Jun Lu

Preface

In an age defined by data—its abundance, its velocity, and its complexity—we face a paradox: the more information we gather, the harder it becomes to extract meaning from it. High-dimensional datasets now permeate every corner of science, engineering, and industry, from medical imaging and genomics to wireless communications and machine learning. Yet, beneath this deluge of numbers lies a powerful insight: much of the data we collect is not as complex as it first appears. In fact, many real-world signals are sparse—they can be accurately described using only a few essential components when viewed through the right lens.

This observation has given rise to a transformative field at the intersection of applied mathematics, signal processing, statistics, and optimization: sparse optimization. At its core, sparse optimization seeks to recover or construct solutions that are as simple as possible—solutions in which most entries are zero or negligible—while still faithfully representing the underlying phenomenon. Whether the goal is to reconstruct an image from a handful of measurements, identify the key genetic markers linked to a disease, or build a predictive model with interpretable features, sparsity offers both computational efficiency and conceptual clarity.

Two major paradigms have emerged within this field. The first, rooted in compressed sensing, reimagines how we acquire data altogether. By recognizing that many signals are sparse in some domain, compressed sensing shows that we can bypass traditional sampling limits and reconstruct signals from far fewer measurements than previously thought possible. The second paradigm, exemplified by the LASSO and related regularization techniques, embeds sparsity directly into the modeling process—encouraging models that are not only accurate but also parsimonious, selecting only the most relevant variables from a sea of candidates.

Though distinct in motivation and application, these approaches share deep mathematical foundations and algorithmic strategies. This book is an invitation to explore those connections. It is designed to serve both as an accessible introduction for students and researchers entering the field, and as a rigorous reference for practitioners seeking to apply sparse optimization methods in their work. We begin with the essential mathematical and algorithmic building blocks, then systematically develop the theory and practice of sparse signal recovery and sparse regularization. Along the way, we emphasize intuition without sacrificing precision, and theory without neglecting application.

The book will take us through the geometry of high-dimensional spaces, the design of measurement systems that preserve sparsity, and the algorithms that make large-scale sparse recovery feasible. We will see how randomness can be harnessed to guarantee recovery, how convex relaxation turns intractable problems into solvable ones, and how modern extensions—such as structured sparsity and non-convex penalties—push the boundaries of what’s possible.

Keywords.

Sparse optimization, LASSO, Generalized LASSO, Group LASSO, Sparse recovery, Convex optimization, Convex relaxation, Design matrices, Nullspace property, Restricted eigenvalue property,
Restricted isometry property, Exact recovery, Gaussian random matrices, Sub-Gaussian random matrices, Primal-dual algorithm,
Gradient descent.

Chapter 1
Introduction

1.1
Introduction and Background

I
In today’s data-driven world, we are encountering a profound shift in how we collect, store, and analyze vast amounts of information.
As sensing technologies and computational methods continue to advance, a key challenge has emerged: how to efficiently manage high-dimensional data that is inherently sparse or compressible.
This challenge lies at the heart of
sparse optimization
, a field that focuses on both the recovery of sparse signals and the formulation of optimization problems that promote sparsity in solutions.

Thanks to rapid progress in digital sensing technologies, we can now capture data with unprecedented resolution.
However, these systems often generate enormous volumes of information, posing significant challenges for storage, processing, and transmission. Fortunately, many real-world signals—ranging from images and audio recordings to genomic sequences and medical scans—are
sparse
or
compressible
in some transform domain.
In other words, although such signals may reside in high-dimensional spaces, they can typically be represented accurately using only a small number of nonzero coefficients. Recognizing and leveraging this inherent sparsity is essential for developing efficient algorithms that reduce dimensionality without sacrificing critical information.

Sparse signal recovery: the role of compressed sensing.

One of the primary applications of sparse optimization techniques is
sparse signal recovery
. This task involves recovering a signal from a reduced number of measurements, taking advantage of the fact that the signal has a sparse representation in some basis or transform domain.

The conventional approach to signal acquisition, governed by the
Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem
, requires sampling a signal at twice the highest frequency present in the signal to ensure perfect reconstruction
(
Nyquist 2002
;
Shannon 2006
)
.
While this theory works well for band-limited signals, it is highly inefficient when the signal is sparse.
Compressed sensing (CS, or compressive sensing)
, a field that emerged in the early 2000s, fundamentally rethinks this paradigm.
Instead of first acquiring signals at a high rate and then compressing them (as in JPEG, MP3, or MPEG), CS advocates for acquiring the data in a compressed form, i.e., directly sampling at a lower rate.
By exploiting sparsity, it becomes possible to reconstruct a signal from a dramatically reduced number of nonadaptive, linear measurements—far fewer than its ambient dimension would suggest. This is not mere data compression; it is compression at the point of acquisition.
This reduces both the number of measurements needed and the computational cost of storing and processing the data
(
Candes and Tao 2006
;
Candes et al. 2011
;
Davenport et al. 2012
)
.

At the heart of CS lies the insight that if a signal is sparse in a known basis (e.g., wavelets, Fourier, or learned dictionaries), we can reconstruct it from far fewer measurements than traditional methods would suggest. The recovery process in CS is typically framed as an
optimization problem
that involves finding the sparsest signal consistent with the available measurements. Formally, given a measurement vector
{\bm{y}}
, the goal is to recover the signal
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
that solves

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{0}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}},

where
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{0}
denotes the
\ell_{0}
-norm
(i.e., the number of nonzero coefficients in
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
),
{\bm{X}}
is the measurement matrix, and
{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}
represents noise.

In practice, minimizing the
\ell_{0}
-norm is computationally intractable because the problem is non-convex and combinatorial.
To overcome this, CS commonly replaces the
\ell_{0}
-norm with the convex
\ell_{1}
-norm
,
leading to the well-known
basis pursuit
formulation:

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}.

This relaxation enables efficient and robust recovery of sparse signals using convex optimization algorithms—a cornerstone of modern compressed sensing theory and practice.

Sparse optimization with LASSO: minimizing loss with sparsity constraints.

While sparse signal recovery focuses on reconstructing signals from compressed measurements,
LASSO (least absolute shrinkage and selection operator)
addresses a related but distinct problem in optimization: it seeks to minimize a loss function while enforcing
sparsity constraints
or
sparse regularization
on the solution
(
Tibshirani 1996
)
.
LASSO is widely used in machine learning and statistics for tasks such as regression, where the goal is to identify a small subset of features that best explain the observed data.

In a standard linear regression setting, the objective is to minimize the squared error between the observed response vector
{\bm{y}}
and the model’s predicted values
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
. LASSO modifies this objective by adding an
\ell_{1}
-norm regularization term, which encourages sparsity in the estimated coefficients.
The LASSO optimization problem can be written as:

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\lambda\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}.

Here,
\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
represents the
least squares loss
, and
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}
is the
\ell_{1}
penalty
or
\ell_{1}
regularization
, which promotes sparsity by penalizing the sum of the absolute values of the coefficients.
The hyperparameter
\lambda
controls the trade-off between fitting the data and enforcing sparsity. A higher value of
\lambda
leads to more coefficients being shrunk to zero, promoting greater sparsity.

LASSO is a versatile and computationally tractable method that has found broad application in areas such as
regression
,
classification
, and
signal denoising
, where sparsity is a desirable property for interpretability, generalization, or efficiency.
While LASSO is not specifically focused on signal recovery from limited measurements, it provides a powerful and general framework for incorporating sparsity directly into optimization-based modeling.

Sparse optimization.

The key distinction between
sparse signal recovery
(as in compressed sensing) and
sparse regularization
or
sparse constraint
(as in LASSO) lies in their objectives and the nature of the underlying optimization problems:

Sparse signal recovery (CS).
The objective is to recover a sparse (or a approximately sparse) signal from a limited number of measurements. The problem is typically posed as finding the sparsest solution consistent with the available data.
CS often leverages optimization techniques like
basis pursuit
(using the
\ell_{1}
-norm) to recover signals from compressed data.

Sparse regularization (LASSO).
In sparse optimization problems like LASSO, the goal is to minimize a data-fitting loss function (e.g., least squares) while encouraging sparsity in the model parameters.
This is achieved by adding an
\ell_{1}
-norm penalty to the objective, which shrinks less important coefficients toward zero and effectively performs feature selection.

Although closely related, these two paradigms serve different purposes and require distinct algorithmic approaches. Compressed sensing is primarily concerned with signal acquisition and reconstruction from limited measurements, whereas LASSO focuses on building predictive models with interpretable, sparse parameter sets—typically in statistical learning and regression contexts.

The field of sparse optimization has profoundly influenced numerous domains, especially those involving high-dimensional data. In medical imaging, compressed sensing enables faster MRI scans with reduced radiation exposure; in communications, it facilitates more efficient data transmission
(
Lustig et al. 2006
;
Lustig et al. 2007
)
. Meanwhile, LASSO and its extensions have become standard tools in machine learning, genomics, and econometrics, where sparse models are crucial for managing large-scale datasets and producing interpretable results
(
Tibshirani 1996
;
Hastie et al. 2015
;
Puig et al. 2011
)
.

This book aims to provide a comprehensive overview of
sparse optimization
, with a focus on both
sparse signal recovery
and
sparse regularization
techniques. We will begin by exploring the foundations of sparse optimization, delving into the mathematical tools and models that underpin sparse signal recovery and LASSO. We will then discuss key algorithms for both
sparse recovery
(e.g., basis pursuit, matching pursuit) and
sparse regularization
(e.g., LASSO, elastic net), along with their applications in real-world problems. Throughout the text, we balance intuitive explanations with rigorous mathematical formulations to provide a comprehensive resource for both newcomers and experts in the field.
Our aim is twofold: to provide a self-contained entry point for students and researchers new to the field, and to offer a rigorous reference for practitioners seeking to apply sparse optimization in science and engineering.

The book is organized as follows.
Chapters
and
lay the groundwork by reviewing essential concepts from (convex) optimization and their relevance to sparse problems.
Chapters
\sim
discuss the design of measurement matrices that guarantee exact or stable recovery of sparse signals, including constructions based on random matrix theory and the restricted isometry property (RIP).
Chapters
\sim
present algorithms for solving various sparse optimization problems, ranging from greedy methods to convex relaxations.

In the remainder of this chapter, we briefly review basic mathematical notation and foundational concepts. Additional definitions will be introduced as needed throughout the text to ensure clarity.

Subarrays are formed by fixing a subset of indices of a matrix.

.
For notational convenience, we adopt
Matlab-style indexing
:

and columns

denotes the submatrix formed by columns

; and

Alternatively, the

.

When the selected indices are not contiguous, let
{\mathbb{I}}
and

be ordered index sets. Then:

{\bm{X}}[{\mathbb{I}},{\mathbb{J}}]
denotes the submatrix of

obtained by extracting the rows and columns of

indexed by

denotes the submatrix of

Definition 1
(Matlab notation).

Let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
, and let
{\mathbb{I}}=\{i_{1},i_{2},\ldots,i_{k}\}
and
{\mathbb{J}}=\{j_{1},j_{2},\ldots,j_{l}\}
be two index sets.
Then
{\bm{X}}[{\mathbb{I}},{\mathbb{J}}]
denotes the
k\times l
submatrix

{\bm{X}}[{\mathbb{I}},{\mathbb{J}}]=\begin{bmatrix}x_{i_{1},j_{1}}&x_{i_{1},j_{2}}&\ldots&x_{i_{1},j_{l}}\\
x_{i_{2},j_{1}}&x_{i_{2},j_{2}}&\ldots&x_{i_{2},j_{l}}\\
\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\
x_{i_{k},j_{1}}&x_{i_{k},j_{2}}&\ldots&x_{i_{k},j_{l}}\\
\end{bmatrix}.

Similarly,
{\bm{X}}[{\mathbb{I}},:]
denotes the
k\times p
submatrix, and
{\bm{X}}[:,{\mathbb{J}}]
denotes the
n\times l
submatrix analogously.
We should also notice that the range of the index satisfies:

\left\{\begin{aligned} 0&\leq\min({\mathbb{I}})\leq\max({\mathbb{I}})\leq n;\\
0&\leq\min({\mathbb{J}})\leq\max({\mathbb{J}})\leq p.\end{aligned}\right.

More compactly, for
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
and
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
, we let

{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}\triangleq{\bm{X}}[:,{\mathbb{I}}]\in\real^{n\times k}\qquad\text{and}\qquad{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}\triangleq{\boldsymbol{\beta}}[{\mathbb{I}}]\in\real^{k}.

(1.1)

Note that
{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{I}}^{\top}
denotes the transpose of the submatrix
{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}
, not a submatrix of
{\bm{X}}^{\top}
.

On the other hand, when an index set
{\mathbb{I}}
appears as an argument of a function—written as
{\bm{X}}({\mathbb{I}})
or
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{I}})
—it denotes a projection operator that zeroes out all entries not indexed by
{\mathbb{I}}
.
Specifically:

For
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
, the vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{I}})\in\real^{p}
equals
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
on the entries in
{\mathbb{I}}
and is zero elsewhere; that is,
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{I}})_{i}=\beta_{i}
if
i\in{\mathbb{I}}
, and 0 otherwise.

For
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
, the matrix
{\bm{X}}({\mathbb{I}})\in\real^{n\times p}
retains the columns of
{\bm{X}}
indexed by
{\mathbb{I}}
and sets all other columns to zero.

With this notation, the matrix-vector product decomposes as

{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\bm{X}}({\mathbb{I}}){\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{I}})+{\bm{X}}({\mathbb{I}}^{c}){\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{I}}^{c})={\bm{X}}[:,{\mathbb{I}}]{\boldsymbol{\beta}}[{\mathbb{I}}]+{\bm{X}}[:,{\mathbb{I}}^{c}]{\boldsymbol{\beta}}[{\mathbb{I}}^{c}]={\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}+{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{I}}^{c}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}^{c}},

where
{\mathbb{I}}^{c}
denotes the complement set of
{\mathbb{I}}
.

Throughout this book, all vectors are assumed to be column vectors unless explicitly transposed. A row vector is denoted as the transpose of a column vector, e.g.,
{\bm{x}}^{\top}
.
Concrete vectors are written using MATLAB-style syntax.
A column vector is written with semicolons
``;"
separating entries, e.g.,

{\bm{x}}=[1;2;3]\qquad\text{(column vector)}

is a column vector in
3
. Similarly, A row vector uses commas
``,"
, e.g.,

{\bm{y}}=[1,2,3]\qquad\text{(row vector)}

is a row vector with 3 values.
Equivalently, a column vector may be expressed as the transpose of a row vector:
{\bm{y}}=[1,2,3]^{\top}
is a column vector.

The transpose of a matrix
{\bm{X}}
is denoted by
{\bm{X}}^{\top}
,
and its inverse (when it exists) by
{\bm{X}}^{-1}
.
The
p\times p
identity matrix is denoted by
{\bm{I}}_{p}
or simply by
{\bm{I}}
.
A vector or matrix of all zeros is denoted by the
boldface
symbol
\boldsymbol{0}
; its dimensions are inferred from context, or explicitly indicated as
\boldsymbol{0}_{p}
for a
p
-dimensional zero vector.
Similarly, a vector or matrix of all ones is denoted by a
boldface
one
{\bm{1}}
, whose sizes are clear from context; or we denote
{\bm{1}}_{p}
to be the vector of all ones with
p
entries.
Subscripts are often omitted when the dimensions are evident from context.

Definition 2
(Eigenvalue, eigenvector).

Let
{\bm{X}}\in\mathbb{C}^{p\times p}
. A scalar
\lambda\in\mathbb{C}
is called a (right) eigenvalue (also known as a proper value, or characteristic value) of
{\bm{X}}
if there exists a nonzero vector
{\bm{u}}\in\mathbb{C}^{p}
such that

{\bm{X}}{\bm{u}}=\lambda{\bm{u}}.

In this case,
{\bm{u}}
is called a (right) eigenvector of
{\bm{X}}
associated with
\lambda
.

For simplicity, we restrict our attention to real-valued matrices unless otherwise stated. Unless explicitly noted, all eigenvalues discussed are assumed to be real as well.

Intuitively, an eigenvector
{\bm{u}}
of a matrix
{\bm{X}}
represents a direction in
p
that is invariant under the linear transformation defined by
{\bm{X}}
: applying
{\bm{X}}
to
{\bm{u}}
does not change its direction—it only scales it by the corresponding eigenvalue
\lambda
.
Note that while real matrices can have complex eigenvalues in general, symmetric real matrices always have real eigenvalues (see Theorem
).

The pair
(\lambda,{\bm{u}})
is commonly referred to as an
eigenpair
.
Importantly, eigenvectors are not unique: if
{\bm{u}}
is an eigenvector, then so is any nonzero scalar multiple
\eta{\bm{u}}
(with
\eta\in\real\setminus\{\boldsymbol{0}\}
).
To resolve this ambiguity, eigenvectors are typically normalized—for example, by requiring
\left\lVert{\bm{u}}\right\rVert_{2}=1
(unit
\ell_{2}
-norm; see Section
).
Furthermore, since both
{\bm{u}}
and
-{\bm{u}}
correspond to the same eigenvalue and represent the same direction up to sign, it is common to fix the sign by convention (e.g., requiring the first nonzero entry of
{\bm{u}}
to be positive).

An important result concerning the eigenvalues of a complex matrix is the
Gershgorin circle theorem
(also known as the
Gershgorin disk theorem
), introduced by the Soviet mathematician Semen Aronovich Gershgorin in 1931
(
Gershgorin 1931
)
.

{theoremHigh}
[Gershgorin circle theorem
(
Gershgorin 1931
)
]
Let
{\bm{X}}=[x_{ij}]
be a
p\times p
complex matrix.
For each row
i
, define the Gershgorin radius
R_{i}
as

R_{i}\triangleq\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j=1,j\neq i\end{subarray}}^{p}\left\lvert x_{ij}\right\rvert.

Then every eigenvalue
\lambda
of
{\bm{X}}
lies within at least one of the
Gershgorin disks
centered at the diagonal entries
x_{ii}
with radius
R_{i}
.
In other words, for every eigenvalue
\lambda
, there exists an index
i
such that:

\left\lvert\lambda-x_{ii}\right\rvert\leq R_{i}.

This means that all eigenvalues of
{\bm{X}}
are located within the union of these
p
disks in the complex plane. Each disk is centered at the diagonal element
x_{ii}
and its radius equals the sum of the absolute values of the off-diagonal entries in the corresponding row.
The Gershgorin circle theorem provides a simple and effective way to estimate the location of eigenvalues without computing them explicitly.
It is especially useful in analyzing matrix properties, stability, and determining whether a matrix is invertible.
For instance, if none of the Gershgorin disks contains the origin, then 0 cannot be an eigenvalue of
{\bm{X}}
, and hence
{\bm{X}}
is invertible.

In linear algebra, every vector space has a basis, and every vector in that space can be expressed uniquely as a linear combination of the basis vectors.
Building on this idea, we define the span and dimension of a subspace using the concept of a basis.

Definition 3
(Subspace and span).

A nonempty subset
\mathcal{V}
of
n
is called a subspace if it is closed under linear combinations; that is,
x{\bm{a}}+y{\bm{b}}\in\mathcal{V}
for every
{\bm{a}},{\bm{b}}\in\mathcal{V}
and every
x,y\in\real
.
Moreover, if every vector
{\bm{v}}
in a subspace
\mathcal{V}
can be written as a linear combination of the vectors
\{{\bm{x}}_{1},{\bm{x}}_{2},\ldots,

{\bm{x}}_{n}\}
, then we say that these vectors span the subspace
\mathcal{V}
.

The concept of linear independence of a set of vectors is central to linear algebra. Two equivalent definitions are given below.

Definition 4
(Linearly independent).

A set of vectors
\{{\bm{x}}_{1},{\bm{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\bm{x}}_{n}\}
is said to be linearly independent if there is no combination can get
a_{1}{\bm{x}}_{1}+a_{2}{\bm{x}}_{2}+\ldots+a_{n}{\bm{x}}_{n}=0
except all
a_{i}
’s are zero. An equivalent definition is that
{\bm{x}}_{1}\neq\boldsymbol{0}
, and for every
k>1
, the vector
{\bm{x}}_{k}
does not lie in the span of
\{{\bm{x}}_{1},{\bm{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\bm{x}}_{k-1}\}
.

Definition 5
(Basis and dimension).

A set of vectors
\{{\bm{x}}_{1},{\bm{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\bm{x}}_{n}\}
is called a basis of a subspace
\mathcal{V}
if the vectors are linearly independent and span
\mathcal{V}
.
Every basis of a given subspace contains the same number of vectors.
This number is called the dimension of the subspace
\mathcal{V}
.
By convention, the trivial subspace
\{\boldsymbol{0}\}
has dimension zero.
Furthermore, any subspace of positive dimension admits an orthogonal basis—that is, one can always choose a basis consisting of mutually orthogonal vectors (see Definition
).

Definition 6
(Column space (range) and row space).

Let
{\bm{X}}
be an
n\times p
real matrix. The column space (or range) of
{\bm{X}}
is defined as the set of all vectors that can be expressed as a linear combination of its columns:

\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}})=\{{\bm{v}}\in\real^{n}\mid\exists\,{\bm{u}}\in\real^{p},\,{\bm{v}}={\bm{X}}{\bm{u}}\}.

Similarly, the row space of
{\bm{X}}
is the set of all vectors spanned by its rows. Equivalently, it is the column space of
{\bm{X}}^{\top}
:

\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}^{\top})=\{{\bm{u}}\in\real^{p}\mid\exists\,{\bm{v}}\in\real^{n},\,{\bm{u}}={\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{v}}\}.

Definition 7
(Null space (nullspace, kernel)).

Let
{\bm{X}}
be an
n\times p
real matrix. The null space (or kernel, or nullspace) of
{\bm{X}}
is defined as the set:

\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})=\{{\bm{v}}\in\real^{p}\mid\,{\bm{X}}{\bm{v}}=\boldsymbol{0}\}.

In some cases, the null space of
{\bm{X}}
is also referred to as the right null space of
{\bm{X}}
.
And the null space of
{\bm{X}}^{\top}
is given by

\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}}^{\top})=\{{\bm{u}}\in\real^{n}\mid\,{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{u}}=\boldsymbol{0}\},

and is commonly called the left null space of
{\bm{X}}
.

Definition 8
(Rank).

The
rank
of a matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
is defined as the dimension of its column space. That is, the rank of
{\bm{X}}
is equal to the maximum number of linearly independent columns of
{\bm{X}}
, which is also equal to the maximum number of linearly independent rows of
{\bm{X}}
. The matrix
{\bm{X}}
and its transpose
{\bm{X}}^{\top}
always have the same rank.
We say that
{\bm{X}}
has full rank if its rank equals
\min\{n,p\}
.
Specifically, given a vector
{\bm{u}}\in\real^{n}
and a vector
{\bm{v}}\in\real^{p}
, then the
n\times p
matrix
{\bm{u}}{\bm{v}}^{\top}
obtained by their outer product of vectors is of rank 1.
In summary, the rank of a matrix can be characterized as:

the number of linearly independent columns;

the number of linearly independent rows;

and remarkably, these two numbers are always equal (see Lemma
).

Both the column space of
{\bm{X}}
and the null space of
{\bm{X}}^{\top}
are subspaces of
n
. In fact, every vector in
\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}}^{\top})
is orthogonal to every vector in
\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}})
, and vice versa.
Similarly, every vector in
\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
is also orthogonal to every vector in
\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}^{\top})
, and vice versa.
This leads to the concept of
orthogonal complementary subspaces
.

Definition 9
(Orthogonal complement in general).

The orthogonal complement
\mathcal{V}^{\perp}\subseteq\real^{n}
of a subspace
\mathcal{V}\subseteq\real^{n}
consists of all vectors that are perpendicular to every vector in
\mathcal{V}
. Formally,

\mathcal{V}^{\perp}=\{{\bm{v}}\in\real^{n}\mid{\bm{v}}^{\top}{\bm{u}}=0,\ \forall\,{\bm{u}}\in\mathcal{V}\}.

These two subspaces are disjoint and together span the entire space
n
.
The dimensions of
\mathcal{V}
and
\mathcal{V}^{\perp}
add up to the dimension of the entire space:
\dim(\mathcal{V})+\dim(\mathcal{V}^{\perp})=n
. Furthermore,
(\mathcal{V}^{\perp})^{\perp}=\mathcal{V}
.

Definition 10
(Orthogonal complement of column space).

Let
{\bm{X}}
be an
n\times p
real matrix. The orthogonal complement of the column space
\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}})
, denoted
\mathcal{C}^{\bot}({\bm{X}})
, is the subspace defined by:

\displaystyle\mathcal{C}^{\bot}({\bm{X}})

\displaystyle=\{{\bm{v}}\in\real^{n}\mid\,{\bm{v}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}{\bm{u}}=\boldsymbol{0},\,\forall\,{\bm{u}}\in\real^{p}\}

\displaystyle=\{{\bm{v}}\in\real^{n}\mid\,{\bm{v}}^{\top}{\bm{w}}=\boldsymbol{0},\,\forall\,{\bm{w}}\in\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}})\}.

For any matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
of rank
r
, we obtain the
four fundamental subspaces
:

\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}})
: Column space of
{\bm{X}}
, i.e., linear combinations of columns with dimension
r
.

\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
: (Right) null space of
{\bm{X}}
, i.e., all
{\bm{u}}
satisfying
{\bm{X}}{\bm{u}}=\boldsymbol{0}
with dimension
p-r
.

\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}^{\top})
: Row space of
{\bm{X}}
, i.e., linear combinations of rows with dimension
r
.

\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}}^{\top})
: Left null space of
{\bm{X}}
, i.e., all
{\bm{v}}
satisfying
{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{v}}=\boldsymbol{0}
with dimension
n-r
.

Furthermore,
\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
is the orthogonal complement of
\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}^{\top})
, and
\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}})
is the orthogonal complement of
\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}}^{\top})
. This is known as the
fundamental theorem of linear algebra
.
See
Lu 2022
for a proof.

We now establish the equivalence of the dimensions of column and row spaces stated in Definition
.

Lemma 11
(Dimension of column space and row space).

The dimension of the column space of a matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
equals the dimension of its
row space, i.e., the row rank and the column rank of a matrix
{\bm{X}}
are identical.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
We first notice that the null space of
{\bm{X}}
is orthogonal complementary to the row space of
{\bm{X}}
:
\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})\bot\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}^{\top})
(where the row space of
{\bm{X}}
is equivalent to the column space of
{\bm{X}}^{\top}
).
That is, vectors in the null space of
{\bm{X}}
are orthogonal to vectors in the row space of
{\bm{X}}
. To see this, suppose
{\bm{X}}=[{\bm{x}}_{1}^{\top};{\bm{x}}_{2}^{\top};\ldots;{\bm{x}}_{n}^{\top}]
is the row partition of
{\bm{X}}
. For any vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
, we have
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\boldsymbol{0}
; that is,
[{\bm{x}}_{1}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\beta}};{\bm{x}}_{2}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\beta}};\ldots;{\bm{x}}_{n}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}]=\boldsymbol{0}
.
And since the row space of
{\bm{X}}
is spanned by
\{{\bm{x}}_{1}^{\top},{\bm{x}}_{2}^{\top},\ldots,{\bm{x}}_{n}^{\top}\}
, thus,
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is perpendicular to any vectors from
\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}^{\top})
. This indicates
\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})\bot\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}^{\top})
.

Now, assuming the dimension of the row space of
{\bm{X}}
is
r
,
let
{\bm{r}}_{1},{\bm{r}}_{2},\ldots,{\bm{r}}_{r}
be a set of vectors in
p
and form a basis for the row space
.
Consequently, the
r
vectors
{\bm{X}}{\bm{r}}_{1},{\bm{X}}{\bm{r}}_{2},\ldots,{\bm{X}}{\bm{r}}_{r}
are in the column space of
{\bm{X}}
; furthermore, they are linearly independent. To see this, suppose we have a linear combination of the
r
vectors:
\beta_{1}{\bm{X}}{\bm{r}}_{1}+\beta_{2}{\bm{X}}{\bm{r}}_{2}+\ldots+\beta_{r}{\bm{X}}{\bm{r}}_{r}=0
, that is,
{\bm{X}}(\beta_{1}{\bm{r}}_{1}+\beta_{2}{\bm{r}}_{2}+\ldots+\beta_{r}{\bm{r}}_{r})=0
, and the vector
{\bm{v}}=\beta_{1}{\bm{r}}_{1}+\beta_{2}{\bm{r}}_{2}+\ldots+\beta_{r}{\bm{r}}_{r}
is in null space of
{\bm{X}}
. But since
\{{\bm{r}}_{1},{\bm{r}}_{2},\ldots,{\bm{r}}_{r}\}
is a basis for the row space of
{\bm{X}}
,
{\bm{v}}
is thus also in the row space of
{\bm{X}}
. We have shown that vectors from null space of
{\bm{X}}
is perpendicular to vectors from row space of
{\bm{X}}
, thus
{\bm{v}}^{\top}{\bm{v}}=0
and
\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}=\ldots=\beta_{r}=0
. Then,
{\bm{X}}{\bm{r}}_{1},{\bm{X}}{\bm{r}}_{2},\ldots,{\bm{X}}{\bm{r}}_{r}
are in the column space of
{\bm{X}}
and they are independent
. This means that the dimension of the column space of
{\bm{X}}
is larger than
r
. This result shows that
row rank of
{\bm{X}}\leq
column rank of
{\bm{X}}
.

Applying the same argument to
{\bm{X}}^{\top}
yields the reverse inequality:
column rank of
{\bm{X}}\leq
row rank of
{\bm{X}}
. Hence, the two ranks are equal, completing the proof.

From the previous proof, we can also conclude that if
\{{\bm{r}}_{1},{\bm{r}}_{2},\ldots,{\bm{r}}_{r}\}
is a basis for the row space of
{\bm{X}}
, then
\{{\bm{X}}{\bm{r}}_{1},{\bm{X}}{\bm{r}}_{2},\ldots,{\bm{X}}{\bm{r}}_{r}\}
forms a basis for the column space of
{\bm{X}}
.
We formalize this observation in the following lemma.

Lemma 12
(Column basis from row basis).

For any matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
, let
\{{\bm{r}}_{1},{\bm{r}}_{2},\ldots,{\bm{r}}_{r}\}
be a set of vectors in
p
, which forms a basis for the row space of
{\bm{X}}
. Then, the set
\{{\bm{X}}{\bm{r}}_{1},{\bm{X}}{\bm{r}}_{2},\ldots,{\bm{X}}{\bm{r}}_{r}\}
forms a basis for the column space of
{\bm{X}}
.

Definition 13
(Permutation matrix).

A permutation matrix
{\bm{P}}\in\real^{p\times p}
is a square binary matrix that has exactly one entry of 1 in each row and each column, and 0’s elsewhere.

Row point.

That is, the permutation matrix
{\bm{P}}
has the rows of the identity
{\bm{I}}
in any order, and the order decides the sequence of the row permutation. If we want to permute the rows of a matrix
{\bm{X}}
, we multiply on the left
{\bm{P}}{\bm{X}}
.

Column point.

Or, equivalently, the permutation matrix
{\bm{P}}
has the columns of the identity
{\bm{I}}
in any order, and the order decides the sequence of the column permutation. To apply a column permutation to
{\bm{X}}
, we multiply on the right
{\bm{X}}{\bm{P}}
.

The permutation matrix
{\bm{P}}
can be represented more compactly by a index set
{\mathbb{J}}\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}^{p}
such that
{\bm{P}}={\bm{I}}[:,{\mathbb{J}}]
, where
{\bm{I}}
is the
p\times p
identity matrix.
Notably, the entries of
{\mathbb{J}}
are a permutation of
\{1,2,\dots,p\}
, so their sum is
1+2+\ldots+p=\frac{p^{2}+p}{2}
.

Definition 14
(Determinant: Laplace expansion by minors).

Let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{p\times p}
be a square matrix, and let
{\bm{X}}_{ij}\in\real^{(p-1)\times(p-1)}
denote the submatrix of
{\bm{X}}
obtained by deleting the
i
-th row and
j
-th column of
{\bm{X}}
.
The determinant of
{\bm{X}}
can be computed recursively using the following formulas:

\det({\bm{X}})=\sum_{k=1}^{p}(-1)^{i+k}x_{ik}\det({\bm{X}}_{ik})=\sum_{k=1}^{p}(-1)^{k+j}x_{kj}\det({\bm{X}}_{kj}),

(1.2)

where the first equation is the Laplace expansion by minors along row
i
, and the second equation is the Laplace expansion by minors along column
j
.
Equivalently, for any integer
r
with
1\leq r\leq p
, let
{\mathbb{J}}\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
be an index set of cardinality
r
(
\left\lvert{\mathbb{J}}\right\rvert=r
), and let
{\mathbb{J}}^{c}=\{1,2,\ldots,n\}\backslash{\mathbb{J}}
denote its complementary set.
Then

\displaystyle\det({\bm{X}})=\sum_{{\mathbb{I}}}(-1)^{\gamma}\det({\bm{X}}[{\mathbb{I}},{\mathbb{J}}])\det({\bm{X}}[{\mathbb{I}}^{c},{\mathbb{J}}^{c}])=\sum_{{\mathbb{I}}}(-1)^{\gamma}\det({\bm{X}}[{\mathbb{J}},{\mathbb{I}}])\det({\bm{X}}[{\mathbb{J}}^{c},{\mathbb{I}}^{c}]),

where
\gamma=\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{I}}}i+\sum_{j\in{\mathbb{J}}}j
, and the sum is taken over all index sets
{\mathbb{I}}\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
with cardinality
r
.
When
r=1
, this reduces to (
).

The determinant assigns to each square matrix a scalar value that encodes geometric and algebraic properties of the associated linear transformation.
For a
2\times 2
matrix, the absolute value of the determinant equals the area of the parallelogram spanned by its column vectors. The sign indicates orientation: it is positive if the columns form a counterclockwise basis, and negative if clockwise.
For a
3\times 3
matrix, the determinant gives the signed volume of the parallelepiped defined by its three column vectors, with the sign again reflecting orientation.
In general, for a linear transformation represented by a
p\times p
matrix, the absolute value of the determinant measures the factor by which
p
-dimensional volume is scaled under the transformation. A positive determinant means the orientation (or “handedness”) of the space is preserved; a negative determinant means it is reversed.
A square matrix is invertible if and only if its determinant is nonzero. Geometrically, this means the transformation does not collapse the space into a lower-dimensional subspace or a single point—both of which occur precisely when the determinant is zero.
Algebraically, the determinant of a matrix equals the product of its eigenvalues (counting multiplicities). Thus, it reflects the cumulative scaling effect of the transformation along its eigenvector directions.

We now summarize key properties of the determinant.

Lemma 15
(Properties of determinant).

The determinant satisfies the following properties:

The determinant of the product of two matrices is
\det({\bm{X}}{\bm{Y}})=\det({\bm{X}})\det({\bm{Y}})
;

The determinant of the transpose is
\det({\bm{X}}^{\top})=\det({\bm{X}})
;

If
\lambda
is an eigenvalue of
{\bm{X}}
, then
\det({\bm{X}}-\lambda{\bm{I}})=0
;

Determinant of any identity matrix is
1
;

For any orthogonal matrix
{\bm{Q}}
(i.e.,
{\bm{Q}}{\bm{Q}}^{\top}={\bm{Q}}^{\top}{\bm{Q}}={\bm{I}}
), we have

\det({\bm{Q}})=\det({\bm{Q}}^{\top})=\pm 1,\qquad\text{since }\det({\bm{Q}}^{\top})\det({\bm{Q}})=\det({\bm{Q}}^{\top}{\bm{Q}})=\det({\bm{I}})=1;

For any square matrix
{\bm{X}}
and orthogonal matrix
{\bm{Q}}
, we have

\det({\bm{X}})=\det({\bm{Q}}^{\top})\det({\bm{X}})\det({\bm{Q}})=\det({\bm{Q}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}{\bm{Q}});

Suppose
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{p\times p}
, then
\det(-{\bm{X}})=(-1)^{p}\det({\bm{X}})
.

Positive definiteness and positive semidefiniteness are among the most important properties a matrix can possess.

Definition 16
(Positive definite and positive semidefinite).

A symmetric matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{p\times p}
is said to be positive definite (PD) if
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}>0
for all nonzero
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
, denoted by
{\bm{X}}\succ\boldsymbol{0}
.
It is called positive semidefinite (PSD) if
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\geq 0
for all
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
, denoted by
{\bm{X}}\succeq\boldsymbol{0}
.

A fundamental result in linear algebra states that a symmetric matrix
{\bm{X}}
is positive definite if and only if all of its eigenvalues are strictly positive. Similarly,
{\bm{X}}
is positive semidefinite if and only if all of its eigenvalues are nonnegative.
This leads to the following theorem:

{theoremHigh}
[Eigenvalue characterization theorem]
A matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{p\times p}
is positive definite if and only if all of its eigenvalues are
positive
. Similarly, a matrix
{\bm{X}}
is positive semidefinite if and only if all of its eigenvalues
nonnegative
.
Moreover, we have the following implications:

{\bm{X}}-\gamma{\bm{I}}\succeq\boldsymbol{0}
if and only if
\lambda_{\min}({\bm{X}})\geq\gamma
;

{\bm{X}}-\gamma{\bm{I}}\succ\boldsymbol{0}
if and only if
\lambda_{\min}({\bm{X}})>\gamma
;

{\bm{X}}-\gamma{\bm{I}}\preceq\boldsymbol{0}
if and only if
\lambda_{\max}({\bm{X}})\leq\gamma
;

{\bm{X}}-\gamma{\bm{I}}\prec\boldsymbol{0}
if and only if
\lambda_{\max}({\bm{X}})<\gamma
;

\lambda_{\min}({\bm{X}}){\bm{I}}\preceq{\bm{X}}\preceq\lambda_{\max}({\bm{X}}){\bm{I}}
,

where
\lambda_{\min}({\bm{X}})
and
\lambda_{\max}({\bm{X}})
represent the minimum and maximum eigenvalues of
{\bm{X}}
, respectively, and
{\bm{B}}\prec{\bm{C}}
means
{\bm{C}}-{\bm{B}}
is PSD.

This theorem provides an alternative characterization of positive definiteness and positive semidefiniteness in terms of eigenvalues.
Given an eigenpair
(\lambda,{\boldsymbol{\beta}})
of
{\bm{X}}
, the forward implication can be verified that
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\lambda{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}>0
such that
\lambda=({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}})/({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\beta}})>0
(resp.,
\geq 0
) if
{\bm{X}}
is PD (resp., PSD).
The full equivalence can be established using the spectral theorem (Theorem
).

A notable subclass of positive semidefinite matrices consists of certain diagonally dominant matrices, which we define rigorously below.

Definition 17
(Diagonally dominant matrices).

Let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{p\times p}
be a symmetric matrix.
Then
{\bm{X}}
is called diagonally dominant if

\left\lvert x_{ii}\right\rvert\geq\sum_{j\neq i}\left\lvert x_{ij}\right\rvert,\qquad\forall\,i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\},

and strictly diagonally dominant if

\left\lvert x_{ii}\right\rvert>\sum_{j\neq i}\left\lvert x_{ij}\right\rvert,\qquad\forall\,i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}.

We now show that a
diagonally dominant matrix
with nonnegative diagonal entries is positive semidefinite, and that a
strictly diagonally dominant matrix
with positive diagonal entries is positive definite.

{theoremHigh}

[Positive definiteness of diagonally dominant matrices]
Let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{p\times p}
be a symmetric matrix.
Then:

1.

If
{\bm{X}}
is diagonally dominant with nonnegative diagonals, then
{\bm{X}}
is positive semidefinite.

2.

If
{\bm{X}}
is strictly diagonally dominant with positive diagonals, then
{\bm{X}}
is positive definite.

This result follows directly from the Gershgorin circle theorem (Theorem
). However, we provide an elementary proof below based on eigenvalue analysis.

Proof
[of Theorem
]

(i).
Suppose, for contradiction, that
{\bm{X}}
is not positive semidefinite with a negative eigenvalue
\lambda
associated with an eigenvector
{\bm{v}}
such that
{\bm{X}}{\bm{v}}=\lambda{\bm{v}}
.
Let
i
be an index such that
\left\lvert v_{i}\right\rvert=\max_{1\leq j\leq p}\left\lvert v_{j}\right\rvert
.
Consider the
i
-th component of
({\bm{X}}-\lambda{\bm{I}}){\bm{v}}=\boldsymbol{0}
, we have

\left\lvert x_{ii}-\lambda\right\rvert\cdot\left\lvert v_{i}\right\rvert=\left\lvert\sum_{j\neq i}x_{ij}v_{j}\right\rvert\leq\left(\sum_{j\neq i}\left\lvert x_{ij}\right\rvert\right)\left\lvert v_{i}\right\rvert\leq\left\lvert x_{ii}\right\rvert\cdot\left\lvert v_{i}\right\rvert.

This implies
\left\lvert x_{ii}-\lambda\right\rvert\leq\left\lvert x_{ii}\right\rvert
.
Since the diagonal entries are nonnegative, we have
x_{ii}<{x_{ii}-\lambda}\leq{x_{ii}}
, and this leads to a contradiction.

(ii).

From part (i), we know that
{\bm{X}}
is positive semidefinite. Suppose, for contradiction, that
{\bm{X}}
is not positive definite with a zero eigenvalue
0
associated with a nonzero eigenvector
{\bm{v}}
such that
{\bm{X}}{\bm{v}}=\boldsymbol{0}
. Similarly, we have

\left\lvert x_{ii}\right\rvert\cdot\left\lvert v_{i}\right\rvert=\left\lvert\sum_{j\neq i}x_{ij}v_{j}\right\rvert\leq\left(\sum_{j\neq i}\left\lvert x_{ii}\right\rvert\right)\left\lvert v_{i}\right\rvert<\left\lvert x_{ii}\right\rvert\cdot\left\lvert v_{i}\right\rvert,

which is impossible and the result follows.

Exercise
\thetheo
(Power of PSD)

Let
{\bm{X}}
be PSD. Show that
{\bm{X}}^{k}
is also PSD for
k=1,2,\ldots
.

From an introductory linear algebra course, we recall the following well-known equivalences characterizing nonsingular (i.e., invertible) square matrices.

Remark 18
(List of equivalence of nonsingularity for a matrix).

Let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{p\times p}
be a square matrix.
The following statements are equivalent:

{\bm{X}}
is nonsingular;

{\bm{X}}
is invertible, i.e.,
{\bm{X}}^{-1}
exists;

{\bm{X}}{\bm{u}}={\bm{y}}
has a unique solution
{\bm{u}}={\bm{X}}^{-1}{\bm{y}}
;

{\bm{X}}{\bm{u}}=\boldsymbol{0}
has a unique, trivial solution:
{\bm{u}}=\boldsymbol{0}
;

Columns of
{\bm{X}}
are linearly independent;

Rows of
{\bm{X}}
are linearly independent;

\det({\bm{X}})\neq 0
;

\dim(\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}}))=0
;

\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})=\{\boldsymbol{0}\}
, i.e., the null space is trivial;

\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}})=\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}^{\top})=\real^{p}
, i.e., the column space or row space span the entire
p
;

{\bm{X}}
has full rank
r=p
;

{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}
is symmetric positive definite (PD);

{\bm{X}}
has
p
nonzero (positive) singular values;

All eigenvalues are nonzero.

It is essential to keep these equivalences in mind, as they appear frequently in both theoretical and applied contexts.
Similarly, the following remark collects equivalent characterizations of singular matrices—particularly in the context of eigenvalues.

Remark 19
(List of equivalence of singularity for a matrix).

Let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{p\times p}
be a square matrix, and let
(\lambda,{\bm{u}})
be an eigenpair of
{\bm{X}}
.
The following statements are equivalent:

({\bm{X}}-\lambda{\bm{I}})
is singular;

({\bm{X}}-\lambda{\bm{I}})
is not invertible;

({\bm{X}}-\lambda{\bm{I}}){\bm{v}}=\boldsymbol{0}
has nonzero
{\bm{v}}\neq\boldsymbol{0}
solutions, and
{\bm{v}}={\bm{u}}
is one of such solutions;

({\bm{X}}-\lambda{\bm{I}})
has linearly dependent columns;

\det({\bm{X}}-\lambda{\bm{I}})=0
;

\dim(\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}}-\lambda{\bm{I}}))>0
;

Null space of
({\bm{X}}-\lambda{\bm{I}})
is nontrivial;

Columns of
({\bm{X}}-\lambda{\bm{I}})
are linearly dependent;

Rows of
({\bm{X}}-\lambda{\bm{I}})
are linearly dependent;

({\bm{X}}-\lambda{\bm{I}})
has rank
r<p
;

Dimension of column space = dimension of row space =
r<p
;

({\bm{X}}-\lambda{\bm{I}})^{\top}({\bm{X}}-\lambda{\bm{I}})
is symmetric semidefinite;

({\bm{X}}-\lambda{\bm{I}})
has
r<p
nonzero (positive) singular values;

Zero is an eigenvalue of
({\bm{X}}-\lambda{\bm{I}})
.

1.2.1
Vector Norms, Dual Norm, Balls

The concept of a
norm
is fundamental for measuring the magnitude of vectors and, consequently, enables the definition of metrics on normed linear spaces. Norms provide a quantitative measure of the “size” of a vector or matrix, which is essential in many applications—such as computing the length of a vector in Euclidean space or assessing the scale of a matrix in multidimensional settings.

Moreover, norms allow us to define distances between vectors or matrices. Specifically, the distance between two vectors
{\bm{u}}
and
{\bm{v}}
can be computed as the norm of their difference,
\left\lVert{\bm{u}}-{\bm{v}}\right\rVert
. This notion is crucial in tasks that rely on proximity measures, including clustering algorithms in machine learning.

For any vector or matrix, a norm must satisfy the following three properties; see, for example,
Lu 2021a
for a more detailed introduction.

Definition 20
(Vector norm and matrix nrom).

Let
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert
denote a norm defined on either vectors or matrices.
Then, for any matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
and any vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
, the following properties must hold:

Nonnegativity.
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert\geq 0
and
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert\geq 0
, with equality if and only if
{\bm{X}}=\boldsymbol{0}
or
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\boldsymbol{0}
, respectively.

Positive homogeneity.
\left\lVert\lambda{\bm{X}}\right\rVert=\left\lvert\lambda\right\rvert\cdot\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert
and
\left\lVert\lambda{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert=\left\lvert\lambda\right\rvert\cdot\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert
for any scale
\lambda\in\real
.

Triangle inequality.
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}+{\bm{Y}}\right\rVert\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert+\left\lVert{\bm{Y}}\right\rVert
for all matrices
{\bm{X}},{\bm{Y}}\in\real^{n\times p}
, and
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert+\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert
for all vectors
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
.

Building on this definition, we now introduce specific types of vector norms: the
\ell_{1}
,
\ell_{2}
, and
\ell_{\infty}
-norms for a vector.

Definition 21
(Vector
\ell_{1},\ell_{2},\ell_{\infty}
,
\ell_{s}
-norms).

For a vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
, the
\ell_{2}
vector norm is defined as
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}=\sqrt{\beta_{1}^{2}+\beta_{2}^{2}+\ldots+\beta_{p}^{2}}
.
Similarly, the
\ell_{1}
-norm can be obtained by

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\left\lvert\beta_{i}\right\rvert.

And the
\ell_{\infty}
-norm can be obtained by

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{\infty}=\mathop{\max}_{i=1,2,\ldots,p}\left\lvert\beta_{i}\right\rvert.

More generally, the
\ell_{s}
-norm is defined as
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{s}=\sqrt[s]{\sum_{i=1}^{p}\left\lvert\beta_{i}\right\rvert^{s}}
for
s\geq 1
.

Exercise
\thetheo
(Standard bounds on vector norms)

Let
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
. Use the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality (see Theorem
), prove the following relationships:

\displaystyle\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{\infty}

\displaystyle\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq p\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{\infty};

\displaystyle\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{\infty}

\displaystyle\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\sqrt{p}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{\infty};

\displaystyle\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}

\displaystyle\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\sqrt{p}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}.

This above exercise shows the equivalence of the
\ell_{1},\ell_{2}
, and
\ell_{\infty}
vector norms on finite-dimensional vector spaces.
Given positive constants
c,C>0
, for two norms
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{a}
and
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{b}
, the inequality
c\cdot\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{a}\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{b}\leq C\cdot\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{a}
for all vectors
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}

means that the norms induce the same notion of “closeness” or topology—they define the same convergent sequences, open sets, continuity, etc.

Dual Norm

Consider the
\ell_{s}
vector norm. By
Hölder’s inequality
(see Theorem
), we have

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{s}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{t},

where
s,t>1
satisfy
\frac{1}{s}+\frac{1}{t}=1
, and
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
. Equality holds if the two sequences
\{\left\lvert\beta_{i}\right\rvert^{s}\}
and
\{\left\lvert\alpha_{i}\right\rvert^{t}\}
are linearly dependent. This implies

\mathop{\max}_{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{t}=1}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{s}.

(1.3)

For this reason,
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{t}
is called the
dual norm
of
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{s}
.
On the other hand, for each
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
with
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{s}=1
, there exists a vector
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}
such that
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{t}=1
and
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=1
.
Notably, the
\ell_{2}
-norm is
self-dual
, while the
\ell_{1}
- and
\ell_{\infty}
-norms are dual to each other.

Definition 22
(Set of primal counterparts).

Let
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert
be any norm on
p
. Then the set of primal counterparts of
{\bm{a}}\in\real^{p}
is defined as

\Lambda_{{\bm{a}}}\triangleq\operatorname*{\text{arg max}}_{{\bm{u}}\in\real^{p}}\left\{\left\langle{\bm{a}},{\bm{u}}\right\rangle\mid\left\lVert{\bm{u}}\right\rVert\leq 1\right\}.

(1.4)

That is,
\left\langle{\bm{a}},{\bm{a}}^{\dagger}\right\rangle=\left\lVert{\bm{a}}\right\rVert_{*}
for any
{\bm{a}}^{\dagger}\in\Lambda_{{\bm{a}}}
, where
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{*}
denotes the dual norm of
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert
.
It follows that

1.

If
{\bm{a}}\neq\boldsymbol{0}
, then
\left\lVert{\bm{a}}^{\dagger}\right\rVert=1
for any
{\bm{a}}^{\dagger}\in\Lambda_{{\bm{a}}}
.

2.

If
{\bm{a}}=\boldsymbol{0}
, then
\Lambda_{{\bm{a}}}=\{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}\mid\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert\leq 1\}
.

Example 23
(Set of primal counterparts).

Below are a few illustrative examples of sets of primal counterparts:

If the norm is the
\ell_{2}
-norm, then for any
{\bm{a}}\neq\boldsymbol{0}
,

\Lambda_{{\bm{a}}}=\left\{{{\bm{a}}}/{\left\lVert{\bm{a}}\right\rVert_{2}}\right\}.

If the norm is the
\ell_{1}
-norm, then for any
{\bm{a}}\neq\boldsymbol{0}
,

\Lambda_{{\bm{a}}}=\left\{\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{I}}({\bm{a}})}\lambda_{i}\sign(a_{i}){\bm{e}}_{i}\mid\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{I}}({\bm{a}})}\lambda_{i}=1,\lambda_{j}\geq 0,j\in{\mathbb{I}}({\bm{a}})\right\},

where
{\mathbb{I}}({\bm{a}})\triangleq\operatorname*{\text{arg max}}_{i=1,2,\ldots,p}\left\lvert a_{i}\right\rvert
.

If the norm is the
\ell_{\infty}
-norm, then for any
{\bm{a}}\neq\boldsymbol{0}
,

\Lambda_{{\bm{a}}}=\left\{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}\mid\beta_{i}=\sign(a_{i}),i\in{\mathbb{I}}_{\neq}({\bm{a}}),\left\lvert\beta_{j}\right\rvert\leq 1,j\in{\mathbb{I}}_{0}({\bm{a}})\right\},

where

{\mathbb{I}}_{\neq}({\bm{a}})\triangleq\left\{i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}\mid a_{i}\neq 0\right\}
and
{\mathbb{I}}_{0}({\bm{a}})\triangleq\left\{i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}\mid a_{i}=0\right\}.

These examples play a crucial role in the development of non-Euclidean gradient descent methods
Lu 2025
.

Balls

Given a specific norm, we introduce the concepts of an open ball and a closed ball as follows:

Definition 24
(Open ball, closed ball).

Let
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{s}:\real^{p}\rightarrow\real_{+}
denote the
\ell_{s}
-norm.
The open ball centered at
{\bm{c}}\in\real^{p}
with radius
r>0
is defined as

{\mathbb{B}}_{s}({\bm{c}},r)\triangleq\{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}\mid\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{c}}\right\rVert_{s}<r\}.

Similarly, the closed ball centered at
{\bm{c}}\in\real^{p}
with radius
r>0
is defined as

{\mathbb{B}}_{s}[{\bm{c}},r]\triangleq\{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}\mid\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{c}}\right\rVert_{s}\leq r\}.

For example,
{\mathbb{B}}_{2}[\boldsymbol{0},1]
represents the
unit closed ball
w.r.t. to the
\ell_{2}
-norm.
To simplify notation, we omit the subscript “2” for
\ell_{2}
-norms and the center
\boldsymbol{0}
for balls centered at the origin, e.g.,

{\mathbb{B}}[1]\triangleq{\mathbb{B}}_{2}[\boldsymbol{0},1].

(1.5)

As a special case, the notation

{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]\triangleq{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[\boldsymbol{0},k]

(1.6)

is used to denote the set of
k
-sparse vectors
, i.e., containing vectors in
p
that have at most
k
nonzero entries.
More generally, let
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert
be any norm, the corresponding open and closed balls are denoted by

{\mathbb{B}}_{\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert}({\bm{c}},r)\qquad\text{and}\qquad{\mathbb{B}}_{\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert}[{\bm{c}},r].

(1.7)

1.2.2
Matrix Norms: Frobenius and Spectral Norms

While vector norms measure the “size” or “length” of a vector, matrix norms extend this concept to matrices—but with the crucial distinction that they must also account for how a matrix acts as a linear operator, often capturing its effect on vectors through properties like scaling or stretching.
For a matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
, we define the (matrix) Frobenius norm as follows.

Definition 25
(Matrix Frobenius norm).

The Frobenius norm of a matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
is defined as

\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{F}=\sqrt{\sum_{i=1,j=1}^{n,p}x_{ij}^{2}}=\sqrt{\mathrm{tr}({\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{\top})}=\sqrt{\mathrm{tr}({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}})}=\sqrt{\sigma_{1}^{2}+\sigma_{2}^{2}+\ldots+\sigma_{r}^{2}},

where
\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2},\ldots,\sigma_{r}
are nonzero singular values of
{\bm{X}}
, and
\mathrm{tr}({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}})
denotes the trace of
{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}
, i.e., sum of diagonal elements of
{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}
.

The spectral norm is defined as follows.

Definition 26
(Matrix spectral norm).

The spectral norm of a matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
is defined as

\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}=\mathop{\max}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\neq\boldsymbol{0}}\frac{\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}}{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}}=\mathop{\max}_{{\bm{u}}\in\real^{p}:\left\lVert{\bm{u}}\right\rVert_{2}=1}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\bm{u}}\right\rVert_{2}.

(1.8)

This quantity equals the largest singular value of
{\bm{X}}
, i.e.,
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}=\sigma_{\max}({\bm{X}})
; see Section
.

If
{\bm{X}}
is
symmetric
, then its spectral norm also equals the maximum absolute eigenvalue:

\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}=\max_{{\bm{u}}\in\real^{p}:\left\lVert{\bm{u}}\right\rVert_{2}=1}\left\lvert{\bm{u}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}{\bm{u}}\right\rvert,\quad\text{if ${\bm{X}}={\bm{X}}^{\top}$}.

(1.9)

Remark 27
(Standard bounds on matrix norms).

Analogous to standard bounds on vector norms (Exercise
), the spectral norm is bounded above by the Frobenius norm

\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{F}.

(1.10)

This follows simply by the definition
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}=\sigma_{\max}({\bm{X}})
and
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{F}=\sqrt{\sigma_{1}^{2}+\sigma_{2}^{2}+\ldots+\sigma_{r}^{2}}
.
Alternatively, this can be proved using

\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{p}x_{ij}\beta_{j}\right)^{2}\leq\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{p}x_{ij}^{2}\right)\left(\sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_{j}^{2}\right)=\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{F}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2},

where the inequality follows from the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality; see Theorem
.

We note that the Frobenius norm serves as the matrix counterpart of the vector
\ell_{2}
-norm.
For simplicity, we e omit the full subscript for the vector
\ell_{2}
-norm or Frobenius norm when the context makes it clear which norm is intended:

\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert=\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{F}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\left\lVert{\bm{x}}\right\rVert=\left\lVert{\bm{x}}\right\rVert_{2}.

However, for the spectral norm, the subscript in
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}
should
not
be omitted.

The vector space
p
, equipped with a given norm
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert
, is called a
normed vector space
.
On the other hand, another way to define norms for matrices is by treating a matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
as a vector in
np
, e.g., via vectorization.
What distinguishes a matrix norm from a generic vector norm on matrices is a key property called
submultiplicativity
:
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\bm{Y}}\right\rVert\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert\left\lVert{\bm{Y}}\right\rVert
if
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert
is a submultiplicative matrix norm (see discussions below).

In some texts, a matrix norm that is not
submultiplicative
is referred to as a
vector norm on matrices
or a
generalized matrix norm
.
Although the definition of a matrix norm applies to both square and rectangular matrices, submultiplicativity is especially important in the analysis of square matrices.
For a submultiplicative matrix norm
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert
satisfying
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\bm{Y}}\right\rVert\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert\left\lVert{\bm{Y}}\right\rVert
, and for a square matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times n}
, it follows by induction that

\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{2}\right\rVert\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert^{2}\quad\implies\quad\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{k}\right\rVert\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert^{k},\ \forall\,k\in\{1,2,\ldots,\}.

(1.11)

Therefore, if
{\bm{X}}
is idempotent (i.e.,
{\bm{X}}^{2}={\bm{X}}
), then
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert\geq 1
.
In particular, this implies

\left\lVert{\bm{I}}\right\rVert\geq 1,\quad\text{if}\quad\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert\text{ is submultiplicative}.

(1.12)

On the other hand, if
{\bm{X}}
is nonsingular, then using submultiplicativity we obtain:

1\leq\left\lVert{\bm{I}}\right\rVert=\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{-1}\right\rVert\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{-1}\right\rVert.

That is, a submultiplicative norm satisfies
\left\lVert{\bm{I}}\right\rVert\geq 1
, and it is said to be
normalized
if and only if
\left\lVert{\bm{I}}\right\rVert=1
.

{theoremHigh}

[Submultiplicativity and orthogonally invariance]
The Frobnenius and spectral norms are submultiplicative. That is,

\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\bm{Y}}\right\rVert_{F}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{F}\left\lVert{\bm{Y}}\right\rVert_{F}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\bm{Y}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\bm{Y}}\right\rVert_{2}.

Moreover, both norms are
orthogonally invariant
. That is, for any orthogonal matrices
{\bm{U}}\in\real^{n\times n}
and
{\bm{V}}\in\real^{p\times p}
, and any
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
,

\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{F}=\left\lVert{\bm{U}}{\bm{X}}{\bm{V}}\right\rVert_{F}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}=\left\lVert{\bm{U}}{\bm{X}}{\bm{V}}\right\rVert_{2}.

Proof

See
Lu 2021a
.

Induced Matrix Norm: Generalizing Spectral Norm

More generally, many matrix norms can be derived using the concept of induced norms.

Definition 28
(Induced matrix norm: General matrix norm).

Let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
be a matrix, and let
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{a}
and
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{b}
be vector norms on
p
and
n
respectively.
The induced matrix norm
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{a,b}
is defined as

\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{a,b}=\mathop{\max}_{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{a}\neq 0}\frac{\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{b}}{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{a}}=\mathop{\max}_{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{a}=1}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{b}.\penalty\

From this definition, the matrix-vector product inequality follows immediately:

\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{b}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{a,b}\cdot\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{a}.

(1.13)

The induced matrix norm can also be referred to as the
(a,b)
-norm.
When
a=b
, it is simply called the
a
-norm, and we write
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{a}
instead of
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{a,a}
.
In particular, when
a=b=2
, we have the classic spectral norm.

Intuitively, the induced norm measures the maximum factor by which the matrix
{\bm{X}}
can stretch a nonzero vector: the input vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is measured using the norm
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{a}
, while the output vector
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is measured using norm
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{b}
.

From the definition above, it follows that the spectral norm is a special case of an induced norm with
a=b=2
, i.e.,
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}=\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2,2}
. Similarly, the
matrix 1-norm
is obtained as

\textbf{Matrix 1-norm:}\quad\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{1}=\mathop{\max}_{j=1,2,\ldots,p}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left\lvert x_{ij}\right\rvert=\mathop{\max}_{j=1,2,\ldots,p}\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{j}\right\rVert_{1},

(1.14)

which is also known as the
maximum absolute column sum norm
.
To verify this, consider
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
.
For any vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
, we have

\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}=\left\lVert\sum_{i=1}^{p}\beta_{i}{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\sum_{i=1}^{p}\left\lvert\beta_{i}\right\rvert\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\sum_{i=1}^{p}\left\lvert\beta_{i}\right\rvert\left(\mathop{\max}_{j=1,2,\ldots,p}\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{j}\right\rVert_{1}\right)=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{1}.

Therefore,
\mathop{\max}_{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}=1}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{1}
.
On the other hand, consider
\mathop{\max}_{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}=1}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}
for
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\bm{e}}_{j},\,\forall\,j\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
, we have

\mathop{\max}_{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}=1}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\geq\mathop{\max}_{j=1,2,\ldots,p}\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{j}\right\rVert_{1}=\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{1}.

By “sandwiching,” we have
\mathop{\max}_{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}=1}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}=\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{1}
.
Likewise, the
matrix
\infty
-norm
is given by

\textbf{Matrix $\infty$-norm:}\quad\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{\infty}=\mathop{\max}_{i=1,2,\ldots,n}\sum_{j=1}^{p}\left\lvert x_{ij}\right\rvert,

(1.15)

which is also called the
maximum absolute row sum norm
.

Exercise
\thetheo
(Maximum absolute row sum norm)

Prove that
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{\infty}
is the matrix norm induced by the vector
\ell_{\infty}
-norm.

Exercise
\thetheo
(Equi-induced and normalized norm)

Let
a=b
and let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{p\times p}
be a square matrix in Definition
.
In this case, the induced norm is called an
equi-induced norm
. Show that the equi-induced norm is normalized:
\left\lVert{\bm{I}}_{p}\right\rVert_{a}=1
and
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{a}\geq 1
.

We have already seen that the spectral norm—an important example of an induced norm—is submultiplicative. In fact, all induced norms are submultiplicative.

{theoremHigh}
[Submultiplicativity of induced norms]
For
a,b,c\geq 1
and matrices
{\bm{X}},{\bm{Y}}
(provided the matrix product
{\bm{X}}{\bm{Y}}
is defined), we have

\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\bm{Y}}\right\rVert_{a,b}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{c,b}\left\lVert{\bm{Y}}\right\rVert_{a,c}.

That is, the norm of a
product is bounded by the product of the norms.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
From the definition of the induced norm, we have

\displaystyle\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\bm{Y}}\right\rVert_{a,b}

\displaystyle=\mathop{\max}_{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{a}=1}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\bm{Y}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{b}\leq\mathop{\max}_{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{a}=1}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{c,b}\left\lVert{\bm{Y}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{c}\leq\mathop{\max}_{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{a}=1}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{c,b}\left\lVert{\bm{Y}}\right\rVert_{a,c}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{a}.

This completes the proof.

Remark 29
(Condition number).

For a nonsingular matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{p\times p}
,
we note that
1=\left\lVert{\bm{I}}\right\rVert_{b,b}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{a,b}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{-1}\right\rVert_{b,a}
. The value
\kappa_{a,b}=\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{a,b}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{-1}\right\rVert_{b,a}
is normally known as the condition number with respect to the induced vector norms
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{a}
and
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{b}
.
The common case is

\kappa({\bm{X}})={\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}}{\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{-1}\right\rVert_{2}}=\frac{\sigma_{\max}({\bm{X}})}{\sigma_{\min}({\bm{X}})},

where
\sigma_{\max}
and
\sigma_{\min}
denote the largest and smallest singular values of
{\bm{X}}
, respectively (Section
).
See
Lu 2021a
for more details.

1.2.3
Orthogonal and Projection Matrices

We often use the letters
{\bm{Q}},{\bm{U}},{\bm{V}}\in\real^{n\times p}
to denote matrices whose columns are orthonormal (called
semi-orthogonal matrices
when
p\neq n
).
If such a matrix is square (i.e.,
p=n
), it is called an orthogonal matrix.
Orthogonal matrices represent linear transformations that preserve the length (magnitude) of any vector—they may change its direction, but not its norm.

Definition 30
(Orthogonal matrix, semi-orthogonal matrix).

A real square matrix
{\bm{Q}}\in\real^{n\times n}
is an orthogonal matrix if its inverse equals its transpose;
that is
{\bm{Q}}^{-1}={\bm{Q}}^{\top}
and
{\bm{Q}}{\bm{Q}}^{\top}={\bm{Q}}^{\top}{\bm{Q}}={\bm{I}}
.
In other words, suppose
{\bm{Q}}=[{\bm{q}}_{1},{\bm{q}}_{2},\ldots,{\bm{q}}_{n}]
, where
{\bm{q}}_{i}\in\real^{n}
for all
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}
, then
{\bm{q}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{q}}_{j}=\delta(i,j)
with
\delta(i,j)
being the Kronecker delta function.
For any vector
{\bm{x}}
, an orthogonal matrix preserves the Euclidean length:
\left\lVert{\bm{Q}}{\bm{x}}\right\rVert_{2}=\left\lVert{\bm{x}}\right\rVert_{2}
, where
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{2}
denotes the
\ell_{2}
-norm (Definition
).
Note that because the columns of an orthogonal matrix are unit vectors and mutually orthogonal, they form an orthonormal set. However, by historical convention, the term orthogonormal matrix is
not
used; instead, such matrices are always referred to as orthogonal matrices, even though their columns are orthonormal.

On the other hand, if
{\bm{Q}}\in\real^{n\times\gamma}
contains only
\gamma<n
of these columns, then
{\bm{Q}}^{\top}{\bm{Q}}={\bm{I}}_{\gamma}
stills holds, where
{\bm{I}}_{\gamma}
is the
\gamma\times\gamma
identity matrix. But
{\bm{Q}}{\bm{Q}}^{\top}={\bm{I}}
will not be true.
In this case,
{\bm{Q}}
referred to as a semi-orthogonal matrix.

The vectors
{\bm{q}}_{1},{\bm{q}}_{2},\ldots,{\bm{q}}_{\gamma}\in\real^{n}
are
mutually orthogonal
if their dot products
{\bm{q}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{q}}_{j}
satisfies
{\bm{q}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{q}}_{j}=0
whenever
i\neq j
.
If, in addition, each vector has unit length (i.e.,
\left\lVert{\bm{q}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}=1
for all i), then the vectors are mutually orthonormal. We typically collect such orthonormal vectors as the columns of a matrix
{\bm{Q}}
.

When
n\neq\gamma
: the matrix
{\bm{Q}}
is easy to work with because
{\bm{Q}}^{\top}{\bm{Q}}={\bm{I}}\in\real^{\gamma\times\gamma}
.

When
n=\gamma
: the matrix
{\bm{Q}}
is square,
{\bm{Q}}^{\top}{\bm{Q}}={\bm{I}}
means that
{\bm{Q}}^{\top}={\bm{Q}}^{-1}
, i.e., the transpose of
{\bm{Q}}
is the inverse of
{\bm{Q}}
. Then we also have
{\bm{Q}}{\bm{Q}}^{\top}={\bm{I}}
, i.e.,
{\bm{Q}}^{\top}
is the two-sided inverse of
{\bm{Q}}
.
Such a matrix
{\bm{Q}}
is called an
orthogonal matrix
.

By definition, the columns
{\bm{q}}_{1},{\bm{q}}_{2},\ldots,{\bm{q}}_{n}
of any
n\times n
orthogonal matrix have unit norm and are orthogonal to each other, so they form an orthonormal basis. Applying
{\bm{Q}}^{\top}
to a vector
{\bm{x}}\in\real^{n}
is equivalent to computing the coefficients of its representation in the basis formed by the columns of
{\bm{Q}}
. Applying
{\bm{Q}}
to
{\bm{Q}}^{\top}{\bm{x}}
recovers
{\bm{x}}
by scaling each basis vector with the corresponding coefficient:

{\bm{x}}={\bm{Q}}{\bm{Q}}^{\top}{\bm{x}}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\langle{\bm{q}}_{i},{\bm{x}}\rangle{\bm{q}}_{i}.

Since orthogonal matrices represent pure rotations (and possibly reflections), it is intuitive that the product of two orthogonal matrices is also orthogonal.
Indeed, if
{\bm{Q}},{\bm{U}}\in\real^{n\times n}
are orthogonal matrices, then their product
{\bm{Q}}{\bm{U}}
is also an orthogonal matrix.

Specifically, the following lemma shows that orthogonal matrices preserve the
\ell_{2}
-norm of any vector.

Lemma 31
.

Let
{\bm{Q}}\in\real^{n\times n}
be an orthogonal matrix.
Then, for any vector
{\bm{x}}\in\real^{n}
,

\left\lVert{\bm{Q}}{\bm{x}}\right\rVert_{2}=\left\lVert{\bm{x}}\right\rVert_{2}.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
By the definition of an orthogonal matrix, we have

\left\lVert{\bm{Q}}{\bm{x}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}={\bm{x}}^{\top}{\bm{Q}}^{\top}{\bm{Q}}{\bm{x}}={\bm{x}}^{\top}{\bm{x}}=\left\lVert{\bm{x}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
.
Taking square roots on both sides yields the desired result.

Semi-orthogonal matrices are closely related to the concept of
orthogonal projection matrices
.
Formally, we define the projection matrix as follows:

Definition 32
(Projection matrix).

A matrix
{\bm{H}}\in\real^{n\times n}
is called a projection matrix or projector onto a subspace
\mathcal{V}\in\real^{n}
if and only if
{\bm{H}}
satisfies the following properties:

(P1).
{\bm{H}}{\bm{y}}\in\mathcal{V}
for all
{\bm{y}}\in\real^{n}
: Any vector can be projected onto the subspace
\mathcal{V}
.

(P2).
{\bm{H}}{\bm{y}}={\bm{y}}
for all
{\bm{y}}\in\mathcal{V}
: Vectors already in
\mathcal{V}
remain unchanged under the projection.

(P3).
{\bm{H}}^{2}={\bm{H}}
: Applying the projection twice has the same effect as applying it once. This property is known as idempotence.

Since we project vectors from
n
onto a subspace of
n
, any projection matrix must be square.
If
{\bm{H}}
were
k\times n
with
k\neq n
, the image would lie in
k
, not in a subspace of
n
.

Observe that
{\bm{H}}{\bm{y}}
always lies in the column space of
{\bm{H}}
, denoted
\mathcal{C}({\bm{H}})
.
One may then ask: what is the relationship between the target subspace
\mathcal{V}
and the column space
\mathcal{C}({\bm{H}})
.
In fact, they are identical (see Lemma
for a hint).

Suppose
\mathcal{V}=\mathcal{C}({\bm{H}})
, and let
{\bm{y}}\in\mathcal{V}
.
Then there exists some vector
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
such that
{\bm{y}}={\bm{H}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
.
Using only condition (P3), we obtain

{\bm{H}}{\bm{y}}={\bm{H}}{\bm{H}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}={\bm{H}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}={\bm{y}}.

Thus, condition (P3) implies both conditions (P1) and (P2).
Consequently, a matrix
{\bm{H}}
is a projection matrix if and only if it is idempotent (
{\bm{H}}^{2}={\bm{H}}
).

Intuitively, we often require more than just idempotence: we want the projected vector
\widehat{\bm{y}}={\bm{H}}{\bm{y}}
to be the closest point in
\mathcal{V}
to the original vector
{\bm{y}}
, in the sense of Euclidean distance. This occurs precisely when the residual
{\bm{y}}-\widehat{\bm{y}}
is orthogonal to
\widehat{\bm{y}}
(and, more generally, to the entire subspace
\mathcal{V}
). Such a projection is called an
orthogonal projection
, and it aligns with the principle of least-squares error minimization.

Definition 33
(Orthogonal and oblique projection matrix).

A matrix
{\bm{H}}
is called an orthogonal projection matrix or an orthogonal projector onto a subspace
\mathcal{V}\subseteq\real^{n}
if and only if
{\bm{H}}
is a projection matrix, and the projection
\widehat{\bm{y}}
of any vector
{\bm{y}}\in\real^{n}
is orthogonal to
{\bm{y}}-\widehat{\bm{y}}
, i.e.,
{\bm{H}}
projects onto
\mathcal{V}
and along
\mathcal{V}^{\perp}
, the orthogonal complement of
\mathcal{V}
.

Otherwise, if
\widehat{\bm{y}}
is not orthogonal to
{\bm{y}}-\widehat{\bm{y}}
, then the projection matrix is called an oblique projection matrix or an oblique projector.
A geometric comparison between orthogonal and oblique projections is illustrated in Figure
.

Exercise
\thetheo

Show that a projection matrix
{\bm{H}}
is an orthogonal projection matrix if and only if it is symmetric.

Intuitively, let
\mathcal{V}
be a subspace of
n
, and let
{\bm{H}}\in\real^{n\times n}
be the orthogonal projection matrix onto
\mathcal{V}
.
As shown in Figure
, for any vector
{\bm{y}}\in\real^{n}
,
the orthogonal projection minimizes the Euclidean distance to
\mathcal{V}
:

\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{H}}{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{v}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},\qquad\forall\,{\bm{v}}\in\mathcal{V}.

(1.16)

(a)

Orthogonal projection: project
{\bm{y}}
to
\widehat{\bm{y}}
.

(b)

Oblique projection: project
{\bm{y}}
to
\widehat{\bm{y}}_{1}
or
\widehat{\bm{y}}_{2}
.

Figure 1.1:
Projection onto the hyperplane
\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}})
, i.e., the column space of
{\bm{X}}
.

It is important to note that the term orthogonal projection does not imply that the projection matrix
{\bm{H}}
itself is an orthogonal matrix (in the sense of Definition
, where
{\bm{Q}}{\bm{Q}}^{\top}={\bm{I}}
).
Rather, “orthogonal” refers to the geometric orthogonality between the projected vector
\widehat{\bm{y}}
and the residua
{\bm{y}}-\widehat{\bm{y}}
.
Unless otherwise stated, the term “projection matrix” in the remainder of this book will refer to an orthogonal projection matrix.

The following result shows that the orthogonal projection onto the column space of a set of linearly independent vectors admits a specific closed-form expression, which is intimately connected to the ordinary least squares (OLS) solution (see Section
).

Lemma 34
(Projection matrix from a set of vectors).

Let
{\bm{x}}_{1},{\bm{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\bm{x}}_{p}\in\real^{n}
be linearly independent vectors such that
\mathcal{C}([{\bm{x}}_{1},{\bm{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\bm{x}}_{p}])=\mathcal{V}
, and assume
n\geq p
.
Then the orthogonal projection onto the subspace
\mathcal{V}
is given by

{\bm{H}}\triangleq{\bm{X}}({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}})^{-1}{\bm{X}}^{\top},

where
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
is the matrix whose columns are
{\bm{x}}_{1},{\bm{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\bm{x}}_{p}
.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
It is straightforward to verify that
{\bm{H}}
is symmetric and idempotent, which characterizes it as an orthogonal projection matrix.
Considering the SVD of
{\bm{X}}={\bm{U}}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}{\bm{V}}^{\top}
(see Section
), we have
{\bm{H}}={\bm{X}}({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}})^{-1}{\bm{X}}^{\top}={\bm{U}}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}({\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}})^{-1}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{\top}{\bm{U}}^{\top}
.
Let
{\bm{U}}=[{\bm{u}}_{1},{\bm{u}}_{2},\ldots,{\bm{u}}_{n}]
be the column partition of
{\bm{U}}
. From Theorem
,
\{{\bm{u}}_{1},{\bm{u}}_{2},\ldots,{\bm{u}}_{p}\}
is an orthonormal basis of
\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}})
. And
{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}({\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}})^{-1}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{\top}
in
{\bm{H}}
is an
n\times n
matrix, where the upper-left part is a
p\times p
identity matrix and the other parts are zero.
Consequently,
{\bm{H}}=\sum_{i=1}^{p}{\bm{u}}_{i}{\bm{u}}_{i}^{\top}
, which implies that
\mathcal{C}({\bm{H}})=\mathrm{span}\{{\bm{u}}_{1},{\bm{u}}_{2},\ldots,{\bm{u}}_{p}\}=\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}})
.
Thus,
{\bm{H}}
is the orthogonal projector onto
\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}})=\mathcal{V}
, as required.

Lemma
shows that
{\bm{H}}={\bm{X}}({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}})^{-1}{\bm{X}}^{\top}
is the orthogonal projector onto
\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}})
if
{\bm{X}}
has full column rank.
More generally, matrices with mutually orthonormal columns (semi-orthogonal matrices) can also be used to construct orthogonal projection matrices.

Lemma 35
(Orthogonal projector onto general subspaces).

Let
\mathcal{V}
be a subspace of
n
with dimension
r
. Let
{\bm{Q}}_{1}\in\real^{n\times r}
and
{\bm{Q}}_{2}\in\real^{n\times(n-r)}
be semi-orthogonal matrices (i.e., their columns are mutually orthonormal; Definition
) such that
\mathcal{C}({\bm{Q}}_{1})=\mathcal{V}
and
\mathcal{C}({\bm{Q}}_{2})=\mathcal{V}^{\perp}
, where
\mathcal{V}^{\perp}
denotes the orthogonal complement of
\mathcal{V}
. Then the orthogonal projectors onto
\mathcal{V}
and
\mathcal{V}^{\perp}
are given by

{\bm{H}}_{1}\triangleq{\bm{Q}}_{1}{\bm{Q}}_{1}^{\top}\qquad\text{and}\qquad{\bm{H}}_{2}\triangleq{\bm{Q}}_{2}{\bm{Q}}_{2}^{\top},

(1.17)

respectively.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
We have
{\bm{H}}_{1}^{2}={\bm{Q}}_{1}{\bm{Q}}_{1}^{\top}{\bm{Q}}_{1}{\bm{Q}}_{1}^{\top}={\bm{Q}}_{1}{\bm{Q}}_{1}^{\top}={\bm{H}}_{1}
since
{\bm{Q}}_{1}^{\top}{\bm{Q}}_{1}={\bm{I}}_{r}
. This shows that
{\bm{H}}_{1}
is a projector onto
\mathcal{V}
.
Since
{\bm{H}}_{1}
is symmetric, this completes the proof for the first part.
An identical argument applies to
{\bm{H}}_{2}={\bm{Q}}_{2}{\bm{Q}}_{2}^{\top}
, showing that it is the orthogonal projector onto
\mathcal{V}^{\perp}
.

1.2.4
Singular Value Decomposition (SVD)

We introduce singular value decomposition (SVD) of a matrix in this section.
Before presenting the general form of the SVD, we begin with the spectral decomposition of a symmetric matrix.
The spectral theorem—also known as the spectral decomposition for symmetric matrices—states that any real symmetric matrix has real eigenvalues and can be diagonalized using a real orthonormal basis.

{theoremHigh}

[Spectral decomposition]
A real matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times n}
is symmetric if and only if there exist an orthogonal matrix
{\bm{Q}}
and a diagonal matrix
{\boldsymbol{\Lambda}}
such that

{\bm{X}}={\bm{Q}}{\boldsymbol{\Lambda}}{\bm{Q}}^{\top},

where the columns of
{\bm{Q}}=[{\bm{q}}_{1},{\bm{q}}_{2},\ldots,{\bm{q}}_{n}]
are mutually orthonormal eigenvectors of
{\bm{X}}
, and the entries of
{\boldsymbol{\Lambda}}=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\ldots,\lambda_{n})
are the corresponding eigenvalues of
{\bm{X}}
, which are real.
In particular, the following properties hold:

1.

All eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix are
real
.

2.

The eigenvectors can be chosen to form an
orthonormal
set.

3.

The rank of
{\bm{X}}
equals the number of its nonzero eigenvalues.

4.

If all eigenvalues are distinct, then the corresponding eigenvectors are linearly independent.

Proof

See
Lu 2022
.

Using spectral decomposition, we can factor a symmetric matrix into a diagonal form.
However, this approach is not always applicable: when
{\bm{X}}
is not symmetric or not square, such a diagonalization is generally impossible.
The singular value decomposition (SVD) addresses this limitation. Instead of relying on a single orthogonal matrix of eigenvectors, the SVD expresses any matrix as a product of two orthogonal matrices and a diagonal (or diagonal-like) matrix of singular values. We now state the SVD theorem.

{theoremHigh}

[Full singular value decomposition]
Every real
n\times p
matrix
{\bm{X}}
of rank
r
admits a decomposition of the form

{\bm{X}}={\bm{U}}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}{\bm{V}}^{\top},

where
{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\in\real^{n\times p}
has the block structure
{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}=\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{r}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}
with
{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{r}=\mathrm{diag}(\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}\ldots,\sigma_{r})\in\real^{r\times r}
, and the singular values satisfy
\sigma_{1}\geq\sigma_{2}\geq\ldots\geq\sigma_{r}
.

The scalars
\sigma_{i}
are the nonzero
singular values
of
{\bm{X}}
. Each
