\sigma_{i}
equals the positive square root of a nonzero eigenvalue of both
{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}
and
{\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{\top}
.

{\bm{U}}\in{\real{}^{n\times n}}
is an orthogonal matrix whose first
r
columns are eigenvectors of
{\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{\top}
corresponding to its
r
nonzero eigenvalues; the remaining
n-r
columns form an orthonormal basis for
\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}}^{\top})
.

{\bm{V}}\in{\real{}^{p\times p}}
is an orthogonal matrix whose first
r
columns are eigenvectors of
{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}
corresponding to its
r
nonzero eigenvalues; the remaining
p-r
columns form an orthonormal basis for
\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
.

The columns of
{\bm{U}}
and
{\bm{V}}
are called the
left and right singular vectors
of
{\bm{X}}
, respectively.

Moreover, the decomposition can be expressed as a sum of rank-one matrices:
{\bm{X}}={\bm{U}}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}{\bm{V}}^{\top}=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\sigma_{i}{\bm{u}}_{i}{\bm{v}}_{i}^{\top}
.

If
{\bm{X}}
has rank
r
, then its singular values satisfy
\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2},\ldots,\sigma_{r}>0
while
\sigma_{r+1}=\sigma_{r+2}=\ldots=0
.
In many applications, it is more convenient to work with the
reduced singular value decomposition (reduced SVD)
.
For
{\bm{X}}
of rank
r
with (full) SVD
{\bm{X}}={\bm{U}}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}{\bm{V}}^{\top}
, we take the submatrices
{\bm{U}}_{r}\in\real^{n\times r}
,
{\bm{V}}_{r}\in\real^{p\times r}
such that
{\bm{U}}=[{\bm{U}}_{r},{\bm{u}}_{r+1},\ldots,{\bm{u}}_{n}]
,
{\bm{V}}=[{\bm{V}}_{r},{\bm{v}}_{r+1},\ldots,{\bm{v}}_{p}]
, and
{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{r}=\mathrm{diag}([\sigma_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{r}])\in\real^{r\times r}
.
Therefore, we obtain the reduced singular value decomposition (reduced SVD) of
{\bm{X}}
:
{\bm{X}}={\bm{U}}_{r}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{r}{\bm{V}}_{r}^{\top}
.
The comparison between the reduced and full SVD is shown in Figure
, where white entries are zero, and blue entries are not necessarily zero.

Given
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
with reduced SVD
{\bm{X}}={\bm{U}}_{r}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{r}{\bm{V}}_{r}^{\top}
, we observe that

\displaystyle{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}

\displaystyle={\bm{V}}_{r}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{r}^{\top}{\bm{U}}_{r}^{\top}{\bm{U}}_{r}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{r}{\bm{V}}_{r}^{\top}={\bm{V}}_{r}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{r}^{2}{\bm{V}}_{r}^{\top};

\displaystyle{\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{\top}

\displaystyle={\bm{U}}_{r}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{r}{\bm{V}}_{r}^{\top}{\bm{V}}_{r}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{r}^{\top}{\bm{U}}_{r}^{\top}={\bm{U}}_{r}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{r}^{2}{\bm{U}}_{r}^{\top}.

Thus, we recover the (reduced) spectral decompositions of symmetric positive semidefinite matrices
{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}
and
{\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{\top}
, respectively.
In particular, the singular values
\sigma_{i}=\sigma_{i}({\bm{X}})
satisfy

\sigma_{i}({\bm{X}})=\sqrt{\lambda_{i}({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}})}=\sqrt{\lambda_{i}({\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{\top})},\quad i=1,\ldots,\min\{n,p\},

(1.18)

where
\lambda_{1}({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}})\geq\lambda_{2}({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}})\geq\ldots
are the eigenvalues of
{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}
in decreasing order. Moreover, the left and right singular vectors listed in
{\bm{U}},{\bm{V}}
can be obtained by the spectral decomposition of the positive semidefinite matrices
{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}
and
{\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{\top}
.
Consequently, one can construct the SVD of
{\bm{X}}
directly from the spectral decompositions of
{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}
and
{\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{\top}
—which also provides an alternative proof of the existence of the SVD.

(a)

Reduced SVD decomposition.

(b)

Full SVD decomposition.

Figure 1.2:
Comparison between the reduced and full SVD. White entries are zero, and blue entries are not necessarily zero

Exercise
\thetheo
(Proof of SVD)

Using the discussion above and the spectral decomposition, prove the existence of the singular value decomposition of a matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
.

Four Orthonormal Bases in SVD

For any matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
, the following properties hold:

The null space
\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
is the orthogonal complement of the row space
\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}^{\top})
in
p
:
\dim(\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}}))+\dim(\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}^{\top}))=p
.

The left null space
\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}}^{\top})
is the orthogonal complement of the column space
\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}})
in
n
:
\dim(\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}}^{\top}))+\dim(\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}))=n
.

This result is known as the fundamental theorem of linear algebra (see the discussion preceding Lemma
).
In particular, the construction of the SVD provides orthonormal bases for all four fundamental subspaces described in this theorem. To establish this, we first require the following lemma.

Lemma 36
(Subspace of
{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}
and
{\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{\top}
).

Let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
be given.
Then,

The column space of
{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}
is identical to the column space of
{\bm{X}}^{\top}
(i.e., row space of
{\bm{X}}
):
\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}})=\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}^{\top})
; this also shows
\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}})=\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
by fundamental theorem of linear algebra (see the discussion preceding Lemma
).

The column space of
{\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{\top}
is identical to the column space of
{\bm{X}}
:
\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{\top})=\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}})
.
Hence, this also shows
\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{\top})=\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}}^{\top})
.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Let
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
, we have

{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\boldsymbol{0}\implies{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\boldsymbol{0},

i.e.,
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})\implies{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}})
. Therefore,
\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})\subseteq\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}})
.
Furthermore, let
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}})
, we have

{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\boldsymbol{0}\implies{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=0\implies\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=0\implies{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\boldsymbol{0},

i.e.,
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}})\implies{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
. Therefore,
\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}})\subseteq\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
.
Combining both inclusions yields

\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})=\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}).

By the fundamental theorem of linear algebra (see the discussion preceding Lemma
), it follows that

\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}^{\top})=\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}).

Applying the same argument to
{\bm{X}}^{\top}
establishes the second claim.

{theoremHigh}

[Four orthonormal bases in SVD]
Let
{\bm{X}}={\bm{U}}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}{\bm{V}}^{\top}
be the full SVD of
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
, where
{\bm{U}}=[{\bm{u}}_{1},{\bm{u}}_{2},\ldots,{\bm{u}}_{n}]
and
{\bm{V}}=[{\bm{v}}_{1},{\bm{v}}_{2},\ldots,{\bm{v}}_{p}]
are the column partitions of
{\bm{U}}
and
{\bm{V}}
, respectively.
Then:

\{{\bm{v}}_{1},{\bm{v}}_{2},\ldots,{\bm{v}}_{r}\}
is an orthonormal basis for the row space
\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}^{\top})
;

\{{\bm{v}}_{r+1},{\bm{v}}_{r+2},\ldots,{\bm{v}}_{p}\}
is an orthonormal basis for the null space
\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
;

\{{\bm{u}}_{1},{\bm{u}}_{2},\ldots,{\bm{u}}_{r}\}
is an orthonormal basis for the column space
\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}})
;

\{{\bm{u}}_{r+1},{\bm{u}}_{r+2},\ldots,{\bm{u}}_{n}\}
is an orthonormal basis for the left null space
\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}}^{\top})
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
By the spectral decomposition, for the symmetric matrix
{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}
, its column space
\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}})
is spanned by the eigenvectors.
Therefore, the set
\{{\bm{v}}_{1},{\bm{v}}_{2},\ldots,{\bm{v}}_{r}\}
forms an orthonormal basis for
\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}})
.
Thus,
\{{\bm{v}}_{1},{\bm{v}}_{2},\ldots,{\bm{v}}_{r}\}
also serves as an orthonormal basis for
\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}^{\top})
by Lemma
.

Since
{\bm{V}}
is orthogonal, the space spanned by the remaining vectors
\{{\bm{v}}_{r+1},{\bm{v}}_{r+2},\ldots,{\bm{v}}_{n}\}
is the orthogonal complement to the space spanned by
\{{\bm{v}}_{1},{\bm{v}}_{2},\ldots,{\bm{v}}_{r}\}
, which is precisely
\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
.
Thus,
\{{\bm{v}}_{r+1},{\bm{v}}_{r+2},\ldots,{\bm{v}}_{n}\}
constitutes an orthonormal basis for
\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
.

A similar argument applied to
{\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{\top}
shows that
\{{\bm{u}}_{1},{\bm{u}}_{2},\ldots,{\bm{u}}_{r}\}
spans
\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}})
and
\{{\bm{u}}_{r+1},{\bm{u}}_{r+2},\ldots,{\bm{u}}_{n}\}
spans
\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}}^{\top})
.
Alternatively, we can see that
\{{\bm{u}}_{1},{\bm{u}}_{2},\ldots,{\bm{u}}_{r}\}
forms a basis for the column space of
{\bm{X}}
by Lemma
, since
{\bm{u}}_{i}=\frac{{\bm{X}}{\bm{v}}_{i}}{\sigma_{i}},\,\forall\,i\in\{1,2,\ldots,r\}
(which is a key property of SVD).

The relationship among the four subspaces is illustrated in Figure
.
Specifically, for each
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,r\}
, the matrix
{\bm{X}}
maps the row-space basis vector
{\bm{v}}_{i}
to the column-space basis vector
{\bm{u}}_{i}
according to the relation
\sigma_{i}{\bm{u}}_{i}={\bm{X}}{\bm{v}}_{i}
.

Figure 1.3:
Orthonormal bases that diagonalize
{\bm{X}}
via the SVD. The set
\{{\bm{v}}_{1},{\bm{v}}_{2},\ldots,{\bm{v}}_{r}\}
forms an orthonormal basis for the row space
\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}^{\top})
, and
\{{\bm{u}}_{1},{\bm{u}}_{2},\ldots,{\bm{u}}_{r}\}
forms an orthonormal basis for the column space
\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}})
.
The action of
{\bm{X}}
links these bases: for each
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,r\}
, it transforms the row-space basis vector
{\bm{v}}_{i}
into the column-space basis vector
{\bm{u}}_{i}
scaled by the singular value
\sigma_{i}
, i.e.,
{\bm{X}}{\bm{v}}_{i}=\sigma_{i}{\bm{u}}_{i}
.

Singular Value Bounds

In its SVD form, a linear map can be interpreted as performing three operations on vectors: an initial rotation, followed by scaling along orthogonal directions according to the singular values, and then a final rotation. This implies that the maximum possible scaling factor equals the largest singular value,
\sigma_{1}
, and occurs in the direction of the corresponding right singular vector
{\bm{v}}_{1}
.
The following theorem formalizes this intuition. It shows that if we restrict attention to the orthogonal complement of
{\bm{v}}_{1}
, the maximum scaling is given by the second singular value,
\sigma_{2}
, due to the orthogonality of the singular vectors. More generally, the direction of maximum scaling that is orthogonal to the first
i-1
right singular vectors corresponds to the
i
-th singular value,
\sigma_{i}
, and is aligned with the
i
-th right singular vector
{\bm{v}}_{i}
.

{theoremHigh}

[Courant–Fischer-type characterization for singular values]
Let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
have the singular value decomposition
{\bm{U}}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}{\bm{V}}^{\top}
.
Then the singular values satisfy

\displaystyle\sigma_{1}

\displaystyle=\max_{\left\{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}=1\mid{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}\right\}}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2},

(1.19)

\displaystyle=\max_{\left\{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}=1\mid{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{n}\right\}}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2},

(1.20)

\displaystyle\sigma_{i}

\displaystyle=\max_{\left\{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}=1\mid{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p},\,{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\perp{\bm{v}}_{1},\ldots,{\bm{v}}_{i-1}\right\}}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2},

(1.21)

\displaystyle=\max_{\left\{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}=1\mid{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{n},\,{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\perp{\bm{u}}_{1},\ldots,{\bm{u}}_{i-1}\right\}}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2},\qquad 2\leq i\leq\min\{n,p\},

(1.22)

the right singular vectors satisfy

\displaystyle{\bm{v}}_{1}

\displaystyle=\operatorname*{\text{arg max}}_{\left\{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}=1\mid{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}\right\}}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2},

(1.23)

\displaystyle{\bm{v}}_{i}

\displaystyle=\operatorname*{\text{arg max}}_{\left\{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}=1\mid{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p},\,{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\perp{\bm{v}}_{1},\ldots,{\bm{v}}_{i-1}\right\}}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2},\qquad 2\leq i\leq p,

(1.24)

and the left singular vectors satisfy

\displaystyle{\bm{u}}_{1}

\displaystyle=\operatorname*{\text{arg max}}_{\left\{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}=1\mid{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{n}\right\}}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2},

(1.25)

\displaystyle{\bm{u}}_{i}

\displaystyle=\operatorname*{\text{arg max}}_{\left\{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}=1\mid{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{n},\,{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\perp{\bm{u}}_{1},\ldots,{\bm{u}}_{i-1}\right\}}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2},\qquad 2\leq i\leq n.

(1.26)

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Consider a unit vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
(i.e.,
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}=1
) that is orthogonal to
{\bm{v}}_{1},\ldots,{\bm{v}}_{i-1}
, where
1\leq i\leq p
(if
i=1
then
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is arbitrary among unit vectors).
We expand
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
in the basis of right singular vectors of
{\bm{X}}
:

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\sum_{j=i}^{p}\gamma_{j}{\bm{v}}_{j}
,
where
1=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\sum_{j=i}^{p}\gamma_{j}^{2}
.
By the ordering of the singular values in Theorem
,

\displaystyle\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle=\left\langle\sum_{k=1}^{p}\sigma_{k}\left\langle{\bm{v}}_{k},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle{\bm{u}}_{k},\sum_{k=1}^{p}\sigma_{k}\left\langle{\bm{v}}_{k},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle{\bm{u}}_{k}\right\rangle=\sum_{k=1}^{p}\sigma_{k}^{2}\left\langle{\bm{v}}_{k},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle^{2}

\displaystyle=\sum_{k=1}^{p}\sigma_{k}^{2}\left\langle{\bm{v}}_{k},\sum_{j=i}^{p}\gamma_{j}{\bm{v}}_{j}\right\rangle^{2}=\sum_{j=i}^{p}\sigma_{j}^{2}\gamma_{j}^{2}\leq\sigma_{i}^{2}\sum_{j=i}^{p}\gamma_{j}^{2}=\sigma_{i}^{2}.

This establishes (
1.19
) and (
1.21
). To verify (
1.23
) and (
1.24
), observe that
{\bm{v}}_{i}
achieves this upper bound:

\displaystyle\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\bm{v}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle=\sum_{k=1}^{p}\sigma_{k}^{2}\left\langle{\bm{v}}_{k},{\bm{v}}_{i}\right\rangle^{2}=\sigma_{i}^{2}.

Applying the same reasoning to
{\bm{X}}^{\top}
yields (
1.20
), (
1.22
), (
1.25
), and (
1.26
).

From the proof above, it also follows that the largest and smallest singular values of a matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
(assuming
p\leq n
) satisfy

\displaystyle\sigma_{\max}({\bm{X}})

\displaystyle=\sigma_{1}({\bm{X}})=\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}=\max_{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}=1}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2};

(1.27)

\displaystyle\sigma_{\min}({\bm{X}})

\displaystyle=\sigma_{p}({\bm{X}})=\min_{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}=1}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}.

(1.28)

This shows that

\sigma_{\min}({\bm{X}})\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\sigma_{\max}({\bm{X}})\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2},\quad\text{for any }{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}.

(1.29)

For the purposes of this book, the following observation is especially useful.

{theoremHigh}
[Singular value bounds under near-orthogonality]
Let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
with
n\geq p
.
Suppose that for some
\delta\in[0,1]
,

\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}-{\bm{I}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\delta.

(1.30)

Then the largest and smallest singular value of
{\bm{X}}
satisfy

\sigma_{\max}({\bm{X}})\leq\sqrt{1+\delta}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\sigma_{\min}({\bm{X}})\geq\sqrt{1-\delta}.

(1.31)

Conversely, if both inequalities in (
) hold, then (
) follows.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Recall that by (
), the eigenvalues of
{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}
are precisely the squared singular values of
{\bm{X}}
,
\lambda_{i}({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}})=\sigma_{i}^{2}({\bm{X}})
,
i=1,2,\ldots,p
.
Consequently, the eigenvalues of
{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}-{\bm{I}}
are given by
\sigma_{i}^{2}({\bm{X}})-1
.
By (
1.27
) and the assumption (
), we have

\max\{\sigma_{\max}^{2}({\bm{X}})-1,\,1-\sigma_{\min}^{2}({\bm{X}})\}=\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}-{\bm{I}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\delta.

This establishes the claim.

The extremal singular values—both the largest and the smallest—are 1-Lipschitz functions (see Definition
) with respect to the spectral norm and the Frobenius norm.
In other words, the difference between the extremal singular values of two matrices is bounded above by the distance between the matrices in either norm.

{theoremHigh}
[Lipschitz continuity of extremal singular values]
The smallest and largest singular values
\sigma_{\min},\sigma_{\max}
, satisfy for all matrices
{\bm{X}},{\bm{Y}}
of the same dimension,

\displaystyle\left\lvert\sigma_{\max}({\bm{X}})-\sigma_{\max}({\bm{Y}})\right\rvert

\displaystyle\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}-{\bm{Y}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}-{\bm{Y}}\right\rVert_{F};

(1.32)

\displaystyle\left\lvert\sigma_{\min}({\bm{X}})-\sigma_{\min}({\bm{Y}})\right\rvert

\displaystyle\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}-{\bm{Y}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}-{\bm{Y}}\right\rVert_{F}.

(1.33)

Proof
[of Theorem
]
By the identification of the largest singular value with the operator norm we have

\left\lvert\sigma_{\max}({\bm{X}})-\sigma_{\max}({\bm{Y}})\right\rvert=\big\lvert\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}-\left\lVert{\bm{Y}}\right\rVert_{2}\big\rvert\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}-{\bm{Y}}\right\rVert_{2}.

By (
1.28
), for the smallest singular value, we have

\displaystyle\sigma_{\min}({\bm{X}})

\displaystyle=\min_{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}=1}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\min_{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}=1}\left(\left\lVert{\bm{Y}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}+\left\lVert({\bm{X}}-{\bm{Y}}){\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}\right)

\displaystyle\leq\min_{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}=1}\left(\left\lVert{\bm{Y}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}+\left\lVert{\bm{X}}-{\bm{Y}}\right\rVert_{2}\right)=\sigma_{\min}({\bm{Y}})+\left\lVert{\bm{X}}-{\bm{Y}}\right\rVert_{2}.

Therefore,
\sigma_{\min}({\bm{X}})-\sigma_{\min}({\bm{Y}})\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}-{\bm{Y}}\right\rVert_{2}
and (
1.33
) follows by symmetry.
Finally, the inequalities involving the Frobenius norm follow from the standard relation
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{2}\leq\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{F}
(see Remark
).

1.2.5
Pseudo-Inverse

For a matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
, we can define its
pseudo-inverse
, denoted by
{\bm{X}}^{+}
, which is a
p\times n
matrix.
Intuitively, when
{\bm{X}}
multiplies a vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
that lies in its row space (i.e.,
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}^{\top})
), the result
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
lies in the column space of
{\bm{X}}
.
Both of these spaces have the same dimension
r
, namely the rank of
{\bm{X}}
.
When restricted to these subspaces,
{\bm{X}}
behaves like an invertible linear transformation, and
{\bm{X}}^{+}
acts as its inverse.
More precisely:

If
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
belongs to the row space of
{\bm{X}}
, then
{\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.

If
{\bm{y}}
belongs to the column space of
{\bm{X}}
, then
{\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{y}}={\bm{y}}
(see Figure
).

The null space of
{\bm{X}}^{+}
coincides with the null space of
{\bm{X}}^{\top}
.
It consists of the vectors
{\bm{y}}\in\real^{n}
such that
{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{y}}=\boldsymbol{0}
.
Those vectors
{\bm{y}}
are orthogonal to every vector in the column space of
{\bm{X}}
, i.e., to every vector of the form
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.
We delay the proof of this property in Theorem
.

More formally, the
pseudo-inverse
, also known as the
Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse
,
{\bm{X}}^{+}
, is defined by the
unique
(see Proposition
)
p\times n
matrix satisfying the following four conditions, commonly called the
Penrose conditions

(
Penrose 1955
)
:

\boxed{\begin{aligned} &(C1)\qquad{\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{X}}&=&{\bm{X}}\qquad&\\
&(C2)\qquad{\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{+}&=&{\bm{X}}^{+}\qquad&\\
&(C3)\qquad({\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{+})^{\top}&=&{\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{+}\qquad&(\text{${\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{+}$ is symmetric})\\
&(C4)\qquad({\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{X}})^{\top}&=&{\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{X}}\qquad&(\text{${\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{+}$ is symmetric})\\
\end{aligned}}

(1.34)

Conditions
(C1)
and
(C2)
imply that
{\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{+}
and
{\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{X}}
are idempotent matrices, and hence they are projection matrices (see Definition
).
Conditions
(C3)
and
(C4)
further ensure that these projection matrices are symmetric, which means they are not merely oblique projections but orthogonal projection matrices (see Exercise
).

The existence and the uniqueness of the pseudo-inverse for any matrix follows from its rank decomposition.

Proposition 37
(Existence and uniqueness of pseudo-inverse).

Every matrix
{\bm{X}}
has a unique pseudo-inverse.

Proof
[of Proposition
]

Existence.

Let
{\bm{X}}={\bm{W}}{\bm{Z}}\in\real^{n\times p}
be a rank decomposition of
{\bm{X}}
, where
{\bm{W}}\in\real^{n\times r}
and
{\bm{Z}}\in\real^{r\times p}
both have full rank.
Define

{\bm{X}}^{+}={\bm{Z}}^{+}{\bm{W}}^{+}={\bm{Z}}^{\top}({\bm{Z}}{\bm{Z}}^{\top})^{-1}({\bm{W}}^{\top}{\bm{W}})^{-1}{\bm{W}}^{\top},

where
{\bm{Z}}^{+}={\bm{Z}}^{\top}({\bm{Z}}{\bm{Z}}^{\top})^{-1}
and
{\bm{W}}^{+}=({\bm{W}}^{\top}{\bm{W}})^{-1}{\bm{W}}^{\top}
. Notably,
{\bm{Z}}{\bm{Z}}^{\top}
and
{\bm{W}}^{\top}{\bm{W}}
are invertible since
{\bm{W}}\in\real^{n\times r}
and
{\bm{Z}}\in\real^{r\times p}
have full rank
r
.

We now verify that
{\bm{X}}^{+}
satisfies the four Penrose conditions:

\displaystyle(C1)\qquad{\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{X}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle{\displaystyle\bm{W}}{\bm{Z}}\left({\bm{Z}}^{\top}({\bm{Z}}{\bm{Z}}^{\top})^{-1}({\bm{W}}^{\top}{\bm{W}})^{-1}{\bm{W}}^{\top}\right){\bm{W}}{\bm{Z}}={\bm{W}}{\bm{Z}}={\bm{X}},

\displaystyle(C2)\qquad{\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{+}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\left({\bm{Z}}^{\top}({\bm{Z}}{\bm{Z}}^{\top})^{-1}({\bm{W}}^{\top}{\bm{W}})^{-1}{\bm{W}}^{\top}\right){\bm{W}}{\bm{Z}}\left({\bm{Z}}^{\top}({\bm{Z}}{\bm{Z}}^{\top})^{-1}({\bm{W}}^{\top}{\bm{W}})^{-1}{\bm{W}}^{\top}\right)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle{\displaystyle\bm{Z}}^{\top}({\bm{Z}}{\bm{Z}}^{\top})^{-1}({\bm{W}}^{\top}{\bm{W}})^{-1}{\bm{W}}^{\top}={\bm{X}}^{+},

\displaystyle(C3)\qquad({\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{+})^{\top}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle{\displaystyle\bm{W}}({\bm{W}}^{\top}{\bm{W}})^{-1}({\bm{Z}}{\bm{Z}}^{\top})^{-1}{\bm{Z}}{\bm{Z}}^{\top}{\bm{W}}^{\top}={\bm{W}}({\bm{W}}^{\top}{\bm{W}})^{-1}{\bm{W}}^{\top}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle{\displaystyle\bm{W}}{\bm{Z}}{\bm{Z}}^{\top}({\bm{Z}}{\bm{Z}}^{\top})^{-1}({\bm{W}}^{\top}{\bm{W}})^{-1}{\bm{W}}^{\top}={\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{+},

\displaystyle(C4)\qquad({\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{X}})^{\top}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle{\displaystyle\bm{Z}}^{\top}{\bm{W}}^{\top}{\bm{W}}({\bm{W}}^{\top}{\bm{W}})^{-1}({\bm{Z}}{\bm{Z}}^{\top})^{-1}{\bm{Z}}={\bm{Z}}^{\top}({\bm{Z}}{\bm{Z}}^{\top})^{-1}{\bm{Z}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle{\displaystyle\bm{Z}}^{\top}({\bm{Z}}{\bm{Z}}^{\top})^{-1}({\bm{W}}^{\top}{\bm{W}})^{-1}{\bm{W}}^{\top}{\bm{W}}{\bm{Z}}={\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{X}}.

This shows the existence of the pseudo-inverse.

Uniqueness.

Suppose
{\bm{X}}_{1}^{+}
and
{\bm{X}}_{2}^{+}
are two matrices satisfying the four Penrose conditions for
{\bm{X}}
. We will show that
{\bm{X}}_{1}^{+}={\bm{X}}_{2}^{+}
.
Starting from
{\bm{X}}_{1}^{+}
and repeatedly applying the Penrose conditions, we obtain:

\displaystyle{\bm{X}}_{1}^{+}

\displaystyle={\bm{X}}_{1}^{+}{\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}_{1}^{+}={\bm{X}}_{1}^{+}({\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}_{2}^{+}{\bm{X}}){\bm{X}}_{1}^{+}={\bm{X}}_{1}^{+}({\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}_{2}^{+})({\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}_{1}^{+})\qquad

\displaystyle(\text{by $(C2),(C1)$})

\displaystyle={\bm{X}}_{1}^{+}({\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}_{2}^{+})^{\top}({\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}_{1}^{+})^{\top}={\bm{X}}_{1}^{+}{\bm{X}}_{2}^{+\top}{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{1}^{+\top}{\bm{X}}^{\top}\qquad

\displaystyle(\text{by $(C3)$})

\displaystyle={\bm{X}}_{1}^{+}{\bm{X}}_{2}^{+\top}({\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}_{1}^{+}{\bm{X}})^{\top}={\bm{X}}_{1}^{+}{\bm{X}}_{2}^{+\top}{\bm{X}}^{\top}\qquad

\displaystyle(\text{by $(C1)$})

\displaystyle={\bm{X}}_{1}^{+}({\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}_{2}^{+})^{\top}={\bm{X}}_{1}^{+}{\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}_{2}^{+}={\bm{X}}_{1}^{+}({\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}_{2}^{+}{\bm{X}}){\bm{X}}_{2}^{+}\qquad

\displaystyle(\text{by $(C3),(C1)$})

\displaystyle=({\bm{X}}_{1}^{+}{\bm{X}})({\bm{X}}_{2}^{+}{\bm{X}}){\bm{X}}_{2}^{+}=({\bm{X}}_{1}^{+}{\bm{X}})^{\top}({\bm{X}}_{2}^{+}{\bm{X}})^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{2}^{+}\qquad

\displaystyle(\text{by $(C4)$})

\displaystyle=({\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}_{1}^{+}{\bm{X}})^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{2}^{+\top}{\bm{X}}_{2}^{+}={\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{2}^{+\top}{\bm{X}}_{2}^{+}\qquad

\displaystyle(\text{by $(C1)$})

\displaystyle=({\bm{X}}_{2}^{+}{\bm{X}})^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{2}^{+}={\bm{X}}_{2}^{+}{\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}_{2}^{+}={\bm{X}}_{2}^{+}.\qquad

\displaystyle(\text{by $(C4),(C2)$})

Thus,
{\bm{X}}_{1}^{+}={\bm{X}}_{2}^{+}
, proving that the pseudo-inverse is unique.

Lemma 38
(Property of pseudo-inverse).

For any matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
, it holds that

{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{+}={\bm{X}}^{\top}.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
By Condition
(C1)

{\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{X}}={\bm{X}}
, we have by taking the transpose of both sides:

({\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{X}})^{\top}={\bm{X}}^{\top}\qquad\implies\qquad{\bm{X}}^{\top}({\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{+})^{\top}={\bm{X}}^{\top}.

Substituting the Condition
(C3)

({\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{+})^{\top}={\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{+}
into the equation above, we get

{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{+}={\bm{X}}^{\top}.

This completes the proof.

The equality
{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{+}={\bm{X}}^{\top}
encodes the idea that applying
{\bm{X}}^{+}
to
{\bm{X}}
does not distort the action of
{\bm{X}}^{\top}
on vectors.

We have shown the four fundamental subspaces associated with the SVD of a matrix in Theorem
.
Similarly, we now describe the four fundamental subspaces associated with the pseudo-inverse.

{theoremHigh}
[Four subspaces in pseudo-inverse]
Let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
be any matrix, and let
{\bm{X}}^{+}
denote its pseudo-inverse.
Then the following relationships hold:

The column space of
{\bm{X}}^{+}
is the same as the row space of
{\bm{X}}
;

The row space of
{\bm{X}}^{+}
is the same as the column space of
{\bm{X}}
;

The null space of
{\bm{X}}^{+}
is the same as the null space of
{\bm{X}}^{\top}
;

The null space of
{\bm{X}}^{+\top}
is the same as the null space of
{\bm{X}}
.

These relationships among the four fundamental subspaces are illustrated in Figure
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Following arguments similar to those in the proof of Lemma
, we can show that

\displaystyle\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{+})

\displaystyle=\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}})\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{X}})=\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})

\displaystyle\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{X}})

\displaystyle=\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}^{+})\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{+})=\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}}^{+}).

Additionally, from Conditions
(C3)
and
(C4)
in the definition of pseudo-inverses, we know that:

({\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{X}})^{\top}={\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{X}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad({\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{+})^{\top}={\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{+}.

Using the fundamental theorem of linear algebra (see the discussion preceding Lemma
), we realize that
\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{+})
is the orthogonal complement to
\mathcal{N}(({\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{+})^{\top})
, and
\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{X}})
is the orthogonal complement to
\mathcal{N}(({\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{X}})^{\top})
:

\displaystyle\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{+})\perp\mathcal{N}(({\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{+})^{\top})

\displaystyle\underrightarrow{\text{leads to}}\qquad\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{+})\perp\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{+})

\displaystyle\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{X}})\perp\mathcal{N}(({\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{X}})^{\top})

\displaystyle\underrightarrow{\text{leads to}}\qquad\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{X}})\perp\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{X}}).

This implies

\displaystyle\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}})\perp\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}}^{+})\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}^{+})\perp\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}}).

That is,
\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}}^{+})=\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}}^{\top})
and
\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}^{+})=\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}^{\top})
.
By the fundamental theorem of linear algebra again, this also implies:
\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}^{+\top})=\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}})
and
\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}}^{+\top})=\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
.

Figure 1.4:
Column space and row space of the pseudo-inverse
{\bm{X}}^{+}
.
{\bm{X}}
transfers from the row space to the column space.
{\bm{X}}^{+}
maps from the column space to the row space.

Pseudo-Inverse in SVD

Given the SVD of a matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
, we provide further discussion on its pseudo-inverse in different cases.
For the full SVD of
{\bm{X}}={\bm{U}}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}{\bm{V}}^{\top}
, we consider the following scenarios:

Case
n>p=r
.

Since the matrix
{\bm{X}}
has independent columns, the left-pseudo-inverse can be obtained by

\displaystyle\text{left-pseudo-inverse}

\displaystyle={\bm{X}}^{+}=({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}})^{-1}{\bm{X}}^{\top}=({\bm{V}}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{\top}{\bm{U}}^{\top}{\bm{U}}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}{\bm{V}}^{\top})^{-1}{\bm{V}}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{\top}{\bm{U}}^{\top}

(1.35)

\displaystyle={\bm{V}}({\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}})^{-1}{\bm{V}}^{\top}{\bm{V}}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{\top}{\bm{U}}^{\top}={\bm{V}}[({\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}})^{-1}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{\top}]{\bm{U}}^{\top}={\bm{V}}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{+}{\bm{U}}^{\top},

where the last equality holds because
{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{+}=({\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}})^{-1}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{\top}
.

Case
p>n=r
.

Since the matrix
{\bm{X}}
has independent rows, the right-pseudo-inverse can be obtained by

\displaystyle\text{right-pseudo-inverse}

\displaystyle={\bm{X}}^{+}={\bm{X}}^{\top}({\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{\top})^{-1}=({\bm{U}}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}{\bm{V}}^{\top})^{\top}[({\bm{U}}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}{\bm{V}}^{\top})({\bm{U}}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}{\bm{V}}^{\top})^{\top}]^{-1}

(1.36)

\displaystyle={\bm{V}}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{\top}{\bm{U}}^{\top}({\bm{U}}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}{\bm{V}}^{\top}{\bm{V}}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{\top}{\bm{U}}^{\top})^{-1}={\bm{V}}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{\top}{\bm{U}}^{\top}{\bm{U}}^{-\top}({\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{\top})^{-1}{\bm{U}}^{-1}

\displaystyle={\bm{V}}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{\top})^{-1}{\bm{U}}^{-1}={\bm{V}}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{+}{\bm{U}}^{\top},

where the last equality follows because
{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{+}={\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{\top})^{-1}
.

Case rank-deficient.

Even when
{\bm{X}}
is rank-deficient, the pseudo-inverse is still given by
{\bm{X}}^{+}={\bm{V}}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{+}{\bm{U}}^{\top}
,
where
{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{+}\in\real^{p\times n}
has the diagonal block
\mathrm{diag}(\frac{1}{\sigma_{1}},\frac{1}{\sigma_{2}},\ldots,\frac{1}{\sigma_{r}})
in its upper-left corner, and zeros elsewhere.
It is straightforward to verify that this definition satisfies the four Penrose conditions in (
).

In all cases,
{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{+}
is obtained by taking the reciprocal of each nonzero singular value in
{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}
.
Thus, the pseudo-inverse via SVD is summarized as:

{\bm{X}}^{+}={\bm{V}}\begin{bmatrix}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}_{1}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}{\bm{U}}^{\top},\quad\text{with }{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}=\begin{bmatrix}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{1}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}\text{ and }{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{1}\in\real^{r\times r}.

(1.37)

If
{\bm{X}}
is nonsingular, then
{\bm{X}}^{+}={\bm{X}}^{-1}
, so (
) is a generalization of the usual inverse.
The pseudo-inverse of a scalar is

\sigma^{+}=\begin{cases}1/\sigma,&\text{if }\sigma\neq 0;\\
0,&\text{if }\sigma=0.\end{cases}

This shows the important fact that the pseudo-inverse
{\bm{X}}^{+}
is not a continuous function of
{\bm{X}}
, unless we allow only perturbations that do not change the rank of
{\bm{X}}
. The pseudo-inverse has the property

{\bm{X}}^{+}=\lim_{\delta\to 0}({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}+\delta{\bm{I}})^{-1}{\bm{X}}^{\top}.

Using the SVD representation of pseudo-inverses in (
), we can derive additional properties of the pseudo-inverse of a matrix
{\bm{X}}
.

Lemma 39
(Properties of pseudo-inverse using SVD).

Let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
. The following properties of the pseudo-inverse follow from (
):

1.

{\bm{X}}^{+}=({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}})^{+}{\bm{X}}^{\top}={\bm{X}}^{\top}({\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{\top})^{+}
.

2.

When
\mathrm{rank}({\bm{X}})=p
, this becomes
{\bm{X}}^{+}=({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}})^{-1}{\bm{X}}^{\top},\ ({\bm{X}}^{\top})^{+}={\bm{X}}({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}})^{-1}
.

3.

({\bm{X}}^{+})^{+}={\bm{X}}
.

4.

(\alpha{\bm{X}})^{+}=\alpha^{+}{\bm{X}}^{+}
.

5.

({\bm{X}}^{+})^{\top}=({\bm{X}}^{\top})^{+}
.

6.

({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}})^{+}={\bm{X}}^{+}({\bm{X}}^{\top})^{+}
.

7.

{\bm{X}}
,
{\bm{X}}^{\top}
,
{\bm{X}}^{+}
, and
{\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{X}}
all have the same rank, which equals
\mathrm{tr}({\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{X}})
.

8.

If
{\bm{U}}
and
{\bm{V}}
are orthogonal, then
({\bm{U}}{\bm{X}}{\bm{V}}^{\top})^{+}={\bm{V}}{\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{U}}^{\top}
.

9.

If
{\bm{X}}=\sum_{i}{\bm{X}}_{i}
, where
{\bm{X}}_{i}{\bm{X}}_{j}^{\top}=\boldsymbol{0}
,
{\bm{X}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{j}=\boldsymbol{0}
,
i\neq j
, then
{\bm{X}}^{+}=\sum_{i}{\bm{X}}_{i}^{+}
.

10.

If
{\bm{X}}
is normal (
{\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{\top}={\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}
), then
{\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{X}}={\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{+}
and
({\bm{X}}^{n})^{+}=({\bm{X}}^{+})^{n}
.

It is important to note that, unlike the standard matrix inverse, the pseudo-inverse does not generally satisfy
{\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{+}={\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{X}}
or
({\bm{X}}{\bm{Y}})^{+}={\bm{Y}}^{+}{\bm{X}}^{+}
.
For example, let
{\bm{X}}=\footnotesize[1,0]
and
{\bm{Y}}=[1,1]^{\top}
. Then
{\bm{X}}{\bm{Y}}=1
, but

{\bm{Y}}^{+}{\bm{X}}^{+}=\frac{1}{2}[1,1]\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}1\\
0\end{bmatrix}\normalsize=\frac{1}{2}.

Necessary and sufficient conditions for the identity
({\bm{X}}{\bm{Y}})^{+}={\bm{Y}}^{+}{\bm{X}}^{+}
to hold were established by
Greville 1966
. The following theorem provides an important sufficient condition under which this equality is valid.

Proposition 40
(Sufficient condition for
({\bm{X}}{\bm{Y}})^{+}={\bm{Y}}^{+}{\bm{X}}^{+}
).

If
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
,
{\bm{Y}}\in\real^{p\times m}
, and
\mathrm{rank}({\bm{X}})=\mathrm{rank}({\bm{Y}})=p
,
then

({\bm{X}}{\bm{Y}})^{+}={\bm{Y}}^{+}{\bm{X}}^{+}={\bm{Y}}^{\top}({\bm{Y}}{\bm{Y}}^{\top})^{-1}({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}})^{-1}{\bm{X}}^{\top}.

Proof
[of Proposition
]
The last equality follows from Lemma
.
. The first equality follows from the proof of Proposition
and is verified by showing that the four Penrose conditions are satisfied.

1.2.6
Famous Inequalities

In this section, we introduce several classical inequalities that will be used frequently throughout the text.
The
Cauchy–Schwarz inequality
is considered one of the most important and widely used inequalities in mathematics.

{theoremHigh}

[Cauchy–Schwarz matrix (vector) inequality]
For any matrices
{\bm{X}},{\bm{Y}}\in\real^{n\times p}
, the following inequality holds:

\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{Y}}\right\rVert_{F}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{F}\cdot\left\lVert{\bm{Y}}\right\rVert_{F}.

This is a direct consequence of the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality applied to the Frobenius inner product
\left\langle{\bm{X}},{\bm{Y}}\right\rangle=\mathrm{tr}{({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{Y}})}
.

Similarly, for any vectors
{\bm{u}},{\bm{v}}\in\real^{n}
, we have

\left\lvert{\bm{u}}^{\top}{\bm{v}}\right\rvert\leq\left\lVert{\bm{u}}\right\rVert_{2}\cdot\left\lVert{\bm{v}}\right\rVert_{2}.

(1.38)

In two dimensions, this becomes the familiar algebraic identity:

(ac+bd)^{2}\leq(a^{2}+b^{2})(c^{2}+d^{2}).

The vector form of the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality plays a crucial role in various branches of modern mathematics, including Hilbert space theory and numerical analysis
(
Wu and Wu 2009
)
.
For completeness, we present a simple proof of the vector case.
Let
{\bm{u}},{\bm{v}}\in\real^{n}
.
Consider the nonnegative sum

\displaystyle 0\leq\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}(u_{i}v_{j}-u_{j}v_{i})^{2}

\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}u_{i}^{2}v_{j}^{2}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}v_{i}^{2}u_{j}^{2}-2\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}u_{i}u_{j}v_{i}v_{j}

\displaystyle=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}u_{i}^{2}\right)\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}v_{j}^{2}\right)+\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}v_{i}^{2}\right)\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}u_{j}^{2}\right)-2\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}u_{i}v_{i}\right)^{2}

\displaystyle=2\left\lVert{\bm{u}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\cdot\left\lVert{\bm{v}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-2\left\lVert{\bm{u}}^{\top}{\bm{v}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},

from which the result follows.
The equality holds if and only if
{\bm{u}}=\eta{\bm{v}}
for some constant
\eta\in\real
, i.e.,
{\bm{u}}
and
{\bm{v}}
are linearly dependent.

Hölder’s inequality, named after
Otto Hölder
, is another cornerstone result with broad applications in optimization, machine learning, probability, and functional analysis. It generalizes the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality (which corresponds to the special case
s=t=2
).

{theoremHigh}

[Hölder’s inequality]
Let
s,t>1
satisfy
\frac{1}{s}+\frac{1}{t}=1
. Then for any vector
{\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}\in\real^{n}
, we have

\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}y_{i}\leq\left\lvert\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}y_{i}\right\rvert\leq\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left\lvert x_{i}\right\rvert\left\lvert y_{i}\right\rvert\leq\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left\lvert x_{i}\right\rvert^{s}\right)^{1/s}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left\lvert y_{i}\right\rvert^{t}\right)^{1/t}=\left\lVert{\bm{x}}\right\rVert_{s}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{t},

where
\left\lVert{\bm{x}}\right\rVert_{s}=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left\lvert x_{i}\right\rvert^{s}\right)^{1/s}
denotes the
\ell_{s}
-norm
of
{\bm{x}}
.
The equality holds if the two sequences
\{\left\lvert x_{i}\right\rvert^{s}\}
and
\{\left\lvert y_{i}\right\rvert^{t}\}
are linearly dependent .
When
s=t=2
, this reduces to the vector Cauchy–Schwarz inequality (
).

Proof

See
Lu 2021a
for a proof.

1.3
Probability Theory and Common Probability Distributions

A
random variable
is a variable that takes on different values according to some underlying randomness, used to model uncertain outcomes or events.
We denote the random variable itself using a lowercase letter in
normal (non-italic) font
, and its possible realizations (observed or potential values) using lowercase letters in
italic font
.
For instance,
y_{1}
and
y_{2}
are possible values (realizations) of the random variable
y
.
For vector-valued random variables, we use
boldface normal
notation: the random vector is written as
{\mathbf{y}}
, and a specific realization is denoted by
{\bm{y}}
in
italic
bold—though to avoid confusion, it’s common to distinguish them typographically.
In this text, we adopt the convention that the random vector is
{\mathbf{y}}
(normal bold), and a realization is
{\bm{y}}
(italic bold).
Similarly, for matrix-valued random variables, we denote the random matrix as
{\mathbf{Y}}
(upright bold) and a particular realization as
{\bm{Y}}
(italic bold).

However, a random variable alone only describes the set of possible outcomes—it must be paired with a probability distribution that specifies how likely each outcome is.
In probability theory, the outcome
x
of a random phenomenon is modeled as a random variable, and the phenomenon itself is described by its
cumulative distribution function (c.d.f., CDF)
, defined as:

F(x)\equiv\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}\leq x].

Now suppose the phenomenon has a characteristic
{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
that influences the probabilities of the outcomes of
x
. Such a characteristic is called a
parameter
. Because the probability of the event
\{{\textnormal{x}}\leq x\}
depends on
{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
, the CDF must also depend on
{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
. We therefore write:

F(x;{\boldsymbol{\theta}})\equiv{\Pr}_{{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}[{\textnormal{x}}\leq x].

In probability theory, if both the functional form
F(x;{\boldsymbol{\theta}})
and the true value of
{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
are known, then for any possible outcome
x
, we can compute the probability:
\Pr_{{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}[{\textnormal{x}}\leq x]=F(x;{\boldsymbol{\theta}})
.

A useful result in probability theory is the union bound, which provides an upper bound on the probability of the union of a collection of events.

{theoremHigh}
[Union bound]
Let
{\mathbb{A}}_{1},{\mathbb{A}}_{2},\dots,{\mathbb{A}}_{n}
be a collection of events in a probability space. Then

\Pr\left(\cup_{i}{\mathbb{A}}_{i}\right)\leq\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Pr({\mathbb{A}}_{i}).

Proof
[of Theorem
]
For each
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}
, refine the set

\widetilde{{\mathbb{A}}}_{i}\triangleq{\mathbb{A}}_{i}\cap\bigcap_{j=1}^{i-1}{\mathbb{A}}_{j}^{c}

It is straightforward to show that
\bigcup_{j=1}^{k}\widetilde{{\mathbb{A}}}_{j}=\bigcup_{j=1}^{k}{\mathbb{A}}_{j}
for any
k
by induction, so
\bigcup_{i}{\mathbb{A}}_{i}=\bigcup_{i}\widetilde{{\mathbb{A}}}_{i}
.
By construction, the sets
\widetilde{{\mathbb{A}}}_{1},\widetilde{{\mathbb{A}}}_{2},\dots
are pairwise disjoint, so

\displaystyle\Pr\left(\bigcup_{i}{\mathbb{A}}_{i}\right)=\Pr\left(\bigcup_{i}\widetilde{{\mathbb{A}}}_{i}\right)=\sum_{i}\Pr\left(\widetilde{{\mathbb{A}}}_{i}\right)\leq\sum_{i}\Pr({\mathbb{A}}_{i})

where the last inequality follows because
\widetilde{{\mathbb{A}}}_{i}\subseteq{\mathbb{A}}_{i}
.

\paragrapharrow

Discrete random variables.
Random variables can be either discrete or continuous. A
discrete random variable
takes on a finite or countably infinite number of distinct states.
These states need not be numerical; they may be symbolic or categorical states without numerical values (e.g., “red,” “blue,” “success,” “failure”).
In contrast, a
continuous random variable
takes values in an uncountable set, typically a subset of the real numbers.

A probability distribution describes how probability is assigned to the possible outcomes of one or more random variables. The way we represent this distribution depends on whether the variables are discrete or continuous.

For discrete random variables, we use a
probability mass function (p.m.f., PMF)
, often denoted by a capital
\Pr
(or sometimes
f
).
The PMF maps each possible state of the random variable to the probability that the variable assumes that state. For example, the notation

\Pr({\textnormal{y}}=y)\quad(\text{or equivalently }\Pr(y),\;f_{{\textnormal{y}}}(y),\;\text{Pr}_{{\textnormal{y}}}(y))

represents the probability that the random variable
y
equals the value
y
.
By definition, probabilities lie in
[0,1]
, where 1 indicates certainty and 0 indicates impossibility.
An alternative and common convention is to first define a random variable and then specify its distribution using the “
\sim
” symbol:

{\textnormal{y}}\sim\Pr({\textnormal{y}}).

PMFs can also be defined over multiple random variables simultaneously. This is called a
joint probability mass distribution functions
or
joint frequency functions
.
For instance,
\Pr({\textnormal{x}}=x,{\textnormal{y}}=y)
denotes the probability that
x=x
and
y=y
occur together.
We often use shorthand notations such as
\Pr(x,y)
or
\Pr_{{\textnormal{x}},{\textnormal{y}}}(x,y)
.
Moreover, if the PMF depends on some known parameters
{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
, we may write it as
\Pr(x,y\mid{\boldsymbol{\theta}})
(or
\Pr_{{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}(x,y)
,
f(x,y;{\boldsymbol{\theta}})
) for brevity.

In many applications, we are interested in the probability of one event given that another event has occurred. This is known as
conditional probability
.
The conditional probability that
{\textnormal{x}}=x
given
{\textnormal{y}}=y
is written as
\Pr({\textnormal{x}}=x\mid{\textnormal{y}}=y)
,
and is computed using the formula:

\Pr({\textnormal{x}}=x\mid{\textnormal{y}}=y)=\frac{\Pr({\textnormal{x}}=x,{\textnormal{y}}=y)}{\Pr({\textnormal{y}}=y)},

provided that
\Pr({\textnormal{y}}=y)>0
.
This relationship is fundamental to
Bayes’ theorem

(
Bayes 1958
)
.

Conversely, when the joint distribution over a set of variables is known, we may wish to find the distribution over a subset of those variables. This is called the
marginal probability mass distribution
(or simply
marginal distribution
).
For example, if
x
and
y
are discrete random variables with known joint PMF
\Pr({\textnormal{x}},{\textnormal{y}})
, the marginal distribution of
x
is obtained by summing over all possible values of
y
:

\Pr({\textnormal{x}}=x)=\sum_{y}\Pr({\textnormal{x}}=x,{\textnormal{y}}=y).

\paragrapharrow

Continuous random variables.

When working with continuous random variables, we describe probability distributions using a
probability density function (p.d.f., PDF)
instead of a probability mass function (PMF).
For a function
p
to qualify as a valid PDF, it must satisfy the following properties:

The domain of
p
must be the set of all possible values (or states) of the random variable
y
.

Unlike a PMF, the PDF is not required to satisfy
p(y)\leq 1
. However, it must be nonnegative everywhere:
\forall\,y\in{\textnormal{y}},p(y)\geq 0
.

It must integrate to 1 over its entire domain:
\int p(y)dy=1
.

Importantly, the value
p(y)
(also denoted as
f_{{\textnormal{y}}}(y)
or
p_{{\textnormal{y}}}(y)
) does not represent a probability. Instead, it describes a density. The probability that the random variable falls within an infinitesimally small interval around y of width
\delta y
is approximately
p(y)\delta y
.
More formally, for any measurable set
{\mathbb{A}}
, the probability that
y\in{\mathbb{A}}
is given by

\Pr(y\in{\mathbb{A}})=\int_{{\mathbb{A}}}p(y)dy.

If the PDF depends on known parameters
{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
, it is commonly written as

p(x\mid{\boldsymbol{\theta}}),\quad f_{{\textnormal{x}}}(x;{\boldsymbol{\theta}}),\quad\text{or simply }\;f(x;{\boldsymbol{\theta}}).

where the semicolon or vertical bar indicates dependence on the parameter(s).

\paragrapharrow

Distribution function.
On the other hand, any probability distribution can also be characterized by its cumulative distribution function (c.d.f., CDF).
Let
x
be a random variable with CDF defined as
F(x)=\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}\leq x]
, where
F(x)
is nondecreasing, right-continuous, and satisfies

0\leq F(x)\leq 1,\qquad\lim_{x\rightarrow-\infty}F(x)=0,\qquad\text{and}\qquad\lim_{x\rightarrow\infty}F(x)=1.

The
expected value (mean)

\mu
and
variance

\omega^{2}
of
x
in the continuous case are defined as

\mu=\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}xdF(x),\qquad\omega^{2}=\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{x}}]=\mathbb{E}[({\textnormal{x}}-\mu)^{2}]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}(x-\mu)^{2}dF(x).

(1.39a)

Similarly, in the discrete case, where
\Pr({\textnormal{x}}=x)
denotes the probability mass function, they are defined as

\mu=\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]=\sum_{x}x\Pr(x),\qquad\omega^{2}=\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{x}}]=\mathbb{E}[({\textnormal{x}}-\mu)^{2}]=\sum_{x}(x-\mu)^{2}\Pr(x).

(1.39b)

It is straightforward to verify the useful identity:

\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{x}}]=\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}^{2}]-(\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}])^{2}.

(1.39c)

The
median
of a random variable
x
is any number
M
satisfying

\Pr({\textnormal{x}}\geq M)\geq\frac{1}{2}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\Pr({\textnormal{x}}\leq M)\geq\frac{1}{2}.

(1.39d)

Exercise
\thetheo
(Uniform distribution)

Let
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\text{Uniform}(x\mid a,b)
be a uniform distributed variable such that
f_{{\textnormal{x}}}(x)=\frac{1}{b-a}
if
a\leq x\leq b
and
f_{{\textnormal{x}}}(x)=0
otherwise. Show that

\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]=\frac{a+b}{2}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{x}}]=\frac{(b-a)^{2}}{12}.

Now consider a random vector
{\mathbf{x}}=[{\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2}\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{n}]^{\top}
.
Its
joint probability distribution function
(or simply called the probability distribution function)—denoted as
F_{{\mathbf{x}}}({\bm{x}})
,
F(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n})
, or
F({\bm{x}})
—is defined as

F_{{\mathbf{x}}}(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n})=\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}_{1}\leq x_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2},\leq x_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{n}\leq x_{n}].

Depending on whether the components are discrete or continuous, we characterize the joint distribution as follows:

When all the variables are discrete, as discussed above, the joint probability mass function or the joint frequency function can be characterized as

f_{{\mathbf{x}}}(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n})=\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}_{1}=x_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2}=x_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{n}=x_{n}].

On the contrary, if the variables are continuous, the
joint probability density function
is a function
f_{{\mathbf{x}}}:\real^{n}\rightarrow[0,\infty)
(or simply
f({\bm{x}})
,
p_{{\mathbf{x}}}({\bm{x}})
,
p({\bm{x}})
) such that

F_{{\mathbf{x}}}(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n})=\int_{-\infty}^{x_{1}}\ldots\int_{-\infty}^{x_{n}}f_{{\mathbf{x}}}(y_{1},y_{2},\ldots,y_{n})dy_{1}\ldots dy_{n}.

In this case, when
f_{{\mathbf{x}}}
is continuous at
{\bm{x}}=[x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n}]^{\top}
, we have

f_{{\mathbf{x}}}(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n})=\frac{\partial^{n}}{\partial x_{1}\partial x_{2}\ldots\partial x_{n}}F_{{\mathbf{x}}}(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n}).

The random variables are independent if and only if

\displaystyle F_{{\mathbf{x}}}(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n})

\displaystyle=F_{{\textnormal{x}}_{1}}(x_{1})\cdot F_{{\textnormal{x}}_{2}}(x_{2})\cdot\ldots\cdot F_{{\textnormal{x}}_{n}}(x_{n});

\displaystyle\text{or}\quad f_{{\mathbf{x}}}(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n})

\displaystyle=f_{{\textnormal{x}}_{1}}(x_{1})\cdot f_{{\textnormal{x}}_{2}}(x_{2})\cdot\ldots\cdot f_{{\textnormal{x}}_{n}}(x_{n}).

The
conditional or marginal probability density functions
for the continuous cases are analogous to those in the discrete case, except that integration is employed instead of summation. For example,
f_{{\textnormal{x}}}(x)=\int f_{{\textnormal{x}},{\textnormal{y}}}(x,y)dy
.

Specifically, the joint distribution of two random variables
{\textnormal{x}}_{i}
and
{\textnormal{x}}_{j}
is is given by the joint cumulative distribution function
F(x_{i},x_{j})\equiv\Pr[{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\leq x_{i},{\textnormal{x}}_{j}\leq x_{j}]
. Then the covariance between
{\textnormal{x}}_{i}
and
{\textnormal{x}}_{j}
, denoted
\omega_{ij}
, is defined as

\omega_{ij}\triangleq\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\textnormal{x}}_{i},{\textnormal{x}}_{j}]\triangleq\mathbb{E}[({\textnormal{x}}_{i}-\mu_{i})({\textnormal{x}}_{j}-\mu_{j})]=\int_{x_{i},x_{j}=-\infty}^{\infty}(x_{i}-\mu_{i})(x_{j}-\mu_{j})dF(x_{i},x_{j}),

where
\mu_{i}=\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{i}]

Equivalently,
\omega_{ij}=\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{i}{\textnormal{x}}_{j}]-\mu_{i}\mu_{j}
.
For a random vector
{\mathbf{x}}\in\real
, the covariance matrix
{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}\in\real^{n\times n}
is defined as

\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\mathbf{x}}]\triangleq{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}=\mathbb{E}[({\mathbf{x}}-{\boldsymbol{\mu}})({\mathbf{x}}-{\boldsymbol{\mu}})^{\top}]=\mathbb{E}({\mathbf{x}}{\mathbf{x}}^{\top})-{\boldsymbol{\mu}}{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{\top},

(1.40)

where
{\boldsymbol{\mu}}=\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{x}}]=[\mu_{1},\mu_{2},\ldots,\mu_{n}]^{\top}
.

The variance of two random variables quantifies the degree of linear dependence between the two.
A closely related measure is the
correlation
, defined as

\mathbb{C}\mathrm{orr}[{\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2}]\triangleq\frac{\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2}]}{\sqrt{\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{x}}_{1}]\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{x}}_{2}]}}.

(1.41)

While covariance and correlation both capture linear dependence, correlation is scale-invariant and always lies in the interval
[-1,1]
.
It also holds that

\left\lvert\mathbb{C}\mathrm{orr}[{\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2}]\right\rvert\leq\sqrt{\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{x}}_{1}]\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{x}}_{2}]}.

(1.42)

Lemma 41
(Linear transformation).

Let
{\mathbf{y}}={\bm{A}}{\mathbf{x}}+{\bm{b}}
, where
{\bm{A}}\in\real^{m\times n}
and
{\bm{b}}\in\real^{m}
are deterministic, and let
{\mathbf{x}}\in\real^{n}
be a random vector with mean
\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{x}}]={\boldsymbol{\mu}}\in\real^{n}
and covariance
{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}\in\real^{n\times n}
.
Then

\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{y}}]={\bm{A}}{\boldsymbol{\mu}}+{\bm{b}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\mathbf{y}}]={\bm{A}}{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}{\bm{A}}^{\top}.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
The first identity follows from the linearity of expectation. For the second, observe that

\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\mathbf{y}}]=\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\bm{A}}{\mathbf{x}}]=\mathbb{E}[{\bm{A}}({\mathbf{x}}-{\boldsymbol{\mu}})({\mathbf{x}}-{\boldsymbol{\mu}})^{\top}{\bm{A}}^{\top}]={\bm{A}}\mathbb{E}[({\mathbf{x}}-{\boldsymbol{\mu}})({\mathbf{x}}-{\boldsymbol{\mu}})^{\top}]{\bm{A}}^{\top}={\bm{A}}{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}{\bm{A}}^{\top}.

This completes the proof.

In the special case when
{\bm{A}}={\bm{a}}^{\top}
is a row vector,
{\mathbf{y}}={\bm{a}}^{\top}{\mathbf{x}}
is a linear functional of
{\mathbf{x}}
. Then, if
\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\mathbf{x}}]=\sigma^{2}{\bm{I}}
,
\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\mathbf{y}}]=\sigma^{2}{\bm{a}}^{\top}{\bm{a}}
.

Lemma 42
(Quadratic transformation).

Let
{\bm{A}}\in\real^{n\times n}
be a symmetric matrix, and let
{\mathbf{x}}\in\real^{n}
be a random vector with mean
{\boldsymbol{\mu}}=[\mu_{i}]\in\real^{n}
and covariance
{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}=[\omega_{ij}]\in\real^{n\times n}
.
Then

\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{x}}^{\top}{\bm{A}}{\mathbf{x}}]={\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{\top}{\bm{A}}{\boldsymbol{\mu}}+\mathrm{tr}({\bm{A}}{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}),

where
\mathrm{tr}({\bm{A}}{\boldsymbol{\Omega}})
denotes the trace of
{\bm{A}}{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}
, i.e., sum of diagonal elements of the matrix.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Since
{\mathbf{x}}^{\top}{\bm{A}}{\mathbf{x}}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_{ij}{\textnormal{x}}_{i}{\textnormal{x}}_{j}
,
it follows that
\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{x}}^{\top}{\bm{A}}{\mathbf{x}}]=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_{ij}\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{i}{\textnormal{x}}_{j}]
.
Substitute the expectations
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{i}{\textnormal{x}}_{j}]=\mu_{i}\mu_{j}+\omega_{ij}
:

\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{x}}^{\top}{\bm{A}}{\mathbf{x}}]={\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_{ij}\mu_{i}\mu_{j}}+{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_{ij}\omega_{ij}}={\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{\top}{\bm{A}}{\boldsymbol{\mu}}+\mathrm{tr}({\bm{A}}{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}).

This completes the proof.

In many applications, we center the random vector so that
{\boldsymbol{\mu}}=\boldsymbol{0}
. In this case, the quadratic expectation simplifies to
\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{x}}^{\top}{\bm{A}}{\mathbf{x}}]=\mathrm{tr}({\bm{A}}{\boldsymbol{\Omega}})
.
If, further,
{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}=\sigma^{2}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}
, then
\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{x}}^{\top}{\bm{A}}{\mathbf{x}}]=\sigma^{2}\mathrm{tr}({\bm{A}}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}})
.
To obtain an unbiased estimator of
\sigma^{2}
, we can choose a matrix
{\bm{A}}
such that
\mathrm{tr}({\bm{A}}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}})=1
.

\paragrapharrow

Other moments.
The quantities
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}^{s}]
,
s>0
are called the
moments
of the random variable
x
, while
\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert^{s}]
are known as its
absolute moments
.
In particular, the mean
\mu=\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]
and the variance
\mathbb{E}[({\textnormal{x}}-\mathbb{E}{\textnormal{x}})^{2}]=\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}^{2}]-(\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}])^{2}
are special cases of moments of
x
.
For
1\leq s<\infty
,
(\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert^{s}])^{1/s}
defines a norm; in particular, the
triangle inequality
holds:

(\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}+{\textnormal{y}}\right\rvert^{s}])^{1/s}\leq(\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert^{s}])^{1/s}+(\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{y}}\right\rvert^{s}])^{1/s}\quad\text{for all }{\textnormal{x}},{\textnormal{y}}.

(1.43)

Similarly,
Hölder’s inequality
for random variables states that, for random variables
{\textnormal{x}},{\textnormal{y}}
on a common probability space, we have

\text{H\"{o}lder's inequality:}\qquad\left\lvert\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}{\textnormal{y}}]\right\rvert\leq\big(\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert^{s}]\big)^{1/s}\big(\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{y}}\right\rvert^{t}]\big)^{1/t},\quad\text{$s,t\geq 1$, $\frac{1}{s}+\frac{1}{t}=1$}.

(1.44a)

The special case
s=t=2
yields the
Cauchy–Schwarz inequality
for random variables:

\text{Cauchy--Schwarz inequality:}\qquad\left\lvert\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}{\textnormal{y}}]\right\rvert\leq\sqrt{\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert^{2}]\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{y}}\right\rvert^{2}]}.

(1.44b)

This extends naturally to random matrices.
For any random
n\times p
matrices
{\mathbf{X}}
and
{\mathbf{Y}}
, the Frobenius norm version of Cauchy–Schwarz reads

\text{Cauchy--Schwarz inequality:}\quad\mathbb{E}\left[\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}^{\top}{\mathbf{Y}}\right\rVert_{F}\right]\leq\mathbb{E}\left[\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}\right]^{1/2}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\lVert{\mathbf{Y}}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}\right]^{1/2},

(1.44c)

where the inner product is defined as
\left\langle{\mathbf{X}},{\mathbf{Y}}\right\rangle=\mathbb{E}\left[\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}^{\top}{\mathbf{Y}}\right\rVert_{F}\right]
.
Analogous matrix extensions also hold for Hölder’s inequality.
Since the constant (deterministic) random variable
1
has expectation
\mathbb{E}[1]=1
, Hölder’s inequality shows that

\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert^{a}]=\mathbb{E}[1\cdot\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert^{a}]\leq(\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert^{b}])^{a/b},\quad\text{for all $a>0,\frac{b}{a}\geq 1$}.

(1.44d)

Therefore,

\big(\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert^{s}]\big)^{1/s}\leq\big(\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert^{t}]\big)^{1/t},\quad\text{for all $0<s\leq t<\infty$}.

(1.44e)

Absolute moments can be expressed in terms of tail probabilities, as shown in the following lemma.

Lemma 43
(Absolute moments lemma).

For any random variable
x
and any
s>0
,

\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert^{s}]=s\int_{0}^{\infty}\Pr(\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert\geq\tau)\tau^{s-1}d\tau,\quad s>0.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Recall that the indicator function
\mathds{1}(\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert^{s}\geq x)
is the random variable that takes the value
1
on the event
\{\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert^{s}\geq x\}
and
0
otherwise.
Using Fubini’s theorem to interchange the order of integration, we compute:

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert^{s}]

\displaystyle=\int_{\Omega}\left\lvert x\right\rvert^{s}dF(x)=\int_{\Omega}\int_{0}^{\left\lvert x\right\rvert^{s}}1dydF(x)=\int_{\Omega}\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathds{1}(\left\lvert x\right\rvert^{s}\geq y)dydF(x)

\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{\Omega}\mathds{1}(\left\lvert x\right\rvert^{s}\geq y)dF(x)dy=\int_{0}^{\infty}\Pr(\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert^{s}\geq y)dy

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle y\triangleq\tau^{s}}}{{\mathrel{\rule[2.15277pt]{20.00003pt}{0.5pt}\hskip-20.00003pt\rule[-2.15277pt]{20.00003pt}{0.5pt}}}}s\int_{0}^{\infty}\Pr(\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert^{s}\geq\tau^{s})\tau^{s-1}d\tau=s\int_{0}^{\infty}\Pr(\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert\geq\tau)\tau^{s-1}d\tau,

where the last equality follows from a change of variables.
This completes the proof.

Exercise
\thetheo

Use Lemma
to show that the expectation of a random variable
x
satisfies

\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]=\int_{0}^{\infty}\Pr({\textnormal{x}}\geq\tau)d\tau-\int_{0}^{\infty}\Pr({\textnormal{x}}\leq-\tau)d\tau.

Hint: Express the random variable
x
as
{\textnormal{x}}={\textnormal{x}}\cdot\mathds{1}\big({\textnormal{x}}\in[0,\infty)\big)+{\textnormal{x}}\cdot\mathds{1}\big(-{\textnormal{x}}\in(0,\infty)\big)
.

\paragrapharrow

Moment generating function (MGF).
The function
\theta\mapsto\mathbb{E}[\exp(\theta{\textnormal{x}})]
is commonly referred to as the
Laplace transform
or the
moment generating function (MGF)
of the random variable
x
.
It is a powerful tool in probability theory and statistics, as it encodes information about the moments of a random variable (or random vector) and can simplify the analysis of sums of independent random variables.

Definition 44
(Moment generating function (MGF)).

Let
x
be a real-valued random variable.
The moment generating function (MGF) of
x
is defined as

\mathbb{M}_{\textnormal{x}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}\left[\exp(\theta{\textnormal{x}})\right]:\real\to\real\cup\{\infty\},\quad\theta\in\real

(1.45a)

Similarly, for a random vector
{\mathbf{x}}\in\real^{n}
, the MGF is defined by

\mathbb{M}_{\mathbf{x}}({\boldsymbol{\theta}})=\mathbb{E}\left[\exp({\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{\top}{\mathbf{x}})\right]:\real^{n}\to\real\cup\{\infty\},\quad{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\in\real^{n}.

(1.45b)

On the other hand, the cumulant generating function (CGF) of
x
is the logarithm of its MGF:

\mathbb{K}_{\textnormal{x}}(\theta)=\ln\mathbb{M}_{\textnormal{x}}(\theta).

(1.45c)

Below are some key properties of moment generating functions:

1.

Moments from MGF.
If the MGF exists in an open interval around zero, then all the moments of
x
exist and can be computed by differentiating the MGF and evaluating at
\theta=0
:

\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}^{k}]=\frac{d^{k}}{d\theta^{k}}\mathbb{M}_{\textnormal{x}}(0),

where
k
is a positive integer representing the order of the moment.

2.

Uniqueness.
If two random variables have the same MGF in an open interval containing zero, then they have the same distribution. That is, if
\mathbb{M}_{\textnormal{x}}(\theta)=\mathbb{M}_{\textnormal{y}}(\theta)
for all
\theta
in an open interval around zero, then the cumulative distribution functions (CDFs) of
x
and
y
are identical (
F_{\textnormal{x}}=F_{\textnormal{y}}
).

3.

Product of independent variables.
For independent random variables
x
and
y
, the MGF of their sum
{\textnormal{x}}+{\textnormal{y}}
is the product of their individual MGFs:

\mathbb{M}_{{\textnormal{x}}+{\textnormal{y}}}(\theta)=\mathbb{M}_{\textnormal{x}}(\theta)\mathbb{M}_{\textnormal{y}}(\theta),\quad\text{if ${\textnormal{x}}$ and ${\textnormal{y}}$ are independent.}

4.

On the other hand, the CGF has
additivity
for independent random variables

\mathbb{K}_{{\textnormal{x}}+{\textnormal{y}}}(\theta)=\mathbb{K}_{{\textnormal{x}}}(\theta)+\mathbb{K}_{{\textnormal{y}}}(\theta),\quad\text{if ${\textnormal{x}}$ and ${\textnormal{y}}$ are independent.}

This makes cumulants particularly useful in limit theorems and asymptotic analysis.
The CGF often simplifies the analysis of sums of independent random variables.

These properties make the moment generating function a valuable tool for analyzing sums of independent random variables, finding moments of distributions, and proving distributional equivalences. However, it should be noted that not all distributions have moment generating functions; for example, the Cauchy distribution does not have an MGF because its moments do not exist. In such cases, other tools like characteristic functions may be used instead.

1.3.1
Some Concentration Inequalities

Markov’s inequality and Chebyshev’s inequality are fundamental concentration inequalities in probability theory.
They provide upper bounds on the probability that a random variable deviates from its expected value, with Markov’s inequality applying to nonnegative variables and Chebyshev’s inequality extending this concept by considering the variance of any random variable.

To be more specific, the function
\tau\mapsto\Pr(\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert\geq\tau)
is called the
tail
(or
tail probability
) of
the random variable
x
.
Markov’s inequality offers a simple yet often useful way to bound this tail using expectations.

{theoremHigh}
[Markov’s inequality]
Let
x
be a
nonnegative
random variable. Then, given any
\tau>0
, we have

\Pr({\textnormal{x}}\geq\tau)\leq\frac{\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]}{\tau}.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Since
x
is nonnegative, we have the pointwise inequality
0\leq\tau\mathds{1}\{{\textnormal{x}}\geq\tau\}\leq{\textnormal{x}}
.
This implies
\mathbb{E}[\tau\mathds{1}\{{\textnormal{x}}\geq\tau\}]\leq\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]
. We also have

\mathbb{E}\left[\tau\mathds{1}\{{\textnormal{x}}\geq\tau\}\right]=\tau\mathbb{E}\left[\mathds{1}\{{\textnormal{x}}\geq\tau\}\right]=\tau\left(1\cdot\Pr({\textnormal{x}}\geq\tau)+0\cdot\Pr({\textnormal{x}}<\tau)\right)=\tau\cdot\Pr({\textnormal{x}}\geq\tau)\leq\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}].

This completes the proof.

Alternatively, let
f(x)
denote the probability density function for
x
. Then,

\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]=\int_{0}^{\infty}xf(x)\,dx\geq\int_{\tau}^{\infty}xf(x)\,dx\geq\int_{\tau}^{\infty}\tau f(x)\,dx=\tau\Pr({\textnormal{x}}\geq\tau),

from which the result follows.

Let
x
be an arbitrary random variable (not necessarily nonnegative).
By applying Markov’s inequality to the nonnegative random variable
\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert
, we obtain a tail bound for
x
:

\Pr(\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert\geq\tau)\leq\frac{\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert]}{\tau},\quad\text{for all }\tau>0.

(1.46a)

Similarly, for
\theta>0
, we obtain

\Pr({\textnormal{x}}\geq\tau)=\Pr\big(\exp(\theta{\textnormal{x}})\geq\exp(\theta\tau)\big)\leq\frac{\mathbb{E}[\exp(\theta{\textnormal{x}})]}{\exp(\theta\tau)},\quad\text{for all }\tau\in\real.

(1.46b)

An important consequence is the following generalized Markov-type bound: for any
s>0
,

\Pr(\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert\geq\tau)=\Pr(\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert^{s}\geq\tau^{s})\leq\tau^{-s}\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert^{s}],\quad\text{for all }t>0.

(1.46c)

The special case
s=2
yields
Chebyshev’s inequality
, provided the variance exists.

{theoremHigh}

[Chebyshev’s inequality]
Let
x
be a random variable with finite mean
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]<\infty
.
Then, for any
\tau>0
, we have

\Pr(\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}-\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]\right\rvert\geq\tau)\leq\frac{\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{x}}]}{\tau^{2}}.

This follows immediately by applying Markov’s inequality to the nonnegative random variable
{\textnormal{y}}\triangleq({\textnormal{x}}-\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}])^{2}
.

The
Chernoff method
leverages the moment generating function to derive exponentially decaying bounds on tail probabilities. The resulting inequalities are known as
Chernoff bounds
.

{theoremHigh}
[Chernoff bound]
Let
x
be a random variable. Then, given any
\theta>0

\Pr({\textnormal{x}}\geq\tau)\leq\min_{\theta>0}\left(\exp({-\theta\tau})\mathbb{M}_{\textnormal{x}}(\theta)\right).

This can be obtained by applying Markov’s inequality to
\exp(\theta{\textnormal{x}})
:
\Pr({\textnormal{x}}\geq\tau)=\Pr(\exp(\theta{\textnormal{x}})\geq\exp(\theta\tau))\leq\mathbb{M}_{\textnormal{x}}(\theta)\exp({-\theta\tau})
and taking the infimum.

A powerful extension of this idea is
Cramér’s theorem
, which provides exponential tail bounds for sums of independent random variables.

{theoremHigh}
[Cramér’s theorem
(
Cramér 1994
)
]
Let
{\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{n}
be a sequence of independent random variables, with cumulant generating functions
\mathbb{K}_{{\textnormal{x}}_{i}}
,
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}
. Then, for any
\tau>0
,

\Pr\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\geq\tau\right)\leq\exp\left(\min_{\theta>0}\left\{-\theta\tau+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{K}_{{\textnormal{x}}_{i}}(\theta)\right\}\right).

Proof
[of Theorem
]
We use the Chernoff method.
For any
\theta>0
, Markov’s inequality (Theorem
) and independence yield

\displaystyle\Pr\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\geq\tau\right)

\displaystyle=\Pr\left(\exp\left(\theta\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\right)\geq\exp(\theta\tau)\right)\leq\exp({-\theta\tau})\mathbb{E}\left[\exp\left(\theta\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\right)\right]

\displaystyle=\exp({-\theta\tau})\mathbb{E}\left[\prod_{i=1}^{n}\exp(\theta{\textnormal{x}}_{i})\right]=\exp({-\theta\tau})\prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}\left[\exp(\theta{\textnormal{x}}_{i})\right]

\displaystyle=\exp({-\theta\tau})\prod_{i=1}^{n}\exp(\mathbb{K}_{{\textnormal{x}}_{i}}(\theta))=\exp\left(-\theta\tau+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{K}_{{\textnormal{x}}_{i}}(\theta)\right).

Since this holds for every
\theta>0
, taking the infimum over
\theta>0
yields the desired bound.

Cramér’s theorem provides an exponential upper bound for the tail probability of the sum of independent random variables. In contrast, Hoeffding’s inequality gives a sharper bound when the summands are almost surely bounded—a common scenario in empirical process theory and learning theory.

Lemma 45
(Hoeffding’s lemma).

Let
x
be a real-valued random variable such that
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]=0
and
{\textnormal{x}}\in[a,b]
almost surely. Then for any
\theta\in\real

\mathbb{M}_{\textnormal{x}}(\theta)\equiv\mathbb{E}\big[\exp(\theta{\textnormal{x}})\big]\leq\exp\!\Big(\frac{\theta^{2}(b-a)^{2}}{8}\Big).

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Let
t\triangleq\theta(b-a)
and
{\textnormal{y}}\triangleq\frac{{\textnormal{x}}-a}{\,b-a\,}\in[0,1]
.
Then
{\textnormal{x}}=a+(b-a){\textnormal{y}}
and
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{y}}]=\dfrac{\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]-a}{b-a}=\dfrac{-a}{b-a}\triangleq\mu
because
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]=0
, where
\mu\in[0,1]
because
a\leq\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]\leq b
.
The exponential function is convex, so for any
\lambda\in[0,1]
and any real
s
,

\exp(\lambda s)\leq(1-\lambda)+\lambda e^{s}.

Applying this inequality with
\lambda={\textnormal{y}}
and
s=t
, where
{\textnormal{y}}=\frac{{\textnormal{x}}-a}{\,b-a\,}\in[0,1]
and
t=\theta(b-a)
, yields

\exp(\theta{\textnormal{x}})=\exp(\theta a)\exp(t{\textnormal{y}})\leq\exp(\theta a)\big(1-{\textnormal{y}}+{\textnormal{y}}e^{t}\big).

Taking expectations on both sides gives

\mathbb{E}[\exp(\theta{\textnormal{x}})]\leq\exp(\theta a)\big(1-\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{y}}]+\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{y}}]e^{t}\big)=\exp(\theta a)\big(1-\mu+\mu e^{t}\big).

Take logarithms and define

g(t)\triangleq\ln\big(1-\mu+\mu e^{t}\big).

Then the cumulant generating function satisfies

\mathbb{K}_{{\textnormal{x}}}(\theta)\equiv\ln\mathbb{E}[\exp(\theta{\textnormal{x}})]\leq\theta a+g(t),\qquad t=\theta(b-a).

(1.47)

We analyze
g(t)
via its second derivative:

g^{\prime\prime}(t)=\frac{\mu(1-\mu)e^{t}}{\big(1-\mu+\mu e^{t}\big)^{2}}.

To bound this, observe the elementary inequality
4uv\leq(u+v)^{2}
.
Setting
u=\sqrt{\mu e^{t}}
and
v=\sqrt{1-\mu}
), we obtain

\mu(1-\mu)e^{t}=(uv)^{2}\leq\Big(\frac{u^{2}+v^{2}}{2}\Big)^{2}=\frac{\big(\mu e^{t}+1-\mu\big)^{2}}{4}.

Dividing both sides by
(1-\mu+\mu e^{t})^{2}
yields

g^{\prime\prime}(t)\leq\frac{1}{4}.

Since
g^{\prime\prime}(t)\leq\tfrac{1}{4}
for all
t
, and
g(0)=\ln(1)=0
,
g^{\prime}(0)=\dfrac{\mu e^{0}}{1-\mu+\mu e^{0}}=\mu
, we can integrate twice.
Moreover, note that the derivative with respect to
\theta
of the right-hand side in (
) at
\theta=0
vanishes:

\left.\frac{d}{d\theta}\big(\theta a+g(\theta(b-a))\big)\right|_{\theta=0}=a+g^{\prime}(0)\,(b-a)=a+\mu(b-a)=0.

Therefore, the Taylor expansion of the right-hand side in (
) about
t=0
with
g^{\prime\prime}(t)\leq 1/4
yields

\ln\mathbb{E}[\exp(\theta{\textnormal{x}})]\leq\theta a+g(t)\leq\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{4}\,t^{2}=\frac{t^{2}}{8}=\frac{\theta^{2}(b-a)^{2}}{8}.

Exponentiating both sides gives the desired bound:

Using the above lemma, we prove Hoeffding’s inequality, which quantifies how tightly the sum of bounded independent random variables concentrates around its mean.

{theoremHigh}
[Hoeffding’s inequality
(
Hoeffding 1963
)
]
Let
{\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2},\dots,{\textnormal{x}}_{n}
be independent random variables such that each
{\textnormal{x}}_{i}
is almost surely bounded in the interval
[a_{i},b_{i}]
, where
a_{i}
and
b_{i}
are known constants.
Let
{\textnormal{s}}_{n}\triangleq\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\textnormal{x}}_{i}
be the sum of these random variables, and let
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{s}}_{n}]
be its mean value.
Then, for any
\tau>0
, Hoeffding’s inequality states:

\Pr({\textnormal{s}}_{n}-\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{s}}_{n}]\geq\tau)\leq\exp\left(-\frac{2\tau^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(b_{i}-a_{i})^{2}}\right).

Similarly, for the lower tail:

\Pr({\textnormal{s}}_{n}-\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{s}}_{n}]\leq-\tau)\leq\exp\left(-\frac{2\tau^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(b_{i}-a_{i})^{2}}\right).

Consequently, the two-sided version holds:

\Pr(\left\lvert{\textnormal{s}}_{n}-\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{s}}_{n}]\right\rvert\geq\tau)\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{2\tau^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(b_{i}-a_{i})^{2}}\right).

The bound decays exponentially in
\tau^{2}
, which implies that large deviations from the mean are extremely unlikely.
The denominator
\sum(b_{i}-a_{i})^{2}
captures the total variability of the random variables: the wider the individual bounds
[a_{i},b_{i}]
, the weaker (i.e., looser) the concentration around the mean.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
We use the Chernoff method.
For any
\theta>0
, by Markov’s inequality (Theorem
) and the independence of
{\textnormal{x}}_{i}
:

\Pr({\textnormal{s}}_{n}-\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{s}}_{n}]\geq\tau)=\Pr(e^{\theta({\textnormal{s}}_{n}-\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{s}}_{n}])}\geq\exp(\theta\tau))\leq\frac{\mathbb{E}[e^{\theta({\textnormal{s}}_{n}-\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{s}}_{n}])}]}{\exp(\theta\tau)}=\exp({-\theta\tau})\prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}[e^{\theta({\textnormal{x}}_{i}-\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{i}])}].

To proceed, we bound the MGF of
{\textnormal{x}}_{i}-\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{i}]
for each
{\textnormal{x}}_{i}
.
Let
{\textnormal{y}}_{i}\triangleq{\textnormal{x}}_{i}-\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{i}]
. Then
{\textnormal{y}}_{i}\in\big[a_{i}-\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{i}],b_{i}-\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{i}]\big]\triangleq[c_{i},d_{i}]
, where
c_{i}\triangleq a_{i}-\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{i}]
,
d_{i}\triangleq b_{i}-\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{i}]
,
d_{i}-c_{i}=b_{i}-a_{i}
, and
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{y}}_{i}]=0
.
Applying Hoeffding’s lemma (Lemma
) to each
{\textnormal{y}}_{i}
:

\mathbb{E}\big[\exp(\theta({\textnormal{x}}_{i}-\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{i}]))\big]\leq\exp\left(\frac{\theta^{2}(b_{i}-a_{i})^{2}}{8}\right),

whence we have

\Pr({\textnormal{s}}_{n}-\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{s}}_{n}]\geq\tau)\leq\exp(-\theta\tau)\prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}\big[\exp(\theta({\textnormal{x}}_{i}-\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{i}]))\big]\leq\exp\left(-\theta\tau+\frac{\theta^{2}}{8}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(b_{i}-a_{i})^{2}\right).

The optimal choice
\theta=\frac{4\tau}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(b_{i}-a_{i})^{2}}
in the above yields the upper tail.
The lower-tail inequality follows analogously by applying the same argument to
-{\textnormal{x}}_{i}
.
Finally, the two-sided bound follows from the union bound:

\Pr(\left\lvert{\textnormal{s}}_{n}-\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{s}}_{n}]\right\rvert\geq\tau)\leq\Pr({\textnormal{s}}_{n}-\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{s}}_{n}]\geq\tau)+\Pr({\textnormal{s}}_{n}-\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{s}}_{n}]\leq-\tau)\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{2\tau^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(b_{i}-a_{i})^{2}}\right).

This completes the proof.

Exercise
\thetheo

Let
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{i}]=0
for all
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}
in Theorem
. Use Cramér’s theorem (Theorem
) to complete an alternative proof.

If the variables
{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\in\{0,1\}
are Bernoulli random variables, then
a_{i}=0,b_{i}=1
, so
b_{i}-a_{i}=1
, and
\sum_{i=1}^{n}(b_{i}-a_{i})^{2}=n
.
Let
\overline{{\textnormal{x}}}\triangleq\frac{1}{n}\sum{\textnormal{x}}_{i}
and
\mu\triangleq\mathbb{E}[\overline{{\textnormal{x}}}]
.
Then Hoeffding’s inequality gives

\Pr(\left\lvert\overline{{\textnormal{x}}}-\mu\right\rvert\geq\varepsilon)\leq 2\exp(-2n\varepsilon^{2}).

This form is widely used in learning theory—for example, in proving the uniform convergence of empirical risk minimization.

A
Rademacher variable
(also known as a
symmetric Bernoulli variable
) is a variant of the Bernoulli random variable: it is a random variable
\epsilon
that takes the values
+1
and
-1
with equal probability. A
Rademacher sequence

{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}
is a vector of independent Rademacher variables.
For such sequences, we obtain the following version of Hoeffding’s inequality.

Corollary 46
(Hoeffding’s inequality for Rademacher sequences).

Let
{\bm{a}}\in\real^{n}
and
{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}=\{\epsilon_{1},\epsilon_{2},\ldots,\epsilon_{n}\}
be a Rademacher sequence. Then, for
\mu>0
,

\Pr\left(\left\lvert\sum_{i=1}^{n}\epsilon_{i}a_{i}\right\rvert\geq\left\lVert{\bm{a}}\right\rVert_{2}\mu\right)\leq 2\exp(-\frac{\mu^{2}}{2}).

Proof
[of Corollary
]
The random variable
\epsilon_{i}a_{i}
has mean zero and is bounded in absolute value by
\left\lvert a_{i}\right\rvert
.
The stated inequality therefore follows directly from Hoeffding’s inequality.

Bernstein’s inequality
provides a useful generalization of Hoeffding’s inequality to sums of independent random variables
that are either bounded or even unbounded, while also incorporating information about their variance (or higher moments). We begin with the version stated below and then derive several useful variants as corollaries.

{theoremHigh}

[Bernstein’s inequality
(
Bernstein 1924
)
]
Let
{\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{n}
be independent zero-mean random variables (i.e.,
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{i}]=0
for all
i
) such that, for all integers
k\geq 2
,

\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\right\rvert^{k}]\leq k!C^{k-2}\sigma_{i}^{2}/2,\quad\text{for all }i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}

for some constants
C>0
and
\sigma_{i}>0
,
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}
. Then, for all
\tau>0
,

\Pr\left(\left\lvert\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\right\rvert\geq\tau\right)\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{\tau^{2}/2}{\sigma^{2}+C\tau}\right),

where
\sigma^{2}\triangleq\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_{i}^{2}
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Using the well-known Taylor expansion
\exp(z)=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^{i}}{i!}
for all
z\in\real
around 0 and the fact that
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{i}]=0
, we have

\mathbb{E}[\exp(\theta{\textnormal{x}}_{i})]=1+\theta\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{i}]+\sum_{k=2}^{\infty}\frac{\theta^{k}\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{i}^{k}]}{k!}=1+\frac{\theta^{2}\sigma_{i}^{2}}{2}\sum_{k=2}^{\infty}\frac{\theta^{k-2}\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{i}^{k}]}{k!\sigma_{i}^{2}/2},

For each
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}
, define
F_{i}(\theta)\triangleq\sum_{k=2}^{\infty}\frac{\theta^{k-2}\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{i}^{k}]}{k!\sigma_{i}^{2}/2}
.
Then,

\mathbb{E}[\exp(\theta{\textnormal{x}}_{i})]=1+\frac{\theta^{2}\sigma_{i}^{2}F_{i}(\theta)}{2}\leq\exp(\frac{\theta^{2}\sigma_{i}^{2}F_{i}(\theta)}{2}),

where we used the inequality
1+x\leq\exp(x)
for all
x\in\real
.
Now let
F(\theta)\triangleq\max_{i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}}F_{i}(\theta)
.
Then by the fact that
\sigma^{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_{i}^{2}
and Cramér’s theorem (Theorem
), we obtain
