\Pr\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\geq\tau\right)\leq\min_{\theta>0}\exp\left(-\theta\tau+\frac{\theta^{2}\sigma^{2}F(\theta)}{2}\right)\leq\min_{0<C\theta<1}\exp\left(-\theta\tau+\frac{\theta^{2}\sigma^{2}F(\theta)}{2}\right),

where we suppose
C\theta<1
.
Combining the inequality
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{i}^{k}]\leq\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\right\rvert^{k}]
and the assumption of the bound for
\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\right\rvert^{k}]
yields

F_{i}(\theta)\leq\sum_{k=2}^{\infty}\frac{\theta^{k-2}\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\right\rvert^{k}]}{k!\sigma_{i}^{2}/2}\leq\sum_{k=2}^{\infty}\frac{(C\theta)^{k-2}}{1-C\theta}=\frac{1}{1-C\theta}.

Hence,
F(\theta)\leq(1-C\theta)^{-1}
, and therefore

\Pr\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\geq\tau\right)\leq\min_{0<C\theta<1}\exp\left(-\theta\tau+\frac{\theta^{2}\sigma^{2}}{2(1-C\theta)}\right).

The choice
\theta=\tau/(\sigma^{2}+C\tau)
satisfies
C\theta<1
, which yields

\displaystyle\Pr\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\geq\tau\right)\leq\exp\left(-\frac{\tau^{2}/2}{\sigma^{2}+C\tau}\right).

Applying the same argument to
-{\textnormal{x}}_{i}
gives an identical bound for
\Pr\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\leq-\tau\right)
.
Combining both tails via the union bound completes the proof.

We present two important consequences of Bernstein’s inequality.
The first is Bernstein’s inequality for bounded random variables, which appears more frequently in the literature.

Corollary 47
(Bernstein’s inequality for bounded random variables).

Let
{\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{n}
be independent zero-mean random variables such that
\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\right\rvert\leq B
almost surely for
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}
, where
B>0
is a constant.
Suppose further that
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{i}^{2}]\leq\sigma_{i}^{2}
for some constants
\sigma_{i}>0
,
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}
. Then, for all
\tau>0
,

\Pr\left(\left\lvert\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\right\rvert\geq\tau\right)\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{\tau^{2}/2}{\sigma^{2}+B\tau/3}\right),

where
\sigma^{2}\triangleq\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_{i}^{2}
.

Proof
[of Corollary
]
For
k=2
, the moment condition in Theorem
is satisfied by assumption.
So let
k\in\mathbb{N}
,
k\geq 3
. Since then
k!\geq 3\cdot 2^{k-2}
, we obtain

\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\right\rvert^{k}]=\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\right\rvert^{k-2}{\textnormal{x}}_{i}^{2}]\leq B^{k-2}\sigma_{i}^{2}\leq\frac{k!B^{k-2}}{k!}\sigma_{i}^{2}\leq\frac{k!B^{k-2}}{2\cdot 3^{k-2}}\sigma_{i}^{2}.

Thus, the moment condition of Theorem
is satisfied for all
k\geq 2
with
C=B/3
and the same
\sigma_{i}
.
The desired inequality follows directly from Theorem
.

As a second consequence, we state Bernstein’s inequality for sub-exponential random variables (see Definition
for more details).

Corollary 48
(Bernstein’s inequality for sub-exponential random variables).

Let
{\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{n}
be independent zero-mean sub-exponential random variables; that is,
\Pr(\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\right\rvert\geq\tau)\leq\Phi\exp(-\xi\tau)
for some constants
\Phi,\xi>0
for all
\tau>0
,
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}
. Then, for all
\tau>0
,

\Pr\left(\left\lvert\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\right\rvert\geq\tau\right)\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{(\xi\tau)^{2}/2}{2\Phi n+\xi\tau}\right).

Proof
[of Corollary
]
Using the absolute moments lemma (Lemma
), for
k\in\mathbb{N}
,
k\geq 2
,

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\right\rvert^{k}]

\displaystyle=k\int_{0}^{\infty}\Pr(\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\right\rvert\geq x)x^{k-1}dx\leq\Phi k\int_{0}^{\infty}\exp(-\xi x)x^{k-1}dx

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle u=\xi x}}{{\mathrel{\rule[2.15277pt]{20.00003pt}{0.5pt}\hskip-20.00003pt\rule[-2.15277pt]{20.00003pt}{0.5pt}}}}\Phi k\xi^{-k}\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-u}u^{k-1}du=\Phi k!\xi^{-k}=k!\xi^{-(k-2)}\frac{2\Phi\xi^{-2}}{2},

where we have used the Gamma function
\Gamma(x)=\int_{0}^{\infty}t^{x-1}\exp(-t)dt
and the fact that
\Gamma(k)=(k-1)!
for any integer
k
. Hence, the moment condition in Theorem
holds with
C=\xi^{-1}
and
\sigma_{i}^{2}=2\Phi\xi^{-2}
. The result follows again from Theorem
.

Recall that the
Gamma function
is defined for
y\geq 0
by

\Gamma(y)=\int_{0}^{\infty}t^{y-1}e^{-t}dt,\qquad y\geq 0.

(1.48)

Utilizing integration by parts
\int_{a}^{b}u(t)v^{\prime}(t)dt=u(t)v(t)|_{a}^{b}-\int_{a}^{b}u^{\prime}(t)v(t)dt
, where
u(t)=t^{y-1}
and
v(t)=-e^{-t}
, we derive

\displaystyle\Gamma(y)

\displaystyle=-t^{y-1}e^{-t}|_{0}^{\infty}-\int_{0}^{\infty}(y-1)t^{y-2}(-e^{-t})dt

\displaystyle=0+(y-1)\int_{0}^{\infty}t^{y-2}e^{-t}dt=(y-1)\Gamma(y-1).

This recurrence relation shows that when
y
is a positive integer,
\Gamma(y)=(y-1)!
.

1.3.2
Gaussian Distribution and Properties

The
Gaussian
(or
normal
) random variable is a widely preferred choice in statistical modeling and signal processing. This preference arises from a fundamental principle: the sum of independent random variables tends to follow a Gaussian distribution—a result formalized by the central limit theorem (see Theorem
below). Consequently, any measurement or quantity formed by the additive combination of many independent, unrelated components is likely to be approximately Gaussian. For this reason, noise in fields such as signal processing and engineering is commonly modeled using a Gaussian distribution due to its desirable mathematical properties.

Gaussian Random Variables

Definition 49
(Gaussian or normal distribution).

A random variable
x
is said to follow the Gaussian distribution (a.k.a., the normal distribution) with mean
\mu
and variance
\sigma^{2}>0
, denoted
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2})
, if

f(x;\mu,\sigma^{2})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^{2}}}\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}(x-\mu)^{2}\right\}=\sqrt{\frac{\tau}{2\pi}}\exp\left\{-\frac{\tau}{2}(x-\mu)^{2}\right\},

where
\tau
is also known as the precision of the distribution.
The mean, variance, and MGF of
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2})
are given by

\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]=\mu,\qquad\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{x}}]=\sigma^{2}=\tau^{-1},\qquad\mathbb{M}_{\textnormal{x}}(\theta)=\exp\{\theta\mu+\theta^{2}\sigma^{2}/2\},

The cumulative distribution function (c.d.f., CDF) of
x
is

F(x;\mu,\sigma^{2})=\Pr({\textnormal{x}}<x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^{2}}}\int_{-\infty}^{x}\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}(z-\mu)^{2}\right\}dz.

In particular, we denote
\Phi(y)=\int_{-\infty}^{y}\mathcal{N}(u\mid 0,1)du=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{y}\exp(-\frac{u^{2}}{2})du
as the cumulative distribution function of
\mathcal{N}(0,1)
, the standard normal distribution.

Figure
illustrates how different values of the parameters
\mu,\sigma^{2}
affect the shape of the Gaussian distribution.

Figure 1.5:
Gaussian probability density functions for different values of the mean and variance parameters
\mu
and
\sigma^{2}
.

As noted above, the central limit theorem states that the distribution of the average of a large number of random variables with finite variances converges to a Gaussian distribution.

{theoremHigh}
[Central limit theorem (CLT)]
Let
{\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2},{\textnormal{x}}_{3},\ldots
be a sequence of i.i.d. random variables with mean
\mu
and finite variance
\sigma^{2}<\infty
. We define the sequence of averages
{\textnormal{y}}_{1},{\textnormal{y}}_{2},{\textnormal{y}}_{3},\ldots
as

{\textnormal{y}}_{n}\triangleq\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\textnormal{x}}_{i}.

Then the normalized sequence
{\textnormal{z}}_{1},{\textnormal{z}}_{2},{\textnormal{z}}_{3},\ldots

{\textnormal{z}}_{n}\triangleq\sqrt{n}({\textnormal{y}}_{n}-\mu)

converges in distribution to a Gaussian random variable with mean
0
and variance
\sigma^{2}
.
That is, for any
x\in\real
,

\lim_{n\to\infty}f_{{\textnormal{z}}_{n}}(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma}e^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}}.

For sufficiently large
n
, the above theorem also implies that the sample average
{\textnormal{y}}_{n}
is approximately Gaussian with mean
\mu
and variance
\sigma^{2}/n
.

While the product of two Gaussian variables remains analytically challenging, the sum of Gaussian variables is itself Gaussian and can be fully characterized by its mean and variance.

Remark 50
(Sum of Gaussians).

Let
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}{\mu_{x},\sigma_{x}^{2}}
and
{\textnormal{y}}\sim\mathcal{N}{\mu_{y},\sigma_{y}^{2}}
be two Gaussian random variables.

If
x
and
y
are uncorrelated, then

{\textnormal{x}}+{\textnormal{y}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_{x}+\mu_{y},\sigma_{x}^{2}+\sigma_{y}^{2}).

If
x
and
y
have correlation coefficient
\rho
, then

{\textnormal{x}}+{\textnormal{y}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_{x}+\mu_{y},\sigma_{x}^{2}+\sigma_{y}^{2}+2\rho\sigma_{x}\sigma_{y}).

An important property of Gaussian random variables is that affine transformations (i.e., scaling and shifting) preserve the Gaussian form.

Lemma 51
(Linear transformation of Gaussian variables).

Let
x
ba a Gaussian random variable with mean
\mu
and variance
\sigma^{2}
.
Then, for any
a,b\in\real
, the random variable

{\textnormal{y}}\triangleq a{\textnormal{x}}+b

(1.49)

is also Gaussian with mean
a\mu+b
and variance
a^{2}\sigma^{2}
.

The proof follows directly from the linear transformation lemma (Lemma
).

Gaussian distributions exhibit strong concentration properties. A fundamental result in this context is the following tail bound for a centered Gaussian random variable.

Exercise
\thetheo
(Chernoff bound for centered Gaussian)

For
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2})
, show that

\Pr(\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert\geq\tau)\leq 2e^{-\frac{\tau^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}},\quad\text{for all }\tau>0.

Hint: Apply the Chernoff bound (Theorem
)

Although the Chernoff bound provide a valid upper bound on
\Pr(\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert\geq\tau)
for a centered Gaussian, the bound is not tight.
A sharper bound can be derived as follows.

Lemma 52
(Tighter tail bound for a centered Gaussian).

For
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2})
, it holds that

\Pr(\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert\geq\tau)\leq\begin{cases}&e^{-\frac{\tau^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}};\\
&\frac{\sigma\sqrt{2}}{\tau\sqrt{\pi}}\exp\left(-\frac{\tau^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right),\end{cases}\quad\text{for all }\tau>0.

Note that the latter inequality is called
Mill’s inequality.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
By definition,
\Pr(\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert\geq\tau)=\frac{2}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^{2}}}\int_{\tau}^{\infty}e^{-x^{2}/2\sigma^{2}}dx
.
Applying the change of variables:

\displaystyle\int_{\tau}^{\infty}e^{-x^{2}/2\sigma^{2}}dx

\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-(x+\tau)^{2}/2\sigma^{2}}dx=e^{-\tau^{2}/2\sigma^{2}}\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-x\tau/\sigma^{2}}e^{-x^{2}/2\sigma^{2}}dx

\displaystyle\leq e^{-\tau^{2}/2\sigma^{2}}\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-x^{2}/2\sigma^{2}}dx=\sqrt{\frac{\pi\sigma^{2}}{2}}e^{-\tau^{2}/2\sigma^{2}},

where the inequality follows from that
e^{-x\tau/\sigma^{2}}\leq 1
for
x,\tau\geq 0
.
This shows that
\Pr(\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert\geq\tau)\leq e^{-\tau^{2}/2\sigma^{2}}
.

For the second part, by symmetry and union bound,
\Pr(\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert\geq\tau)\leq 2\Pr({\textnormal{x}}\geq\tau)
:

\displaystyle 2\Pr({\textnormal{x}}\geq\tau)

\displaystyle=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{\pi}\sigma}\int_{\tau}^{+\infty}\exp\left(-\frac{x^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right)dx\leq\frac{\sigma^{2}\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{\pi}\sigma^{2}}\int_{\tau}^{+\infty}\frac{x}{\sigma^{2}\tau}\exp\left(-\frac{x^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right)dx

\displaystyle=\frac{\sigma\sqrt{2}}{\tau\sqrt{\pi}}\int_{\tau}^{+\infty}-\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\exp\left(-\frac{x^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right)dx=\frac{\sigma\sqrt{2}}{\tau\sqrt{\pi}}\exp\left(-\frac{\tau^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right).

This completes the proof.

The definition of a standard Gaussian random variable
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)
shows that
\mathbb{M}_{{\textnormal{x}}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}[\exp(\theta{\textnormal{x}})]=\exp(\theta^{2}/2)
. A more general result holds for expectations involving quadratic functions of
x
.

Lemma 53
(Moment of standard Gaussian variables).

Let
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)
. Then, for
a,b,c\in\real
with
a<1/2
,

\mathbb{E}[\exp(a{\textnormal{x}}^{2}+b{\textnormal{x}}+c)]=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-2a}}\exp\left(\frac{b^{2}}{2(1-2a)}+c\right).

Proof
[of Lemma
]
By definition of expectation under the standard normal density,

\mathbb{E}[\exp(a{\textnormal{x}}^{2}+b{\textnormal{x}}+c)]=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\exp(ax^{2}+bx+c)\exp\left(-\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right)dx.

Noting the identity

ax^{2}-\frac{x^{2}}{2}+bx=-\frac{1-2a}{2}\left(x-\frac{b}{1-2a}\right)^{2}+\frac{b^{2}}{2(1-2a)}+c.

After a change of variable, the latter integral reduces to the integral of the Gaussian probability density function with variance
1/(1-2a)
, so it equals one. This completes the proof.

Note that the above lemma implies a bound on the higher-order moments of a standard Gaussian
x
, since

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\exp(\theta{\textnormal{x}}^{2})]

\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\frac{(\theta{\textnormal{x}}^{2})^{i}}{i!}\right]=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\frac{\mathbb{E}[(\theta{\textnormal{x}}^{2})^{i}]}{i!},

where the first equality follows from the well-known Taylor expansion
\exp(z)=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^{i}}{i!}
for all
z\in\real
around 0.
Bounds that exploit the behavior of higher-order moments to control tail probabilities through the expectation of an exponential are often called Chernoff bounds or Chernoff methods; see also Theorem
.

Gaussian Random Vectors

A
multivariate Gaussian distribution
(also known as a
multivariate normal distribution
or simply a Gaussian distribution) is a continuous probability distribution that describes a set of jointly normally distributed random variables.
It is completely characterized by its mean vector and covariance matrix.
The covariance matrix captures the pairwise covariances between all variables, thereby encoding both their individual variances (along the diagonal) and their linear dependencies (off-diagonal entries).
Due to its mathematical tractability and flexibility, the multivariate Gaussian distribution is widely used across fields such as machine learning, statistics, and signal processing.
We now provide the formal definition of the multivariate Gaussian distribution.

Definition 54
(Multivariate Gaussian distribution).

A random vector
{\mathbf{x}}\in\real^{p}
is said to follow the multivariate Gaussian distribution (multivariate normal, MVN) with parameters
{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\in\real^{p}
and
{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\in\real^{p\times p}
, denoted
{\mathbf{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}({\boldsymbol{\mu}},{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}})
, if

\displaystyle f({\bm{x}};{\boldsymbol{\mu}},{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}})

\displaystyle=(2\pi)^{-p/2}\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\right\rvert^{-1/2}\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2}({\bm{x}}-{\boldsymbol{\mu}})^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}({\bm{x}}-{\boldsymbol{\mu}})\right\},\penalty\

where
{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\in\real^{p}
is called the mean vector, and
{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\in\real^{p\times p}
is positive definite and is called the covariance matrix.
\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\right\rvert=\det({\boldsymbol{\Sigma}})
denotes the determinant of
{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}
.
The mean, mode, and covariance of the multivariate Gaussian distribution are given by

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{x}}]

\displaystyle={\boldsymbol{\mu}},\qquad\mathrm{Mode}[{\mathbf{x}}]={\boldsymbol{\mu}},\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\mathbf{x}}]={\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}.

The covariance matrix can also be expressed as:

\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\mathbf{x}}]=\mathbb{E}[({\mathbf{x}}-{\boldsymbol{\mu}})({\mathbf{x}}-{\boldsymbol{\mu}})^{\top}]=\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{x}}{\mathbf{x}}^{\top}]-{\boldsymbol{\mu}}{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{\top}.

Figure
illustrates Gaussian density plots under different covariance structures.
When the covariance matrix of a Gaussian vector is the identity and its mean is zero, then its entries are i.i.d. standard Gaussians with mean zero and unit variance. We refer to such vectors as
i.i.d. standard Gaussian vectors
.
Additionally, a multivariate Gaussian random vector can be generated from univariate Gaussian samples; see Problem
.

(a)

Gaussian,
{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\
0&1\end{bmatrix}.

(b)

Gaussian,
{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\
0&3\end{bmatrix}.

(c)

Gaussian,
{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}=\begin{bmatrix}1&\textendash 0.5\\
\textendash 0.5&1.5\end{bmatrix}.

(d)

Gaussian,
{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}=\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\
0&2\end{bmatrix}.

(e)

Gaussian,
{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}=\begin{bmatrix}3&0\\
0&1\end{bmatrix}.

(f)

Gaussian,
{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}=\begin{bmatrix}3&\textendash 0.5\\
\textendash 0.5&1.5\end{bmatrix}.

Figure 1.6:
Density and contour plots (
blue
=low,
yellow
=high) of the multivariate Gaussian distribution over the
2
space for various values of the covariance/scale matrix with a zero-mean vector. Fig
and
: A spherical covariance matrix has a circular shape;
Fig

Fig

Two important distributions related to the multivariate Gaussian distribution are the
Gamma distribution
and its special case, the
Chi-squared distribution
. Definitions for these distributions are provided below.

Definition 55
(Gamma distribution).

A random variable
x
is said to follow the Gamma distribution with shape parameter
r>0
and rate parameter
\lambda>0
, denoted by
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{G}(r,\lambda)
, if its probability density function is given by

f(x;r,\lambda)=\left\{\begin{aligned} &\frac{\lambda^{r}}{\Gamma(r)}x^{r-1}\exp(-\lambda x),&\mathrm{\,\,if\,\,}x\geq 0.\\
&0,&\mathrm{\,\,if\,\,}x<0,\end{aligned}\right.

where
\Gamma(x)=\int_{0}^{\infty}t^{x-1}\exp(-t)dt
is the Gamma function (see (
)), which normalizes the distribution so that it integrates to 1.
The mean and variance of
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{G}(r,\lambda)
are given by

\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]=\frac{r}{\lambda},\qquad\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{x}}]=\frac{r}{\lambda^{2}}.

Figure
illustrates different parameters for the Gamma distribution.
It is worth noting that the shape parameter
r
in the Gamma distribution is not restricted to natural numbers; instead, it can take any positive value.
However, when
r
is a positive integer, the Gamma distribution can be interpreted as the sum of
r
independent
exponential variables
, each with rate
\lambda

(
Lu 2023
)
.
This summation property extends more generally to Gamma-distributed variables with the same rate parameter. If
{\textnormal{x}}_{1}
and
{\textnormal{x}}_{2}
are random variables drawn from
\mathcal{G}(r_{1},\lambda)
and
\mathcal{G}(r_{2},\lambda)
, respectively, then their sum
{\textnormal{x}}_{1}+{\textnormal{x}}_{2}
follows a Gamma distribution
\mathcal{G}(r_{1}+r_{2},\lambda)
.

(a)

Gamma probability density
functions for different values of the parameters
r
and
\lambda
.

(b)

Chi-squared probability density
functions for different values of the parameter
p
.

Figure 1.7:
Comparison between the Gamma distribution and the Chi-squared distribution.

Although the Chi-squared distribution is a special case of the Gamma distribution, it plays a particularly important role in statistical theory.

Definition 56
(Chi-squared distribution,
\chi^{2}
-distribution).

Let
{\textnormal{a}}_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)
for
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
(equivalently,
{\mathbf{a}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},{\bm{I}}_{p})
; see Definition
).
Then the random variable
{\textnormal{x}}=\sum_{i=1}^{p}{\textnormal{a}}_{i}^{2}
follows the Chi-squared distribution (or Chi-square distribution,
\chi^{2}
-distribution) with
p
degrees of freedom.
We write
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\chi_{(p)}^{2}
, which is equivalent to
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{G}(p/2,1/2)
in Definition
. The probability density function of
x
is given by

f(x;p)=\left\{\begin{aligned} &\frac{1}{2^{p/2}\Gamma(\frac{p}{2})}x^{\frac{p}{2}-1}\exp(-\frac{x}{2}),&\mathrm{\,\,if\,\,}x\geq 0;\\
&0,&\mathrm{\,\,if\,\,}x<0.\end{aligned}\right.

The mean and variance of
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\chi_{(p)}^{2}
are given by

\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]=p,\qquad\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{x}}]=2p.

Figure
shows the effect of varying the degrees of freedom
p
on the shape of the Chi-squared distribution.
The definition shows that if
{\mathbf{a}}=[{\textnormal{a}}_{1},{\textnormal{a}}_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{a}}_{p}]^{\top}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},{\bm{I}}_{p})
(the multivariate Gaussian distribution; see Definition
), then
{\textnormal{x}}={\mathbf{a}}^{\top}{\mathbf{a}}\sim\chi_{(p)}^{2}
.
More generally, let
{\bm{H}}
be an orthogonal projection matrix of rank
r<p
(see Definition
).
Then it follows that

{\mathbf{a}}^{\top}{\bm{H}}{\mathbf{a}}\sim\chi_{(r)}^{2},\text{ with orthogonal projector $\mathrm{rank}({\bm{H}})=r<p$}.

(1.50a)

Furthermore, suppose
{\mathbf{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}({\boldsymbol{\mu}},{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}})
, where
{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\in\real^{p}
and
{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}
is nonsingular. Then,

({\mathbf{x}}-{\boldsymbol{\mu}})^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}({\mathbf{x}}-{\boldsymbol{\mu}})\sim\chi^{2}_{(p)}.

(1.50b)

To see this, note that since
{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}
is symmetric and positive definite, it admits the spectral decomposition
{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}={\bm{Q}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\Lambda}}{\bm{Q}}
, where
{\bm{Q}}
is a
p\times p
orthogonal matrix and
{\boldsymbol{\Lambda}}=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\ldots,\lambda_{p})
with
\lambda_{j}>0
(see Theorem
).
Define the standardized vector
{\mathbf{y}}\triangleq{\boldsymbol{\Lambda}}^{-1/2}{\bm{Q}}({\mathbf{x}}-{\boldsymbol{\mu}})
.
Vector
{\mathbf{y}}
then is normally distributed (as a hindsight, see Lemma
):

{\mathbf{y}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},{\boldsymbol{\Lambda}}^{-1/2}{\bm{Q}}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}{\bm{Q}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\Lambda}}^{-1/2})=\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},{\boldsymbol{\Lambda}}^{-1/2}{\bm{Q}}{\bm{Q}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\Lambda}}{\boldsymbol{\Lambda}}^{-1/2})=\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},{\bm{I}}_{p}).

It follows that the components of
{\mathbf{y}}
are independent (see Lemma
) and that
{\textnormal{y}}_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)
. So,

({\mathbf{x}}-{\boldsymbol{\mu}})^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}({\mathbf{x}}-{\boldsymbol{\mu}})={\mathbf{y}}^{\top}{\mathbf{y}}\sim\chi^{2}_{(p)}
.

We may also be interested in the quadratic form of
{\mathbf{x}}^{\top}{\bm{A}}{\mathbf{x}}
where
{\bm{A}}
is symmetric.
The following theorem provides key characterizations of when such quadratic forms follow a Chi-squared distribution.

Proposition 57
(Quadratic of Gaussians).

We have the following results with quadratic forms of Gaussians:

Given
{\mathbf{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\lambda{\bm{I}})
(of length
p
) and symmetric matrix
{\bm{A}}\in\real^{p\times p}
. Then, it follows that

\frac{{\mathbf{x}}^{\top}{\bm{A}}{\mathbf{x}}}{\lambda}\sim\chi^{2}_{(r)},

if and only if
{\bm{A}}
is idempotent (
{\bm{A}}^{2}={\bm{A}}
) with rank
r<p
.

Given
{\mathbf{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}})\in\real^{p}
and symmetric matrix
{\bm{A}}\in\real^{p\times p}
. Then, it follows that

{\mathbf{x}}^{\top}{\bm{A}}{\mathbf{x}}\sim\chi^{2}_{(r)},

if and only if
{\bm{A}}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}
is idempotent with rank
r<p
.

Properties of Multivariate Gaussian Distribution

A fundamental property of Gaussian random vectors is that affine transformations preserve Gaussianity.
This is a multidimensional generalization of Lemma
, and it can be derived using the linear transformation rule for probability distributions (Lemma
) or via moment generating functions of the multivariate Gaussian distribution.

Lemma 58
(Affine transformation of multivariate Gaussian distribution).

Given fixed matrices and vector,
{\bm{A}},{\bm{B}}\in\real^{p\times d}
and
{\bm{c}}\in\real^{p}
,
let
{\mathbf{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}({\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{x},{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{x})
and
{\mathbf{y}}\sim\mathcal{N}({\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{y},{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{y})
be independent random vectors (of length
d
).
Then,

{\mathbf{z}}={\bm{A}}{\mathbf{x}}+{\bm{B}}{\mathbf{y}}+{\bm{c}}\sim\mathcal{N}({\bm{A}}{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{x}+{\bm{B}}{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{y}+{\bm{c}},{\bm{A}}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{x}{\bm{A}}^{\top}+{\bm{B}}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{y}{\bm{B}}^{\top}).

Moreover, for any fixed vector
{\bm{d}}\in\real^{d}
, the linear combination
{\bm{d}}^{\top}{\mathbf{x}}
follows from a univariate Gaussian:

{\bm{d}}^{\top}{\mathbf{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}({\bm{d}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{x},{\bm{d}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{x}{\bm{d}}).

The result also relies on the
sum of independent Gaussians
:

\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\mathbf{x}}_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}\big(\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{i},\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{i}\big)\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\text{if }{\mathbf{x}}_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}({\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{i},{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{i}),\ \forall\,i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}.

As a special case, let
{\bm{A}}={\bm{e}}_{i}^{\top}
be the
i
-th standard basis vector in
d
.
Then
{\textnormal{x}}_{i}={\bm{e}}_{i}^{\top}{\mathbf{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_{x,i},\sigma_{x,ii}^{2})
, where
\mu_{x,i}
represents the
i
-th component of
{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{x}
and
\sigma_{x,ii}^{2}
denotes the
i
-th diagonal of
{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{x}
.

An immediate consequence of Lemma
is that any subvector of a multivariate Gaussian vector is itself Gaussian.
Another consequence of Lemma
is that an i.i.d. standard Gaussian vector is
isotropic
, meaning its distribution is invariant under rotations.
Formally, for any orthogonal matrix
{\bm{Q}}
, if
{\mathbf{x}}
is an i.i.d. standard Gaussian vector, then by Lemma
,
{\bm{Q}}{\mathbf{x}}
has the same distribution, since its mean equals
{\bm{Q}}\boldsymbol{0}=\boldsymbol{0}
and its covariance matrix equals
{\bm{Q}}{\bm{I}}{\bm{Q}}^{\top}={\bm{Q}}{\bm{Q}}^{\top}={\bm{I}}
.
This rotational invariance is stronger than merely having equal variance in all directions (which holds for any vector with uncorrelated, identically distributed components). Isotropy implies that the entire distribution—not just second-order moments—is unchanged under orthogonal transformations.

Lemma 59
(Rotations on multivariate Gaussian distribution).

Rotations on the Gaussian distribution do not affect the distribution.
That is, for any orthogonal matrix
{\bm{Q}}
with
{\bm{Q}}{\bm{Q}}^{\top}={\bm{Q}}^{\top}{\bm{Q}}={\bm{I}}
, if
{\mathbf{v}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\sigma^{2}{\bm{I}})
, then
{\bm{Q}}{\mathbf{v}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\sigma^{2}{\bm{I}})
.

\paragrapharrow

“Standardization and decorrelation.”
The distribution
\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},{\bm{I}})
is called the
i.i.d. standard Gaussian vector
.
Given
{\mathbf{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}({\boldsymbol{\mu}},{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}})
, then the
decorrelation
of
{\mathbf{x}}
follows that

{\mathbf{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}({\boldsymbol{\mu}},{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}})\quad\implies\quad{\mathbf{z}}={\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1/2}({\mathbf{x}}-{\boldsymbol{\mu}})\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},{\bm{I}}).

(1.51)

This also shows that if
{\mathbf{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}({\boldsymbol{\mu}},{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}})
, then

{\mathbf{x}}={\boldsymbol{\mu}}+{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{1/2}{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}},\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\text{where }{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},{\bm{I}}).

(1.52)

Suppose
\{{\bm{x}}_{i},{\bm{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\bm{x}}_{n}\}
are
n
random samples of
\mathcal{N}({\boldsymbol{\mu}},{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}})
and let
\overline{{\bm{x}}}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\bm{x}}_{i}
. Then, it follows that

\sqrt{n}(\overline{{\bm{x}}}-{\boldsymbol{\mu}})\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}).

(1.53)

Lemma 60
(Uncorrelation implies mutual independence for Gaussian random vectors).

If all components of a Gaussian random vector
{\mathbf{x}}
are uncorrelated, then they are mutually independent.

This result follows directly by observing that the joint p.d.f. of
{\mathbf{x}}
factorizes into the product of its marginal p.d.f.s when the covariance matrix is diagonal (i.e., when components are uncorrelated).

We now turn to the partitioning of Gaussian vectors.
Let
{\mathbf{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}({\boldsymbol{\mu}},{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}})
where
{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\in\real^{p}
,
and consider a partition of
{\mathbf{x}}
into two subvectors:

\begin{bmatrix}{\mathbf{x}}_{1}\\
{\mathbf{x}}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\sim\mathcal{N}({\boldsymbol{\mu}},{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}})=\mathcal{N}\left(\begin{bmatrix}{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{1}\\
{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{11}&{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{12}\\
{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{21}&{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{22}\end{bmatrix}\right).

Then
{\mathbf{x}}_{1}
and
{\mathbf{x}}_{2}
are independent if and only if
{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{12}=\boldsymbol{0}
.
More generally, let
{\mathbf{x}}=[{\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{1},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{p}]^{\top}\sim\mathcal{N}({\boldsymbol{\mu}},{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}})
. Then,

the
{\textnormal{x}}_{i}
’s are mutually independent if and only if
{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}
is diagonal.

(1.54)

This can be rigorously established as follows:

Proof
[of Lemma
and Equation (
)]
Suppose that the
{\textnormal{x}}_{i}
’s are independent. Then
{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_{i},\sigma_{i}^{2})
for some
\sigma_{i}>0
. Thus the density of
{\mathbf{x}}
is

\displaystyle p_{{\mathbf{x}}}({\bm{x}})\

\displaystyle=\prod_{i=1}^{p}p_{{\textnormal{x}}_{i}}(x_{i})=\prod_{i=1}^{p}\frac{1}{\sigma_{i}\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2}\frac{(x_{i}-\mu_{i})^{2}}{\sigma_{i}^{2}}\right\}

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{p/2}\left\lvert\mathrm{diag}(\sigma_{1}^{2},\ldots,\sigma_{p}^{2})\right\rvert^{1/2}}\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2}({\bm{x}}-{\boldsymbol{\mu}})^{\top}\mathrm{diag}(\sigma_{1}^{-2},\ldots,\sigma_{p}^{-2})({\bm{x}}-{\boldsymbol{\mu}})\right\}.

Hence
{\mathbf{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}({\boldsymbol{\mu}},\mathrm{diag}(\sigma_{1}^{2},\ldots,\sigma_{p}^{2}))
, i.e., the covariance
{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}
is diagonal.

Conversely, assume
{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}
is diagonal, say
{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}=\mathrm{diag}(\sigma_{1}^{2},\ldots,\sigma_{p}^{2})
. Then we can reverse the steps of the first part to see that the joint density
p_{{\mathbf{x}}}({\bm{x}})
can be written as a product of the marginal densities
p_{{\textnormal{x}}_{i}}(x_{i})
, thus proving independence.

The results above immediately imply the following corollary.

Corollary 61
(Independence of linear combinations in Gaussian Distributions).

Let
{\mathbf{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}({\boldsymbol{\mu}},{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}})
be a random vector in
p
, and let
{\bm{A}}\in\real^{m\times p}
,
{\bm{B}}\in\real^{d\times p}
be fixed matrices.
Then,

{\bm{A}}{\mathbf{x}}

is independent of

{\bm{B}}{\mathbf{x}}

\quad\iff\quad

{\bm{A}}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}{\bm{B}}^{\top}=\boldsymbol{0}
.

(1.55)

An alternative proof can be obtained using properties of the moment generating function of the multivariate Gaussian distribution; we omit the details here.

It also follows from basic probability theory that measurable functions of independent random vectors remain independent. That is, if
{\mathbf{x}}_{1}
and
{\mathbf{x}}_{2}
are independent, then
g_{1}({\mathbf{x}}_{1})
and
g_{2}({\mathbf{x}}_{2})
are independent for any measurable functions
g_{1}({\mathbf{x}}_{1})
and
g_{2}({\mathbf{x}}_{2})
.

As an important example, suppose variables
{\textnormal{x}}_{i}
are i.i.d.
\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2})
for
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
. Then, we can define a vector populated by
\overline{{\textnormal{x}}}
and
{\textnormal{x}}_{i}-\overline{{\textnormal{x}}}
:

\begin{bmatrix}\overline{{\textnormal{x}}}\\
{\textnormal{x}}_{1}-\overline{{\textnormal{x}}}\\
\vdots\\
{\textnormal{x}}_{p}-\overline{{\textnormal{x}}}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{p}&\frac{1}{p}&\ldots&\frac{1}{p}\\
&{\bm{I}}_{p}-\frac{1}{p}{\bm{J}}_{p}&\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{\textnormal{x}}_{1}\\
{\textnormal{x}}_{2}\\
\vdots\\
{\textnormal{x}}_{p}\end{bmatrix}\qquad\text{where}\qquad{\bm{J}}_{p}=\begin{bmatrix}1&1&\ldots&1\\
1&\ddots&&1\\
1&&\ddots&\vdots\\
1&1&\ldots&1\end{bmatrix}\in\real^{p\times p}.

It then follows that

\begin{bmatrix}\overline{{\textnormal{x}}}\\
{\textnormal{x}}_{1}-\overline{{\textnormal{x}}}\\
\vdots\\
{\textnormal{x}}_{p}-\overline{{\textnormal{x}}}\end{bmatrix}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(\begin{bmatrix}\mu\\
0\\
\vdots\\
0\end{bmatrix},\sigma^{2}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{p}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&{\bm{I}}_{p}-\frac{1}{p}{\bm{J}}_{p}\end{bmatrix}\right).

Therefore, we find that
\overline{{\textnormal{x}}}
is independent of
{\textnormal{x}}_{1}-\overline{{\textnormal{x}}},{\textnormal{x}}_{2}-\overline{{\textnormal{x}}},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{p}-\overline{{\textnormal{x}}}
.
In many applications, we may construct a random variable:

t\triangleq\sqrt{p}\frac{(\overline{{\textnormal{x}}}-\mu)/\sigma}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{p-1}\sum_{i}(x_{i}-\overline{{\textnormal{x}}})^{2}/\sigma^{2}}},

in which case, the numerator and the denominator are independent variables.

Induced norm properties
(
Lu 2021a

Consider the induced matrix norm in Definition

(a).

Given
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{n}

\frac{1}{a}+\frac{1}{a^{\star}}=1

{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{n}

.

(c).

.

Equivalence of matrix norms.

Similarly to the vector norms in Exercise

Let

The equivalence theorem again states that if a matrix is small in one norm, it is also small in other norms, and vice versa.

16.

Properties of expectation of conditionals.

Let
x
and
y
be two random variables, and let
h
be a function.
Show that

(a).

Note that
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}\mid{\textnormal{y}}]
is a function of
y
. However, if
x
is independent of

, then
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}\mid{\textnormal{y}}]={\textnormal{x}}
.

(b).

\mathbb{E}[c\mid{\textnormal{x}}]={\textnormal{x}}
, where
c
is a constant.

(c).

Linearity:
\mathbb{E}[a{\textnormal{x}}_{1}+b{\textnormal{x}}_{2}\mid{\textnormal{y}}]=a\cdot\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{1}\mid{\textnormal{y}}]+b\cdot\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{2}\mid{\textnormal{y}}]
.

(d).

Conditional constant:
\mathbb{E}[h({\textnormal{y}}){\textnormal{x}}\mid{\textnormal{y}}]=h({\textnormal{y}})\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}\mid{\textnormal{y}}]
, where
h({\textnormal{y}})
is called a
conditional constant
w.r.t.
y
.

(e).

Monotonicity: if
{\textnormal{x}}_{1}\leq{\textnormal{x}}_{2}
, then
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{1}\mid{\textnormal{y}}]\leq\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{2}\mid{\textnormal{y}}]
.

(f).

Tower property:
\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}\mid{\textnormal{y}}]\mid h({\textnormal{y}})\right]=\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}\mid h({\textnormal{y}})]
; that is,
h({\textnormal{y}})
conveys information at most as
y
.

(g).

Unbiasedness:
\mathbb{E}\big\{\mathbb{E}[h({\textnormal{x}},{\textnormal{y}})\mid{\textnormal{y}}]\big\}=\mathbb{E}[h({\textnormal{x}},{\textnormal{y}})]
; specially,
\mathbb{E}\big[\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}\mid{\textnormal{y}}]\big]=\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]
.

(h).

Least squares:
\mathbb{E}\big[\big({\textnormal{y}}-\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{y}}\mid{\textnormal{x}}]\big)^{2}\big]\leq\mathbb{E}\big[\big({\textnormal{y}}-h({\textnormal{x}})\big)^{2}\big]
for any function
h
. This also means
g({\textnormal{x}})\triangleq\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{y}}\mid{\textnormal{x}}]
is the best estimate in the least squares sense.

Theory

\nopagecolor

Chapter 2
Basics of Optimization

T
This chapter provides a concise yet self-contained introduction to the fundamental concepts of convex analysis and convex optimization. It covers essential topics such as convex sets and functions, subdifferentials, and optimality conditions. While the presentation is designed to equip the reader with the core tools needed for applications in statistics, machine learning, and signal processing, it is not intended to be exhaustive.
For a deeper and more comprehensive treatment—including advanced theoretical results, duality theory, constrained optimization, and specialized algorithms—the reader is encouraged to consult standard references in the field, such as
Bertsekas et al.
;
Boyd and Vandenberghe 2004
;
Bertsekas 2009
;
Foucart and Rauhut 2013
;
Rockafellar 1970
;
Lu 2025
.

2.1
Differentiable Functions and Differential Calculus

Differentiability and differential calculus form the backbone of mathematical analysis, particularly in the study of functions defined on multidimensional spaces.
This section introduces the fundamental concepts that allow us to quantify how a function changes with respect to its input variables.

Central to this discussion is the directional derivative, which measures the instantaneous rate of change of a function
f
at a point
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
in the direction of a given vector
{\bm{d}}
.

Definition 62
(Directional derivative, partial derivative).

Let
f
be a real-valued function defined on a set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}
, and let
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}
.
For any nonzero vector
{\bm{d}}\in\real^{p}
, the directional derivative of
f
at
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}
in the direction
{\bm{d}}
is defined—provided the limit exists—by

f^{\prime}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}};{\bm{d}})\triangleq\mathop{\lim}_{\mu\rightarrow 0}\frac{f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+\mu{\bm{d}})-f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})}{\mu}.

This quantity is also sometimes referred to as the Gâteaux derivative.

For each
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
, the directional derivative at
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
in the direction of the
i
-th standard basis vector
{\bm{e}}_{i}
(if it exists) is called the
i
-th partial derivative.
It is commonly denoted by
\frac{\partial f}{\partial\alpha_{i}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
,
D_{{\bm{e}}_{i}}f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
, or
\partial_{i}f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
.

Figure 2.1:
Plot for the function
f(\alpha,\beta)=\sqrt{\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}}
.
The partial derivatives at
[0,0]^{\top}
do not exist.

It is important to note that the existence of directional derivatives in all nonzero directions at a point does not guarantee the existence of partial derivatives—or, more generally, differentiability—at that point.
A classic example is the function
f(\alpha,\beta)=\sqrt{\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}}
(see Figure
).
Consider a direction
{\bm{d}}=[a,b]^{\top}
.
The partial derivatives at
[0,0]^{\top}
are

\displaystyle\frac{\partial f}{\partial\alpha}(0,0)

\displaystyle=\mathop{\lim}_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{\sqrt{(0+h)^{2}+0^{2}}}{h}=\mathop{\lim}_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{\left\lvert h\right\rvert}{h},

\displaystyle\frac{\partial f}{\partial\beta}(0,0)

\displaystyle=\mathop{\lim}_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{\sqrt{0^{2}+(0+h)^{2}}}{h}=\mathop{\lim}_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{\left\lvert h\right\rvert}{h}.

When
h>0
, the partial derivatives are 1; when
h<0
, the partial derivaties are
-1
. Since the left- and right-hand limits differ, the limit does not exist.

Definition 63
(Gradient).

If all the partial derivatives of a function
f
exist at a point
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}
, then the gradient of
f
at
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
is defined as the column vector consisting of these partial derivatives:

\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\partial f}{\partial\alpha_{1}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}),\frac{\partial f}{\partial\alpha_{2}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}),\ldots,\frac{\partial f}{\partial\alpha_{p}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\end{bmatrix}^{\top}\in\real^{p}.

Exercise
\thetheo

Show that a function may have all partial derivatives at a point yet fail to be continuous there (see Definition
).
Conversely, demonstrate that a function can be continuous everywhere but still lack partial derivatives at some points.

A function
f
defined on an open set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}
(see Definition
) is said to be
differentiable

at a point
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
if it admits a linear approximation near
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
.
This notion is formalized by
Fréchet differentiability
, which is stronger than merely requiring the existence of partial derivatives.

Definition 64
((Fréchet) differentiability).

Let
f:\real^{p}\rightarrow\real
.
The function
f
is said to be differentiable or Fréchet differentiability at
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
if there exists a vector
{\bm{g}}\in\real^{p}
such that

\mathop{\lim}_{{\bm{d}}\rightarrow\boldsymbol{0}}\frac{f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+{\bm{d}})-f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-{\bm{g}}^{\top}{\bm{d}}}{\left\lVert{\bm{d}}\right\rVert_{2}}=0.

The vector
{\bm{g}}
is unique and equals the gradient
\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
.

Moreover, a function
f
defined on an open set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}
is called
continuously differentiable
on
{\mathbb{S}}
if all its partial derivatives exist and are also continuous on
{\mathbb{S}}
.

Note that a function can be differentiable without being continuously differentiable.
A classical example is the univariate function:

f(\alpha)=\begin{cases}\alpha^{2}\sin(\frac{1}{\alpha}),&\text{if }\alpha\neq 0,\\
0,&\text{if }\alpha=0.\end{cases}

This function is differentiable everywhere on , including at
\alpha=0
. To see this, for
\alpha\neq 0
,
f(\alpha)
is a product of two differentiable functions (
\alpha^{2}
and
\sin(1/\alpha)
), hence it is differentiable.
At
\alpha=0
, the derivative is computed via the limit definition:

f^{\prime}(0)=\mathop{\lim}_{\mu\rightarrow 0}\frac{f(\mu)-f(0)}{\mu}=\mathop{\lim}_{\mu\rightarrow 0}\frac{\mu^{2}\sin(\frac{1}{\mu})-0}{\mu}=\mu\sin(\frac{1}{\mu})

Since
\left\lvert\sin(1/\mu)\right\rvert\leq 1
for all
\mu\neq 0
, the limit exists and is equal to 0. Thus,
f(\alpha)
is differentiable at
\alpha=0
with
f^{\prime}(0)=0
.
However,
f(\alpha)
is not continuously differentiable at
\alpha=0
. The derivative of
f(\alpha)
when
\alpha\neq 0
is

f^{\prime}(\alpha)=2\alpha\sin(\frac{1}{\alpha})-\cos(\frac{1}{\alpha}).

The limit
\mathop{\lim}_{\alpha\rightarrow 0}f^{\prime}(\alpha)
does not exist because the sine and cosine functions oscillate as
\alpha
approaches 0.

Lemma 65
(Gradient formula for directional derivatives).

If
f
is differentiable at
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}
, then for every direction
{\bm{d}}\in\real^{p}
, the directional derivative of
f
at
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
in the direction
{\bm{d}}
satisfies

f^{\prime}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}};{\bm{d}})=\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})^{\top}{\bm{d}},\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\text{for all }{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{S}}\text{ and }{\bm{d}}\in\real^{p}.

(2.1)

Proof
[of Lemma
]
The formula is obviously correct for
{\bm{d}}=\boldsymbol{0}
. We then assume that
{\bm{d}}\neq\boldsymbol{0}
. The differentiability of
f
implies that

0=\lim_{\mu\to 0^{+}}\frac{f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+\mu{\bm{d}})-f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\left\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}),\mu{\bm{d}}\right\rangle}{\left\lVert\mu{\bm{d}}\right\rVert_{2}}=\lim_{\mu\to 0^{+}}\left[\frac{f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+\mu{\bm{d}})-f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})}{\mu\left\lVert{\bm{d}}\right\rVert_{2}}-\frac{\left\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}),{\bm{d}}\right\rangle}{\left\lVert{\bm{d}}\right\rVert_{2}}\right].

Therefore,

\displaystyle f^{\prime}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}};{\bm{d}})=\lim_{\mu\to 0^{+}}\frac{f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+\mu{\bm{d}})-f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})}{\mu}

\displaystyle=\lim_{\mu\to 0^{+}}\left\{\left\lVert{\bm{d}}\right\rVert_{2}\left[\frac{f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+\mu{\bm{d}})-f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})}{\mu\left\lVert{\bm{d}}\right\rVert_{2}}-\frac{\left\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}),{\bm{d}}\right\rangle}{\left\lVert{\bm{d}}\right\rVert_{2}}\right]+\left\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}),{\bm{d}}\right\rangle\right\}

\displaystyle=\left\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}),{\bm{d}}\right\rangle.

This proves (
).

Recalling the differentiability of
f
at
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
, we have

\mathop{\lim}_{{\bm{d}}\rightarrow\boldsymbol{0}}\frac{f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+{\bm{d}})-f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})^{\top}{\bm{d}}}{\left\lVert{\bm{d}}\right\rVert_{2}}=0,\quad\text{for all }{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{S}},

(2.2)

or

f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+o(\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}),

(2.3)

where the
small-oh
function
o(\cdot):\real_{+}\rightarrow\real
is a one-dimensional function satisfying
\frac{o(\mu)}{\mu}\rightarrow 0
as
\mu\rightarrow 0^{+}
.
Therefore, any differentiable function ensures that
\mathop{\lim}_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\rightarrow{\bm{a}}}f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=f({\bm{a}})
. Hence,
any differentiable function is continuous
.

\paragrapharrow

Descent direction and steepest direction.
An important consequence of the gradient-directional derivative relationship (
) is that the gradient encodes the directions of steepest ascent and descent.

Lemma 66
(Steepest direction).

Let
f:\real^{p}\rightarrow\real
be differentiable at
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
. Among all unit directions
{\bm{d}}\in\real^{p}
(i.e.,
\left\lVert{\bm{d}}\right\rVert_{2}=1
), the directional derivative
f^{\prime}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}};{\bm{d}})
is maximized when
{\bm{d}}
points in the direction of
\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
, and minimized (most negative) when
{\bm{d}}
points in the opposite direction.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
For all
{\bm{d}}\in\real^{p}
satisfying
\left\lVert{\bm{d}}\right\rVert_{2}=1
,
by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality (Theorem
), we have

\displaystyle\left\lvert f^{\prime}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}};{\bm{d}})\right\rvert

\displaystyle=\left\lvert\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})^{\top}{\bm{d}}\right\rvert\leq\left\lVert\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\bm{d}}\right\rVert_{2}=\left\lVert\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\right\rVert_{2}.\quad

Equality holds if and only if
{\bm{d}}
is a scalar multiple of
{\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})}
. Since
\left\lVert{\bm{d}}\right\rVert_{2}=1
, the maximizing direction is
{\bm{d}}=\pm\frac{\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})}{\left\lVert\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\right\rVert_{2}}
.

Figure
illustrates the gradient field of a function
f:\real^{2}\to\real
.
The gradient vectors (shown as black arrows) are orthogonal to the contour lines. This orthogonality arises because the function is constant along each contour line, so the directional derivative in any tangent direction is zero. By (
), this implies
\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})^{\top}{\bm{d}}=0
for all tangent vectors
{\bm{d}}
, meaning the gradient must be normal to the level set.

Figure 2.2:
Contour lines of a function
f:\real^{2}\to\real
. The gradients at different points are represented by
black arrows, which are orthogonal to the contour lines.

Note that
{\bm{d}}=-\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
is called the
steepest descent direction
. More generally, any direction
{\bm{d}}
satisfying

f^{\prime}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}};{\bm{d}})<0

is called a
descent direction
at
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
.

Lemma 67
(Unconstrained and constrained descent property).

Let
f
be a continuously differentiable function over
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}
(resp.,
p
), and let
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
(resp.,
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}
). Suppose that
{\bm{d}}
is a descent direction of
f
at
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
. Then, there exists
\varepsilon>0
such that

f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+\eta{\bm{d}})<f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}),\quad\text{for any $\eta\in(0,\varepsilon]$.}

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Since
f^{\prime}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}};{\bm{d}})=\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})^{\top}{\bm{d}}<0
, it follows from the definition of the directional derivative (Definition
) that

\lim_{\eta\to 0^{+}}\frac{f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+\eta{\bm{d}})-f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})}{\eta}=f^{\prime}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}};{\bm{d}})<0.

Therefore, there exists an
\varepsilon>0
such that

\frac{f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+\eta{\bm{d}})-f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})}{\eta}<0

for any
\eta\in(0,\varepsilon]
, which completes the proof.

2.1.1
Second-Order Partial Derivative

The partial derivative
\frac{\partial f}{\partial\alpha_{i}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
is itself a real-valued function of
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
, and it may be partially differentiated again.
The
j
-th partial derivative of
\frac{\partial f}{\partial\alpha_{i}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
is defined as

\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial\alpha_{j}\partial\alpha_{i}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\frac{\partial\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial\alpha_{i}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\right)}{\partial\alpha_{j}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}).

This is called the (
j,i
)-th
second-order partial derivative
of function
f
.

A function
f
defined on an open set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq
is called
twice continuously differentiable
over
{\mathbb{S}}
if all its second-order partial derivatives exist and are continuous on
{\mathbb{S}}
.
In the setting of twice continuously differentiability,
the mixed partial derivatives are symmetric:

\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial\alpha_{j}\partial\alpha_{i}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial\alpha_{i}\partial\alpha_{j}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}).

The
Hessian
of the function
f
at a point
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{S}}

is the
p\times p

matrix of second-order partial derivatives:

\nabla^{2}f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial\alpha_{1}^{2}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})&\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial\alpha_{1}\partial\alpha_{2}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})&\ldots&\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial\alpha_{1}\partial\alpha_{p}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\\
\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial\alpha_{2}\partial\alpha_{1}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})&\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial\alpha_{2}\partial\alpha_{2}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})&\ldots&\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial\alpha_{2}\partial\alpha_{p}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\\
\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\
\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial\alpha_{p}\partial\alpha_{1}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})&\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial\alpha_{p}\partial\alpha_{2}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})&\ldots&\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial\alpha_{p}^{2}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\end{bmatrix}.

When
f
is twice continuously differentiable, this matrix is symmetric due to the equality of mixed partials.

Definition 68
(Twice differentiable).

By its definition, a differentiable function
f:{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}\rightarrow\real
is twice differentiable at a point
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
if there exist a matrix
\nabla^{2}f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\in\real^{p\times p}
such that

\mathop{\lim}_{{\bm{d}}\rightarrow\boldsymbol{0}}\frac{\left\lVert\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+{\bm{d}})-\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\nabla^{2}f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}){\bm{d}}\right\rVert_{2}}{\left\lVert{\bm{d}}\right\rVert_{2}}=0.

The matrix
\nabla^{2}f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\in\real^{p\times p}
is unique and coincides with the Hessian matrix of
f
at
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
.

Geometrically, the curvature of a function describes how quickly its slope changes; in one dimension, this is captured by the second derivative. In higher dimensions, the Hessian matrix encodes the curvature of the function in every direction.

Analogously to the gradient formula for directional derivatives (Lemma
), the second directional derivative is related to the Hessian as follows.

Lemma 69
(Hessian-directional derivative identity).

If a function
f:{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}\to\real
is twice differentiable, the second directional derivative
f^{\prime\prime}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}};{\bm{d}})
of
f
at
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
equals

f^{\prime\prime}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}};{\bm{d}})={\bm{d}}^{\top}\nabla^{2}f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}){\bm{d}},

(2.4)

for any unit-norm vector
{\bm{d}}\in\real^{p}
.

2.1.2
Functions of Several Real Variables

We now present several classical approximation theorems that rely on derivatives and related concepts.

{theoremHigh}

[Rolle’s theorem]
Let
f(\alpha)
be continuous on the closed interval
[a,b]
and differentiable on
(a,b)
.
If
f(a)=f(b)
, then there exist at least one point
\xi\in(a,b)
such that
f^{\prime}(\xi)=0
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
We simply note that either
f
is constant, in which case
f^{\prime}(\alpha)=0
for all
\alpha
in
(a,b)
, or it has a local maximum or minimum at
\xi\in(a,b)
, in which case
f^{\prime}(\xi)=0
.

Rolle’s Theorem is primarily used as a key step in proving the ordinary mean value theorem (OMVT).

{theoremHigh}
[Ordinary mean value theorem (OMVT)]
Let
f(\alpha)
be continuous on the closed interval
[a,b]
and differentiable on
(a,b)
. Then, there exists a point
\xi\in(a,b)
such that

f(b)-f(a)=f^{\prime}(\xi)(b-a).

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Define the auxiliary function

g(\alpha)\triangleq f(\alpha)-\left(\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}\right)(\alpha-a).

It holds that
g(a)=g(b)
. Then by Rolle’s theorem, there exists
\xi\in(a,b)
such that
g^{\prime}(\xi)=0
, which rearranges to the desired identity:

f(b)-f(a)=f^{\prime}(\xi)(b-a).

This completes the proof.

For functions of several variables, an analogous result holds, though it takes a slightly different form due to the vector-valued nature of the gradient.

{theoremHigh}
[Mean value theorem (MVT)]
Let
f:{\mathbb{S}}\rightarrow\real
be a continuously differentiable function on an open set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}
, and given two points
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
. Then, there exists a point
{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\in[{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}]
such that

f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\xi}})^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}).

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Without loss of generality, we assume
{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t)={\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+t({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
with
t\in[0,1]
.
Then we define
g(t)\triangleq f({\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t))
. We can apply the ordinary mean value theorem to
g(t)
, to get

g(1)=g(0)+g^{\prime}(\gamma),

for some
\gamma
in the interval
[0,1]
. The derivative of
g(t)
is

g^{\prime}(t)=\left\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t)),{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rangle,

where

\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t))=\left[\frac{\partial f}{\partial\alpha_{1}}({\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t)),\frac{\partial f}{\partial\alpha_{2}}({\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t)),\ldots,\frac{\partial f}{\partial\alpha_{p}}({\boldsymbol{\xi}}(t))\right]^{\top}.

Therefore,

g^{\prime}(\gamma)=\left\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\xi}}(\gamma)),{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rangle.

Since
{\boldsymbol{\xi}}(\gamma)=(1-\gamma){\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+\gamma{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
, this completes the proof.

{theoremHigh}

[Linear approximation theorem]
Let
f:{\mathbb{S}}\rightarrow\real
be a twice continuously differentiable function on an open set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}
, and let
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
. Then, there exists a point
{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\in[{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}]
such that

\displaystyle f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})

\displaystyle=f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\frac{1}{2}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})^{\top}\nabla^{2}f({\boldsymbol{\xi}})({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}),

\displaystyle\text{or}\quad f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})

\displaystyle=f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+o(\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}),

\displaystyle\text{or}\quad f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})

\displaystyle=f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\mathcal{O}(\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}).

This theorem, also known as the
first-order Taylor series expansion
, suggests that the error in the linear approximation is of the order of the square of the distance between
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
and
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.
And the first-order Taylor series expansion
f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\approx f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
is exact only for the neighborhood of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
at the point
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
,

{theoremHigh}

[Quadratic approximation theorem]
Let
f:{\mathbb{S}}\rightarrow\real
be a twice continuously differentiable function on an open set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}
, and let
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
. Then it follows that

\displaystyle f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})

\displaystyle=f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\frac{1}{2}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})^{\top}\nabla^{2}f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+o(\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}),

\displaystyle\text{or}\quad f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})

\displaystyle=f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\frac{1}{2}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})^{\top}\nabla^{2}f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\mathcal{O}(\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{3}).

This theorem indicates that the error in the quadratic approximation is of the order of the cube of the distance between
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
and
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
, making it a more accurate approximation when
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is close to
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
.

2.1.3
Fundamental Theorem of Calculus

We now present the
undamental theorem of calculus
in a multivariate setting. This result plays a pivotal role in connecting differential and integral calculus, offering deep insight into the structure and behavior of smooth functions.

{theoremHigh}
[Fundamental theorem of calculus]
Let
f:\real^{p}\rightarrow\real
be a continuously differentiable function, and let
{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}
.
Then the difference between function values can be expressed as

f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\int_{0}^{1}\left\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+\mu({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})),{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rangle d\mu.

(2.5a)

If, in addition,
f
is twice continuously differentiable, then the difference between gradients satisfies

\displaystyle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})

\displaystyle=\left(\int_{0}^{1}\nabla^{2}f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+\mu({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}))d\mu\right)\cdot({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}});

(2.5b)

\displaystyle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+\eta{\bm{d}})-\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})

\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{\eta}\nabla^{2}f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+\mu{\bm{d}}){\bm{d}}d\mu.

(2.5c)

where
\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
denotes the gradient of
f
evaluated at
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
,

\nabla^{2}f(\cdot)
the Hessian matrix, and
\left\langle\cdot,\cdot\right\rangle
the standard Euclidean inner product.
Furthermore, use directional derivative for twice continuously differentiable functions, we also have

f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\left\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}),({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\right\rangle+\int_{0}^{1}(1-\mu)\frac{\partial^{2}f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+\mu({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}))}{\partial\mu^{2}}d\mu.

(2.5d)

The first equality (
) can be derived by defining the auxiliary scalar function
g(t)\triangleq f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+t({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}))
. Then we can obtain
f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
as

f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=g(1)=g(0)+\int_{0}^{1}g^{\prime}(t)dt.

The remaining identities can be demonstrated similarly.

2.2
Convex Combinations and Convex Sets

This section introduces the concepts of affine, convex, and conic combinations and their associated hulls, in the context of vector sets in
p
.
We provide precise definitions and mathematical formulations for these fundamental geometric constructs.

Interior Points and Closed Sets

Given a set of vectors
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{1},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{2},\ldots,{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{k}\in\real^{p}
,
an
affine combination
of these
k
vectors is a vector of the form
\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{i}
, where
\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i}=1
, i.e., a linear combination of these points where the coefficients (not necessarily nonnegative) sum to 1.
A
convex combination
of these
k
vectors is a vector of the form
\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{i}
, where
\lambda_{i}\geq 0
for
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,k\}
satisfying
\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i}=1
(i.e.,
\{\lambda_{i}\}
belongs to the unit-simplex in
p
:
{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\Delta_{k}
);
when only requiring
\lambda_{i}\geq 0
without the constraint on their sum, the combination is referred to as a
conic combination
of these vectors.

After fixing a norm on
p
, we introduced open and closed balls in Definition
.
These notions lead naturally to the concepts of interior and relative interior points, which are foundational in topology and convex analysis.

Definition 70
(Affine hulls).

The affine hull of a set
{\mathbb{S}}
, denoted
\text{aff}({\mathbb{S}})
, is the smallest affine subspace (a translation of a vector subspace) that contains
{\mathbb{S}}
.
Formally, given a set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}
, the affine hull of
{\mathbb{S}}
is defined as the set of all affine combinations of points from
{\mathbb{S}}
:

\text{aff}({\mathbb{S}})\triangleq\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{i}\mid{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{1},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{2},\ldots,{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{k}\in{\mathbb{S}},\lambda_{i}\in\real,{\bm{1}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}=1,k\in\mathbb{N}\right\}.

Definition 71
(Interior and relative interior points).

The interior of a set
{\mathbb{S}}
in a topological space is the set of all points in
{\mathbb{S}}
that admit a neighborhood entirely contained in
{\mathbb{S}}
.
Formally, the interior of
{\mathbb{S}}
, denoted
\text{int}({\mathbb{S}})
, is defined as:

\text{int}({\mathbb{S}})=\{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{S}}\mid\exists\,\epsilon>0\text{ such that }{\mathbb{B}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}},\epsilon)\subseteq{\mathbb{S}}\}.

where
{\mathbb{B}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}},\epsilon)
denotes the open ball centered at
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
with radius
\epsilon
.

The relative interior of a set
{\mathbb{S}}
in a topological space is the interior of
{\mathbb{S}}
relative to its affine hull.
The relative interior of
{\mathbb{S}}
, denoted
\text{relint}({\mathbb{S}})
, is given by:

\text{relint}({\mathbb{S}})=\{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{S}}\mid\exists\,\epsilon>0\text{ such that }{\mathbb{B}}_{\text{aff}({\mathbb{S}})}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}},\epsilon)\subseteq{\mathbb{S}}\}.

where
{\mathbb{B}}_{\text{aff}({\mathbb{S}})}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}},\epsilon)
is the open ball centered at
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
with radius
\epsilon
in the subspace topology of
\text{aff}({\mathbb{S}})
.

In other words, the
interior
of a set is concerned with the open balls in the ambient space; the
relative interior
is concerned with open balls in the affine hull of the set, i.e., it considers neighborhoods only within the lower-dimensional affine subspace that actually contains
{\mathbb{S}}
.
This is particularly important in higher dimensions and in convex analysis where the set may lie in a lower-dimensional subspace.

Example 72
(Interior and relative interior points).

Interval in .
Let
{\mathbb{S}}=[0,1]
. Then
\text{int}({\mathbb{S}})=(0,1)
and
\text{relint}({\mathbb{S}})=(0,1)
. Here, the interior and relative interior are the same because the set
[0,1]
is a subset of and
\text{aff}({\mathbb{S}})=\real
.

Line Segment in
2
.

Let
{\mathbb{S}}=\{(x,y)\in\real^{2}\mid 0\leq x\leq 1,y=0\}
with

\text{aff}({\mathbb{S}})=\{(x,0)\in\real^{2}\mid x\in\real\}
. Then
\text{int}({\mathbb{S}})=\varnothing
and
\text{relint}({\mathbb{S}})=\{(x,0)\mid 0<x<1\}
.
The interior is empty because there are no open balls in
2
entirely contained within
{\mathbb{S}}
. However, the relative interior is the open interval (0, 1) in the context of the line segment (the affine hull is the line
y=0
).

Triangle in
2
.

Let
{\mathbb{S}}
be the (filled) triangle with vertices at
(0,0)
,
(1,0)
, and
(0,1)
. Then the interior consists of all points strictly inside the triangle, excluding the boundary;
and the relative interior is the same as the interior in this case because the affine hull of the triangle is the entire plane
2
.

Definition 73
(Open, closed, compact, and level sets).

A set
{\mathbb{S}}_{1}
is said to be open if it consists of only interior points. That is, for every
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
, there exists a scalar
s>0
such that
{\mathbb{B}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}},s)\subseteq{\mathbb{S}}_{1}
.

A set
{\mathbb{S}}_{2}
is said to be closed if its complement
{\mathbb{S}}_{2}^{c}
is open.
Alternatively,
{\mathbb{S}}_{2}
is closed if it contains all the limit points of convergent sequence of points in
{\mathbb{S}}_{2}
; that is, for every sequence of points
\{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{i}\}_{i\geq 1}\subseteq{\mathbb{S}}_{2}
satisfying
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{i}\rightarrow{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{\star}
as
i\rightarrow\infty
, it follows that
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{\star}\in{\mathbb{S}}_{2}
.
In the meantime, the closure of a set
{\mathbb{S}}
, denoted
\text{cl}({\mathbb{S}})
, is defined as the smallest closed set containing
{\mathbb{S}}
:

\text{cl}({\mathbb{S}})=\cap\left\{{\mathbb{T}}\mid{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq{\mathbb{T}},{\mathbb{T}}\text{ is closed}\right\}.

A set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}
is called bounded if there exists
M>0
for which
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq{\mathbb{B}}(\boldsymbol{0},M)
, where
{\mathbb{B}}(\boldsymbol{0},M)
is the ball of finite radius
M
centered at the origin.
A set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}
is called compact if it is closed and bounded.

Given a function
f:{\mathbb{S}}\rightarrow\real
where
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}
, the level set of
f
at a particular value
c\in\real
is defined as:

\mathrm{Lev}[f,c]=\{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{S}}\mid f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\leq c\}.\penalty\

In other words, the level set
\mathrm{Lev}[f,c]
consists of all points
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
in the domain
{\mathbb{S}}
for which the function
f
evaluates to smaller than or equal to the constant
c
.

Exercise
\thetheo
(Interior and closure)

Let
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}
be a convex set with a nonempty interior. Show that

\text{cl}(\text{int}({\mathbb{S}}))=\text{cl}({\mathbb{S}})\qquad\text{and}\qquad\text{int}(\text{cl}({\mathbb{S}}))=\text{int}({\mathbb{S}}).

Convex Sets

For vectors
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
and
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
, any point of the form
\lambda{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+(1-\lambda){\boldsymbol{\beta}}
with
\lambda\in[0,1]
is called a
convex combination
of the two vectors.
A set that is closed under all such convex combinations is known as a convex set.
The standard definition follows:

Definition 74
(Convex sets).

A set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}
is called convex if, for any
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
and
\lambda\in[0,1]
, the point
\lambda{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+(1-\lambda){\boldsymbol{\beta}}
also belongs to
{\mathbb{S}}
.

By definition, it is straightforward to verify that a set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}
is convex if and only if it contains every convex combination of finitely many of its points.
That is, for any
k\in\mathbb{N}
, any
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{1},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{2},\ldots,{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{k}\in{\mathbb{S}}
and
\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\ldots,\lambda_{k}\geq 0
such that
\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i}=1
, the convex combination
\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{i}
is also contained in
{\mathbb{S}}
.
For an arbitrary (possibly non-convex) set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}
, its
convex hull
is defined as the collection of all such convex combinations:

Definition 75
(Convex hulls).

The convex hull of a set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}
, denoted
\text{conv}({\mathbb{S}})
, is the set of all convex combinations of points in
{\mathbb{S}}
:

\text{conv}({\mathbb{S}})\triangleq\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{i}\mid{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{1},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{2},\ldots,{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{k}\in{\mathbb{S}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\Delta_{k},k\in\mathbb{N}\right\},

where
\Delta_{k}=\{(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\ldots,\lambda_{k})\mid\lambda_{i}\geq 0,\sum_{i}^{k}\lambda_{i}=1\}
is the standard
(k-1)
unit-simplex.

The intersection of any collection of convex sets is itself convex. Geometrically, a convex set contains the entire line segment joining any two of its points (see Figure
). Consequently, such sets have no “inward dents” or concave regions.

Example 76
.

Common examples of convex sets include affine subspaces, linear subspaces, half spaces,
polygons, and norm balls of the form
{\mathbb{B}}_{\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert}[{\bm{c}},r]
, where
{\bm{c}}
is the center,
r>0
is the radius, and
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert
is a given norm (see Definition
).

Exercise
\thetheo
(Closure of convex)

Let
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}
be a convex set. Show that the closure
\text{cl}({\mathbb{S}})
is also convex.

Figure 2.3:

A set is convex if it contains all convex combinations of its points. If even a single convex combination of points in the set lies outside the set, then the set is not convex. Thus, convex sets must be “bulge-free” and lack inward indentations. Notably, the set of sparse vectors fails this property and is therefore non-convex. The illustration is adapted from
Jain et al. 2017
.

Definition 77
(Cones and convex cones).

A set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}
is called a cone if, for every
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
and
\lambda\geq 0
, the scaled vector
\lambda{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
also belongs to
{\mathbb{S}}
.
A set
{\mathbb{S}}
is a convex cone if it is both a cone and a convex set.

The conic hull of a set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}
is the smallest
convex cone
that contains
{\mathbb{S}}
.

Definition 78
(Conic hulls).

The conic hull of
{\mathbb{S}}
, denoted
\text{cone}({\mathbb{S}})
, is the set consisting of all the conic combinations of vectors from
{\mathbb{S}}
:

\text{cone}({\mathbb{S}})\triangleq\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{i}\mid{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{1},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{2},\ldots,{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{k}\in{\mathbb{S}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{k}_{+},k\in\mathbb{N}\right\}.

Obviously, the zero vector always belongs to any cone.
A set
{\mathbb{S}}
is a convex cone if, for all
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
and
a,b\geq 0
, the conic combination
a{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+b{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
.

Example 79
(Convex cone).

Common examples of convex cones include: the positive orthant
\real{}_{+}^{p}=\{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}\mid\beta_{i}\geq 0\text{ for all }i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}\}
or the set of positive semidefinite matrices in
p×p
.
Another important example of a convex cone is the second-order cone (also known as the Lorentz cone):

\left\{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p+1}\mid\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{p}\beta_{i}^{2}}\leq\beta_{p+1}\right\}.

Definition 80
(Dual cone and polar cone).

Let
{\mathbb{S}}\subset\real^{p}
be a cone.
Its dual conej, denoted
{\mathbb{S}}^{*}
, is defined as

{\mathbb{S}}^{*}\triangleq\left\{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}\mid\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle\geq 0\text{ for all }{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{S}}\right\}.

(2.6)

The polar cone, denoted
{\mathbb{S}}^{\circ}
, is closely related to the dual cone, which is defined as

{\mathbb{S}}^{\circ}\triangleq\left\{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}\mid\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle\leq 0\text{ for all }{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{S}}\right\}=-{\mathbb{S}}^{*}.

(2.7)

Since the dual cone is defined as the intersection of half spaces,
{\mathbb{S}}^{*}
is always closed and convex, and it is straightforward to check that
{\mathbb{S}}^{*}
is itself a cone.
If
{\mathbb{S}}
is a closed cone, then
{\mathbb{S}}^{**}={\mathbb{S}}
. Moreover, if
{\mathbb{T}},{\mathbb{S}}\subset\real^{p}
are cones such that
{\mathbb{T}}\subset{\mathbb{S}}
, then
{\mathbb{S}}^{*}\subset{\mathbb{T}}^{*}
.

Example 81
(Dual cone).

The dual cone of the positive orthant
\real{}_{+}^{p}
is
\real{}_{+}^{p}
itself; in other words,
\real{}_{+}^{p}
is self-dual.

We now turn to the notion of extreme points.

Definition 82
(Extreme points).

Let
{\mathbb{S}}\subset\real^{p}
be a convex set. A point
{\bm{z}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
is called an extreme point of
{\mathbb{S}}
if,
whenever
{\bm{z}}=\lambda{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+(1-\lambda){\boldsymbol{\beta}}
for
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
and
\lambda\in(0,1)
,
it follows that
{\bm{z}}={\boldsymbol{\alpha}}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.

Compact (i.e., closed and bounded) convex sets can be fully characterized by their extreme points, as formalized below.

{theoremHigh}
[Compact convex sets via extreme points]
Every compact (i.e., closed and bounded) convex set is equal to the convex hull of its extreme points.

Proof

See
Rockafellar 1970
, Section 18.

For instance, if
{\mathbb{S}}
is a polygon in
2
, its extreme points are precisely its vertices (the zero-dimensional faces), and the theorem aligns with the intuitive idea that the polygon is “built” from its corners.

2.3
Convex Functions

A closely related concept is that of convex functions, which exhibit a specific inequality behavior under convex combinations.
Before introducing convex functions, we note that we work with
extended real-valued
functions
f:\real^{p}\to\widetilde{\real}\triangleq(-\infty,\infty]=\real\cup\{+\infty\}
.
Arithmetic operations and inequalities in
(-\infty,\infty]
are interpreted in the natural way; for instance,
\alpha+\infty=\infty
for all
\alpha\in\real
,
\lambda\cdot\infty=\infty
for
\lambda>0
,
\alpha<\infty
for all
\alpha\in\real
,
\infty\leq\infty
. The
domain
of an extended real-valued function
f
is defined as

\mathrm{dom}(f)=\{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}\mid f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\neq\infty\}.

A function with
\mathrm{dom}(f)\neq\varnothing
is called
proper
: that is, (i). The function never takes on the value
-\infty
; (ii). The function does not attain the value
+\infty
everywhere.
A function
f:{\mathbb{S}}\to\real
defined on a subset
{\mathbb{S}}\subset\real^{p}
can be extended to an extended valued function by setting
f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\infty
for
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\notin{\mathbb{S}}
.
This extension satisfies
\mathrm{dom}(f)={\mathbb{S}}
and is referred to as the
canonical extension
of
f
.

We now recall the definition of a convex function.

Definition 83
(Convex functions).

A function
f:{\mathbb{S}}\rightarrow\real
defined over a convex set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}
is called convex if

f(\lambda{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+(1-\lambda){\boldsymbol{\beta}})\leq\lambda f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+(1-\lambda)f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}),\text{ for any }{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}},\lambda\in[0,1].

Moreover,
f
is called strictly convex if

f(\lambda{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+(1-\lambda){\boldsymbol{\beta}})<\lambda f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+(1-\lambda)f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}),\text{ for any }{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\neq{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}},\lambda\in(0,1).

A function
f
is
concave
(resp.,
strictly concave
) if
-f
is convex (resp., strictly convex).
Note that the domain of any convex function is necessarily a convex set, and a function
f:{\mathbb{S}}\to\real
on a convex subset
{\mathbb{S}}\subset\real^{p}
is called convex if its canonical extension to
p
is convex.

An equivalent and geometrically insightful characterization is that a function
f
is convex if and only if its
epigraph

\mathrm{epi}(f)\triangleq\{({\boldsymbol{\alpha}},r)\in{\mathbb{S}}\times\real\mid f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\leq r\}\subseteq\real^{p}\times\real

(2.8)

is a convex set of
p+1
.

Example 84
(Convex, strictly convex).

Let
f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})={\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+{\bm{y}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+z
.
Then the function is

Convex if and only if
{\bm{X}}\succeq\boldsymbol{0}
; strictly convex if and only if
{\bm{X}}\succ\boldsymbol{0}
.

Concave if and only if
{\bm{X}}\preceq\boldsymbol{0}
; strictly concave if and only if
{\bm{X}}\prec\boldsymbol{0}
.

The proofs are easy if we use the second-order characterization of convexity (see Theorem
).

Exercise
\thetheo
(Convexity of directional derivatives)

Suppose the function
f
is a continuously differentiable convex function.
Show that the directional derivative (Definition
)
g({\bm{d}})\triangleq f^{\prime}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}};{\bm{d}})
is also convex.

Exercise
\thetheo
(Convexity of quadratic functions)

Let
f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\frac{1}{2}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+{\bm{y}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+z
, where
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{p\times p}
is symmetric,
{\bm{y}}\in\real^{p}
, and
z\in\real
. Show that
f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
is convex (resp., strictly convex) if and only if
{\bm{X}}\succeq\boldsymbol{0}
(resp.,
{\bm{X}}\succ\boldsymbol{0}
).

Exercise
\thetheo
(Convexity of indicator)

Show that the
indicator function
(also called the
characterization function
)
\delta_{\mathbb{S}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}):\real^{p}\rightarrow\real
, which is
0
if
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
belongs to the set
{\mathbb{S}}
and
+\infty
otherwise, is convex if and only if the set
{\mathbb{S}}
is convex.

Exercise
\thetheo
(Convexity of norm functions)

Show that the norm functions
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
and
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{1}
are convex.
More generally, show that

The
\ell_{s}
-norm functions
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{s}
are strictly convex if
1<s<\infty
, and they are
not
strictly convex if
s=1
or
s=\infty
.

For a nondecreasing convex function
f:\real\to(-\infty,\infty]
and a norm
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert
on
p
, the function
g({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=f(\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert)
is convex.
In particular, the function
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\mapsto\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert^{k}
is convex provided that
k\geq 1
.

The exercises above show that standard norm functions are convex. However, the so-called “
\ell_{0}
-norm”—defined as the number of nonzero entries in a vector—is not convex.
Despite its name, it is not a true norm because it fails to satisfy positive homogeneity: for any nonzero
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}
, we have
\left\lVert 2{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{0}=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{0}\neq 2\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{0}
; see Definition
.

Lemma 85
(
\ell_{0}
-norm is not convex).

The
\ell_{0}
-norm function, defined as the number of nonzero entries in a vector, is not convex.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Consider a simple counterexample in
2
.
Let
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\triangleq\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}1\\
0\end{bmatrix}\normalsize
and
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\triangleq\footnotesize\begin{bmatrix}0\\
1\end{bmatrix}\normalsize
.
Then, for any
\lambda\in(0,1)
,

\left\lVert\lambda{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+(1-\lambda){\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{0}=2>1=\lambda\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{0}+(1-\lambda)\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{0}.

This violates the definition of convexity. The same idea extends directly to
p
, completing the proof.

The rank of a matrix, when viewed as a function of its entries, is also not convex.

Lemma 86
(The rank is not convex).

The rank function
\mathrm{rank}(\cdot):\real^{p\times p}\rightarrow\real
is not convex on the space of square matrices.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
