We provide a counterexample analogous to the one used in the proof of Lemma
.
Let

{\bm{X}}\triangleq\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\
0&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad{\bm{Y}}\triangleq\begin{bmatrix}0&0\\
0&1\end{bmatrix}.

For any
\lambda\in(0,1)
,

\mathrm{rank}\left(\lambda{\bm{X}}+(1-\lambda){\bm{Y}}\right)=2>1=\lambda\,\mathrm{rank}({\bm{X}})+(1-\lambda)\,\mathrm{rank}({\bm{Y}}).

Extending this counterexample into
p×p
completes the proof.

2.3.1
Properties of Convex Functions

A well-known inequality that follows from the definition of convex functions is stated below without proof.

{theoremHigh}
[Jensen’s inequality]
Let
f:{\mathbb{S}}\rightarrow\real
be a convex function defined on a convex subset
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}
. For any finite sequence of points
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{1},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{2},\ldots,{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{k}\in{\mathbb{S}}
and any sequence of nonnegative weights
\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3},\ldots,\lambda_{k}
such that
\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i}=1
, Jensen’s inequality states:

f\left(\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{i}\right)\leq\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i}f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{i}).

If
f
is concave, the inequality is reversed:

f\left(\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{i}\right)\geq\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i}f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{i}).

In the context of probability theory, if
{\mathbf{x}}
is a random vector taking values in
{\mathbb{S}}
and
f
is a convex function,
Jensen’s inequality takes the form:

f(\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{x}}])\leq\mathbb{E}[f({\mathbf{x}})],

where
\mathbb{E}[\cdot]
denotes the expectation operator over the random vector
{\mathbf{x}}
. For a concave function, the inequality is again reversed.

Next, we consider the maximum of a convex function over a convex set.

{theoremHigh}

[Attainment of maximum]
Let
{\mathbb{S}}\subset\real^{p}
be a compact (closed and bounded) convex set, and
f:{\mathbb{S}}\to\real
be a convex function. Then
f
attains its maximum at an extreme point of
{\mathbb{S}}
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Let
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
such that
f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\geq f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
for all
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
. Since
{\mathbb{S}}
is the convex hull of its extreme points (Theorem
), we can write
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{i}
for some
k
,
where
\lambda_{i}>0
,
\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i}=1
, and each
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{i}
is an extreme point of
{\mathbb{S}}
.
By convexity and the assumption of
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
, we have

f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=f\left(\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{i}\right)\leq\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i}f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{i})\leq\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i}f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}).

Hence, both inequalities are equalities, which implies
f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{i})=f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
for all
i=1,2,\ldots,k
. Therefore, the maximum of
f
is attained at an extreme point of
{\mathbb{S}}
.

We say that a function
f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}})
of two arguments
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{q}
,
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
is jointly convex if it is convex as a function of the variable
{\bm{z}}=({\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}})
.
Partial minimization of a jointly convex function with respect to one block of variables preserves convexity, as stated below.

{theoremHigh}
[Preservation under partial infimum]
Let
f:\real^{q}\times\real^{p}\to(-\infty,\infty]
be a jointly convex function. Then the function
g({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\triangleq\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}})
,
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{q}
, is convex.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
For simplicity, assume that the infimum is attained for every
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
.
The general case has to be treated with an
\varepsilon
-argument.
Given
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{1},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{2}\in\real^{q}
, there exist
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}\in\real^{p}
such that

f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{1},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1})=\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{1},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}),\quad f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{2},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2})=\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{2},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}).

For any
\lambda\in[0,1]
, the minimization of
g
and joint convexity of
f
implies that

\displaystyle g(\lambda{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{1}+(1-\lambda){\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{2})

\displaystyle\leq f(\lambda{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{1}+(1-\lambda){\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{2},\lambda{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1}+(1-\lambda){\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2})

\displaystyle\leq\lambda f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{1},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1})+(1-\lambda)f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{2},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2})=\lambda g({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{1})+(1-\lambda)g({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{2}).

Thus,
g
is convex, completing the proof.

Clearly, the same reasoning shows that partial maximization of a jointly concave function yields a concave function.
The following operations also preserve convexity. These results are left as an exercise.

Exercise
\thetheo
(Preservation of convexity)

Prove the following results:

1.

Let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{p\times p}
and
{\bm{y}}\in\real^{p}
, and let
f:\real^{p}\rightarrow(-\infty,\infty]
be an extended real-valued convex function. Then the function

g({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=f({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+{\bm{y}})

is convex.

2.

Let
f:\real\to\real
be convex and nondecreasing, and let
g:\real^{p}\to\real
be convex. Then the function
h({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=f(g({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}))
is convex.

3.

Let
f_{1},f_{2},\ldots,f_{k}:\real^{p}\rightarrow(-\infty,\infty]
be extended real-valued convex functions, and let
\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2},\ldots,\sigma_{k}\in\real_{+}
. Then the function
f=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sigma_{i}f_{i}
is convex.

4.

Let
f_{i}:\real^{p}\rightarrow(-\infty,\infty],i\in{\mathbb{I}}
be extended real-valued convex functions, where
{\mathbb{I}}
is a given index set. Then the function

f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\max_{i\in{\mathbb{I}}}f_{i}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})

is convex.

Hint: the epigraph of
\max_{i\in{\mathbb{I}}}f_{i}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
is the intersection of the epigraphs of functions
f_{i}
.

{theoremHigh}

[Local is global in convex functions]
Let
f:{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}\to\real
(or
f:\real^{p}\to\real\cup\{\infty\}
) be convex over a convex set
{\mathbb{S}}
.

1.

A local minimum of
f
is a global minimum. If
f
is strictly convex, then the minimum is unique.

2.

The set of minimizers of
f
is convex. If
f
is strictly convex, then the set is a
singleton
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]

(i).
Suppose
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}
is a local minimum of
f
over
{\mathbb{S}}
. There exists a scalar
\tau>0
such that
f({\boldsymbol{\theta}})\geq f({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}})
for any
{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
satisfying
{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\in{\mathbb{B}}[{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}},\tau]
. Now let
{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
satisfy
{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}\neq{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}
. It suffices to show that
f({\boldsymbol{\gamma}})\geq f({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}})
. Let
\lambda\in(0,1]
be such that
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}+\lambda({\boldsymbol{\gamma}}-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}})\in{\mathbb{B}}[{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}},\tau]
. An example of such
\lambda
is
\lambda=\frac{\tau}{\left\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}\right\rVert_{2}}
. Since
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}+\lambda({\boldsymbol{\gamma}}-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}})\in{\mathbb{B}}[{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}},\tau]\cap{\mathbb{S}}
, it follows that

f({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}})\leq f({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}+\lambda({\boldsymbol{\gamma}}-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}})),

and hence by Jensen’s inequality (Theorem
)

f({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}})\leq f({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}+\lambda({\boldsymbol{\gamma}}-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}))\leq(1-\lambda)f({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}})+\lambda f({\boldsymbol{\gamma}}).

Therefore, we obtain
f({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}})\leq f({\boldsymbol{\gamma}})
.

A slight modification of the above argument shows that any local minimum of a strictly convex function over a convex set is indeed a strict global minimum of the function over the set.

(ii).

Let
\Theta\triangleq\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}\{f({\boldsymbol{\theta}}):{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}\}
. If
\Theta=\varnothing
, the result follows trivially.
We then assume that
\Theta\neq\varnothing
and denote the optimal value by
f^{*}
.
Let
{\boldsymbol{\theta}},{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}\in\Theta
be two different minimizers and
\lambda\in[0,1]
. Then, by Jensen’s inequality
f(\lambda{\boldsymbol{\theta}}+(1-\lambda){\boldsymbol{\gamma}})\leq\lambda f^{*}+(1-\lambda)f^{*}=f^{*}
, and hence
\lambda{\boldsymbol{\theta}}+(1-\lambda){\boldsymbol{\gamma}}
is also a minimmizer, i.e., it belongs to
\Theta
, establishing the convexity of
\Theta
.
Suppose now that
f
is strictly convex and
\Theta
is nonempty; to show that
\Theta
is a singleton, suppose in contradiction that there exist
{\boldsymbol{\theta}},{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}\in\Theta
such that
{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\neq{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}
. Then
\frac{1}{2}{\boldsymbol{\theta}}+\frac{1}{2}{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
, and by the strict convexity of
f
, we have

f\left(\frac{1}{2}{\boldsymbol{\theta}}+\frac{1}{2}{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}\right)<\frac{1}{2}f({\boldsymbol{\theta}})+\frac{1}{2}f({\boldsymbol{\gamma}})=\frac{1}{2}f^{*}+\frac{1}{2}f^{*}=f^{*},

which leads to a contradiction to the fact that
f^{*}
is the optimal value.
Therefore,
\Theta
must be a singleton.

The fact that every local minimum of a convex function is automatically a global minimum is the key reason why convex optimization problems admit efficient solution methods; see Section
for further details.

2.3.2
Characterization of Convex Functions

\paragrapharrow

First-order characterizations of convex functions.
Convex functions need not be differentiable. However, when they are differentiable, they can be characterized by the
gradient inequality
.

{theoremHigh}
[Gradient inequality]
Let
f:{\mathbb{S}}\rightarrow\real
be a continuously differentiable function defined on a convex set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}
. Then,
f
is convex over
{\mathbb{S}}
if and only if

f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\leq f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}),\text{ for any ${\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}$}.

(2.9a)

Similarly, the function is strictly convex on
{\mathbb{S}}
if and only if

f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})<f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}),\text{ for any ${\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\neq{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}$}.

(2.9b)

Geometrically, this means that the graph of a convex function lies above its tangent hyperplane at any point. For concave (or strictly concave) functions, the inequality signs are reversed.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
For brevity, we prove only (
); the proof of (
) is analogous.
Suppose that
f
is convex. Let
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
and
\lambda\in[0,1]
. If
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}
, then (
) trivially holds. We will therefore assume that
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\neq{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.
By convexity

f(\lambda{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+(1-\lambda){\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\leq\lambda f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+(1-\lambda)f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\;\implies\;\frac{f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+\lambda({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}))-f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})}{\lambda}\leq f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}).

Taking
\lambda\to 0^{+}
, the left-hand side converges to the directional derivative of
f
at
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
in the direction
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
(Definition
), whence we have

f^{\prime}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}};{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\leq f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}).

Since
f
is continuously differentiable, it follows that
f^{\prime}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}};{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
by (
), and hence (
) follows.

Conversely, assume that the gradient inequality (
) holds.
Let
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
, and let
\lambda\in[0,1]
. We will show that
f(\lambda{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+(1-\lambda){\boldsymbol{\beta}})\leq\lambda f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+(1-\lambda)f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
. The cases for
\lambda=0
or
\lambda=1
holds trivially. We will therefore assume that
\lambda\in(0,1)
.
Let
{\bm{z}}\triangleq\lambda{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+(1-\lambda){\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
. Then

-\frac{\lambda}{1-\lambda}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\bm{z}})=({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{z}}).

Combining with the gradient inequality implies that

f({\bm{z}})+\nabla f({\bm{z}})^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\bm{z}})\leq f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\qquad\text{and}\qquad f({\bm{z}})-\frac{\lambda}{1-\lambda}\nabla f({\bm{z}})^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\bm{z}})\leq f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}).

Multiplying the first inequality by
\frac{\lambda}{1-\lambda}
and adding it to the second one, we obtain

\frac{1}{1-\lambda}f({\bm{z}})\leq\frac{\lambda}{1-\lambda}f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}),

establishing convexity of
f
.
This completes the proof.

{theoremHigh}

[Monotonicity of gradient of convex functions]
Let
f:{\mathbb{S}}\rightarrow\real
be a continuously differentiable function defined on a convex set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}
. Then
f
is convex over
{\mathbb{S}}
if and only if

\big\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}),({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\big\rangle\geq 0,\quad\text{for all }{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}.

(2.10a)

Similarly,
f
is strictly convex over
{\mathbb{S}}
if and only if

\big\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}),({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\big\rangle>0,\quad\text{for all }{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\neq{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}.

(2.10b)

Proof
[of Theorem
]
We prove only (
); the strict case follows similarly.
Assume that
f
is convex over
{\mathbb{S}}
. Then by the gradient inequality, for any
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
, we have

f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\geq f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\qquad\text{and}\qquad f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\geq f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}).

Adding these two inequalities eliminates the function values and yields (
).

Conversely, assume that (
) holds, and let
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
. Define
g(\mu)\triangleq f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+\mu({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})),\mu\in[0,1]
as a one-dimensional function.
By the fundamental theorem of calculus (Theorem
), we have

\displaystyle f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})

\displaystyle=g(1)=g(0)+\int_{0}^{1}g^{\prime}(\mu)\,d\mu=f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\int_{0}^{1}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})^{\top}\nabla f\big({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+\mu({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\big)\,d\mu

\displaystyle=f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\int_{0}^{1}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})^{\top}\big(\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+\mu({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}))-\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\big)\,d\mu

\displaystyle\geq f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}),

where the last inequality follows from the monotonicity of the gradient. This shows that
f
is convex by Definition
.

\paragrapharrow

Second-order characterizations of convex functions.

When the function is further assumed to be twice continuously differentiable,
its convexity can be characterized by the positive semidefiniteness (see Definition
) of its Hessian matrix

{theoremHigh}
[PSD Hessian of convex functions]
Let
f:{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}\rightarrow\real
be a twice continuously differentiable function defined on an
open
convex set
{\mathbb{S}}
. Then
f
is convex
if and only if

\nabla^{2}f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\succeq\boldsymbol{0}
for any
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
.
Moreover,
if

\nabla^{2}f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\succ\boldsymbol{0}
for any
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
, then the function is strictly convex over
{\mathbb{S}}
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Assume that
\nabla^{2}f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\succeq\boldsymbol{0}
for all
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
, and let
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
.
By the linear approximation theorem (Theorem
), there exists
{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\in[{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}]
(and hence
{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
) such that

f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\frac{1}{2}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})^{\top}\nabla^{2}f({\boldsymbol{\xi}})({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}),\quad{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\in[{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}].

(2.12)

Given that
\nabla^{2}f({\boldsymbol{\xi}})\succeq\boldsymbol{0}
, it follows that
({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})^{\top}\nabla^{2}f({\boldsymbol{\xi}})({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\geq 0
, whence by (
) we have
f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\geq f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
, establishing the convexity by Theorem
.

Conversely, assume that
f
is convex over
{\mathbb{S}}
. Let
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
and let
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
. Since
{\mathbb{S}}
is open, there exists a scalar
\varepsilon>0
such that
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+\lambda{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
for any
\lambda\in(0,\varepsilon)
.
The gradient inequality (Theorem
) shows that

f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+\lambda{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\geq f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\lambda\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}.

(2.13)

Additionally, by the quadratic approximation theorem (Theorem
), we have

f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+\lambda{\boldsymbol{\beta}})=f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\lambda\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+\frac{\lambda^{2}}{2}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\top}\nabla^{2}f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}){\boldsymbol{\beta}}+o(\lambda^{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}),

which combined with (
) yields the inequality

\frac{\lambda^{2}}{2}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\top}\nabla^{2}f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}){\boldsymbol{\beta}}+o(\lambda^{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2})\geq 0

for any
\lambda\in(0,\varepsilon)
. Dividing the latter inequality by
\lambda^{2}
yields that

\frac{1}{2}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\top}\nabla^{2}f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}){\boldsymbol{\beta}}+\frac{o(\lambda^{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2})}{\lambda^{2}}\geq 0.

Taking
\lambda\to 0^{+}
, we conclude that

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\top}\nabla^{2}f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}){\boldsymbol{\beta}}\geq 0

for any
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
, implying that
\nabla^{2}f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\succeq\boldsymbol{0}
for any
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
.
The strict convexity can be proved analogously.

2.4
Continuous and Closed Functions, and Weierstrass Theorem

Since we will use the notion of closed functions to analyze properties of proximal operators in Section
—a step that relies on the closedness condition in the Weierstrass theorem (Theorem
)—and since this theorem is, in turn, essential for studying the convergence of
proximal gradient methods
in Section
, we review the relevant concepts in this section.

A continuous function is one that does not exhibit abrupt changes in value—i.e., it has no
discontinuities
. More formally, continuity means that arbitrarily small changes in the input produce arbitrarily small changes in the output. Continuous functions are fundamental in calculus and mathematical analysis and enjoy several key properties.

Definition 87
(Continuous functions).

Let
f:{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}\rightarrow\real
. The function
f
is said to be continuous at a point
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
if for every
\epsilon>0
, there exists a
\delta>0
such that for all
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
in
{\mathbb{S}}
:

\forall\,\epsilon>0,\exists\,\delta>0:\quad\forall\,{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{S}},\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}<\delta\quad\implies\quad\left\lvert f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rvert<\epsilon.

(2.14)

In simpler terms, this means that the values
f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
can be made arbitrarily close to
f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
by choosing
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
sufficiently close to
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.

If
f
is continuous at every point in its domain
{\mathbb{S}}
, then
f
is said to be continuous on
{\mathbb{S}}
, or simply continuous.

Remark 88
(Properties of continuous functions).

Continuous functions satisfy several important properties:

1.

Intermediate value theorem. If
f
is continuous on a closed interval
[a,b]
and
y
lies between
f(a)
and
f(b)
, then there exists some
c\in[a,b]
such that
f(c)=y
. This is known as Rolle’s theorem (Theorem
).

2.

Extreme value theorem. If
f
is continuous on a closed interval
[a,b]
, then
f
attains both a maximum and a minimum value on that interval. This will be discussed further in the Weierstrass theorem (Theorem
).

3.

Composition of continuous functions. If
g
is continuous at
c
and
f
is continuous at
g(c)
, then the composition
f\circ g
is continuous at
c
.

4.

Arithmetic operations. If
f
and
g
are continuous at
c
, then so are
f+g
,
f-g
,
fg
, and
\frac{f}{g}
(provided
g(c)\neq 0
).

5.

Continuity and limits. A function
f
is continuous at
c
if and only if
\lim_{x\to c}f(x)=f(c)
.

Example 89
(Continuous functions).

The following are examples of continuous functions:

Polynomial functions are continuous everywhere.

Rational functions are continuous wherever they are defined (i.e., where the denominator is not zero).

Trigonometric functions like sine and cosine are continuous everywhere.

Exponential and logarithmic functions are continuous on their respective domains.

Absolute value function
\left\lvert\alpha\right\rvert
is continuous everywhere.

In contrast, common types of discontinuities include:

Removable discontinuity. The function has a hole at a point, but it can be “filled” to become continuous.

Jump discontinuity. The left-hand limit and right-hand limit exist but are not equal.

Infinite discontinuity. The function approaches positive or negative infinity at a point.

Oscillating discontinuity. The function does not approach a single value as the input approaches a point.

Continuous functions are generally easier to analyze and manipulate, while discontinuities can lead to complex behaviors that require special handling. Identifying the type of discontinuity is crucial for selecting appropriate analytical or numerical strategies in applications.

Definition 90
(Lower semicontinuity (LSC)).

A function
f:\real^{p}\rightarrow\real\cup\{\infty\}
is called lower semicontinuous (LSC) at
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}\in\real^{p}
if

f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*})\leq\liminf_{t\rightarrow\infty}f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)})

for any sequence
\{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)}\}_{t\geq 1}\subseteq\real^{p}
such that
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)}\rightarrow{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}
as
t\rightarrow\infty
.
In other words, the limit inferior of the function values at points approaching
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}
must be greater than or equal to the function value at
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}
.
This means the function cannot exhibit a sudden drop at
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}
.
A function
f:\real^{p}\rightarrow\real\cup\{\infty\}
is called lower semicontinuous if it is lower semicontinuous at each point in
p
.

Figure
illustrates examples of lower semicontinuous and non-lower semicontinuous functions.
Note that allowing the extended real value
\{\infty\}
in the codomain is standard when defining lower semicontinuity. While not strictly necessary for all functions, this extension provides greater generality and is essential in optimization and variational analysis. It enables us to treat functions that become unbounded above (e.g., indicator functions of constraints) while still discussing their continuity-like properties.

In optimization, lower semicontinuity plays a crucial role because it helps ensure the existence of minimizers. Specifically, if a sequence of feasible points approaches a candidate solution and the objective function is lower semicontinuous, then the function value at the limit point does not exceed the limit inferior of the sequence’s values. Under suitable compactness or coercivity conditions, this guarantees that a global minimum is attained.

For instance, in the calculus of variations and optimal control, one often proves existence of minimizers by showing that a functional is both lower semicontinuous and coercive (i.e.,
f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\to\infty
as
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}\to\infty
). Combined with weak compactness arguments, this yields existence results (see Property
in Theorem
).

In numerical optimization and iterative algorithms, lower semicontinuity is also valuable for analyzing convergence. For example, if an algorithm generates a minimizing sequence for a lower semicontinuous function, then any cluster point of the sequence is guaranteed to have a function value no larger than the limit inferior—often implying that such points are stationary or optimal. Moreover, when combined with strong convexity, lower semicontinuity (or closedness) ensures uniqueness and existence of the optimizer (Theorem
).

For these reasons, throughout this work we primarily consider lower semicontinuous (i.e.,
closed
) functions in our analysis.

(a)

A lower semicontinuous funtion.

(b)

A non-lower semicontinuous funtion

(c)

A lower semicontinuous funtion.

Figure 2.4:
Lower semicontinuous and non-lower semicontinous funtions. In numerical methods and iterative algorithms, lower semicontinuity can help in proving convergence properties. For instance, if a sequence generated by an algorithm is minimizing a lower semicontinuous function, it can be shown that the limit points of the sequence are stationary points.

Definition 91
(Closed functions).

A function
f:{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}\rightarrow\real\cup\{\infty\}
is said to be closed if its epigraph is a closed subset in the product topology of
{\mathbb{S}}\times\real
. In other words, for every sequence
({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)},r_{t})
in
\text{epi}(f)
that converges to a limit
({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*},r^{*})
, we have
f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*})\leq r^{*}
, meaning that the limit point
({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*},r^{*})
also belongs to the epigraph.

Exercise
\thetheo
(Closedness of indicator)

Show that the indicator function
\delta_{\mathbb{S}}
, which is
0
if
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
belongs to a set
{\mathbb{S}}
and
+\infty
otherwise, is closed if and only if
{\mathbb{S}}
is a closed set.

The following exercise demonstrates that closedness is preserved under several common operations: affine transformations, nonnegative linear combinations, and pointwise maximization.

Exercise
\thetheo
(Preservation of closedness)

Prove the following results:

1.

Let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{p\times p}
, and let
f:\real^{p}\rightarrow(-\infty,\infty]
be an extended real-valued closed function. Then the function

g({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=f({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+{\bm{y}})

is closed.

2.

Let
f_{1},f_{2},\ldots,f_{k}:\real^{p}\rightarrow(-\infty,\infty]
be extended real-valued closed functions, and let
\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2},\ldots,\sigma_{k}\in\real_{+}
. Then the function
f=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sigma_{i}f_{i}
is closed.

3.

Let
f_{i}:\real^{p}\rightarrow(-\infty,\infty],i\in{\mathbb{I}}
be extended real-valued closed functions, where
{\mathbb{I}}
is a given index set. Then the function

f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\max_{i\in{\mathbb{I}}}f_{i}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})

is closed.

Hint: the epigraph of
\max_{i\in{\mathbb{I}}}f_{i}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
is the intersection of the epigraphs of functions
f_{i}
.

An important property of closed functions is the equivalence among three fundamental concepts: lower semicontinuity, closedness of the function (i.e., closed epigraph), and closedness of all its sublevel sets.

{theoremHigh}
[Equivalence of closedness, LSC, and closedness of level sets]
Let
f:\real^{p}\rightarrow\real\cup\{-\infty,\infty\}
. Then the following three statements are equivalent:

(i)

f
is lower semicontinuous (LSC).

(ii)

f
is closed.

(iii)

For any
\gamma\in\real
, the level set

\mathrm{Lev}[f,\gamma]=\{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}\mid f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\leq\gamma\}

is closed.

Proof
[of Theorem
]

(i)
\implies
(ii).
Assume that
f
is lower semicontinuous. We will demonstrate that
\mathrm{epi}(f)
is closed.
Let
\{({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)},y^{(t)})\}_{t\geq 1}\subseteq\mathrm{epi}(f)
be a sequence such that
({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)},y^{(t)})\rightarrow({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*},y^{*})
as
t\rightarrow\infty
. By definition, for any
t\geq 1
,

f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)})\leq y^{(t)}.

Due to the lower semicontinuity of
f
at
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}
, we have

f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*})\leq\liminf_{t\rightarrow\infty}f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)})\leq\liminf_{t\rightarrow\infty}y^{(t)}=y^{*},

which shows that
({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*},y^{*})\in\mathrm{epi}(f)
, proving that
f
is closed.

(ii)
\implies
(iii).

Suppose that
f
is closed, i.e., the epigraph
\mathrm{epi}(f)
is closed.
For any
\gamma\in\real
, we aim to show that
\mathrm{Lev}[f,\gamma]
is closed. If
\mathrm{Lev}[f,\gamma]=\varnothing
, the claim holds trivially.
Otherwise, take a sequence
\{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)}\}_{t\geq 1}\subseteq\mathrm{Lev}[f,\gamma]
that converges to
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}
. Obviously,
({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)},\gamma)\in\mathrm{epi}(f)
for any
t
and
({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)},\gamma)\rightarrow({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}},\gamma)
as
t\rightarrow\infty
. By the closedness of
\mathrm{epi}(f)
, it follows that
({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}},\gamma)\in\mathrm{epi}(f)
, establishing the fact that
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}\in\mathrm{Lev}[f,\gamma]
.

(iii)
\implies
(i).

Assuming all level sets of
f
are closed, we prove that it is lower semicontinuous. Suppose for contradiction that
f
is not lower semicontinuous, meaning that there exists
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}\in\real^{p}
and
\{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)}\}_{t\geq 1}\subseteq\real^{p}
such that
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)}\rightarrow{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}
and
\liminf_{t\rightarrow\infty}f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)})<f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*})
.
Choose
\gamma
satisfying

\liminf_{t\rightarrow\infty}f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)})<\gamma<f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}).

(2.15)

Then there exists a subsequence
\{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{n_{t}}\}_{t\geq 1}
such that
f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{n_{t}})\leq\gamma
for all
t\geq 1
. By the closedness of the level set
\mathrm{Lev}[f,\gamma]
and the fact that
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{n_{t}}\rightarrow{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}
as
t\rightarrow\infty
, it follows that
f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*})\leq\gamma
, which is a contradiction to (
), establishing that (iii) implies (i).

To guarantee the existence of a
global minimizer
(also called a global optimum point)—that is, a point where a function attains its smallest value over a given set—the classical Weierstrass theorem provides sufficient conditions. Below, we present the Weierstrass theorem and several of its extensions for continuous and proper closed functions.

{theoremHigh}
[Weierstrass theorem and variants]
We consider the Weierstrass theorem and its variants for different types of functions and sets:

1.

Let
f:{\mathbb{S}}\rightarrow(-\infty,\infty]
be a
continuous function
defined over a
nonempty and compact (closed and bounded) set

{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}
.
Then, there exists a global minimum point and a global maximum point of
f
over
{\mathbb{S}}
.

2.

Let
f:{\mathbb{S}}\rightarrow(-\infty,\infty]
be a
continuous function
defined over a
nonempty and closed set

{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}
. Suppose that all the level sets
\mathrm{Lev}[f,\gamma]=\{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{S}}\mid f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\leq\gamma\}
are bounded. Then,
f
has a global minimum point over
{\mathbb{S}}
.

3.

Let
f:{\mathbb{S}}\rightarrow(-\infty,\infty]
be a
continuous and coercive function
and let
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}
be a
nonempty and closed set
. Then,
f
has a global minimum point over
{\mathbb{S}}
. (
The coerciveness ensures the function is bounded over a subset.
)

4.

Let
f:{\mathbb{S}}\rightarrow(-\infty,\infty]
be a
proper closed function
, and one of the following is satisfied:

(a).

f
is defined over a
nonempty and compact set

{\mathbb{S}}
.

(b).

There exists a
nonempty and bounded level set

\mathrm{Lev}[f,\gamma]=\{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{S}}\mid f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\leq\gamma\}
.

(c).

f
is coercive, i.e.,
\mathop{\lim}_{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}\rightarrow\infty}f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\infty
.

Then, there exists a global minimum point of
f
over
{\mathbb{S}}
. And the set of minimizers
\{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{S}}\mid f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\leq f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}),\forall\,{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}\}
of
\mathop{\min}_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{S}}}f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
is nonempty and compact.

Note the coerciveness in
ensures the function is bounded over a subset. The three conditions of
.
\sim
.
essentially ensure that the minimum value of
f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
cannot be attained at infinity.
The results in
are used more extensively in optimization analysis. To provide a counterexample, let
f=\exp(-x)
be defined on , which is a proper closed function.
However, the domain and some level sets of
f
are not bounded, and
f
is not coercive. Therefore, the attainment of the global optimal point is not guaranteed.

2.5
Subgradient and Conjugate Functions

The gradient inequality for convex functions applies specifically to continuously differentiable functions. However, this concept can be generalized using the notion of a
subgradient
, which plays a crucial role in optimization, particularly for non-differentiable or non-smooth functions.

Definition 92
(Subgradient and subdifferential).

Let
f:{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}\rightarrow\real
. A vector
{\bm{g}}\in\real^{p}
is called a subgradient of
f
at
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
if

f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\geq f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\left\langle{\bm{g}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rangle,\quad\text{for all ${\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}$}.

This inequality is known as the subgradient inequality.
The set of all subgradients of
f
at
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
, denoted by
\partial f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
, is called the subdifferential of
f
at
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
:

\partial f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\triangleq\left\{{\bm{g}}\in\real^{p}\mid f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\geq f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\left\langle{\bm{g}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rangle,\text{ for all ${\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}$}\right\}.

Any subgradient of
f
at
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
may be denoted by

f^{\prime}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\in\partial f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}).

It is worth noting that the concept of a subgradient applies not only to convex functions but also extends to non-convex settings.
However, for convex functions, it is guaranteed that the subdifferential at any point in the interior of the domain is nonempty (Theorem
).
If
f
is differentiable at
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
, then the subdifferential contains only the gradient:

\partial f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\{\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\},

Exercise
\thetheo
(Subdifferential of norms)

Let
f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}
. Show that

\partial f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\begin{cases}\left\{\frac{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}}\right\},&{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\neq\boldsymbol{0};\\
{\mathbb{B}}_{2}[\boldsymbol{0},1],&{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=\boldsymbol{0},\end{cases}

where
{\mathbb{B}}_{2}[\boldsymbol{0},1]
denotes the closed unit ball in the
\ell_{2}
-norm.
Additionally, let
g({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{1}
. Show that
\partial g({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\partial g_{i}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
, where
g_{i}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\left\lvert\alpha_{i}\right\rvert
and

\partial g_{i}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\begin{cases}\{\sign(\alpha_{i}){\bm{e}}_{i}\},&\alpha_{i}\neq 0;\\
[-{\bm{e}}_{i},{\bm{e}}_{i}],&\alpha_{i}=0.\end{cases}

Let
{\bm{u}}\in\partial g({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
. We have
\left\lVert{\bm{u}}\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq 1
and
{\bm{u}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{1}
.
This also indicates that

\sign({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\in\partial g({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}),

where
\sign({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
returns the sign for each component.
This also shows the subgradient inequality for the absolute value function. Specifically, for any
a\neq 0
and any
b\in\real
, we have

\left\lvert a+b\right\rvert\geq\left\lvert a\right\rvert+\sign(a)b,

with equality if and only if
\left\lvert a+b\right\rvert-\left\lvert a\right\rvert
is linear in
b
, i.e., when

b
does not cause a sign change or zero-crossing.

An established result in convex analysis states that the relative interior of a convex set is always nonempty. Moreover, for a proper convex function, the subdifferential is guaranteed to be nonempty at every point in the relative interior of its effective domain.
The following theorem summarizes these key facts without proof.

{theoremHigh}
[Nonemptiness of relative interior
(
Rockafellar 1970
)
]
Let
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}
be a nonempty convex set. Then, the relative interior of
{\mathbb{S}}
, denoted
\text{relint}({\mathbb{S}})
, is nonempty.
Moreover, let
f:\real^{p}\rightarrow(-\infty,\infty]
be a proper convex function, and let
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\text{relint}(\mathrm{dom}(f))
.
Then the subdifferential of
f
at
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
, denoted
\partial f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
, is nonempty.

Fermat’s theorem
, also known as
Fermat’s theorem on stationary points
, is a fundamental result in calculus and mathematical optimization. It provides a necessary condition for a differentiable function to attain a local optimum (either a local maximum or a local minimum) at an interior point of its domain.
In the univariate case, Fermat’s theorem gives the optimality condition for a point that lies in the interior of an interval—i.e., for a one-dimensional constrained optimization problem where the constraint set is an open interval.

{theoremHigh}

[Fermat’s theorem: Necessary condition for univariate functions]
Let
f:(a,b)\rightarrow\real
be a one-dimensional differentiable function defined on an open interval (
a,b
).
If a point
\alpha^{*}\in(a,b)
(i.e.,
\alpha^{*}\in\text{int}([a,b])
) is a local maximum or minimum of
f
, then
f^{\prime}(\alpha^{*})=0
.

In other words, if a differentiable function
f
has a local maximum or minimum at a point
\alpha^{*}
, then the slope of the tangent line at that point is zero; the derivative of the function at that point must be zero.
It’s important to emphasize that this condition is necessary but
not
sufficient for
\alpha^{*}
to be an optimum. There are cases where the derivative is zero but the point is neither a maximum nor a minimum, such as in the case of an inflection point. Additionally, Fermat’s theorem does
not
apply to boundary points of the domain of
f
or to points where
f
is not differentiable.

We now present the first-order necessary condition for a local minimum in multivariate optimization.

Corollary 93
(First-order necessary condition for a minimum point).

Let
f:\real^{p}\rightarrow\real
be a differentiable function. If
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}
is a (local) minimizer of
f
, then

\nabla f({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}})=\boldsymbol{0}.

Such a point is called a stationary point of
f
.

Proof
[of Corollary
]
Fix an index
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
, and define the one-dimensional function
g(\mu)=f({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}+\mu{\bm{e}}_{i})
. Note that
g
is differentiable at
\mu=0
and that
g^{\prime}(0)=\frac{\partial f}{\partial\theta_{i}}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}})
. Since
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}
is a local minimum point of
f
, it follows that
\mu=0
is a local minimum point of
g
, which immediately implies that
g^{\prime}(0)=0
by Theorem
. This equality is exactly the same as
\frac{\partial f}{\partial\theta_{i}}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}})=0
. Since this holds for any
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
, we obtain
\nabla f({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}})=\boldsymbol{0}
.

Most objective functions, especially those with multiple local minima, also contain local maxima and other critical points that satisfy the necessary condition from Fermat’s theorem.
To distinguish true local minima from these irrelevant or non-optimal critical points, we require additional criteria, such as second-order conditions or convexity assumptions
(
Lu 2025
)
.
Subdifferentials are particularly useful for characterizing minimizers, especially in non-smooth or non-differentiable settings. A fundamental result in convex optimization provides a complete characterization of global minima via the subdifferential.
In essence, this is a generalization of Fermat’s optimality condition at points of differentiability:
\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*})=\boldsymbol{0}
.

{theoremHigh}

[Necessity/sufficiency of unconstrained convex]
Let
f:\real^{p}\rightarrow(-\infty,\infty]
be a proper convex function. Then,

{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}\in\mathop{\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}}_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}}f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})

if and only if
\boldsymbol{0}\in\partial f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*})
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
By the definition of the subgradient (Definition
), it holds that
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}\in\mathop{\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}}_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}}f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
if and only if

f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\geq f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*})+\left\langle\boldsymbol{0},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}\right\rangle,\quad\text{for any }{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\mathrm{dom}(f),

which is the same as the inclusion
\boldsymbol{0}\in\partial f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*})
, where the existence of this subdifferential is stated by Theorem
.

We now introduce the definition and key properties of conjugate functions.

Definition 94
(Conjugate functions).

Let
f:\real^{p}\rightarrow\real\cup\{\infty\}
be an extended real-valued function. The conjugate function
f^{*}:\real^{p}\rightarrow\real\cup\{\infty\}
of
f
is defined by

f^{*}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\max_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}}\{\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rangle-f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\},\quad{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}.

Note that
f^{*}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
is the pointwise maximum of affine functions of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
, each of which is convex and closed.
Consequently, the conjugate function
f^{*}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
is always convex and closed, regardless of whether the original function
f
possesses these properties (see Exercises
and
).
This leads to the following fundamental result:

Lemma 95
(Closedness and convexity of conjugate).

Let
f:\real^{p}\rightarrow\real\cup\{\infty\}
be an extended real-valued function. Then its conjugate
f^{*}
is closed and convex.

A direct consequence of the definition is Fenchel’s inequality.

{theoremHigh}
[Fenchel’s inequality]
Let
f:\real^{p}\rightarrow\real\cup\{\infty\}
be a proper extended real-valued function. Then for any
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
,

f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+f^{*}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\geq\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rangle.

The
biconjugate

f^{**}
(i.e., the conjugate of
f^{*}
) plays a central role in convex analysis.

Exercise
\thetheo
(Bounds on biconjugate
(
Rockafellar 1970
)
)

Let
f:\real^{p}\rightarrow[-\infty,\infty]
be an extended real-valued function. Show that
f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\geq f^{**}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
for any
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}
.
Additionally, let
g:\real^{p}\rightarrow\real\cup\{\infty\}
be a proper
closed and convex
function. Show that
g({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=g^{**}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})

Because of this property, the biconjugate
f^{**}

is often referred to as the
convex envelope
(or
convex closure
,
convex relaxation
) of
f
—it is the largest convex lower semicontinuous function that lies below
f
.

Exercise
\thetheo
(Properness of conjugate)

Let
f:\real^{p}\rightarrow\real\cup\{\infty\}
be a proper convex function. Show that
f^{*}
is also proper.

Exercise
\thetheo
(Conjugate calculus)

Let
f:\real^{p}\to\real\cup\{\infty\}
. Show that

1.

Let
f_{\tau}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\triangleq f(\tau{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
, where
\tau\neq 0
. Then
(f_{\tau})^{*}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=f^{*}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}/\tau)
.

2.

For
\tau>0
,
(\tau f)^{*}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\tau f^{*}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}/\tau)
.

3.

Let
f_{({\boldsymbol{\zeta}})}\triangleq f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\zeta}})
, where For
{\boldsymbol{\zeta}}\in\real^{p}
. Then
(f_{({\boldsymbol{\zeta}})})^{*}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=f^{*}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\zeta}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle
.

Let us compute the convex conjugate for some examples.

Example 96
(Self-conjugate).

Let
f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
for
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}
.
Then
f^{*}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
,
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
. Indeed, since

\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rangle\leq\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
,
we have

f^{*}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\max_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}}\{\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rangle-f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\}\leq\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

For the reverse inequality, we just set
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}
in the definition of the convex conjugate to obtain

f^{*}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\geq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

Hence, equality holds. This function is self-conjugate: it is the unique (up to scaling and translation in certain contexts) function on
p
satisfying
f=f^{*}
.

The central result relating subgradients and conjugates is the so-called
conjugate subgradient theorem
,
which establishes an elegant duality between a convex function and its Fenchel conjugate through their subdifferentials. In essence, it characterizes when a pair of points
({\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}})
are dual to each other—not only in the sense of achieving equality in Fenchel’s inequality
f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+f^{*}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\geq\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle
, but also in the geometric sense that one is a subgradient of the function at the other. This connection lies at the heart of convex analysis and plays a crucial role in optimization, duality theory, and sensitivity analysis. Moreover, when the function is closed (i.e., lower semicontinuous), the relationship becomes symmetric: subgradients of
f
correspond precisely to subgradients of
f^{*}
, reflecting the involutive nature of the conjugate operation.

{theoremHigh}

[Conjugate subgradient theorem]
Let
f:\real^{p}\to\real\cup\{\infty\}
be a proper
convex
function. The following two claims are equivalent for any
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
:

1.

\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle=f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+f^{*}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
.

2.

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\partial f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
.

If, in addition,
f
is
closed
, then (i) and (ii) are also equivalent to

{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\partial f^{*}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
.

Alternatively, let
f:\real^{p}\to\real\cup\{\infty\}
be a proper
closed convex
function. Then for any
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
,

\displaystyle\partial f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})

\displaystyle=\operatorname*{\text{arg max}}_{{\bm{u}}\in\real^{p}}\left\{\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\bm{u}}\right\rangle-f^{*}({\bm{u}})\right\};

(2.16a)

\displaystyle\partial f^{*}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})

\displaystyle=\operatorname*{\text{arg max}}_{{\bm{v}}\in\real^{p}}\left\{\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\bm{v}}\right\rangle-f({\bm{v}})\right\}.

(2.16b)

Proof
[of Theorem
]
By the subgradient inequality of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\partial f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
, it follows that

f({\bm{u}})\geq f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\bm{u}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rangle\quad\implies\quad\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rangle-f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\geq\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\bm{u}}\right\rangle-f({\bm{u}}),\text{ for all }{\bm{u}}\in\real^{p}.

Taking the maximum over
{\bm{u}}
, the above inequality is equivalent to

\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rangle-f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\geq f^{*}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}),

which by Fenchel’s inequality (Theorem
) is the same as the equality
\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle=f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+f^{*}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
, establishing the equivalence between (i) and (ii).
When
f
is proper closed and convex, by Exercise
,
f^{**}=f
, which implies that (i) is equivalent to

\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle=f^{*}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+f^{**}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
. By the above argument, we conclude that (i) is equivalent to
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\partial f^{*}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
.
This completes the proof.

2.6
Lipschitz Functions

This section further explores the properties of Lipschitz continuity, defining the relevant concepts and examining their implications for function behavior—particularly the boundedness of subdifferential sets for convex functions.

Definition 97
(Lipschitz functions).

Let
L\geq 0
, and let
f:{\mathbb{S}}\rightarrow\real
be a function defined on a set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}
. Then, the function
f
is called L-Lipschitz if, for all
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
, it follows that

\left\lvert f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rvert\leq L\cdot\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}.

If
f
is continuously differentiable, its gradient is said to be Lipschitz continuous over
{\mathbb{S}}
(or, equivalently,
f
is called Lipschitz continuously differentiable) with constant
L
if, for all
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
, it follows that

\left\lVert\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rVert_{2}\leq L\cdot\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}.\penalty\

The class of functions whose gradients are Lipschitz continuous with constant
L
is denoted by
C_{L}^{1,1}({\mathbb{S}})
or simply by
C_{L}^{1,1}
.

Similarly, the function is called twice Lipschitz continuously differentiable with constant
L
, denoted by
C_{L}^{2,2}({\mathbb{S}})
, if, for all
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
, it follows that

\left\lVert\nabla^{2}f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\nabla^{2}f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rVert_{2}\leq L\cdot\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}.

More generally, let
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}
. We denote by
C_{L}^{k,s}({\mathbb{S}})
the class of functions satisfying the following properties:

Any
f\in C_{L}^{k,s}({\mathbb{S}})
is
k
times continuously differentiable on
{\mathbb{S}}
.

Its
s
-th derivative is Lipschitz continuous on
{\mathbb{S}}
with constant
L
:

\left\lVert\nabla^{s}f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\nabla^{s}f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rVert_{2}\leq L\cdot\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}

for all
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
.

In this book, we primarily consider the cases
s=0
,
s=1
, and
s=2
. Clearly, we always have
s\leq k
.
Moreover, if
t\geq k
, then
C_{L}^{t,s}({\mathbb{S}})\subseteq C_{L}^{k,s}({\mathbb{S}})
.
For simplicity, we also denotes
C^{k}({\mathbb{S}})
as the set of
k
times continuously differentiable functions on
{\mathbb{S}}
.

Example 98
.

Consider the following examples:

Since
\big\lvert\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{1}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\big\rvert\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\sqrt{p}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}
for any
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
(see Exercise
), the function
f_{1}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{1}
is thus
\sqrt{p}
-Lipschitz.

Since
\big\lvert\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}-\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}\big\rvert\leq\left\lVert({\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-({\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rVert_{2}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}
, the function
f_{2}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}
is
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}
-Lipschitz, where
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}
denotes the spectral norm of
{\bm{X}}
.

The function
f_{3}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\triangleq f_{2}^{2}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
is not Lipschitz. However, it can be shown that
f_{3}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
is (gradient) Lipschitz continuously differentiable with constant
2\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}
.

Exercise
\thetheo
(Gradient Lipschitzness of quadratic functions)

Let
f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\frac{1}{2}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+{\bm{y}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+z
, where
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{p\times p}
is symmetric,
{\bm{y}}\in\real^{p}
, and
z\in\real
. Show that the gradient of
f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
is
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}
-Lipschitz. This also indicates that the gradient function is 0-Lipschitz when
{\bm{X}}=\boldsymbol{0}
(an affine function).

Remark 99
(Lipschitz continuity implies continuity).

Recall that a function
f
is continuous (Definition
) at a point
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
if, for every
\epsilon>0
, there exists a
\delta>0
such that:

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}<\delta\implies\left\lvert f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rvert<\epsilon.

Now, suppose
f
is Lipschitz continuous with constant
L
, i.e.,
\left\lvert f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rvert\leq L\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}
.
Given
\epsilon>0
, choose
\delta=\frac{\epsilon}{L}
. Then, if
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}<\delta
, we have:

\left\lvert f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rvert\leq L\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}<L\cdot\frac{\epsilon}{L}=\epsilon.

Thus,
f
is continuous at
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
. Since
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
was arbitrary,
f
is continuous on
{\mathbb{S}}
.
The Lipschitz condition bounds the “rate of change” of the function, preventing any infinite slopes or wild oscillations that could break continuity.

Exercise
\thetheo

Let
f_{1}\in C^{k,s}_{L_{1}}({\mathbb{S}})
,
f_{2}\in C^{k,s}_{L_{2}}({\mathbb{S}})
, and let
a_{1},a_{2}\in\real
.
Define
L_{3}=\left\lvert a_{1}\right\rvert\cdot L_{1}+\left\lvert a_{2}\right\rvert\cdot L_{2}
.
Show that
a_{1}f_{1}+a_{2}f_{2}\in C^{k,s}_{L_{3}}({\mathbb{S}})
.

Exercise
\thetheo

Show that a function
f:\real^{p}\rightarrow\real
belongs to the class
C^{2,1}_{L}(\real^{p})\subset C^{1,1}_{L}(\real^{p})
if and only if for all
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}
we have

\left\lVert\nabla^{2}f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\right\rVert_{2}\leq L.

Hint: use the fundamental theorem of calculus (Theorem
).

We now establish the boundedness of the subdifferential under Lipschitz continuity.

{theoremHigh}
[Lipschitzness and boundedness of subdifferential sets]
Let
f:{\mathbb{S}}\rightarrow\real
be a
convex
function, and let
{\mathbb{X}}\subseteq\text{int}({\mathbb{S}})
. Consider the following two claims:

1.

\left\lvert f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rvert\leq L\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}
for any
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{X}}
.

2.

\left\lVert{\bm{g}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq L
for any
{\bm{g}}\in\partial f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}),{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{X}}
.

Then,

1.

The implication (ii)
\implies
(i) holds,

2.

If
{\mathbb{X}}
is open, then statement (i) holds if and only if statement (ii) holds.

Proof
[of Theorem
]

(a).
Assume that (ii) is satisfied, and let
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{X}}
. Let
{\bm{g}}_{x}\in\partial f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
and
{\bm{g}}_{y}\in\partial f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
.
By the definitions of
{\bm{g}}_{x},{\bm{g}}_{y}
and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality (Theorem
),

\displaystyle f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})

\displaystyle\leq\left\langle{\bm{g}}_{x},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle\leq\left\lVert{\bm{g}}_{x}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq L\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2};

\displaystyle f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})

\displaystyle\leq\left\langle{\bm{g}}_{y},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rangle\leq\left\lVert{\bm{g}}_{y}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq L\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2},

which establishes the validity of (i).

(b).

The implication (ii)
\implies
(i) was shown in (a). Conversely, assume that (i) is satisfied. Take
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{X}}
and
{\bm{g}}\in\partial f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
. Let
\widetilde{\bm{g}}\triangleq\frac{{\bm{g}}}{\left\lVert{\bm{g}}\right\rVert_{2}}
such that
\left\lVert\widetilde{\bm{g}}\right\rVert_{2}=1
and
\left\langle\widetilde{\bm{g}},{\bm{g}}\right\rangle=\left\lVert{\bm{g}}\right\rVert_{2}
. Since
{\mathbb{X}}
is open, we can take
\epsilon>0
small enough such that
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+\epsilon\widetilde{\bm{g}}\in{\mathbb{X}}
.
Given the subgradient inequality, it follows that

f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+\epsilon\widetilde{\bm{g}})\geq f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\epsilon\left\langle{\bm{g}},\widetilde{\bm{g}}\right\rangle,

whence we have

\epsilon\left\lVert{\bm{g}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+\epsilon\widetilde{\bm{g}})-f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\leq L\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+\epsilon\widetilde{\bm{g}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}=L\epsilon\quad\implies\quad\left\lVert{\bm{g}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq L.

This completes the proof.

2.7
Strongly Convex, Strongly Smooth Functions

This section provides rigorous definitions of
strong convexity (SC)
and
strong smoothness (SS, or simply smoothness)
. Although both concepts can be extended to non-differentiable convex functions using subgradients, we restrict our attention in this book to differentiable functions.

Figure 2.5:

A convex function always lies above its tangent at any point. In contrast, a strongly convex function is not only bounded below by its tangent but also by a quadratic function, which limits how slowly it can grow. Similarly, a smooth function is bounded above by a quadratic model, preventing it from increasing too rapidly. Together, strong convexity and smoothness confine the function’s behavior between two quadratic envelopes. The shaded region in each plot indicates where the graph of the function is allowed to lie. The figure is adapted from
Jain et al. 2017
.

Definition 100
(Strongly convex/smooth functions).

Let
f:{\mathbb{S}}\rightarrow\real
be a differentiable function defined on a
convex
set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}
. Then,
f
is said to be
L_{a}
-strongly convex (SC, or simply
L_{a}
-convex) and
L_{b}
-strongly smooth (SS, or simply
L_{b}
-smooth) if, for every
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
, it follows that

\frac{L_{a}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\left\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}),({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\right\rangle\leq\frac{L_{b}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.\penalty\

(2.17)

When the function is twice differentiable, Theorem
also indicates that

L_{a}{\bm{I}}\preceq\nabla^{2}f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\preceq L_{b}{\bm{I}},\quad\text{for all }{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\text{int}({\mathbb{S}}).\penalty\

(2.18)

That is, the smallest eigenvalue of
\nabla^{2}f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
is at least
L_{a}
, and the largest eigenvalue of
\nabla^{2}f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
is at most
L_{b}
:

L_{a}\leq\frac{{\bm{v}}^{\top}\nabla^{2}f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}){\bm{v}}}{\left\lVert{\bm{v}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}\leq L_{b},\quad\text{for all }{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{S}},\text{and nonzero }{\bm{v}}\in\real^{p}.\penalty\

(2.19)

It is evident that if the function is
L_{b}^{\prime}
-strongly smooth, it is also
L_{b}^{\prime\prime}
-strongly smooth for any
L_{b}^{\prime\prime}\geq L_{b}^{\prime}
.
An
L_{a}
-strongly convex function is necessarily a convex function (when
L_{a}=0
, it reduces to a standard convex function).
While if the function is
L_{a}^{\prime}
-strongly convex, it is also
L_{a}^{\prime\prime}
-strongly convex for any
L_{a}^{\prime\prime}\in(0,L_{a}^{\prime}]
.

Strong convexity and smoothness are fundamental in the analysis of gradient-based optimization algorithms (see Chapter
). Strong convexity ensures that the function curves upward sufficiently fast, providing a positive lower bound on its curvature and preventing gradients from vanishing too quickly near minima. Conversely, strong smoothness imposes an upper bound on the curvature, guaranteeing that the gradient does not change too abruptly. This controls the size of allowable steps in gradient descent and prevents overly aggressive updates (see Figure
).

Definition
later extends these notions to functions defined on non-convex domains.

Exercise
\thetheo
(Sum of SC and convex, SS)

Prove the following two statements:

Let
f
be
L_{a}
-SC and
g
be convex. Show that
f+g
is
L_{a}
-SC.

Let
f
be
L_{b}^{\prime}
-SS and
g
be
L_{b}^{\prime\prime}
-SS. Show that
f+g
is
(L_{b}^{\prime}+L_{b}^{\prime\prime})
-SS.

{theoremHigh}

[SS Property-O: Equivalence between gradient Lipschitzness and smoothness]
Let
f:{\mathbb{S}}\rightarrow\real
be a differentiable function defined on a
convex
set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}
.
If
f
is gradient Lipschitz continuous with constant
L_{b}
, i.e.,
f\in C_{L_{b}}^{1,1}({\mathbb{S}})
, then it is also
L_{b}
-smooth.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
By the fundamental theorem of calculus (Equation (
)), it follows that

f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\left\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}),{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rangle+\int_{0}^{1}\left\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+\mu({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}))-\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}),{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rangle d\mu.

Since
{\mathbb{S}}
is a convex set, the function
f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+\mu({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}))
is well-defined for
\mu\in[0,1]
.
This results in

\displaystyle\left\lvert f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\left\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}),{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rangle\right\rvert=\left\lvert\int_{0}^{1}\left\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+\mu({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}))-\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}),{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rangle d\mu\right\rvert

\displaystyle\overset{{\dagger}}{\leq}\int_{0}^{1}\left\lVert\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+\mu({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}))-\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\right\rVert_{2}\cdot\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}d\mu\leq\int_{0}^{1}L_{b}\mu\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}d\mu=\frac{L_{b}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},

where the inequality
({\dagger})
follows from the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality (Theorem
).
Hence,
f
is
L_{b}
-smooth.

If
f
is
L_{b}
-smooth and admits a global minimizer
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}
, an important consequence is
that the quadratic upper bound provided by smoothness can be used to relate the function suboptimality
f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*})
to the norm of the gradient at any point
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
. This relationship is particularly powerful when combined with strong convexity, as it yields tight two-sided bounds.

{theoremHigh}

[SS&SC Property-I: Bound of
f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*})
]
Let
f:\real^{p}\rightarrow\real
be a differentiable function defined on
p
that possesses a global minimizer
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}
. Suppose
f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
is
L_{b}
-smooth and
L_{a}
-strongly convex.
Then,

\frac{1}{2L_{b}}\left\lVert\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*})\leq\frac{1}{2L_{a}}\left\lVert\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\right\rVert_{2}^{2},\quad\text{ for any }{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Since
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}
is a global minimuizer, for any
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
, applying the quadratic upper bound from the smoothness gives

f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*})\leq f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\leq f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\frac{L_{b}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

Fixing
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
, note that the above inequality holds for any
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
, thus we can take the infimum on the right side of the inequality:

\displaystyle f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*})

\displaystyle\leq\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\left\{f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\frac{L_{b}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right\}=f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\frac{1}{2L_{b}}\left\lVert\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\right\rVert_{2}^{2},

where the minimum is attained at
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-\frac{1}{L_{b}}\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
(since the domain is
p
).

For the second part, since
f
is strongly convex, we have

\displaystyle f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})

\displaystyle\geq f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\frac{L_{a}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle\geq f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})^{\top}({\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\frac{L_{a}}{2}\left\lVert{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\frac{1}{2L_{a}}\left\lVert\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\right\rVert_{2}^{2},

where
{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\triangleq{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-(1/L_{a})\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
minimizes the right-hand side of the above inequality.
Letting
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\triangleq{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}
completes the proof.

An immediate implication of the upper bound is the following practical criterion: for any tolerance
\varepsilon>0
,

\left\lVert\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\right\rVert_{2}\leq(2L_{a}\varepsilon)^{1/2}\quad\implies\quad f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*})\leq\varepsilon,

(2.20)

Thus, controlling the gradient norm provides a certificate of near-optimality.
This generalizes the classical
optimality condition for convex functions
stated in Theorem
, which states that
\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\boldsymbol{0}
characterizes exact minimizers in the differentiable case.
Moreover, the theorem reveals a key growth property: near the minimizer, a strongly convex and smooth function behaves like a quadratic—neither too flat nor too steep.

The next result establishes that strong convexity alone (even without smoothness) guarantees both existence and uniqueness of a minimizer, along with a quadratic growth condition around it.

{theoremHigh}

[SC Property-II: Existence and uniqueness of a minimizer of closed SC functions]
Let
f:\real^{p}\rightarrow(-\infty,\infty]
be a differentiable , proper closed, and
L_{a}
-strongly convex function (
L_{a}>0
). Then,

1.

f
has a unique minimizer.

2.

f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*})\geq\frac{L_{a}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
for all
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}
, where
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}
is the unique minimizer of
f
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]

(i).
Fix any
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{0}\in\real^{p}
. By strong convexity, it follows that

\displaystyle f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\geq f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{0})+\left\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{0}),{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{0}\right\rangle+\frac{L_{a}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{0}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle\implies f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\geq f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{0})-\frac{1}{2L_{a}}\left\lVert\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{0})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac{L_{a}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-\left({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{0}-\frac{1}{L_{a}}\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{0})\right)\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\quad\text{for any }{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}.

This indicates that

\mathrm{Lev}[f,f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{0})]\subseteq{\mathbb{B}}_{2}\left[{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{0}-\frac{1}{L_{a}}\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{0}),\frac{1}{L_{a}}\left\lVert\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{0})\right\rVert_{2}\right].

Since
f
is closed, the above level set is closed (Theorem
); and since it is contained in a ball, it is also bounded. Therefore,
\mathrm{Lev}[f,f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{0})]
is compact. We can thus deduce that the optimal set for minimizing
f
over
\mathrm{dom}(f)
is identical to the optimal set for minimizing
f
over the nonempty compact set
\mathrm{Lev}[f,f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{0})]
. Invoking Weierstrass theorem for proper closed functions (
.
in Theorem
), it follows that a minimizer exists. To show the uniqueness, assume that
{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}
and
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}
are minimizers of
f
. Then
f({\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}})=f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*})
, where
f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*})
is the minimal value of
f
. Then by property (iv) of Theorem
,

f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*})\leq f\left(\frac{1}{2}{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}+\frac{1}{2}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}\right)\leq\frac{1}{2}f({\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}})+\frac{1}{2}f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*})-\frac{L_{a}}{8}\left\lVert{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*})-\frac{L_{a}}{8}\left\lVert{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},

implying that
{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}={\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}
, thus proving the uniqueness of the minimizer of
f
.

(ii).

Let
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}
be the unique minimizer of
f
. Then by optimality condition for convex functions (Theorem
),
\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*})=\boldsymbol{0}
. Thus, by the definition of strong convexity,

f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*})\geq\left\langle\boldsymbol{0},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}\right\rangle+\frac{L_{a}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\frac{L_{a}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},\;\text{ for any ${\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}$},

establishing claim (ii).

The definition of smoothness does not require the function to be convex. However, when it indeed is, the function can be equivalently characterized as follows.

{theoremHigh}
[Characterization theorem of SS and convexity
(
Beck 2017
)
]
Let
f:{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}\rightarrow\real
be a differentiable
convex
function defined on a convex set
{\mathbb{S}}
, and let
L_{b}>0
. Then the following statements are equivalent:

1.

f
is
L_{b}
-smooth.

2.

The function
g({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\triangleq\frac{L_{b}}{2}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
is convex.

3.

f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\leq f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\left\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}),{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rangle+\frac{L_{b}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
for all
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
.

4.

f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\geq f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\left\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}),{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rangle+\frac{1}{2L_{b}}\left\lVert\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
for all
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
.

5.

f(\lambda{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+(1-\lambda){\boldsymbol{\beta}})\geq\lambda f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+(1-\lambda)f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-\frac{L_{b}}{2}\lambda(1-\lambda)\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
for any
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
and
\lambda\in[0,1]
.

Reversing
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
and
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
in (iii) and (iv), we can also obtain

\frac{1}{L_{b}}\left\lVert\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\left\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}),{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle\leq L_{b}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},\text{ for all ${\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}$.}

(2.21)

Proof
[of Theorem
]

(i)
\implies
(ii).
For any
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
, it follows that

\displaystyle\big(\nabla g({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\nabla g({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\big)^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}})

\displaystyle=L_{b}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\big(\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\big)^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}})

\displaystyle\geq L_{b}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rVert_{2}\geq 0,

where the last inequality follows from Theorem
and the definition of smoothness.
Thus,
g({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
is a convex function by Theorem

(ii)
\implies
(iii).

Since
g({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\triangleq\frac{L_{b}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
is convex, this implies

g({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\geq g({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\nabla g({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}),\quad\forall\,{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}},

where

\nabla g({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=L_{b}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}).

Substituting the gradient into the convexity condition yields that

\displaystyle\frac{L_{b}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\geq\frac{L_{b}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\big(L_{b}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\big)^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})

\displaystyle\quad\implies\quad f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\leq\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\frac{L_{b}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

(2.22)

(iii)
\implies
(iv).

We can assume that
\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\neq\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
since otherwise the inequality (iv) is trivial by the convexity of
f
. For a fixed
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
