g_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\triangleq f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\left\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}),{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rangle,\quad{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}},

which is convex w.r.t.
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.
Note that
\nabla g_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
for any
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
.
By the condition of (iii), for any
{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\bm{u}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
, we have

\displaystyle g_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}({\bm{u}})

\displaystyle=f({\bm{u}})-f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\left\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}),{\bm{u}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rangle

(2.23)

\displaystyle\leq\big\{f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+\left\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}),{\bm{u}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle+\frac{L_{b}}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{u}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\big\}-f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\left\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}),{\bm{u}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rangle

\displaystyle=f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\left\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}),{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rangle+\left\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}),{\bm{u}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle+\frac{L_{b}}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{u}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle=g_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+\left\langle\nabla g_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}),{\bm{u}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle+\frac{L_{b}}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{u}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},

Since
\nabla g_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\boldsymbol{0}
, which by the convexity of
g_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}
implies that
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
is a global minimizer of
g_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}
such that

0=g_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\leq g_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}({\bm{u}}),\,\text{for all }{\bm{u}}\in{\mathbb{S}}.

Let
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
, and let
\widetilde{\bm{g}}\triangleq\frac{\nabla g_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})}{\left\lVert\nabla g_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rVert_{2}}
such that
\left\lVert\widetilde{\bm{g}}\right\rVert_{2}=1
and
\left\langle\nabla g_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}),\widetilde{\bm{g}}\right\rangle=\left\lVert\nabla g_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rVert_{2}
. Defining

{\bm{u}}\triangleq{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\frac{\left\lVert\nabla g_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rVert_{2}}{L_{b}}\widetilde{\bm{g}}
, the optimum of
g_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
shows that

0=g_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\leq g_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}\left({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\frac{\left\lVert\nabla g_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rVert_{2}}{L_{b}}\widetilde{\bm{g}}\right).

Combining the preceding inequality with (
), we obtain

\displaystyle 0

\displaystyle=g_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\leq g_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-\frac{\left\lVert\nabla g_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rVert_{2}}{L_{b}}\left\langle\nabla g_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}),\widetilde{\bm{g}}\right\rangle+\frac{\left\lVert\nabla g_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\cdot\left\lVert\widetilde{\bm{g}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}{2L_{b}}=g_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-\frac{\left\lVert\nabla g_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}{2L_{b}}

\displaystyle=f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\left\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}),{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rangle-\frac{1}{2L_{b}}\left\lVert\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rVert_{2}^{2},

establishing (iv).

(iii)
\implies
(v).

Let
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
and
\lambda\in[0,1]
, and denote
{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\triangleq\lambda{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+(1-\lambda){\boldsymbol{\beta}}
. Since

is convex, we also have
{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
.
Invoking (iii) with
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\xi}}
and
{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\xi}}
, and plugging in the expression of

yields that

\displaystyle f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})

\displaystyle\leq f({\boldsymbol{\xi}})+(1-\lambda)\left\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\xi}}),{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle+\frac{L_{b}(1-\lambda)^{2}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},

\displaystyle f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})

\displaystyle\leq f({\boldsymbol{\xi}})+\lambda\left\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\xi}}),{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rangle+\frac{L_{b}\lambda^{2}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

Multiplying the first inequality by
\lambda
and the second by

and adding them yields the inequality (v).

(v)
\implies
(iii).

Rearranging terms in the inequality (v), we obtain that it is equivalent to

f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\leq f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\frac{f\big({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+(1-\lambda)({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\big)-f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})}{1-\lambda}+\frac{L_{b}}{2}\lambda\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

Taking

, the preceding inequality becomes

f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\leq f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+f^{\prime}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}};{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\frac{L_{b}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
.
Since

is differentiable, (
) shows that
f^{\prime}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}};{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\left\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}),{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rangle
, establishing the desired result.

{theoremHigh}

[Characterization theorem of SC
(
Beck 2017
)
]
Let
f:{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}\rightarrow\real
be a convex and differentiable function defined on a convex set
{\mathbb{S}}
, and let
L_{a}>0
. Then the following statements are equivalent:

1.

f
is
L_{a}
-strongly convex.

2.

f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\geq f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\left\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}),{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rangle+\frac{L_{a}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

for any
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
.

3.

\left\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}),{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle\geq L_{a}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

for any
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
.

4.

f(\lambda{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+(1-\lambda){\boldsymbol{\beta}})\leq\lambda f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+(1-\lambda)f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-\frac{L_{a}}{2}\lambda(1-\lambda)\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
for any

and
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
.

The proof is similar to that of Theorem
and is left as an exercise.
The theorem shows that a strongly convex function is strictly convex.
Notably, combining Theorem
and Theorem

L_{a}

\displaystyle\frac{L_{a}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\;

\displaystyle\leq f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\left\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}),{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rangle

\displaystyle\leq

\displaystyle\frac{L_{b}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2};

(2.24a)

\displaystyle L_{a}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\;

\displaystyle\leq\left\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}),{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle

\displaystyle\leq

\displaystyle L_{b}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2};

(2.24b)

\displaystyle\frac{L_{a}\zeta}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\;

\displaystyle\leq\big\{\lambda f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+(1-\lambda)f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\}-f\big(\lambda{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+(1-\lambda){\boldsymbol{\beta}}\big)

where

for any

.
In some texts, the definitions of SC and SS are defined using (

Again, we focus on differentiable functions in this book.
When the function is not differentiable, the gradient in Theorem

.
Additionally, we have the following characterization theorem for SC and SS functions.

{theoremHigh}
[Characterization theorem of SC and SS]
Let
f:{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}\rightarrow\real
be a differentiable,
L_{a}
-strongly convex, and
L_{b}
-smooth function defined on a convex set
{\mathbb{S}}

\left\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}),{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle\geq\frac{L_{a}L_{b}}{L_{a}+L_{b}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac{1}{L_{a}+L_{b}}\left\lVert\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

(2.25)

When
L_{a}=0
, this reduces to the implication in (
) of Theorem
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Let
g({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\triangleq f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\frac{1}{2}L_{a}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
. Then
\nabla g({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-L_{a}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
.
Using (iii) in Theorem
and (
) in Theorem
, this implies
g({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
is
(L_{b}-L_{a})
-smooth and

\frac{1}{L_{b}-L_{a}}\left\lVert\nabla g({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\nabla g({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\left\langle\nabla g({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\nabla g({\boldsymbol{\beta}}),{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle,

which is equivalent to the result.

In non-convex optimization, we are often interested not in global convexity or smoothness, but in restricted versions of these properties that hold only over certain subsets of the domain—even when the function is non-convex overall.

Definition 101
(Restricted strong convexity/smoothness).

Let
f:{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}\rightarrow\real
be a differentiable function.
Then
f
is said to satisfy restricted convexity over a (possibly non-convex) set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}
if, for every
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
, it follows that

f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\geq f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}).

(2.26)

Additionally,
f
is said to satisfy
L_{a}
-restricted strong convexity (RSC) and
L_{b}
-restricted strong smoothness (RSS) over a (possibly non-convex) set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}
if, for every
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
, it follows that

\frac{L_{a}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\leq\frac{L_{b}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

(2.27)

When the function is twice differentiable, Theorem
also indicates that

L_{a}{\bm{I}}\preceq\nabla^{2}f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\preceq L_{b}{\bm{I}},

(2.28)

for any
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\text{int}({\mathbb{S}})
and there exists a vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
such that
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+\lambda{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
for some sufficiently small
\lambda
(see proof of Theorem
).
That is,

L_{a}\leq\frac{{\bm{v}}^{\top}\nabla^{2}f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}){\bm{v}}}{\left\lVert{\bm{v}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}\leq L_{b},

(2.29)

for any
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\text{int}({\mathbb{S}})
and
{\bm{v}}\in\real^{p}
such that
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+\lambda{\bm{v}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
for some sufficiently small
\lambda
.

Figure
illustrates these restricted properties.
We note that when
f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\frac{1}{2n}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
, where
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
and
{\bm{y}}\in\real^{n}
, (
) becomes
L_{a}\leq\frac{{\bm{v}}^{\top}(\frac{1}{n}{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}){\bm{v}}}{\left\lVert{\bm{v}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}\leq L_{b}
.
This yields the RSC and RSS properties for sparse problems (Definition
).

Figure 2.6:

An illustration of restricted convexity properties. The first function
f
exhibits non-convex behavior over the entire real line, yet it shows convex characteristics within the shaded region delineated by the dotted vertical lines. The second and third functions are also non-convex overall but demonstrate restricted strong convexity. Outside the shaded area, these functions fail to maintain convexity. However, within the defined region, they exhibit strong convexity. Figure is adapted from
Jain et al. 2017
.

2.8
Projection, Proximal, Bregman-Proximal, and Separation

In this section, we introduce the fundamental concepts of projection and proximal operators, which are essential tools in optimization theory and convex analysis. These concepts play a central role in the projected and proximal gradient descent methods discussed in Chapter
, as well as in the proofs of various theoretical results.

We begin by defining a divergence measure based on a convex function.

Definition 102
(Bregman distance
(
Bregman 1965
)
).

The Bregman distance (also called Bregman divergence) generalizes the concept of squared Euclidean distance and measures the difference between two points in a space.
It is defined for a convex and differentiable function
\phi:{\mathbb{S}}\rightarrow\real
, where
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}
is a convex set. The Bregman distance from point
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
to point
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
with respect to
\phi
is given by:

\mathcal{D}_{\phi}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\phi({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\phi({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-\left\langle\nabla\phi({\boldsymbol{\beta}}),{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle.

(2.30)

If
\phi
is a non-smooth convex function, let
{\bm{g}}\in\partial\phi({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
be a subgradient vector of the function
\phi
at the point
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.
The Bregman distance between the points
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
and
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
, denoted
D_{\phi}^{{\bm{g}}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}})
, is defined as

D_{\phi}^{{\bm{g}}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\phi({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\phi({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-\left\langle{\bm{g}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle.

(2.31)

For brevity, we summarize the key properties of the Bregman distance in the following remark.

Remark 103
(Properties of Bregman distance).

The Bregman distance satisfies the following properties:

1.

Nonnegativity.

\mathcal{D}_{\phi}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\geq 0,\text{for all }{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}.

When
\phi
is strictly convex, equality holds if and only if
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.

2.

The Bregman distance for the same point is zero, i.e.,
D_{\phi}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=0
.

3.

Convexity in the first argument.
For a fixed
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
,
\mathcal{D}_{\phi}(\cdot,{\boldsymbol{\beta}})
is convex in its first argument.
This property ensures that minimization problems involving
\mathcal{D}_{\phi}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}})
over
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
are well-posed—a feature frequently exploited in optimization algorithms.

4.

Not symmetric.
In general,
\mathcal{D}_{\phi}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\neq\mathcal{D}_{\phi}({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
. Thus, Bregman distances/divergences do not satisfy the symmetry property required for a distance metric. The term “distance” is retained for historical reasons.

5.

Closedness. The Bregman distance can measure the closeness of two points
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
and
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
since
D_{\phi}({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\geq D_{\phi}({\boldsymbol{\xi}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
for any point
{\boldsymbol{\xi}}
on the line connecting
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
and
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
.

6.

Linearity in the gradient.
If
\phi
is a quadratic function, then the Bregman distance reduces to a scaled version of the squared Euclidean distance.
If
\phi
is linear, the Bregman distance becomes zero.

7.

Pythagorean property.
Let
{\mathbb{T}}\subseteq{\mathbb{S}}
be a nonempty, closed, and convex subset of
{\mathbb{S}}
, and let
\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{T}}^{\phi}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
denote the projection of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
onto
{\mathbb{T}}
with respect to
\mathcal{D}_{\phi}
(Definition
). Then for any
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{T}}
,

\mathcal{D}_{\phi}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\mathcal{D}_{\phi}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}},\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{T}}^{\phi}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}))+\mathcal{D}_{\phi}(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{T}}^{\phi}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}),{\boldsymbol{\beta}})

This identity mirrors the classical Pythagorean theorem and is instrumental in analyzing the convergence of iterative algorithms.

8.

Three-point property.
For any three points
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
, the following relation holds:

\mathcal{D}_{\phi}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}})+\mathcal{D}_{\phi}({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\xi}})=\mathcal{D}_{\phi}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\xi}})+\left\langle\nabla\phi({\boldsymbol{\xi}})-\nabla\phi({\boldsymbol{\beta}}),{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle

(2.32)

This identity is often used to derive bounds and establish algorithmic guarantees.

9.

Local behavior.
When
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
is close to
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
,
\mathcal{D}_{\phi}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}})
approximates the second-order Taylor expansion of
\phi
around
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
(by the quadratic approximation theorem in Theorem
). Specifically, if
\phi
is twice continuously differentiable, then for small
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}
,

\mathcal{D}_{\phi}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\approx\frac{1}{2}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}})^{\top}\nabla^{2}\phi({\boldsymbol{\beta}})({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}})

where
\nabla^{2}\phi({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
denotes the Hessian of
\phi
at
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.

Two commonly used examples of strongly convex functions are given below.

Example 104
(Bregman with Euclidean and negative entropy).

Note that when
\phi({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\triangleq\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}:\real^{p}\rightarrow\real\cup\{\infty\}
,
\mathcal{D}_{\phi}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}})
becomes

\mathcal{D}_{\phi}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},

which corresponds to the squared Euclidean distance.
Let
\phi({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
be the negative entropy function, defined as

\phi({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\triangleq\begin{cases}\sum_{i=1}^{p}\alpha_{i}\ln(\alpha_{i})&{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}_{+};\\
\infty&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}

the Bregman distance
\mathcal{D}_{\phi}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}})
becomes

\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{\phi}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}})

\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\alpha_{i}\ln(\alpha_{i})-\sum_{i=1}^{p}\beta_{i}\ln(\beta_{i})-\sum_{i=1}^{p}(\ln(\beta_{i})+1)(\alpha_{i}-\beta_{i})

\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\alpha_{i}\ln(\alpha_{i}/\beta_{i})-\sum_{i=1}^{p}(\alpha_{i}-\beta_{i}).

If
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
and
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
lie on the probability simplex (i.e.,
\sum_{i=1}^{p}\alpha_{i}=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\beta_{i}=1
), the linear terms cancel, and we obtain the standard Kullback–Leibler divergence.

Bregman distances have broad applications across optimization, machine learning, statistics, and information theory. They are especially valuable in the design of algorithms for convex optimization because they provide a geometry-aware measure of progress toward an optimal solution—one that respects the structure induced by the convex function
\phi
.
For instance, Bregman distances are central to
mirror descent methods
, a powerful generalization of gradient descent that operates in non-Euclidean geometries; see, e.g.,
Lu 2025
.

Next, we introduce the definitions of the projection and proximal operators, along with a generalization known as the
Bregman-proximal operator

(
Lu 2025
)
.

Definition 105
(Projection, proximal, Bregman-proximal operators).

Let
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}
be a nonempty
closed
set, and let
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
.
The (orthogonal) projection of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
, denoted
\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{S}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}):\real^{p}\rightarrow{\mathbb{S}}
, is defined as

\textbf{(Projection)}:\quad{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{S}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\triangleq\mathop{\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}}_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{S}}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}=\mathop{\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}}_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{S}}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

(2.33)

Let
f:\real^{p}\rightarrow\real\cup\{\infty\}
be a
proper
function, and let
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
.
The proximal mapping of
f
, denoted
\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{f}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
, is defined as

\textbf{(Proximal)}:\quad{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\in\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{f}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\triangleq\mathop{\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}}_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}}\left(f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right).

(2.34)

Using the indicator function
\delta_{\mathbb{S}}
(defined in Exercise
), and assuming
{\mathbb{S}}
is nonempty,
one can verify that the projection and proximal operators are related by

\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{\delta_{\mathbb{S}}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{S}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}),\quad\text{for all }{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}.

(2.35)

Replacing the squared Euclidean distance in (
) with the Bregman distance, we obtain the Bregman-proximal mapping, denoted
\mathcal{B}\mathrm{rox}_{f}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
, as

\textbf{(Bregman)}:\qquad{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}\in\mathcal{B}\mathrm{rox}_{f,\phi}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\triangleq\mathop{\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}}_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}}\big(f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\mathcal{D}_{\phi}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\big),

(2.36)

where
\phi:\real^{p}\rightarrow\real\cup\{\infty\}
is a proper
convex
function.
By Example
,

\mathcal{B}\mathrm{rox}_{f,\phi}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\equiv\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{f}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\quad\text{if $\phi({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}$}.

Unless otherwise stated, we assume that projection operators act on nonempty closed sets and that proximal operators are applied to proper functions. The following example illustrates why these assumptions are necessary.

Example 106
(Counterexample for non-closed
{\mathbb{S}}
and non-proper functions).

Consider the open set
{\mathbb{S}}=\{\alpha\in\real\mid\alpha>0\}
and let
\beta=0
. The projection problem then becomes:

\widehat{\beta}=\arg\min_{\alpha>0}\alpha^{2}.

The infimum of
\alpha^{2}
is
0
, but this value is not attained because
\alpha=0\notin{\mathbb{S}}
. Thus, there is no point in
{\mathbb{S}}
achieving the infimum.

Any sequence
\{\alpha_{t}\}_{t>0}\subset{\mathbb{S}}
with
\alpha_{t}\rightarrow 0
minimizes
\alpha^{2}
, but the “solution” is not unique since it depends on the sequence chosen.

Hence, the projection is not well-defined for non-closed sets. A similar issue arises for proximal operators when
f
is not proper—for instance, if
f\equiv+\infty
, the minimization problem has no feasible solution.

Exercise
\thetheo
(Proximal calculus)

Let
g:\real^{p}\to(-\infty,\infty]
be proper, and let
\eta\neq 0
. Show that

1.

Let
f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\eta g({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}/\eta)
. Then

\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{f}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\eta\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{g/\eta}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}/\eta).

2.

Let
\eta\neq 0
and
{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\in\real^{p}
. Define
f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\triangleq g(\eta{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+{\boldsymbol{\xi}})
. Then

\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{f}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\frac{1}{\eta}\left(\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{\eta^{2}g}(\eta{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+{\boldsymbol{\xi}})-{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\right).

In the following subsections, we discuss the properties of projection and proximal operators.
The properties of Bregman-proximal operators are discussed in Problems
\sim
.

2.8.1
Properties of Projection Operators

We now present some key properties of projection operators.

Lemma 107
(Projection Property-O).

Let
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}
be any
closed set
, and let
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
such that
{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\triangleq\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{S}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
is the projection of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
onto the set
{\mathbb{S}}
. Then, for all
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
, we have
\big\lVert{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\big\rVert_{2}\leq\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\big\rVert_{2}
.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
This follows directly from the definition of the projection:

\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{S}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\mathop{\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}}_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{S}}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
.

Note that Projection Property-O holds for any closed set, whether convex or not.
However, the following three properties require convexity of the set.

Lemma 108
(Projection Property-I).

Let
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}
be a closed
convex set
, and let
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
such that
{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\triangleq\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{S}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
. Then, for all
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
, we have
\big\langle{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rangle\leq 0
, i.e., the angle between the two vectors is greater than or equal to 90°.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Assume, for contradiction, that
\big\langle{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rangle>0
for some
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
.
Since
{\mathbb{S}}
is convex and both
{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
, for any
\lambda\in[0,1]
, we have

{\boldsymbol{\xi}}_{\lambda}\triangleq\lambda\cdot{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+(1-\lambda)\cdot{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\in{\mathbb{S}}.

We will now show that there exists a value of
\lambda\in[0,1]
such that
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\xi}}_{\lambda}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}<\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}
, which contradicts the fact that
{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is the closest point in the convex set to
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
and prove the lemma.
To see this, let
\lambda_{1}\triangleq\frac{2\big\langle{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rangle}{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}
for the moment. We have

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\xi}}_{\lambda_{1}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-2\lambda_{1}\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\right\rangle+\lambda_{1}^{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

Let
g(\lambda)\triangleq\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}-2\lambda\big\langle{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rangle+\lambda^{2}\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}
. It can be shown that
\lambda=\lambda_{1}
does not obtain the minimum of
g(\lambda)
by the property of quadratic. Indeed, the minimal value is achieved at
\lambda=\frac{\lambda_{1}}{2}
.
Since we assumed
\big\langle{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rangle>0
,
letting
0<\lambda<\min\left\{1,\frac{2\big\langle{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rangle}{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}\right\}
, we have
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\xi}}_{\lambda}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}<\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}
. This contradict the property of projection operators, and completes the proof.

Lemma 109
(Projection Property-II).

Let
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}
be a closed
convex set
, and let
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
such that
{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\triangleq\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{S}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
. Then, for all
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
, we have
\big\lVert{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}
, which also implies
\big\lVert{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\big\rVert_{2}\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}
(the former inequality can be viewed as a generalized Pythagorean theorem for projections onto convex sets.).

Proof
[of Lemma
]
We expand the squared norm as follows:

\displaystyle\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle=\left\lVert({\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-({\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left\lVert{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\left\lVert{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-2\left\langle{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\dagger}}}{{\geq}}\left\lVert{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\left\lVert{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\geq\left\lVert{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},

where inequality (
{\dagger}
) follows from the Projection Property-I.

Lemma 110
(Projection Property-III).

Let
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}
be a closed
convex set
, and let
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
. Then,
\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{S}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\triangleq\mathop{\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}}_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{S}}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
has a
unique
optimal solution.

Proof
[Lemma
]
Since the objective function in
\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{S}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\triangleq\mathop{\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}}_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{S}}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
is a quadratic function associated with a positive definite
matrix, it follows by Problem
that the objective function is coercive and hence, by Weierstrass theorem
in Theorem
, that the problem has at least one optimal solution. In addition, since the
objective function is strictly convex (again, since the objective function is quadratic associated with a
positive definite matrix), it follows by Theorem
that there exists only one optimal
solution.

Convexity matters.

Note that Projection Properties-I, II, and III are often referred to as first-order properties of projections and rely crucially on the convexity of
{\mathbb{S}}
. However, Projection Property-O, often called a zeroth-order property, holds for any nonempty closed set, convex or not; see Figure
.

Figure 2.7:

Projection operators map a point
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
to the closest point
{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
in a set
{\mathbb{S}}
.
For convex sets, Projection Property-I ensures that the angle
\theta
between the vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
(from the projection to the original point) and any vector
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
(from the projection to another point in the set) is at least
90^{\circ}
.
Sets satisfying Property-I automatically satisfy Property-II, which guarantees that projecting
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
onto
{\mathbb{S}}
never increases its distance to any other point
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
.
However, non-convex sets may violate Property-II.

Example 111
(Projection onto subsets of
p
).

Below are examples of nonempty closed and convex sets together with their orthogonal projections:

1.

Nonnegative orthant
{\mathbb{S}}_{1}=\real^{p}_{+}
:
\mathcal{P}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{1}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\{\max\{\beta_{i},0\}\}_{i=1}^{p}
.

2.

Box
{\mathbb{S}}_{2}=\text{Box}[\bm{\ell},{\bm{u}}]\triangleq\{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}\mid\bm{\ell}\leq{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\leq{\bm{u}}\}
:
\mathcal{P}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{2}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\left\{\min(\max(\beta_{i},\ell_{i}),u_{i})\right\}_{i=1}^{p}
.

3.

Closed
\ell_{2}
-ball
{\mathbb{S}}_{3}={\mathbb{B}}_{2}[{\bm{a}},\gamma]
:
\mathcal{P}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{3}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})={\bm{a}}+\frac{\gamma}{\max\{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{a}}\right\rVert_{2},\gamma\}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{a}})
.

4.

Half-space
{\mathbb{S}}_{4}=\{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\mid{\bm{c}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\leq\eta\}
:
\mathcal{P}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{4}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})={\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\frac{\max\{{\bm{c}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\eta,0\}}{\left\lVert{\bm{c}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}{\bm{c}}
.

5.

Affine set
{\mathbb{S}}_{5}=\{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}\mid{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}={\bm{y}}\}
:
\mathcal{P}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{5}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})={\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{X}}^{\top}({\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{\top})^{-1}({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}})
.

where
\bm{\ell}\in[-\infty,\infty)^{p},{\bm{u}}\in(-\infty,\infty]^{p}
satisfying
\bm{\ell}\leq{\bm{u}}
,
{\bm{a}}\in\real^{p}
,
\gamma>0
,
{\bm{c}}\in\real^{p}\setminus\{\boldsymbol{0}\}
,
\eta\in\real
,
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
has full row rank such that
{\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{\top}
is nonsingular, and
{\bm{y}}\in\real^{n}
.
The results in (i)–(iv) holds trivially.
For (v),
it’s equivalent to solving the following optimization problem:

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}}\quad\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}={\bm{y}},

where
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
,
{\bm{y}}\in\real^{n}
and
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
are given matrices and vectors.
We assume that the matrix
{\bm{X}}
has full row rank (for matrices that do not have full row rank, we can remove linearly dependent rows to obtain a reduced constraint condition).
For the equality constraint, we introduce the Lagrange multiplier
{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n}
and construct the Lagrangian function (see Section
):

L({\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})=\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{\top}({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\bm{y}}).

Since the objective is convex and the constraints are affine, Slater’s condition holds trivially.
Theorem
shows that
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}
is a global optimum if and only if there exists
{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{*}\in\real^{n}
such that

\begin{cases}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{*}=\boldsymbol{0},\\
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}={\bm{y}}.\end{cases}

This yields that

{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+{\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{*}=\boldsymbol{0}\qquad\implies\qquad{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{*}=({\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{\top})^{-1}({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}).

Plugging
{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{*}
back yields the claimed formula.

2.8.2
Separation Theorem

Using properties of projections, we can prove the following strict separation theorem, which is essential for establishing Farkas’ lemma (Problem
). Farkas’ lemma, in turn, plays a fundamental role in the derivation of the KKT conditions; see, for example,
Lu 2025
for further details. Additional separation results are discussed in Problems
\sim
.

{theoremHigh}
[Strict separation theorem]
Let
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}
be a closed
convex
set, and let
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\notin{\mathbb{S}}
. Then there exist
{\bm{w}}\in\real^{p}\setminus\{\boldsymbol{0}\}
and
\gamma\in\real
such that

{\bm{w}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}>\gamma\qquad\text{and}\qquad{\bm{w}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\leq\gamma,\quad\text{for all }{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{S}}.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Let
{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\triangleq\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{S}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\in{\mathbb{S}}
. By the Projection Property-I (Lemma
),

\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\right\rangle\leq 0\quad\implies\quad({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\leq({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})^{\top}{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}},\quad\text{for all }{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{S}}.

Denote
{\bm{w}}\triangleq{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\neq\boldsymbol{0}
(since
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\notin{\mathbb{S}}
) and
\gamma\triangleq({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})^{\top}{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
. Then we have that
{\bm{w}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\leq\gamma
for all
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
. On the other hand,

{\bm{w}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})+({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})^{\top}{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\gamma>\gamma,

establishing the desired result.

2.8.3
Properties of Proximal Operators

Analogously to projection operators, for the proximal operator, if the function is closed and satisfies a mild coerciveness condition (i.e.,
f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\to\infty
as
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}\to\infty
) then the proximal map
\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{f}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
is guaranteed to be nonempty for every
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
.

Lemma 112
(Proximal Property-O: Nonemptiness of prox under closedness and coerciveness).

Let
f:\real^{p}\rightarrow(-\infty,\infty]
be a proper
closed
function, and assume that the following condition holds:

\text{the function }{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\mapsto f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\text{ is coercive for any }{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}.

Then
\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{f}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
is
nonempty
for any
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
For any
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real
, the proper function
g({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\triangleq f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
is closed as a sum of two closed functions.
Therefore, by the standard existence result for minimizers of proper, closed, and coercive functions (e.g., Weierstrass theorem
in Theorem
),
the set of minimizers of
g
, which is precisely
\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{f}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
, is nonempty.

Lemma 113
(Proximal Property-I).

Let
f:\real^{p}\rightarrow(-\infty,\infty]
be a proper
closed and convex
function. Then for any
{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\in\real^{p}
, the following three statements are equivalent:

1.

{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}=\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{f}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
.

2.

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\in\partial f({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})
.

3.

\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}},{\boldsymbol{\xi}}-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\right\rangle\leq f({\boldsymbol{\xi}})-f({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})
for any
{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\in\real^{p}
.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
By definition,
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}=\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{f}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
if and only if
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is the minimizer of the problem

\mathop{\min}_{{\bm{v}}}\left\{f({\bm{v}})+\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{v}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right\},

which, by the optimality condition (Theorem
) and the sum rule of subdifferential calculus, is equivalent to the relation

\boldsymbol{0}\in\partial f({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})+{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}.

This establishes the equivalence between (i) and (ii).
Finally, by the definition of the subgradient (Definition
), the membership relation of claim (ii) is equivalent to (iii).

When
f=\delta_{\mathbb{S}}
, with
{\mathbb{S}}
being a nonempty closed and convex set, the equivalence between claims (i) and (iii) in the Proximal Property-I reduces exactly to the Projection Property-I (Lemma
).

For consistency with the projection properties, we also state Proximal Property-II, although it is less frequently used in practice.

Lemma 114
(Proximal Property-II).

Let
f:\real^{p}\rightarrow(-\infty,\infty]
be a proper
closed and convex
function. Then for any
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\triangleq\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{f}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
and
{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\in\real^{p}
, it follows that

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\geq\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\xi}}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}+\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}+2\left(f({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})-f({\boldsymbol{\xi}})\right).

Lemma 115
(Proximal Property-III).

Let
f:\real^{p}\rightarrow(-\infty,\infty]
be a proper
closed and convex
function. Then
\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{f}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
is a
singleton
for any
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
For any
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}
,

\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{f}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\arg\min_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}}g({\boldsymbol{\beta}};{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}),

(2.37)

where
g({\boldsymbol{\beta}};{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
. The function
g({\boldsymbol{\beta}};{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
is a closed and strongly convex function as a sum of the closed and strongly convex function
\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
and the closed and convex function
f
(Exercise
and Exercise
). The properness of
g({\boldsymbol{\beta}};{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
immediately follows from the properness of
f
. Therefore, by the SC Property-II (Theorem
, or Theorem
for the uniqueness under strict convexity), there exists a unique minimizer to the problem in (
).

The Proximal Property-III also proves the Projection Property-III (Lemma
) by noting that
\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{\delta_{\mathbb{S}}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{S}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
for any
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
if
{\mathbb{S}}
is convex and closed (the indicator function is closed convex due to Exercises
and
).

When
f
is proper closed and convex, the preceding lemma shows that
\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{f}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
is a singleton for any
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
. In these cases, which will constitute the vast majority of cases that will be discussed in this book, we will treat
\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{f}
as a single-valued mapping from
p
to
p
, meaning that we will simply write
\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{f}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})={\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
instead of
\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{f}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\{{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\}
.

Convexity and Closedness.

Note again that Proximal Properties-I, II, and III are often referred to as first-order properties and can be violated if the underlying function is non-convex. However, Projection Property-O, often called a zeroth-order property, always holds, whether the underlying function is convex or not.
In all cases, we require the function to be closed to ensure the attainment due to the Weierstrass theorem (Theorem
).

{theoremHigh}

[Projection and Proximal Property-IV: Nonexpansiveness]
Let
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}
be a closed
convex set
, and let
f:\real^{p}\rightarrow(-\infty,\infty]
be a proper
closed and convex
function. Then,

1.

Firm nonexpansiveness.
For any
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
, it follows that

\displaystyle\left\lVert\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{S}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{S}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle\leq\left\langle\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{S}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{S}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}),{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle;

\displaystyle\left\lVert\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{f}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{f}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle\leq\left\langle\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{f}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{f}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}),{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle.

2.

Nonexpansiveness.
For any
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
, it follows that

\displaystyle\left\lVert\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{S}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{S}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rVert_{2}

\displaystyle\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2};

\displaystyle\left\lVert\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{f}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{f}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rVert_{2}

\displaystyle\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}.

Proof
[of Theorem
]

Projection operator.
By the Projection Property-I (Lemma
), for any
{\bm{u}}\in\real^{p}
and
{\bm{v}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
, we have that

\left\langle{\bm{v}}-\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{S}}({\bm{u}}),{\bm{u}}-\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{S}}({\bm{u}})\right\rangle\leq 0.

Invoking this inequality with
{\bm{u}}\triangleq{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\bm{v}}\triangleq\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{S}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
and
{\bm{u}}\triangleq{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\bm{v}}\triangleq\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{S}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
:

\displaystyle\left\langle\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{S}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{S}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}),{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{S}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\right\rangle

\displaystyle\leq 0\qquad\text{and}\qquad\left\langle\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{S}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{S}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}),{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{S}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rangle

\displaystyle\leq 0.

Adding the two inequalities yields that

\left\langle\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{S}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{S}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}),{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{S}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{S}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\right\rangle\leq 0,

showing the firm nonexpansiveness of projection operators.

To prove the nonexpansiveness, note that if
\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{S}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{S}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
, the inequality holds trivially. We will therefore assume that
\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{S}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\neq\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{S}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality we have

\left\langle\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{S}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{S}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}),{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle\leq\left\lVert\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{S}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{S}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rVert_{2}\cdot\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2},

which combined with the firm nonexpansivess yields the desired result.

Proximal operator.

Denoting
{\bm{u}}\triangleq\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{f}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
,
{\bm{v}}\triangleq\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{f}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
, by the equivalence of (i) and (ii) in the Proximal Property-I (Lemma
), it follows that

{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\bm{u}}\in\partial f({\bm{u}})\qquad\text{and}\qquad{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{v}}\in\partial f({\bm{v}}).

By the subgradient inequality, we have

f({\bm{v}})\geq f({\bm{u}})+\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\bm{u}},{\bm{v}}-{\bm{u}}\right\rangle\qquad\text{and}\qquad f({\bm{u}})\geq f({\bm{v}})+\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{v}},{\bm{u}}-{\bm{v}}\right\rangle.

Adding the two inequalities yields that

0\geq\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+{\bm{u}}-{\bm{v}},{\bm{u}}-{\bm{v}}\right\rangle,

showing the firm nonexpansiveness of proximal operators.

To prove the nonexpansiveness, if
\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{f}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{f}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
, then the inequality is trivial. Therefore, we assume that
\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{f}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\neq\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{f}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, it follows that

\left\langle\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{f}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{f}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}),{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle\leq\left\lVert\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{f}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{f}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rVert_{2}\cdot\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2},

which combined with the firm nonexpansivess yields the desired result.

Finally, note that the (firm) nonexpansiveness of the projection operator is a special case of the proximal operator result. Indeed, setting
f\triangleq\delta_{\mathbb{S}}
(the indicator function of
{\mathbb{S}}
), we have
\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{f}=\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{S}}
, and since
\delta_{\mathbb{S}}
is proper, closed, and convex whenever
{\mathbb{S}}
is nonempty, closed, and convex (Exercises
and
), the proximal nonexpansiveness theorem directly implies the projection version.

Example 116
(Soft-thresholding, proximal of
\ell_{1}
-norms).

Let
f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\lambda\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{1}=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\psi(\alpha_{i})
, where
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}
,
\lambda>0
, and
\psi(u)=\lambda\left\lvert u\right\rvert
.
Then
\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{f}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\big\{\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{\psi}(\beta_{i})\big\}_{i=1}^{p},

where
\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{\psi}(\beta)=\mathcal{T}_{\lambda}(\beta)
, and
\mathcal{T}_{\lambda}
is known as the soft-thresholding function and is defined as

\mathcal{T}_{\lambda}(\beta)\triangleq[\left\lvert\beta\right\rvert-\lambda]_{+}\cdot\sign(\beta)=\begin{cases}\beta-\lambda,&\beta\geq\lambda;\\
0,&\left\lvert\beta\right\rvert<\lambda;\\
\beta+\lambda,&\beta\leq-\lambda.\end{cases}

(2.38)

where
[u]_{+}=\max\{u,0\}
for any
u\in\real
, and the sign function is given by
\sign(u)=u/\left\lvert u\right\rvert
for
u\neq 0
, as usual.
See Figure
for an illustration of this soft-thresholding function.
More compactly, the proximal operation of
f
can be denoted as

\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{f}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\mathcal{T}_{\lambda}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\left\{\mathcal{T}_{\lambda}(\beta_{i})\right\}_{i=1}^{p}=[\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rvert-\lambda{\bm{1}}]_{+}\circ\sign({\boldsymbol{\beta}}),

where
\circ
denotes the Hadamard product, and
{\bm{1}}
is the all-ones vector.

Figure 2.8:
Illustration of the soft-thresholding function
\mathcal{T}_{\lambda}(\beta)
for different values of
\lambda
.

Example 117
(Block soft-thresholding).

The proximal operator of the function
f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\lambda\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}
with
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}
, the scaled
\ell_{2}
-norm, is known as the block soft-thresholding function.
This is often used in group sparsity (see Section
).
The proximal operator has a closed-form solution:

\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{\lambda\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{2}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\left[1-\frac{\lambda}{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}}\right]_{+}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\left(1-\frac{\lambda}{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}}\right){\boldsymbol{\beta}},&\text{if }\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}>\lambda;\\
\boldsymbol{0},&\text{if }\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\lambda,\end{cases}

(2.39)

where
[u]_{+}=\max(u,0)
.
To see this, we observe that the objective is radially symmetric, so the minimizer
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}
must be colinear with
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
:
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}=\gamma{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
for some
\gamma\geq 0
.
Substitute into the objective:

\lambda\left\lVert\gamma{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}+\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert\gamma{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\lambda\gamma\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}+\frac{1}{2}(\gamma-1)^{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

Minimize over
\gamma\geq 0
, we differentiate with respect to
\gamma
:

\lambda\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}+(\gamma-1)\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=0\quad\implies\quad\gamma=1-\frac{\lambda}{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}}.

However, since
\gamma\geq 0
, this solution is valid only when
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}>\lambda
.
If
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\lambda
, the minimum occurs at
\gamma=0
, yielding
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}=\boldsymbol{0}
.

As a special case, when the dimension
p=1
, then
\left\lVert\beta\right\rVert_{2}=\left\lvert\beta\right\rvert
and

\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{\lambda\left\lvert\cdot\right\rvert}(\beta)=\sign(\beta)\max(\left\lvert\beta\right\rvert-\lambda,0),

which reduces to the scalar soft-thresholding operator from Example
.

2.8.4
Moreau Decomposition

A key property of the proximal operator is the so-called
Moreau decomposition
theorem,
which establishes a relationship between the proximal operator of a proper closed convex function and that of its convex conjugate (Definition
).

{theoremHigh}
[Moreau decomposition]
Let
f:\real^{p}\to(-\infty,\infty]
be a proper closed and convex function. Then, for all
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
,

\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{f}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{f^{*}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})={\boldsymbol{\beta}}.

(2.40)

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Let
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\triangleq\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{f}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
. Then by the equivalence between claims (i) and (ii) in the Proximal Property-I (Lemma
), it follows that
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\in\partial f({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})
, which by the conjugate subgradient theorem (Theorem
) is equivalent to
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\in\partial f^{*}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})
.
Using the Proximal Property-I (Lemma
) again, we conclude that
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}=\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{f^{*}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
. Therefore,

\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{f}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{f^{*}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})={\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}+({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})={\boldsymbol{\beta}}.

This completes the proof.

The next result provides a useful generalization of the Moreau decomposition theorem.

{theoremHigh}
[Extended Moreau decomposition]
Let
f:\real^{p}\to(-\infty,\infty]
be a proper closed and convex function, and let
\eta>0
. Then, for all
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
,

\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{\eta f}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+\eta\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{\eta^{-1}f^{*}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}/\eta)={\boldsymbol{\beta}}.

(2.41)

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Using Moreau decomposition, for any
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
,

\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{\eta f}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})={\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{(\eta f)^{*}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})={\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{\eta f^{*}(\cdot/\eta)}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}),

(2.42)

where the second equality follows from conjugate calculus (Exercise
).
By proximal calculus (Exercise
),

\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{\eta f^{*}(\cdot/\eta)}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\eta\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{\eta^{-1}f^{*}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}/\eta),

which, combined with (
), yields the desired identity.

2.9
Convex Optimization and Optimaliy Conditions

We have already encountered the general form of optimization problems in previous chapters.
More precisely, a
convex optimization problem
(or simply a convex problem) involves minimizing a convex function over a convex set:

\textbf{(Convex optimization)}:\qquad\begin{aligned} &\min\quad f({\boldsymbol{\theta}})\quad&&\text{(convex function)}\\
&\text{s.t.}\quad{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}\quad&&\text{(convex set)},\end{aligned}

(2.43)

where the function
f:\real^{p}\to(-\infty,\infty]
is called the
objective function
(or
loss function
),
and
{\mathbb{S}}
is the
constraint set
.
A point
{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
that satisfies the constraints is called
feasible
.
The problem (
) is said to be feasible if at least one feasible point exists.
A feasible point
{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{*}
that achieves the minimum—i.e.,
f({\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{*})\leq f({\boldsymbol{\theta}})
for all feasible
{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
—is called a
minimizer
,
minimum point
, or
optimal point
.
And the value
f({\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{*})
is referred to as the
optimal value
.

Example 118
(Equality and inequality constraints).

Consider the following problem:

\displaystyle\min

\displaystyle f({\boldsymbol{\theta}})

(2.44)

\displaystyle\text{s.t.}

\displaystyle g_{i}({\boldsymbol{\theta}})\leq 0,\quad i=\{1,2,\ldots,m\},

\displaystyle h_{j}({\boldsymbol{\theta}})=0,\quad j=\{1,2,\ldots,n\},

where
f,g_{1},g_{2},\ldots,g_{m}:\real^{p}\rightarrow\real
are convex functions, and
h_{1},h_{2},\ldots,h_{n}:\real^{p}\rightarrow\real
are affine functions.
Since the objective function is convex and the feasible set is a convex set, this problem is a convex optimization problem.
The feasible set can be expressed as

{\mathbb{S}}=\bigg(\bigcap_{i=1}^{m}\mathrm{Lev}[g_{i},0]\bigg)\cap\bigg(\bigcap_{j=1}^{n}\{{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mid h_{j}({\boldsymbol{\theta}})=0\}\bigg),

which is a convex set since it is the intersection of level sets of convex functions and hyperplanes, both of which are also convex sets.

Example 119
(Linear programming (LP)).

A linear programming (LP) problem involves minimizing a linear objective function subject to linear equality and inequality constraints:

\text{(LP)}\qquad\begin{aligned} \min&\quad{\bm{c}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\theta}}+d\\
\text{s.t.}&\quad{\bm{G}}{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\leq{\bm{h}},\\
&\quad{\bm{A}}{\boldsymbol{\theta}}={\bm{b}},\end{aligned}

where
{\bm{G}}\in\real^{n\times p}
,
{\bm{h}}\in\real^{n}
,
{\bm{A}}\in\real^{m\times p}
,
{\bm{b}}\in\real^{m}
, and
{\bm{c}}\in\real^{p}
. (For convenience, we write
{\bm{a}}\leq\boldsymbol{0}
if
a_{i}\leq 0
for all
i
.)
This is a convex optimization problem because affine functions are inherently convex. The constant term
d
in the objective does not affect the location of the minimizer and can be omitted when identifying optimal solutions.
A commonly used formulation is the “standard form” of an LP:

\text{(Standard LP)}\qquad\begin{aligned} \min&\quad{\bm{c}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\\
\text{s.t.}&\quad{\bm{A}}{\boldsymbol{\theta}}={\bm{b}},\\
&\quad{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\geq\boldsymbol{0}.\end{aligned}

Any LP can be converted into this standard form. To do so, we introduce nonnegative slack variables
{\bm{s}}
to turn inequalities into equalities:
{\bm{G}}{\boldsymbol{\theta}}+{\bm{s}}={\bm{h}}
.
Additionally, we express
{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
as the difference of two nonnegative variables
{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\triangleq{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{+}-{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{-}
, where
{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{+},{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{-}\geq\boldsymbol{0}
:

\text{(LP${}^{\prime}$)}\qquad\begin{aligned} \min&\quad{\bm{c}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{+}-{\bm{c}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{-}+d\\
\text{s.t.}&\quad{\bm{G}}{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{+}-{\bm{G}}{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{-}+{\bm{s}}={\bm{h}},\\
&\quad{\bm{A}}{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{+}-{\bm{A}}{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{-}={\bm{b}},\\
&\quad{\bm{s}}\geq\boldsymbol{0},{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{+}\geq\boldsymbol{0},{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{-}\geq\boldsymbol{0},\end{aligned}\quad\iff\quad\begin{aligned} \min&\quad[{\bm{c}}^{\top},-{\bm{c}}^{\top},\boldsymbol{0}]{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}+d\\
\text{s.t.}&\quad[{\bm{G}},-{\bm{G}},{\bm{I}}]{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}={\bm{h}},\\
&\quad[{\bm{A}},-{\bm{A}},\boldsymbol{0}]{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}={\bm{b}},\\
&\quad{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}\geq\boldsymbol{0},\end{aligned}

where

{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}\triangleq\scriptsize\begin{bmatrix}{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{+}\\
{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{-}\\
{\bm{s}}\end{bmatrix}
.
This reformulation is in standard LP form with decision variable
{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}
. For each feasible solution
{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{*}
of (LP), we can set
{\bm{s}}\triangleq{\bm{h}}-{\bm{G}}{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{*}
,
\theta_{i}^{+}\triangleq\max\{0,\theta_{i}\}
, and
\theta_{i}^{-}\triangleq\max\{0,-\theta_{i}\}
for all
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
, which is a feasible solution of (LP
′
). This shows the optimal value of (LP
′
) is less than or equal to the optimal value of (LP).
Conversely, suppose
{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{+},{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{-}
, and
{\bm{s}}
are feasible solutions of (LP
′
). Then,
{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\triangleq{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{+}-{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{-}
is a feasible solution of (LP), demonstrating that the optimal value of (LP) is less than or equal to the optimal value of (LP
′
). Therefore, the optimization problems (LP) and (LP
′
) are equivalent.

Example 120
(Quadratic Programming).

The convex optimization problem (
) is called a quadratic program (QP) if the objective function is quadratic with positive semidefinite (convex), and the constraint functions are affine. A general form can be written as:

\displaystyle\text{min}

\displaystyle{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{\top}{\bm{P}}{\boldsymbol{\theta}}+2{\bm{q}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\theta}}+r

\displaystyle\text{s.t.}

\displaystyle{\displaystyle\bm{G}}{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\leq{\bm{h}},

\displaystyle{\displaystyle\bm{A}}{\boldsymbol{\theta}}={\bm{b}},

where
{\bm{P}}\in\real^{p\times p}
is positive semidefinite,
{\bm{q}}\in\real^{p}
,
{\bm{G}}\in\real^{n\times p}
,
{\bm{h}}\in\real^{n}
,
{\bm{A}}\in\real^{m\times p}
, and
{\bm{b}}\in\real^{m}
.
If both the objective function and inequality constraints are convex quadratic:

\displaystyle\text{min}

\displaystyle{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{\top}{\bm{P}}{\boldsymbol{\theta}}+2{\bm{q}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\theta}}+r

\displaystyle\text{s.t.}

\displaystyle{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{\top}{\bm{G}}_{i}{\boldsymbol{\theta}}+2{\bm{h}}_{i}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\theta}}+c_{i}\leq 0,\quad i=\{1,2,\ldots,k\},

\displaystyle{\displaystyle\bm{A}}{\boldsymbol{\theta}}={\bm{b}},

where
{\bm{P}},{\bm{G}}_{1},{\bm{G}}_{2},\ldots,{\bm{G}}_{k}
are positive semidefinite, the problem is called a quadratically constrained quadratic program (QCQP).
In a QCQP, we minimize a convex quadratic function over a feasible region defined as the intersection of ellipsoids (when each
{\bm{G}}_{i}\succ\boldsymbol{0}
) and affine subspaces.

2.9.1
Constrained Optimization over Convex Sets

We begin by restricting our attention to optimization problems defined over a
convex
set
{\mathbb{S}}
.
In this setting, if the objective function
f
is also convex, the problem becomes a convex optimization problem, as previously discussed.
Earlier, in Corollary
or Theorem
, we introduced
stationary points
for unconstrained problems—specifically, points
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
where gradient vanishes
\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})=\boldsymbol{0}
, or
\boldsymbol{0}\in\partial f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})
when the function is not smooth.
However, for constrained problems, this definition no longer suffices, and a more general notion is required.

Definition 121
(Stationary points of constrained problems on a convex set).

Consider the constrained optimization problem

\text{(P${}_{C}$)}\quad\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}.

(2.45)

Let
f
be a continuously differentiable function over a closed
convex
set
{\mathbb{S}}
. Then
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\in{\mathbb{S}}
is called a stationary point of (P
C
) if
\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})\geq 0
for any
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
.

The following result shows that a local minimum point of a constraint optimization problem must be a stationary point.

{theoremHigh}

[First-order necessary condition for (P
C
) over a convex set]
Consider the constrained optimization problem (P
C
):
\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
subject to
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
.
Let
f
be a continuously differentiable function on a closed
convex
set
{\mathbb{S}}
, and let
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
be a local minimum of (P
C
). Then
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
is a stationary point of (P
C
).

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Let
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
be a local minimum of (P
C
), and assume in contradiction that
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
is not a stationary point of (P
C
). Then there exists some
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
such that
\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})<0
. By Lemma
, it follows that there exists
\varepsilon\in(0,1)
such that
f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}+\eta{\bm{d}})<f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})
for all
\eta\in(0,\varepsilon)
, where
{\bm{d}}\triangleq{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
. Since
{\mathbb{S}}
is convex we have that
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}+\eta{\bm{d}}=(1-\eta){\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}+\eta{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
, contradicting the assumption that
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
is a local minimum point of (P
C
).
Hence,
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
must be a stationary point.

When the projection onto the convex set
{\mathbb{S}}
admits a closed-form expression, the first-order condition can be equivalently stated using the projection operator. This leads to the following characterization.

Corollary 122
(Necessity/sufficiency for (P
C
) on a convex set under projection).

Consider the constrained optimization problem (P
C
):
\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
subject to
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
.
Let
f
be a continuously differentiable function on a closed
convex
set
{\mathbb{S}}
, and let
\eta>0
be an arbitrary positive scalar. Then
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
is a stationary point of (P
C
)
if and only if

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}=\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{S}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-\eta\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})).

Proof
[of Corollary
]
By the Projection Property-I (Lemma
), it follows that
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}=\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{S}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-\eta\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}))
if and only if

\displaystyle\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-\eta\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rangle\leq 0\quad\implies\quad\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})\geq 0,\text{ for any }{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}.

This is precisely the definition of a stationary point in Definition
, completing the proof.

2.9.2
Equality/Inequality Constraints

We now consider the problem presented in Example
.
Such an optimization problem is typically formulated as

\displaystyle\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}f_{0}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})

(P)

s.t.

\displaystyle{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\bm{y}},

\displaystyle f_{i}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\leq z_{i},\quad i\in\{1,2,\ldots,q\},

where the function
f_{0}:\real^{p}\to(-\infty,\infty]
is again called the objective function or loss function,
the functions
f_{1},f_{2},\ldots,f_{q}:\real^{p}\to(-\infty,\infty]
are referred to as
(inequality) constraint functions
, and
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
,
{\bm{y}}\in\real^{n}
define the
equality constraint
.
Note that if
f_{0},f_{1},\ldots,f_{q}
are all convex functions, then problem (
P
) is a
convex
optimization problem.

The equality constraint can be equivalently expressed using inequality constraints. Specifically, for each row
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{i}^{\top}
of
{\bm{X}}
(i.e., the
i
-th row), the condition
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{i}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=y_{i}
is equivalent to the pair of inequalities

{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{i}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\leq y_{i}\qquad\text{and}\qquad-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{i}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\leq-y_{i}.

Note that the set of feasible points described by the constraints can be obtained as

{\mathbb{S}}=\{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}\mid{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\bm{y}},f_{i}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\leq z_{i},i\in\{1,2,\ldots,q\}\}.

(2.46)

Thus, problem (
P
) is equivalent to minimizing
f_{0}
over the feasible set
{\mathbb{S}}
,

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}}f_{0}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}).

(2.47)

Furthermore, by introducing the indicator function
\delta_{\mathbb{S}}
(see Example
), the constrained problem can be reformulated as an unconstrained optimization problem involving the composite objective

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}F({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\triangleq f_{0}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+\delta_{\mathbb{S}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}).

(2.48)

2.9.3
Dual Problem

The
Lagrange function
(or simply the
Lagrangian
) associated with an optimization problem of the form (
P
) is defined for
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
,
{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n}
,
{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\in\real^{q}
,
\nu_{i}\geq 0
,
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,q\}
(for brevity, we write
{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\geq\boldsymbol{0}
when all components of
{\boldsymbol{\nu}}
are nonnegative), by

L({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\boldsymbol{\nu}})\triangleq f_{0}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{\top}({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}})+\sum_{i=1}^{q}\nu_{i}(f_{i}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-z_{i})\triangleq f_{0}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{\top}({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}})+{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{\top}{\bm{f}},

(2.49)

where the vectors
{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}
and
{\boldsymbol{\nu}}
are called
Lagrange multipliers
, and

{\bm{f}}\triangleq\{f_{i}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-z_{i}\}_{i=1}^{q}\in\real^{q}.

The
Lagrange dual function
(or simply the
dual function
) is defined by

D({\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\boldsymbol{\nu}})\triangleq\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}L({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\boldsymbol{\nu}}),\quad{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n},{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\in\real^{q},{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\geq\boldsymbol{0}.

(2.50)

If the function
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\mapsto L({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\boldsymbol{\nu}})
is unbounded from below, we set
D({\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\boldsymbol{\nu}})=-\infty
.
Importantly, the dual function is always
concave
because it is the pointwise infimum of a family of affine functions in
({\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\boldsymbol{\nu}})
, even if the original problem (
P
) is not convex (see Exercise
by noting that the negative of a concave function is convex).

Now, suppose
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is a feasible point for (
P
).
Then
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}=\boldsymbol{0}
and
f_{i}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\leq z_{i}
,
i=1,2,\ldots,q
.
Since
{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\geq\boldsymbol{0}
, it follows that

\displaystyle{\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{\top}({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}})+{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{\top}{\bm{f}}\leq 0

\displaystyle\implies

\displaystyle L({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\boldsymbol{\nu}})=f_{0}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{\top}({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}})+{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{\top}{\bm{f}}\leq f_{0}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}).

Taking the infimum over all
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
on the left-hand side (which yields
D({\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\boldsymbol{\nu}})
), and over all feasible
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
on the right-hand side (which gives the optimal value
f_{0}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})
)
leads to the fundamental inequality

D({\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\boldsymbol{\nu}})\leq f_{0}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}),\quad\text{for all }{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n},{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\geq\boldsymbol{0}.

(2.51)

Thus, the dual function provides a lower bound on the optimal value of the primal problem. To obtain the tightest possible lower bound, we maximize this dual function, which gives rise to the
dual problem
to (
P
):

\max_{{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n},{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\geq\boldsymbol{0}}D({\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\boldsymbol{\nu}}).

(D)

Consequently, the original problem (
P
) is often referred to as the
primal problem
.

Strong Duality

Since problem (
) involves maximizing a concave function, it is equivalent to the convex optimization problem of minimizing the convex function
-D
subject to the positivity constraint
{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\geq\boldsymbol{0}
.
A pair
({\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\boldsymbol{\nu}})
with
{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n}
and
{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\geq\boldsymbol{0}
is called
dual feasible
.
A (dual feasible) maximizer
({\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{*},{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{*})
of (
) is referred to as
dual optimal
or as the
optimal Lagrange multipliers
. If
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
is optimal for the primal problem (
P
), then the triple
({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{*},{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{*})
is called
primal-dual optimal
.
Inequality (
) implies that, for dual optimal
({\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{*},{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{*})
and primal optimal
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
,

D({\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{*},{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{*})\leq f_{0}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}).

(2.52)

This relationship is known as
weak duality
.
For most—but not all—convex optimization problems,
strong duality
holds, meaning that equality is achieved:

D({\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{*},{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{*})=f_{0}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}).

(2.53)

See Problem
\sim
for the strong duality of linear programs.

A well-known sufficient condition for strong duality in convex problems is Slater’s condition, stated below in a simplified form.

{theoremHigh}

[Slater’s condition qualification for convex problems]
Assume that
f_{0},f_{1},f_{2},\ldots,f_{q}
are convex functions with
\mathrm{dom}(f_{0})=\real^{p}
. If there exists
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
such that
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\bm{y}}
and
f_{i}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})<0
for all
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,q\}
, then strong duality holds for the optimization problem (
P
).

Proof

See, for example, Chapter 6 of
Bertsekas et al.
or Chapter 2 of
Lu 2025
.

We also recall some well-known optimality conditions expressed in terms of the Lagrangian function in cases where strong duality holds

{theoremHigh}

[KKT conditions: Optimality under strong duality]
Suppose strong duality holds; that is, the optimal values of problems (
P
) and (
) are finite and equal.
Then
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
and
({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}},{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}})
are optimal solutions to the primal and dual problems, respectively, if and only if the following conditions hold:

1.

Primal feasibility.

{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is a feasible solution of (
P
), i.e.,
{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}={\bm{y}}
and
f_{i}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})\leq z_{i}
for all
i=1,2,\ldots,q
.

2.

Dual feasibility.

{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}\geq\boldsymbol{0}
.

3.

Complementary slackness.

{\widehat{\nu}}_{i}(f_{i}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})-z_{i})=0

for all
i=1,2,\ldots,q
.

4.

Stationarity.

{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\in\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}L({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}},{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}})
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]

Necessity.

Let
\widehat{f}
and
\widehat{d}
denote the optimal values of the primal and dual problems, respectively.
By assumption, strong duality holds, so
\widehat{f}=\widehat{d}
.
If
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
and
({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}},{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}})
are the optimal solutions of problems (
P
) and (
), then (i) and (ii) follow immediately from feasibility.
In addition,

\displaystyle\widehat{f}

\displaystyle=\widehat{d}=D({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}},{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}})=\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}L({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}},{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}})\leq L({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}},{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}},{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}})

\displaystyle=f({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})+\left\langle{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}},{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rangle+\sum_{i=1}^{q}{\widehat{\nu}}_{i}\big(f_{i}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})-z_{i}\big)\leq f({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}),

where the last inequality follows by the facts that
{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}={\bm{y}}
, and
f_{i}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})\leq z_{i}
. Since
\widehat{f}=f({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})
, all inequalities above must be equalities.
This implies that
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\in\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}L({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}},{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}})
, meaning property (iv),
and that
\sum_{i=1}^{q}{\widehat{\nu}}_{i}(f_{i}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})-z_{i})=0
, which by the fact that
{\widehat{\nu}}_{i}(f_{i}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})-z_{i})\leq 0
for any
i
, implies that
{\widehat{\lambda}}_{i}(f_{i}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})-z_{i})=0
for any
i
, showing the property (iii).

Sufficiency.

Conversely, assume that properties (i)-(iv) hold. Then,

\displaystyle D({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}},{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}})

\displaystyle=\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}L({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}},{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}})=L({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}},{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}},{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}})
