\displaystyle=f({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})+\left\langle{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}},{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rangle+\sum_{i=1}^{q}{\widehat{\nu}}_{i}(f_{i}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})-z_{i})=f({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}).

where the second equality follows from property (iv), and the last equality follows from properties (i) and (iii).
By the weak duality theorem, since
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
and
({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}},{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}})
are primal and dual feasible solutions with equal primal and dual objective functions, it follows that they are the optimal solutions of their corresponding problems.

Remark 123
(KKT conditions for convex optimization with equality constraints).

Consider the special case of an optimization problem with only equality constraints:

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}f_{0}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\bm{y}},

where
f_{0}
is
convex
and differentiable.
Then Theorems
and
show that
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is a solution if and only if
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is feasible and there exists
{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n}
such that:

\nabla_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}L({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})=\boldsymbol{0}=\nabla f_{0}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})-{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},

where the Lagrangian is defined as
L({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})=f_{0}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle
, and the vector
{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}
is the Lagrange multiplier associated with the equality constraint.
The geometric interpretation is that
\nabla f_{0}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})\perp\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
.

When
f_{0}
is not differentiable, the stationarity condition generalizes to:

{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is feasible and there exists
{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n}
such that

{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\text{ is a subgradient of }f_{0}\text{ at }{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}.

Given a primal-dual feasible triple
({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\boldsymbol{\nu}})
—that is,
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is feasible for (
P
) and
{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n}
,
{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\geq\boldsymbol{0}
—the
primal-dual gap
is defined as

H({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\boldsymbol{\nu}})=F({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-D({\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\boldsymbol{\nu}}),\quad\text{with }F({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\triangleq f_{0}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+\delta_{\mathbb{S}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}).

(2.54)

This quantity serves as a measure of how close
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is to a primal minimizer, and how close
({\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\boldsymbol{\nu}})
is to a dual maximizer.
If
({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}},{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}},{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}})
is a primal-dual optimal solution and strong duality holds, then the gap vanishes:
H({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}},{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}},{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}})=0
.
In practice, the primal-dual gap is commonly used as a stopping criterion in iterative optimization algorithms.

To illustrate these concepts, we now derive the dual of the
\ell_{\infty}
-minimization problem. (Its counterpart, the
\ell_{1}
-minimization problem, will be discussed in greater detail in Chapter
.)

Example 124
(
\ell_{\infty}
-minimization problem).

Consider the
\ell_{\infty}
-minimization problem:

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{\infty}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\bm{y}}.

(2.55)

The Lagrangian associated with this problem is

L({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{\infty}+\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}})\right\rangle.

The corresponding dual function is obtained by minimizing the Lagrangian over
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
:

D({\boldsymbol{\lambda}})=\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\left\{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{\infty}+\left\langle{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle-\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\bm{y}}\right\rangle\right\}.

By Hölder’s inequality, we have
\left\langle{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rVert_{1}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{\infty}
.
This implies that
if
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rVert_{1}>1
, then there exists
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
(by picking its sign appropriately) such that
\left\langle{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle<-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{\infty}
.
Replacing
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
by
\mu{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
and letting
\mu\to\infty
shows that
D({\boldsymbol{\lambda}})=-\infty
in this case.
On the other hand, if
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq 1
, then
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{\infty}+\left\langle{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle\geq 0
. The choice
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\boldsymbol{0}
yields the infimum, and
D({\boldsymbol{\lambda}})=-\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\bm{y}}\right\rangle
. Therefore, the dual problem is equivalent to:

\max_{{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n}}D({\boldsymbol{\lambda}})=\begin{cases}-\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\bm{y}}\right\rangle,&\text{if }\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq 1;\\
-\infty,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

Since maximizing
D({\boldsymbol{\lambda}})
is only meaningful where it is finite, the dual problem is equivalent to

\max_{{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n}}-\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\bm{y}}\right\rangle\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\big\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\big\rVert_{1}\leq 1.

(2.56)

Equivalently, one may write the objective as
\max_{{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n}}\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\bm{y}}\right\rangle
by absorbing the minus sign into the maximization (though the constraint remains unchanged).
Finally, by Slater’s condition (Theorem
), strong duality holds for this primal-dual pair provided the primal problem (
) is feasible—since the objective
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{\infty}
is convex and the equality constraints are affine.

Saddle-Point Property

Lagrange duality admits a natural
saddle-point interpretation
.
For simplicity, we consider the primal problem (
P
) without inequality constraints; however, the same reasoning extends straightforwardly to problems with inequality constraints.

Let
({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{*})
be a primal-dual optimal pair.
By definition of the Lagrangian
L
, we have

\displaystyle\max_{{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n}}L({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})

\displaystyle=\max_{{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n}}f_{0}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{\top}({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}})=\begin{cases}f_{0}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}),&\text{if }{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\bm{y}},\\
\infty,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

(2.57)

In other words, this supremum is infinite whenever
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
violates the equality constraints.
Consequently, the (feasible) minimizer
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
of the primal problem (
P
) satisfies

f_{0}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})=\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\max_{{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n}}L({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}).

(2.58)

On the other hand, by the definition of the Lagrange dual function, a dual optimal vector
{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{*}
achieves

D({\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{*})=\max_{{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n}}\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}L({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})

(2.59)

Weak duality then implies the general inequality

\max_{{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n}}\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}L({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})\leq\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\max_{{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n}}L({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}).

(2.60)

When strong duality holds, equality is achieved:

\max_{{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n}}\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}L({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})=\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\max_{{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n}}L({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}).

(2.61)

In this case, the order of minimization and maximization can be interchanged in the case of strong duality.
This is known as the strong
max-min property
or the
saddle-point property
.
Indeed, under strong duality, any primal-dual optimal pair
({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{*})
forms a saddle point of the Lagrangian:

L({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})\leq L({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{*})\leq L({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{*})\quad\text{for all }{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n}.

(2.62)

Thus, solving the primal and dual problems jointly is equivalent to finding a saddle point of the Lagrangian, provided that strong duality holds.

2.9.4
Composite Function

Conjugate functions arise naturally in dual optimization problems, most notably in the celebrated
Fenchel’s duality theorem
, which we now recall. Consider the following composite optimization problem:

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}F({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+G({\boldsymbol{\beta}}).

All the relevant optimization problems discussed in this book belong to this class; see Chapter
.

Example 125
.

Many problems covered in this book take this form.
For example, setting
F({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\triangleq\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
and
G({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\lambda\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}
yields the Lagrangian LASSO problem (
LL
); the choice
G({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}
and
\widetilde{F}({\bm{z}})\triangleq F({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}})
with
\widetilde{F}=\delta_{\{{\bm{y}}\}}
(the indicator function of the singleton
\{{\bm{y}}\}
) gives the
\ell_{1}
-minimization problem (
);
the choice
G({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}
and
\widetilde{F}({\bm{z}})\triangleq F({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}})
with
\widetilde{F}=\delta_{{\mathbb{B}}[{\bm{y}},\epsilon]}
(the indicator function of the the
\ell_{2}
-ball with center
{\bm{y}}
and radius
\epsilon
) leads to the quadratically-constrained
\ell_{1}
-minimization problem (
).

We begin by reformulating the original problem as a constrained optimization problem:

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}}\left\{F({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+G({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\right\}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\boldsymbol{\alpha}}.

The associated Lagrangian is then

L({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})=F({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+G({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle=-[\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle-F({\boldsymbol{\beta}})]-[\left\langle-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rangle-G({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})].

The dual function is obtained by minimizing the Lagrangian over the primal variables
{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
:

D({\boldsymbol{\lambda}})=\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}L({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}};{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})=-F^{*}({\boldsymbol{\lambda}})-G^{*}(-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}).

Thus, the corresponding dual problem—commonly referred to as
Fenchel’s dual
—is

\max_{{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{p}}\left\{-F^{*}({\boldsymbol{\lambda}})-G^{*}(-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})\right\}.

Fenchel’s duality theorem, stated below, provides sufficient conditions under which strong duality holds between the primal problem and its Fenchel dual.

{theoremHigh}

[Fenchel’s duality theorem;
Rockafellar 1970
, Theorem 31.1]
Let
F,G:\real^{p}\to(-\infty,\infty]
be proper convex functions. If
\text{relint}(\mathrm{dom}(F))\cap\text{relint}(\mathrm{dom}(G))\neq\varnothing
, then

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\{F({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+G({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\}=\max_{{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{p}}\left\{-F^{*}({\boldsymbol{\lambda}})-G^{*}(-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})\right\},

and the maximum on the right-hand side is attained whenever it is finite.

Chapter 3
Sparse Optimization Problems and Optimality Conditions

I
In the fields of
sparse representation
and
compressed sensing
(also known as
compressive sensing
,
compressive sampling
, or
sparse sampling
), a central challenge is to recover a high-dimensional signal from a relatively small number of linear measurements. This task is mathematically formulated as solving an underdetermined linear system

{\bm{X}}\boldsymbol{\beta}={\bm{y}},

where
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
(with
n\ll p
) is a measurement or sensing matrix,
{\bm{y}}\in\real^{n}
is the observed data vector, and
\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\real^{p}
is the unknown coefficient vector assumed to be
sparse
, meaning that only a small subset of its entries are nonzero. The sparsity assumption is crucial: without it, the system admits infinitely many solutions due to its underdetermined nature. However, when
\boldsymbol{\beta}
is known (or believed) to be sparse—or approximately sparse—it becomes possible, under suitable conditions on
{\bm{X}}
(e.g., the restricted isometry property or incoherence; see Chapters
and
), to uniquely and stably reconstruct
\boldsymbol{\beta}
from
{\bm{y}}
.

This chapter focuses on how tools from optimization theory can be leveraged to solve such sparse inverse problems. Specifically, we explore two closely related but conceptually distinct classes of sparse optimization problems:

1.

Optimization with sparse regression (or sparse constraints).
In this setting, sparsity is imposed as a constraint or regularizer within a broader regression or estimation framework. Typical formulations include minimizing a loss function (e.g., least squares) subject to a constraint on the number of nonzero coefficients (an “
\ell_{0}
-norm” constraint) or, more tractably, adding an
\ell_{1}
-norm penalty (as in the
LASSO
). These approaches are widely used in statistics, machine learning, and signal processing for feature selection and model interpretability.

2.

Sparse recovery problems.
Here, the primary goal is exact or stable reconstruction of a sparse signal from incomplete measurements, often in the presence of noise. This perspective is common in applied mathematics and engineering, particularly in compressed sensing. Recovery is typically achieved by solving convex relaxations (e.g.,
basis pursuit
) or non-convex approximations of the original combinatorial problem, with theoretical guarantees provided under assumptions about the sensing matrix
{\bm{X}}
.

While both paradigms aim to exploit sparsity, they differ in emphasis: sparse regression often prioritizes predictive performance and model simplicity in data-rich contexts, whereas sparse recovery emphasizes faithful signal reconstruction from minimal measurements. In what follows, we develop the mathematical foundations, and theoretical insights underlying these two approaches, illustrating how optimization serves as a unifying framework for sparse modeling.

3.1
Sparse Optimization Problems

On the one hand,
compressed sensing
—a term pioneered by David Donoho, Emmanuel Candès, and Terence Tao
(
Donoho et al. 2001
;
Donoho and Elad 2003
;
Candes and Tao 2005
)
—has emerged as a groundbreaking paradigm for sparse signal recovery, fundamentally reshaping how we tackle underdetermined linear systems.
It exploits the fact that many natural signals admit sparse representations in some basis or frame, enabling accurate reconstruction from far fewer measurements than required by the Nyquist rate. This directly challenges the classical view that such inverse problems are inherently ill-posed. Beyond its theoretical elegance, compressed sensing has had a profound practical impact, transforming fields such as signal processing, information theory, and statistics, while also catalyzing new research directions—including low-rank matrix completion and phase retrieval
(
Baraniuk et al. 2011
;
Foucart and Rauhut 2013
;
Jain et al. 2017
)
. In doing so, it stands as a quintessential example of how a unifying mathematical insight can redefine data acquisition and analysis in today’s data-intensive era.

A key advantage of compressed sensing is its ability to combine sampling and compression into a single, efficient step. Instead of collecting large volumes of raw data and compressing them afterward, compressed sensing leverages signal sparsity at the point of acquisition, dramatically reducing the number of measurements needed. This not only lowers data storage and transmission costs but also accelerates the acquisition process—making it especially valuable in time-critical applications such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and wireless communications, where it enables shorter scan times or reduced bandwidth usage without compromising fidelity
(
Han et al. 2013
)
. Moreover, its inherent robustness to noise and resilience to missing observations allow high-quality signal reconstruction even from highly incomplete data, yielding substantial gains in speed, efficiency, and overall system performance.

Although the basis pursuit formulation for sparse recovery was introduced by S. Chen, D. Donoho, and M. Saunders
(
Chen et al. 2001
)
as a principled method to find the sparsest solution to an underdetermined linear system via
\ell_{1}
-norm minimization, the
LASSO (least absolute shrinkage and selection operator)
, proposed earlier by R. Tibshirani
(
Tibshirani 1996
)
, has become the dominant framework within the statistics and machine learning communities
(
Hastie et al. 2015
)
.
This divergence in popularity stems largely from differences in problem framing and disciplinary priorities. In the compressed sensing literature—rooted in applied mathematics, signal processing, and information theory—the emphasis is on exact or stable recovery of a true sparse signal from incomplete measurements, often under stringent assumptions about the sensing matrix (e.g., the restricted isometry property or mutual coherence; see Chapters
and
). Basis pursuit and its noise-aware variants, such as
basis pursuit denoising (BPDN)
, are naturally aligned with this goal, as they directly minimize the
\ell_{1}
-norm subject to explicit data fidelity constraints.

By contrast, the LASSO originated in the context of regression modeling, where the primary objectives are prediction accuracy, model interpretability, and variable selection in high-dimensional settings.
Rather than enforcing hard constraints on residual error, the LASSO formulates sparsity as a trade-off: it minimizes the sum of squared residuals plus an
\ell_{1}
-penalty on the coefficients. This Lagrangian formulation offers greater practical flexibility—it eliminates the need to pre-specify a noise level or tolerance parameter and integrates seamlessly into cross-validation pipelines for tuning the regularization strength.
Consequently, the LASSO resonated strongly with statisticians and data scientists seeking robust, scalable tools for feature selection and model regularization.
Over time, the distinction between the two approaches has blurred, as they can be shown to be equivalent under appropriate choices of parameters. Nevertheless, their historical origins and methodological emphases continue to shape how researchers in different fields conceptualize and apply sparse optimization.

We now turn to the precise mathematical formulations of these two canonical problems, along with their closely related variants.

3.1.1
Sparse Regression Problems

In this subsection, we start by the challenge of minimizing a (general) continuously differentiable objective function subject to a sparsity constraint. Specifically, we consider the following problem:

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{0}\leq R,

(S
0
)

where
f:\real^{p}\to\real
is continuously differentiable with a Lipschitz continuous gradient of constant
L_{b}
(in our case, if we take
f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
, the least squares objective, then
L_{b}=\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}
; see Example
),
R>0
is an integer satisfying
R<p
, and
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{0}
is the so-called “
\ell_{0}
-norm” of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
, which counts the number of nonzero components in
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.
For any positive number
s>0
, the
\ell_{s}
-norm of a vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is defined as

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{s}=\left(\sum_{i}\left\lvert\beta_{i}\right\rvert^{s}\right)^{1/s}.

Thus, the
\ell_{0}
-norm of a
p\times 1
vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
can be defined as

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{0}=\lim_{s\to 0}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{s}^{s}=\lim_{s\to 0}\sum_{i=1}^{p}\left\lvert\beta_{i}\right\rvert^{s}=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\mathds{1}(\beta_{i}\neq 0)=\left\lvert\{i\mid\beta_{i}\neq 0,\forall\,i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}\}\right\rvert.

Thus, if
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{0}\ll p
, the vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is said to be sparse.
It is important to note that the
\ell_{0}
-norm is not actually a norm, as it fails to satisfy the homogeneity property: for any nonzero scalar
\lambda
, we have
\left\lVert\lambda{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{0}=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{0}
(Definition
).

Problem (
) is a constrained optimization problem in which we seek the best model—i.e., the one that minimizes
f
—under a hard sparsity constraint. By restricting the solution to have at most
R
nonzero coefficients, we explicitly control model complexity, promoting interpretability and mitigating overfitting.

LASSO

From the above sparse optimization analysis,
we observe that—although convergence of algorithms like
iterative hard-thresholding
(IHT; see Section
) can be guaranteed under very specific conditions—the use of the
\ell_{0}
-norm (or hard-thresholding), which counts the number of nonzero elements in a vector, presents several significant challenges and drawbacks:

Non-convexity.
The
\ell_{0}
-norm is inherently non-convex. Consequently, optimization problems involving it are generally NP-hard. Finding the global minimum becomes computationally prohibitive, especially as the problem dimension grows.

Combinatorial nature.
Minimizing the
\ell_{0}
-norm requires evaluating all possible subsets of variables to identify the sparsest solution satisfying the constraints. This combinatorial search has exponential complexity, rendering it infeasible for high-dimensional datasets.

Instability.
Solutions obtained by direct
\ell_{0}
minimization are highly sensitive to small perturbations in the data. This lack of robustness is particularly problematic in noisy settings or when working with real-world data containing errors or outliers.

Lack of continuity and differentiability.
The
\ell_{0}
-norm is neither continuous nor differentiable, making it incompatible with standard gradient-based optimization methods. This absence of smoothness hinders the use of iterative algorithms designed for differentiable objectives.

Difficulty in incorporating into optimization algorithms.
Due to its discrete and discontinuous nature, the
\ell_{0}
-norm is difficult to incorporate directly into most optimization frameworks. As a result, practical approaches often rely on relaxations or surrogates—most notably the convex
\ell_{1}
-norm—to render the problem tractable.

In contrast, the
\ell_{1}
-norm also promotes sparsity: it encourages solutions in which many coefficients are exactly zero. This behavior arises from its geometric structure—in high dimensions, the corners of the
\ell_{1}
-ball (a polytope) lie along the coordinate axes, which favors sparse solutions; see Figures
and
.
Importantly, the
\ell_{1}
-norm is convex. Therefore, any local minimum of an
\ell_{1}
-regularized problem is also a global minimum. This property dramatically simplifies optimization compared to the non-convex
\ell_{0}
setting.

To be more concrete, consider the standard linear regression model in matrix-vector form:

{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}+{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}},

(3.1)

where
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
is the design (or model) matrix,
{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\in\real^{n}
is a vector of noise variables, and
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\in\real^{p}
is the unknown coefficient vector.
The
standard linear regression
or
least squares problem
then corresponds to the following unconstrained optimization:

(\textbf{Least squares}):\qquad\mathop{\min}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\triangleq\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

(L
2
)

By employing convex relaxation via the
\ell_{1}
-norm, later sections of this chapter will develop the
LASSO (least absolute selection and shrinkage operator)
framework, covering both its constrained and Lagrangian formulations. Practical algorithms and theoretical guarantees are discussed in Sections
and
, respectively:

\displaystyle(\textbf{Constrained LASSO}):\qquad

\displaystyle\mathop{\min}_{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\Sigma}f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\triangleq\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2};

(L
C
)

\displaystyle(\textbf{Lagrangian LASSO}):\qquad

\displaystyle\mathop{\min}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}F({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\triangleq\left\{\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\lambda\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\right\}.

(L
L
)

The constrained LASSO uses the same least squares loss as in (
), but restricts the solution to lie within the
\ell_{1}
-ball
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}<\Sigma
.
The Lagrangian LASSO, also known as the
\ell_{1}
-regularized least squares
problem, incorporates sparsity through an additive penalty term.
Through Lagrangian duality, these two formulations are equivalent in the following sense: for every
\Sigma>0
, there exists a
\lambda\geq 0
such that the solutions to (
LC
) and (
LL
) coincide, with
\lambda
interpretable as the Lagrange multiplier associated with the constraint
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\Sigma
; see Corollary
.

For sufficiently large
\lambda
(or sufficiently small
\Sigma
), any solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
to either (
LC
) or (
LL
) is typically sparse—i.e., it has only a few nonzero entries—and thus identifies the relevant features (columns of
{\bm{X}}
) that are useful for predicting
{\bm{y}}
.
With the gradual decrease of
\lambda
, the sparsity of the solution vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
also gradually decreases. As
\lambda
tends to 0, the solution vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
becomes the vector such that
\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
is minimized. That is to say,
\lambda>0
can balance the twin objectives by minimizing the error squared sum cost function
\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
and the
\ell_{1}
-norm cost function
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}
.
See Section
for further details.

Note that a scaled version of the LASSO is also commonly used, particularly in statistical learning contexts where normalization by the sample size
n
improves interpretability:

\displaystyle(\textbf{Constrained LASSO-II}):\qquad

\displaystyle\mathop{\min}_{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\Sigma}f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\triangleq\frac{1}{2n}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2};

(L
{}_{C}^{\prime}
)

\displaystyle(\textbf{Lagrangian LASSO-II}):\qquad

\displaystyle\mathop{\min}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}F({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\triangleq\left\{\frac{1}{2n}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\lambda\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\right\}.

(L
{}_{L}^{\prime}
)

The LASSO admits numerous generalizations; here are a few examples. In machine learning, sparse kernel regression is sometimes referred to as the
generalized LASSO

(
Roth 2004
)
.
The
group LASSO
extends sparsity to predefined groups of variables
(
Puig et al. 2011
)
.
The
distributed LASSO
addresses sparse linear regression in decentralized or networked settings
(
Mateos et al. 2010
)
.
See Chapter
for a more comprehensive discussion of these extensions.

3.1.2
Sparse Recovery Problems

The success of the LASSO in promoting sparsity and enabling feature selection is not an isolated phenomenon; it is deeply rooted in a broader mathematical framework known as
sparse recovery
, which originated in signal processing and compressed sensing.
As noted above, while the LASSO was developed in a statistical context—where the primary goals are prediction, estimation, and interpretability in the presence of noise—the same
\ell_{1}
-regularization principle also arises in deterministic settings,
where the objective is to exactly reconstruct a sparse signal from incomplete linear measurements.
This leads naturally to formulations such as
basis pursuit
and its noise-robust extension,
basis pursuit denoising (BPDN)
, which frame sparse recovery as a constrained optimization problem rather than a penalized one.
Although their motivations differ—statistical inference versus exact or stable signal reconstruction—the underlying geometry of the
\ell_{1}
-norm and the conditions that guarantee successful recovery (e.g., restricted isometry or nullspace properties; see Chapters
and
) provide a unifying foundation for these approaches.
This subsection introduce this complementary perspective.

There exist a wide variety of approaches to recover a sparse signal
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
from a small number of linear measurements. We begin by considering a natural first approach to the problem of sparse recovery.
Given measurements
{\bm{y}}\in\real^{n}
(e.g., generated via
{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
, where
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
) and the knowledge that our original signal
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
is sparse, it is natural to attempt recovery by solving an optimization problem of the form

{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}=\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{0}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\mathcal{B}({\bm{y}}),

(PS
0
)

where
\mathcal{B}({\bm{y}})
enforces consistency between
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
and the observed measurements
{\bm{y}}
.
Recall that
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{0}=\left\lvert\mathrm{supp}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rvert
simply counts the number of nonzero entries in
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
;
thus, (
) seeks the sparsest signal consistent with the data.
Common choices for
\mathcal{B}({\bm{y}})
include:

If our measurements are
exact and noise-free
, then we can set
\mathcal{B}({\bm{y}})=\{{\bm{z}}\mid{\bm{X}}{\bm{z}}={\bm{y}}\}
.

If the measurements are contaminated by a small amount of
bounded noise
, we may instead use
\mathcal{B}({\bm{y}})=\{{\bm{z}}\mid\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\bm{z}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\epsilon\}
.

In both cases, (
) identifies the sparsest
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
that remains consistent with the observations. Further details on these two scenarios are provided below.

The key differences between problem (
) (p.
) and (
) are as follows:

1.

Objective function.
In (
), the goal is to minimize a data-fidelity term (e.g., least squares error) subject to a sparsity constraint. In contrast, (
) directly minimizes sparsity (i.e.,
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{0}
) subject to data consistency.

2.

Constraints.
Problem (
) imposes a hard constraint on the sparsity level (e.g.,
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{0}\leq R
), allowing flexibility in how well the model fits the data. Conversely, (
) enforces strict data fidelity (exact or approximate), with sparsity as the objective.

3.

Application.
Formulation (
) is typically used in statistical settings where data are noisy, and a trade-off between fit and sparsity is desired (e.g., regression). In contrast, (
) arises in signal processing and compressed sensing, where the priority is exact or stable reconstruction of a truly sparse signal from limited measurements.

4.

Computational complexity.
Although both problems involve the nonconvex
\ell_{0}
-norm, (
) can sometimes be tackled with iterative heuristics (e.g., IHT) under additional assumptions. However, (
) is generally NP-hard due to the combinatorial nature of minimizing
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{0}
, as it requires evaluating all possible support patterns of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}

(
Mallat and Zhang 1993
;
Natarajan 1995
;
Davis et al. 1997
)
.

\paragrapharrow

Data transformation.
Note that in (
), we implicitly assume that the signal
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
itself is sparse.
In many practical settings, however, sparsity holds not in the standard basis but in some transformed domain, i.e.,
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\boldsymbol{\Phi}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
, where
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}
is sparse and
{\boldsymbol{\Phi}}\in\real^{p\times p}
is a known dictionary (e.g., a wavelet or Fourier basis). In this case, we can reformulate the recovery problem as

\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}=\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{0}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\mathcal{B}({\bm{y}}),

(PS
{}_{0}^{\prime}
)

where
\mathcal{B}({\bm{y}})=\{{\bm{z}}\mid{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\Phi}}{\bm{z}}={\bm{y}}\}
for noise-free measurements, or
\mathcal{B}({\bm{y}})=\{{\bm{z}}\mid\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\Phi}}{\bm{z}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\epsilon\}
in the presence of bounded noise.
By defining
\widetilde{\bm{X}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\Phi}}
, we see that (
) is structurally identical to (
), with
\widetilde{\bm{X}}
replacing
{\bm{X}}
.
Moreover, in many applications, the introduction of
{\boldsymbol{\Phi}}
does not substantially complicate the design of
{\bm{X}}
such that

\widetilde{\bm{X}}
satisfies desirable properties (e.g., restricted isometry).
Therefore, for most of the remainder of this book, we restrict our attention to the case
{\boldsymbol{\Phi}}={\bm{I}}
, i.e., when sparsity is assumed directly in the canonical basis. It is important to note, however, that this simplification imposes limitations when
{\boldsymbol{\Phi}}
is a general (possibly overcomplete) dictionary rather than an orthonormal basis. In particular,

\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{2}=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Phi}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\Phi}}\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}\right\rVert_{2}\neq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}\right\rVert_{2},

so a bound on
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}\right\rVert_{2}
does not directly translate into a bound on
\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{2}
, which is often the quantity of interest in applications. Further discussion of these implications can be found in
Candes et al. 2011
.

\paragrapharrow

Convex relaxation.
Although the performance of (
) can be analyzed under suitable assumptions on
{\bm{X}}
, we do not pursue this route because the objective function
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{0}
is nonconvex—and consequently, the optimization problem is generally intractable. In fact, for an arbitrary measurement matrix
{\bm{X}}
, even approximating the optimal solution is NP-hard.
Recall that the number of nonzero entries of a vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
can be viewed as the limit of its
\ell_{s}
-quasinorm as
s\to 0
:

\sum_{i=1}^{p}\left\lvert\beta_{i}\right\rvert^{s}\quad\stackrel{{\scriptstyle s\to 0}}{{\longrightarrow}}\quad\sum_{i=1}^{p}\mathds{1}(\{\beta_{i}\neq 0\})=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{0}.

This observation suggests to replace the
\ell_{0}
-minimization problem (
) with the following family of problems:

{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}=\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{s}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\mathcal{B}({\bm{y}}),\quad 0<s<1.

(PS
s
)

However, this approach has significant drawbacks.
For
s>1
, the
\ell_{s}
-norm fails to promote sparsity—even 1-sparse vectors may not be recovered (see Problem
). For
0<s<1
, although sparsity is better encouraged, the resulting problem remains non-convex and is still NP-hard (see Problem
).
A more practical alternative is to replace
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{0}
with its convex envelope over the unit
\ell_{\infty}
-ball (see Lemma
for further details): the
\ell_{1}
-norm. This leads to the convex program

{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}=\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\mathcal{B}({\bm{y}}).

(PS
1
)

Provided that
\mathcal{B}({\bm{y}})
is convex, (
) is computationally feasible.
In the noiseless setting
\mathcal{B}({\bm{y}})=\{{\bm{z}}\mid{\bm{X}}{\bm{z}}={\bm{y}}\}
, it can even be cast as a linear program
(
Chen and Donoho 1994
;
Chen et al. 2001
;
Foucart and Rauhut 2013
)
.

It is clear that replacing (
) with (
) transforms an intractable combinatorial problem into a tractable convex one. Less obvious, however, is whether the solution to (
) resembles that of (
). Nevertheless, there are strong intuitive and geometric reasons to expect that
\ell_{1}
-minimization promotes sparsity.
For instance, as illustrated later in Example
and Figure
, the solution to the
\ell_{1}
-minimization problem coincides exactly with the solution to
\ell_{s}
-minimization for any
s<1
—and is indeed sparse.

Moreover, historical precedent supports this intuition. As early as 1965,
Logan 1965
showed that a bandlimited signal corrupted on a small interval can be perfectly reconstructed by minimizing the
\ell_{1}
-norm of the error. This method—searching for the bandlimited signal closest to the observations in
\ell_{1}
—can be interpreted as an early instance of robust recovery via
\ell_{1}
-minimization, further reinforcing the idea that the
\ell_{1}
-norm is well-suited to handling sparse errors.

Basis Pursuit and other Forms

In summary, the core problem of sparse representation is the
\ell_{0}
-norm minimization

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{0}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}},

(P
0
)

where
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
, and
{\bm{y}}\in\real^{n}
.
Since this problem is NP-hard, we instead consider its convex relaxation known as the
basis pursuit
problem also referred to as
noise-free signal recovery
,
\ell_{1}
-norm minimization
, or simply
\ell_{1}
-minimization
problem):

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\qquad\text{s.t.}\quad{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}.

(P
1
)

This is a convex optimization problem because the objective function
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}
is convex and the constraint
{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is affine.
Thus, this basis pursuit problem can be seen as a convex relaxation of (
).
Problem (
) is equivalent to

\displaystyle\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\bm{u}}}\sum_{i=1}^{p}u_{i}\qquad\text{s.t.}

\displaystyle{\displaystyle\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}};

(P
{}_{1}^{\prime}
)

\displaystyle-u_{i}\leq\beta_{i}\leq u_{i},\quad\forall\,i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}.

This is a linear program formulation (see Example
).
While (
) enforces an exact equality constraint, it can also be reformulated as a penalized problem:

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}+\sigma\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},

(P
1,σ
)

where
\sigma>0
is a
penalty parameter
.
This formulation is known as the
basis pursuit denoising (BPDN)
problem
(
Chen et al. 2001
)
.
As
\sigma\rightarrow\infty
, the solution of (
) converges to that of (
), making the two problems asymptotically equivalent.

Apparently, the penalized
\ell_{1}
problem (
) is equivalent to the Lagrangian LASSO problem (
LL
) (p.
LL
) by setting
\sigma\triangleq\frac{1}{2\lambda}
.

\paragrapharrow

Signal recovery vs sparse regression.
As noted previously, although the formulations of (
) and (
LL
) are mathematically equivalent under the correspondence
\sigma\triangleq\frac{1}{2\lambda}
, their interpretations and typical application contexts differ significantly.
In the Lagrangian LASSO problem (
LL
), the primary objective is to minimize the least squares loss
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}
subject to an
\ell_{1}
regularization term
\lambda\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}
.
Here, the underlying goal is predictive modeling: we seek a good fit to the data while encouraging sparsity in the estimated coefficients to improve interpretability and prevent overfitting.
When the setting arises in overdetermined systems (
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
with
n\geq p
, also the LASSO can also work when
p\geq n
), where the equation
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\bm{y}}
generally has no exact solution due to noise or model mismatch, the regularization term
\lambda\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}
thus serves as a mechanism to control model complexity
(
Lu 2021a
)
.

In contrast, the penalized
\ell_{1}
-minimization problem (
) originates in sparse signal recovery, particularly in compressed sensing. Here, the goal is not prediction but exact or stable reconstruction of a truly sparse signal from incomplete and possibly noisy measurements. The system is usually underdetermined (
p\gg n
), meaning there are far more unknowns than observations. Sparsity is not a convenience—it is a structural assumption that makes recovery possible.

This distinction has practical implications in communication systems. When
p\gg n
, transmitting the full signal
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
is inefficient. Instead, the sender can transmit only the low-dimensional measurement vector
{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{n}
, which requires far less bandwidth since
n\gg p
. If the receiver knows both
{\bm{X}}
and
{\bm{y}}
, it can reconstruct the original sparse signal
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
by solving a problem such as (
).

Example 126
(Sparse signal recovery using
\ell_{0},\ell_{1}
, and
\ell_{2}
-norm minimization).

We compare the recovery of a sparse signal from underdetermined measurements using
\ell_{0}
- and
\ell_{1}
-norm minimization.
We also compare with the
\ell_{2}
-norm minimization:

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}.

(P
2
)

The process begins with a random matrix
{\bm{X}}
of size
60\times 120
and a sparse vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
of length 120, where sparsity is enforced by zeroing out small values in a dense random vector. The measurements
{\bm{y}}
are then computed as
{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
, simulating a compressed sensing scenario where only 60 linear measurements are available for a 120-dimensional sparse signal.

The first subplot of Figure
the solution obtained via
\ell_{0}
-minimization.
The second subplot presents the
\ell_{2}
-minimization solution. Because the
\ell_{2}
-norm favors energy spreading and smoothness, the recovered signal is dense and distributes error across all coordinates, leading to a large reconstruction error relative to
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
.
The third subplot shows the
\ell_{1}
-minimization solution. Thanks to its sparsity-promoting geometry, the
\ell_{1}
-norm yields a solution that closely matches the support and magnitude of the original sparse signal. As expected, the reconstruction error is significantly lower than that of the
\ell_{2}
approach, illustrating the effectiveness of
\ell_{1}
-minimization for sparse recovery.

Figure 3.1:
Illustration of
\ell_{0},\ell_{1}
, and
\ell_{2}
-norm minimization for sparse signal recovery.

Constrained Sparse Recovery

On the other hand, observed signals are typically contaminated by noise. Therefore, the equality constraint in the idealized optimization problem should be relaxed to allow for a bounded measurement error. This leads to the following
\ell_{0}
-norm minimization with an inequality constraint:

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{0}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\epsilon,

(P
0,ϵ
)

where
\epsilon\geq 0
controls the permissible deviation between the measurements
{\bm{y}}
and the model prediction
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.

In realistic settings, it is also impossible to measure a signal
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
with infinite precision. Consequently, the observed measurement vector
{\bm{y}}\in\real^{n}
is only an approximation of the true linear measurement
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
, satisfying

\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert\leq\epsilon

for some
\epsilon\geq 0
and some norm
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert
on
n
(most commonly the
\ell_{2}
-norm).
In such cases, a good reconstruction method should produce an estimate
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
whose distance to the true signal
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is controlled by the measurement error
\epsilon
.
This desirable property is known as
robustness
to measurement noise.

Accordingly, the noiseless basis pursuit problem (
) is replaced by the following convex optimization problem:

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\epsilon,

(P
1,ϵ
)

which is commonly referred to as
quadratically-constrained basis pursuit
(or
quadratically-constrained
\ell_{1}
-minimization
,
\ell_{1}
-minimization with noise measurement
) problem and is known as the problem of
signal recovery in noise
.

Another prominent variant is the
Dantzig selector (DS)
(
Candes and Tao 2007
)
, defined as

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}})\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq D.

(P
1,D
)

This is again a convex optimization problem.
The intuition behind the constraint is that the residual
{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}
should exhibit only small correlations with all columns
{\bm{x}}_{i}
of the measurement matrix
{\bm{X}}
.
Indeed,

\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}})\right\rVert_{\infty}=\max_{i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}}\left\lvert\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}},{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rangle\right\rvert.

A theoretical framework analogous to the one developed later in this chapter for problems (
) and (
) also applies to the Dantzig selector. However, we do not delve into those details here. For further insight, see Problem
.

3.1.3
Equivalence of Some Problems

The solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
of the quadratically-constrained basis pursuit problem (
) is closely related to the solutions of the Lagrangian and constrained LASSO problems in (
LL
) and (
LC
) (p.
LC
). To establish this connection, we first prove a more general result.

{theoremHigh}

[Equivalence between constrained and regularized problems]
Let
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{a}
,
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{b}
be two norms on
p
.
Given
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
,
{\bm{y}}\in\real^{n}
and
\epsilon>0
,
consider the optimization problem

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{a}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{b}\leq\epsilon.

(3.4)

Assume that (
) is strictly feasible; that is, there exists some vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
such that
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{b}<\epsilon
.
Let
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
be a minimizer of (
). Then there exists a parameter
\sigma\geq 0
such that
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
also minimizes the regularized problem

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{a}+\sigma\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{b}.

(3.5)

Conversely, for any
\sigma>0
, if
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
minimizes (
), then there exists
\epsilon\geq 0
such that
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is a minimizer of (
).

Proof
[of Theorem
]
The Lagrange function of problem (
) is

L({\boldsymbol{\beta}},\lambda)=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{a}+\lambda(\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{b}-\epsilon).

By Slater’s condition (Theorem
), strong duality holds for (
) under the stated strict feasibility assumption.
Therefore, there exists an optimal dual multiplier
{\widehat{\lambda}}\geq 0
. The saddle point property (
) implies that

L({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}},{\widehat{\lambda}})\leq L({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\widehat{\lambda}})

for all
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
.
Thus,
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
minimizes the function
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\mapsto L({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\widehat{\lambda}})
. Since the constant term
-{\widehat{\lambda}}\epsilon
does not affect the location of the minimizer,
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
also minimizes

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{a}+{\widehat{\lambda}}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{b},

which establishes the first claim with
\sigma={\widehat{\lambda}}
.

Conversely, let
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
be the minimizer of (
) and set
\lambda=\sigma
. Choose
\epsilon=\big\lVert{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\bm{y}}\big\rVert_{b}
. Then the Lagrange dual function
D
satisfies

D(\lambda)=L({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}},\lambda)=\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{a}.

By weak duality, it holds that
D(\lambda)\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{a}
for all feasible
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
. Because
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is feasible and achieves this lower bound by the choice of
\epsilon=\big\lVert{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\bm{y}}\big\rVert_{b}
, it must be a minimizer of (
).

This general equivalence immediately clarifies the relationships among the problems (
), (
), (
LC
), and (
LL
).

Corollary 127
(Equivalence of (
), (
), (
LC
), and (
LL
)).

Consider the problems (
), (
), (
LC
), and (
LL
):

1.

As mentioned above, the penalized
\ell_{1}
problem (
) is equivalent to the Lagrangian LASSO problem (
LL
) by setting
\sigma\triangleq\frac{1}{2\lambda}
.

2.

If
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is a minimizer of Lagrangian LASSO problem (
LL
), then there exists
\epsilon=\epsilon_{{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}
such that
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is a minimizer of the quadratically-constrained basis pursuit problem (
).

3.

If
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is a minimizer of the constrained LASSO problem (
LC
), then there exists
\lambda=\lambda_{{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}
such that
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is a minimizer of the Lagrangian LASSO problem (
LL
).

4.

If
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is a minimizer of quadratically-constrained basis pursuit (
), then there is
\Sigma=\Sigma_{{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}
such that
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is a minimizer of the constrained LASSO problem (
LC
).

It is important to note that these equivalences are implicit: the mapping between parameters (e.g., between
\lambda
and
\epsilon
or
\lambda
and
\Sigma
) depends on the specific minimizer
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
. Consequently, the transformation cannot be performed a priori—it requires knowledge of the solution itself. For this reason, while the equivalences are theoretically insightful, they are of limited practical use when selecting regularization parameters in real-world applications.

3.1.4
\ell_{1}
-Analysis Models

Note that the models (
), (
), and (
) are collectively known as the
\ell_{1}
-synthesis models
.
We also consider the following
\ell_{1}
-minimization formulations:

\displaystyle\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1},\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\bm{y}},

(Q
1
)

\displaystyle\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}+\sigma\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},

(Q
1,σ
)

\displaystyle\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1},\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\epsilon,

(Q
1,ϵ
)

where
\epsilon,\sigma
are positive parameters.
Model (
Q1
) is appropriate in the noiseless setting, i.e., when the measurement error satisfies
{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}=\boldsymbol{0}
.
If
{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}={\bm{I}}
, the identity matrix, these models reduce exactly to the
\ell_{1}
-synthesis models.
If
{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}\neq{\bm{I}}
, they are referred to as the
\ell_{1}
-analysis models

(
Elad et al. 2007
;
Candes et al. 2011
;
Liu et al. 2012
;
Nam et al. 2013
;
Zhang et al. 2016
)
.

It is important to distinguish these models from the data transformation described in (
) (p.
): in the analysis framework, the transformation is applied to the signal itself, not to the measurements.

In the
\ell_{1}
-synthesis approaches, the signal of interest is synthesized as
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}={\bm{D}}{\bm{b}}
, where
{\bm{D}}
is a certain dictionary and
{\bm{b}}
is a sparse coefficient vector.
The
\ell_{1}
-analysis model, including the cosparse analysis model
(
Nam et al. 2013
)
and the total variation model
(
Rudin et al. 1992
)
, has widely known examples and has attracted a lot of attention. The underlying signal is expected to make sparse correlations with the columns (atoms) in an (overcomplete) dictionary
{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}\in\real^{p\times q}
with
q\geq p
, i.e.,
{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
is sparse.

Typically, we require the analysis operator
{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}
to have full row rank such that
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}}\triangleq\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}\cdot\big\rVert_{1}
is a valid norm for
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
(Problem
).
When
{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}
has full row rank, we can invoke Theorem
with
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{a}\triangleq\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}}
to prove the equivalence between problems (
Q1,σ
) and (
Q1,ϵ
).

Corollary 128
(Equivalence of (
Q1,σ
) and (
Q1,ϵ
)).

Suppose
{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}
has full row rank and
consider the problems (
Q1,σ
) and (
Q1,ϵ
):

1.

If
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is a minimizer of problem (
Q1,σ
), then there exists
\epsilon=\epsilon_{{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}
such that
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is a minimizer of the problem (
Q1,ϵ
).

2.

If
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is a minimizer of the problem (
Q1,ϵ
), then there exists
\sigma=\sigma_{{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}
such that
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is a minimizer of the problem (
Q1,σ
).

3.2
Optimality Condition of Least Squares Problems

To introduce optimality conditions for sparse optimization problems, we begin with the basic least squares problem:
\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
.
For this problem, we consider the following questions:

Q1: What is the least squares solution?

Q2: When can uniqueness of the least squares solution be claimed?

Q3: When can uniqueness of the least squares solution with minimum-norm be claimed?

To address these questions, we rely on the following fundamental result characterizing the optimality condition for the least squares problem:

{\bm{X}}^{\top}({\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\boldsymbol{0}.

(3.7)

This condition arises because the objective function
f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
is convex and differentiable. Therefore, any minimizer
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
must satisfy the first-order optimality condition
\nabla f({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})=2{\bm{X}}^{\top}({\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\boldsymbol{0}
(Corollary
).

We now present a unified perspective on the least squares problem in the following theorem. The underlying ideas will become clearer as we proceed. This theorem answers Question Q1.

{theoremHigh}
[A unified view of least squares problems
(
Lu 2021b
)
]
Let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
and
{\bm{y}}\in\real^{n}
.
Then the least squares problem
f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
admits a minimizer
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\in\real^{n}
if and only if there exists a vector
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}
such that

{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}={\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{y}}+({\bm{I}}-{\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{X}}){\boldsymbol{\alpha}},

(3.8)

where
{\bm{X}}^{+}
denotes the pseudo-inverse of
{\bm{X}}
(see Section
):

This shows that the least squares problem has a
unique
minimizer of
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}={\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{y}}
only when
{\bm{X}}^{+}
is a left inverse of
{\bm{X}}
(i.e.,
{\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{X}}={\bm{I}}
, and
{\bm{X}}
is left-invertible only when
{\bm{X}}
has full column rank
(
Lu 2021a
)
).

The optimal value is
f({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})={\bm{y}}^{\top}({\bm{I}}-{\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{+}){\bm{y}}
.

If
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\neq\boldsymbol{0}
:
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{y}}+({\bm{I}}-{\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{X}}){\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}
.

This means that any vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
that minimizes
f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
must be of the form given in (
), where:

{\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{y}}\perp\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
(by Theorem
) is the particular solution (the minimum-norm solution).

({\bm{I}}-{\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{X}}){\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
is the homogeneous solution, which captures the degrees of freedom in
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
arising from the null space of
{\bm{X}}
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
From (
), any minimizer
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
must satisfy the normal equation:
{\bm{X}}^{\top}({\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\boldsymbol{0}
.
This equation means that the vector
{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is orthogonal to the column space of
{\bm{X}}
, i.e., the error
{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
lies in the null space of
{\bm{X}}^{\top}
:

{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\perp\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}})\qquad\text{and}\qquad{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}}^{\top}).

(3.9)

To solve for
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
, note that the system
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\bm{y}}
may not have an exact solution when
{\bm{y}}\notin\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}})
.
In such cases, we seek the minimum-norm solution that minimizes
\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}
.
The pseudo-inverse
{\bm{X}}^{+}
provides the best possible solution by giving the unique minimum-norm least squares solution (see the argument in the sequel):

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{particular}}={\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{y}}.

(3.10)

To see
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{particular}}
satisfies (
), we have

{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{particular}}={\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{y}}
, where we used the fact that
{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{+}={\bm{X}}^{\top}
(Lemma
).

However, this is only
one
solution among possibly many. To characterize the full solution set, we consider two cases.

Case 1:
{\bm{y}}\in\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}})
.

For this case, the solution in (
) is obvious by the properties (
{\bm{X}}({\bm{I}}-{\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{X}}){\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=\boldsymbol{0}
) and uniqueness of the pseudo-inverse of a matrix (Proposition
).

Case 2:
{\bm{y}}\notin\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}})
.

Define the residual
{\bm{e}}\triangleq{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{particular}}={\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{y}}
. We seek all vectors
{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
such that
\big\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left\lVert{\bm{e}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
.
Two algebraic possibilities arise:

{\bm{X}}{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\bm{y}}={\bm{e}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}={\bm{e}}.

The former scenario implies that
{\bm{e}}={\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{particular}}={\bm{X}}{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\bm{y}}
, which leads to
{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}\frac{{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}+{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{particular}}}{2}
, i.e.,
{\bm{y}}\in\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}})
, contradicting the assumption of Case 2. Hence, only the second scenario is valid.

Since
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is in
p
, the complete set of minimizers consists of the particular solution
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{particular}}={\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{y}}
plus any vector in the null space of
{\bm{X}}
(i.e., any
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{null}}
that satisfies
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{null}}=\boldsymbol{0}
,
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{null}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})\triangleq\{{\bm{z}}\mid{\bm{X}}{\bm{z}}=\boldsymbol{0}\}
).
Thus, the general solution for
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
must then take the form:

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{y}}+{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{null}},\qquad\text{with}\quad{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{null}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}}).

(3.11)

Since
{\bm{X}}-{\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{X}}=\boldsymbol{0}
by (
), the projection onto the null space of
{\bm{X}}
is given by:

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{null}}=({\bm{I}}-{\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{X}}){\boldsymbol{\alpha}},\quad\text{for some }{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}.

(3.12)

This follows because
({\bm{I}}-{\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{X}})
is an orthogonal projection matrix onto
\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
(see Sections
and
).

On the other hand, since
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{null}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
and
\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}^{+})\equiv\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}^{\top})
(see Theorem
), it follows that

\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{y}}+({\bm{I}}-{\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{X}}){\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\left\lVert({\bm{I}}-{\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{X}}){\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

This shows that
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{y}}+({\bm{I}}-{\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{X}}){\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}
if
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\neq\boldsymbol{0}
and completes the proof.

3.2.1
LS in Convex Optimization

The theorems on convex functions provide rigorous answers to Questions Q2 and Q3 posed at the beginning of this section.
Theorem
partially addresses Question Q2—concerning the uniqueness of the least squares solution—in the context of the large-sample setting.
Specifically, if
n>p=\mathrm{rank}({\bm{X}})
, the least squares solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}=({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}})^{-1}{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{y}}
is unique.
In this case, the matrix

{\bm{H}}\triangleq{\bm{X}}({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}})^{-1}{\bm{X}}^{\top}

is is known as the
hat matrix
, which orthogonally projects
{\bm{y}}
onto the column space of
{\bm{X}}
(see Section
).
Indeed, this is the
only
scenario in which the least squares solution is guaranteed to be unique.

Note that both Q2 and Q3 can be formulated as convex optimization problems:

\displaystyle\text{(P2)}:

\displaystyle\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-2{\bm{y}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+{\bm{y}}^{\top}{\bm{y}};

(3.13)

\displaystyle\text{(P3)}:

\displaystyle\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{Q}}_{2}}g({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},\quad{\mathbb{Q}}_{2}\triangleq\{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}\mid\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\min\}.

Here, both
f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
and
g({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
are convex functions (Exercise
), and the set
{\mathbb{Q}}_{2}
is convex (see Theorem
).
Therefore, both (P2) and (P3) are convex optimization problems.
Theorem
also states that if the function is strictly convex, then the minimizer is unique.
Apparently,
g({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
is strictly convex (this again confirms Q3).
And
f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
is strictly convex only when
{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}
is positive definite, i.e., when
{\bm{X}}
has full column rank (i.e.,
n>p=\mathrm{rank}({\bm{X}})
).
This provides a rigorous answer to question Q2.

Combining this analysis with Theorem
, we establish the uniqueness of the minimum-norm least squares solution in the following corollarys.

Corollary 129
(Minimum-norm and unique LS solutions).

Let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
and
{\bm{y}}\in\real^{n}
.

Let
{\mathbb{Q}}_{2}\subset\real^{p}
denote the set of all minimizers of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\mapsto\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}
. The optimization problem

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{Q}}_{2}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

(3.14)

has the unique solution
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{+}={\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{y}}
.

If
n\geq p
and
{\bm{X}}
has full column rank, then the least squares problem

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

(3.15)

has the unique solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}={\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{y}}
.

Note that the minimizer of (
) corresponds to the orthogonal projection of
{\bm{y}}
onto the column space of
{\bm{X}}
.
Consequently, the matrix
{\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{+}
represents the orthogonal projector onto
{\bm{X}}
.
When
{\bm{X}}
has full rank and
n\geq p
, the matrix
{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}
is invertible.
By (
), we have
{\bm{X}}^{+}=({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}})^{-1}{\bm{X}}^{\top}
. Therefore,
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}={\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{y}}
satisfies the normal equation

{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}={\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{y}}.

(3.16)

Corollary 130
(High-dimensional LS solution,
\ell_{2}
-minimization).

Let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
with
p\geq n
, assume
{\bm{X}}
has full rank, and let
{\bm{y}}\in\real^{n}
.
Then the constrained optimization problem

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\bm{y}}

(3.17)

has the unique solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}={\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{y}}
.

In this setting, by (
), we have
{\bm{X}}^{+}={\bm{X}}^{\top}({\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{\top})^{-1}
if
{\bm{X}}
has full rank and
p\geq n
; thus, the system
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\bm{y}}
is consistent.
Therefore, in the situation of the above corollary, the minimizer
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
of (
) satisfies the
normal equation of the second kind

{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}={\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\gamma}},\quad\text{where }{\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}={\bm{y}}.

(3.18)

Finally, although the normal equations (
) and (
) suggest that least squares problems can be solved by standard linear system solvers (e.g., Gaussian elimination), it is numerically advantageous to use specialized algorithms designed for least squares. These include methods based on Cholesky factorization, QR decomposition, or singular value decomposition (SVD), which offer greater stability and accuracy
(
Lu 2021b
;
Björck 2024
)
.

3.2.2
Weighted LS Problems

Corollary
introduces the unique solution of the
\ell_{2}
-minimization problem.
We can also consider the
weighted
\ell_{2}
-minimization problem
:

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2,{\bm{w}}}\triangleq\left(\sum_{i=1}^{p}\alpha_{i}^{2}w_{i}\right)^{1/2}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}={\bm{y}},

(L
2,w
)

where
{\bm{w}}
is a vector of positive weights (
w_{i}>0
for all
i
).
Introduce the diagonal weight matrix
{\bm{D}}_{{\bm{w}}}=\mathrm{diag}([w_{1},w_{2},\ldots,w_{p}])\in\real^{p\times p}
, and define the change of variables

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\triangleq{\bm{D}}_{{\bm{w}}}^{1/2}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}.

Then
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2,{\bm{w}}}^{2}=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
, and the constraint becomes
{\bm{X}}{\bm{D}}_{{\bm{w}}}^{-1/2}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\bm{y}}
.
Thus, the minimizer
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}
of (
) corresponds to the minimizer
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
of the standard minimum-norm problem:

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\bm{X}}{\bm{D}}_{{\bm{w}}}^{-1/2}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\bm{y}},

By Corollary
, the solution is

{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}={\bm{D}}_{{\bm{w}}}^{-1/2}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}={\bm{D}}_{{\bm{w}}}^{-1/2}({\bm{X}}{\bm{D}}_{{\bm{w}}}^{-1/2})^{+}{\bm{y}}.

(3.19)

In particular, if
p\geq n
and
{\bm{X}}
has full rank, then Corollary
implies that the pseudo-inverse simplifies, yielding

{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}={\bm{D}}_{{\bm{w}}}^{-1}{\bm{X}}^{\top}({\bm{X}}{\bm{D}}_{{\bm{w}}}^{-1}{\bm{X}}^{\top})^{-1}{\bm{y}}.

(3.20)

Theorem
shows that the standard least squares solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}={\bm{X}}^{+}{\bm{y}}
is orthogonal to
\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
. Similar result can be observed in the weighted LS case.

{theoremHigh}
[Orthogonal relation of LS-III]
A vector
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}\in\real^{p}
is a minimizer of (
) if and only if

\left\langle{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}},{\bm{n}}\right\rangle_{{\bm{w}}}=0,\quad\text{for all }{\bm{n}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}}),

(3.21)

where
\left\langle{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}},{\bm{n}}\right\rangle_{{\bm{w}}}\triangleq\sum_{i=1}^{p}\beta_{i}n_{i}w_{i}
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Let
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}
satisfy
{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}={\bm{y}}
.
Any feasible vector
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}
for (
) can be written as
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}={\widehat{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}+{\bm{n}}
with
{\bm{n}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
.
For any scalar
\eta\in\real
and
{\bm{n}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
, consider the perturbed vector
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}+\eta{\bm{n}}
.
Its weighted norm squared is

\left\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}+\eta{\bm{n}}\right\rVert_{2,{\bm{w}}}^{2}=\left\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}\right\rVert_{2,{\bm{w}}}^{2}+\eta^{2}\left\lVert{\bm{n}}\right\rVert_{2,{\bm{w}}}^{2}+2\eta\left\langle{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}},{\bm{n}}\right\rangle_{{\bm{w}}}.

(3.22)

Therefore, if
\left\langle{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}},{\bm{n}}\right\rangle_{{\bm{w}}}=0
for all
{\bm{n}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
, then
\eta=0
is the minimizer of
\eta\mapsto\left\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}+\eta{\bm{n}}\right\rVert_{2,{\bm{w}}}
. Hence, (
) implies that
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}
is a minimizer of (
).

Conversely, suppose
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}
is a minimizer of (
).
Then
\eta=0
is a minimizer of
\eta\mapsto\left\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}+\eta{\bm{n}}\right\rVert_{2,{\bm{w}}}
for all
{\bm{n}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
. However, if
\left\langle{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}},{\bm{n}}\right\rangle_{{\bm{w}}}
would be nonzero, then by (
), we could find a nonzero
\eta
sufficiently close to
0
and of opposite sign as
\left\langle{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}},{\bm{n}}\right\rangle_{{\bm{w}}}
such that
\left\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}+\eta{\bm{n}}\right\rVert_{2,{\bm{w}}}<\left\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}\right\rVert_{2,{\bm{w}}}
, which leads to a contradiction to
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}
being a minimizer.

3.2.3
Regression and other Forms

Since the least squares model is commonly used for regression problems, it typically assumes that the number of samples exceeds the number of features (
n>p
).
In this setting, if the design matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
has full column rank, the least squares solution is given by

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{OLS}\triangleq({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}})^{-1}{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{y}},

which is widely known as the
ordinary least squares (OLS)
solution.

A common issue with the ordinary least squares solution arises when
{\bm{X}}
is nearly singular.
Let the SVD of
{\bm{X}}
be
{\bm{X}}={\bm{U}}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}{\bm{V}}^{\top}\in\real^{n\times p}
, where
{\bm{U}}\in\real^{n\times n}
and
{\bm{V}}\in\real^{p\times p}
are orthogonal, and the main diagonal of
{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\in\real^{n\times p}
contains the singular values
\sigma_{1}\geq\sigma_{2}\geq\ldots\geq\sigma_{p}\geq 0
.
Consequently,
{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}={\bm{V}}({\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}){\bm{V}}^{\top}\triangleq{\bm{V}}{\bm{S}}{\bm{V}}^{\top}
, where
{\bm{S}}\triangleq{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}=\mathrm{diag}(\sigma_{1}^{2},\sigma_{2}^{2},\ldots,\sigma_{p}^{2})\in\real^{p\times p}
contains the squared singular values of
{\bm{X}}
. When
{\bm{X}}
is nearly singular, the smallest singular value satisfies
\sigma_{p}^{2}\approx 0
, which renders the inversion
({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}})^{-1}={\bm{V}}{\bm{S}}^{-1}{\bm{V}}^{\top}
numerically unstable.
As a result, the solution
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{OLS}=({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}})^{-1}{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{y}}
may become highly sensitive to perturbations or even diverge.
To mitigate this instability, an
\ell_{2}
-regularization term is often added, leading to the following regularized optimization problem:

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{Tik}=\mathop{\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\lambda\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

(3.23)

This approach is known as
Tikhonov regularization
(or the
ridge regression
)
(
Tikhonov 1963
)
.
The gradient of the objective function is
2({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}+\lambda{\bm{I}}){\boldsymbol{\beta}}-2{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{y}}
, and setting it to zero yields the closed-form solution

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{Tik}=({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}+\lambda{\bm{I}})^{-1}{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{y}}.

Using the SVD of
{\bm{X}}
, the inverse becomes
({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}+\lambda{\bm{I}})^{-1}={\bm{V}}({\bm{S}}+\lambda{\bm{I}})^{-1}{\bm{V}}^{\top}
, where
\widetilde{\bm{S}}\triangleq({\bm{S}}+\lambda{\bm{I}})=\mathrm{diag}(\sigma_{1}^{2}+\lambda,\sigma_{2}^{2}+\lambda,\ldots,\sigma_{p}^{2}+\lambda)
.
Thus, the OLS and Tikhonov-regularized solutions can be expressed as

\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{OLS}

\displaystyle=({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}})^{-1}{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{y}}={\bm{V}}\left({\bm{S}}^{-1}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\right){\bm{U}}^{\top}{\bm{y}};

(3.24a)

\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{Tik}

\displaystyle=({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}+\lambda{\bm{I}})^{-1}{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{y}}={\bm{V}}\left(({\bm{S}}+\lambda{\bm{I}})^{-1}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\right){\bm{U}}^{\top}{\bm{y}},

(3.24b)

where the main diagonals of
\left({\bm{S}}^{-1}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\right)
are
\mathrm{diag}(\frac{1}{\sigma_{1}},\frac{1}{\sigma_{2}},\ldots,\frac{1}{\sigma_{p}})
; and the main diagonals of
\left(({\bm{S}}+\lambda{\bm{I}})^{-1}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\right)
are
\mathrm{diag}(\frac{\sigma_{1}}{\sigma_{1}^{2}+\lambda},\frac{\sigma_{2}}{\sigma_{2}^{2}+\lambda},\ldots,\frac{\sigma_{p}}{\sigma_{p}^{2}+\lambda})
.
The latter expression remains well-behaved even when
\sigma_{p}\approx 0
, provided that
\lambda
is chosen larger than the smallest nonzero squared singular value. This regularization also improves the condition number of the system (see Remark
): when
\sigma_{p}
is close to zero,

\kappa({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}})={\sigma_{1}^{2}}/{\sigma_{p}^{2}}\qquad\rightarrow\qquad\kappa({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}+\lambda{\bm{I}})={(\lambda+\sigma_{1}^{2})}/{(\lambda+\sigma_{p}^{2})}.

In summary, Tikhonov regularization effectively prevents divergence in the least squares estimate
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{OLS}
when
{\bm{X}}
is ill-conditioned or rank-deficient. This stabilization enhances the numerical convergence of least squares algorithms and their variants—such as alternating least squares
(
Lu 2022
)
—making Tikhonov regularization a widely adopted technique in practice.

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{Tik}=({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}+\lambda{\bm{I}})^{-1}{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{y}}

has a norm that is non-increasing as

increases.

The global minimum of this objective lies at the center of the innermost ellipse. However, the addition of a constraint restricts the feasible region for

In contrast, the
\ell_{1}

Among them, the
\ell_{1}

\ell_{2}
-regularization term confines the parameters within a circular region.
As illustrated in the figure, the optimal solution under
\ell_{1}

\beta_{1}

By contrast, the circular geometry of the

The
\ell_{0}
-unit ball promotes sparsity, while it is not convex.
And the
\ell_{\infty}
-unit ball includes all vectors where each entry has magnitude less than or equal to
1
.
The intersection of the
\ell_{0}
- and
\ell_{\infty}
-unit balls yields precisely the set of 1-sparse vectors with entries in
[-1,1]
.
This observation provides another justification for using the
\ell_{1}
-norm to induce sparsity:
the

-norm—that is, the convex hull of the intersection between the

\ell_{\infty}

This relationship is illustrated in two dimensions in Figure
