Lemma 131
(
\ell_{1}
-unit ball).

The
\ell_{1}
-unit ball is the convex hull of the intersection between the
\ell_{0}
-unit ball and the
\ell_{\infty}
-unit ball.

Proof
[of Lemma
]

{\mathbb{B}}_{1}\subseteq\text{conv}({\mathbb{B}}_{0}\cap{\mathbb{B}}_{\infty})
.

Let
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{1}\subset\real^{p}
so that
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq 1
.
If we set
\theta_{i}\triangleq\left\lvert\beta_{i}\right\rvert
and
\theta_{0}\triangleq 1-\sum_{i=1}^{p}\theta_{i}
, we have
\sum_{i=0}^{p}\theta_{i}=1
by construction,
\theta_{i}=\left\lvert\beta_{i}\right\rvert\geq 0
and

\displaystyle\theta_{0}

\displaystyle=1-\sum_{i=1}^{p}\theta_{i}=1-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\geq 0.

(3.25)

We can express now
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
as a convex combination of the standard basis vectors multiplied by the sign of the entries of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
as
\sign(\beta_{1}){\bm{e}}_{1}
,
\sign(\beta_{2}){\bm{e}}_{2}
, …,
\sign(\beta_{p}){\bm{e}}_{p}
and the zero vector
\boldsymbol{0}
:

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\theta_{i}\sign(\beta_{i}){\bm{e}}_{i}+\theta_{0}\boldsymbol{0},

(3.26)

where the vectors all belong to
{\mathbb{B}}_{0}\cap{\mathbb{B}}_{\infty}
. Hence,
{\mathbb{B}}_{1}\subseteq\text{conv}({\mathbb{B}}_{0}\cap{\mathbb{B}}_{\infty})
.

\text{conv}({\mathbb{B}}_{0}\cap{\mathbb{B}}_{\infty})\subseteq{\mathbb{B}}_{1}
.

Let
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\text{conv}({\mathbb{B}}_{0}\cap{\mathbb{B}}_{\infty})\subset\real^{p}
.
By definition of the convex hull, we can express
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
as

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\theta_{i}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{i},

(3.27)

where
m>0
,
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{1},\dots,{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{m}\in\real^{p}
have a single entry bounded by one,
\theta_{i}\geq 0
for all
1\leq i\leq m
and
\sum_{i=1}^{m}\theta_{i}=1
.
By the triangle inequality, we have

\displaystyle\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}

\displaystyle\leq\sum_{i=1}^{m}\theta_{i}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{i}\right\rVert_{1}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\theta_{i}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{i}\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq\sum_{i=1}^{m}\theta_{i}\leq 1,

(3.28)

where the equality follows since each vector
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{i}
has only one nonzero entry.
This immediately implies
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{1}
and completes the proof.

3.3
Optimality Condition of
\ell_{1}
-Regularized Problems

We have previously demonstrated that the
\ell_{1}
-regularized least squares estimator promotes sparsity in the solution: many components of the estimated coefficient vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
are driven exactly to zero, leading to interpretable and compact models. This property makes
\ell_{1}
-regularization especially valuable in high-dimensional settings where feature selection is desired.

To analyze this behavior more formally, we now turn to the optimality conditions of the
\ell_{1}
-regularized least squares problem—commonly known as the Lagrangian LASSO (see (
LL
), p.
LL
). In its penalized (Lagrangian) form, the problem is stated as

\text{(L${}_{L}$)}\quad\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}F(\lambda,{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\triangleq\left\{\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\lambda\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\right\}.

(3.29)

The subgradient of the objective function (
) with respect to
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is given by

\partial_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}F(\lambda,{\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\frac{\partial F(\lambda,{\boldsymbol{\beta}})}{\partial{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}=-{\bm{X}}^{\top}({\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}})+\lambda\nabla_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\triangleq-{\bm{c}}+\lambda\partial\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1},

(3.30)

where
{\bm{c}}\triangleq{\bm{X}}^{\top}({\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}})
is the
residual correlation vector
, and the vector
\partial\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}=[\partial_{\beta_{1}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1},\partial_{\beta_{2}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1},\ldots,\partial_{\beta_{p}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}]^{\top}
denotes the subdifferential of the
\ell_{1}
-norm
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}
(Exercise
), with
i
-th entry

\partial\left\lvert\beta_{i}\right\rvert=\begin{cases}\{+1\},&\beta_{i}>0;\\
\{-1\},&\beta_{i}<0;\\
[-1,+1],&\beta_{i}=0,\end{cases}\qquad\forall\,i=1,2,\ldots,p.

(3.31)

From (
), it follows that a stationary point of the Lagrangian LASSO problem (
LL
) must satisfy
\partial_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}F(\lambda,{\boldsymbol{\beta}})=-{\bm{c}}+\lambda\partial\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}=\boldsymbol{0}
, i.e.,

{\bm{c}}=\lambda\partial\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}.

(3.32)

Equivalently, for each
i=1,2,\ldots,p
, we have
c_{i}=\lambda\partial\left\lvert\beta_{i}\right\rvert
.
Because the Lagrangian LASSO problem is convex, this stationary-point condition is both necessary and sufficient for optimality (Theorem
).

The optimality condition (
) can be expressed in terms of the support set
{\mathbb{S}}\triangleq\{i\mid\beta_{i}\neq 0\}
and its complement
{\mathbb{S}}^{c}=\{1,2,\ldots,p\}\setminus{\mathbb{S}}
as

{\bm{c}}[{\mathbb{S}}]=\lambda\cdot\mathrm{sign}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}[{\mathbb{S}}])\qquad\text{and}\qquad\left\lvert{\bm{c}}[{\mathbb{S}}^{c}]\right\rvert\leq\lambda{\bm{1}},

(3.33)

This reveals that, for indices in the support
{\mathbb{S}}
, the residual correlations have magnitude exactly equal to
\lambda
and share the same sign as the corresponding coefficients in
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.
Equivalently, condition (
) can be written as

\left\lvert c_{i}\right\rvert=\lambda,\quad\forall\,i\in{\mathbb{S}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\left\lvert c_{i}\right\rvert\leq\lambda,\quad\forall\,i\in{\mathbb{S}}^{c}.

(3.34)

In other words, the absolute value of the residual correlation equals
\lambda
for active (nonzero) coefficients and does not exceed
\lambda
for inactive (zero) coefficients. Consequently, the maximum absolute residual correlation satisfies
\left\lVert{\bm{c}}\right\rVert_{\infty}=\max\{c_{i}\}=\lambda
.

Remark 132
(KKT conditions of constrained LASSO).

The conditions in (
) are similar to the KKT conditions of the constrained LASSO problem (
LC
) (p.
LC
).
This equivalence arises from the shared optimality structure between the penalized and constrained formulations of LASSO.
At the optimal solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
for a given
\ell_{1}
-norm constraint
\Sigma
, the following KKT conditions (Theorem
) must hold:

1.

Subgradient condition. The gradient of the least squares loss (
-{\bm{X}}^{\top}({\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})
) must be in the subdifferential of
\nu\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}
, where
\nu
is the Lagrange multiplier associated with the constraint.
This translates to:

For any
i
where
{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}\neq 0
:
\big\lvert{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}({\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})\big\rvert=\nu
(the absolute correlation between predictor
i
and the residual is exactly
\nu
).

For any
i
where
{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}=0
:
\big\lvert{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}({\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})\big\rvert\leq\nu
(the absolute correlation does not exceed
\nu
).

2.

Complementary slackness.
\nu(\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}-\Sigma)=0
. If
\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}<\Sigma
, then
\nu=0
(no regularization). If
\nu>0
, then
\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}=\Sigma
(the constraint is active).

3.3.1
LASSO Dual

For the Lagrangian LASSO problem (
LL
),
introducing the residual vector
{\bm{r}}={\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
, we can equivalently reformulate the primal problem as

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p},{\bm{r}}\in\real^{n}}\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{r}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\lambda\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\bm{r}}={\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}.

(3.35)

Letting
{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\in\real^{n}
denote the vector of Lagrange multipliers associated with the equality constraint. The Lagrangian function for this problem is

L({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\bm{r}},{\boldsymbol{\nu}})=\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{r}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\lambda\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}-{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{\top}({\bm{r}}-{\bm{y}}+{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}).

(3.36)

The Lagrangian dual function is obtained by minimizing
L({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\bm{r}},{\boldsymbol{\nu}})
over
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
and
{\bm{r}}
.
In order to obtain the Lagrangian dual function
\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\bm{r}}}L({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\bm{r}},{\boldsymbol{\nu}})
,
isolating those terms involving
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
, and noting that
\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rvert\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\right\rVert_{\infty}
by Hölder’s inequality (Theorem
), we find

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\lambda\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}-{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\begin{cases}0,&\text{if }\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq\lambda;\\
-\infty,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

(3.37)

Next, we isolate terms involving
{\bm{r}}
and find

\min_{{\bm{r}}\in\real^{n}}\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{r}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{\top}{\bm{r}}=-\frac{1}{2}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\nu}},\quad\text{with ${\bm{r}}={\boldsymbol{\nu}}$}.

(3.38)

Substituting relations (
) and (
) into the Lagrangian representation (
), we obtain

\displaystyle\text{LASSO Dual:}\qquad\phi(\lambda)

\displaystyle\triangleq\max_{{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}\frac{1}{2}\left(\left\lVert{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right)\triangleq\max_{{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}D({\boldsymbol{\nu}})

(3.39)

\displaystyle\text{s.t.}\quad\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq\lambda,

where
D({\boldsymbol{\nu}})\triangleq\frac{1}{2}\left(\left\lVert{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right)
is the dual objective function,
and
\phi(\lambda)
denotes the optimal dual value corresponding to the penalty parameter
\lambda
.

Geometrically, this dual formulation amounts to projecting the response vector
{\bm{y}}
onto the feasible set
{\mathbb{S}}_{\lambda}\triangleq\{{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\in\real^{n}\mid\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq\lambda\}
.
The set
{\mathbb{S}}_{\lambda}
is the intersection of the
2p
half-spaces defined by
\left\lvert{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\right\rvert\leq\lambda
, each one is a convex polytope in
n
. In the language of projection and proximal operators, the solution is given by the projection or proximal map
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}=\mathcal{P}_{{{\mathbb{S}}_{\lambda}}}({\bm{y}})\equiv\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{\delta_{{\mathbb{S}}_{\lambda}}}({\bm{y}})
.
In other words,
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}
is the projection onto the polytope
{\mathbb{S}}_{\lambda}
.
Figure
illustrates this geometric interpretation.

Figure 3.4:
The Lagrange dual of the LASSO, with
D({\boldsymbol{\nu}})=\frac{1}{2}(\left\lVert{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2})
. The shaded region is the feasible set
{\mathbb{S}}_{\lambda}
. The unconstrained dual solution is
{\boldsymbol{\nu}}={\bm{y}}
, the null residual.
The dual solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}=\mathcal{P}_{{{\mathbb{S}}_{\lambda}}}({\bm{y}})
, the projection of
{\bm{y}}
onto the convex set
{\mathbb{S}}_{\lambda}
.

\paragrapharrow

Dual feasibility condition for sparsity.
For the primal LASSO problem (
LL
), strong duality holds (Theorem
).
The optimal primal
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
and dual
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}
solutions then satisfy

{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}+{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}.

(3.40)

The dual problem plays a crucial role in identifying sparsity in the primal solution: by examining the dual variable
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}
, we can determine which coefficients in
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
must be exactly zero. Specifically, the optimality condition

\left\lvert{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}\right\rvert<\lambda\quad\implies\quad{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}(\lambda)=0,\quad i=1,2,\dots,p,

(3.41)

follows directly from (
) and (
).
Note that the above condition is sufficient for that
{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}(\lambda)
must be an inactive predictor, but it is not necessary.
Indeed, it is possible for
{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}(\lambda)=0
even when
\left\lvert{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}\right\rvert=\lambda
. In such cases, the predictor lies on the boundary of the active set and is considered marginally inactive.

\paragrapharrow

Largest
\lambda
for a nontrivial solution.

This form of the LASSO dual also reveals the largest value of the penalty parameter, denoted
\lambda=\lambda_{\max}
, for which the primal LASSO problem admits a nontrivial solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\max}\neq\boldsymbol{0}
.
If
\lambda=\lambda_{\max}
is chosen large enough, the optimal primal solution becomes identically zero:
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}={\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\max}=\boldsymbol{0}
.
To determine such a
\lambda_{\max}
, we substitute
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\max}=\boldsymbol{0}
in the primal LASSO problem (
LL
) to obtain
\phi(\lambda_{\max})=\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
since
{\bm{y}}={\boldsymbol{\nu}}
in (
).
By strong duality, the dual problem under
\lambda=\lambda_{\max}
achieves a value of
\phi(\lambda_{\max})=\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
at the unique solution

{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}_{\max}={\bm{y}}.

(3.42)

The point
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}_{\max}
is a dual feasible point and satisfies the constraints
\left\lvert{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{y}}\right\rvert\leq\lambda_{\max}
,
i=1,2,\dots,p
.
Therefore, this form of the LASSO dual shows the largest
\lambda=\lambda_{\max}
such that the solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\max}
is nontrivial is

\lambda_{\max}=\max_{1\leq i\leq p}\left\lvert{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{y}}\right\rvert=\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{\infty}.

(3.43)

3.3.2
Dual Polytope Projections and Screening Rules

The quantity in (
) reveals an important intuition: covariates that have small inner products with the response vector
{\bm{y}}
are less likely to receive nonzero coefficients in the LASSO solution compared to those with larger inner products

This observation suggests a practical strategy: we may be able to eliminate irrelevant predictors before solving the full optimization problem, thereby reducing computational cost. For instance, in genomic applications—where datasets often involve millions of single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs)—we typically expect only a handful of variables to appear in the final model.

In this subsection, we discuss
screening rules
that exploit this intuition. These rules can dramatically accelerate LASSO computations by efficiently identifying and removing inactive predictors—i.e., features that are guaranteed to have zero coefficients in the optimal solution—without compromising numerical accuracy. The resulting reduced problem yields the exact same solution as the original, but at a fraction of the computational cost.

We begin with a geometric screening rule based on projections onto the dual feasible set, known as the
dual polytope projections (DPPs)
rule
(
Ghaoui et al. 2010
;
Wang et al. 2013
)
.

{theoremHigh}
[Dual polytope projections (DPP)]
Suppose we are given a solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}(\lambda^{\prime})
to the LASSO dual (
) and a primal solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}(\lambda^{\prime})
at some penalty parameter
0<\lambda^{\prime}\leq\lambda_{\max}
.
Let
\lambda
be a nonnegative value different from
\lambda^{\prime}
.
If, for a given index
i
, the following inequality holds:

\left\lvert{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}(\lambda^{\prime})\right\rvert<\lambda^{\prime}-\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lvert 1-\frac{\lambda^{\prime}}{\lambda}\right\rvert,

(3.44)

then the
i
-th coefficient in the LASSO solution at
\lambda
is zero:

{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}(\lambda)=0
, where
{\bm{x}}_{i}
denotes the
i
-th column of
{\bm{X}}
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Introduce the change of variable
{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\triangleq{\boldsymbol{\nu}}/\lambda
.
Then the LASSO dual problem (
) becomes

\text{LASSO Dual:}\quad\max_{{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}\frac{1}{2}\left(\left\lVert{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\lambda^{2}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}/\lambda-{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq 1.

(3.45)

Thus, the feasible set in the scaled dual space is the fixed convex polytope
\widetilde{{\mathbb{S}}}\triangleq\{{\bm{z}}\in\real^{n}\mid\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{z}}\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq 1\}
, which is independent of
\lambda
.
The optimal scaled dual variable
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}(\lambda)
is the projection of
{\bm{y}}/\lambda
into the feasible set
\widetilde{{\mathbb{S}}}
.

By (
), the stationarity conditions for the LASSO problem, we have

\left\lvert{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}(\lambda)\right\rvert<1\quad\implies\quad{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}(\lambda)=0,\quad i=1,2,\dots,n.

(3.46)

Since the polytopes for different penalty parameters
\lambda
are the same,
by the nonexpansiveness of projection operators (Theorem
), we have

\left\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}(\lambda)-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}(\lambda^{\prime})\right\rVert_{2}=\left\lVert\mathcal{P}_{\widetilde{{\mathbb{S}}}}(\frac{{\bm{y}}}{\lambda})-\mathcal{P}_{\widetilde{{\mathbb{S}}}}(\frac{{\bm{y}}}{\lambda^{\prime}})\right\rVert_{2}\leq\left\lVert\frac{{\bm{y}}}{\lambda}-\frac{{\bm{y}}}{\lambda^{\prime}}\right\rVert_{2}=\left\lVert{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lvert\frac{1}{\lambda}-\frac{1}{\lambda^{\prime}}\right\rvert.

(3.47)

Using triangle inequality and Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, the above inequality and the assumption (
) yield

\displaystyle\left\lvert{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}(\lambda)\right\rvert

\displaystyle\leq\left\lvert{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}(\lambda)-{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}(\lambda^{\prime})\right\rvert+\left\lvert{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}(\lambda^{\prime})\right\rvert

\displaystyle<\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}(\lambda)-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}(\lambda^{\prime})\right\rVert_{2}+1-\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lvert\frac{1}{\lambda^{\prime}}-\frac{1}{\lambda}\right\rvert

\displaystyle\leq\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lvert\frac{1}{\lambda^{\prime}}-\frac{1}{\lambda}\right\rvert+1-\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lvert\frac{1}{\lambda^{\prime}}-\frac{1}{\lambda}\right\rvert=1.

Using (
) completes the proof.

The above theorem shows that if

\left\lvert{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}\big({\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}(\lambda^{\prime})\big)\right\rvert<\lambda^{\prime}-\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lvert 1-\frac{\lambda^{\prime}}{\lambda}\right\rvert,

(3.48a)

then variable
i
does not belong to the active set at penalty level
\lambda
(i.e.,
{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}(\lambda)=0
).
In particular, at
\lambda^{\prime}=\lambda_{\max}\equiv\big\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{y}}\big\rVert_{\infty}
by (
), the above inequality becomes

\left\lvert{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{y}}\right\rvert<\lambda_{\max}-\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}\left(\frac{\lambda_{\max}}{\lambda}-1\right).

(3.48b)

The
dual polytope projection (DPP)
rule then suggests to discard the
i
-th predictor whenever (
) holds
(
Wang et al. 2013
)
.

\paragrapharrow

Variant of DPP rule.
On the other hand, suppose
\frac{{\bm{y}}}{\lambda^{\prime}}\notin\widetilde{{\mathbb{S}}}\triangleq\{{\bm{z}}\in\real^{n}\mid\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{z}}\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq 1\}
, i.e.,
\lambda^{\prime}\in(0,\lambda_{\max})
.
In this case, the scaled dual solution satisfies
\frac{{\bm{y}}}{\lambda^{\prime}}\neq\mathcal{P}_{\widetilde{{\mathbb{S}}}}(\frac{{\bm{y}}}{\lambda^{\prime}})\equiv{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}(\lambda^{\prime})
(recall that
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}(\lambda^{\prime})={\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}(\lambda^{\prime})/\lambda^{\prime}
is the scaled dual solution under the penalth parameter
\lambda=\lambda^{\prime}
).
Let
{\boldsymbol{\mu}}(\eta)\triangleq{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}(\lambda^{\prime})+\eta\left(\frac{{\bm{y}}}{\lambda^{\prime}}-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}(\lambda^{\prime})\right)
for
\eta\geq 0
, i.e.,
{\boldsymbol{\mu}}(\eta)
is a point lying on the ray starting from
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}(\lambda^{\prime})
and pointing to the same direction as
\frac{{\bm{y}}}{\lambda^{\prime}}-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}(\lambda^{\prime})
. We can observe that
\mathcal{P}_{\widetilde{{\mathbb{S}}}}({\boldsymbol{\mu}}(\eta))={\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}(\lambda^{\prime})
, i.e., the projection of
{\boldsymbol{\mu}}(\eta)
onto the set
\widetilde{{\mathbb{S}}}
is
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}(\lambda^{\prime})
as well. By the nonexpansiveness of the projection operator (Theorem
), we have

\displaystyle\left\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}(\lambda)-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}(\lambda^{\prime})\right\rVert_{2}

\displaystyle=\left\lVert\mathcal{P}_{\widetilde{{\mathbb{S}}}}\big(\frac{{\bm{y}}}{\lambda}\big)-\mathcal{P}_{\widetilde{{\mathbb{S}}}}\big({\boldsymbol{\mu}}(\eta)\big)\right\rVert_{2}

\displaystyle\leq\left\lVert\frac{{\bm{y}}}{\lambda}-{\boldsymbol{\mu}}(\eta)\right\rVert_{2}=\left\lVert\eta\big(\frac{{\bm{y}}}{\lambda^{\prime}}-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}(\lambda^{\prime})\big)-\big(\frac{{\bm{y}}}{\lambda}-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}(\lambda^{\prime})\big)\right\rVert_{2}.

(3.49)

Clearly, when
\eta=1
, the inequality in (
3.49
) reduces to the one in (
).
Because the inequality in (
3.49
) holds for all
\eta\geq 0
, we may get a tighter bound by

\left\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}(\lambda)-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}(\lambda^{\prime})\right\rVert_{2}\leq\min_{\eta\geq 0}\left\lVert\eta{\bm{u}}_{1}-{\bm{u}}_{2}\right\rVert_{2},

(3.50)

where
{\bm{u}}_{1}\triangleq\frac{{\bm{y}}}{\lambda^{\prime}}-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}(\lambda^{\prime})
and

{\bm{u}}_{2}\triangleq\frac{{\bm{y}}}{\lambda}-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}(\lambda^{\prime})
.
When
\lambda^{\prime}=\lambda_{\max}
, we can set
{\bm{u}}_{1}=\sign({\bm{x}}_{*}^{\top}{\bm{y}}){\bm{x}}_{*}
where
{\bm{x}}_{*}\triangleq\arg\max_{{\bm{x}}_{i}}\left\lvert{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{y}}\right\rvert
.
The minimization problem on the right-hand side of the inequality (
) has a closed-form solution:

\min_{\eta\geq 0}\left\lVert\eta{\bm{u}}_{1}-{\bm{u}}_{2}\right\rVert_{2}=\varphi(\lambda^{\prime},\lambda)\triangleq\begin{cases}\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{2}\right\rVert_{2},&\text{if }\left\langle{\bm{u}}_{1},{\bm{u}}_{2}\right\rangle<0;\\
\left\lVert\frac{\left\langle{\bm{u}}_{1},{\bm{u}}_{2}\right\rangle}{\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{1}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}{\bm{u}}_{1}-{\bm{u}}_{2}\right\rVert_{2},&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

(3.51)

This refined bound leads to an enhanced DPP screening rule, as stated below.

Corollary 133
(Enhanced DPP rule).

Suppose we are given a solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}(\lambda^{\prime})
to the LASSO dual (
) and a primal solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}(\lambda^{\prime})
at some penalty parameter
0<\lambda^{\prime}\leq\lambda_{\max}
.
Let
\lambda
be a nonnegative value different from
\lambda^{\prime}
.
If, for a given index
i
, the following inequality holds:

\left\lvert{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}(\lambda^{\prime})\right\rvert<\lambda^{\prime}-\lambda^{\prime}\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}\varphi(\lambda^{\prime},\lambda),

(3.52)

then
{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}(\lambda)=0
, where
{\bm{x}}_{i}
is the
i
-th column of
{\bm{X}}
.

The above corollary shows that if

\left\lvert{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}\big({\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}(\lambda^{\prime})\big)\right\rvert<\lambda^{\prime}-\lambda^{\prime}\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}\varphi(\lambda^{\prime},\lambda),

(3.53a)

then variable
i
is not part of the activate set at penalty level
\lambda
.
At
\lambda^{\prime}=\lambda_{\max}\equiv\big\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{y}}\big\rVert_{\infty}
by (
), this condition becomes

\left\lvert{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{y}}\right\rvert<\lambda_{\max}-\lambda_{\max}\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}\varphi(\lambda_{\max},\lambda).

(3.53b)

Again, the enhanced DPP rule then suggests to discard the
i
-th variable if (
) is satisfied.

\paragrapharrow

The screening rule.
Equation (
) or (
) provides a practical screening rule for efficiently solving the Lagrangian LASSO problem (
LL
).
Suppose we know the optimal dual solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}(\lambda^{\prime})
at some penalty parameter
\lambda^{\prime}
(e.g., the well-known case
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}(\lambda_{\text{max}})={\bm{y}}
).
Using this information, we can bound the possible location of the dual solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}(\lambda)
at a nearby parameter
\lambda
.
By bounding this possible location of
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}(\lambda)
, we can check if
\left\lvert{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}(\lambda)\right\rvert
is
guaranteed
to be less than
\lambda
. If so, the corresponding predictor
{\bm{x}}_{i}
is inactive at
\lambda
(i.e.,
{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}(\lambda)=0
) and can be safely removed from the optimization problem without affecting the final solution.

Sequential DDP

Motivated by the dual polytope projection theorem (Theorem
) and the screening principle above, we can construct a sequential DPP strategy.
Specifically, consider a decreasing sequence of penalty parameters:
\lambda_{0}=\lambda_{\max}>\lambda_{1}>\lambda_{2}>\ldots>\lambda_{m}
,
We begin by applying the DPP screening rule at
\lambda_{0}=\lambda_{\max}
to eliminate predictors that are guaranteed to be inactive.
Since
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}(\lambda_{\max})={\bm{y}}
, this initial screening is particularly simple and effective.

After discarding inactive variables, we solve the reduced LASSO problem at
\lambda_{1}
using any algorithm from Section
, obtaining the exact primal solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}(\lambda_{1})
. From the primal-dual relationship (
), we then recover the dual solution:

{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}(\lambda_{1})={\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}(\lambda_{1})
.
This newly computed dual solution enables us to apply the DPP rule again—now with tighter bounds—to screen out inactive predictors for the next parameter
\lambda_{2}
. Repeating this process iteratively yields a sequential screening framework that progressively reduces the problem size at each step, significantly accelerating computation while preserving exactness.

Corollary 134
(Sequential DPP).

For the Lagrangian LASSO problem (
LL
), suppose we are given a sequence of parameter values
\lambda_{\max}=\lambda_{0}>\lambda_{1}>\ldots>\lambda_{m}
. Then for any integer
0\leq t<m
, we have
{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}(\lambda_{t+1})=0
if
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}(\lambda_{t})
is known, and the following holds:

\left\lvert{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}(\lambda_{t})\right\rvert\equiv\left\lvert{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}\big({\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}(\lambda_{t})\big)\right\rvert<\lambda_{t}-\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}\left(\frac{\lambda_{t}}{\lambda_{t+1}}-1\right),\quad i=1,2,\ldots,p.

or

\left\lvert{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}(\lambda_{t})\right\rvert\equiv\left\lvert{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}\big({\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}(\lambda_{t})\big)\right\rvert<\lambda_{t}-\lambda_{t}\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}\varphi(\lambda_{t},\lambda_{t+1}),\quad i=1,2,\ldots,p.

3.3.3
Safe Feature Elimination (SAFE)

The
SAFE (Safe FEature Elimination)
rule is another powerful technique used in sparse optimization problems, especially in LASSO-type regression, to efficiently identify and eliminate features (columns of the design matrix) that are guaranteed to have zero coefficient in the optimal solution without solving the full problem.
This significantly speeds up computation, particularly when dealing with high-dimensional data where many features are irrelevant.

The intuition behind SAFE stems from the stationarity condition in (
), which we recall here:

\left\lvert{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}\right\rvert<\lambda\quad\implies\quad{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}(\lambda)=0,\quad i=1,2,\dots,p,

(3.54)

The SAFE rule constructs a constraint set
\Theta
known to contain the dual optimal solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}
.
It then replaces
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}
in the inequality test with this entire set
\Theta
. Specifically, if

\left\lvert{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\right\rvert<\lambda,\quad\text{for all }{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\in\Theta,

(3.55)

then the condition in (
) holds uniformly over
\Theta
. Consequently, the
i
-th component of the primal optimal solution must be zero:
{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}=0
.

Constructing the Dual Constraint Set

We begin by constructing a set
\Theta
that is guaranteed to contain the dual optimal solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}
of the LASSO dual problem (
):

\displaystyle\text{LASSO Dual:}\qquad\phi(\lambda)

\displaystyle\triangleq\max_{{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}\left\{D({\boldsymbol{\nu}})\triangleq\frac{1}{2}\left(\left\lVert{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right)={\bm{y}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}-\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right\}

(3.56)

\displaystyle\text{s.t.}\quad\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq\lambda,

under the penalty parameter
\lambda
.
To this end, we define
\Theta
as the intersection of two sets,
\Theta_{1}
and
\Theta_{2}
, each derived from a different optimality condition.

\paragrapharrow

Constructing
\Theta_{1}
.
The first set,
\Theta_{1}
, is based on the fact that the dual objective
D({\boldsymbol{\nu}})
achieves its maximum at
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}
. That is, for any dual-feasible point
{\boldsymbol{\nu}}
, we have
D({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}})\geq D({\boldsymbol{\nu}})
.
Let
{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{\eta}
be a specific dual-feasible point for problem (
), and define
\gamma\triangleq D({\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{\eta})
.
Then we must have
D({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}})\geq\gamma
, so the set
\Theta_{1}\triangleq\{{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\mid D({\boldsymbol{\nu}})\geq\gamma\}
contains the dual optimum
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}
, i.e.,
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}\in\Theta_{1}
.

One practical way to obtain such a feasible point
{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{\eta}
is via
dual scaling
.
Specifically, let
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}_{0}
be a known dual-feasible point corresponding to a larger penalty parameter
\lambda_{0}>\lambda
(e.g., as in (
)).
We then define
{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{\eta}\triangleq\eta{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}_{0}
where the scalar
\eta\in\real
is chosen so that
{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{\eta}
remains feasible for the dual problem with penalty
\lambda
; that is,
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{\eta}\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq\lambda
or
\left\lvert\eta\right\rvert\leq\lambda/\lambda_{0}
.
We now choose
\eta
to maximize the dual objective over this interval:

\gamma=\max_{\eta}\left\{D(\eta{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}_{0})\mid\left\lvert\eta\right\rvert\leq\frac{\lambda}{\lambda_{0}}\right\}=\max_{\eta}\left\{-\frac{1}{2}a\eta^{2}+b\eta\mid\left\lvert\eta\right\rvert\leq\frac{\lambda}{\lambda_{0}}\right\},

where
a\triangleq\left\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}_{0}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}>0

and
b\triangleq\left\lvert{\bm{y}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}_{0}\right\rvert
.
We obtain by
\eta=\lambda/\lambda_{0}
that

\gamma=-\frac{a}{2}\left(\frac{\lambda}{\lambda_{0}}\right)^{2}+b\frac{\lambda}{\lambda_{0}}
,
such that

{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}\in\Theta_{1}\triangleq\{{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\mid D({\boldsymbol{\nu}})\geq\gamma\}.

(3.57)

\paragrapharrow

Constructing
\Theta_{2}
.
The second set,
\Theta_{2}
, arises from a first-order optimality condition for the dual problem (
).
Recall that for a convex maximization problem over a convex feasible set, a point
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}_{0}
is optimal if and only if
{\bm{g}}^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\nu}}-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}_{0})\geq 0
for every dual point
{\boldsymbol{\nu}}
that is feasible for the dual problem (
) under the penalty parameter
\lambda_{0}
,
where
{\bm{g}}\triangleq\nabla D({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}_{0})={\bm{y}}-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}_{0}

(see Theorem
for the general optimality condition in convex-constrained optimization).
Now consider a penalty parameter
\lambda\leq\lambda_{0}
.
Any dual point
{\boldsymbol{\nu}}
feasible for the dual problem (
) under the penalty parameter
\lambda
satisfies
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq\lambda\leq\lambda_{0}
, and is therefore also dual feasible for the dual problem (
) with parameter
\lambda_{0}
.
Since
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}
(the dual optimum for penalty
\lambda
) is feasible under
\lambda
, it is also feasible under
\lambda_{0}
.
Therefore, we define

{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}\in\Theta_{2}\triangleq\left\{{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\mid{\bm{g}}^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\nu}}-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}_{0})\geq 0\right\}.

(3.58)

Combining both conditions, the dual optimal solution must lie in the intersection of these two sets:

\Theta=\Theta_{1}\cap\Theta_{2}.

This set
\Theta
provides a tight region that provably contains
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}
, enabling safe feature elimination via the rule described earlier.

Safe Feature Elimination

The task of identifying whether the
i
-th component of the primal solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is zero—and thus safely removing the
i
-th feature (i.e., the
i
-th column
{\bm{x}}_{i}
of the design matrix
{\bm{X}}
) from the Lagrangian LASSO problem (
LL
)—reduces to verifying the condition:

\lambda>\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{\top}{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rvert=\max({\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{\top}{\bm{x}}_{i},-{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{\top}{\bm{x}}_{i})\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\in\Theta.

(3.59)

Equivalently, this can be expressed as:

\lambda>\max(S(\gamma,{\bm{x}}_{i}),S(\gamma,-{\bm{x}}_{i})),

where
S(\gamma,{\bm{x}}_{i})
denotes the optimal value of the following convex optimization problem with constraints
{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\in\Theta_{1}
and
{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\in\Theta_{2}
:

S(\gamma,{\bm{x}}_{i})\triangleq\max_{{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}\left\{{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad D({\boldsymbol{\nu}})\geq\gamma,\ {\bm{g}}^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\nu}}-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}_{0})\geq 0\right\}.

(3.60)

Remarkably, this problem admits a closed-form solution:

S(\gamma,{\bm{x}}_{i})=\begin{cases}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}_{0}{}^{\top}{\bm{x}}_{i}+A_{i}B,&\text{ if }\left\lVert{\bm{g}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}<C{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{g}};\\
{\bm{y}}^{\top}{\bm{x}}_{i}-\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}C,&\text{ if }\left\lVert{\bm{g}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}\geq C{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{g}},\end{cases}

(3.61)

where
A_{i}\triangleq(\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-{({\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{g}})^{2}}/{\left\lVert{\bm{g}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}})^{1/2}
,

B\triangleq(C^{2}-\left\lVert{\bm{g}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2})^{1/2}
, and
C\triangleq(\left\lVert{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-2\gamma)^{1/2}
.

Proof
[of (
)]
We derive the result by forming the Lagrangian dual of problem (
). Introducing nonnegative dual variables
\mu_{1}
and
\mu_{2}
for the two constraints, we obtain:

\displaystyle S(\gamma,{\bm{x}}_{i})

\displaystyle=\max_{\mu_{1},\mu_{2}\geq 0}L(\mu_{1},\mu_{2})\triangleq\max_{\mu_{1},\mu_{2}\geq 0}\min_{\boldsymbol{\nu}}{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}-\mu_{1}(D({\boldsymbol{\nu}})-\gamma)-\mu_{2}{\bm{g}}^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\nu}}-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}_{0})

\displaystyle=\max_{\mu_{1},\mu_{2}\geq 0}\left\{\{\mu_{1}\gamma+\mu_{2}{\bm{g}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}_{0}\}+\min_{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\{{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}-\mu_{1}D({\boldsymbol{\nu}})-\mu_{2}{\bm{g}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\}\right\}

\displaystyle=\max_{\mu_{1},\mu_{2}\geq 0}\left\{\{\mu_{1}\gamma+\mu_{2}{\bm{g}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}_{0}\}+\mu_{1}\min_{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\left(\frac{{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}-\mu_{1}{\bm{y}}^{\top}-\mu_{2}{\bm{g}}^{\top}}{\mu_{1}}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}+\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right)\right\}.

Therefore,

S(\gamma,{\bm{x}}_{i})=\max_{\mu_{1},\mu_{2}\geq 0}L(\mu_{1},\mu_{2}),

where by
{\bm{g}}={\bm{y}}-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}_{0}
, we have

L(\mu_{1},\mu_{2})={\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{y}}-\frac{\mu_{1}}{2}C^{2}-\frac{1}{2\mu_{1}}\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\frac{\mu_{2}^{2}}{2\mu_{1}}\left\lVert{\bm{g}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac{\mu_{2}}{\mu_{1}}{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{g}}-\mu_{2}\left\lVert{\bm{g}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},

(3.62)

and
C\triangleq(\left\lVert{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-2\gamma)^{1/2}
.
To maximize
L(\mu_{1},\mu_{2})
, we first differentiate (
) w.r.t.
\mu_{2}
and set it to zero:

-\mu_{2}\left\lVert{\bm{g}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{g}}-\mu_{1}\left\lVert{\bm{g}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=0.

Since
\mu_{2}\geq 0
, we obtain the threshold condition:
\mu_{2}=\max\{0,{{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{g}}}/{\left\lVert{\bm{g}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\mu_{1}}\}
.
This leads to two cases.
When
\mu_{1}\geq{{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{g}}}/{\left\lVert{\bm{g}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}
, we have
\mu_{2}=0
,
\mu_{1}={\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}}/{C}
, and consequently,
S(\gamma,{\bm{x}}_{i})
takes the value:

S(\gamma,{\bm{x}}_{i})={\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{y}}-\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}C.

On the other hand, when
\mu_{1}\leq{{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{g}}}/{\left\lVert{\bm{g}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}
, we have
\mu_{2}={{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{g}}}/{\left\lVert{\bm{g}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\mu_{1}}
.
Substituting this into
L(\mu_{1},\mu_{2})
and differentiating with respect to
\mu_{1}
leads to the optimality condition:

B^{2}\mu_{1}^{2}=A_{i}^{2},

where
A_{i}\triangleq(\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-{({\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{g}})^{2}}/{\left\lVert{\bm{g}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}})^{1/2}
and
B\triangleq(C^{2}-\left\lVert{\bm{g}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2})^{1/2}
. Substituting
\mu_{1}
and
\mu_{2}
in (
),
S(\gamma,{\bm{x}}_{i})
takes the value:

S(\gamma,{\bm{x}}_{i})={\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}_{0}^{\top}{\bm{x}}_{i}+A_{i}B.

The analysis above leads directly to the SAFE rule for LASSO.

{theoremHigh}
[SAFE–LASSO
(
Ghaoui et al. 2010
)
]
Consider the LASSO problem (
LL
) with penalty parameter
\lambda
. Let
\lambda_{0}\geq\lambda
be a regularization parameter for which an optimal primal solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{0}\in\real^{p}
is known. Denote by
{\bm{x}}_{i}
the
i
-th column of the design matrix
{\bm{X}}
. Define the index set

{\mathbb{I}}=\left\{i\mid\lambda>\max(S(\gamma,{\bm{x}}_{i}),S(\gamma,-{\bm{x}}_{i}))\right\},

where the function
S(\gamma,{\bm{x}}_{i})
is given by

S(\gamma,{\bm{x}}_{i})=\begin{cases}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}_{0}{}^{\top}{\bm{x}}_{i}+A_{i}B(\gamma),&\text{ if }\left\lVert{\bm{g}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}<C(\gamma){\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{g}};\\
{\bm{y}}^{\top}{\bm{x}}_{i}-\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}C(\gamma),&\text{ if }\left\lVert{\bm{g}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}\geq C(\gamma){\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{g}},\end{cases}

with

\displaystyle{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}_{0}

\displaystyle={\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{0},\quad{\bm{g}}\triangleq{\bm{y}}-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}_{0},\quad a_{0}\triangleq\left\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}_{0}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},

\displaystyle b_{0}

\displaystyle\triangleq\left\lvert{\bm{y}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}_{0}\right\rvert,\quad\gamma\triangleq-\frac{a_{0}}{2}\left(\frac{\lambda}{\lambda_{0}}\right)^{2}+b_{0}\frac{\lambda}{\lambda_{0}},

\displaystyle C(\gamma)

\displaystyle=\left(\left\lVert{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-2\gamma\right)^{1/2},\quad B(\gamma)=\left(C(\gamma)^{2}-\left\lVert{\bm{g}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right)^{1/2},\quad A_{i}\triangleq\left(\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\frac{({\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{g}})^{2}}{\left\lVert{\bm{g}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}\right)^{1/2}.

Then, for every index
i\in{\mathbb{I}}
, the corresponding entry of
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is zero:
{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}=0
.
Consequently, the feature
{\bm{x}}_{i}
can be safely eliminated from
{\bm{X}}
before solving the full LASSO problem (
LL
).

In practice, if no prior solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{0}
is available, we can initialize using the trivial solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{0}=\boldsymbol{0}
, which corresponds to the maximal regularization parameter
\lambda_{0}=\lambda_{\max}\triangleq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{\infty}
.
In this case, the SAFE test simplifies significantly. Specifically, the condition
\lambda>\max(S(\gamma,{\bm{x}}_{i}),S(\gamma,-{\bm{x}}_{i}))
reduces to
\lambda>\rho_{i}\lambda_{\max}
, where

\rho_{i}\triangleq\frac{\left\lVert{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}+\left\lvert{\bm{y}}^{\top}{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rvert}{\left\lVert{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}+\lambda_{\max}}.

(3.63)

For scaled datasets, where the response and all features are normalized such that
\left\lVert{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}=1
and
\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}=1
for every
i
, the quantity
\rho_{i}
admits a clean geometric interpretation:

\rho_{i}=\frac{1+\left\lvert\cos\alpha_{i}\right\rvert}{1+\max\limits_{1\leq j\leq p}\left\lvert\cos\alpha_{j}\right\rvert},

(3.64)

where
\alpha_{i}
denotes the angle between the
i
-th feature
{\bm{x}}_{i}
and the response vector
{\bm{y}}
.
Thus, the SAFE test eliminates features based on their relative alignment with the response—specifically, how closely they align compared to the most aligned feature. In this setting, the SAFE rule closely resembles standard correlation-based feature selection methods
(
Ghaoui et al. 2010
)
.

3.4
Optimality Condition of
\ell_{1}
-Minimization Problems

As a recap, given measurements
{\bm{y}}
and the assumption that the original signal
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is sparse or compressible, a natural approach to recover
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is to solve an optimization problem of the form

{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}=\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{0}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\mathcal{B}({\bm{y}}),

(3.65)

where
\mathcal{B}({\bm{y}})
ensures that the reconstructed signal
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is consistent with the measurements
{\bm{y}}
.
For example, if the measurements are exact and noise-free, we can define
\mathcal{B}({\bm{y}})=\{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\mid{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\bm{y}}\}
.
In the presence of small bounded noise, we might instead use
\mathcal{B}({\bm{y}})=\{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\mid\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\epsilon\}
.
In both cases, (
) seeks the sparsest solution
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
that satisfies the measurement constraints.

To make the problem more tractable, a common strategy is to replace the
\ell_{0}
-norm with its convex surrogate, the
\ell_{1}
-norm. This leads to the relaxed optimization problem:

{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}=\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\mathcal{B}({\bm{y}}).

(3.66)

Provided that
\mathcal{B}({\bm{y}})
is convex, (
) becomes a convex optimization problem and can be solved efficiently.

The use of
\ell_{1}
-minimization to promote sparsity has a long history. It dates back at least to Beurling’s work on Fourier transform extrapolation from partial observations
(
Beurling 1938
)
. In a different context,
Logan 1965
showed in 1965 that a bandlimited signal can be perfectly recovered even when corrupted on a small interval (with later extensions provided by
Donoho and Logan 1992
). His method involved finding the bandlimited signal closest to the observed data in the
\ell_{1}
-norm—further supporting the intuition that
\ell_{1}
is well-suited for handling sparse errors.

Thus, there are multiple compelling reasons to expect that
\ell_{1}
-minimization yields accurate solutions for sparse signal recovery. Moreover, it provides a computationally efficient alternative to the intractable
\ell_{0}
-minimization problem. In this section, we present an optimality analysis of
\ell_{1}
-minimization, followed by a later discussion of algorithms for solving it in Chapter
.

3.4.1
Necessary and Sufficient Condition

Specifically, we now consider the
system
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
and the
\ell_{1}
-minimization problem (
) (p.
):

(\text{P}_{1})\quad\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\bm{y}}.

(3.67)

A vector
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is a solution to (
) if and only if:

\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}+{\bm{n}}\big\rVert_{1}\geq\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1},\quad\forall\,{\bm{n}}\in\real^{p}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\bm{n}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})\quad\text{and}\quad{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}},

where
{\bm{n}}
is in the nullspace of
{\bm{X}}
, i.e.,
{\bm{X}}{\bm{n}}=\boldsymbol{0}
.
Given that
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is supported on
{\mathbb{S}}\triangleq\mathrm{supp}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})=\{i\mid{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}\neq 0\}
and the inequality
\big\lvert{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}+n_{i}\big\rvert\geq\big\lvert{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}\big\rvert+\mathrm{sign}({\widehat{\beta}}_{i})n_{i}
, we have

\left\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}+{\bm{n}}\right\rVert_{1}=\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}}\left\lvert{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}+n_{i}\right\rvert+\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\left\lvert n_{i}\right\rvert\geq\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}}\left\lvert{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}\right\rvert+\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}}\mathrm{sign}({\widehat{\beta}}_{i})n_{i}+\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\left\lvert n_{i}\right\rvert.

This analysis indicates the necessary and sufficient condition for (
).

{theoremHigh}
[Necessary and sufficient condition for (
)]
Consider the optimization problem (
).
Then,
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is a solution of (
) if and only if, for all
{\bm{n}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
, it follows that

\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}}\mathrm{sign}({\widehat{\beta}}_{i})n_{i}\leq\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\left\lvert n_{i}\right\rvert,

where
{\mathbb{S}}\triangleq\mathrm{supp}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})=\{i\mid{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}\neq 0,\,i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}\}
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]

Necessity.

Suppose
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is a solution of (
).
Choose
\gamma>0
sufficiently small so that the sign of each nonzero component
{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}
is preserved in
{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}-\gamma n_{i}
.
Then for
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
,

\left\lvert{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}-\gamma n_{i}\right\rvert=\begin{cases}{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}-\gamma n_{i}={\widehat{\beta}}_{i}-\gamma\mathrm{sign}({\widehat{\beta}}_{i})n_{i},&\text{if }{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}>0;\\
-({\widehat{\beta}}_{i}-\gamma n_{i})=-{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}-\gamma\mathrm{sign}({\widehat{\beta}}_{i})n_{i},&\text{if }{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}<0;\\
\gamma\left\lvert n_{i}\right\rvert,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}\qquad\forall\,i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}.

Now assume, for contradiction, that there exists
{\bm{n}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
such that
\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}}\mathrm{sign}({\widehat{\beta}}_{i})n_{i}>\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\left\lvert n_{i}\right\rvert
.
This implies

\left\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-\gamma{\bm{n}}\right\rVert_{1}=\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}-\gamma\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}}\mathrm{sign}({\widehat{\beta}}_{i})n_{i}+\gamma\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\left\lvert n_{i}\right\rvert<\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1},

leading to a contradiction. Hence, the stated inequality must hold.

Sufficiency.

Suppose that there exists another feasible point
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}
such that
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}={\bm{y}}
and
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}\right\rVert_{1}<\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}
.
Define
{\bm{n}}\triangleq{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}
, which satisfies
{\bm{X}}{\bm{n}}=\boldsymbol{0}
since
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}={\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
. This means
{\bm{n}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
.
Using the identity
\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}\big\rVert_{1}=\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\bm{n}}\big\rVert_{1}
, we analyze:

\displaystyle\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}\big\rVert_{1}=\left\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\bm{n}}\right\rVert_{1}

\displaystyle=\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}}\left\lvert{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}-n_{i}\right\rvert+\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\left\lvert n_{i}\right\rvert

\displaystyle\geq\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}}\big\lvert{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}\big\rvert-\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}}\mathrm{sign}({\widehat{\beta}}_{i})n_{i}+\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\left\lvert n_{i}\right\rvert\geq\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}}\left\lvert{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}\right\rvert=\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1},

where the first inequality follows from the fact that
\big\lvert{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}-n_{i}\big\rvert\geq\big\lvert{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}\big\rvert-\mathrm{sign}({\widehat{\beta}}_{i})n_{i}
,
and the second inequality follows from the given condition that
\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}}\mathrm{sign}({\widehat{\beta}}_{i})n_{i}\leq\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\left\lvert n_{i}\right\rvert
.
Since the assumption was
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}\right\rVert_{1}<\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}
, we obtain a contradiction.
This completes the proof.

3.4.2
Dual Certificate and Uniqueness

We introduced the dual of the
\ell_{\infty}
-minimization problem in Example
.
Let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
.
The dual of the optimization problem of

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{\infty}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\bm{y}}

(3.68a)

is

\max_{{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n}}\left\langle{\bm{y}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rangle\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq 1.

(3.68b)

The dual of the
\ell_{1}
-minimization problem can be derived analogously.

Proposition 135
(Dual of
\ell_{1}
-minimization).

Let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
.
The dual of the optimization problem (
)

(\text{P}_{1})\quad\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\bm{y}}

(3.69a)

is

\max_{{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n}}D({\boldsymbol{\lambda}})=\begin{cases}\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\bm{y}}\right\rangle,&\text{if }\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq 1;\\
-\infty,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

(3.69b)

Clearly, it is enough to maximize over the points
{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}
for which
D({\boldsymbol{\lambda}})>-\infty
. Making this constraint explicit, the dual program to (
) is given by

\max_{{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n}}\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\bm{y}}\right\rangle\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\big\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\big\rVert_{\infty}\leq 1.

(3.69c)

Proof
[of Proposition
]
The Lagrangian associated with (
) is

L({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}+\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle.

The Lagrange dual function is therefore

D({\boldsymbol{\lambda}})\triangleq\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}-\left\langle{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle+\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\bm{y}}\right\rangle.

If
({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})_{i}>1
, then one can set
\beta_{i}
arbitrarily large so that
D({\boldsymbol{\lambda}})\to-\infty
. The same happens if
({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})_{i}<-1
. If
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq 1
, by Hölder’s inequality (Theorem
)

\displaystyle\left\lvert({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rvert\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\cdot\big\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\big\rVert_{\infty}\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1},

so the Lagrangian is minimized by setting
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
to zero and
D({\boldsymbol{\lambda}})=\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\bm{y}}\right\rangle
. This completes the proof.

By Theorem
, strong duality holds for this pair of primal and dual optimization problems provided the primal problem (
) is feasible.

Interestingly, the solution to the dual problem of the
\ell_{1}
-minimization problem often provides valuable information about the support of the primal optimal solution.
Let the primal optimal solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
be supported on

{\mathbb{S}}\triangleq\mathrm{supp}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})=\{i\mid{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}\neq 0\}.

Note that
{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}={\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
, where
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\triangleq{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}[{\mathbb{S}}]\in\real^{\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert}
denotes a subvector of
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
indexed by
{\mathbb{S}}
, and
{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\triangleq{\bm{X}}[:,{\mathbb{S}}]\in\real^{n\times\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert}
denotes a submatrix of
{\bm{X}}
consisting of the columns indexed by
{\mathbb{S}}
.

Lemma 136
(Support of primal optimum using dual optimum).

Suppose the primal problem (
) is feasible.
Let
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}}
be an optimal solution to the dual problem (
). Then, for every primal optimal solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
,

({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}})_{i}=\mathrm{sign}({\widehat{\beta}}_{i}),\quad\text{for all }{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}\neq 0\ (\text{i.e., }i\in{\mathbb{S}}).

(3.70)

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Feasibility of the primal implies strong duality (by Theorem
). Hence,

\displaystyle\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}

\displaystyle={\bm{y}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}}=({\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}}=({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})^{\top}({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}})=\sum_{i=1}^{p}({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}})_{i}{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}.

On the other hand, by‘ Hölder’s inequality, we have

\sum_{i=1}^{p}({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}})_{i}{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}\leq\big\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}}\big\rVert_{\infty}\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}\leq\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1},

with equality if and only if

({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}})_{i}=\mathrm{sign}({\widehat{\beta}}_{i})
,
\text{for all }{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}\neq 0.

This completes the proof.

In the study of sparse recovery or
\ell_{1}
-regularized optimization, a central question is whether an optimal solution to the
\ell_{1}
-minimization problem (
) is
unique
.
While existence of solutions is guaranteed under mild conditions due to convexity, uniqueness often hinges on additional structural assumptions—particularly those related to the geometry of the data matrix
{\bm{X}}
and the support of the solution.
The previous analysis established necessary optimality conditions, revealing that the optimal solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}

satisfies certain sign and dual feasibility conditions involving the Lagrange multipliers. In particular, the vector
{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}
plays a crucial role in characterizing the support and sparsity pattern of
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
. Building upon these insights, we now turn to the important question: under what conditions is this optimal solution uniquely determined? This leads us to the following key result, which provides sufficient conditions for the uniqueness of the solution to the
\ell_{1}
-minimization problem (
) based on the properties of the
dual certificate
and sheds lights on the
restricted isometry property (RIP)
of the design matrix (Chapters
and
).

Consider a certain sparse vector
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\in\real^{p}
with support
{\mathbb{S}}
such that
{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}={\bm{y}}
. If there exists a vector
{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n}
such that
{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}
is equal to the sign of
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
on
{\mathbb{S}}
and has magnitude smaller than one elsewhere, then
{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}
is feasible for the dual problem (
), so by weak duality,
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\geq{\bm{y}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}
for any
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
that is feasible for the primal problem (
).
By Lemma
, we then have

\displaystyle\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}

\displaystyle\geq{\bm{y}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}=({\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}=({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})^{\top}({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})=\sum_{i=1}^{p}{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}\,\mathrm{sign}({\widehat{\beta}}_{i})=\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}.

(3.71)

Since
({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})_{i}=\mathrm{sign}({\widehat{\beta}}_{i})
for all
{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}\neq 0
, geometrically,
{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}
is a subgradient of the
\ell_{1}
-norm at
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
. The subgradient is
orthogonal
to the feasibility hyperplane given by
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\bm{y}}
(any vector
{\bm{n}}
within the hyperplane is the difference between two feasible vectors and therefore satisfies
{\bm{X}}{\bm{n}}=\boldsymbol{0}
). As a result, for any other feasible vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}

\displaystyle\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\geq\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}+({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})=\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}+{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{\top}({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})=\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1},

(3.72)

where the first inequality follows from the subgradient inequality (Definition
).

Alternatively,
we have discussed the KKT conditions of convex optimization problems with equality constraints in Remark
, which is a result of Slater’s condition for convex optimization problems and the KKT conditions under strong duality (Theorems
and
).
Since
f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}
is convex, Remark
and Equation (
) show that

{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is an optimal solution if
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is feasible and there exists
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}={\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}
, where
{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n}
denotes the Lagrangian multipliers (i.e.,
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
lies in the row space of
{\bm{X}}
, and
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\perp\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
) with

\begin{cases}\alpha_{i}=\mathrm{sign}({\widehat{\beta}}_{i}),&{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}\neq 0\ (\text{i.e., }i\in{\mathbb{S}});\\
\left\lvert\alpha_{i}\right\rvert\leq 1,&{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}=0\ (\text{i.e., }i\in{\mathbb{S}}^{c}),\end{cases}

(3.73)

where
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is supported on
{\mathbb{S}}\triangleq\mathrm{supp}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})=\{i\mid{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}\neq 0\}
.

These two arguments show that the existence of a certain dual vector can be used to verify that a given primal feasible vector is optimal, but they do not guarantee uniqueness.
It turns out that requiring the magnitude of
{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}
to be strictly smaller than one on
{\mathbb{S}}^{c}
is enough to guarantee it (as long as
{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
has full rank). In that case, we call the dual variable
{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}
a
dual certificate
for the
\ell_{1}
-minimization problem.

{theoremHigh}

[Dual certificate for (
)]
Consider the
\ell_{1}
-minimization problem (
).
Let
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
be an optimal solution of (
) such that
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}={\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}
satisfies the following conditions:
Suppose further that

1.

\alpha_{i}=({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})_{i}=\mathrm{sign}({\widehat{\beta}}_{i})
, when
{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}\neq 0
for all
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
.

2.

\left\lvert\alpha_{i}\right\rvert=\big\lvert({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})_{i}\big\rvert<1
, when
{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}=0
for all
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
.

3.

{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
has full column rank , where
{\mathbb{S}}\triangleq\mathrm{supp}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})=\{i\mid{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}\neq 0\}
.

Then
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is the
unique
solution of (
).
Any such
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
or
{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}
satisfying (i)–(iii) is called a dual certificate.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Let
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
be any feasible point, and define
{\bm{n}}\triangleq{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
.
Since
{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
is full-rank, we have
{\bm{n}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\neq\boldsymbol{0}
unless
{\bm{n}}=\boldsymbol{0}
, because otherwise
{\bm{n}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
would be a nonzero vector in the null space of
{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
.
Condition (ii) implies

\left\lVert{\bm{n}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}>{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{\top}{\bm{n}}({\mathbb{S}}^{c}),

where
{\bm{n}}({\mathbb{S}}^{c})\in\real^{p}
a projection that sets to zero all entries of a vector except the ones indexed by
{\mathbb{S}}^{c}
(see Definition
).
Using the fact that
\big\lvert{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}+n_{i}\big\rvert\geq\big\lvert{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}\big\rvert+\mathrm{sign}({\widehat{\beta}}_{i})n_{i}

and that
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is supported on
{\mathbb{S}}
, the above inequality implies

\displaystyle\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}

\displaystyle=\left\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}+{\bm{n}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}+\left\lVert{\bm{n}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}>\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}+{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{\top}{\bm{n}}({\mathbb{S}})+{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{\top}{\bm{n}}({\mathbb{S}}^{c})=\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}+{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}{\bm{n}}=\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}.

On the other hand, if
{\bm{n}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}=\boldsymbol{0}
, then since
{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
has full column rank,

{\bm{X}}{\bm{n}}={\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}{\bm{n}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}=\boldsymbol{0}\quad\implies\quad{\bm{n}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}=\boldsymbol{0}\quad\implies\quad{\bm{n}}=\boldsymbol{0}.

Therefore, for any
{\bm{n}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
,
\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}+{\bm{n}}\big\rVert_{1}>\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}
unless
{\bm{n}}=\boldsymbol{0}
.
This completes the proof.

Note that ideally we would like to analyze the vector
{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}
satisfying this underdetermined system of
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert
equations such that
{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}
has the smallest possible
\ell_{\infty}
-norm. Unfortunately, the solution to the optimization problem

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rVert_{\infty}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}=\sign({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{S}})

(3.74)

does not have a closed-form solution. However, the related least squares problem

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rVert_{2}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}=\sign({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{S}})

(3.75)

does have an explicit solution, so we can analyze it instead. Note that since
{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
has full column rank (
{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
invertible), the solution is

{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}={\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}({\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}})^{-1}\sign({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{S}})\qquad\text{and}\qquad{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\triangleq{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},

(3.76)

which is a high-dimensional LS problem (Corollary
) of the form
{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}=\sign({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{S}})
.
Therefore,

if
\left\lvert\alpha_{i}\right\rvert\leq 1
for all
i\in{\mathbb{S}}^{c}
, then
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is a solution;

if
\left\lvert\alpha_{i}\right\rvert<1
for all
i\in{\mathbb{S}}^{c}
, then
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is the unique solution.

For a given coefficient vector
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\in\real^{p}
, the conditions in Theorem
can be restated as follows:
The index sets
{\mathbb{S}}\triangleq\mathrm{supp}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})
and
{\mathbb{T}}\triangleq{\mathbb{S}}^{c}
satisfy:

1.

\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}}({\mathbb{S}}))=\{\boldsymbol{0}\}
: this guarantees that the linear system
{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}={\bm{y}}
has a unique solution.

2.

There exists a vector
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}
such that
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}^{\top})
,
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}=\mathrm{sign}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{{\mathbb{S}}})
, and
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{\mathbb{T}}\right\rVert_{\infty}<1
: this ensures that any optimal solution must satisfy
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{T}}=\boldsymbol{0}
.

In fact, the
restricted isometry property (RIP)
guarantees that such conditions hold for all sufficiently small supports
{\mathbb{S}}
and for arbitrary sign patterns; see Definition
and Section
for further details.

The argument in Theorem
can thus be naturally split into two parts.

\paragrapharrow

Condition (i)
\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}}({\mathbb{S}}))=\{\boldsymbol{0}\}
is necessary for the uniqueness.

If
\boldsymbol{0}\neq{\bm{n}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}}({\mathbb{S}}))\in\real^{p}
,
then all
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\eta}\triangleq{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}+\eta\widetilde{\bm{n}}
for any scalar
\eta
is also optimal, where
\widetilde{\bm{n}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}={\bm{n}}_{\mathbb{S}}
and
\widetilde{\bm{n}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}=\boldsymbol{0}
.
To see this, we have that
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\eta}
is feasible since
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\eta}={\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}={\bm{y}}
.
Since
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is the unique minimizer, we have
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\eta}\right\rVert_{1}>\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}
.
But for small
\eta
around 0, namely
\left\lvert\eta\right\rvert<\min_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}}\big\lvert{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}\big\rvert/\left\lVert{\bm{n}}\right\rVert_{\infty}
, it follows that
\mathrm{sign}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}+\eta\widetilde{\bm{n}})=\mathrm{sign}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})
, whence we have

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\eta}\right\rVert_{1}=\left\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}+\eta{\bm{n}}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{1}=\left\langle\mathrm{sign}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}),({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}+\eta{\bm{n}}_{\mathbb{S}})\right\rangle=\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}+\left\langle\mathrm{sign}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}),\eta{\bm{n}}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rangle.

This is a contradiction, because we can always choose a small
\eta\neq 0
such that
\big\langle\mathrm{sign}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}),\eta{\bm{n}}_{\mathbb{S}}\big\rangle<0
.
Therefore,
{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
must have full column rank.

\paragrapharrow

Condition (ii) guarantees that
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{T}}=\boldsymbol{0}
.
To see this, we introduce the following optimization problem:

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{\mathbb{T}}\right\rVert_{\infty}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}^{\top}),\;{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}=\mathrm{sign}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}).

(3.77)

If the optimal objective value is strictly less than
1
, then there exists
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
obeying Condition (ii), so Condition (ii) is also necessary.

Let
{\bm{v}}\in\real^{p}
with
{\bm{v}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}=\mathrm{sign}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{{\mathbb{S}}})
and
{\bm{v}}_{{\mathbb{T}}}=\boldsymbol{0}
, and let
{\bm{Q}}\in\real^{p\times r}
contains the mutually orthonormal basis of
\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
.
If
{\bm{v}}\in\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}^{\top})
, set
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\triangleq{\bm{v}}
, and the proof is complete.
Otherwise, let
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\triangleq{\bm{v}}+{\bm{u}}
for some
{\bm{u}}\in\real^{p}
. Then the following problems are equivalent

{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}^{\top})\quad\iff\quad{\bm{Q}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=\boldsymbol{0}\quad\iff\quad{\bm{Q}}^{\top}{\bm{u}}=-{\bm{Q}}^{\top}{\bm{v}},

where
{\bm{u}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}=\boldsymbol{0}
since
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}=\mathrm{sign}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{{\mathbb{S}}})={\bm{v}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
. Since
{\bm{v}}_{\mathbb{T}}=\boldsymbol{0}
, we also have
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{\mathbb{T}}\right\rVert_{\infty}=\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{\mathbb{T}}\right\rVert_{\infty}
.
We can therefore translate (
) and rewrite
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}^{\top})
as the following equivalent problem:

\min_{{\bm{u}}\in\real^{p}}\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{\mathbb{T}}\right\rVert_{\infty}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\bm{Q}}^{\top}{\bm{u}}=-{\bm{Q}}^{\top}{\bm{v}},\;{\bm{u}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}=\boldsymbol{0}.

(3.78)

If the optimal objective value is strictly less than
1
, then Condition (ii) is necessary.

Problem (
) is feasible and has a finite objective value. The dual of (
) is

\max_{{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}\in\real^{p}}\,({\bm{Q}}^{\top}{\bm{v}})^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\left\lVert({\bm{Q}}{\boldsymbol{\gamma}})_{\mathbb{T}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq 1.

(3.79)

By assumption, the strong duality of problem (
) holds.
Then if the optimal objective value of (
) is strictly less than
1
, Condition (ii) is necessary.

Lemma 137
.

Suppose
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is unique with support
{\mathbb{S}}\triangleq\mathrm{supp}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})
and let
{\mathbb{T}}\triangleq{\mathbb{S}}^{c}
.
Then the optimal objective of the following primal-dual problems is strictly less than 1:

\displaystyle\min_{{\bm{u}}}\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{{\mathbb{T}}}\right\rVert_{\infty}\quad

\displaystyle\text{s.t.}\quad{\bm{Q}}^{\top}{\bm{u}}=-{\bm{Q}}^{\top}{\bm{v}},\;{\bm{u}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}=\boldsymbol{0};

\displaystyle\max_{{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}}\,({\bm{Q}}^{\top}{\bm{v}})^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}\quad

\displaystyle\text{s.t.}\quad\left\lVert({\bm{Q}}{\boldsymbol{\gamma}})_{\mathbb{T}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq 1.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Since
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is the unique solution of the
\ell_{1}
-minimization problem (
),

\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}<\left\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}+{\bm{n}}\right\rVert_{1}=\left\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}+{\bm{n}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}+\left\lVert{\bm{n}}_{\mathbb{T}}\right\rVert_{1},\quad\forall\,{\bm{n}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})\setminus\{\boldsymbol{0}\}.

Similar to the argument in the proof of Theorem
,
this shows
\left\langle{\bm{v}}_{\mathbb{S}},{\bm{n}}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rangle<\left\lVert{\bm{n}}_{\mathbb{T}}\right\rVert_{1}
.
Therefore,

if
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}}=\boldsymbol{0}
, then
\left\lVert\widehat{\bm{u}}_{\mathbb{T}}\right\rVert_{\infty}=({\bm{Q}}^{\top}{\bm{v}})^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}}=\boldsymbol{0}
.

if
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}}\neq\boldsymbol{0}
, then
{\bm{n}}\triangleq{\bm{Q}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})\setminus\{\boldsymbol{0}\}
satisfies

\left\lVert\widehat{\bm{u}}_{\mathbb{T}}\right\rVert_{\infty}=({\bm{Q}}^{\top}{\bm{v}})^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}}=\left\langle{\bm{v}}_{\mathbb{S}},{\bm{n}}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rangle<\left\lVert{\bm{n}}_{\mathbb{T}}\right\rVert_{1}=\left\lVert({\bm{Q}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}})_{\mathbb{T}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq 1.

In both cases, the optimal objective value is strictly less than
1
.

3.4.3
\ell_{1}
-Minimization with Noise Measurements

We now consider the case where the observations are contaminated by noise; that is,
{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}
.
In this setting, we employ the following two robust variants of the
\ell_{1}
-minimization problem, i.e., (
) and (
) (p.
and
):

(P
1,σ
)

\displaystyle\min\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}+\sigma\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2};

(3.80a)

(P
1,ϵ
)

\displaystyle\min\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\epsilon.

(3.80b)

As shown in Corollary
, problems (
) and (
) are equivalent in the sense that, for appropriate choices of
\sigma
and
\epsilon
, they share the same set of solutions.
The following lemma establishes a stronger property: both the residual norm and the
\ell_{1}
-norm are constant over the entire solution set of each problem.

Lemma 138
(Constants over the set of solutions in (
) and (
)).

Let
\sigma>0
.
Suppose the function
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}+\sigma\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
is constant on a convex set
{\mathbb{C}}
.
Then both
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}
and
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}
are constants on
{\mathbb{C}}
.

Let
{\mathbb{Q}}_{\sigma}
denote the set of solutions to problem (
).
Since
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}+\sigma\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
is constant over
{\mathbb{Q}}_{\sigma}
, the above result shows that
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}
and
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}
are constants on
{\mathbb{Q}}_{\sigma}
in problem (
).

Moreover, let
{\mathbb{Q}}_{\epsilon}
denote the set of solutions to problem (
). Then both
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}
and
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}
are constant on
{\mathbb{Q}}_{\epsilon}

Proof
[of Lemma
]
It suffices to consider the case where the convex set contains more than one point.
Let
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}\in{\mathbb{C}}
with
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1}\neq{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}
.
Consider the line segment
{\mathbb{L}}
connecting
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1}
and
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}
.
By convexity of
{\mathbb{C}}
, we know
{\mathbb{L}}\subset{\mathbb{C}}
. Thus,
c\triangleq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}+\sigma\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
is a constant on
{\mathbb{L}}
.
Suppose
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1}-{\bm{y}}\neq{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}-{\bm{y}}
. Then for any
0<\lambda<1
, we have

\displaystyle\sigma\left\lVert{\bm{X}}(\lambda{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1}+(1-\lambda){\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2})-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\big\lVert(\lambda{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1}+(1-\lambda){\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2})\big\rVert_{1}

\displaystyle=\sigma\left\lVert\lambda({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1}-{\bm{y}})+(1-\lambda)({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}-{\bm{y}})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\big\lVert\lambda({\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1})+(1-\lambda)({\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2})\big\rVert_{1}

\displaystyle<\lambda\left(\sigma\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1}\big\rVert_{1}\right)+(1-\lambda)\left(\sigma\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}\big\rVert_{1}\right)

\displaystyle=\lambda c+(1-\lambda)c=c,

where the strict inequality follows from the strict convexity of
\sigma\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
and the convexity of
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}
. This means that the points
\lambda{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1}+(1-\lambda){\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}
on
{\mathbb{L}}
attain a lower value than
c
, which leads to a contradiction. Therefore, we have
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1}-{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}-{\bm{y}}
, which in turn implies that
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1}\right\rVert_{1}=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}\right\rVert_{1}
.

For problem (
), if
\boldsymbol{0}\in{\mathbb{Q}}_{\epsilon}
, then we have
{\mathbb{Q}}_{\epsilon}=\{\boldsymbol{0}\}
, and the claim holds trivially.
Otherwise, suppose
\boldsymbol{0}\not\in{\mathbb{Q}}_{\epsilon}
.
Since the optimal objective
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}
is constant for all
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{Q}}_{\epsilon}
, it remains to show that
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}=\epsilon
for all
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{Q}}_{\epsilon}
.
Suppose on the contrary that there exists a nonzero
{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\in{\mathbb{Q}}_{\epsilon}
such that
\big\lVert{\bm{X}}{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\bm{y}}\big\rVert_{2}<\epsilon
, we can find a non-empty ball
{\mathbb{T}}
centered at
{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
with a sufficiently small radius
r>0
such that
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}<\epsilon
for all
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{T}}
.
Let
\gamma\triangleq\min\left(\frac{r}{2\left\lVert{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\right\rVert_{2}},\frac{1}{2}\right)
.
We have
(1-\gamma){\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\in{\mathbb{T}}
such that
(1-\gamma){\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
satisfies the constraint in problem (
), implying
\big\lVert(1-\gamma){\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}<\big\lVert{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}
, which leads to a contradiction and concludes the result.

Using Lemma
, we can establish a dual certificate for the two robust models under the same conditions as in Theorem
for the noiseless problem (
