{theoremHigh}
[Dual certificate for (
) and (
)]
Suppose
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is a solution to either (

{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is the unique solution if and only if the same condition stated in Theorem
holds for
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Since the results of Lemma
are identical for problems (
) and (
), we present the proof for problem (
) only.

By assumption, the solution set
{\mathbb{Q}}_{\sigma}
of (
) is nonempty, so we pick
{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\in{\mathbb{Q}}_{\sigma}
. Let
\widetilde{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
, which is independent of the choice of
{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
according to Lemma
.
Now consider the following noiseless
\ell_{1}
-minimization problem:

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\widetilde{\bm{y}},

(3.81)

and let
{\mathbb{Q}}_{q}
denote its solution set.

Now, we show that
{\mathbb{Q}}_{\sigma}={\mathbb{Q}}_{q}
. Since
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\bm{X}}{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
and
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}=\big\lVert{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}
for all
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{Q}}_{\sigma}

and conversely any point
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
obeying

and

for any

.
Assuming this does not hold, then since problem (

{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
as a feasible solution and has a finite objective, we have a nonempty

and there exists

satisfying

.
However,

and

mean that

is a strictly better solution to problem (

{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
, contradicting the assumption
{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\in{\mathbb{Q}}_{\sigma}
.
Thus,
{\mathbb{Q}}_{\sigma}={\mathbb{Q}}_{q}
.

Since
{\mathbb{Q}}_{\sigma}={\mathbb{Q}}_{q}
,
{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is the unique solution to problem (
) if and only if it is the unique solution to problem (
). Since problem (

for problem (
), we conclude that
{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is the unique solution to problem (

holds.

{theoremHigh}

[Error bound of (
) under measurement noise]
Let
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
be the original signal satisfying
{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}+{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}
with
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\epsilon
. And let
\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
be a solution to the problem (

\text{(P${}_{1,\epsilon}$)}\qquad\min\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\epsilon.

Define the support of the true signal as
{\mathbb{S}}\triangleq\mathrm{supp}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})
and its complement as
{\mathbb{T}}\triangleq{\mathbb{S}}^{c}
.
Then the reconstruction error satisfies

\big\lVert\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\big\rVert_{1}\leq C_{3}\epsilon+C_{4}\big\lVert\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{T}}\big\rVert_{1},

where
C_{3}\triangleq 2\sqrt{\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert}\cdot\mathcal{U}({\mathbb{S}})
,
C_{4}\triangleq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}\sqrt{\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert}\cdot\mathcal{U}({\mathbb{S}})+1
, and

\mathcal{U}({\mathbb{S}})\triangleq\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathrm{supp}({\bm{u}})={\mathbb{S}},\\
{\bm{u}}\neq\boldsymbol{0}\end{subarray}}\frac{\left\lVert{\bm{u}}\right\rVert_{2}}{\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\bm{u}}\right\rVert_{2}}.\penalty\

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Observe that
\big\lVert\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\big\rVert_{1}=\big\lVert\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{S}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}_{\mathbb{S}}\big\rVert_{1}+\big\lVert\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{T}}\big\rVert_{1}
, where the first term satisfies

\left\lVert\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{S}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\sqrt{\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert}\cdot\left\lVert\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{S}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\sqrt{\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert}\cdot\mathcal{U}({\mathbb{S}})\cdot\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}(\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{S}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}_{\mathbb{S}})\right\rVert_{2},

where the first inequality follows from standard bounds on vector norms (Exercise
), and the last inequality follows from the definition of
\mathcal{U}({\mathbb{S}})
.
Let
{\bm{d}}\in\real^{p}
such that
{\bm{d}}_{\mathbb{S}}=\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{S}}
and
{\bm{d}}_{\mathbb{T}}=\boldsymbol{0}
, that is
\mathrm{supp}({\bm{d}})={\mathbb{S}}
.
Therefore, by the triangle inequality,

\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}(\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{S}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}_{\mathbb{S}})\right\rVert_{2}=\left\lVert{\bm{X}}({\bm{d}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})\right\rVert_{2}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}({\bm{d}}-\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})\right\rVert_{2}+{\big\lVert{\bm{X}}(\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})\big\rVert_{2}}.

Since both
\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
and
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
are feasible, we have
{\big\lVert{\bm{X}}(\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})\big\rVert_{2}}\leq 2\epsilon
.
The definition of the spectral norm and standard bounds on vector norms (Exercise
) also show that

\left\lVert{\bm{X}}({\bm{d}}-\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})\right\rVert_{2}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\bm{d}}-\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\bm{d}}-\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\right\rVert_{1}=\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}\big\lVert\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{T}}\big\rVert_{1}

Combining the results shows

\left\lVert\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{S}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\sqrt{\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert}\cdot\mathcal{U}({\mathbb{S}})\cdot(\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}\big\lVert\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{T}}\big\rVert_{1}+2\epsilon).

This concludes the result after rearrangement.

Suppose
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
and
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
satisfy the same condition as Theorem
.
The vector then
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}={\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}
satisfies

{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{\mathbb{S}}=\mathrm{sign}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{*})\qquad\text{and}\qquad\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{\mathbb{T}}\right\rVert_{\infty}<1,

where
{\mathbb{S}}=\mathrm{supp}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})
and
{\mathbb{T}}={\mathbb{S}}^{c}
.
Let
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
be a solution of (
). Then

\displaystyle\big\lVert\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{S}}\big\rVert_{1}

\displaystyle\geq\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{\mathbb{S}},\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rangle;

\displaystyle\big\lVert\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{T}}\big\rVert_{1}

\displaystyle\leq(1-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{\mathbb{T}}\right\rVert_{\infty})^{-1}\left(\big\lVert\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{T}}\big\rVert_{1}-\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{\mathbb{T}},\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{T}}\right\rangle\right),

where the second inequality follows from the triangle inequality

\big\lVert\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{T}}\big\rVert_{1}-\big\lVert\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{T}}\big\rVert_{1}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{\mathbb{T}}\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq\big(\big\lVert\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{T}}\big\rVert_{1}-\big\langle{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{\mathbb{T}},\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{T}}\big\rangle\big)
.
Therefore,

\big\lVert\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{T}}\big\rVert_{1}\leq(1-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{\mathbb{T}}\right\rVert_{\infty})^{-1}\left(\big\lVert\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}-\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\right\rangle\right)\triangleq(1-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{\mathbb{T}}\right\rVert_{\infty})^{-1}D_{1}^{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}(\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}),

where

D_{1}^{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}(\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})\triangleq\big\lVert\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{1}-\big\langle{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\big\rangle

is the Bregman distance associated with

(see Definition

{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\partial\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{1}

Since

using the optimality of

shows

\displaystyle D_{1}^{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}(\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})

\displaystyle\triangleq\big\lVert\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{1}-\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rangle

\displaystyle\leq 0+\left\langle{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\right\rangle\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})\right\rVert_{2}\leq 2\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rVert_{2}\epsilon.

Therefore, we can bound the optimal solution in the complement set by

\big\lVert\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{T}}\big\rVert_{1}\leq 2(1-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{\mathbb{T}}\right\rVert_{\infty})^{-1}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rVert_{2}\epsilon.

The above analysis shows the following corollary from Theorem

Corollary 139

3.5
Optimality Condition of

We now consider the following

\displaystyle(Q_{1})\qquad

\displaystyle\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1},\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\bm{y}};

(3.83a)

\displaystyle(Q_{1,\sigma})\qquad

\displaystyle\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}+\sigma\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2};

(3.83b)

\displaystyle(Q_{1,\epsilon})\qquad

\displaystyle\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1},\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\epsilon,

(3.83c)

where
\epsilon,\sigma
are positive parameters,
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
,
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
, and
{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}\in\real^{p\times q}
.
Problem (
3.83a
) is appropriate when the observations are noise-free, i.e.,
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}={\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}=\boldsymbol{0}
. If
{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}={\bm{I}}
, the identity matrix, these models reduce to the standard
\ell_{1}
-synthesis models (i.e., (

, and (

).
We focus on the high-dimensional regime
n\leq p
(see Lemma

for justification).

For certificates of these models, we consider the following condition.

Condition
\thetheo

Let
{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}\in\real^{q\times p}
and
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
.
Given
{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}}\in\real^{p}
, index set
{\mathbb{S}}=\mathrm{supp}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}})\subset\{1,2,\ldots,q\}
and
{\mathbb{T}}\triangleq{\mathbb{S}}^{c}
satisfy

1.

\mathcal{N}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}({\mathbb{T}})^{\top})\cap\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})=\{\boldsymbol{0}\}
;

2.

There exists
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{q}
such that
{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}^{\top})
,
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{\mathbb{S}}=\mathrm{sign}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}})
, and
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{T}}}\right\rVert_{\infty}<1
.

This condition is a natural extension of the dual certificate condition in Theorem
for the classical
\ell_{1}
-minimization problem (
).
Note again that
{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}({\mathbb{T}})\in\real^{q\times p}
and
{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{{\mathbb{T}}}={\boldsymbol{\Psi}}[:,{\mathbb{T}}]\in\real^{n\times\left\lvert{\mathbb{T}}\right\rvert}
; see Definition
.
When
{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}={\bm{I}}_{p}
,
\mathcal{N}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}({\mathbb{T}})^{\top})=\{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}\mid\beta_{i}=0\text{ for all }i\in{\mathbb{T}}\}
. Then Condition
(i) reduces to requiring that
{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
has full column rank, exactly as in Theorem
.

More generally, Condition
(i) ensures that there is no nonzero perturbation
\Delta{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
satisfying both
{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}({\mathbb{T}})^{\top}{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}}={\boldsymbol{\Psi}}({\mathbb{T}})^{\top}({{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}}+\Delta{\boldsymbol{\beta}})
and
{\bm{X}}{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}}={\bm{X}}({{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}}+\Delta{\boldsymbol{\beta}})
. Otherwise, there exists a nonempty interval
{\mathbb{M}}=[{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}}-\gamma\Delta{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}}+\gamma\Delta{\boldsymbol{\beta}}]
for some sufficiently small
\gamma>0
so that
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\bm{X}}{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}}
and
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}
is constant for
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{M}}
;
consequently,
{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}}
could not be the unique minimizer.

Condition
(ii) asserts the existence of a strictly complementary
dual certificate

{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
.
To see this, recall the optimality condition for problem (
Q1
):
\boldsymbol{0}\in{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}\partial\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}-{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}
, where
{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}
is the vector of Lagrangian multipliers (see Remark
).
In the synthesis case (
{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}={\bm{I}}
),
{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}
is a subgradient of the
\ell_{1}
-norm at
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
(see Theorem
); however,
{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}
is no longer a subgradient in this
\ell_{1}
-analysis case due to the transformation of
{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}
.
We can rewrite the condition as
\boldsymbol{0}={\boldsymbol{\Psi}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}
, where
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\partial\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}
, which translates to
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{\mathbb{S}}=\mathrm{sign}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\beta}})
and
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{\mathbb{T}}\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq 1
by the subdifferential of the
\ell_{1}
-norm (Exercise
).
The vector
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
thus certifies the optimality of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}}
.
For uniqueness and robustness, we will later show that the strict inequality
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{\infty}<1
is essential.

Taken together, these observations confirm that Condition
is indeed a natural generalization of the dual certificate condition in Theorem
to the
\ell_{1}
-analysis framework.
We also introduce a slightly more general version:

Condition
\thetheo

Let
{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}\in\real^{q\times p}
and
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
.
Given
{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}}\in\real^{p}
, let
{\mathbb{S}}=\mathrm{supp}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}})
. There exists a nonempty index set
{\mathbb{T}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\subseteq}{\mathbb{S}}^{c}
such that the index sets
{\mathbb{S}}
,
{\mathbb{T}}
and
{\mathbb{I}}\triangleq({\mathbb{S}}\cup{\mathbb{T}})^{c}
satisfy

1.

\mathcal{N}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}({\mathbb{T}})^{\top})\cap\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})=\{\boldsymbol{0}\}
;

2.

There exists
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{q}
such that
{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}^{\top})
,
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{\mathbb{S}}=\mathrm{sign}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}})
,
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{\mathbb{T}}\right\rVert_{\infty}<1
, and
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{\mathbb{I}}\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq 1
.

In Condition
, choosing a smaller
{\mathbb{T}}
relaxes requirement (b) but enlarges the nullspace
\mathcal{N}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}({\mathbb{T}})^{\top})
, thereby tightening requirement (a).
Although this formulation allows greater flexibility in selecting
{\mathbb{T}}
, we will show that Conditions
and
are in fact equivalent.

We also impose the following standard assumptions:

Assumption
\thetheo

Consider the problems in (
), we assume that

1.

Matrix
{\bm{X}}
has full row rank.

2.

Matrix
{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}
has full row rank.

3.

Maximum singular value
\sigma_{\max}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}})=1
.

Assumptions 1 and 2 prevent redundant equations or transform coefficients and are commonly adopted in compressed sensing and inverse problems. Assumption 3 is non-essential: any matrix
{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}
can be normalized by dividing by
\sigma_{\max}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}})
, which simply rescales the
\ell_{1}
-penalty and leaves the solution set unchanged.

3.5.1
Unique Recovery in Noise-Free Settings

We begin by establishing a necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of a solution to problem (
Q1
).

{theoremHigh}
[Necessary and sufficient condition for (
Q1
)]
Consider the optimization problem (
Q1
).
A vector
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is a solution of (
Q1
) if and only if, for all
{\bm{n}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
,

\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\bm{n}},\mathrm{sign}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})\right\rangle\leq\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}^{\top}{\bm{n}}\big\rVert_{1},

where
{\mathbb{S}}\triangleq\mathrm{supp}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]

Necessity.

Suppose
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is a solution of (
Q1
).
Since the function
f(\eta)={\bm{X}}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}+\eta{\bm{n}})
is continuously differentiable, we can find
\eta
small enough around 0 such that
\mathrm{sign}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}+\eta{\bm{n}}))=\mathrm{sign}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})
.
For small and nonzero
\eta
, we have

\displaystyle\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}

\displaystyle\leq\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}+\eta{\bm{n}})\big\rVert_{1}=\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}+\eta{\bm{n}})\big\rVert_{1}+\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}^{\top}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}+\eta{\bm{n}})\big\rVert_{1}

\displaystyle\leq\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}+\eta{\bm{n}}),\mathrm{sign}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}+\eta{\bm{n}}))\right\rangle+\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}+\big\lVert\eta{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}^{\top}{\bm{n}}\big\rVert_{1}

\displaystyle=\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}+\eta{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\bm{n}},\mathrm{sign}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})\right\rangle+\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}+\big\lVert\eta{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}^{\top}{\bm{n}}\big\rVert_{1}

\displaystyle=\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}},\mathrm{sign}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})\right\rangle+\eta\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\bm{n}},\mathrm{sign}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})\right\rangle+\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}+\big\lVert\eta{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}^{\top}{\bm{n}}\big\rVert_{1}

\displaystyle=\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}+\eta\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\bm{n}},\mathrm{sign}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})\right\rangle+\big\lVert\eta{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}^{\top}{\bm{n}}\big\rVert_{1}.

Therefore, for any
{\bm{n}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
, we have

\big\langle{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\bm{n}},\mathrm{sign}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})\big\rangle\leq\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}^{\top}{\bm{n}}\big\rVert_{1}
.

Sufficiency.

Suppose the stated inequality holds for all
{\bm{n}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
.
Assume, for contradiction, that there exists a feasible point
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}
such that
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}={\bm{y}}
and
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}\right\rVert_{1}<\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}
.
Define
{\bm{n}}\triangleq{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}
, which satisfies
{\bm{X}}{\bm{n}}=\boldsymbol{0}
since
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}={\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
. This means
{\bm{n}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
.
Using the identity
\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}\big\rVert_{1}=\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\bm{n}}\big\rVert_{1}
, we consider the decomposition of the objective:

\displaystyle\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}\big\rVert_{1}

\displaystyle=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\bm{n}})\right\rVert_{1}=\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}}\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}_{i}({\widehat{\beta}}_{i}-n_{i})\right\rvert+\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}_{i}n_{i}\right\rvert

\displaystyle\geq\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}}\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}_{i}{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}\right\rvert-\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}}\mathrm{sign}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}_{i}{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}){\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}_{i}n_{i}+\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}_{i}n_{i}\right\rvert\geq\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}}\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}_{i}{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}\right\rvert=\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1},

where the first inequality follows from the fact that
\big\lvert b-n\big\rvert\geq\big\lvert b\big\rvert-\mathrm{sign}(b)n
,
and the second inequality follows from the given condition that
\big\langle{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\bm{n}},\mathrm{sign}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})\big\rangle\leq\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}^{\top}{\bm{n}}\big\rVert_{1}
.
Since the assumption was
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}\right\rVert_{1}<\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}
, we obtain a contradiction.
Hence, no such
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}
exists, and
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is indeed optimal.
This completes the proof.

The following theorem states that Conditions
and
are equivalent, and they are necessary and sufficient for the
unique solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
to problem (
Q1
).

{theoremHigh}
[Dual certificate for (
Q1
)
(
Zhang et al. 2016
)
]
Under Assumption 1, let
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
be a solution to problem (
Q1
). The following are equivalent:

1.

Solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is unique.

2.

Condition
holds for
{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}}={\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
.

3.

Condition
holds for
{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}}={\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
This proof adapts arguments from
Grasmair et al. 2011
;
Zhang et al. 2015
;
Zhang et al. 2016
.
We establish the equivalence by proving the implications (iii)
\Rightarrow
(i)
\Rightarrow
(ii)
\Rightarrow
(iii).

(iii)
\Rightarrow
(i).

Consider any perturbation
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}+{\bm{n}}
where
{\bm{n}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})\setminus\{\boldsymbol{0}\}
.
Since by Condition
,
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{\mathbb{S}}=\mathrm{sign}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})
,
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{\mathbb{T}}\right\rVert_{\infty}<1
, and
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{\mathbb{I}}\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq 1
,
we can take a subgradient
{\bm{g}}\in\partial\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}
satisfying

{\bm{g}}_{\mathbb{S}}={\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{\mathbb{S}}\equiv\mathrm{sign}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})
,

{\bm{g}}_{\mathbb{I}}={\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{\mathbb{I}}
(
\left\lVert{\bm{g}}_{\mathbb{I}}\right\rVert_{\infty}=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{\mathbb{I}}\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq 1
),
and
\left\lVert{\bm{g}}_{\mathbb{T}}\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq 1

such that
\left\langle{\bm{g}}_{\mathbb{T}},{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{T}}^{\top}{\bm{n}}\right\rangle=\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{T}}^{\top}{\bm{n}}\big\rVert_{1}
(which is similar to
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
while we do not require strict inequality here; actually
\left\lVert{\bm{g}}_{\mathbb{T}}\right\rVert_{\infty}=1
is required to satisfy the latter equality).
Then the subgradient inequality (Definition
) shows

\displaystyle\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}+{\bm{n}})\big\rVert_{1}

\displaystyle\geq\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}+\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}{\bm{g}},{\bm{n}}\right\rangle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\dagger}}}{{=}}\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}+\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}{\bm{g}}-{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\bm{n}}\right\rangle

\displaystyle=\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}+\left\langle{\bm{g}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{\bm{n}}\right\rangle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\ddagger}}}{{=}}\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}+\left\langle{\bm{g}}_{\mathbb{T}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{\mathbb{T}},{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{T}}^{\top}{\bm{n}}\right\rangle

\displaystyle\geq\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}+\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{T}}^{\top}{\bm{n}}\big\rVert_{1}(1-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{\mathbb{T}}\right\rVert_{\infty}),

where the equality
({\dagger})
follows from
{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}^{\top})=\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})^{\perp}
and
{\bm{n}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
, the equality (
{\ddagger}
) follows from the definition of
{\bm{g}}
, and the last inequality is an application of the Hölder’s inequality
\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{\mathbb{T}},{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{T}}^{\top}{\bm{n}}\right\rangle\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{\mathbb{T}}\right\rVert_{\infty}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{T}}^{\top}{\bm{n}}\right\rVert_{1}
and
\left\langle{\bm{g}}_{\mathbb{T}},{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{T}}^{\top}{\bm{n}}\right\rangle=\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{T}}^{\top}{\bm{n}}\big\rVert_{1}
.
Since
{\bm{n}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})\setminus\{\boldsymbol{0}\}
and
\mathcal{N}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}({\mathbb{T}})^{\top})\cap\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})=\{\boldsymbol{0}\}
, we have
\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{T}}^{\top}{\bm{n}}\big\rVert_{1}>0
. Together with the condition
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{\mathbb{T}}\right\rVert_{\infty}<1
, we have
\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}+{\bm{n}})\big\rVert_{1}>\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}
for every
{\bm{n}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})\setminus\{\boldsymbol{0}\}
.
This proves that
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is the unique minimizer of problem (
Q1
).

(i)
\Rightarrow
(ii).

For every
{\bm{n}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})\setminus\{\boldsymbol{0}\}
, we have
{\bm{X}}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}+\eta{\bm{n}})={\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
.
Since the function
f(\eta)={\bm{X}}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}+\eta{\bm{n}})
is continuously differentiable, we can find
\eta
small enough around 0 such that
\mathrm{sign}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}+\eta{\bm{n}}))=\mathrm{sign}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})
. Since
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is the unique solution, for small and nonzero
\eta
, the proof of Theorem
shows the following strict inequality

\displaystyle\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}<\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}+\eta\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\bm{n}},\mathrm{sign}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})\right\rangle+\big\lVert\eta{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}^{\top}{\bm{n}}\big\rVert_{1}.

Therefore, for any
{\bm{n}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})\setminus\{\boldsymbol{0}\}
, we have

\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\bm{n}},\mathrm{sign}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})\right\rangle<\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}^{\top}{\bm{n}}\big\rVert_{1}.

(3.84)

If the condition
\mathcal{N}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}({\mathbb{S}}^{c})^{\top})\cap\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})=\{\boldsymbol{0}\}
does not hold, we can choose a nonzero vector
{\bm{n}}\in\mathcal{N}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}({\mathbb{S}}^{c})^{\top})\cap\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
.
We also have
-{\bm{n}}\in\mathcal{N}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}({\mathbb{S}}^{c})^{\top})\cap\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
.
By (
), we have
\big\langle{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\bm{n}},\mathrm{sign}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})\big\rangle<0
and
-\big\langle{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\bm{n}},\mathrm{sign}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})\big\rangle<0
, which leads to a contradiction, and shows that
\mathcal{N}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}({\mathbb{S}}^{c})^{\top})\cap\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})=\{\boldsymbol{0}\}
, i.e., Condition
(i).

Next, we construct
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
satisfying Condition
(ii).
Define
{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}\in\real^{q}
by
{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}_{\mathbb{S}}=\mathrm{sign}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})
and
{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}=\boldsymbol{0}
.

If such
{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}
satisfies
{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}\in\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}^{\top})
, we are done.

If
{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}\notin\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}^{\top})\equiv\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})^{\perp}
, then we will construct a new vector to satisfy Condition
(ii).

Let
{\bm{Q}}\in\real^{p\times r}
be a matrix whose columns form a basis for
\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
.
It follows that
{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}\triangleq{\bm{Q}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}\in\real^{r}
must be a nonzero vector.
Consider the optimization problem

\min_{{\bm{u}}\in\real^{q}}\left\lVert{\bm{u}}\right\rVert_{\infty}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\bm{Q}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}{\bm{u}}=-{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}\text{ and }{\bm{u}}_{\mathbb{S}}=\boldsymbol{0}.

(3.85)

For any minimizer
\widehat{\bm{u}}
of problem (
), we have
{\bm{Q}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}({\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}+\widehat{\bm{u}})=\boldsymbol{0}
such that
{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}({\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}+\widehat{\bm{u}})
is orthogonal to the nullspace
\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
,
which implies
{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}({\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}+\widehat{\bm{u}})\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})^{\perp}\equiv\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}^{\top})
and
({\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}+\widehat{\bm{u}})_{\mathbb{S}}={\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}_{\mathbb{S}}=\mathrm{sign}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})
.
Thus, we shall show that the objective of problem (
) is strictly less than 1 using strong duality, thus completing for the proof of the part (ii) of Condition
.
To this end, we rewrite problem (
) in an equivalent form as:

\min_{{\bm{u}}\in\real^{q}}\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{\infty}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\bm{Q}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}{\bm{u}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}=-{\boldsymbol{\gamma}},

(3.86)

whose Lagrange dual problem (i.e., the dual of an
\ell_{\infty}
-minimization problem; see Example
) is

\max_{{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{r}}\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}\right\rangle\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}^{\top}{\bm{Q}}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\big\rVert_{1}\leq 1.

(3.87)

Note that
{\bm{Q}}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
, and

\left\lvert\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}\right\rangle\right\rvert=\big\lvert\big\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\bm{Q}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}\big\rangle\big\rvert=\big\lvert\big\langle{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\bm{Q}}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},\mathrm{sign}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})\big\rangle\big\rvert
.
Using (
), for any
{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}
, we have

\left\lvert\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}\right\rangle\right\rvert=\begin{cases}\left\lvert\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\bm{Q}}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},\mathrm{sign}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})\right\rangle\right\rvert=0,&\text{if }{\bm{Q}}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}=\boldsymbol{0};\\
\left\lvert\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\bm{Q}}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},\mathrm{sign}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})\right\rangle\right\rvert<\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}^{\top}{\bm{Q}}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq 1,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

Hence, problem (
) is feasible, and its objective value is strictly less than 1. By the strong duality property (which holds because the primal is feasible and the objective is convex and continuous), problems (
) and (
) attain their minimum, and the optimal value is also strictly less than 1.
Let
\widehat{\bm{u}}
be an optimal solution. Define
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=\widetilde{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}+\widehat{\bm{u}}
. Then:

{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{\mathbb{S}}={\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}_{\mathbb{S}}=\sign({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})
,

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{\infty}=\left\lVert\widehat{\bm{u}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{\infty}<1
,

{\bm{Q}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}={\bm{Q}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}(\widetilde{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}+\widehat{\bm{u}})={\boldsymbol{\gamma}}-{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}=\boldsymbol{0}
, so
{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})^{\perp}\equiv\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}^{\top})
.

Hence,
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
satisfies Condition
(ii).

(ii)

3.5.2
Unique Recovery in Noisy Signal

Similarly to Theorem

Lemma 140

{theoremHigh}

[Dual certificate for (

(

]
Under Assumption 1, let

Proof
[of Theorem
]
The proof closely mirrors that of Theorem

Since Lemma

) and (

Let
{\mathbb{Q}}_{\sigma}

Q1,σ

Let
\widehat{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\widehat{\bm{y}},

(3.88)

and let
{\mathbb{Q}}_{q}
denote its solution set.

We claim that

{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}

Applying Theorem

3.5.3
Stable Recovery in Noisy Signal

To state the robustness result, define

\mathcal{U}({\mathbb{T}})\triangleq\max_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\mathcal{N}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}({\mathbb{T}})^{\top})\setminus\{\boldsymbol{0}\}}\frac{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}}{\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}}.

(3.89)

Condition
(i) guarantees that
0<\mathcal{U}({\mathbb{T}})<+\infty
.
If
{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}={\bm{I}}
,
any nonzero
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\mathcal{N}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}({\mathbb{T}})^{\top})\setminus\{\boldsymbol{0}\}
is a sparse (nonzero) vector supported on
{\mathbb{T}}^{c}
;
consequently,
\mathcal{U}({\mathbb{T}})
equals the reciprocal of the smallest singular value of the submatrix
{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{T}}^{c}}
(see (
)).

Lemma 141
.

Assume that vectors
{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}}
and
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
satisfy Condition
. Let
{\mathbb{S}}\triangleq\mathrm{supp}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}})
and
{\mathbb{T}}\triangleq{\mathbb{S}}^{c}
.
Then,

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq C_{3}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}})\right\rVert_{2}+C_{4}D_{1}^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}}),\quad\forall\,{\boldsymbol{\beta}},

(3.90)

where
D_{1}^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}})\triangleq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}}\right\rVert_{1}-\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}}\right\rangle
is the Bregman distance associated with the function
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}\cdot\right\rVert_{1}
, with
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\partial\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}}\right\rVert_{1}
(see Definition
), the absolute constants
C_{3},C_{4}
are given by

C_{3}=\mathcal{U}({\mathbb{T}})\sqrt{\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert},\quad\text{and}\quad C_{4}=\frac{1+\text{cond}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}})\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}C_{3}}{1-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{\mathbb{T}}\right\rVert_{\infty}},

where
\text{cond}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}})=\sigma_{\max}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}})/\sigma_{\min}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}})
denotes the condition number of
{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}
.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
This proof adapts the argument in
Zhang et al. 2016
and proceeds in two steps.
The first part shows that for any
{\bm{u}}\in\mathcal{N}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}({\mathbb{T}})^{\top})
,

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\left(1+\frac{C_{3}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}}{\sigma_{\min}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}})}\right)\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{u}})\right\rVert_{1}+C_{3}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}})\right\rVert_{2}.

(3.91a)

The second part shows that

f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\triangleq\min\left\{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{u}})\right\rVert_{1}\mid\;{\bm{u}}\in\mathcal{N}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}({\mathbb{T}})^{\top})\right\}\leq(1-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{\mathbb{T}}\right\rVert_{\infty})^{-1}D_{1}^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}}).

(3.91b)

Combining the two parts and using the definition of
C_{4}
prove the desired result.

Proof of (
).

Let
{\bm{u}}\in\mathcal{N}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}({\mathbb{T}})^{\top})
, which also means
{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{T}}^{\top}{\bm{u}}=\boldsymbol{0}
and
\mathrm{supp}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{\bm{u}})={\mathbb{S}}
.
By the triangle inequality, we get

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{u}})\right\rVert_{1}+\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}({\bm{u}}-{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}})\right\rVert_{1}.

(3.92)

Since
\mathrm{supp}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}})={\mathbb{S}}
, implying
{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}}\in\mathcal{N}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}({\mathbb{T}})^{\top})
, we have
{\bm{u}}-{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}}\in\mathcal{N}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}({\mathbb{T}})^{\top})
and thus
\left\lVert{\bm{u}}-{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\mathcal{U}({\mathbb{T}})\left\lVert{\bm{X}}({\bm{u}}-{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}})\right\rVert_{2}
, where
\mathcal{U}({\mathbb{T}})<+\infty
follows from Condition
(i).
It can be shown that

\displaystyle\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}({\bm{u}}-{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}})\right\rVert_{1}

\displaystyle\leq\sqrt{\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}({\bm{u}}-{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}})\right\rVert_{2}\leq\sqrt{\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert}\left\lVert{\bm{u}}-{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}}\right\rVert_{2}

(3.93)

\displaystyle\leq\sqrt{\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert}\,\mathcal{U}({\mathbb{T}})\left\lVert{\bm{X}}({\bm{u}}-{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}})\right\rVert_{2}=C_{3}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}({\bm{u}}-{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}})\right\rVert_{2},

where the first inequality follows from the standard bounds on vector norms (Exerciser

\sigma_{\max}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}})=1
(Assumption 3) and the definition

Furthermore, using the singular value bound (
) and the standard bounds on vector norms (Exerciser

\displaystyle\left\lVert{\bm{X}}({\bm{u}}-{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}})\right\rVert_{2}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{u}})\right\rVert_{2}+\left\lVert{\bm{X}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}})\right\rVert_{2}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{u}}\right\rVert_{2}+\left\lVert{\bm{X}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}})\right\rVert_{2}

(3.94)

\displaystyle\leq\frac{\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{u}})\right\rVert_{2}}{\sigma_{\min}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}})}+\left\lVert{\bm{X}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}})\right\rVert_{2}\leq\frac{\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{u}})\right\rVert_{1}}{\sigma_{\min}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}})}+\left\lVert{\bm{X}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}})\right\rVert_{2}.

Therefore, we get (
) after combining (

Proof of (
).

Since
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{\mathbb{S}}=\sign({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}})
and
{\mathbb{S}}=\mathrm{supp}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}})
, we have

\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}}\right\rangle=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}}\right\rVert_{1}
, so the Bregman distance simplifies to
D_{1}^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}})=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}-\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle
.
Thus, it suffices to show

f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\leq(1-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{\mathbb{T}}\right\rVert_{\infty})^{-1}(\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\big\rVert_{1}-\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle).

Since
{\bm{u}}\in\mathcal{N}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}({\mathbb{T}})^{\top})
is equivalent to
{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{T}}^{\top}{\bm{u}}=\boldsymbol{0}
, the Lagrangian of the minimization problem in (
) is

L({\bm{u}},{\boldsymbol{\nu}})=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{u}})\right\rVert_{1}+\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\nu}},{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{T}}^{\top}{\bm{u}}\right\rangle=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{u}})\right\rVert_{1}+\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{T}}{\boldsymbol{\nu}},{\bm{u}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle+\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{T}}{\boldsymbol{\nu}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle.

Then,
f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\min_{\bm{u}}\max_{\boldsymbol{\nu}}L({\bm{u}},{\boldsymbol{\nu}})
. Following the minimax theorem, we derive that

\displaystyle f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})

\displaystyle=\max_{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\min_{\bm{u}}L({\bm{u}},{\boldsymbol{\nu}})=\max_{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\min_{\bm{u}}\left\{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{u}})\right\rVert_{1}+\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{T}}{\boldsymbol{\nu}},{\bm{u}}\right\rangle\right\}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\dagger}}}{{=}}\max_{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\min_{\bm{u}}\max_{{\bm{w}}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{\infty}}\left\{\left\langle{\bm{w}},{{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{u}})}\right\rangle+\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{T}}{\boldsymbol{\nu}},{\bm{u}}\right\rangle\right\}

\displaystyle=\max_{{\bm{z}}\in\mathcal{C}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{T}})}\min_{\bm{u}}\max_{{\bm{w}}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{\infty}}\left\{\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}{\bm{w}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle+\left\langle{\bm{u}},{\bm{z}}-{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}{\bm{w}}\right\rangle\right\}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\ddagger}}}{{=}}\max_{{\bm{z}}}\left\{\left\langle{\bm{z}},{\bm{w}}\right\rangle\mid{\bm{z}}\in{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}\cdot{\mathbb{B}}_{\infty}\cap\mathcal{C}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{T}})\right\}

\displaystyle=\max_{\bm{z}}\left\{\left\langle c{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+{\bm{z}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle\mid{\bm{z}}\in{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}\cdot{\mathbb{B}}_{\infty}\cap\mathcal{C}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{T}})\right\}-\left\langle c{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle,\;\forall\,c>0

\displaystyle=c\max_{\bm{z}}\left\{\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+{\bm{z}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle\mid{\bm{z}}\in c^{-1}{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}\cdot{\mathbb{B}}_{\infty}\cap\mathcal{C}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{T}})\right\}-c\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle,\;\forall\,c>0,

where the equality (
{\dagger}
) follows from the definition of the dual norm (see (
)), the equality (
{\ddagger}
) follows by letting
{\bm{z}}-{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}{\bm{w}}=\boldsymbol{0}
(otherwise the minimum over
{\bm{u}}
is
-\infty
),
{\mathbb{B}}_{\infty}\triangleq\{{\bm{w}}\mid\left\lVert{\bm{w}}\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq 1\}
denotes the unit
\ell_{\infty}
-ball, and
\mathcal{C}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{T}})
denotes the column space of
{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{T}}
.
Let
c\triangleq(1-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{\mathbb{T}}\right\rVert_{\infty})^{-1}

and
{\mathbb{B}}_{\mathbb{T}}\triangleq\{{\bm{b}}\in\real^{q}\mid{\bm{b}}_{\mathbb{S}}=\boldsymbol{0}\}
.
Since
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{\mathbb{S}}=\sign({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}})
and
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{\mathbb{T}}\right\rVert_{\infty}<1
from Condition
(ii), we have
c<+\infty
and get

({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+c^{-1}{\mathbb{B}}_{\infty}\cap{\mathbb{B}}_{\mathbb{T}})\subset{\mathbb{B}}_{\infty},

from which we conclude

({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+c^{-1}{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}\cdot{\mathbb{B}}_{\infty}\cap\mathcal{C}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{T}}))\subset{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}\cdot{\mathbb{B}}_{\infty}.

Hence, for any
{\bm{z}}\in c^{-1}{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}\cdot{\mathbb{B}}_{\infty}\cap\mathcal{C}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}_{\mathbb{T}})

f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\leq c(\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}-\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle)
.
This completes the proof.

Lemma 142
.

Let
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\in\real^{p}
be a fixed vector such that
\mathrm{supp}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})={\mathbb{S}}
.
Suppose there exists a subgradient
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\partial\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{1}
satisfying
{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}={\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}^{\top})
,
where from

{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}=({\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{\top})^{-1}{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}

Then, for every

and every data vector

satisfying
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\epsilon

1.

Every minimizer
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\sigma}
of problem (
Q1,σ

D_{1}^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\sigma},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})\leq\frac{(\epsilon+\sigma\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rVert_{2}/2)^{2}}{\sigma}\quad\text{and}\quad\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\sigma}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\epsilon+\sigma\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rVert_{2};

2.

Every minimizer
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\epsilon}
of problem (
Q1,ϵ
) satisfies
D_{1}^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\epsilon},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})\leq 2\epsilon\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rVert_{2}
.

Proof

See Theorem 3 of
Burger and Osher 2004
and Lemma 3.5 of
Grasmair et al. 2011
.

From the above lemmas, we now show that Condition
guarantees robustness of problems (

{theoremHigh}
[Error bound of (
Q1,σ
) and (
Q1,ϵ
) under measurement noise
(
Zhang et al. 2016
)
]
Under Assumptions 1
\sim
3, let
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\in\real^{p}
be a given signal, and let
{\mathbb{S}}\triangleq\mathrm{supp}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})
and
{\mathbb{T}}\triangleq{\mathbb{S}}^{c}
. For arbitrary noise
{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}
, let
{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}+{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}
and
\epsilon=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\right\rVert_{2}

If Condition

{{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}

1.

For any
C_{0}>0
, there exists constant
C_{1}>0
such that every minimizer
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\sigma}

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\epsilon}

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\epsilon}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})\right\rVert_{1}\leq C_{2}\epsilon.

The constants
C_{1}
and
C_{2}
are given explicitly as follows. Define

{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}=({\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{\top})^{-1}{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},\quad C_{3}=\mathcal{U}({\mathbb{T}})\sqrt{\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert},\quad\text{and}\quad C_{4}=\frac{1+\text{cond}({\boldsymbol{\Psi}})\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}C_{3}}{1-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{\mathbb{T}}\right\rVert_{\infty}},

with which we have

\displaystyle C_{1}

\displaystyle=2C_{3}+C_{3}C_{0}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rVert_{2}+\frac{(1+C_{0}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rVert_{2}/2)^{2}C_{4}}{C_{0}},

\displaystyle C_{2}

\displaystyle=2C_{3}+2C_{4}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rVert_{2}.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Firstly, we derive that

\displaystyle\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\sigma}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{1}

\displaystyle\leq C_{3}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\sigma}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})\right\rVert_{2}+C_{4}D_{1}^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\sigma},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})

\displaystyle\leq C_{3}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\sigma}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}+C_{3}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}+C_{4}D_{1}^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\sigma},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})

\displaystyle\leq C_{3}(\epsilon+\sigma\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rVert_{2})+C_{3}\epsilon+C_{4}\frac{(\epsilon+\sigma\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rVert_{2}/2)^{2}}{\sigma},

where the first and the third inequalities follow from Lemmas
and
, respectively. Substituting
\sigma=C_{0}\epsilon
and simplifying yields the bound in part (i).
Part (ii) follows analogously by applying the corresponding bound from Lemma
for the constrained formulation.

Note that the condition
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{\mathbb{T}}\right\rVert_{\infty}<1
plays a crucial role: the constant
C_{4}
is inversely proportional to
1-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{\mathbb{T}}\right\rVert_{\infty}
, so this gap directly controls stability.
Moreover, the numerator of
C_{4}
also depends on global properties of
{\boldsymbol{\Psi}}
and
{\bm{X}}
,
whereas,
C_{3}
depends only on the restricted geometry of the support
{\mathbb{S}}
.

Data least squares.

While the OLS method accounts for errors in the response variable
{\bm{y}}

data least sqaures (DLS)
method considers errors in the predictor variables:

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{DLS}=\mathop{\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}},\widetilde{\bm{X}}}\big\lVert\widetilde{\bm{X}}\big\rVert_{F}^{2},\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\bm{y}}\in\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}+\widetilde{\bm{X}}),

(3.97)

where
\widetilde{\bm{X}}
represents a perturbation of
{\bm{X}}
(i.e., a noise in the predictor variables).
That is,
({\bm{X}}+\widetilde{\bm{X}}){\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{DLS}={\bm{y}}
, assuming the measured response
{\bm{y}}
is noise-free.
The Lagrangian function and its gradient w.r.t.
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
are, respectively, given by

\displaystyle L({\boldsymbol{\beta}},\widetilde{\bm{X}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})

\displaystyle=\mathrm{tr}(\widetilde{\bm{X}}\widetilde{\bm{X}}^{\top})+{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{\top}({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+\widetilde{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}});

\displaystyle\nabla_{\widetilde{\bm{X}}}L({\boldsymbol{\beta}},\widetilde{\bm{X}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})

\displaystyle=\widetilde{\bm{X}}+{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\top}=\boldsymbol{0}\quad\implies\quad\widetilde{\bm{X}}=-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\top},

where
{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n}
is a vector of Lagrange multipliers.
Show that the original problem is equivalent to

\mathop{\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\frac{({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}})^{\top}({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}})}{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}.

Total least squares.
Similar to data least squares, the

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{TLS}=\mathop{\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}},\widetilde{\bm{X}},\widetilde{\bm{y}}}\left\lVert[\widetilde{\bm{X}},\widetilde{\bm{y}}]\right\rVert_{F}^{2},\quad\text{s.t.}\quad({\bm{y}}+\widetilde{\bm{y}})\in\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}+\widetilde{\bm{X}}),

(3.98)

where
\widetilde{{\bm{X}}}
and

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{TLS}=\mathop{\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}}_{{\bm{z}},{\bm{D}}}\left\lVert{\bm{D}}\right\rVert_{F}^{2},\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\bm{D}}{\bm{z}}=-{\bm{C}}{\bm{z}},

Part II
Design Matrices

\nopagecolor

Chapter 4
Design Matrices and Properties

I
In sparse representation and
compressed sensing
(also known as
compressive sensing
,
compressive sampling
, or
sparse sampling
; see Section
), one must solve an underdetermined linear system

{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\bm{y}},

where
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is a sparse vector containing only a few nonzero entries,
{\bm{y}}
is the vector of
measurements
(or
reesponse
), and
{\bm{X}}
is the
design matrix
(or
sensing matrix
).
Sparsity has long been leveraged in signal processing and approximation theory—for tasks such as image compression
(
Pennebaker and Mitchell 1992
;
Taubman et al. 2002
;
Rabbani and Joshi 2002
;
Foucart and Rauhut 2013
)
and denoising
(
Donoho 2002
;
Joy et al. 2013
)
—as well as in statistics and learning theory as a means to prevent overfitting
(
Vapnik 2013
;
Lu 2021b
)
. It also plays a central role in statistical estimation and model selection
(
Tibshirani 1996
;
Lu 2021b
)
, in modeling the human visual system
(
Olshausen and Field 1996
)
, and especially in image processing, where the multiscale wavelet transform yields nearly sparse representations for natural images
(
Mallat 1999
)
.
In this chapter, we discuss the role of design matrices in solving sparse linear systems.

Transforming a signal into a new basis or frame—i.e., expressing it as
{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
so that
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
represents the signal in that basis—can lead to a more concise representation.
Such compression is valuable for reducing data storage and transmission costs, which can be substantial in many applications. Consequently, rather than transmitting the original high-dimensional signal, one may instead transmit only the (typically few) nonzero analysis coefficients from the basis or frame expansion. When the number of nonzero coefficients is small, we say the signal admits a sparse representation.
Sparse signal models enable high compression rates, and in compressive sensing, the prior knowledge that a signal is sparse in some known basis or frame allows us to reconstruct the original signal from far fewer measurements than its ambient dimension would suggest. For sparse data, only the nonzero coefficients generally need to be stored or transmitted; all others can safely be assumed to be zero.

Mathematically, a signal
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is called
k
-sparse if it contains at most
k
nonzero entries, i.e.,
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{0}\leq k
. We denote the set of all
k
-sparse signals
by

{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]=\{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}:\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{0}\leq k\},

(4.1)

where square brackets are used to emphasize that equality is allowed.
Using this notation, problem (
) (p.
) can be restated as:

\min\;f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\quad\text{ s.t. }\quad{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[R].

In practice, many signals are not sparse in the standard basis but admit a sparse representation in some other basis
{\boldsymbol{\Phi}}
. In such cases, we still refer to
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
as
k
-sparse, with the understanding that
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\boldsymbol{\Phi}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
for some coefficient vector
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
satisfying
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{0}\leq k
.

In many applications, sparse optimization involves minimizing the objective function

f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},

where
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
is the
design matrix
, and
{\bm{y}}\in\real^{n}
is the observed response vector.
Notably, when the design matrix is the identity, it preserves the geometric structure of the signal, thereby enabling exact recovery of sparse vectors. We will formalize this idea and establish precise conditions on
{\bm{X}}
that guarantee universal recovery—that is, the ability to uniquely reconstruct every
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]
from its measurements
{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.

However, a design matrix that can identify some sparse vectors does not necessarily ensure universal recovery. For example, consider a matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
and two distinct
k
-sparse vectors
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]
with
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1}\neq{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}
, yet
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}={\bm{y}}
. In this case, the measurements provide no way to distinguish between
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1}
and
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}
, making unique recovery impossible. Consequently, such a design matrix fails to support universal recovery. Moreover, this failure is not limited to a single pair of vectors: it typically implies that an entire subspace—or infinitely many pairs—of sparse vectors cannot be uniquely identified from their measurements.

Therefore, it is essential that the design matrix preserves the geometric structure of sparse vectors when projecting them from a high-dimensional space (of dimension
p
) into a lower-dimensional space (of dimension
n
), particularly in settings where
n\ll p
. The nullspace property and other properties in this chapter formalize this requirement.

Basic Notations

We now introduce some basic notation.
For any index set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
, define the following sets:

\displaystyle{\mathbb{C}}[{\mathbb{S}}]

\displaystyle\triangleq\{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}\mid\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}\};

(4.2a)

\displaystyle{\mathbb{C}}[{\mathbb{S}};\gamma]

\displaystyle\triangleq\{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}\mid\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\gamma\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}\};

(4.2b)

\displaystyle{\mathbb{C}}[k]

\displaystyle\triangleq\bigcup_{{\mathbb{S}}:\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert=k}{\mathbb{C}}[{\mathbb{S}}],

(4.2c)

where
{\mathbb{S}}^{c}
denotes the complement of
{\mathbb{S}}
.
Here, “square brackets” are used (rather than parentheses) to indicate that equality is allowed in the defining inequalities.
Thus,
{\mathbb{C}}[{\mathbb{S}}]={\mathbb{C}}[{\mathbb{S}};1]
is the convex cone consisting of vectors whose
\ell_{1}
-mass outside
{\mathbb{S}}
does not exceed that inside
{\mathbb{S}}
, i.e., vectors that concentrate most of their weight on the coordinates in
{\mathbb{S}}
.
In contrast,
{\mathbb{C}}[k]
is the (non-convex) union of all such cones over index sets of size
k
; it captures vectors that concentrate most of their
\ell_{1}
-norm on some subset of
k
coordinates.
Note that

{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]\subset{\mathbb{C}}[k],

since any
k
-sparse vector places all its nonzero entries—and hence all its
\ell_{1}
-mass—within a set of at most
k
coordinates.
Additionally, for a fixed
{\mathbb{S}}
, we have

{\mathbb{C}}[{\mathbb{S}};\gamma_{1}]\subseteq{\mathbb{C}}[{\mathbb{S}};\gamma_{2}],\quad\text{whenever }\gamma_{1}\leq\gamma_{2}.

In certain contexts, strict inequalities are required. In such cases, the above definitions can be restated using “parentheses” to exclude equality:

\displaystyle{\mathbb{C}}({\mathbb{S}})

\displaystyle\triangleq\{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}\mid\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}<\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}\};

(4.3a)

\displaystyle{\mathbb{C}}({\mathbb{S}};\gamma)

\displaystyle\triangleq\{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}\mid\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}<\gamma\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}\};

(4.3b)

\displaystyle{\mathbb{C}}(k)

\displaystyle\triangleq\bigcup_{{\mathbb{S}}:\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert=k}{\mathbb{C}}({\mathbb{S}}),

(4.3c)

Before discussing these properties further, we introduce one more definition.
The
\ell_{s}
-error of best
k
-sparse approximation
(also called the
\ell_{s}
-distance to the set of
k
-sparse vectors
) is defined as:

\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})_{s}\triangleq\min_{\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]}\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{s}.

(4.4)

4.1
Nullspace, Restricted Eigenvalue, and Other Design Properties

We now introduce several desirable properties of the design matrix that are widely studied in the literature (see, e.g.,
Candes and Tao 2005
;
Cohen et al. 2009
;
Raskutti et al. 2010
;
Baraniuk et al. 2011
;
Jain et al. 2014
;
Hastie et al. 2015
;
Jain et al. 2017
).

We begin with the nullspace property.

Definition 143
(Nullspace property (NSP)).

A matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
is said to satisfy the nullspace property (NSP) or restricted nullspace property (RNP) over the set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
, denoted NSP(
{\mathbb{S}}
), if

\qquad\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})\cap{\mathbb{C}}[{\mathbb{S}}]=\{\boldsymbol{0}\},

(4.5a)

where
\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})\triangleq\{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}\mid{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\boldsymbol{0}\}
denotes the nullspace of
{\bm{X}}
(Definition
).
Equivalently, this condition can be expressed as:

\text{or }\quad\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}<\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1},\qquad\text{ for all }{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})\setminus\{\boldsymbol{0}\};

(4.5b)

\text{or }\quad 2\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}<\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1},\qquad\text{ for all }{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})\setminus\{\boldsymbol{0}\}.

(4.5c)

On the other hand,
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
is said to satisfy the NSP of order
k
, denoted NSP(
k
), if
\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})\cap{\mathbb{C}}[k]=\{\boldsymbol{0}\}
.
Note that, for a given
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})\setminus\{\boldsymbol{0}\}
, the
inequality
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}<\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}
holds for any index set
{\mathbb{S}}\subset\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
with
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert\leq k
as soon as it holds for an index set of
k
largest (in absolute value) entries of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.
Consequently, for NSP of order
k
, (
) or (
) can be equivalently stated as

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}<2\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})_{1},\qquad\text{ for all }{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})\setminus\{\boldsymbol{0}\},

(4.5d)

where
\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})_{s}\triangleq\min_{\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]}\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{s}
is the
\ell_{s}
-distance to
k
-sparse vectors.

While the NSP of order
k
(i.e., NSP(
k
)) is defined with respect to the union
{\mathbb{C}}[k]=\bigcup_{{\mathbb{S}}:\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert=k}{\mathbb{C}}[{\mathbb{S}}]
, the NSP over
{\mathbb{S}}
(i.e, NSP(
{\mathbb{S}}
)) applies to a fixed index set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
.
Therefore, NSP over
{\mathbb{S}}
is a less strict condition compared with NSP of order
k
if
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert=k
.
In words, the NSP(
{\mathbb{S}}
) property holds when the only vector in the cone
{\mathbb{C}}[{\mathbb{S}}]
that lies in the nullspace of
{\bm{X}}
is the zero vector.

Recall that the NSP of order
k
states the following: for every nonzero vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})\setminus\{\boldsymbol{0}\}
and for every index set
{\mathbb{S}}\subset\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
with
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert\leq k
, we have
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}<\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}
.
In other words, any nonzero vector in the nullspace of
{\bm{X}}
must be more “spread out” outside any subset of at most
k
coordinates than inside it.
This implies that no nonzero vector in
\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
can concentrate most of its
\ell_{1}
-mass on any
k
coordinates.
As a direct consequence, the nullspace cannot contain any nonzero
k
-sparse vector.

Exercise
\thetheo

Let
{\bm{X}}
be a design matrix that satisfies the NSP of order
2k
. Show that for any two distinct
k
-sparse vectors
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]
with
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1}\neq{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}
, it holds that
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1}\neq{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}
.

\paragrapharrow

Rescaled, reshuffled, and augmented properties of NSP.
Consider replacing the original measurement matrix
{\bm{X}}
with new measurement matrices
\widehat{\bm{X}}
or
\widetilde{\bm{X}}
, defined as follows:

\displaystyle\widehat{\bm{X}}

\displaystyle\triangleq{\bm{P}}{\bm{X}},\quad\text{where }{\bm{P}}\text{ is some invertible }n\times n\text{ matrix};

\displaystyle\widetilde{\bm{X}}

\displaystyle\triangleq\begin{bmatrix}{\bm{X}}\\
{\bm{Y}}\end{bmatrix},\quad\text{where }{\bm{Y}}\text{ is some }n^{\prime}\times p\text{ matrix}.

When
{\bm{P}}
is a diagonal matrix,
{\bm{P}}{\bm{X}}
corresponds to a rescaled version of
{\bm{X}}
; when
{\bm{P}}
is a permutation matrix (Definition
),
{\bm{P}}{\bm{X}}
represents a reshuffled (i.e., row-permuted) version of
{\bm{X}}
.
We observe that

\mathcal{N}(\widehat{\bm{X}})=\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathcal{N}(\widetilde{\bm{X}})\subseteq\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}}).

(4.6)

Consequently, if the NSP condition holds for
{\bm{X}}
, it also holds for both
\widehat{\bm{X}}
and
\widetilde{\bm{X}}
.

If a design matrix satisfies the NSP of order
2k
, then no two distinct
k
-sparse vectors can be mapped to the same measurement vector (see Exercise
).
This injectivity on the set of
k
-sparse vectors is essential for guaranteeing global uniqueness in sparse recovery.
A stronger condition than NSP is the restricted eigenvalue (RE) property, which not only rules out sparse vectors in the nullspace but also ensures that sparse vectors retain a significant portion of their norm under the action of the measurement matrix.

Definition 144
(Restricted eigenvalue (RE) property).

A matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
is said to satisfy the restricted eigenvalue (RE) property with constant
\mu>0
over a set
{\mathbb{S}}
if, for all
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
, we have

\mu\leq\frac{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}\qquad\iff\qquad\mu\cdot\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},

where the right-hand side of the first inequality represents the Rayleigh quotient of the vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
associated with the matrix
{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}
, which also serves as the Hessian of the least squares loss function
f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
.

This property implies that sparse vectors are not only excluded from the nullspace of
{\bm{X}}
, but are also well-conditioned under the linear transformation defined by
{\bm{X}}
: their Euclidean norm is preserved up to a factor of
\mu
.
In particular, if the RE property holds over the set of all
2k
-sparse vectors (i.e.,
{\mathbb{S}}={\mathbb{B}}_{0}[2k]
), then for any two
k
-sparse vectors
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}\in{\mathbb{B}}[k]
, their difference
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}
is
2k
-sparse, and we have

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]\quad\implies\quad\left\lVert{\bm{X}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\geq\mu\cdot\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

(4.7)

Consequently, the mapping
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\mapsto{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
preserves distances between
k
-sparse vectors up to the constant
\mu
.
This stability is crucial for both identifiability and robust recovery in high-dimensional statistics and compressed sensing.

4.1.1
Nullspace Property-II

The NSP condition is not the only condition that enforces the non-concentration of vectors in the nullspace.
In practice, the vectors we aim to recover—whether via basis pursuit or other reconstruction methods—are rarely exactly sparse.
Exact sparsity is typically an idealization; more realistically, signals are only approximately sparse, meaning they are close (in some norm) to a
k
-sparse vector.
In such cases, we would like the reconstruction error to be controlled by how well the true vector can be approximated by a
k
-sparse one. This desirable behavior is known as
stability
with respect to sparsity defect.

To formalize this idea, we introduce an alternative formulation called the nullspace property-II (NSP
′
).

Definition 145
(Nullspace property-II (NSP
′
)).

A matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
satisfies the NSP
′
over a set
{\mathbb{S}}\subset\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
with constant
C
, denoted NSP
′
(
{\mathbb{S}},C
),
if
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert=k
and there exists a constant
C>0
such that

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq C\frac{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}}{\sqrt{k}},\quad\text{for all }{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}}).

(4.8)

It is said to satisfy the NSP
′
of order
k
with constant
C
, denoted NSP
′
(
k,C
), if it satisfies the NSP
′
with constant
C
relative to any set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
with
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert\leq k
.

Note that the equality can be achieved in the definition of the NSP
′
, while the equality is not achieved in the definition of the standard NSP.

Like the standard NSP, the NSP
′
condition formalizes the idea that no nonzero vector in the nullspace of
{\bm{X}}
can be overly concentrated on a small subset of coordinates.
For example, suppose
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is exactly
k
-sparse.
Then there exists a set
{\mathbb{S}}
with
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert\leq k
such that
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}=\boldsymbol{0}
.
Plugging this into (
) yields
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\mathbb{S}}=\boldsymbol{0}
, which implies
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\boldsymbol{0}
.
Consequently, if
{\bm{X}}
satisfies NSP
′
, the only
k
-sparse vector in
\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
is the zero vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\boldsymbol{0}
.
That is,
\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})\cap{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]=\{\boldsymbol{0}\}
, which is similar to the standard NSP condition.

To fully understand the implications of NSP
′
in sparse recovery, we now consider how to evaluate the performance of reconstruction algorithms when the true signal
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is not necessarily sparse.
Let
\Delta:\real^{n}\rightarrow\real^{p}
denote a specific recovery map (e.g., a decoder). We are particularly interested in error guarantees of the form

\left\lVert\Delta({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}})-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq C\frac{\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})_{1}}{\sqrt{k}},\quad\text{for all ${\boldsymbol{\beta}}$},

(4.9)

where
\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})_{1}
denotes the
\ell_{1}
-distance of best
k
-term approximation
:

\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})_{1}\triangleq\min_{\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]}\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1},

i.e., the distance between a vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
and the ball
{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]
under the
\ell_{1}
-norm.
This bound ensures two important properties:

Exact recovery
of all possible
k
-sparse solutions (i.e.,
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}=\Delta({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime})
if
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]
).

Robustness
to non-sparse signals, where the reconstruction error scales with how well
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
can be approximated by a
k
-sparse vector.

Such guarantees are called
instance-optimal

(
Cohen et al. 2009
;
Foucart and Rauhut 2013
)
, because the error bound adapts to each individual signal
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
, rather than holding only for a restricted class (e.g., strictly sparse vectors). These are also referred to as
uniform guarantees
, since they hold uniformly over all possible
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.

The choice of norms in (
) is not unique. One could measure reconstruction error using other
\ell_{s}
-norms.
However, the choice of norm affects both the strength of achievable guarantees and the corresponding nullspace conditions. For example, replacing the
\ell_{2}
-
\ell_{1}
structure in (
) with an
\ell_{2}
-
\ell_{2}
bound would generally require significantly more measurements—and, in fact, such a guarantee is impossible without a prohibitively large number of samples; see Theorem
or
Cohen et al. 2009
.
Thus, the form in (
) represents the strongest feasible uniform guarantee for stable recovery from linear measurements.
Moreover, a specific
\ell_{1}
-
\ell_{1}
bound will be discussed in Section
.

The following result, adapted from
Cohen et al. 2009
, shows that any recovery algorithm satisfying (
) necessarily requires the measurement matrix
{\bm{X}}
to satisfy NSP
′
of order
2k
.

Lemma 146
(Sparse recovery under NSP
′

(
Cohen et al. 2009
)
).

Let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
be a measurement matrix and
\Delta:\real^{n}\rightarrow\real^{p}
an arbitrary recovery map.
If the pair
({\bm{X}},\Delta)
satisfies the error bound (
), then
{\bm{X}}
satisfies the NSP
′
of order
2k
.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Let
{\bm{n}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
, and let
{\mathbb{S}}
be the index set corresponding to the
2k
largest (in magnitude) entries of
{\bm{n}}
.
Partition
{\mathbb{S}}
into two disjoint subsets
{\mathbb{S}}_{0}
and
{\mathbb{S}}_{1}
,each of size
k
.
Define
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\triangleq{\bm{n}}({\mathbb{S}}_{1})+{\bm{n}}({\mathbb{S}}^{c})
and
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}\triangleq-{\bm{n}}({\mathbb{S}}_{0})
, so that
{\bm{n}}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}
.
By construction,
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]
.
Therefore, the instance-optimal guarantee (
) implies exact recovery:
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}=\Delta({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime})
. Moreover, since
{\bm{n}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
, we have

{\bm{X}}{\bm{n}}={\bm{X}}\left({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}\right)=\boldsymbol{0}\qquad\implies\qquad{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}.

(4.10)

It follows that
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}=\Delta({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}})
.
Now consider the reconstruction error:

\left\lVert{\bm{n}}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{n}}\right\rVert_{2}=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}\right\rVert_{2}=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\Delta({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rVert_{2}\leq C\frac{\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})_{1}}{\sqrt{k}}=\sqrt{2}C\frac{\left\lVert{\bm{n}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}}{\sqrt{2k}},

(4.11)

where the last inequality follows from (
).
This completes the proof.

4.1.2
Stable Nullspace Property

We have introduced the NSP
′
property, which provides an
\ell_{1}
-
\ell_{2}
bound on vectors in the nullspace.
Now we turn to an analogous condition based on an
\ell_{1}
-
\ell_{1}
bound.
In particular, we will show that basis pursuit is stable under a slightly strengthened version of the nullspace property, known as the stable nullspace property (see Theorem
).

Definition 147
(Stable nullspace property).

A matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
is said to satisfy the stable nullspace property (stable NSP) over a set
{\mathbb{S}}\subset\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
with constant
0<\rho<1
, denoted SNSP(
{\mathbb{S}},\rho
), if

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\rho\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1},\quad\text{for all }{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}}).

It is said to satisfy the stable NSP of order
k
with constant
0<\rho<1
, denoted SNSP(
k,\rho
), if it satisfies the stable NSP with constant
0<\rho<1
for every subset
{\mathbb{S}}\subset\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
with
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert\leq k
.

Note again that the equality can be achieved in the definition of the stable NSP, while the equality is not achieved in the definition of the standard NSP.

The following result shows that, under the stable NSP relative to a set
{\mathbb{S}}
, the
\ell_{1}
-distance between a vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
and another vector
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}
that yields the same measurements (
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
) is controlled by the difference between their
\ell_{1}
-norms.
