This fact plays a key role in establishing error bounds for basis pursuit under the stable NSP (see Theorem
).

{theoremHigh}

[Standard consequence of stable NSP]
A matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
satisfies the stable NSP with constant
0<\rho<1
over
{\mathbb{S}}
if and only if

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\frac{1+\rho}{1-\rho}(\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{1}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}+2\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1})

(4.12)

for all vectors
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
with
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.

Observe that if
{\mathbb{S}}
consists of the indices of the
k
largest (in magnitude) entries of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
, then
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}=\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})_{1}
, the best
k
-term
\ell_{1}
approximation error.
Consequently, if
{\bm{X}}
satisfies the stable NSP of order
k
with constant
0<\rho<1
, it holds that

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\frac{1+\rho}{1-\rho}\big(\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{1}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}+2\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})_{1}\big),\quad\text{for all ${\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ with ${\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$.}

(4.13)

Before proving Theorem
, we establish a useful auxiliary inequality.

Lemma 148
.

For any set
{\mathbb{S}}\subset\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
and any vectors
{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}
, the following inequality holds:

\left\lVert({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{1}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}+\left\lVert({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})_{{{\mathbb{S}}}}\right\rVert_{1}+2\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
By the triangle inequality, we have

\displaystyle\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}

\displaystyle=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}+\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}+\left\lVert({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{1}+\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{1};

\displaystyle\left\lVert({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}

\displaystyle\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}+\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}.

Taking the summation over the two inequalities yields the desired result.

Proof
[of Theorem
]

\Leftarrow
.
Suppose that the matrix
{\bm{X}}
satisfies (
) for all vectors
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
with
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.
Given a vector
{\bm{u}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
, since
{\bm{X}}{\bm{u}}({\mathbb{S}}^{c})=-{\bm{X}}{\bm{u}}({\mathbb{S}})
, we can invoke (
) with
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\triangleq-{\bm{u}}({\mathbb{S}})
and
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\triangleq{\bm{u}}({\mathbb{S}}^{c})
.
Since
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}}^{c})=\boldsymbol{0}
, we have

\displaystyle\left\lVert{\bm{u}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\frac{1+\rho}{1-\rho}(\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}-\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{1})\qquad\implies\qquad\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\rho\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}.

This proves the stable NSP with constant
0<\rho<1
over
{\mathbb{S}}
.

\Rightarrow
.

Conversely, suppose that the matrix
{\bm{X}}
satisfies the stable NSP with constant
0<\rho<1
over
{\mathbb{S}}
.
For
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
with
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
, since
{\bm{u}}\triangleq{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
, the stable NSP yields

\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\rho\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}
.
Applying Lemma
to
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
and
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}+{\bm{u}}
, we obtain

\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{1}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}+\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{1}+2\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}.

Substituting
\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\rho\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}
into this inequality yields

\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{1}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}+\rho\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}+2\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}.

Since
\rho<1
, we can rearrange to get

\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\frac{1}{1-\rho}(\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{1}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}+2\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}).

Using
\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\rho\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}
once again, we conclude

\left\lVert{\bm{u}}\right\rVert_{1}=\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}+\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq(1+\rho)\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\frac{1+\rho}{1-\rho}(\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{1}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}+2\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}).

This completes the proof.

4.1.3
Robust Nullspace Property

In realistic settings, it is impossible to measure a signal
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
with infinite precision.
This means that the observed measurement vector
{\bm{y}}\in\real^{n}
only approximates the ideal measurement
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{n}
, satisfying

\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert\leq\epsilon

for some
\epsilon\geq 0
and some norm
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert
on
n
(typically the
\ell_{2}
-norm).
In such cases, a reconstruction algorithm should produce an estimate
\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\in\real^{p}
whose distance to the original vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\in\real^{p}
is controlled by the measurement error
\epsilon\geq 0
.
This desirable behavior is commonly referred to as
robustness
to measurement error.
We will show that if the standard basis pursuit problem (
) is replaced by the convex optimization program (
) (p.
):

\text{(P${}_{1,\epsilon}$)}\qquad\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert\leq\epsilon,

(4.14)

then robust recovery is guaranteed under a further strengthening of the nullspace property—namely, the robust nullspace property; see Theorem
for further results.

Definition 149
(
\ell_{s}
-robust nullspace property).

Let
s\geq 1
.
A matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
is said to satisfy the
\ell_{s}
-robust nullspace property (
\ell_{s}
-robust NSP) of order
k
(with respect to the norm
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert
on
n
) with constants
0<\rho<1
and
\tau>0
over a set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
, denoted RNSP(
\ell_{s},{\mathbb{S}},\rho,\tau
), if

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{s}\leq\frac{\rho}{k^{(1-\frac{1}{s})}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}+\tau\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert,\quad\text{for all }{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}.

(4.15a)

When
s=2
,
\rho=C
, and
\tau=0
, this reduces to the NSP
′
(Definition
).
In the special case
s=1
, the matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
is simply said to satisfy the robust NSP (with respect to
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert
) with constants
0<\rho<1
and
\tau>0
over a set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
, denoted RNSP(
{\mathbb{S}},\rho,\tau
), if

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\rho\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}+\tau\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert,\quad\text{for all }{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}.

(4.15b)

It is said to satisfy the
\ell_{s}
-robust NSP or robust NSP of order
k
with constants
0<\rho<1
and
\tau>0
if it satisfies the
\ell_{s}
-robust NSP or the robust NSP with constants
\rho,\tau
relative to
any
set
{\mathbb{S}}\subset\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
with
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert\leq k
, respectively.

Note that the robust NSP generalizes the stable NSP (Definition
): when
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\boldsymbol{0}
, the term
\tau\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert
vanishes, and the robust NSP reduces exactly to the stable NSP.

Remark 150
.

For
1\leq t\leq s
, the norm inequality
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{t}\leq k^{(\frac{1}{t}-\frac{1}{s})}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{s}
(see Problem
) implies that the
\ell_{s}
-robust NSP with constants
0<\rho<1
and
\tau>0
entails, for any
{\mathbb{S}}\subset\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
with
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert\leq k
,

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{t}\leq\frac{\rho}{k^{(1-\frac{1}{t})}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}+\tau k^{(\frac{1}{t}-\frac{1}{s})}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert,\quad\text{for all }{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}.

(4.16)

Thus, for
1\leq t\leq s
, the
\ell_{s}
-robust NSP implies the
\ell_{t}
-robust NSP with the same constants, up to a factor of
k^{(\frac{1}{t}-\frac{1}{s})}
in the measurement-dependent term.
In particular, the
\ell_{s}
-robust NSP is a stronger condition than the
\ell_{1}
-robust NSP, since it controls the signal on
{\mathbb{S}}
in a stronger norm (e.g.,
\ell_{2}
or
\ell_{\infty}
) while still depending only on the
\ell_{1}
-norm of the tail and the measurement residual.

Note that the definition above does not require
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
to lie in the nullspace of
\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
.
In fact, if
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
, then the term
\tau\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert
vanishes.
In this case, the robust NSP reduces exactly to the stable NSP given in Definition
. Thus, the robust NSP indeed generalizes the stable NSP.

Similar to Theorem
, we now establish a stronger equivalence that holds for any fixed index set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
.

{theoremHigh}
[Standard consequence of robust NSP]
A matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
satisfies the robust NSP with constants
0<\rho<1
and
\tau>0
relative to a set
{\mathbb{S}}
if and only if

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\frac{1+\rho}{1-\rho}\big(\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{1}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}+2\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}\big)+\frac{2\tau}{1-\rho}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rVert

(4.17)

for all vectors
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]

\Leftarrow
.
The proof follows similarly from that of Theorem
.
Assume that inequality (
) holds for all
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
. For any
{\bm{u}}\in\real^{p}
, invoking (
) with
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\triangleq-{\bm{u}}({\mathbb{S}})
and
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\triangleq{\bm{u}}({\mathbb{S}}^{c})
yields

\left\lVert{\bm{u}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\frac{1+\rho}{1-\rho}(\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}-\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{1})+\frac{2\tau}{1-\rho}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\bm{u}}\right\rVert\qquad\implies\qquad\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\rho\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}+\tau\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\bm{u}}\right\rVert.

This proves the robust NSP with constants
0<\rho<1
and
\tau>0
over
{\mathbb{S}}
.

\Rightarrow
.

Conversely, suppose that the matrix
{\bm{X}}
satisfies the robust NSP with constants
0<\rho<1
and
\tau>0
over
{\mathbb{S}}
.
Let
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
be arbitrary, and set
{\bm{u}}\triangleq{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.
Then
{\bm{u}}\in\real^{p}
, and the robust NSP and Lemma
give

\displaystyle\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{1}

\displaystyle\leq\rho\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}+\tau\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\bm{u}}\right\rVert;

\displaystyle\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}

\displaystyle\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{1}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}+\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}+2\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}.

Replacing the term
\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{1}
in the second inequality with the first inequality yields

\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\frac{1}{1-\rho}(\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{1}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}+2\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}+\tau\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\bm{u}}\right\rVert).

Using the robust NSP inequality once again, we derive

\displaystyle\left\lVert{\bm{u}}\right\rVert_{1}

\displaystyle=\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}+\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq(1+\rho)\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}+\tau\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\bm{u}}\right\rVert

\displaystyle\leq\frac{1+\rho}{1-\rho}(\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{1}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}+2\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1})+\frac{2\tau}{1-\rho}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\bm{u}}\right\rVert.

This completes the proof.

Similarly, for the
\ell_{s}
-robust NSP, we obtain the following standard consequence.
This result strengthens the previous error bound by replacing the
\ell_{1}
-error estimate with an
\ell_{t}
-error estimate for
s\geq t\geq 1
.

{theoremHigh}

[Standard consequence of
\ell_{s}
-robust NSP]
Let
1\leq t\leq s
.
Suppose that the matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
satisfies the
\ell_{s}
-robust NSP of order
k
with constants
0<\rho<1
and
\tau>0
. Then, for all
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
,

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{t}\leq\frac{C}{k^{(1-\frac{1}{t})}}(\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{1}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}+2\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})_{1})+Dk^{(\frac{1}{t}-\frac{1}{s})}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rVert,

(4.18)

where
C\triangleq(1+\rho)^{2}/(1-\rho)
and
D\triangleq\tau(3+\rho)/(1-\rho)
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
By (
), the
\ell_{s}
-robust NSP implies the
\ell_{1}
-robust and
\ell_{t}
-robust NSP (
t\leq s
) in the forms:

\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\rho\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}+\tau k^{(1-\frac{1}{s})}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\bm{u}}\right\rVert,

(4.19)

\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{t}\leq\frac{\rho}{k^{(1-\frac{1}{t})}}\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}+\tau k^{(\frac{1}{t}-\frac{1}{s})}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\bm{u}}\right\rVert,

(4.20)

for all
{\bm{u}}\in\real^{p}
and all
{\mathbb{S}}\subset\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
with
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert\leq k
. Thus, in view of (
), applying Theorem
with
{\mathbb{S}}
chosen as an index set of
k
largest (in modulus) entries of
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
leads to

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\frac{1+\rho}{1-\rho}(\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{1}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}+2\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})_{1})+\frac{2\tau}{1-\rho}k^{(1-\frac{1}{s})}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rVert.

(4.21)

Then, choosing
{\mathbb{S}}
as an index set of
k
largest (in modulus) entries of
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
, Problem
shows that

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{t}=\left\lVert({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}})_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{t}+\left\lVert({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}})_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{t}\leq\frac{1}{k^{(1-\frac{1}{t})}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}+\left\lVert({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}})_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{t}.

Now substitute the bounds from (
) with
{\bm{u}}={\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
and (
) into this inequality:

\displaystyle\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{t}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\eqref{equation:lsrob_nsp_gen_e2}}}{{\leq}}\frac{1}{k^{(1-\frac{1}{t})}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}+\frac{\rho}{k^{(1-\frac{1}{t})}}\left\lVert({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}})_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}+\tau k^{(\frac{1}{t}-\frac{1}{s})}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rVert

\displaystyle\leq\frac{1+\rho}{k^{(1-\frac{1}{t})}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}+\tau k^{(\frac{1}{t}-\frac{1}{s})}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rVert

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\eqref{equation:lsrob_nsp_gen_e3}}}{{\leq}}C(\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{1}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}+2\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})_{1})+D\left\lVert{\bm{X}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rVert.

This completes the proof.

4.2
Spark, Mutual Coherence, and Uniqueness of Sparse Recovery

A full row rank underdetermined linear system

{\bm{X}}_{n\times p}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{p\times 1}={\bm{y}}_{n\times 1},\quad\text{with}\quad n<p,

has infinitely many solutions.
Suppose we seek the sparsest solution—that is, the one with the fewest nonzero entries.
Can such a solution ever be unique? And how can we find the sparsest solution? This section briefly addresses the first question (see also Chapter
for further discussion); the second will be covered in Chapters
and
.

4.2.1
Spark

If we wish to be able to recover all sparse signals
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
from the measurements
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
,
then for any two distinct vectors
{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]=\{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\mid\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{0}\leq k\}
, we must have
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\neq{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}
.
Otherwise, the measurements
{\bm{y}}
would not allow us to distinguish between
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
and
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}
.
More formally, if
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}
, then
{\bm{X}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime})=\boldsymbol{0}
, and the difference satisfies
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[2k]
.
Therefore,
{\bm{X}}
uniquely represents all
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]
if and only if its nullspace
\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
contains no (nonzero) vector from
{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[2k]
.

This condition can be characterized in several equivalent ways. One of the most common is via the spark of the matrix
{\bm{X}}
, a key concept introduced in
Donoho and Elad 2003
that plays a central role in analyzing the uniqueness of sparse solutions.

Definition 151
(Spark
(
Gorodnitsky and Rao 1997
;
Donoho and Elad 2003
)
).

Given a matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
, its spark, denoted
\sigma=\mathrm{spark}({\bm{X}})
, is defined as the smallest possible number such that there exists a subgroup of
\sigma
columns from
{\bm{X}}
that are linearly dependent.
That is,

\sigma=\min\{s:\text{ there exists a subset of $s$ columns of ${\bm{X}}$ that are linearly dependent}\}.

It always holds that

\sigma=\mathrm{spark}({\bm{X}})\in[2,\min\{n,p\}+1].

The spark is closely related to the
Kruskal rank
, denoted
\mathrm{rank}_{k}({\bm{X}})
or
k_{{\bm{X}}}
, which is defined as the largest integer
r
such that every set of
r
columns of
{\bm{X}}
is linearly independent (see, e.g.,
Lu 2021a
for further details).
Recall that the (standard) rank of a matrix is the maximum number of linearly independent columns in
{\bm{X}}
(Definition
).
While the definitions of rank and Kruskal rank (or spark) appear similar, computing the spark is significantly more difficult: it requires a combinatorial search over all possible subsets of columns of
{\bm{X}}
.
By definition, any nonzero vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
satisfying
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\boldsymbol{0}
must have at least
\mathrm{spark}({\bm{X}})
nonzero entries. In other words,

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{0}\geq\mathrm{spark}({\bm{X}})\qquad\text{if}\qquad{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\boldsymbol{0},\text{ and }{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\neq\boldsymbol{0},

(4.22)

since fewer than
\mathrm{spark}({\bm{X}})
columns cannot form a nontrivial linear combination equal to zero.

This property leads to a simple and powerful criterion for the uniqueness of sparse solutions to underdetermined systems.

{theoremHigh}
[Uniqueness under spark
(
Gorodnitsky and Rao 1997
;
Donoho and Elad 2003
;
Bruckstein et al. 2009
)
]
If the linear system
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\bm{y}}
admits a solution
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
satisfying
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{0}<\mathrm{spark}({\bm{X}})/2
, then this solution is necessarily the (unique) sparsest solution.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Let
\widetilde{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
be any other solution such that
{\bm{X}}\widetilde{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}={\bm{y}}
.
Then
{\bm{X}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})=\boldsymbol{0}
, so
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\widetilde{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
lies in the nullspace of
{\bm{X}}
.
By (
),

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{0}+\big\lVert\widetilde{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{0}\geq\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\widetilde{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{0}\geq\mathrm{spark}({\bm{X}}).

(4.23)

Since we have a solution satisfying
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{0}<\mathrm{spark}({\bm{X}})/2
, we conclude that any alternative solution
\widetilde{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
necessarily has more than
\mathrm{spark}({\bm{X}})/2
nonzeros, proving that
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is the unique sparsest solution.

The theorem can be put in a different way as follows.

Corollary 152
.

For any vector
{\bm{y}}\in\real^{n}
, there exists at most one solution
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]
such that
{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
if and only if
\mathrm{spark}({\bm{X}})>2k
.

Proof
[of Corollary
]
We first assume that, for every
{\bm{y}}\in\real^{n}
, there is at most one solution
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]
satisfying
{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
. Suppose, for contradiction, that
\mathrm{spark}({\bm{X}})\leq 2k
.
By definition of spark, this implies that there exists a set of at most
2k
columns of
{\bm{X}}
that are linearly dependent.
Consequently, there exists a nonzero vector
{\bm{n}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
such that
{\bm{n}}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[2k]
.
In this case, since
{\bm{n}}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[2k]
we can write
{\bm{n}}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}
, where
{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]
, whence we have that
{\bm{X}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime})=\boldsymbol{0}
and hence
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}
.
But this contradicts the assumption there exists at most one solution
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]
such that
{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.
Hence, we must have that
\mathrm{spark}({\bm{X}})>2k
.

Conversely, suppose
\mathrm{spark}({\bm{X}})>2k
. Assume that for some
{\bm{y}}\in\real^{n}
, there exist two vectors
{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]
such that
{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}
.
Then
{\bm{X}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime})=\boldsymbol{0}
, so
{\bm{n}}\triangleq{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{x}})
.
Moreover, since both
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
and
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}
have at most
k
nonzeros, their difference satisfies
\left\lVert{\bm{n}}\right\rVert_{0}\leq 2k
.
However, because
\mathrm{spark}({\bm{X}})>2k
,
the nullspace of
{\bm{X}}
contains no nonzero vector with
\ell_{0}
-norm
\leq 2k
.
Therefore,
{\bm{n}}=\boldsymbol{0}
, which implies
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}
. This proves uniqueness, completing the proof.

Clearly, the spark of a matrix is highly informative: larger values of
\mathrm{spark}({\bm{X}})
guarantee uniqueness for sparser solutions. How large can the spark be? By definition,

2\leq\mathrm{spark}({\bm{X}})\leq\min\{n,p\}+1
.
For example, if
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
has entries drawn independently from a continuous distribution (e.g., Gaussian), then with probability one, every subset of
\min\{n,p\}
columns is linearly independent. In particular, when
n<p
, we have
\mathrm{spark}({\bm{X}})=n+1
almost surely, since no more than
n
columns can be linearly independent in
n
. Thus, uniqueness is guaranteed for any solution with fewer than
(n+1)/2
nonzeros.

4.2.2
Mutual Coherence

While the spark, the standard NSP, and its robust variants all provide theoretical guarantees for the recovery of sparse signals (see Section
for details),
verifying that a general matrix
{\bm{X}}
satisfies any of these properties is computationally intractable.
Specifically, each condition requires examining on the order of
\binom{p}{k}
submatrices, leading to combinatorial complexity.
For example, Theorem
shows that for any sparsest solution
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
to the linear system
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\bm{y}}
, it holds that
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{0}\leq\mathrm{spark}({\bm{X}})/2
.
However, computing the spark of a matrix is at least as difficult as solving the
\ell_{0}
-minimization problem in (
) (p.
).
In many practical settings, it is therefore preferable to use easily computable properties of
{\bm{X}}
that still yield meaningful recovery guarantees. One such property is the
mutual coherence
of the matrix.

Mutual coherence provides a simple yet effective measure of how suitable a measurement matrix is for sparse recovery. In general, the smaller the mutual coherence, the better the performance of recovery algorithms.

Definition 153
(Mutual coherence
(
Mallat and Zhang 1993
;
Donoho et al. 2001
;
Bruckstein et al. 2009
)
).

The mutual coherence (also known as pairwise coherence or simply coherence) of a given matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
is defined as the largest absolute value of the normalized inner product between any two distinct columns of
{\bm{X}}
. Denoting the
i
-th column in
{\bm{X}}
by
{\bm{x}}_{i}
, mutual coherence is given by

\mu({\bm{X}})=\max_{1\leq i,j\leq p,i\neq j}\frac{\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{x}}_{i},{\bm{x}}_{j}\right\rangle\right\rvert}{\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{j}\right\rVert_{2}}\in[0,1].

(4.24)

Mutual coherence characterizes the degree of linear dependence among the columns of
{\bm{X}}
. It quantifies the maximum similarity between any pair of distinct columns: lower coherence implies that the columns are closer to being orthogonal. This is advantageous because it suggests that each column contributes unique information—a key requirement for reliable sparse representation and recovery.

For an orthogonal matrix (Definition
), the columns are mutually orthonormal, so the mutual coherence is exactly zero. In contrast, for underdetermined systems where
p>n
(i.e., more columns than rows),
\mu({\bm{X}})
must be strictly positive. In such cases, we aim to minimize
\mu({\bm{X}})
to emulate the favorable properties of orthogonal matrices as closely as possible.

To illustrate the extremes, consider now a matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
with
n\geq p
. In this case,
\mu({\bm{X}})=0
if and only if the columns of
{\bm{X}}
are orthonormal. In particular, when
{\bm{X}}
is square (
n=p
), this occurs precisely when
{\bm{X}}
is an orthogonal matrix.

In compressed sensing, however, we are primarily interested in the underdetermined setting where
n<p
. Here, perfect orthogonality among all columns is impossible, and there are fundamental limits on how small the coherence can be. Roughly speaking, small coherence implies that submatrices formed by a moderate number of columns are well-conditioned, which is crucial for stable sparse recovery.
It can be shown that the mutual coherence of any matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
with
p>n
always satisfies

\mu({\bm{X}})\in\left[\sqrt{\frac{p-n}{n(p-1)}},1\right].

The lower bound is known as the
Welch bound

(
Rosenfeld 1997
;
Strohmer and Heath Jr 2003
;
Welch 2003
)
; a proof is provided in Theorem
.
Note that when
p\gg n
, this bound simplifies approximately to
\mu({\bm{X}})\geq 1/\sqrt{n}
.

Equivalently, mutual coherence reflects—on an entry-wise level—how close the Gram matrix
{\bm{G}}={\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}
is to the
p
-dimensional identity matrix
{\bm{I}}
.

Lemma 154
(Interpretation of mutual coherence w.r.t. spectral norm).

Let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
be a matrix with unit-norm columns.
Then

\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}-{\bm{I}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\max_{i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}}\sum_{j\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}\setminus\{i\}}\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{x}}_{i},{\bm{x}}_{j}\right\rangle\right\rvert,

(4.25)

where
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{2}
denotes the spectral norm of a matrix.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Let
{\bm{H}}\triangleq{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}-{\bm{I}}
.
By the Gershgorin circle theorem (Theorem
), every eigenvalue
\lambda
of
{\bm{H}}
satisfies

\left\lvert\lambda-h_{ii}\right\rvert\leq\sum_{j\neq i}\left\lvert h_{ij}\right\rvert.

Since the diagonal entries of
{\bm{H}}
are zero (
h_{ii}=0
), this simplifies to

\left\lvert\lambda\right\rvert\leq\sum_{j\neq i}\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{x}}_{i},{\bm{x}}_{j}\right\rangle\right\rvert.

Taking the maximum over all
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
, we obtain

\left\lVert{\bm{H}}\right\rVert_{2}=\max_{\lambda\in\Lambda({\bm{H}})}\left\lvert\lambda\right\rvert\leq\max_{i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}}\sum_{j\neq i}\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{x}}_{i},{\bm{x}}_{j}\right\rangle\right\rvert.

where
\Lambda({\bm{H}})
denotes the spectrum of
{\bm{H}}
.
This completes the proof.

A stronger condition than mutual coherence is the
mutual incoherence condition
.
This condition is defined with respect to any subset
{\mathbb{S}}\subset\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
.

Definition 155
(Mutual incoherence).

The mutual incoherence (also known as the irrepresentable condition) for a matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
holds for a subset
{\mathbb{S}}\subset\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
if there exists some
\gamma>0
such that

\max_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\left\lVert({\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}})^{-1}{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{1}\leq 1-\gamma.

(4.26)

To interpret this condition, observe that the submatrix
{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}\in\real^{n\times k}
(where
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert=k
) consists of the columns of
{\bm{X}}
indexed by the support set
{\mathbb{S}}
. For each index
i
in the complement
{\mathbb{S}}^{c}
, the vector
({\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}})^{-1}{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\bm{x}}_{i}
contains the coefficients obtained by regressing
{\bm{x}}_{i}
onto the columns of
{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}
. The
\ell_{1}
-norm of this vector quantifies how well
{\bm{x}}_{i}
can be represented as a linear combination of the columns in
{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}
.
In the ideal scenario, every column
{\bm{x}}_{i}
with
i\in{\mathbb{S}}^{c}
would be orthogonal to all columns in
{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}
. In that case, the regression coefficients would all be zero, and we would have
\gamma=1
. Of course, in high-dimensional settings where
p\gg n
, such perfect orthogonality is impossible. Nevertheless, we may still hope for a form of “near orthogonality,” which is precisely what the mutual incoherence condition captures when
\gamma
is close to 1.

It is worth noting that the term “mutual incoherence” is sometimes used informally to refer to small pairwise correlations between columns—i.e., a small mutual coherence
\mu({\bm{X}})
. However, the formal mutual incoherence condition in Definition
is strictly stronger, as it involves collective behavior of groups of columns rather than just pairwise interactions.

Mutual coherence can sometimes be related to other fundamental properties such as spark, the NSP, and the restricted isometry property (RIP, as a hindsight, see Definition
for reference). For instance, spark and mutual coherence are connected via the Gershgorin circletheorem (Theorem
), as shown in the following proposition.

Proposition 156
(Spark
\&
mutual coherence).

For any matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
, it follows that

\textup{spark}({\bm{X}})\geq 1+\frac{1}{\mu({\bm{X}})}.

(4.27)

Proof
[of Proposition
]
First, normalize the columns of
{\bm{X}}
to unit
\ell_{2}
-norm, obtaining a new matrix
\widetilde{{\bm{X}}}
.
This operation preserves both the spark and the mutual coherence. Let
{\bm{G}}=\widetilde{{\bm{X}}}^{\top}\widetilde{{\bm{X}}}
be the corresponding Gram matrix. Its entries satisfy:

\{g_{kk}=1,\;\forall\,1\leq k\leq p\}\quad\text{and}\quad\{\left\lvert g_{ij}\right\rvert\leq\mu({\bm{X}}),\;\forall\,1\leq i,j\leq p,\;i\neq j\}.

Now consider any
l\times l
principal submatrix of
{\bm{G}}
, corresponding to a subset of
l
columns from
\widetilde{{\bm{X}}}
(and computing their sub-Gram matrix). From the Gershgorin circle theorem (Theorem
or Theorem
), if this minor is diagonally dominant (i.e., if
\sum_{j\neq i}\left\lvert g_{ij}\right\rvert<\left\lvert g_{ii}\right\rvert
for every
i
), then this submatrix of
{\bm{G}}
is positive definite, and so those
l
columns from
\widetilde{{\bm{X}}}
are linearly independent satisfying:

g_{ii}=1
,
1\leq i\leq l
;

\left\lvert g_{ij}\right\rvert\leq\mu({\bm{X}})
,
1\leq i,j\leq l
,
i\neq j
.

Since
l<\mathrm{spark}({\bm{X}})
, the spark condition and the positive definiteness implies
(l-1)\mu({\bm{X}})<1
or, equivalently,
l<1+1/\mu({\bm{X}})
.
Therefore, we can choose
l
such that
l<1+1/\mu({\bm{X}})\leq l+1\leq\mathrm{spark}({\bm{X}})
, yielding
\mathrm{spark}({\bm{X}})\geq 1+1/\mu({\bm{X}})
.

By combining Theorem
or Corollary
with Proposition
, we obtain the following condition on
{\bm{X}}
that guarantees uniqueness of sparse solutions.

{theoremHigh}

[Uniqueness under mutual coherence
(
Donoho et al. 2001
;
Donoho and Elad 2003
)
]
Consider the linear system
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\bm{y}}
.
If this system admits a solution
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
satisfying

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{0}<\frac{1}{2}\left(1+\frac{1}{\mu({\bm{X}})}\right),

then the solution
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is necessarily the (unique) sparsest solution.
Equivalently, if

k<\frac{1}{2}\left(1+\frac{1}{\mu({\bm{X}})}\right),

then for each measurement vector
{\bm{y}}\in\real^{n}
, there exists at most one signal
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]
such that
{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.

This theorem once again partially answers the following fundamental questions:

When can we guarantee uniqueness of the sparsest solution?

Can a candidate solution be verified as globally optimal for (
)?

We have seen that any solution sufficiently sparse—specifically, sparser than the bounds above—is guaranteed to be unique among all solutions of comparable sparsity. Consequently, such a solution must also be the global minimizer of (
). This shows that seeking sparse solutions is not merely a heuristic; under appropriate conditions, it leads to a well-posed inverse problem with strong theoretical guarantees.

Comparing Theorems
and
, we observe that they are structurally similar but rely on different assumptions. Theorem
, which is based on the spark, is sharp and generally much stronger than Theorem
, which depends only on mutual coherence—a quantity that provides a lower bound on the spark.

Indeed, mutual coherence cannot be smaller than approximately
1/\sqrt{n}
(as implied by the Welch bound, i.e.,
\mu({\bm{X}})\in\left[\sqrt{\frac{p-n}{n(p-1)}},1\right]
), so the sparsity level guaranteed by Theorem
never exceeds roughly
\sqrt{n}/2
.
That is, Theorem
, together with the Welch bound, provides an upper bound on the level of sparsity
k
that guarantees uniqueness using coherence:
k=\mathcal{O}\left(\sqrt{n}\right)
.
In contrast, the spark can be as large as
n
(assuming
p>n
), in which case Theorem
allows sparsity levels up to
n/2
—a significantly more permissive bound.

We now show that mutual coherence also implies the NSP condition.

Proposition 157
(Coherence
\implies
NSP).

Let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
.
Suppose that for some integer
k\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
, the mutual coherence satisfies the bound
\mu({\bm{X}})<\frac{1}{3k}
.
Then
{\bm{X}}
satisfies the NSP of order
k
.

Proof
[of Proposition
]
Without loss of generality, we may assume that all columns of
{\bm{X}}
are normalized to unit
\ell_{2}
-norm, i.e.,
\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}=1
for all
i
(since mutual coherence and the NSP are invariant under column rescaling).
To simplify the analysis, suppose more generally that
\mu({\bm{X}})<\frac{\delta}{k}
for some
\delta>0
, and determine the smallest
\delta
that guarantees the NSP. We will see that
\delta=1/3
suffices.

Let
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
be any subset with
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert=k
, and let
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{C}}[{\mathbb{S}}]\setminus\{\boldsymbol{0}\}
.
To verify the NSP
\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})\cap{\mathbb{C}}[{\mathbb{S}}]=\{\boldsymbol{0}\}
, it suffices to show that
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}>0
, and so we begin with the lower bound

\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}+{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\geq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+2{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}.

We now bound the cross term. Using the definition of mutual coherence and the triangle inequality,

\displaystyle 2\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rvert

\displaystyle\leq 2\Big\lvert\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}}\sum_{j\in{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\left\lvert\beta_{i}\right\rvert\left\lvert\beta_{j}\right\rvert\left\langle{\bm{x}}_{i},{\bm{x}}_{j}\right\rangle\Big\rvert

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(i)}}{{\leq}}2\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}\mu({\bm{X}})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(ii)}}{{\leq}}\frac{2\delta\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}^{2}}{k}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(iii)}}{{\leq}}2\delta\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},

where the inequality (i) follows from the definition of the mutual coherence; the inequality (ii) exploits the assumed bound on
\mu({\bm{X}})
combined with the fact that
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{C}}[{\mathbb{S}}]
; and the inequality (iii) follows from the fact that
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\sqrt{k}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}
(Exercise
) since the cardinality of
{\mathbb{S}}
is at most
k
.
Combining the two inequalities, we have

\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\geq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-2\delta\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

(4.28)

It remains to lower-bound
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
.
By Lemma
, we have

\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}-{\bm{I}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\max_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}}\sum_{j\in{\mathbb{S}}\setminus\{i\}}\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{x}}_{i},{\bm{x}}_{j}\right\rangle\right\rvert\leq k\frac{\delta}{k}=\delta.

This shows all eigenvalues of
{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}-{\bm{I}}
lie in the interval
[-\delta,\delta]
and
-\delta{\bm{I}}\preceq{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}-{\bm{I}}\preceq\delta{\bm{I}}
.
Therefore,
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\geq(1-\delta)\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
, and combined with the bound (
), we conclude that
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}>(1-3\delta)\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
, so that
\delta=1/3
ensures strict positivity, which proves that
{\bm{X}}
satisfies the NSP of order
k
.

Moreover, another direct application of the Gershgorin circle theorem (Theorem
) links mutual coherence to the RIP (see Definition
for reference).

Proposition 158
(Coherence
\implies
RIP).

If
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
has unit-norm columns and coherence
\mu=\mu({\bm{X}})
, then
{\bm{X}}
satisfies the RIP of order
k
with
\delta=(k-1)\mu
for all
k<1/\mu
.

The proof follows the same reasoning as in Proposition
, using diagonal dominance of sub-Gram matrices.

These results underscore the importance of small mutual coherence in compressed sensing matrix design. Coherence bounds have been studied extensively for both deterministic and random constructions. For instance, there exist explicit deterministic matrices of size
n\times n^{2}
that achieve the Welch lower bound
\mu({\bm{X}})=1/\sqrt{n}
, such as Gabor frames generated from the Alltop sequence
(
Herman and Strohmer 2009
)
and equiangular tight frames
(
Tropp 2008
)
. Using such matrices, stable recovery of
k
-sparse signals is possible with
n=\mathcal{O}(k^{2}\ln p)
measurements.

In contrast, for random matrices with i.i.d. entries having zero mean and finite variance, the coherence concentrates around
\mu({\bm{X}})=\sqrt{(2\ln p)/n}

in the asymptotic regime
(n,p\rightarrow\infty)

(
Cai and Jiang 2011
;
Cand 2008
;
Donoho 2006
)
. Substituting this into the coherence-based sparsity bound yields

k=\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{n/(\ln p)})
,
which—after rearrangement—again gives
n=\mathcal{O}(k^{2}\ln p)
.
However, we will not delve into these details in this book,
while the RIP related results will be introduced in Chapters
and
.

4.2.3
\ell_{1}
-Coherence

A more general notion than mutual coherence is the
\ell_{1}
-coherence, also known as the Babel function.

Definition 159
(
\ell_{1}
-coherence
(
Foucart and Rauhut 2013
)
).

Let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
. The
\ell_{1}
-coherence function (or Babel function)
\mu_{1}
of the matrix
{\bm{X}}
is defined for
1\leq k\leq p-1
by

\mu_{1}({\bm{X}},k)=\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}{\mathbb{S}}\subset\{1,\ldots,p\}\\
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert=k\end{subarray}}\max_{j\notin{\mathbb{S}}}\left\{\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}}\frac{\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{x}}_{i},{\bm{x}}_{j}\right\rangle\right\rvert}{\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{j}\right\rVert_{2}}\right\}.

It is straightforward to verify that, for
1\leq k\leq p-1
,

\mu({\bm{X}})\leq\mu_{1}({\bm{X}},k)\leq k\cdot\mu({\bm{X}}),

(4.29a)

and more generally that, for
1\leq k,t\leq p-1
with
k+t\leq p-1
,

\max\{\mu_{1}({\bm{X}},k),\mu_{1}({\bm{X}},t)\}\leq\mu_{1}({\bm{X}},k+t)\leq\mu_{1}({\bm{X}},k)+\mu_{1}({\bm{X}},t).

(4.29b)

Mutual coherence captures the worst-case pairwise correlation between any two distinct columns of
{\bm{X}}
, measuring only the largest absolute normalized inner product. In contrast,
\ell_{1}
-coherence quantifies the total interference that any set of
k
columns can exert on another column. Specifically, it measures the maximum sum of absolute normalized inner products between a fixed column
{\bm{x}}_{j}
and any collection of
k
other columns.

Note that by (
), we have
\mu_{1}({\bm{X}},1)=\mu_{1}({\bm{X}})
, so mutual coherence is simply the special case of
\ell_{1}
-coherence with
k=1
.

Both mutual coherence and the
\ell_{1}
-coherence function are
invariant
under left multiplication by an orthogonal matrix
{\bm{Q}}\in\real^{n\times n}
.
Indeed, the columns of
{\bm{Q}}{\bm{X}}
are
{\bm{Q}}{\bm{x}}_{1},{\bm{Q}}{\bm{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\bm{Q}}{\bm{x}}_{p}
, and since orthogonal transformations preserve inner products,

\left\langle{\bm{Q}}{\bm{x}}_{i},{\bm{Q}}{\bm{x}}_{j}\right\rangle=\left\langle{\bm{x}}_{i},{\bm{x}}_{j}\right\rangle.

Moreover, by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality
\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{x}}_{i},{\bm{x}}_{j}\right\rangle\right\rvert\leq\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{j}\right\rVert_{2}
, so the normalized inner product is always at most 1 in magnitude.
Consequently, the mutual coherence satisfies

\mu({\bm{X}})\leq 1
.

As previously discussed,
\mu({\bm{X}})=0
if and only if the columns of
{\bm{X}}
form an orthonormal system. In particular, when
{\bm{X}}
is square (
n=p
), this occurs precisely when
{\bm{X}}
is an orthogonal matrix.
However, in compressive sensing we are primarily interested in the underdetermined regime, where
n<p
. In this setting, perfect orthogonality among all columns is impossible, and there are fundamental limits on how small the mutual coherence can be. These limitations will be explored in Section
.
For now, we simply note that small coherence implies that submatrices formed by a moderate number of columns are well-conditioned, which is essential for stable sparse recovery.

We have already shown in Proposition
that mutual coherence implies the RIP (Definition
) under mild conditions. An analogous result holds for
\ell_{1}
-coherence.

{theoremHigh}
[
\ell_{1}
-coherence and RIP]
Let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
be a matrix with
\ell_{2}
-normalized columns (i.e., each column has unit norm), and let
1\leq k\leq p
.
Then, for every vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
with
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]
(i.e.,
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{0}\leq k
),

\big(1-\mu_{1}({\bm{X}},k-1)\big)\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\big(1+\mu_{1}({\bm{X}},k-1)\big)\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

Equivalently, for every index set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
with
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert\leq k
, all eigenvalues of the Gram matrix
{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
lie in the interval

\lambda({\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}})\in\left[1-\mu_{1}({\bm{X}},k-1),1+\mu_{1}({\bm{X}},k-1)\right].

In particular, if
\mu_{1}({\bm{X}},k-1)<1
,
then
{\bm{X}}
satisfies the RIP of order
k
with constant
\delta=\mu_{1}({\bm{X}},k-1)
(see Definition
), and
{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
is nonsingular for all such
{\mathbb{S}}
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Let
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
with
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert\leq k
.
Since
{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
is symmetric and positive semidefinite, it admits an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors with real, nonnegative eigenvalues (Theorem
).
Denote its smallest and largest eigenvalues by
\lambda_{\min}
and
\lambda_{\max}
, respectively.
For any
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
supported on
{\mathbb{S}}
, we have
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
, thus the maximum of

\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

over the set
\{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p},\;\mathrm{supp}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\subseteq{\mathbb{S}},\;\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}=1\}
is
\lambda_{\max}
and that its minimum is
\lambda_{\min}
.
Hence, the stated bounds on
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}
are equivalent to the eigenvalue inclusion claimed in the theorem.

Now, because the columns of
{\bm{X}}
are normalized, the diagonal entries of
{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
are all equal to 1.
Applying the Gershgorin circle theorem (Theorem
), each eigenvalue lies within at least one disc centered at 1 with radius

r_{i}=\sum_{j\in{\mathbb{S}},j\neq i}\left\lvert({\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}})_{ij}\right\rvert=\sum_{j\in{\mathbb{S}},j\neq i}\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{x}}_{j},{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rangle\right\rvert\leq\mu_{1}({\bm{X}},k-1),\quad i\in{\mathbb{S}},

where the inequality follows from the definition of
\mu_{1}({\bm{X}},k-1)
(since
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\setminus\{i\}\right\rvert\leq k-1
).
Because all eigenvalues are real, they must lie in the interval
\left[1-\mu_{1}({\bm{X}},k-1),1+\mu_{1}({\bm{X}},k-1)\right]
, as claimed.

The above result shows that if
\mu_{1}({\bm{X}},k-1)<1
, then
{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
is nonsingular for all such
{\mathbb{S}}
. Expand writing here…

The result above shows that if
\mu_{1}({\bm{X}},k-1)<1
, then the Gram matrix
{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
is nonsingular for every index set
{\mathbb{S}}
with
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert\leq k
.
This guarantees that any
k
columns of
{\bm{X}}
are linearly independent—a crucial property for sparse recovery. The following corollary strengthens this observation by providing a condition under which any
2k
columns remain linearly independent, which is often required in the analysis of algorithms like orthogonal matching pursuit or in establishing uniqueness of
k
-sparse solutions.

Corollary 160
.

Let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
have
\ell_{2}
-normalized columns, and let
k\geq 1
be an integer.
If

\mu_{1}({\bm{X}},k)+\mu_{1}({\bm{X}},k-1)<1,

then for every index set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
with
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert\leq 2k
, the matrix
{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
is invertible.
Consequently,
{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
has full column rank.
In particular, this conclusion holds whenever

\mu({\bm{X}})<\frac{1}{2k-1}.

‘

Proof
[of Corollary
]
By inequality (
), we have
\mu_{1}({\bm{X}},2k-1)\leq\mu_{1}({\bm{X}},k)+\mu_{1}({\bm{X}},k-1)<1
.
Now consider any index set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
with
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert\leq 2k
. Applying Theorem
with sparsity level
2k
, we obtain that the smallest eigenvalue of
{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
satisfies
\lambda_{\min}\geq 1-\mu_{1}({\bm{X}},2k-1)>0
.
Hence,
{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
is positive definite and therefore invertible.
To see that
{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
has full column rank, suppose
{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}{\bm{z}}=\boldsymbol{0}
for some vector
{\bm{z}}\in\real^{\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert}
, which implies
{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}{\bm{z}}=\boldsymbol{0}
.
Since
{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
is invertible, it follows that
{\bm{z}}=\boldsymbol{0}
. This proves the first statement.
Finally, using inequality (
), we bound
\mu_{1}({\bm{X}},k)+\mu_{1}({\bm{X}},k-1)\leq(2k-1)\mu({\bm{X}})<1
if
\mu({\bm{X}})<1/(2k-1)
.

4.2.4
Bounds for Mutual Coherence and
\ell_{1}
-Coherence

In this subsection, we establish lower bounds for both the mutual coherence and the
\ell_{1}
-coherence function of a matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}

with
n<p
.

Matrices that achieve these lower bounds share a distinctive structure: their columns form equiangular tight frames, defined below.

Definition 161
(Equiangular system, and tight frame system).

A matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
with
\ell_{2}
-normalized columns is called equiangular if there is a exists
C\geq 0
such that

\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{x}}_{i},{\bm{x}}_{j}\right\rangle\right\rvert=C\quad\text{for all }i\neq j,\;i,j\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}.

A matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
is called a tight frame if there exists a constant
\lambda>0
such that any of the following equivalent conditions holds:

1.

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\lambda\sum_{j=1}^{p}\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\bm{x}}_{j}\right\rangle^{2}
for all
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{n}
,

2.

{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=\lambda\sum_{j=1}^{p}\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\bm{x}}_{j}\right\rangle{\bm{x}}_{j}
for all
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{n}
,

3.

{\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{\top}=\frac{1}{\lambda}{\bm{I}}_{n}
.

As the name suggests, a system of
\ell_{2}
-normalized vectors is called an equiangular tight frame if it satisfies both properties above.

Such systems are precisely those that attain the lower bound stated next, known as the
Welch bound
.

{theoremHigh}
[Welch bound: lower bound of mutual coherence
(
Rosenfeld 1997
;
Strohmer and Heath Jr 2003
;
Welch 2003
)
]
Let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
with
p>n
.
Then its mutual coherence satisfies

\mu({\bm{X}})\geq\sqrt{\frac{p-n}{n(p-1)}}.

(4.30)

Equality holds if and only if the columns of
{\bm{X}}
form an equiangular tight frame.
Note that when
p\gg n
, the lower bound is approximately
\mu({\bm{X}})\geq 1/\sqrt{n}
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Without loss of generality, we assume that
{\bm{X}}
have
\ell_{2}
-normalized columns.
Define the Gram matrix
{\bm{G}}\triangleq{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}\in\real^{p\times p}
and the matrix
{\bm{H}}\triangleq{\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{\top}\in\real^{n\times n}
.
Since the columns of
{\bm{X}}
are
\ell_{2}
-normalized, we have

\mathrm{tr}({\bm{G}})=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=p
.
Recall that the Frobenius inner product

\left\langle{\bm{A}},{\bm{B}}\right\rangle_{F}\triangleq\mathrm{tr}({\bm{A}}{\bm{B}}^{\top})=\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}a_{ij}b_{ij}

induces the Frobenius norm
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{F}
(Definition
).
By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality,

\mathrm{tr}({\bm{H}})\leq\left\lVert{\bm{H}}\right\rVert_{F}\left\lVert{\bm{I}}_{n}\right\rVert_{F}=\sqrt{n}\sqrt{\mathrm{tr}({\bm{H}}{\bm{H}}^{\top})}.

(4.31)

Using the cyclic invariance of the trace, we compute

\displaystyle\mathrm{tr}({\bm{H}}{\bm{H}}^{\top})

\displaystyle=\mathrm{tr}\big(({\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{\top})({\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{\top})\big)=\mathrm{tr}({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}})=\mathrm{tr}({\bm{G}}{\bm{G}}^{\top})=\sum_{i,j=1}^{p,p}\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{x}}_{i},{\bm{x}}_{j}\right\rangle\right\rvert^{2}

\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\sum_{i,j=1,i\neq j}^{p,p}\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{x}}_{i},{\bm{x}}_{j}\right\rangle\right\rvert^{2}=p+\sum_{i,j=1,i\neq j}^{p,p}\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{x}}_{i},{\bm{x}}_{j}\right\rangle\right\rvert^{2}.

By the cyclic invariance of the trace again, it follows that
\mathrm{tr}({\bm{G}})=\mathrm{tr}({\bm{H}})
, whence we have

p^{2}\leq n\left(p+\sum_{i,j=1,i\neq j}^{p,p}\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{x}}_{i},{\bm{x}}_{j}\right\rangle\right\rvert^{2}\right).

(4.32)

By the definition of mutual coherence,

\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{x}}_{i},{\bm{x}}_{j}\right\rangle\right\rvert\leq\mu({\bm{X}}),\quad\text{ for all }1\leq i\neq j\leq p,

(4.33)

we obtain

p^{2}\leq n(p+(p^{2}-p)\mu({\bm{X}})^{2}),

which rearranges to the claimed bound (
).
Finally, equality holds if and only if equality holds in both (
) and (
). Equality in (
) implies
{\bm{H}}=\lambda{\bm{I}}_{n}
for some
\lambda>0
, i.e.,
{\bm{X}}
is a tight frame. Equality in (
) implies that all off-diagonal inner products have the same magnitude, i.e.,
{\bm{X}}
is equiangular. Hence, equality occurs precisely when
{\bm{X}}
forms an equiangular tight frame.

The Welch bound can be extended to the
\ell_{1}
-coherence function for small values of its argument.

{theoremHigh}
[Welch bound: lower bound of
\ell_{1}
-coherence]
Let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
with
p>n
.
Then its
\ell_{1}
-coherence function satisfies

\mu_{1}({\bm{X}},k)\geq k\sqrt{\frac{p-n}{n(p-1)}},\quad\text{for}\quad k<\sqrt{p-1}.

(4.34)

Equality holds if and only if the columns of
{\bm{X}}
form an equiangular tight frame.

The proof relies on the following auxiliary result.

Lemma 162
.

Let
s<\sqrt{m}
, and let
(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\ldots,\alpha_{m})
be a nonnegative, nonincreasing sequence satisfying

\alpha_{1}\geq\alpha_{2}\geq\ldots\geq\alpha_{m}\geq 0\quad\text{and}\quad\alpha_{1}^{2}+\alpha_{2}^{2}+\ldots+\alpha_{m}^{2}\geq\frac{m}{s^{2}}.

Then

\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}+\ldots+\alpha_{s}\geq 1,

with equality if and only if
\alpha_{1}=\alpha_{2}=\ldots=\alpha_{m}=1/s
.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
It suffices to prove the contrapositive:

\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\alpha_{1}\geq\alpha_{2}\geq\ldots\geq\alpha_{m}\geq 0\\
\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}+\ldots+\alpha_{s}\leq 1\end{array}\right\}\implies\alpha_{1}^{2}+\alpha_{2}^{2}+\ldots+\alpha_{m}^{2}\leq\frac{m}{s^{2}},

with equality only when all
\alpha_{i}=1/s
.
This is equivalent to maximizing the convex function

f(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\ldots,\alpha_{m})\triangleq\alpha_{1}^{2}+\alpha_{2}^{2}+\ldots+\alpha_{m}^{2}

over the convex set

{\mathbb{S}}\triangleq\{(\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{m})\in\real^{m}\mid\alpha_{1}\geq\ldots\geq\alpha_{m}\geq 0\text{ and }\alpha_{1}+\ldots+\alpha_{s}\leq 1\}.

Since
f
is convex and
{\mathbb{S}}
is a compact convex polytope, the maximum of
f
over
{\mathbb{S}}
is attained at an extreme point (vertex) of
{\mathbb{S}}
.
The vertices of
{\mathbb{S}}
arise when enough of the inequality constraints become equalities. Up to symmetry and ordering, the relevant cases are:

if
\alpha_{1}=\alpha_{2}=\ldots=\alpha_{m}=0
, then
f(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\ldots,\alpha_{m})=0
;

if
\alpha_{1}+\ldots+\alpha_{s}=1
and
\alpha_{1}=\ldots=\alpha_{\ell}>\alpha_{\ell+1}=\ldots=\alpha_{m}=0
for
1\leq\ell\leq s
, then
\alpha_{1}=\ldots=\alpha_{\ell}=1/\ell
, and consequently
f(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\ldots,\alpha_{m})=1/\ell
;

if
\alpha_{1}+\ldots+\alpha_{s}=1
and
\alpha_{1}=\ldots=\alpha_{\ell}>\alpha_{\ell+1}=\ldots=\alpha_{m}=0
for
s<\ell\leq m
, then
\alpha_{1}=\ldots=\alpha_{\ell}=1/s
, and consequently
f(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\ldots,\alpha_{m})=\ell/s^{2}
.

Since
s<\sqrt{m}
, we have

\max_{(\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{m})\in{\mathbb{S}}}f(\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{m})=\max\left\{\max_{1\leq\ell\leq k}\frac{1}{\ell},\max_{s<\ell\leq m}\frac{\ell}{s^{2}}\right\}=\max\left\{1,\frac{m}{s^{2}}\right\}=\frac{m}{s^{2}},

with equality only when
\ell=m
and
\alpha_{1}=\alpha_{2}=\ldots=\alpha_{m}=1/s
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Without loss of generality, we assume that
{\bm{X}}
have
\ell_{2}
-normalized columns.
From inequality (
), we have

\sum_{i,j=1,i\neq j}^{p,p}\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{x}}_{i},{\bm{x}}_{j}\right\rangle\right\rvert^{2}\geq\frac{p^{2}}{n}-p=\frac{p(p-n)}{n}
.
This implies

\max_{i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}}\sum_{j=1,j\neq i}^{p}\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{x}}_{i},{\bm{x}}_{j}\right\rangle\right\rvert^{2}\geq\frac{1}{p}\sum_{i,j=1,i\neq j}^{p,p}\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{x}}_{i},{\bm{x}}_{j}\right\rangle\right\rvert^{2}\geq\frac{p-n}{n}.

For an index
i^{\dagger}\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
that achieves this maximum, and consider the
(p-1)
-dimensional vector of absolute inner products:
\big\{\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{x}}_{i^{\dagger}},{\bm{x}}_{j}\right\rangle\right\rvert\big\}_{j=1,j\neq i^{\dagger}}^{p}
.
Reorder these values in nonincreasing order as
\beta_{1}\geq\beta_{2}\geq\ldots\geq\beta_{p-1}\geq 0
, so that

\beta_{1}^{2}+\beta_{2}^{2}+\ldots+\beta_{p-1}^{2}\geq\frac{p-n}{n}.

Invoking Lemma
with
m=p-1
and
s=k
, and defining
\alpha_{\ell}\triangleq(\frac{1}{k}\sqrt{n(p-1)/(p-n)})\beta_{\ell}
gives
\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}+\ldots+\alpha_{k}\geq 1
.
By the definition of
\ell_{1}
-coherence, it follows that

\mu_{1}({\bm{X}},k)\geq\beta_{1}+\beta_{2}+\ldots+\beta_{k}\geq k\sqrt{\frac{p-n}{n(p-1)}},

which yields the desired bound (
).

Finally, suppose equality holds in (
). Then all intermediate inequalities must be tight. In particular:

Equality in (
) implies that
{\bm{X}}
is a tight frame (as in the proof of Theorem
).

Equality in Lemma
implies that all off-diagonal inner products involving column
i^{\dagger}
have the same magnitude:

\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{x}}_{i^{\dagger}},{\bm{x}}_{j}\right\rangle\right\rvert=\sqrt{(p-n)/(n(p-1))}
for all
j\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
,
j\neq i^{\dagger}
.

This ensures that the choice of
i^{\dagger}
must be arbitrary in
\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
, it follows that all pairwise inner products between distinct columns have identical magnitude. Hence,
{\bm{X}}
is equiangular.
Conversely, the proof that equiangular tight frames yield equality in (
) follows easily from the above discussions.

4.3
Restricted Isometry Property (RIP)

The NSP condition is both necessary and sufficient for establishing error guarantees of the form

\left\lVert\Delta({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}})-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq C\frac{\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})_{1}}{\sqrt{k}},\quad\text{with }\quad\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})_{s}\triangleq\min_{\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]}\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{s}.

(4.35)

However, these guarantees assume noise-free measurements.
In practical settings—where measurements are corrupted by noise (e.g., due to sensor error or quantization)—stronger conditions are required to ensure stable and robust recovery.
To address this,
Candes and Tao 2005
introduced the restricted isometry property (RIP), a fundamental condition in compressive sensing that we briefly touched upon in the discussion of mutual coherence.

Definition 163
(Restricted isometry property (RIP)).

A matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
is said to satisfy the restricted isometry property (RIP) of order
k
(
k<p
) with constant
\delta_{k}\in[0,1)
, denoted RIP
(k,\delta_{k})
, if for
k
-sparse vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]\triangleq\{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\mid\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{0}\leq k\}
, we have

(1-\delta_{k})\cdot\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq(1+\delta_{k})\cdot\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

(4.36a)

Using the spectral norm identity
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}-{\bm{I}}\right\rVert_{2}=\mathop{\max}_{{\bm{u}}\in\real^{p}:\left\lVert{\bm{u}}\right\rVert_{2}=1}\left\lvert{\bm{u}}^{\top}({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}-{\bm{I}}){\bm{u}}\right\rvert=\mathop{\max}_{{\bm{u}}\in\real^{p}:\left\lVert{\bm{u}}\right\rVert_{2}=1}\left\lvert\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\bm{u}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-1\right\rvert
by (
), condition (
) can be equivalently restated as

\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}-{\bm{I}}_{\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\delta_{k},\quad\text{for all }{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots,p\}\text{ with }\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert\leq k.,

(4.36b)

where
{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\triangleq{\bm{X}}[:,{\mathbb{S}}]\in\real^{n\times\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert}
denotes the columns of
{\bm{X}}
from the index set
{\mathbb{S}}
.

The smallest constant
\delta_{k}
for which RIP
(k,\delta_{k})
holds is called the restricted isometry constant (RIC) of order
k
. It can be defined as

\displaystyle\delta_{k}

\displaystyle=\min\left\{\delta\mid(1-\delta)\left\lVert{\bm{v}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}{\bm{v}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq(1+\delta)\left\lVert{\bm{v}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},\;\forall\,\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert\leq k,\forall\,{\bm{v}}\in\real^{\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert}\right\}

(4.37a)

\displaystyle=\max_{{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots,p\},\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert\leq k}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}-{\bm{I}}_{\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert}\right\rVert_{2}.

(4.37b)

Note that either expression in (
4.37a
) or (
4.37b
) implies that all singular values of
{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
lie in the interval

\sigma({\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}})\in[\sqrt{1-\delta_{k}},\sqrt{1+\delta_{k}}]\qquad\text{with}\qquad\delta_{k}\leq 1.

(see Theorem
).
Equivalently, the eigenvalues of
{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
lie in

\lambda({\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}})\in[1-\delta_{k},1+\delta_{k}]\qquad\text{with}\qquad\delta_{k}\leq 1.

The strict inequality
\delta_{k}<1
further implies that the smallest eigenvalue of
{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
is positive, which means that
{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
has full column rank for any index set
{\mathbb{S}}
with
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert\leq k
, by the eigenvalue characterization theorem of positive definite matrices (Theorem
).
Consequently,
{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
is nonsingular.

This relationship between eigenvalues (or singular values) and the RIP constant is instrumental in deriving key inequalities used later.

Remark 164
(IHT inequalities).

From (
), we obtain

\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}=\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}-{\bm{I}}_{\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\delta_{k}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2},

(4.38)

where
\mathrm{supp}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})={\mathbb{S}}
.
This is a standard bound used in iterative algorithms such as iterative hard-thresholding (IHT).
Alternatively, applying the triangle inequality yields:

\displaystyle\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}

\displaystyle\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}+\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq(1+\delta_{k})\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2};

\displaystyle\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}

\displaystyle\geq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}-\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}\geq(1-\delta_{k})\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}.

Thus, we arrive at the key inequality:

(1-\delta_{k})\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq(1+\delta_{k})\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}.

(4.39)

Informally, a matrix
{\bm{X}}
is said to
possess the RIP
if
\delta_{k}
is small for sufficiently large sparsity level
k
.
Note that for a vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
with support
{\mathbb{S}}
, we have
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
.
Thus, the RIP essentially requires that every submatrix of
{\bm{X}}
formed by selecting up to
k
columns is well-conditioned—that is, it acts approximately like an isometry on sparse vectors.
In fact, for sparse optimization problems, the RIP of order
2k
is particularly relevant (see, e.g., Theorem
).
Indeed, condition (
) implies that
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2})\right\rVert_{2}>0

for any two distinct
k
-sparse vectors
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]
.
Consequently, their measurement vectors are also distinct:
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1}\neq{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}
.

For a concrete example of sparse recovery, suppose that
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
is
k
-sparse. Then:

We can uniquely recover
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]
from the noiseless measurements
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}={\bm{y}}
provided that any
2k
columns of
{\bm{X}}
are linearly independent.
This is because if
{\bm{X}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2})=\boldsymbol{0}
for two
k
-sparse vectors
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1}
and
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}
, then
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}
, ensuring uniqueness of the solution.

Conversely, if
{\bm{X}}
contains a set of
2k
linearly dependent columns, then unique recovery of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
is not guaranteed. In this case, there exists a nonzero vector
{\bm{n}}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}
(with
\left\lVert{\bm{n}}\right\rVert_{0}\leq 2k
) such that
{\bm{X}}{\bm{n}}=\boldsymbol{0}
, meaning
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}
for two distinct
k
-sparse vectors.

This example motivates the need for a lower bound in the RIP of order
2k
.
If this lower bound fails—i.e., if
(1-\delta_{2k})
is too small or zero—then it becomes possible to find two distinct
k
-sparse vectors
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1}
and
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}
with disjoint supports such that
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}
.
The lower bound in the RIP ensures that distinct sparse signals are mapped to well-separated measurement vectors, preventing ambiguity in recovery.

However, the RIP can be somewhat restrictive, as it requires the distortion of vector norms to be bounded symmetrically in the form
(1\pm\delta_{k})
for
\delta_{k}\in[0,1)
.
By definition, if the matrix
{\bm{X}}
is orthogonal (i.e.,
{\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{\top}={\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}={\bm{I}}
), then
\delta_{k}=0
, since
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}
for all
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.
Consequently, a nonzero RIC
\delta_{k}
can be interpreted as a measure of how far
{\bm{X}}
deviates from orthogonality, but only when considering sparse linear combinations involving at most
k
columns.

Recall that the expression
{{\bm{v}}^{\top}{\bm{A}}{\bm{v}}}/{\left\lVert{\bm{v}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}
is known as the
Rayleigh quotient
of a nonzero vector
{\bm{v}}
with respect to a matrix
{\bm{A}}\in\real^{p\times p}
. This quantity always lies between the largest and smallest eigenvalues of
{\bm{A}}
.
The ratio of the largest to the smallest eigenvalue—known as the condition number—characterizes how well-conditioned a matrix is
(
Lu 2021a
;
Lu 2025
)
; a smaller condition number indicates better conditioning. In this context, the RIP condition implies two important properties:

Norm preservation controlled by
\delta_{k}
.
The inequality
(1-\delta_{k})\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq(1+\delta_{k})\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
guarantees that
{\bm{X}}
approximately preserves the Euclidean norm of every
k
-sparse vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
, with the deviation governed by
\delta_{k}
.

Well-conditioned submatrices.

When
\delta_{k}
is not too large, every submatrix of
{\bm{X}}
formed by selecting any
k
columns is well-conditioned. In other words, such submatrices are close to being orthonormal. This property is essential for ensuring the stability and accuracy of sparse recovery algorithms.

\paragrapharrow

Rescaled, reshuffled, and augmented properties of RIP?
We recall from (
) that the NSP is invariant under certain transformations of the measurement matrix—specifically, when measurements are rescaled, reshuffled, or augmented. (Consequently,
k
-sparse recovery via
\ell_{1}
-minimization remains unaffected by such operations; see Chapter
.)
However, these same operations can deteriorate the RICs.
Reshuffling measurements corresponds to replacing the measurement matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
with
{\bm{P}}{\bm{X}}
, where
{\bm{P}}\in\real^{n\times n}
is a permutation matrix (a special case of an orthogonal matrix).
Since orthogonal transformations preserve singular values—i.e.,
\sigma_{i}({\bm{Q}}{\bm{X}})=\sigma_{i}({\bm{X}})
for any orthogonal matrix
{\bm{Q}}\in\real^{n\times n}
—this operation leaves the RICs unchanged.

Rescaling measurements—i.e., replacing
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
with
{\bm{D}}{\bm{X}}
, where
{\bm{D}}\in\real^{n\times n}
is a diagonal matrix—can also increase the RIC. This holds even for scalar rescaling: replacing
{\bm{X}}
by
\eta{\bm{X}}
for some
\eta\in\real
.
For instance, if
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
satisfies
\delta_{k}({\bm{X}})<1/3
, then the scaled matrix
2{\bm{X}}
has RIC
\delta_{k}(2{\bm{X}})=5/6
.

Augmenting a measurement, on the other hand, corresponds to appending a row to
{\bm{X}}
, which can also increase the RIC.
For example, let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
satisfy
\delta_{k}({\bm{X}})<1
, and choose any
\delta>\delta_{k}({\bm{X}})
. Construct a new matrix
\widetilde{\bm{X}}
by appending the row vector
[0,\ldots,0,\sqrt{1+\delta}]
.
Consider the 1-sparse vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\triangleq[0,\ldots,0,1]^{\top}
.
Then
\big\lVert\widetilde{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}\geq 1+\delta
, implies that
\delta_{1}(\widetilde{\bm{X}})\geq\delta
, and hence
\delta_{k}(\widetilde{\bm{X}})>\delta_{k}({\bm{X}})
(by Exercise
).

Exercise
\thetheo

Given
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
, let
\mu>0
and
\nu>0
be the largest and smallest constants such that

\mu\cdot\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\nu\cdot\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},\quad\text{for all $k$-sparse vectors ${\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}$.}

Find the scaling factor
\eta>0
that minimizes
\delta_{k}(\eta\b{)}
.

Hint: Think about
(\nu-\mu)/(\nu+\mu)
.

It is also important to note that in our definition of the RIP, we assume symmetric bounds around 1 (i.e., of the form
1\pm\delta_{k}
).
However, this symmetry is adopted for notational convenience only. In practice, one may consider asymmetric bounds, leading to a useful generalization of the RIP—particularly relevant in settings where the design matrix is not tightly controlled, such as in gene expression analysis. This generalization is captured by the concepts of restricted strong convexity (RSC) and restricted smoothness (RSS).

Definition 165
(Restricted strong convexity/smoothness property).

A matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
is said to satisfy the
\mu
-restricted strong convexity (RSC) and
\nu
-restricted smoothness (RSS) property of order
k
if, for all
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]
,

\mu\cdot\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\nu\cdot\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

(4.40)

The key difference between RIP and RSC/RSS lies in their constants.
RIP requires the lower and upper bounds to be symmetric about 1, i.e.,
1\pm\delta_{k}
, whereas RSC/RSS imposes no such symmetry.
Readers may notice a close connection between Definition
and Definition
, where restricted strong convexity and smoothness are defined for general functions. Indeed, Definition
can be viewed as a generalization of Definition
to arbitrary (possibly non-quadratic) functions
(
Jain et al. 2014
;
Lu 2025
)
. For twice-differentiable functions, both definitions essentially constrain the restricted eigenvalues of the Hessian matrix.

Importantly, given any matrix
{\bm{X}}
satisfying the asymmetric bounds in (
), we can always rescale it to meet the symmetric RIP condition in (
). Specifically, define

\widetilde{\bm{X}}\triangleq\sqrt{2/(\nu+\mu)}{\bm{X}}.

Then
\widetilde{\bm{X}}
satisfies the RIP of order
k
with constant
\delta_{k}=(\nu-\mu)/(\nu+\mu)
.
While we do not prove this explicitly here, it is straightforward to verify. Moreover, all theorems in this book that assume the RIP actually remain valid as long as some scaling of
{\bm{X}}
satisfies the RIP. Therefore, without loss of generality, we may restrict our attention to the symmetric formulation in (
).

Another useful property of the RIP is its monotonicity with respect to sparsity level:
If
{\bm{X}}
satisfies the RIP of order
k
with constant
\delta_{k}
, then for any
k^{\prime}<k
it automatically satisfies the RIP of order
k^{\prime}
with constant
\delta_{k^{\prime}}\leq\delta_{k}
.

Exercise
\thetheo
(Nondecreasing of RICs)

Let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
satisfy the RIP condition. Show that

\delta_{1}\leq\delta_{2}\leq\ldots\leq\delta_{p}.

(4.41)

Furthermore, if
{\bm{X}}

satisfies the RIP of order
k
with a sufficiently small constant, then it will also automatically satisfy the RIP of order
\gamma k
for certain
\gamma
, albeit with a somewhat worse constant.

Exercise
\thetheo
(RIP variants
(
Needell and Tropp 2009
)
)

Suppose that
{\bm{X}}
satisfies the RIP of order
k
with constant
\delta_{k}
. Let
\gamma
be a positive integer.
Show that
{\bm{X}}
satisfies the RIP of order
k^{\prime}=\gamma\lfloor\frac{k}{2}\rfloor
with constant
\delta_{k^{\prime}}<\gamma\cdot\delta_{k}
, where
\lfloor\cdot\rfloor
denotes the floor function.

This result is immediate for
\gamma=1,2
, but for
\gamma\geq 3
(and
k\geq 4
),
it enables us to extend RIP guarantees from order
k
to significantly higher sparsity levels. Note, however, that for the resulting bound to be meaningful (e.g.,
\delta_{k^{\prime}}<1
), the original constant
\delta_{k}
must be sufficiently small.

4.3.1
Restricted Orthogonality Property (ROP)

Note that inequality (
) implies that for any index set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
with
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert<k
,
the eigenvalues of the Gram matrix
{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
lie in interval
[1-\delta_{k},1+\delta_{k}]
.
In particular, when
k=1
, the constant
\delta_{1}
reflects the deviation of the column norms of
{\bm{X}}
from unity:
\delta_{1}=0
if and only if every column of
{\bm{X}}
has unit Euclidean norm.
A related concept that captures the non-orthogonality between distinct columns (or disjoint subsets of columns) is the
restricted orthogonality property (ROP)
.

To motivate this notion, we begin with a simple but essential observation, which leads naturally to the definition of the
restricted orthogonality constant (ROC)
.

Proposition 166
(Standard consequence of RIP).

Let
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
be vectors such that
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{0}\leq s
and
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{0}\leq t
. If
\mathrm{supp}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\cap\mathrm{supp}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\varnothing
, then

\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle\right\rvert\leq\delta_{s+t}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}.

Proof
[of Proposition
]
Let
{\mathbb{S}}\triangleq\mathrm{supp}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\cup\mathrm{supp}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
, and denote by
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\in\real^{\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert}
the restrictions of
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
to the coordinates in
{\mathbb{S}}
.
Since the supports of
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
and
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
