are disjoint,
\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rangle=0
.
We then compute:

\displaystyle\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle\right\rvert

\displaystyle=\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}},{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rangle-\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rangle\right\rvert=\left\lvert\left\langle({\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}-{\bm{I}}){\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rangle\right\rvert

\displaystyle\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}-{\bm{I}}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\delta_{s+t}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2},

where the last inequality follows from (
4.37b
) and the facts that
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}
and
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}
.

This result motivates a complementary condition to the RIP, known as the restricted orthogonality property.

Definition 167
(Restricted orthogonality property (ROP)).

A matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
is said to satisfy the restricted orthogonality property (ROP) of order (
k,k^{\prime}
) with constant
\theta_{k,k^{\prime}}
(
k+k^{\prime}\leq p
), denoted ROP
(k,k^{\prime},\theta_{k,k^{\prime}})
, if for all
disjoint
vectors
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]
and
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k^{\prime}]
(i.e.,
\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}\right\rangle=0
), we have

\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}\right\rangle\right\rvert\leq\theta_{k,k^{\prime}}\cdot\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}\right\rVert_{2}.

(4.42a)

The smallest such constant
\theta_{k,k^{\prime}}
is called the restricted orthogonality constant (ROC).
It can be defined as the infimum of all parameters
\theta
such that ROP
(k,k^{\prime},\theta_{k,k^{\prime}})
holds, i.e.,

\displaystyle\theta_{k,k^{\prime}}=\min{\mathbb{S}};

(4.42b)

\displaystyle{\mathbb{S}}

\displaystyle\triangleq\left\{\theta\mid\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}{\bm{v}}_{1},{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{I}}^{\prime}}{\bm{v}}_{2}\right\rangle\right\rvert\leq\theta\cdot\left\lVert{\bm{v}}_{1}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\bm{v}}_{2}\right\rVert_{2},\forall\left\lvert{\mathbb{I}}\right\rvert\leq k,\left\lvert{\mathbb{I}}^{\prime}\right\rvert\leq k^{\prime},\forall{\bm{v}}_{1}\in\real^{\left\lvert{\mathbb{I}}\right\rvert},{\bm{v}}_{2}\in\real^{\left\lvert{\mathbb{I}}^{\prime}\right\rvert},{\mathbb{I}}\cap{\mathbb{I}}^{\prime}=\varnothing\right\}.

Equivalently, the ROC admits the explicit characterization

\theta_{k,k^{\prime}}=\max\Big\{\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{I}}^{\prime}}\right\rVert_{2},{\mathbb{I}}\cap{\mathbb{I}}^{\prime}=\varnothing,\left\lvert{\mathbb{I}}\right\rvert\leq k,\left\lvert{\mathbb{I}}^{\prime}\right\rvert\leq k^{\prime}\Big\}.

(4.42c)

Note that
\theta_{k,k^{\prime}}\equiv\theta_{k^{\prime},k}
due to symmetry.

The RIP and ROP constants are closely related. To see this, consider the setting of Definition
and assume without loss of generality that
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}\right\rVert_{2}=1
(since both properties are scale-invariant).
Since
{\mathbb{I}}
and
{\mathbb{I}}^{\prime}
are disjoint, there exist
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\triangleq{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k+k^{\prime}]
and
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{\prime}\triangleq{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k+k^{\prime}]
—
(k+k^{\prime})
-sparse vectors satisfying
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}
and
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{\prime}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}
—such that

\displaystyle(1-\delta_{k+k^{\prime}})\cdot\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}+{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq(1+\delta_{k+k^{\prime}})\cdot\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}\right\rVert_{2}^{2};

\displaystyle(1-\delta_{k+k^{\prime}})\cdot\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq(1+\delta_{k+k^{\prime}})\cdot\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

Since
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=2
,
these inequalities simplify to:

\displaystyle 2(1-\delta_{k+k^{\prime}})\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}+{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq 2(1+\delta_{k+k^{\prime}});

(4.43)

\displaystyle 2(1-\delta_{k+k^{\prime}})\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq 2(1+\delta_{k+k^{\prime}}).

Subtracting the two squared norms and using the identity

\left\lVert{\bm{X}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}+{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\left\lVert{\bm{X}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=4\left\langle{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}\right\rangle,

one can further derive a quantitative link between
\theta_{k,k^{\prime}}

and
\delta_{k+k^{\prime}}
, showing that small RIP constants imply small ROC constants; see Proposition
.

Exercise
\thetheo
(Nondecreasing of ROC)

Show that the ROC defined in (
) satisfies the following monotonicity properties:

\displaystyle\theta_{k,k^{\prime}}

\displaystyle\leq\theta_{s,k^{\prime}},\quad\text{if}\quad k\leq s;

(4.44)

\displaystyle\theta_{k,k^{\prime}}

\displaystyle\leq\theta_{k,s},\quad\text{if}\quad k^{\prime}\leq s.

4.3.2
Relationship between RIC, ROC, and other Constants

In this subsection, we explore the connections among various constants associated with the design matrix
{\bm{X}}
, including the RIC, mutual coherence, and the ROC.

Proposition 168
(RIC and coherence).

Let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
have
\ell_{2}
-normalized columns, i.e.,
\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}=1
for all
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
. Then, the RICs satisfy

\delta_{1}=0,\quad\delta_{2}=\mu({\bm{X}}),\quad\delta_{k}\leq\mu_{1}({\bm{X}},k-1)\leq(k-1)\mu({\bm{X}}),\quad k\geq 2.

Proof
[of Proposition
]
The
\ell_{2}
-normalization of the columns implies that
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\bm{e}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left\lVert{\bm{e}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
for each standard basis vector
{\bm{e}}_{i}
.
Hence, the RIP condition holds exactly for 1-sparse vectors, yielding
\delta_{1}=0
.
For
\delta_{2}
, consider any pair of distinct indices
i\neq j
. The Gram matrix of the corresponding submatrix satisfies

\delta_{2}=\max_{1\leq i\neq j\leq p}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}[:,\{i,j\}]^{\top}{\bm{X}}[:,\{i,j\}]-{\bm{I}}_{2}\right\rVert_{2}.

The eigenvalues of this symmetric matrix
{\bm{X}}[:,\{i,j\}]^{\top}{\bm{X}}[:,\{i,j\}]-{\bm{I}}=\scriptsize\begin{bmatrix}0&\left\langle{\bm{x}}_{i},{\bm{x}}_{j}\right\rangle\\
\left\langle{\bm{x}}_{i},{\bm{x}}_{j}\right\rangle&0\end{bmatrix}\normalsize
are

\pm\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{x}}_{i},{\bm{x}}_{j}\right\rangle\right\rvert
, and thus its spectral norm equals
\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{x}}_{i},{\bm{x}}_{j}\right\rangle\right\rvert
. Taking the maximum over
1\leq i\neq j\leq p
gives
\delta_{2}=\mu({\bm{X}})
, the mutual coherence.
The inequality
\delta_{k}\leq\mu_{1}({\bm{X}},k-1)\leq(k-1)\mu({\bm{X}})
follows from Theorem
and (
).

We now present a comparison between restricted isometry constants and restricted orthogonality constants.
This result provides control over the principal angles between subspaces spanned by disjoint subsets of columns of
{\bm{X}}
of sizes
s
and
t
, respectively. Such control is valuable because it enables guarantees of exact sparse recovery based solely on bounds involving the RICs; see Section
for further details.

Proposition 169
(RIC and ROC
(
Candes and Tao 2005
;
Foucart and Rauhut 2013
)
).

For all positive integers
s,t
, we have that

\theta_{s,t}\leq\delta_{s+t}\leq\begin{cases}&\theta_{s,t}+\max\{\delta_{s},\delta_{t}\};\\
&\frac{1}{s+t}(s\delta_{s}+t\delta_{t}+2\sqrt{st}\theta_{s,t}).\end{cases}

In the special case
t=s
, this yields

\theta_{s,s}\leq\delta_{2s}\leq\delta_{s}+\theta_{s,s}.

Proof
[of Proposition
]

The inequality
\theta_{s,t}\leq\delta_{s+t}
.

The inequality
\theta_{s,t}\leq\delta_{s+t}
follows directly from definition.
Alternatively, by homogeneity, it suffices to show that

\left\lvert\left\langle\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{I}}}\beta_{i}{\bm{x}}_{i},\sum_{j\in{\mathbb{J}}}\beta_{j}{\bm{x}}_{j}\right\rangle\right\rvert\leq\delta_{s+t}

(4.45)

whenever
{\mathbb{I}},{\mathbb{J}}\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
are disjoint (
{\mathbb{I}}\cap{\mathbb{J}}=\varnothing
),
\left\lvert{\mathbb{I}}\right\rvert\leq s
,
\left\lvert{\mathbb{J}}\right\rvert\leq t
,
and
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
satisfies
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}\right\rVert_{2}=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{J}}}\right\rVert_{2}=1
, i.e.,

\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{I}}}\left\lvert\beta_{i}\right\rvert^{2}=\sum_{j\in{\mathbb{J}}}\left\lvert\beta_{j}\right\rvert^{2}=1
.
To see this, (
) indicates that

\displaystyle 2(1-\delta_{s+t})

\displaystyle\leq\left\lVert\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{I}}}\beta_{i}{\bm{x}}_{i}+\sum_{j\in{\mathbb{J}}}\beta_{j}{\bm{x}}_{j}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq 2(1+\delta_{s+t});

\displaystyle 2(1-\delta_{s+t})

\displaystyle\leq\left\lVert\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{I}}}\beta_{i}{\bm{x}}_{i}-\sum_{j\in{\mathbb{J}}}\beta_{j}{\bm{x}}_{j}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq 2(1+\delta_{s+t}).

Inequality (
) then follows from the parallelogram identity

4\left\langle{\bm{a}},{\bm{b}}\right\rangle={\left\lVert{\bm{a}}+{\bm{b}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\left\lVert{\bm{a}}-{\bm{b}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}
for any vectors
{\bm{a}},{\bm{b}}
.

The inequality
\delta_{s+t}\leq\theta_{s,t}+\max\{\delta_{s},\delta_{t}\}
.

For the reverse inequality, again by homogeneity, consider any
(s+t)
-sparse vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
with
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}=1
.
Partition its support as
{\mathbb{S}}={\mathbb{I}}\cup{\mathbb{J}}
, where
\left\lvert{\mathbb{I}}\right\rvert\leq s
,
\left\lvert{\mathbb{J}}\right\rvert\leq t
, and define
\nu\triangleq\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{I}}}\left\lvert\beta_{i}\right\rvert^{2}
, so that
1-\nu=\sum_{j\in{\mathbb{J}}}\left\lvert\beta_{j}\right\rvert^{2}
.
Then

\displaystyle\left\lvert\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-1\right\rvert

\displaystyle=\left\lvert\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right\rvert

(4.46)

\displaystyle\leq\left\lvert\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\nu\right\rvert+\left\lvert\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{J}}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{J}}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-(1-\nu)\right\rvert+2\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}},{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{J}}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{J}}}\right\rangle\right\rvert

\displaystyle\leq\delta_{s}\nu+\delta_{t}(1-\nu)+2\theta_{s,t}\sqrt{\nu(1-\nu)}\leq\max\{\delta_{s},\delta_{t}\}(\nu+1-\nu)+\theta_{s,t}

\displaystyle=\max\{\delta_{s},\delta_{t}\}+\theta_{s,t},

where the first inequality follows from the triangle inequality, and the second inequality follows from (
) and (
), the definitions of RICs and ROCs.

The inequality
\delta_{s+t}\leq\frac{1}{s+t}(s\delta_{s}+t\delta_{t}+2\sqrt{st}\theta_{s,t})
.

This inequality provides a sharper relationship between RICs and ROCs.
Once again, let
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
be
(s+t)
-sparse with
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}=1
.
By (
), we have

\left\lvert\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right\rvert\leq\delta_{s}\nu+\delta_{t}(1-\nu)+2\theta_{s,t}\sqrt{\nu(1-\nu)}\triangleq f(\nu),

(4.47)

where
f(\nu):[0,1]\rightarrow\real
.
It can be shown that there is a scalar
\nu^{*}\in[0,1]
such that this function is nondecreasing on
[0,\nu^{*}]
and then nonincreasing on
[\nu^{*},1]
; see Problem
. Depending on the location of this
\nu^{*}
with respect to
s/(s+t)
, the function
f
is either nondecreasing on
[0,s/(s+t)]
or nonincreasing on
[s/(s+t),1]
. By properly choosing the vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}
, we can always assume that
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
is in one of these intervals. Indeed, if
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}
is made of
s
smallest modulus components of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
while
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{J}}}
is made of
t
largest modulus components of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
, then we have

\frac{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}{s}\leq\frac{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{J}}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}{t}=\frac{1-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}{t},\quad\text{so that }\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\frac{s}{s+t}.

Otherwise, if
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}
is made of
s
largest modulus components of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
, then we have
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\geq s/(s+t)
.
Therefore, we obtain

\left\lvert\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right\rvert\leq f\left(\frac{s}{s+t}\right)=\delta_{s}\frac{s}{s+t}+\delta_{t}\frac{t}{s+t}+2\theta_{s,t}\frac{\sqrt{st}}{s+t}.

This completes the proof.

We conclude this subsection by showing that RICs and ROCs of higher order can be bounded in terms of those of lower order.

Proposition 170
(Different orders of RICs and ROCs).

Let
k,s,t\geq 1
be integers with
t\geq s
.
Then

\displaystyle\theta_{t,k}

\displaystyle\leq\sqrt{\frac{t}{s}}\theta_{s,k},

\displaystyle\delta_{t}

\displaystyle\leq\frac{t-d}{s}\delta_{2s}+\frac{d}{s}\delta_{s},\quad\text{where }d\triangleq\gcd(s,t).

In the special case
t=cs
for some integer
c\geq 1
, this simplifies to

\delta_{cs}\leq c\cdot\delta_{2s}.

Proof
[of Proposition
]
Let
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}
be a
t
-sparse vector and
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
a
k
-sparse vector, with disjoint supports.
We aim to establish the two inequalities:

\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle\right\rvert\leq\sqrt{\frac{t}{s}}\theta_{s,k}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2},

(4.48)

\left\lvert\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right\rvert\leq\left(\frac{t-d}{s}\delta_{2s}+\frac{d}{s}\delta_{s}\right)\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

(4.49)

Let
d
be a common divisor of
s
and
t
. We define integers
\mu,\nu
such that

s=\mu d,\qquad t=\nu d.

Let
{\mathbb{T}}=\{j_{1},j_{2},\ldots,j_{t}\}
denote the support of
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
. We consider the
\nu
subsets
{\mathbb{S}}_{1},{\mathbb{S}}_{2},\ldots,{\mathbb{S}}_{\nu}\subseteq{\mathbb{T}}
of size
s
defined by

{\mathbb{S}}_{i}=\{j_{(i-1)d+1},j_{(i-1)d+2},\ldots,j_{(i-1)d+s}\},

where indices are taken modulo
t
.
With this construction, every index
j\in{\mathbb{T}}
appears in exactly
s/d=\mu
of the subsets
{\mathbb{S}}_{i}
.
Consequently, we can decompose
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
as

{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=\frac{1}{\mu}\sum_{i=1}^{\nu}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}({\mathbb{S}}_{i}),\qquad\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\frac{1}{\mu}\sum_{i=1}^{\nu}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}({\mathbb{S}}_{i})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

Note again that
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}({\mathbb{S}}_{i})\in\real^{p}
(while
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}\in\real^{s}
; see Definition
).

Proof of (
).

Using the decomposition above and the definition of the ROC, we obtain

\displaystyle\left\langle{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle

\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{\mu}\sum_{i=1}^{\nu}\left\langle{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}({\mathbb{S}}_{i}),{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle\leq\frac{1}{\mu}\sum_{i=1}^{\nu}\theta_{s,k}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}({\mathbb{S}}_{i})\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}

\displaystyle\leq\theta_{s,k}\frac{\sqrt{\nu}}{\mu}\sqrt{\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\nu}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right)}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}=\theta_{s,k}\sqrt{\frac{\nu}{\mu}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2},

where the last inequality follows from the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality
{\bm{a}}^{\top}{\bm{b}}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{a}}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\bm{b}}\right\rVert_{2}
by invoking with
{\bm{a}}={\bm{1}}
and
b_{i}=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}({\mathbb{S}}_{i})\right\rVert_{2}
for all
i
.

Proof of (
).

We begin by writing

\displaystyle\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left\lvert\left\langle\big({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}-{\bm{I}}\big){\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rangle\right\rvert\leq\frac{1}{\mu^{2}}\sum_{1\leq i\leq\nu}\sum_{1\leq j\leq\nu}\left\lvert\left\langle\big({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}-{\bm{I}}\big){\boldsymbol{\alpha}}({\mathbb{S}}_{i}),{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}({\mathbb{S}}_{j})\right\rangle\right\rvert

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\mu^{2}}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\neq j\leq\nu}\left\lvert\left\langle\big({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}-{\bm{I}}\big){\boldsymbol{\alpha}}({\mathbb{S}}_{i}),{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}({\mathbb{S}}_{j})\right\rangle\right\rvert+\sum_{1\leq i\leq\nu}\left\lvert\left\langle\big({\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}-{\bm{I}}\big){\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}\right\rangle\right\rvert\right)

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\dagger}}}{{\leq}}\frac{1}{\mu^{2}}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\neq j\leq\nu}\delta_{2s}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{j}}\right\rVert_{2}+\sum_{1\leq i\leq\nu}\delta_{s}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right)=\frac{\delta_{2s}}{\mu^{2}}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\nu}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}\right\rVert_{2}\right)^{2}-\frac{\delta_{2s}-\delta_{s}}{\mu^{2}}\sum_{1\leq i\leq\nu}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\ddagger}}}{{\leq}}\left(\frac{\delta_{2s}\nu}{\mu^{2}}-\frac{\delta_{2s}-\delta_{s}}{\mu^{2}}\right)\sum_{1\leq i\leq\nu}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left(\frac{\nu}{\mu}\delta_{2s}-\frac{\delta_{2s}-\delta_{s}}{\mu}\right)\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left(\frac{t}{s}\delta_{2s}-\frac{1}{\mu}(\delta_{2s}-\delta_{s})\right)\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},

where the inequality (
{\dagger}
) follows from Proposition
, and the inequality
({\ddagger})

follows again from the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality
{\bm{a}}^{\top}{\bm{b}}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{a}}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\bm{b}}\right\rVert_{2}
by invoking with
{\bm{a}}={\bm{1}}
and
b_{i}=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}\right\rVert_{2}
for all
i
.
To make the latter bound as tight as possible, we take
\mu
as small as possible, i.e., we choose
d
as the greatest common divisor of
s
and
t
. This completes the proof.

4.3.3
Bounds for Restricted Isometry Property

Just as with mutual coherence or
\ell_{1}
-coherence (see Section
), it is important to understand how small the
k
-th RIC of a matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
can be.
In the regime relevant to compressive sensing—namely, when
p\geq Cn
—Theorem
below shows that the RIC must satisfy

\delta_{k}\geq c\sqrt{k/n}
.
For
k=2
, this implies the mutual coherence satisfies
\mu({\bm{X}})\geq c^{\prime}/\sqrt{n}
by Proposition
, which is reminiscent of the Welch bound of Theorem
.

{theoremHigh}

[Bounds for RICs
(
Krahmer and Ward 2011
;
Foucart and Rauhut 2013
)
]
Let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
and
2\leq k\leq p
.
Suppose
p\geq Cn
and
\delta_{k}\leq\delta_{*}
, where the constants
c
,
C
, and
\delta_{*}
depend only on each other.
Then

n\geq c\frac{k}{\delta_{k}^{2}}.

(4.50)

For example, the choices
c=1/162
,
C=30
, and
\delta_{*}=2/3
are valid.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
We first observe that the statement cannot hold for
k=1
, since
\delta_{1}=0
whenever all columns of
{\bm{X}}
are normalized to unit
\ell_{2}
-norm (see Proposition
).
Set
t\triangleq\lfloor k/2\rfloor\geq 1
, and partition
{\bm{X}}
in blocks of size
n\times t
(with possibly fewer columns in the last block):

{\bm{X}}=[{\bm{X}}_{1},{\bm{X}}_{2},\ldots,{\bm{X}}_{\nu}],\quad p\leq\nu t.

By Definitions
and
, Exercise
, and Proposition
, we have for all distinct
i,j\in\{1,2,\ldots,\nu\}
,
i\neq j
,

\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{i}-{\bm{I}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\delta_{t}\leq\delta_{k},\qquad\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{j}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\theta_{t,t}\leq\delta_{2t}\leq\delta_{k}.

Thus, all the eigenvalues of
{\bm{X}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{i}
and all the singular values of
{\bm{X}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{j}
satisfy

1-\delta_{k}\leq\lambda_{h}({\bm{X}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{i})\leq 1+\delta_{k},\qquad\sigma_{h}({\bm{X}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{j})\leq\delta_{k},\qquad h=1,2,\ldots,t

Define the Gram matrix and its dual:

{\bm{G}}\triangleq{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}=[{\bm{X}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{j}]_{1\leq i,j\leq\nu}\in\real^{p\times p},\qquad{\bm{H}}\triangleq{\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{\top}\in\real^{n\times n}.

Lower bound on
\mathrm{tr}({\bm{H}})
.

Using the cyclic invariance of the trace and the fact that each
{\bm{X}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{i}
is symmetric, we obtain

\mathrm{tr}({\bm{H}})=\mathrm{tr}({\bm{G}})=\sum_{i=1}^{\nu}\mathrm{tr}({\bm{X}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{i})=\sum_{i=1}^{\nu}\sum_{h=1}^{t}\lambda_{h}({\bm{X}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{i})\geq\nu t(1-\delta_{k}).

(4.51)

Upper bound via Frobenius norm.

Recall that for any matrices
{\bm{A}}_{1},{\bm{A}}_{2}
, the Frobenius inner product satisfies
\left\langle{\bm{A}}_{1},{\bm{A}}_{2}\right\rangle_{F}=\mathrm{tr}({\bm{A}}_{2}^{\top}{\bm{A}}_{1})
, and by Cauchy–Schwarz,

\mathrm{tr}({\bm{H}})^{2}=\left\langle{\bm{I}}_{n},{\bm{H}}\right\rangle_{F}^{2}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{I}}_{n}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}\left\lVert{\bm{H}}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}=n\mathrm{tr}({\bm{H}}^{\top}{\bm{H}}).

Now, using cyclic invariance again and the fact that
{\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{\top}=\sum_{i}{\bm{X}}_{i}{\bm{X}}_{i}^{\top}
, we have

\displaystyle\mathrm{tr}({\bm{H}}^{\top}{\bm{H}})

\displaystyle=\mathrm{tr}({\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{\top})=\mathrm{tr}({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}})=\mathrm{tr}({\bm{G}}{\bm{G}}^{\top})

\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{\nu}\mathrm{tr}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{\nu}{\bm{X}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{j}{\bm{X}}_{j}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{i}\right)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\dagger}}}{{=}}\sum_{1\leq i\neq j\leq\nu}\sum_{h=1}^{t}\sigma_{h}({\bm{X}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{j})^{2}+\sum_{i=1}^{\nu}\sum_{h=1}^{t}\lambda_{h}({\bm{X}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{i})^{2}

\displaystyle\leq\nu(\nu-1)t\delta_{k}^{2}+\nu t(1+\delta_{k})^{2}.

where the equality
({\dagger})
follows from the fact that the trace of a symmetric matrix is equal to the sum of its eigenvalues, and the fact that
\sigma({\bm{A}})^{2}=\lambda({\bm{A}}^{\top}{\bm{A}})=\lambda({\bm{A}}{\bm{A}}^{\top})
for any matrix
{\bm{A}}
.
This implies the upper bound

\mathrm{tr}({\bm{H}})^{2}\leq n\mathrm{tr}({\bm{H}}^{\top}{\bm{H}})\leq n\nu t\big((\nu-1)\delta_{k}^{2}+(1+\delta_{k})^{2}\big).

(4.52)

Combining the bounds (
) and (
) yields the lower bound for the number of samples:

n\geq\frac{\nu t(1-\delta_{k})^{2}}{(\nu-1)\delta_{k}^{2}+(1+\delta_{k})^{2}}.

(4.53)

If
(\nu-1)\delta_{k}^{2}<(1+\delta_{k})^{2}/5
, we would obtain, using
\delta_{k}\leq 2/3
,

n>\frac{\nu t(1-\delta_{k})^{2}}{6(1+\delta_{k})^{2}/5}\geq\frac{5(1-\delta_{k})^{2}}{6(1+\delta_{k})^{2}}p\geq\frac{1}{30}p,

which contradicts our assumption. We therefore have
(\nu-1)\delta_{k}^{2}\geq(1+\delta_{k})^{2}/5
, which yields, using
\delta_{k}\leq 2/3
again and
k\leq 3t
,

n\geq\frac{\nu t(1-\delta_{k})^{2}}{6(\nu-1)\delta_{k}^{2}}\geq\frac{1}{54\delta_{k}^{2}}t\geq\frac{1}{162\delta_{k}^{2}}k.

This completes the proof.

We will see later in Chapter
(e.g., Corollary
) that certain random matrices
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
satisfy
\delta_{k}\leq\delta
with high probability for any fixed
\delta\in(0,1)
, provided that

n\geq C\delta^{-2}k\ln(ep/k).

Thus, the lower bound (
) is optimal up to the logarithmic factor.

Theorem
examines measurement bounds when the RIP constant
\delta
is fixed.
We can also ask a complementary question: How many measurements are necessary to satisfy the RIP, if we ignore the specific value of
\delta
and focus only on the problem dimensions
n,p
, and
k
?
In this setting, we can derive a simple lower bound on
n
. To do so, we first establish a key lemma that will be used in the proof of the main result.

Lemma 171
.

Let
k
and
p
be integers satisfying
k<p/2
.
Then there exists a set
{\mathbb{S}}\subset{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]
such that

1.

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\sqrt{k}
for all
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
.

2.

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}\geq\sqrt{k/2}
for all distinct
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
with
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\neq{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
.

3.

\ln\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert\geq\frac{k}{2}\ln\left(\frac{p}{k}\right)
.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Consider the set

{\mathbb{T}}\triangleq\{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\{0,+1,-1\}^{p}\mid\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{0}=k\}.

By construction, every
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{T}}
satisfies
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}=\sqrt{k}
.
Thus, any subset of
{\mathbb{T}}
automatically satisfies condition (i).

Note that the cardinality of
{\mathbb{T}}
is
\left\lvert{\mathbb{T}}\right\rvert=\binom{p}{k}2^{k}
.
Moreover, since
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{0}\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
(when
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{T}}
),
it follows that if
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq k/2
, then
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{0}\leq k/2
.
Hence, for any fixed
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{T}}
, the number of
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{T}}
within squared
\ell_{2}
-distance
k/2
satisfies

\left\lvert\{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{T}}:\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq k/2\}\right\rvert\leq\big\lvert\{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{T}}\mid\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{0}\leq k/2\}\big\rvert\leq\binom{p}{k/2}3^{k/2}.

We now construct
{\mathbb{S}}
greedily: starting from
{\mathbb{T}}
, we iteratively select vectors that are at least
\sqrt{k/2}
apart in
\ell_{2}
-norm. After selecting
j
points, at most
j\binom{p}{k/2}3^{k/2}
points in
{\mathbb{T}}
are excluded from further selection.
Therefore, as long as

\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert\binom{p}{k/2}3^{k/2}\leq\binom{p}{k}2^{k}\equiv\left\lvert{\mathbb{T}}\right\rvert.

(4.54)

such a set
{\mathbb{S}}
of size
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert
exists.
To verify this inequality, observe that

\frac{\binom{p}{k}}{\binom{p}{k/2}}=\frac{(k/2)!(p-k/2)!}{k!(p-k)!}=\prod_{i=1}^{k/2}\frac{p-k+i}{k/2+i}\geq\left(\frac{p}{k}-\frac{1}{2}\right)^{k/2},

where the inequality holds because the function
f(i)\triangleq(p-k+i)/(k/2+i)
is decreasing in
i
.
Now set
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert=(p/k)^{k/2}
. Then

\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^{k/2}=\left(\frac{3p}{4k}\right)^{k/2}=\left(\frac{p}{k}-\frac{p}{4k}\right)^{k/2}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\dagger}}}{{\leq}}\left(\frac{p}{k}-\frac{1}{2}\right)^{k/2}\leq\frac{\binom{p}{k}}{\binom{p}{k/2}},

(4.55)

where the inequality (
{\dagger}
) follows from the assumption that
k<p/2
.
Combining (
) and (
), it follows that (
) holds for
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert=(p/k)^{k/2}
, which establishes the lemma.

Using this packing lemma, we now derive a fundamental lower bound on the number of measurements required for the RIP.

{theoremHigh}

[Measurement bound for RIP
(
Garnaev and Gluskin 1984
;
Baraniuk et al. 2011
)
]
Let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
satisfy the RIP of order
2k
with constant
\delta\in(0,\frac{1}{2}]

.
Then,

n\geq Ck\ln\left(\frac{p}{k}\right),\quad\text{with }C\triangleq\frac{1}{2\ln(\sqrt{24}+1)}\approx 0.28.

(4.56)

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Since
{\bm{X}}
satisfies the RIP or order
2k
,
for any
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
(with
{\mathbb{S}}
from Lemma
),
we have
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[2k]
, and thus

\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}\geq\sqrt{1-\delta}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}\geq\sqrt{k/4},\quad\forall\,{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}.

(4.57)

Similarly, using the upper RIP bound,

\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\sqrt{1+\delta}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\sqrt{3k/2},\quad\forall\,{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}.

(4.58)

The lower bound tells us that for any pair of points
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
, if we center balls of radius
\sqrt{k/4}/2=\sqrt{k/16}
at
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
and
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
, then these balls will be disjoint. In turn, the upper bound tells
us that the entire set of balls is itself contained within a larger ball of radius
\sqrt{3k/2}+\sqrt{k/16}
.
Let
{\mathbb{B}}_{2}[r]=\{{\bm{x}}\in\real^{n}\mid\left\lVert{\bm{x}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq r\}
denote the
\ell_{2}
-ball. This implies that

\displaystyle\text{Vol}\left({\mathbb{B}}_{2}\left[\sqrt{3k/2}+\sqrt{k/16}\right]\right)

\displaystyle\geq

\displaystyle\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert\cdot\text{Vol}\left({\mathbb{B}}_{2}\left[\sqrt{k/16}\right]\right)

(4.59)

\displaystyle\implies

\displaystyle\left(\sqrt{3k/2}+\sqrt{k/16}\right)^{n}

\displaystyle\geq

\displaystyle\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert\cdot\left(\sqrt{k/16}\right)^{n}

\displaystyle\implies

\displaystyle(\sqrt{24}+1)^{n}

\displaystyle\geq

\displaystyle\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert

\displaystyle\implies

\displaystyle n

\displaystyle\geq

\displaystyle\frac{\ln\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert}{\ln(\sqrt{24}+1)}.

By the bound for
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert
from Lemma
, this completes the proof.

Theorem
provides a lower bound on
n
that depends explicitly on the RIP constant
\delta_{k}
and the sparsity level
k
, but does not depend on
p
(the ambient dimension), except through the condition
p\geq Cn
.
Theorem
gives a lower bound on
n
that depends on
k
and the logarithmic ratio
\ln(p/k)
, but assumes a fixed range for
\delta
(e.g.,
\delta\leq 1/2
) and does not explicitly involve
\delta
in the bound.
Although the proofs above are somewhat indirect, a similar scaling in
p
and
k
can also be derived via the Gelfand width of the
\ell_{1}
-ball
(
Garnaev and Gluskin 1984
)
.

4.3.4
The RIP and Stability

We will see later in this book that if a matrix
{\bm{X}}
satisfies the RIP, then this condition is sufficient to guarantee that a wide range of algorithms can successfully recover a sparse signal from noisy measurements; see Section
.
Here, we examine whether the RIP is also necessary. It should be clear that the lower bound in the RIP is necessary if we wish to recover all
k
-sparse signals
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
exactly from noiseless measurements
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
, for the same reasons that the NSP is necessary (see Exercise
).
In fact, we can say even more about the necessity of the RIP by introducing the following notion of stability.

Definition 172
(
C
-stable
(
Baraniuk et al. 2011
)
).

Let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
be a sensing matrix and
\Delta:\real^{n}\rightarrow\real^{p}
a recovery algorithm.
We say that the pair
({\bm{X}},\Delta)
is
C
-stable if, for any
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]
and any
{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\in\real^{n}
,

\left\lVert\Delta({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}})-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq C\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\right\rVert_{2}.

(4.60)

This definition simply states that adding a small amount of noise to the measurements should not cause an arbitrarily large error in the recovered signal.
The following lemma shows that the existence of any decoding algorithm—even one that may be computationally impractical—that can stably recover signals from noisy measurements implies that
{\bm{X}}
must satisfy the lower bound of (
), with a constant determined by
C
.

Lemma 173
(
C
-stable
(
Baraniuk et al. 2011
)
).

If the pair
({\bm{X}},\Delta)
is
C
-stable, then

\frac{1}{C}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}

(4.61)

for all
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[2k]
.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Let
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]
. Define

{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{\beta}\triangleq\frac{{\bm{X}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\gamma}})}{2}\qquad\text{and}\qquad{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{\alpha}=\frac{{\bm{X}}({\boldsymbol{\gamma}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})}{2},

and observe that

{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}+{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{\beta}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{\alpha}=\frac{{\bm{X}}({\boldsymbol{\gamma}}+{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})}{2}.

Let
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\triangleq\Delta({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}+{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{\beta})=\Delta({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{\alpha})
.
By the triangle inequality and the definition of
C
-stability,

\displaystyle\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}

\displaystyle=\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}+{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\big\rVert_{2}\leq\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{2}+\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\big\rVert_{2}

\displaystyle\leq C\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{\beta}\right\rVert_{2}+C\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{\alpha}\right\rVert_{2}\leq C\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}.

Since this holds for any
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]
, it follows that for any
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[2k]
(by setting
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\boldsymbol{\gamma}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
), we have
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq C\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}
, which completes the proof.

Note that as
C\to 1
, the matrix
{\bm{X}}
must satisfy the lower bound of (
) with
\delta_{k}\triangleq 1-1/C^{2}\to 0
. Thus, to reduce the impact of noise on the reconstructed signal, we must choose
{\bm{X}}
so that it satisfies the RIP lower bound with a tighter (i.e., smaller) constant.

Since only the lower bound of RIP is necessary—and not the upper bound—we could avoid redesigning
{\bm{X}}
altogether by simply rescaling it. Indeed, if
{\bm{X}}
satisfies the RIP with
\delta_{2k}<1
, then the rescaled matrix
\eta{\bm{X}}
will satisfy inequality (
) for any desired constant
C
, provided
\eta
is chosen appropriately. In settings where the noise magnitude is independent of
{\bm{X}}
, this reasoning is valid: scaling
{\bm{X}}
increases the “signal” component of the measurements without affecting the noise, thereby improving the signal-to-noise ratio. In principle, this allows the noise to become negligible relative to the signal.

However, in practice, we cannot arbitrarily scale
{\bm{X}}
, since the noise does depend on
{\bm{X}}
in many real-world scenarios.
For example, suppose the noise vector
{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}
arises from quantization using a finite dynamic-range quantizer with
B
bits. If the original measurements lie in
[-R,R]
, and the quantizer is calibrated to this range, then rescaling
{\bm{X}}
by a factor
\eta
causes the measurements to span
[-\eta R,\eta R]
.
To accommodate this, the quantizer’s dynamic range must also be scaled by
\eta
, resulting in quantization error
\eta{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}
. Consequently, the reconstruction error does not decrease—it scales proportionally with
\eta
, offering no net improvement.

4.3.5
The RIP, NSP, and Variants

In this subsection, we show that if a matrix satisfies the RIP, then it also satisfies various forms of the NSP. Consequently, the RIP is strictly stronger than the NSP.

We begin by illustrating how RIP implies the standard NSP. The following observation—which is an extension to the standard bounds on vector norms (Exercise
)—is frequently used in our arguments, so we isolate it from the proof.

Lemma 174
(Ordered entry norm inequality
(
Foucart and Rauhut 2013
)
).

Given
s>t>0
, if
{\bm{u}}\in\real^{p}
and
{\bm{v}}\in\real^{m}
satisfy

\max_{i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}}\left\lvert u_{i}\right\rvert\leq\min_{j\in\{1,2,\ldots,m\}}\left\lvert v_{j}\right\rvert,

(4.62)

then

\left\lVert{\bm{u}}\right\rVert_{s}\leq\frac{p^{1/s}}{m^{1/t}}\left\lVert{\bm{v}}\right\rVert_{t}.

A special case occurs when
t=1
,
s=2
, and
p=m
, yielding

\left\lVert{\bm{u}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\frac{1}{\sqrt{p}}\left\lVert{\bm{v}}\right\rVert_{1}.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
To prove this, observe that:

\frac{\left\lVert{\bm{u}}\right\rVert_{s}}{p^{1/s}}=\left[\frac{1}{p}\sum_{i=1}^{p}\left\lvert u_{i}\right\rvert^{s}\right]^{1/s}\leq\max_{1\leq i\leq p}\left\lvert u_{i}\right\rvert,

\frac{\left\lVert{\bm{v}}\right\rVert_{t}}{m^{1/t}}=\left[\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\left\lvert v_{j}\right\rvert^{t}\right]^{1/t}\geq\min_{1\leq j\leq m}\left\lvert v_{j}\right\rvert.

This completes the proof.

The following lemma establishes a key relationship between the
\ell_{1}
-norms of the largest and smallest entries in any vector from the null space of a matrix satisfying the RIP, showing that the energy of the significant components is strictly bounded by that of the less significant ones under suitable RIP conditions.

Lemma 175
(RIP
\ell_{1}
-
\ell_{1}
bound lemma).

Let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
satisfy the RIP of order
2k
with constant
\delta_{2k}
.
For any nonzero
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
and any index set
{\mathbb{S}}
consisting of the
k
largest (in magnitude) coordinates of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
, we have

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\rho\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}\quad\text{with}\quad\rho=\frac{\delta_{2k}}{1-2\delta_{2k}}.

In particular, if
\delta_{2k}<\tfrac{1}{3}
, then
\rho<1
.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Consider
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})\setminus\{\boldsymbol{0}\}
, and let
{\mathbb{S}}\triangleq{\mathbb{S}}_{0}
be the set of indices corresponding to the
k
largest entries of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
in absolute value.
Partition
{\mathbb{S}}^{c}
into disjoint blocks
{\mathbb{S}}_{1},{\mathbb{S}}_{2},\dots
,
each containing at most
k
elements, such that the magnitudes of entries within each block are nonincreasing across blocks.
Since
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
, We have the decomposition

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}})+\sum_{i\geq 1}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}}_{i})\qquad\implies\qquad\boldsymbol{0}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}})+\sum_{i\geq 1}{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}}_{i}),

where
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}})\in\real^{p}
(see Definition
).
Taking the inner product with
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}})
yields

\boldsymbol{0}=\left\langle{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}}),{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle=\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\sum_{i\geq 1}\left\langle{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}}),{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}}_{i})\right\rangle.

Rearranging and taking absolute values gives

\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\sum_{i\geq 1}\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}}),{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}}_{i})\right\rangle\right\rvert.

From the RIP, for any two disjointly supported vectors
{\bm{u}},{\bm{v}}
with
\left\lVert{\bm{u}}\right\rVert_{0}+\left\lVert{\bm{v}}\right\rVert_{0}\leq 2k
, Proposition
shows that

\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{X}}{\bm{u}},{\bm{X}}{\bm{v}}\right\rangle\right\rvert\leq\delta_{2k}\,\left\lVert{\bm{u}}\right\rVert_{2}\,\left\lVert{\bm{v}}\right\rVert_{2}.

Also, the RIP lower bound provides
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\geq(1-\delta_{2k})\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
.
Applying these results, we obtain:

(1-\delta_{2k})\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\delta_{2k}\,\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}\sum_{i\geq 1}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}\right\rVert_{2}\quad\implies\quad(1-\delta_{2k})\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\delta_{2k}\sum_{i\geq 1}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}\right\rVert_{2}.

(4.63)

Because entries are nonincreasing across blocks, we have, for every
i\geq 1
,

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq\frac{1}{k}\sum_{v\in{\mathbb{S}}_{i-1}}\left\lvert\beta_{v}\right\rvert=\frac{1}{k}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i-1}}\right\rVert_{1},\quad\forall\,i\geq 1.

By the standard bounds on vector norms (Exercise
),
the
\ell_{2}
-norm of block
{\mathbb{S}}_{i}
satisfies:

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\sqrt{k}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq\sqrt{k}\cdot\frac{1}{k}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i-1}}\right\rVert_{1}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{k}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i-1}}\right\rVert_{1},\quad\forall\,i\geq 1.

(Note that the inequality can be directly obtained by Lemma
such that
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\frac{1}{\sqrt{k}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i-1}}\right\rVert_{1}
.)
Summing these inequalities over
i\geq 1
yields:

\sum_{i\geq 1}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\frac{1}{\sqrt{k}}\sum_{i\geq 1}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i-1}}\right\rVert_{1}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{k}}\sum_{i\geq 0}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}\right\rVert_{1}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{k}}\big(\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}+\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}\big).

(4.64)

Use (
) to bound the right-hand side of (
), and use
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\sqrt{k}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}
(Exercise
) to replace
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}
:

\displaystyle(1-\delta_{2k})\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}

\displaystyle\leq\delta_{2k}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt{k}}\big(\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}+\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}\big)

\displaystyle\leq\delta_{2k}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt{k}}\big(\sqrt{k}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}+\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}\big)=\delta_{2k}\big(\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}+\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{k}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}\big).

Rearrange to collect the
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}
terms and use
\frac{1}{\sqrt{k}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}
to obtain:

\frac{1}{\sqrt{k}}(1-2\delta_{2k})\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq(1-2\delta_{2k})\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\frac{\delta_{2k}}{\sqrt{k}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}.

Therefore, it holds that

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\frac{\delta_{2k}}{1-2\delta_{2k}}\,\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}.

So we can take
\rho\triangleq\dfrac{\delta_{2k}}{1-2\delta_{2k}}
. In particular if
\delta_{2k}<\tfrac{1}{3}
, then
1-2\delta_{2k}>1/3
and
\rho<1
.

Remark 176
.

In
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\geq(1-\delta_{2k})\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
, the vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
is actually
k
-sparse, yet it was treated as
2k
-sparse.
Consequently, a tighter bound could have been used
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}/(1-\delta_{k})
(see Exercise
).
The ROC
\theta_{k,k}<\delta_{2k}
could also have been used instead of
\delta_{2k}
(see Proposition
).
Using these refinements would lead to the improved sufficient condition
\delta_{k}+2\theta_{k,k}<1
rather than the more conservative requirement
\delta_{2k}<1/3
.

Using the lemma above, we now show that the RIP is a sufficient condition for the NSP (Definition
) to hold.

{theoremHigh}
[RIP
\implies
NSP]
If a matrix
{\bm{X}}
satisfies RIP(
2k,\delta_{2k}
) with
\delta_{2k}<1/3
, then it satisfies the NSP of order
k
.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
By the technical lemma
: if
{\bm{X}}
satisfies RIP
(2k,\delta_{2k})
, then for any nonzero
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
and
{\mathbb{T}}
being the set of
k
largest-magnitude entries of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
,

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{T}}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\rho\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{T}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1},\quad\rho=\frac{\delta_{2k}}{1-2\delta_{2k}}.

If
\delta_{2k}<\frac{1}{3}
, then
\rho<1
.

Let
{\mathbb{S}}\subset\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
with
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert=k
be arbitrary, and let
{\mathbb{T}}
be the set of
k
largest-magnitude entries of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.
By construction of
{\mathbb{T}}
:

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{T}}}\right\rVert_{1},\quad\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}\geq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{T}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}.

Therefore,

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{T}}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\rho\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{T}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\rho\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1},\quad\text{for {all} ${\mathbb{S}}$ with $\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert=k$}.

This establishes the NSP of order
k
for
{\bm{X}}
.

It is worth noting that the RIP(
2k,\delta_{2k}
) condition imposes constraints on a very large number of submatrices—specifically, on
\binom{p}{2k}
of them. In contrast to the pairwise incoherence condition, however, the RIP constant
\delta_{2k}
itself does not inherently depend on
k
(beyond the order of the property).

Results from random matrix theory show that various random ensembles satisfy the RIP with high probability, provided the number of measurements
n
scales as
n\gtrsim k\ln\frac{ep}{k}
. For example, this holds for a standard Gaussian random matrix
{\bm{X}}
with i.i.d. entries drawn from
\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{n})
; see Corollary
for details.
Thus, the RIP-based framework enables exact sparse recovery from significantly fewer measurements than what is required by pairwise incoherence—which typically demands
n\gtrsim k^{2}\ln p

(
Foucart and Rauhut 2013
)
. On the other hand, a major practical limitation of RIP is that, unlike pairwise incoherence, it is extremely difficult to verify directly, due to the combinatorial number
\binom{p}{2k}
of submatrices that must be checked.

We next show that the RIP also implies NSP
′
.
We begin with a key lemma that will be used in the proof of Theorem
. This result holds for arbitrary vectors
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
, not only those in the null space of
{\bm{X}}
. (Note that if
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
, the argument could be significantly simplified.)

Lemma 177
.

Suppose
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
and
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
are orthogonal vectors. Then

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}+\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\sqrt{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Define the
2\times 1
vector
{\bm{u}}=[\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2},\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}]^{\top}
.
By the standard bounds on vector norms (Exercise
), we have
\left\lVert{\bm{u}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\sqrt{2}\left\lVert{\bm{u}}\right\rVert_{2}
. This gives

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}+\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\sqrt{2}\sqrt{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}.

Since
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
and
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
are orthogonal,
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
, which completes the proof.

The next lemma bounds the sum of the
\ell_{2}
-norms of successive blocks of
k
largest entries (in magnitude) of a vector, in terms of the
\ell_{1}
-norm of its tail. It quantifies how the energy of a vector decays across increasingly less significant components.

Lemma 178
(Partitioned ordered-set inequality).

Let
{\mathbb{S}}_{0}\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
be any index set with
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}_{0}\right\rvert\leq k
.
For any vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
, define
{\mathbb{S}}_{1}
as the indices of the
k
largest entries (in absolute value) of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}^{c}}
,

{\mathbb{S}}_{2}
as the indices of the next
k
largest entries, and so on.
Then

\sum_{i\geq 2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\frac{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}}{\sqrt{k}}.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
By construction, the magnitudes of entries in
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}
are nonincreasing with
i
. In particular, for
i\geq 2
,

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq\frac{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i-1}}\right\rVert_{1}}{k},\quad\text{for $i\geq 2$},

since each entry in
{\mathbb{S}}_{i}
no larger (in absolute value) than the average magnitude of the entries in
{\mathbb{S}}_{i-1}
.
Using this result and applying standard bounds on vector norms (Exercise
), we obtain

\sum_{i\geq 2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\sqrt{k}\sum_{i\geq 2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq\frac{1}{\sqrt{k}}\sum_{i\geq 1}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}\right\rVert_{1}=\frac{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}}{\sqrt{k}}.

This completes the proof.

The following result, due to Emmanuel Candes, provides a crucial estimate for the norm of a vector restricted to a support set of size at most
2k
. It plays a central role in connecting the RIP to sparse recovery guarantees.

Lemma 179
(Candes RIP
\ell_{2}
-
\ell_{1}
bound lemma
(
Candes 2008
)
).

Let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
satisfy the RIP of order
2k
(with
2k\leq p
), and let
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
,
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\neq\boldsymbol{0}
be arbitrary.
Let
{\mathbb{S}}_{0}\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
satisfy
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}_{0}\right\rvert\leq k
.
Define
{\mathbb{S}}_{1}
as the indices of the
k
largest entries (in magnitude) of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}^{c}}
, and set
{\mathbb{S}}\triangleq{\mathbb{S}}_{0}\cup{\mathbb{S}}_{1}
.
Then,

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\mu\frac{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}}{\sqrt{k}}+\nu\frac{\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}},{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle\right\rvert}{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}},

(4.65)

where
\mu={\sqrt{2}\delta_{2k}}/{(1-\delta_{2k})}

and

\nu={1}/{(1-\delta_{2k})}
.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Since
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\mathbb{S}}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[2k]
, the lower RIP bound gives

(1-\delta_{2k})\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left\langle{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\mathbb{S}},{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle-\left\langle{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\mathbb{S}},\sum_{i\geq 2}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}\right\rangle,

(4.66)

where the sets
{\mathbb{S}}_{i}
for
i\geq 2
are defined as in Lemma
, i.e., as
{\mathbb{S}}_{1}
is the index set corresponding to the
k
largest entries of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}^{c}}
in absolute value, define
{\mathbb{S}}_{2}
as the index set corresponding to the next
k
largest entries, and so on. The above equality holds since
{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\mathbb{S}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\sum_{i\geq 2}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}
.
We now bound the second term. Using linearity of the inner product,

\displaystyle\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\mathbb{S}},\sum_{i\geq 2}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}\right\rangle\right\rvert

\displaystyle=\left\lvert\sum_{i\geq 2}\left\langle{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}},{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}\right\rangle+\sum_{i\geq 2}\left\langle{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{1}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{1}},{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}\right\rangle\right\rvert

\displaystyle\leq\sum_{i\geq 2}\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}},{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}\right\rangle\right\rvert+\sum_{i\geq 2}\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{1}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{1}},{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}\right\rangle\right\rvert

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\dagger}}}{{\leq}}\delta_{2k}\sum_{i\geq 2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}\right\rVert_{2}+\delta_{2k}\sum_{i\geq 2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{1}}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}\right\rVert_{2}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\ddagger}}}{{\leq}}\sqrt{2}\delta_{2k}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{2}\sum_{i\geq 2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\sqrt{2}\delta_{2k}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{2}\frac{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}}{\sqrt{k}}.

where the inequality (
{\dagger}
) follows from the standard consequence of RIP (Proposition
),
the inequality (
{\ddagger}
) follows from the fact that
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}}\right\rVert_{2}+\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{1}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\sqrt{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{2}
by Lemma
,
and the last inequality follows from Lemma
.
Substituting this bound back, we get

\displaystyle(1-\delta_{2k})\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle\leq\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\mathbb{S}},{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle\right\rvert+\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\mathbb{S}},\sum_{i\geq 2}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}\right\rangle\right\rvert

\displaystyle\leq\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\mathbb{S}},{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle\right\rvert+\sqrt{2}\delta_{2k}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{2}\frac{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}}{\sqrt{k}}.

This proves the desired result after rearrangement.

A refined version of this lemma—tailored to bound
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}
with
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}
—is presented in Lemma
and will be used to establish noise-free signal recovery guarantees.

We now show that if a matrix satisfies the RIP, then it also satisfies the NSP
′
(Definition
).

{theoremHigh}
[RIP
\implies
NSP
′
]
Suppose that
{\bm{X}}
satisfies the RIP of order
2k
with
\delta_{2k}<\sqrt{2}-1
. Then
{\bm{X}}
satisfies the NSP
′
of order
2k
with constant

C=\frac{\sqrt{2}\delta_{2k}}{1-(1+\sqrt{2})\delta_{2k}}.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Recall that Lemma
holds for arbitrary vectors
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
.
To prove the theorem, we apply this lemma to the special case where
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
, i.e.,
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\boldsymbol{0}
.
Let
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
denote the index set corresponding to the
2k
largest entries (in absolute value) of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
. It suffices to show that

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq C\frac{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}}{\sqrt{k}}.

(4.67)

To this end, let
{\mathbb{S}}_{0}
be the subset of
{\mathbb{S}}
containing the
k
largest entries of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
, and define
{\mathbb{S}}_{1}={\mathbb{S}}\setminus{\mathbb{S}}_{0}
(so that
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}_{1}\right\rvert\leq k
). Applying Lemma
and noting that
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\boldsymbol{0}
, the second term in the lemma vanishes, yielding

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\mu\frac{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}}{\sqrt{k}},

(4.68)

where
\mu={\sqrt{2}\delta_{2k}}/{(1-\delta_{2k})}
.
Using the standard bounds on vector norms (Exercise
), we have

\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}^{c}}\big\rVert_{1}=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{1}}\right\rVert_{1}+\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\big\rVert_{1}\leq\sqrt{k}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{1}}\right\rVert_{2}+\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}.

(4.69)

Combining (
) and (
) leads to

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\mu\left(\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{1}}\right\rVert_{2}+\frac{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}}{\sqrt{k}}\right)\quad\implies\quad(1-\mu)\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\mu\frac{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}}{\sqrt{k}},

where the implication follows since
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{1}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}
.
The assumption
\delta_{2k}<\sqrt{2}-1
ensures that
\mu<1
, and thus we may divide by
1-\mu
without changing the direction of the inequality to establish (
) with constant

C\triangleq\frac{\mu}{1-\mu}=\frac{\sqrt{2}\delta_{2k}}{1-(1+\sqrt{2})\delta_{2k}}.

This completes the proof.

The next argument establishes that the RIP implies the robust NSP (see Definition
).
This proof relies on the following auxiliary result, known as the
square root lifting inequality
.
It can be viewed as a refined counterpart of the standard vector norm inequality

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\sqrt{p}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}
(see Exercise
).

Lemma 180
(Square root lifting inequality).

Let
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
satisfy
\beta_{1}\geq\beta_{2}\geq\ldots\geq\beta_{p}\geq 0
.
Then

\sqrt{\beta_{1}^{2}+\beta_{2}^{2}+\ldots+\beta_{p}^{2}}\leq\frac{\beta_{1}+\beta_{2}+\ldots+\beta_{p}}{\sqrt{p}}+\frac{\sqrt{p}}{4}(\beta_{1}-\beta_{p}).

That is,
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\frac{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}}{\sqrt{p}}+\frac{\sqrt{p}}{4}(\beta_{1}-\beta_{p})
.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
It suffices to prove the equivalent implication:

\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\beta_{1}\geq\beta_{2}\geq\ldots\geq\beta_{p}\geq 0\\
\frac{\beta_{1}+\beta_{2}+\ldots+\beta_{p}}{\sqrt{p}}+\frac{\sqrt{p}}{4}\beta_{1}\leq 1\end{array}\right\}\implies\sqrt{\beta_{1}^{2}+\beta_{2}^{2}+\ldots+\beta_{p}^{2}}+\frac{\sqrt{p}}{4}\beta_{p}\leq 1.

Define the convex function

f(\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\ldots,\beta_{p})\triangleq\sqrt{\beta_{1}^{2}+\beta_{2}^{2}+\ldots+\beta_{p}^{2}}+\frac{\sqrt{p}}{4}\beta_{p}

and consider the convex polytope

{\mathbb{T}}\triangleq\left\{[\beta_{1},\ldots,\beta_{p}]\in\real^{p}\mid\beta_{1}\geq\ldots\geq\beta_{p}\geq 0\text{ and }\frac{\beta_{1}+\beta_{2}+\ldots+\beta_{p}}{\sqrt{p}}+\frac{\sqrt{p}}{4}\beta_{1}\leq 1\right\}.

Since
f
is convex and
{\mathbb{T}}
is a compact convex set, the maximum of
f
over
{\mathbb{T}}
is attained at an extreme point (vertex) of
{\mathbb{T}}
. The vertices arise by setting
p
of the
p+1
defining inequalities to equality. We examine the relevant cases:

If
\beta_{1}=\ldots=\beta_{p}=0
, then
f(\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\ldots,\beta_{p})=0
.

If
(\beta_{1}+\beta_{2}+\ldots+\beta_{p})/\sqrt{p}+\sqrt{p}\beta_{1}/4=1
and
\beta_{1}=\ldots=\beta_{k}>\beta_{k+1}=\ldots=\beta_{p}=0
for some
1\leq k\leq n-1
, then we have
\beta_{1}=\ldots=\beta_{k}=4\sqrt{p}/(4k+p)
, and consequently
f(\beta_{1},\ldots,\beta_{p})=4\sqrt{p}/(4k+p)\leq 1
.

If
(\beta_{1}+\beta_{2}+\ldots+\beta_{p})/\sqrt{p}+\sqrt{p}\beta_{1}/4=1
and
\beta_{1}=\ldots=\beta_{p}>0
, then we have
\beta_{1}=\ldots=\beta_{p}=4/(5\sqrt{p})
, and consequently
f(\beta_{1},\ldots,\beta_{p})=4/5+1/5=1
.

Thus,

\max_{[\beta_{1},\ldots,\beta_{p}]\in{\mathbb{T}}}f(\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\ldots,\beta_{p})=1
,
which proves the lemma.

{theoremHigh}

[RIP
\implies
robust NSP]
Let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
satisfy the RIP condition of order
2k
with the RIC

\delta_{2k}<\frac{77-\sqrt{1337}}{82}\approx 0.4931.

(4.70)

Then
{\bm{X}}
satisfies the
\ell_{2}
-robust NSP of order
k
(w.r.t.
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert=\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{2}
) with constants
0<\rho<1
and
\tau>0
that depend only on
\delta_{2k}
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
We need to find constants
0<\rho<1
and
\tau>0
such that, for any
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
and any
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
with
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert=k
,

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\frac{\rho}{\sqrt{k}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}+\tau\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}.

(4.71)

Given
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
, it suffices to consider an index set
{\mathbb{S}}\triangleq{\mathbb{S}}_{0}
of
k
largest entries of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
in modulus.
As before, we partition
{\mathbb{S}}^{c}
into disjoint blocks
{\mathbb{S}}_{1},{\mathbb{S}}_{2},\dots
,
each containing at most
k
elements, such that the magnitudes of entries within each block are nonincreasing across blocks.
We begin by applying the RIP to the vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}}_{0})+{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}}_{1})
, which is
2k
-sparse:

\displaystyle(1-\delta_{2k})(\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}}_{0})+{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}}_{1})\right\rVert_{2}^{2})

\displaystyle\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}}_{0})+{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}}_{1}))\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\big\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\sum_{i\geq 2}{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}}_{i})\big\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle=\big\lVert\sum_{i\geq 2}{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}}_{i})\big\rVert_{2}^{2}-2\left\langle{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}},\sum_{i\geq 2}{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}}_{i})\right\rangle+\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

(4.72)

Denote the sum of the last two terms by
\mu
.
For the first term, expand the squared norm:

\displaystyle\left\lVert\sum_{i\geq 2}{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}}_{i})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle=\left\langle\sum_{i\geq 2}{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}}_{i}),\sum_{j\geq 2}{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}}_{j})\right\rangle

\displaystyle=\sum_{i\geq 2}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}}_{i})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\sum_{i,j\geq 2,i\neq j}\left\langle{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}}_{i}),{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}}_{j})\right\rangle

\displaystyle\leq(1+\delta_{2k})\sum_{i\geq 2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}}_{i})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\sum_{i,j\geq 2,i\neq j}\delta_{2k}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}}_{i})\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}}_{j})\right\rVert_{2}

\displaystyle=\sum_{i\geq 2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}}_{i})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\delta_{2k}\left(\sum_{i\geq 2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}}_{i})\right\rVert_{2}\right)^{2},

(4.73)

where the inequality follows from the RIP condition, and the standard consequence of RIP (Proposition
).

For each block
{\mathbb{S}}_{i}
, let
\beta_{i}^{-}
and
\beta_{i}^{+}
denote the smallest and largest absolute values of entries of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
on
{\mathbb{S}}_{i}
.
Define
\eta\triangleq\sum_{i\geq 2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}\right\rVert_{1}=\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}^{c}}\big\rVert_{1}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{1}}\right\rVert_{1}
.
Then we can bound:

\sum_{i\geq 2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\sum_{i\geq 2}\sum_{j\in{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}\left\lvert\beta_{j}\right\rvert^{2}\leq\sum_{i\geq 2}\beta_{2}^{+}\sum_{j\in{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}\left\lvert\beta_{j}\right\rvert=\beta_{2}^{+}\eta.

Second, by Lemma
and the monotonicity of the blocks (such that
\beta_{i}^{-}\geq\beta_{i+1}^{+}
), it follows that

\sum_{i\geq 2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\sum_{i\geq 2}\left(\frac{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}\right\rVert_{1}}{\sqrt{k}}+\frac{\sqrt{k}}{4}(\beta_{i}^{+}-\beta_{i}^{-})\right)\leq\frac{\eta}{\sqrt{k}}+\frac{\sqrt{k}}{4}\beta_{2}^{+}.

Substituting the above two inequalities into (
4.73
) yields

\left\lVert\sum_{i\geq 2}{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}}_{i})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\beta_{2}^{+}\eta+\delta_{2k}\left(\frac{\eta}{\sqrt{k}}+\frac{\sqrt{k}}{4}\beta_{2}^{+}\right)^{2}.

Substituting the above inequality into (
4.72
), taking into account the fact that
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}}+{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{1}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{1}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\geq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+k\beta_{2}^{+2}
, and using the inequality that

\eta=\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}^{c}}\big\rVert_{1}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{1}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}^{c}}\big\rVert_{1}-k\beta_{2}^{+}=(1-\nu)\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}^{c}}\big\rVert_{1},
with
\nu\triangleq k\beta_{2}^{+}/\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}^{c}}\big\rVert_{1}

gives

\displaystyle(1

\displaystyle-\delta_{2k})\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq-(1-\delta_{2k})k\beta_{2}^{+2}+\beta_{2}^{+}\eta+\delta_{2k}\left(\frac{\eta}{\sqrt{k}}+\frac{\sqrt{k}}{4}\beta_{2}^{+}\right)^{2}+\mu

(4.74)

\displaystyle\leq-(1-\delta_{2k})\frac{\nu^{2}}{k}\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}^{c}}\big\rVert_{1}^{2}+\frac{\nu(1-\nu)}{k}\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}^{c}}\big\rVert_{1}^{2}+\delta_{2k}\left(\frac{1-\nu}{\sqrt{k}}+\frac{\nu}{4\sqrt{k}}\right)^{2}\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}^{c}}\big\rVert_{1}^{2}+\mu

\displaystyle=\left[-(1-\delta_{2k})\nu^{2}+\nu(1-\nu)+\delta_{2k}\left(1-\frac{3\nu}{4}\right)^{2}\right]\frac{\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}^{c}}\big\rVert_{1}^{2}}{k}+\mu.

We need to prove that the quantity in square brackets divided by

is negative. This difference is the quadratic expression in

This expression is maximized at

f(\nu)\leq f(\nu^{*})=\frac{b^{2}}{4a}-c=\frac{(1-3\delta_{2k}/2)^{2}}{4(2-25\delta_{2k}/16)}-1+2\delta_{2k}.

It is easy to show that

Under this condition, the quantity in square brackets of (

To show the desired inequality (

), we have

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\frac{\rho^{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}^{2}}{k}+\frac{\mu}{1-\delta_{2k}}.

(4.75)

For the estimation of

\mu\leq 2\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}\sum_{i\geq 2}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}}_{i})\right\rVert_{2}+\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq 2\sqrt{1+\delta_{2k}}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}\sum_{i\geq 2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}\right\rVert_{2}+\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

By Lemma

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i-1}}\right\rVert_{1}/\sqrt{k}

\sum_{i\geq 2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\frac{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}}{\sqrt{k}}.

Substituting the above two inequalities into (

\displaystyle\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle\leq\frac{\rho^{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}^{2}}{k}+2\frac{\sqrt{1+\delta_{2k}}}{1-\delta_{2k}}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}\frac{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}}{\sqrt{k}}+\frac{\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}{1-\delta_{2k}}

\displaystyle\leq\left(\frac{\rho^{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}^{2}}{k}+2\frac{\sqrt{1+\delta_{2k}}}{1-\delta_{2k}}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}\frac{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}}{\sqrt{k}}+\frac{1+\delta_{2k}}{\rho^{2}(1-\delta_{2k})^{2}}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right)

\displaystyle=\left(\frac{\rho\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}}{\sqrt{k}}+\frac{\sqrt{1+\delta_{2k}}}{\rho(1-\delta_{2k})}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}\right)^{2}.

This completes the proof by letting
\tau\triangleq\sqrt{1+\delta_{2k}}/(\rho(1-\delta_{2k}))
