Chapter 5
Sparse Optimization Analysis

I
In many real-world applications—from signal processing and imaging to machine learning and genomics—the data we encounter often exhibit sparsity: that is, only a small number of components carry meaningful information. Exploiting this structural property allows us to recover signals or estimate models from limited or noisy observations with high accuracy and computational efficiency. This chapter delves into the theoretical foundations of sparse optimization, focusing on conditions under which sparse signals can be accurately recovered from linear measurements.

We begin in Section
by examining recovery guarantees based on the nullspace property (NSP), a fundamental condition that ensures exact recovery of sparse signals via convex optimization. We analyze both noiseless and noisy settings, providing theoretical insights into stability and robustness.

Section
investigates recovery under coherence, a measure of similarity between columns of the measurement matrix. This approach offers intuitive understanding and practical tools for designing sensing matrices with favorable recovery properties. Moving forward, Section
focuses on the restricted isometry property (RIP), which provides stronger and more versatile guarantees for sparse recovery. We present results for both noiseless and noisy scenarios, including instance-optimal error bounds and an analysis of the Dantzig selector—an alternative to
\ell_{1}
-minimization.

The theoretical foundations of
\ell_{1}
-minimization leads naturally to the discussion of LASSO (least absolute shrinkage and selection operator) in Section
, a widely used technique in statistics and machine learning for regression with sparsity-inducing regularization. We compare LASSO with robust linear regression methods and examine its behavior under different conditions.

To illustrate the relevance of the design matrix’s properties to sparse recovery, consider the following result:

{theoremHigh}
[Exact recovery of
\ell_{0}
under RIP]
Suppose
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
is a design matrix satisfying the RIP condition of order
2k
with
k\geq 1
and restricted isometry constant
\delta_{2k}<1
, and let
{\mathbb{S}}\subset\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
be such that
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert\leq k
. Let
{\bm{y}}\triangleq{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
where
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
is any vector supported on
{\mathbb{S}}
(i.e.,
{\mathbb{S}}=\mathrm{supp}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})
). Then
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
is the
unique
minimizer of problem (
) (p.
):

(\text{P}_{0})\quad\min\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{0}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\bm{y}}.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Assume, for contradiction, that
{\bm{y}}
admits two distinct
k
-sparse representations:
{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}
, where
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
and
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}
are supported on sets
{\mathbb{S}}
and
{\mathbb{S}}^{\prime}
, respectively, with
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert,\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}^{\prime}\right\rvert\leq k
.
Then

{\bm{X}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime})=\boldsymbol{0}.

By construction, the difference
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}
is supported on
{\mathbb{S}}\cup{\mathbb{S}}^{\prime}
, which has cardinality at most
2k
.
Applying the RIP condition (see Equation (
)) and using
\delta_{2k}<1
, we obtain
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=0
, contradicting the assumption that the two representations are distinct.

Note that this theorem is an abstract existence result: it establishes what is theoretically possible but does not provide an efficient algorithm to recover
{\mathbb{S}}
or the coefficients
\beta^{*}_{i}
from
{\bm{y}}
and
\{{\bm{x}}_{i}\}_{i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}}
, other than exhaustive (brute-force) search—as discussed in Chapter
.
In contrast, as we show next, imposing slightly stronger conditions—such as a stricter bound on the restricted isometry constant
\delta_{2k}
or alternative structural properties—ensures that the convex
\ell_{1}
-minimization program (
) recovers
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
exactly.

For example,

Candes and Tao 2005
demonstrated that if
{\bm{X}}\in\text{RIP}(2k,0.33)
(Definition
), then the non-convex
\ell_{0}
-norm minimization problem (
) and the convex
\ell_{1}
-minimization problem (
) (p.
) share identical solutions for all
k
-sparse vectors.
Moreover, in the presence of noise (
{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}
),
\ell_{1}
-minimization stably approximates the sparsest near-solution, with a well-controlled stability constant (see Section
).
Later,
Candes 2008
established a sharper sufficient condition:
\delta_{2k}<0.4142
.
Under this bound,
\ell_{1}
-minimization exactly recovers any
k
-sparse signal in the noiseless case and provides robust estimates in the presence of noise. This chapter discusses further results related to this condition and extends the analysis to LASSO-type problems as well.

5.1
Sparse Recovery under NSP

In Exercise
, we demonstrated that the NSP of order
2k
is sufficient for the unique recovery of distinct
k
-sparse signals, and that NSP
′
is necessary when the recovery algorithm satisfies a specific bound as stated in (
) of Lemma
. In this section, we investigate the conditions under which the NSP is both sufficient and necessary for the unique recovery of sparse signals in the noiseless case. We further show that in noisy settings, the associated error bounds remain stable.

5.1.1
Signal Recovery without Noise

We begin by establishing the connection between the NSP (Definition
) and the exact recovery of sparse vectors via basis pursuit (i.e.,
\ell_{1}
-minimization).

{theoremHigh}
[Exact recovery of
\ell_{1}
under NSP(
{\mathbb{S}}
)]
Let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
.
Then, every vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\in\real^{p}
supported on a set
{\mathbb{S}}
is the
unique
solution of (
) with
{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
if and only if
{\bm{X}}
satisfies the NSP condition relative to
{\mathbb{S}}
, i.e., NSP(
{\mathbb{S}}
).

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Fix an index set
{\mathbb{S}}
, and assume that every vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\in\real^{p}
supported on
{\mathbb{S}}
is the unique minimizer of
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{1}
subject to
{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
, where
{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}={\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
.
Consider any nonzero
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})\setminus\{\boldsymbol{0}\}
.
Then
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}})
satisfies
{\bm{X}}(-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}}^{c}))={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}})
,
and since
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\neq\boldsymbol{0}
, we have
-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}}^{c})\neq{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}})
.
By the assumed uniqueness of the
\ell_{1}
minimizer, it follows that
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}<\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}
, which is precisely the NSP(
{\mathbb{S}}
) condition.

Conversely, suppose the NSP(
{\mathbb{S}}
) condition holds.
Let
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
be supported on
{\mathbb{S}}
, and let
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}
,
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\neq{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
, satisfy
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.
Define
{\bm{u}}\triangleq{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})\setminus\{\boldsymbol{0}\}
.
Then, using the triangle inequality and the NSP(
{\mathbb{S}}
) condition,

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}+\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}=\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}+\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}<\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}+\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}=\left\lVert-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}+\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{1}.

Thus,
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
uniquely minimizes the
\ell_{1}
-norm among all feasible solutions, completing the proof.

Allowing the support set
{\mathbb{S}}
to vary over all subsets of size at most
k
, we immediately obtain the following corollary.

Corollary 181
(Exact recovery of
\ell_{1}
under NSP of order

).

Let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
.
Then, every
k
-sparse vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\in\real^{p}
is the
unique

{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
if and only if
{\bm{X}}
satisfies the NSP of order
k
.

This result shows that, whenever the NSP of order
k
holds, the
\ell_{1}
-minimization problem (

\ell_{0}
-minimization problem (

Indeed, suppose
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
is
k

-minimization from

. Let
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
be a solution to (

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{0}\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{0}\leq k

The following theorem formalizes this equivalence between the
\ell_{0}
and

{theoremHigh}

[
\ell_{0}
and

Suppose that
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\in\real^{p}

Then the basis pursuit problem (

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
if and only if
{\bm{X}}
satisfies the NSP condition relative to
{\mathbb{S}}
, i.e., NSP(
{\mathbb{S}}
).

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Assume
{\bm{X}}
satisfies NSP(
{\mathbb{S}}
).
Let
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\in\real^{p}
be the unique solution to problem (
), and define the error vector
\Delta\triangleq{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
. Our goal is to show that
\Delta=\boldsymbol{0}
, and in order to do so, it suffices to show that
\Delta\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})\cap{\mathbb{C}}({\mathbb{S}})
.
Since
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
and
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
are optimal (and hence feasible) solutions to the
\ell_{0}
and
\ell_{1}
problems, respectively, they yield the same measurement
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}={\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}

{\bm{X}}\Delta=\boldsymbol{0}
, and thus
\Delta\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
.
Moreover, since
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
is feasible for the
\ell_{1}
-minimization problem (

implies that

, whence we have

\displaystyle\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}>\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}\geq\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\big\rVert_{1}=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}_{{\mathbb{S}}}+\Delta_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}+\left\lVert\Delta_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}\geq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}-\left\lVert\Delta_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}+\left\lVert\Delta_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1},

where the equality follows from the fact that
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}+\Delta
and
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}=\boldsymbol{0}
, and the last inequality follows by the triangle inequality. Rearranging terms shows that
\Delta\in{\mathbb{C}}({\mathbb{S}})
.
However, since
\Delta\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})\cap{\mathbb{C}}({\mathbb{S}})\neq\{\boldsymbol{0}\}

{\mathbb{S}}
), we must have

. Thus
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
.

Conversely, suppose the problem (

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\in\real^{p}
with support
{\mathbb{S}}
.
For any nonzero
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})\setminus\{\boldsymbol{0}\}
, the vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}})
is the unique minimizer of
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{1}
subject to
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}})
.
Since
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\boldsymbol{0}
and
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\neq\boldsymbol{0}
, we have
{\bm{X}}(-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}}^{c}))={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}})
and
-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}}^{c})\neq{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}})
.
Hence, it follows that
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}<\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}
, which establishes the NSP(
{\mathbb{S}}
) condition.
This completes the proof.

Note that it is also desirable that any reconstruction method be robust to certain transformations of the measurement system—such as rescaling, reordering, or augmenting rows of
{\bm{X}}
. Basis pursuit enjoys such invariance properties, as shown in (
).

To conclude this section, we extend the analysis to the more general
\ell_{s}
-minimization
problem:

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\qquad\text{s.t.}\quad{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}},

(P
s
)

where

.
While the case

Intuitively, smaller values of
s
should yield solutions closer to the true
\ell_{0}
minimizer. To formalize this, we introduce an
\ell_{s}
-analogue of the NSP.

The proof of the next result mirrors that of Theorem
and is left as an exercise. It relies on the fact that the function
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\mapsto\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{s}^{s}
satisfies the triangle inequality for
0<s\leq 1
; see Problem
.

{theoremHigh}

[Exact recovery of
\ell_{s}
]
Let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
and
0<s\leq 1
.
Then every
k
-sparse vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\in\real^{p}
is the
unique
solution of (
) with
{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
if and only if, for every index set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
with
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert\leq k
,

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{s}<\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{s},\quad\text{for all }{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})\setminus\{\boldsymbol{0}\}.

(5.1)

The condition in (
) is actually the
\ell_{s}
-analogue of the standard NSP condition (
) in Definition
.

We now show that successful sparse recovery via
\ell_{s}
-minimization implies successful recovery via
\ell_{t}
-minimization whenever
0<t<s\leq 1
—that is, using a smaller exponent yields at least as strong a recovery guarantee.

{theoremHigh}

[Exact recovery of
\ell_{t}<\ell_{s}
]
Let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
and
0<t<s\leq 1
.
If every
k
-sparse vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\in\real^{p}
is the
unique
solution of (
) with
{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
, then every
k
-sparse vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\in\real^{p}
is also the
unique
solution of (P
t
) with
{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
By Theorem
, it suffices to show the following: for any nonzero
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})\setminus\{\boldsymbol{0}\}
, if
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
denotes a set of
k
indices corresponding to the largest (in magnitude) entries of
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
, then

\sum_{j\in{\mathbb{S}}}\left\lvert\alpha_{j}\right\rvert^{t}<\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\left\lvert\alpha_{i}\right\rvert^{t},

(5.2)

provided that the same inequality holds with
s
in place of
t
.

Note that, since
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\neq\boldsymbol{0}
and
{\mathbb{S}}
contains the
k
largest entries in absolute value, the complement
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}
cannot be identically zero unless
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
is
k
-sparse—but even in that case, the NSP condition would require
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=\boldsymbol{0}
, a contradiction. Hence
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\neq\boldsymbol{0}
, and the denominator below is positive.

Dividing both sides of (
) by
\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\left\lvert\alpha_{i}\right\rvert^{t}>0
, the desired inequality is equivalent to

\sum_{j\in{\mathbb{S}}}\frac{\left\lvert\alpha_{j}\right\rvert^{t}}{\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\left\lvert\alpha_{i}\right\rvert^{t}}=\sum_{j\in{\mathbb{S}}}\frac{1}{\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}(\left\lvert\alpha_{i}\right\rvert/\left\lvert\alpha_{j}\right\rvert)^{t}}<1.

(5.3)

Now observe that for each
i\in{\mathbb{S}}^{c}
and
j\in{\mathbb{S}}
, the ratio
\left\lvert\alpha_{i}\right\rvert/\left\lvert\alpha_{j}\right\rvert\leq 1
by construction of
{\mathbb{S}}
.
This makes the left-hand side of (
) a nondecreasing function of
0<t\leq 1
. Hence, its value at
t<s
does not exceed its value at
s
.
But by assumption and Theorem
, the inequality holds strictly for
s
, i.e., the expression is
<1
when
t=s
. Therefore, it is also
<1
for
t<s
, which establishes (
). This completes the proof.

5.1.2
Signal Recovery with Noise

The ability to perfectly reconstruct a sparse signal from noise-free measurements is a promising theoretical result. However, in most real-world applications, measurements are inevitably contaminated by some form of noise. For example, when processing data on a digital computer, we must represent signals using a finite number of bits, which introduces quantization error. Moreover, physical measurement systems are subject to various types of noise—such as thermal, electronic, or sensor noise—depending on the specific implementation and environment.

Perhaps somewhat surprisingly, it is possible to modify the standard
\ell_{1}
-minimization program

{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}=\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\qquad\text{s.t.}\quad{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\mathcal{B}({\bm{y}}).

so that it stably recovers sparse (or approximately sparse) signals under a wide range of common noise models, e.g., model (
) (p.
) uses
\mathcal{B}({\bm{y}})=\{{\bm{z}}\mid\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\bm{z}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\epsilon\}
.

The previous results establish exact recovery for the basis pursuit problem under various NSP conditions.
We then start by using the stable NSP (Definition
) or robust NSP (Definition
) to show that any solution lies in a neighborhood of the true vector, with the size of the neighborhood controlled by the best
k
-term approximation error.

{theoremHigh}
[Stability of
\ell_{1}
under stable NSP]
Let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
satisfy the stable NSP of order
k
with constant
0<\rho<1
.
Then, for any
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\in\real^{p}
, every solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
of (
) with measurements
{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
satisfies the
\ell_{1}
-error bound:

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\frac{2(1+\rho)}{(1-\rho)}\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})_{1},

(5.4)

where
\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})_{1}\triangleq\min_{\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]}\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}
denotes the
\ell_{1}
-error of the best
k
-term approximation.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Let
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
be a set of
k
indices corresponding to the largest (in magnitude) entries of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
.
Then, by definition,
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}=\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})_{1}
.
Since
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is a minimizer of (
), it satisfies
\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{1}
and
{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
.
Applying Theorem
with
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}={\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
and
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
, we obtain

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\frac{2(1+\rho)}{(1-\rho)}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}=\frac{2(1+\rho)}{(1-\rho)}\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})_{1},

which is precisely the bound in (
).

In contrast to Theorem
and Corollary
, we can no longer guarantee uniqueness of the
\ell_{1}
-minimizer under the stable NSP alone—although non-uniqueness occurs only in degenerate cases.
Nevertheless, even when multiple minimizers exist, the theorem ensures that every solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
of (
) with
{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
satisfies the error bound (
).

The following theorem extends Theorem
, recovering it as the special case
\epsilon=0
for the quadratically-constrained
\ell_{1}
-minimization problem (
).

{theoremHigh}

[Stability of (
) under robust NSP]
Let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
satisfy the robust NSP of order
k
with constants
0<\rho<1
,
\tau>0
, and
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert=\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{2}
.
Then, for any
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\in\real^{p}
, every solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
of (
) with measurements
{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}+{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}
and noise satisfying
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\epsilon
obeys the
\ell_{1}
-error bound:

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\frac{2(1+\rho)}{(1-\rho)}\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})_{1}+\frac{4\tau}{1-\rho}\epsilon.

(5.5)

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Let
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
be a set of
k
indices corresponding to the largest (in magnitude) entries of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
.
By definition,
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}=\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})_{1}
.
Since
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is a minimizer of (
), it satisfies
\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{1}
and
\big\lVert{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\big\rVert\leq 2\epsilon
.
Applying Theorem
(standard consequence of robust NSP) with
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}={\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
and
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
, we obtain

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\frac{2(1+\rho)}{(1-\rho)}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}+\frac{2\tau}{1-\rho}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})\right\rVert_{2}\leq\frac{2(1+\rho)}{(1-\rho)}\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})_{1}+\frac{4\tau}{1-\rho}\epsilon.

which is precisely the bound in (
).

Note that when
\mathrm{supp}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})={\mathbb{S}}
with
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert=k
, i.e.,
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
is exactly
k
-sparse, the bound becomes

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\frac{4\tau}{1-\rho}\epsilon.

Moreover, when
\epsilon=0
, the result reduces to Corollary
.

The following corollary strengthens the above robustness guarantee by providing error bounds not only in
\ell_{1}
, but in
\ell_{t}
for all

1\leq t\leq 2
.

Corollary 182
(Stability of (
) under
\ell_{2}
-robust NSP).

Let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
satisfy the
\ell_{2}
-robust NSP of order
k
with constants
0<\rho<1
,
\tau>0
, and
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert=\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{2}
.
Then, for any
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\in\real^{p}
, every solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
of (
) with measurements
{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}+{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}
and noise
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\epsilon
satisfies the
\ell_{t}
-error bound:

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\right\rVert_{t}\leq\frac{C}{k^{(1-\frac{1}{t})}}\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})_{1}+Dk^{(\frac{1}{t}-\frac{1}{2})}\epsilon,\quad 1\leq t\leq 2,

(5.6)

where the constants
C,D>0
depend only on
\rho
and
\tau
(specifically,
C\triangleq 2(1+\rho)^{2}/(1-\rho)
and
D\triangleq 2\tau(3+\rho)/(1-\rho)
).
In particular, the bounds for the extremal cases are:

\displaystyle\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\right\rVert_{1}

\displaystyle\leq C\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})_{1}+D\sqrt{k}\epsilon,\qquad t=1;

\displaystyle\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\right\rVert_{2}

\displaystyle\leq\frac{C}{\sqrt{k}}\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})_{1}+D\epsilon,\qquad t=2.

Proof
[of Corollary
]
The error bound (
) follows from Theorem
(standard consequence of
\ell_{s}
-robust NSP) as follows:
Let
{\mathbb{S}}
to be a set of
k
indices corresponding to the largest (in magnitude) entries of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
.
Then
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}=\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})_{1}
.
The solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
of (
) satisfies
\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{1}
and
\big\lVert{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\big\rVert_{2}\leq 2\epsilon
.
Invoking Theorem
with
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}={\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
and
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
can therefore prove the desired bound (
).

We observe that the coefficient of
\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})_{1}
is constant when
t=1
and decays like
1/\sqrt{k}
when
t=2
,
whereas the coefficient of
\epsilon
grows like
\sqrt{k}
for
t=1
but remains constant for
t=2
.
This reflects the well-known trade-off between sparsity-driven approximation error and noise sensitivity across different norms.

5.2
Sparse Recovery under Coherence

In this section,
we show that a small
\ell_{1}
-coherence (see Definition
) also guarantees the success of
\ell_{1}
-minimization.

{theoremHigh}

Let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
be a matrix with
\ell_{2}
-normalized columns. If

\mu_{1}({\bm{X}},k)+\mu_{1}({\bm{X}},k-1)<1,

(5.7)

then every
k
-sparse vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\in\real^{p}
is exactly recovered from the measurements
{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
by solving the
\ell_{1}
-minimization problem (
).

Proof
[of Theorem
]
By Corollary
, it suffices to verify that
{\bm{X}}
satisfies the NSP condition of order
k
, i.e., that

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}<\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}

(5.8)

for every nonzero vector
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})\setminus\{\boldsymbol{0}\}
and every index set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
with
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert=k
.
Since
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=\boldsymbol{0}
, we have
\sum_{j=1}^{p}\alpha_{j}{\bm{x}}_{j}=\boldsymbol{0}
.
Taking the inner product of both sides with a column
{\bm{x}}_{i}
for some
i\in{\mathbb{S}}
, and using the fact that
\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}=1
, we obtain

\alpha_{i}=\alpha_{i}\left\langle{\bm{x}}_{i},{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rangle=-\sum_{j=1,j\neq i}^{p}\alpha_{j}\left\langle{\bm{x}}_{j},{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rangle=-\sum_{h\in{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\alpha_{h}\left\langle{\bm{x}}_{h},{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rangle-\sum_{j\in{\mathbb{S}},j\neq i}\alpha_{j}\left\langle{\bm{x}}_{j},{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rangle,

whence we have

\left\lvert\alpha_{i}\right\rvert\leq\sum_{h\in{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\left\lvert\alpha_{h}\right\rvert\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{x}}_{h},{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rangle\right\rvert+\sum_{j\in{\mathbb{S}},j\neq i}\left\lvert\alpha_{j}\right\rvert\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{x}}_{j},{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rangle\right\rvert.

Summing over all
i\in{\mathbb{S}}
and interchanging the order of summation gives

\displaystyle\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}

\displaystyle=\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}}\left\lvert\alpha_{i}\right\rvert\leq\sum_{h\in{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\left\lvert\alpha_{h}\right\rvert\left(\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}}\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{x}}_{h},{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rangle\right\rvert\right)+\sum_{j\in{\mathbb{S}}}\left\lvert\alpha_{j}\right\rvert\left(\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}},i\neq j}\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{x}}_{j},{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rangle\right\rvert\right)

\displaystyle\leq\sum_{h\in{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\left\lvert\alpha_{h}\right\rvert\cdot\mu_{1}({\bm{X}},k)+\sum_{j\in{\mathbb{S}}}\left\lvert\alpha_{j}\right\rvert\cdot\mu_{1}({\bm{X}},k-1)

\displaystyle=\mu_{1}({\bm{X}},k)\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}+\mu_{1}({\bm{X}},k-1)\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}.

Rearranging terms, we obtain
\big(1-\mu_{1}({\bm{X}},k-1)\big)\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\mu_{1}({\bm{X}},k)\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}
.
Under the assumption (
), we have
1-\mu_{1}({\bm{X}},k-1)>\mu_{1}({\bm{X}},k)
, which implies (
). Thus, the NSP of order
k
holds, and exact recovery via
\ell_{1}
-minimization follows from Corollary
.

5.3
Sparse Recovery under RIP

In this section, we establish the success of sparse recovery via basis pursuit for measurement matrices with small restricted isometry constants. We present several proofs of this result.
The first proof uses the condition
\delta_{k}+\theta_{k,k}+\theta_{k,2k}<1
, which is derived from the dual certificate theorem (Theorem
).
The second proof is simpler and more intuitive. It shows that the condition
\delta_{2k}<1/3
is sufficient to guarantee exact recovery of all
k
-sparse vectors via
\ell_{1}
-minimization.
The remaining proofs are more involved. We show that the weaker conditions
\delta_{2k}<0.4142
or
\delta_{2k}<0.4931
are actually sufficient to ensure stable and robust recovery of all
k
-sparse vectors via
\ell_{1}
-minimization.

5.3.1
Dual Certificate: Revisited

As stated in Theorem
, a vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
, supported on
{\mathbb{S}}=\mathrm{supp}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})
, is the unique minimizer of (
) if the submatrix
{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
has full rank and there exists a vector
{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}
satisfying the following two properties:

1.

\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rangle=\sign(\beta^{*}_{i})
for all
i\in{\mathbb{S}}
;

2.

\left\lvert\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rangle\right\rvert<1
, for all
i\in{\mathbb{S}}^{c}
.

This vector
{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}
is known as the
dual certificate for problem (
)
.
The next two lemmas demonstrate the existence of such a dual certificate under the restricted isometry property (RIP).
Lemma
establishes that the inner products
\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rangle
for
i\in{\mathbb{S}}^{c}
are suitably bounded, except possibly on a small “exceptional set.” Lemma
strengthens this result by eliminating the exceptional set entirely.

Lemma 183
(Dual reconstruction property,
\ell_{2}
version).

Suppose
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
is a design matrix that satisfies the RIP condition or order
k\geq 1
with constant
\delta_{k}<1
, and let
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
be a real vector supported on
{\mathbb{S}}\subset\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
with
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert\leq k
.
Then there exists a vector
{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}})
such that
\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rangle=\sign(\beta^{*}_{i})
for all
i\in{\mathbb{S}}
. Furthermore, there exists an “exceptional set”
{\mathbb{T}}\subset\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
which is disjoint from
{\mathbb{S}}
, with cardinality at most

\left\lvert{\mathbb{T}}\right\rvert\leq k^{\prime}
(
k^{\prime}\geq 1
),
such that

\left\lvert\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rangle\right\rvert\leq\frac{\theta_{k,k^{\prime}}}{(1-\delta_{k})\sqrt{k^{\prime}}}\cdot\sqrt{k},\quad\text{for all }i\in({\mathbb{S}}\cup{\mathbb{T}})^{c}

and

\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{T}}}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rVert_{2}=\left(\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{T}}}\left\lvert\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rangle\right\rvert^{2}\right)^{1/2}\leq\frac{\theta_{k,k^{\prime}}}{1-\delta_{k}}\cdot\sqrt{k}.

Additionally,
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq C\sqrt{k}
for some constant
C>0
depending only upon
\delta_{k}
.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
The proof differs slightly but is based on
Candes and Tao 2005
.
The RIP condition (
) implies that the eigenvalue satisfies
\lambda({\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}})\in[1-\delta_{k},1+\delta_{k}]
.
Since we assume
\delta_{k}<1
,
{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}
is invertible with

\left\lVert({\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}})^{-1}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\frac{1}{1-\delta_{k}}\quad\text{ and }\quad\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}({\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}})^{-1}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\frac{\sqrt{1+\delta_{k}}}{1-\delta_{k}}

(5.9)

by Problem
.
Define
{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}})
by

{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\triangleq{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}({\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}})^{-1}\sign({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}_{\mathbb{S}})
.
It is then clear that
{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}=\sign({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}_{\mathbb{S}})
, i.e.,
\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rangle=\sign(\beta^{*}_{i})
for all
i\in{\mathbb{S}}
.
Moreover,
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq C\cdot\left\lVert\sign(\beta^{*}_{i})\right\rVert_{2}
with
C\triangleq\sqrt{1+\delta_{k}}/(1-\delta_{k})
by (
) and (
).
Now let
{\mathbb{S}}^{\prime}\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots,p\}\setminus{\mathbb{S}}
, i.e.,
{\mathbb{S}}^{\prime}
is any set in
\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
disjoint from
{\mathbb{S}}
with
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}^{\prime}\right\rvert\leq k^{\prime}
, and let
{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{\prime}}\triangleq\{d_{i}\}_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}^{\prime}}\in\real^{\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}^{\prime}\right\rvert}
be arbitrary.
Then the ROP condition (
) and (
) give

\displaystyle\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{\prime}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{\prime}}\right\rangle\right\rvert

\displaystyle=\left\lvert\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{\prime}}{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{\prime}}\right\rangle\right\rvert=\left\lvert\left\langle\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}}\big(({\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}})^{-1}\sign({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}_{\mathbb{S}})\big)_{i}{\bm{x}}_{i},\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}^{\prime}}d_{i}{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rangle\right\rvert

\displaystyle\leq\theta_{k,k^{\prime}}\cdot\left\lVert({\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}})^{-1}\sign({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}_{\mathbb{S}})\right\rVert_{2}\cdot\left\lVert{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{\prime}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\frac{\theta_{k,k^{\prime}}}{1-\delta_{k}}\left\lVert\sign({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}_{\mathbb{S}})\right\rVert_{2}\cdot\left\lVert{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{\prime}}\right\rVert_{2}.

Since
{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{\prime}}
is arbitrary, it follows from Hölder’s inequality by setting
{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{\prime}}\triangleq{{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{\prime}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}}/{\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{\prime}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rVert_{2}}
that

\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{\prime}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rVert_{2}=\left(\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}^{\prime}}\left\lvert\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rangle\right\rvert^{2}\right)^{1/2}\leq\frac{\theta_{k,k^{\prime}}}{1-\delta_{k}}\left\lVert\sign({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}_{\mathbb{S}})\right\rVert_{2}

(5.10)

whenever
{\mathbb{S}}^{\prime}\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots,p\}\setminus{\mathbb{S}}
and
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}^{\prime}\right\rvert\leq k^{\prime}
.
Finally, define the exceptional set

{\mathbb{T}}\triangleq\left\{i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}\setminus{\mathbb{S}}\mid\left\lvert\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rangle\right\rvert>\frac{\theta_{k,k^{\prime}}}{(1-\delta_{k})\sqrt{k^{\prime}}}\cdot\left\lVert\sign({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}_{\mathbb{S}})\right\rVert_{2}\right\},

then
\left\lvert{\mathbb{T}}\right\rvert
must obey
\left\lvert{\mathbb{T}}\right\rvert\leq k^{\prime}
, since otherwise we could contradict (
) by taking a subset
{\mathbb{S}}^{\prime}
of
{\mathbb{T}}
of cardinality
k^{\prime}
.

We now construct a dual vector with improved control over
\left\lvert\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rangle\right\rvert
for indices
i
outside the support
{\mathbb{S}}
, by iteratively eliminating the exceptional set
{\mathbb{T}}
while keeping the values on
{\mathbb{S}}
fixed.
The following result and its proof are adapted from
Candes and Tao 2005
.

Lemma 184
(Dual reconstruction property,
\ell_{\infty}
version).

Suppose
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
is a design matrix that satisfies the RIP and ROP condition with
k\geq 1
and constants such that
\delta_{k}+\theta_{k,k}+\theta_{k,2k}<1
,
and let
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
be a real vector supported on
{\mathbb{S}}\subset\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
with
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert\leq k
.
Then there exists a vector
{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}})
such that
\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rangle=\sign(\beta^{*}_{i})
for all
i\in{\mathbb{S}}
. Furthermore,
{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}
satisfies

\left\lvert\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rangle\right\rvert\leq\frac{\theta_{k,k}}{(1-\delta_{k}-\theta_{k,2k})}<1,\quad\text{for all $i\in{\mathbb{S}}^{c}$.}

(5.11)

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Set
{\mathbb{S}}_{0}\triangleq{\mathbb{S}}
.
By Lemma
, there exists a vector
{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(1)}\triangleq{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}}({\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}})^{-1}\sign({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}})\in\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}})
and a set
{\mathbb{S}}_{1}\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
such that

\displaystyle{\displaystyle\mathbb{S}}_{0}\cap{\mathbb{S}}_{1}=\varnothing\ \text{ with }\ \left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}_{1}\right\rvert\leq k;

\displaystyle\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(1)},{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rangle=\sign(\beta^{*}_{i}),\qquad\text{for all }i\in{\mathbb{S}}_{0};

\displaystyle\left\lvert\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(1)},{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rangle\right\rvert\leq\frac{\theta_{k,k}}{(1-\delta_{k})},\qquad\text{for all }i\in({\mathbb{S}}_{0}\cup{\mathbb{S}}_{1})^{c};

\displaystyle\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{1}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t+1)}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\frac{\theta_{k,k}}{1-\delta_{k}}\sqrt{k};

\displaystyle\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(1)}\big\rVert_{2}\leq C\sqrt{k}.

Since the assumption
\delta_{k}+\theta_{k,k}+\theta_{k,2k}<1
implies that
\delta_{2k}\leq\delta_{k}+\theta_{k,k}<1
by Proposition
such that
{\bm{X}}
satisfies the RIP condition of order
2k
.
We then iteratively construct a set
{\mathbb{S}}_{t}
with
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}_{t}\right\rvert\leq k
for
t\geq 2
.
Let
{\mathbb{I}}_{t}\triangleq{\mathbb{S}}_{t}\cup{\mathbb{S}}_{0}
, and for
i\in{\mathbb{I}}_{t}
define
{\bm{b}}^{(t)}\in\real^{\left\lvert{\mathbb{I}}_{t}\right\rvert}
with

b_{i}^{(t)}=\begin{cases}\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)},{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rangle,\quad&i\in{\mathbb{S}}_{t};\\
0,\quad&i\in{\mathbb{S}}_{0}.\end{cases}

Define further
{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t+1)}\triangleq{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{I}}_{t}}({\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{I}}_{t}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{I}}_{t}})^{-1}{\bm{b}}^{(t)}
,
where
({\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{I}}_{t}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{I}}_{t}})
is invertible since
{\bm{X}}
satisfies the RIP condition of order
2k
.
Applying Lemma
iteratively gives a sequence of vectors

{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t+1)}\triangleq{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{I}}_{t}}({\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{I}}_{t}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{I}}_{t}})^{-1}{\bm{b}}^{(t)}\in\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}})
and sets
{\mathbb{S}}_{t+1}\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
for all
t\geq 1
satisfying

\displaystyle{\mathbb{S}}_{t}\cap({\mathbb{S}}_{0}\cup{\mathbb{S}}_{t+1})=\varnothing\ \text{ with }\ \left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}_{t+1}\right\rvert\leq k;

(5.12a)

\displaystyle\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t+1)},{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rangle=\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)},{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rangle,\qquad\text{for all }i\in{\mathbb{S}}_{t};

(5.12b)

\displaystyle\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t+1)},{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rangle=0,\qquad\text{for all }i\in{\mathbb{S}}_{0};

(5.12c)

\displaystyle\left\lvert\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t+1)},{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rangle\right\rvert\leq\frac{\theta_{k,k}}{1-\delta_{k}}\left(\frac{\theta_{k,2k}}{1-\delta_{2k}}\right)^{t}\leq\frac{\theta_{k,k}}{1-\delta_{2k}}\left(\frac{\theta_{k,2k}}{1-\delta_{2k}}\right)^{t},\quad\forall\,i\in({\mathbb{S}}_{0}\cup{\mathbb{S}}_{t}\cup{\mathbb{S}}_{t+1})^{c};

(5.12d)

\displaystyle\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{t+1}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t+1)}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\frac{\theta_{k,k}}{1-\delta_{k}}\left(\frac{\theta_{k,2k}}{1-\delta_{2k}}\right)^{t}\sqrt{k}\leq\frac{\theta_{k,k}}{1-\delta_{2k}}\left(\frac{\theta_{k,2k}}{1-\delta_{2k}}\right)^{t}\sqrt{k};

(5.12e)

\displaystyle\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t+1)}\right\rvert\leq\left(\frac{\theta_{k,2k}}{1-\delta_{2k}}\right)^{t-1}C,

(5.12f)

where we have used the facts that
\delta_{k}\leq\delta_{2k}
(Exercise
).
The inequality (
5.12d
) follows since
\left\lvert{\mathbb{I}}_{t}\right\rvert\leq 2k
(the ROC has
\theta_{k,2k}\equiv\theta_{2k,k}
, hence the parameter
\theta_{k,2k}
instead of
\theta_{k,k}
) and the iterative argument of
\left\lVert{\bm{b}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}=\big\lVert{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{t}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}\big\rVert_{2}
:

\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{t+1}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t+1)}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\frac{\theta_{k,2k}}{1-\delta_{2k}}\left\lVert{\bm{b}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}=\frac{\theta_{k,2k}}{1-\delta_{2k}}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{t}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}.

The inequality (
5.12e
) hence follows accordingly.

By hypothesis, we have
\theta_{k,2k}+\delta_{2k}\leq\theta_{k,2k}+\delta_{k}+\theta_{k,k}<1
(Proposition
) such that
\frac{\theta_{k,2k}}{1-\delta_{2k}}<1
. Thus, if we set

{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\triangleq\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{t-1}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}
, then the series is absolutely convergent and, therefore,
{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}
is a well-defined vector in
\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}})
. We now examine the coefficients

\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rangle=\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{t-1}\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)},{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rangle,\quad\text{for $i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}$}.

(5.13)

On the one hand, for
i\in{\mathbb{S}}_{0}
, it follows from the construction that
\big\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(1)},{\bm{x}}_{i}\big\rangle=\sign(\beta^{*}_{i})
and
\big\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)},{\bm{x}}_{i}\big\rangle=0
for all
t\geq 2
, and hence,

\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rangle=\sign(\beta^{*}_{i}),\quad\text{for all }i\in{\mathbb{S}}_{0}.

On the other hand, we examine
i
with
i\in{\mathbb{S}}_{0}^{c}
. For example, let
i\in{\mathbb{S}}_{2}
, it holds that

\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rangle=\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{t-1}\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)},{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rangle=\sum_{t\notin\{2,3\}}^{\infty}(-1)^{t-1}\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)},{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rangle,

where the term
-\big\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(2)},{\bm{x}}_{i}\big\rangle+\big\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(3)},{\bm{x}}_{i}\big\rangle
cancels out by (
5.12b
).
And the other terms satisfy (
5.12d
).
Therefore,
\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rangle
follows from a geometric series:

\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rangle\leq\frac{\theta_{k,k}}{1-\delta_{2k}-\theta_{k,2k}},\quad\text{for all $i\in{\mathbb{S}}^{c}$.}

This completes the proof.

Lemma
effectively solves the dual reconstruction problem: it guarantees the existence of a vector
{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}})
satisfying both properties (i) and (ii) stated at the beginning of this section.
Combining this lemma with the dual certificate result in Theorem
immediately establishes the uniqueness of the solution to the
\ell_{1}
-minimization problem (
).
Alternatively, the same conclusion can be reached directly using only the RIP. This leads to the following recovery guarantee.

{theoremHigh}

[Exact recovery of
\ell_{1}
under RIP and ROP
(
Candes and Tao 2005
)
]
Let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
be a design matrix satisfying the RIP and ROP conditions with
k\geq 1
and

\delta_{k}+\theta_{k,k}+\theta_{k,2k}<1,

(5.14)

and let
{\mathbb{S}}\subset\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
be any index set with
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert\leq k
.
Let
{\bm{y}}\triangleq{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
where
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
is an arbitrary vector supported on
{\mathbb{S}}
.
Then
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
is the
unique
minimizer of the optimization problem

(\text{P}_{1})\qquad\min\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\bm{y}}.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Standard results from convex analysis ensure that at least one minimizer
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
of (
) exists.
We need to prove that
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
.
Since
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
is a feasible point of (
) and
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is a minimizer of (
), it follows that

\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{1}=\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}}\left\lvert\beta^{*}_{i}\right\rvert.

(5.15)

By Lemma
, there exists a vector
{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}
satisfying the properties (i) and (ii) at the beginning of this Section.
Then, it follows that

\displaystyle\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}

\displaystyle=\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}}\left\lvert\beta^{*}_{i}+({\widehat{\beta}}_{i}-\beta^{*}_{i})\right\rvert+\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\left\lvert{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}\right\rvert\geq\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}}\sign(\beta^{*}_{i})\big(\beta^{*}_{i}+({\widehat{\beta}}_{i}-\beta^{*}_{i})\big)+\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}{\left\lvert\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rangle\right\rvert}

(5.16)

\displaystyle=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{1}+\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}}({\widehat{\beta}}_{i}-\beta^{*}_{i}){\left\lvert\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rangle\right\rvert}+\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}{\left\lvert\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rangle\right\rvert}=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{1}+\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rangle

\displaystyle=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{1}+\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\bm{y}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rangle=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{1}.

Combining (
) and (
) yields
\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{1}
.
Since
\left\lvert\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rangle\right\rvert
is strictly less than 1 for all
i\in{\mathbb{S}}^{c}
, this in particular forces
{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}=0
for all
i\in{\mathbb{S}}^{c}
.
To see this, if
\mathrm{supp}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})\neq{\mathbb{S}}
, (
) also indicates that

0=\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}}(\beta^{*}_{i}-{\widehat{\beta}}_{i})\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rangle-\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rangle=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{1}-\underbrace{\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}}\sign(\beta^{*}_{i}){\widehat{\beta}}_{i}}_{\leq\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}}\left\lvert{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}\right\rvert}-\underbrace{\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rangle}_{<\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\left\lvert{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}\right\rvert}>0,

leading to a contradiction with the fact that
\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{1}
.
Thus,
\mathrm{supp}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})={\mathbb{S}}
and
{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}={\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
,

Applying the RIP condition in (
) and the fact that
\delta_{k}<1
, we conclude that
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
. This proves the uniqueness of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
.

Note from Proposition
that the hypothesis of (
) implies
\delta_{2k}<1
, and is in turn implied by
\delta_{k}+\delta_{2k}+\delta_{3k}<1
. Thus, the condition (
) is roughly “three times as strict” as the condition required for Theorem
under the
\ell_{0}
-minimization model (
\delta_{2k}<1
).
By virtue of the previous discussion, we have the following simple result, which requires
\delta_{2k}<1/3
and is also roughly “three times as strict” as the condition required for Theorem
.

{theoremHigh}

[Exact recovery of
\ell_{1}
under RIP]
Let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
satisfy the RIP condition of order
2k
with RIC

\delta_{2k}<\frac{1}{3}.

(5.17)

Then every
k
-sparse vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\in\real^{p}
is the
unique
solution of

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
The proof follows simply from Corollary
and Theorem
.

It is instructive to go beyond exact recovery and establish stability and robustness—i.e., guarantees that persist when the measurements are noisy or the signal is only approximately sparse. The following exercise invites such a refinement.

Exercise
