to establish stability and robustness of
k
-sparse recovery via basis pursuit under the condition
\delta_{2k}<1/3
.
Specifically, show that the reconstruction error remains bounded in terms of the measurement noise level and the best
k
-term approximation error of the true signal.

Hint: See Theorem
, or see Section
for further details.

5.3.2
Signal Recovery without Noise

Exercise
addressed stable recovery under the RIP of order
2k
with constant
\delta_{2k}<1/3
.
We now relax this requirement to the weaker condition
\delta_{2k}<\sqrt{2}-1
.
To achieve this, we rely on the following general result, which refines the Candes RIP bound lemma (Lemma
).

Lemma 185
(Candes RIP bound refinement lemma
(
Candes 2008
)
).

Suppose that
{\bm{X}}
satisfies the RIP condition of order
2k
with constant
\delta_{2k}<\sqrt{2}-1
. Let
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}},\in\real^{p}
be given, and define
{\bm{d}}\triangleq{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.
Let
{\mathbb{S}}_{0}
denote the index set of the
k
largest-magnitude entries of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
,
and let
{\mathbb{S}}_{1}
denote the index set of the
k
largest-magnitude entries of
{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}^{c}}
.
Set
{\mathbb{S}}\triangleq{\mathbb{S}}_{0}\cup{\mathbb{S}}_{1}
. If
\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\big\rVert_{1}\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}
, then

\left\lVert{\bm{d}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq C_{0}\frac{\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})_{1}}{\sqrt{k}}+C_{1}\frac{\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}},{\bm{X}}{\bm{d}}\right\rangle\right\rvert}{\left\lVert{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}},

(5.18)

where

C_{0}=2\frac{1-(1-\sqrt{2})\delta_{2k}}{1-(1+\sqrt{2})\delta_{2k}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad C_{1}=\frac{2}{1-(1+\sqrt{2})\delta_{2k}}.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Since
{\bm{d}}={\bm{d}}({\mathbb{S}})+{\bm{d}}({\mathbb{S}}^{c})
, the triangle inequality gives

\left\lVert{\bm{d}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}+\left\lVert{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{2}.

(5.19)

We first bound
\left\lVert{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{2}
.
By the partitioned ordered sets inequality (Lemma
), we have

\left\lVert{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{2}=\left\lVert\sum_{i\geq 2}{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\sum_{i\geq 2}\left\lVert{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{i}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\frac{\left\lVert{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}}{\sqrt{k}},

(5.20)

where the sets
{\mathbb{S}}_{i}
are defined as before, i.e.,
{\mathbb{S}}_{1}
is the index set corresponding to the
k
largest entries of
{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}^{c}}
(in absolute value),
{\mathbb{S}}_{2}
as the index set corresponding to the next
k
largest entries, and so on.

Next, we bound
\left\lVert{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}
.
Since
\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+{\bm{d}}\big\rVert_{1}=\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\big\rVert_{1}\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}
, the triangle inequality yields

\displaystyle\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}

\displaystyle\geq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+{\bm{d}}\right\rVert_{1}=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}}+{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}}\right\rVert_{1}+\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}^{c}}+{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}

\displaystyle\geq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}}\right\rVert_{1}-\left\lVert{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}}\right\rVert_{1}+\left\lVert{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}-\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}^{c}}\big\rVert_{1}.

Rearranging terms and recalling that
\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})_{1}=\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}^{c}}\big\rVert_{1}=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}}_{0})\right\rVert_{1}
, we obtain

\displaystyle\left\lVert{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}

\displaystyle\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}}\right\rVert_{1}+\left\lVert{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}}\right\rVert_{1}+\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}^{c}}\big\rVert_{1}

\displaystyle\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{S}}_{0})\right\rVert_{1}+\left\lVert{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}}\right\rVert_{1}+\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}^{c}}\big\rVert_{1}=\left\lVert{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}}\right\rVert_{1}+2\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})_{1}.

(5.21)

Substituting (
5.21
) into (
) gives

\left\lVert{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\frac{\left\lVert{\bm{d}}_{{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}}}\right\rVert_{1}+2\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})_{1}}{\sqrt{k}}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}}\right\rVert_{2}+\frac{2\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})_{1}}{\sqrt{k}},

(5.22)

where the last inequality follows from the standard bounds on vector norms (Exercise
).
By observing that
\left\lVert{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}
, substituting the above inequality into (
) yields

\left\lVert{\bm{d}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq 2\left\lVert{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}+\frac{2\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})_{1}}{\sqrt{k}}.

(5.23)

We now bound
\left\lVert{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}
. Combining Candes RIP bound lemma (Lemma
) with (
5.21
) and again applying standard bounds on vector norms (Exercise
), we obtain

\displaystyle\left\lVert{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}

\displaystyle\leq\mu\frac{\left\lVert{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}}{\sqrt{k}}+\nu\frac{\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}},{\bm{X}}{\bm{d}}\right\rangle\right\rvert}{\left\lVert{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}}\leq\mu\frac{\left\lVert{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}}\right\rVert_{1}+2\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})_{1}}{\sqrt{k}}+\nu\frac{\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}},{\bm{X}}{\bm{d}}\right\rangle\right\rvert}{\left\lVert{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}}

\displaystyle\leq\mu\left\lVert{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}}\right\rVert_{2}+2\mu\frac{\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})_{1}}{\sqrt{k}}+\nu\frac{\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}},{\bm{X}}{\bm{d}}\right\rangle\right\rvert}{\left\lVert{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}},

(5.24)

where
\mu,\nu
are defined in Lemma
.
Since
\left\lVert{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}
, the above inequality becomes

(1-\mu)\left\lVert{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq 2\mu\frac{\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})_{1}}{\sqrt{k}}+\nu\frac{\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}},{\bm{X}}{\bm{d}}\right\rangle\right\rvert}{\left\lVert{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}}.

(5.25)

The assumption that
\delta_{2k}<\sqrt{2}-1
ensures that
\mu=\frac{\sqrt{2}\delta_{2k}}{1-\delta_{2k}}<1
. Dividing by
(1-\mu)
and substituting the resulting bound into (
) yield

\left\lVert{\bm{d}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\left(\frac{4\mu}{1-\mu}+2\right)\frac{\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})_{1}}{\sqrt{k}}+\frac{2\nu}{1-\mu}\frac{\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}},{\bm{X}}{\bm{d}}\right\rangle\right\rvert}{\left\lVert{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}}.

(5.26)

Using the definitions of
\mu
and
\nu
yields the desired constants.

Lemma
establishes an error bound for the class of
\ell_{1}
-minimization algorithms, assuming the measurement matrix
{\bm{X}}
satisfies the RIP.
To derive concrete recovery guarantees, one must analyze how the constraint
\mathcal{B}({\bm{y}})
influences the term
\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}},{\bm{X}}{\bm{d}}\right\rangle\right\rvert
.
As an illustration, consider the noiseless setting where measurements are exact:
\mathcal{B}({\bm{y}})=\{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\mid{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}={\bm{y}}\}
.
In this case, we obtain the following result.

{theoremHigh}

[Error bound of (
) under RIP
(
Candes 2008
)
]
Suppose that
{\bm{X}}
satisfies the RIP of order
2k
with
\delta_{2k}<\sqrt{2}-1
, and let
{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
for some
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\in\real^{p}
.
Then the solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
to (
) satisfies

\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\big\rVert_{2}\leq C_{0}\frac{\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})_{1}}{\sqrt{k}},

(5.27)

where
C_{0}
is the constant defined in Lemma
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Invoking Lemma
with
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\triangleq{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
and
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\triangleq{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
yields that, for
{\bm{d}}={\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
,

\left\lVert{\bm{d}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq C_{0}\frac{\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})_{1}}{\sqrt{k}}+C_{1}\frac{\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}},{\bm{X}}{\bm{d}}\right\rangle\right\rvert}{\left\lVert{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}}.

(5.28)

Furthermore, since
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*},{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
are feasible (i.e.,
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}={\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
), we also have that
{\bm{X}}{\bm{d}}=\boldsymbol{0}
.
Thus, the second term in the bound vanishes, yielding the claimed inequality.

Theorem
is quite remarkable. In particular, if
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]\triangleq\{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\mid\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{0}\leq k\}
, then—provided
{\bm{X}}
satisfies the RIP—we can recover any
k
-sparse vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
exactly.
At first glance, this exact recovery might seem surprising, suggesting that the method could be highly sensitive to noise. However, as we will see next, Lemma
can also be used to show that the approach is in fact stable (see Theorem
).

Finally, note that Theorem
assumes the RIP holds for
{\bm{X}}
. The argument can be easily adapted to instead assume the NSP, using the known implication that RIP implies NSP (see Section
).

5.3.3
Instance-Optimal Guarantees

We now briefly return to the noise-free setting to examine
instance-optimal guarantees
for recovering non-sparse signals more closely.
To begin, we introduce the concept of instance optimality.

Definition 186
(Instance optimality).

Given
s\geq 1
, a pair of measurement matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
and reconstruction map
\Delta:\real^{n}\to\real^{p}
is called
\ell_{s}
-instance optimal of order
k
with constant
C>0
if

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\Delta({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rVert_{s}\leq C\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})_{s},\quad\text{for all ${\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}$},

where
\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})_{s}\triangleq\min_{\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]}\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{s}
.

In Theorem
, we bounded the
\ell_{2}
-norm of the reconstruction error of problem (
)
as

\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\big\rVert_{2}\leq C_{0}\frac{\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})_{1}}{\sqrt{k}}.

(5.29)

This result can be generalized to other norms: for any
s\in[1,2]
, one can bound the reconstruction error in the
\ell_{s}
-norm.
For instance, with minor modifications to the same arguments, it can also be shown that

\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\big\rVert_{1}\leq C\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})_{1};

see Theorem
and
Candes 2008
for details.
This naturally raises the question: Can we replace the right-hand side with
\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})_{2}
, i.e., obtain a bound of the form

\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\big\rVert_{2}\leq C\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})_{2}?

Unfortunately, such an
\ell_{2}
-instance optimal guarantee comes at a steep cost in terms of the number of measurements, as quantified by the following theorem.

{theoremHigh}

[
\ell_{2}
-instance optimality
(
Cohen et al. 2009
)
]
Let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
have full rank
n
(
p\geq n
), and let
\Delta:\real^{n}\to\real^{p}
be a recovery algorithm satisfying

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\Delta({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rVert_{2}\leq C\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})_{2},\qquad\text{for some $k\geq 1$},

(5.30)

(i.e.,
\ell_{2}
-instance optimal of order
k
).
Then the number of measurements must satisfy
n>\left(1-\sqrt{1-1/C^{2}}\right)p
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Let
{\bm{d}}\in\real^{p}
be any vector in the nullspace of
{\bm{X}}
, i.e.,
{\bm{d}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
.
Decompose
{\bm{d}}
as
{\bm{d}}={\bm{d}}({\mathbb{S}})+{\bm{d}}({\mathbb{S}}^{c})
, where
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
is an arbitrary index set with
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert\leq k
.
Set
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\bm{d}}({\mathbb{S}}^{c})
.
Since
{\bm{d}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
, we have
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}={\bm{X}}{\bm{d}}-{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}=-{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
.
On the other hand, since
{\bm{d}}({{\mathbb{S}}})\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]
,
\sigma_{k}({\bm{d}}({{\mathbb{S}}}))_{2}=0
;
(
) implies that
\Delta({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\equiv\Delta(-{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}})=-{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
.
Hence,
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\Delta({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rVert_{2}=\left\lVert{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}-(-{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}})\right\rVert_{2}=\left\lVert{\bm{d}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq C\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
.
Furthermore, by definition of
\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})_{2}
, we have
\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})_{2}\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}
for all
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]
, including
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=\boldsymbol{0}
.
Thus, we obtain
\left\lVert{\bm{d}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq C\left\lVert{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{2}
by setting
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=\boldsymbol{0}
.
Using the fact that
\left\lVert{\bm{d}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left\lVert{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\left\lVert{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
, this yields

\left\lVert{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left\lVert{\bm{d}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\left\lVert{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{d}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\frac{1}{C^{2}}\left\lVert{\bm{d}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left(1-\frac{1}{C^{2}}\right)\left\lVert{\bm{d}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

Since the choices of
{\bm{d}}
and
{\mathbb{S}}
are arbitrary whenever
{\bm{d}}\in\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
and
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert\leq k
; in particular, let
\{{\bm{u}}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{p-n}
be an orthonormal basis for
\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
, and define the vectors
\{{\bm{d}}_{j}\}_{j=1}^{p}
as follows:

{\bm{d}}_{j}=\sum_{i=1}^{p-n}u_{ij}{\bm{u}}_{i}\equiv\sum_{i=1}^{p-n}\left\langle{\bm{e}}_{j},{\bm{u}}_{i}\right\rangle{\bm{u}}_{i}=\sum_{i=1}^{p-n}({\bm{u}}_{i}{\bm{u}}_{i}^{\top}){\bm{e}}_{j}\triangleq{\bm{P}}_{\mathcal{N}}{\bm{e}}_{j},

where
{\bm{e}}_{j}
denotes the
j
-th canonical basis vector,
u_{ij}
denotes the
j
-th entry of
{\bm{u}}_{i}
,
and
{\bm{P}}_{\mathcal{N}}\triangleq\sum_{i=1}^{p-n}({\bm{u}}_{i}{\bm{u}}_{i}^{\top})
denotes the orthogonal projection onto
\mathcal{N}({\bm{X}})
(see Definition
).
Since
\left\lVert{\bm{P}}_{\mathcal{N}}{\bm{e}}_{j}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\left\lVert{\bm{P}}_{\mathcal{N}}^{\perp}{\bm{e}}_{j}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left\lVert{\bm{e}}_{j}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=1
, we have that
\left\lVert{\bm{d}}_{j}\right\rVert_{2}\leq 1
. Thus, by setting
{\mathbb{S}}=\{j\}
for
{\bm{d}}_{j}
, we observe that

\left\lvert\sum_{i=1}^{p-n}(u_{ij})^{2}\right\rvert^{2}=(d_{jj})^{2}\leq\left(1-\frac{1}{C^{2}}\right)\left\lVert{\bm{d}}_{j}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq 1-\frac{1}{C^{2}}.

Summing over
j=1,2,\ldots,p
, we obtain

p\sqrt{1-1/C^{2}}\geq\sum_{j=1}^{p}\sum_{i=1}^{p-n}(u_{ij})^{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{p-n}\sum_{j=1}^{p}(u_{ij})^{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{p-n}\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=p-n,

which completes the proof after rearrangement.

Thus, if we desire a bound of the form (
) that holds for all signals
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
with a constant
C\approx 1
, then—regardless of the reconstruction algorithm—we must take nearly as many measurements as the ambient dimension, i.e.,
n\approx p
.

5.3.4
Signal Recovery with Noise

In Section
, we discussed recovery guarantees under the stable or robust NSP, which ensure robust signal reconstruction in noisy settings.
The RIP also supports such stability and robustness guarantees and plays a central role in compressed sensing theory.
Significant effort has been devoted in the literature to identifying the largest allowable value of the RIC
\delta_{2k}
.
Specifically,
Candes 2008
showed that
\delta_{2k}<\sqrt{2}-1\approx 0.4142
is sufficient to ensure exact recovery of any
k
-sparse signal.
This bound was subsequently improved by
Foucart and Lai 2009
to
\delta_{2k}<2(3-\sqrt{2})/7\approx 0.4531
,
and later by
Foucart 2010
to
\delta_{2k}<0.4652
.
Further refinements include the result of
Cai et al. 2009
, who established that
\delta_{2k}<0.4721
suffices when
k
is a multiple of 4 or when
k
is very large.
The same authors (in
Foucart 2010
) later pushed this to
\delta_{2k}<0.4734
for large values of
k
.
Most notably,
Mo and Li 2011
derived the current best-known general bound, showing that exact recovery is guaranteed whenever
\delta_{2k}<(77-\sqrt{1337})/{82}\approx 0.4931
for arbitrary
k
.

We now turn to the analysis of reconstruction error under uniformly bounded noise. The following result provides a worst-case error bound for problem (
) and improves upon Theorem
by relaxing the sufficient condition from
\delta_{2k}<1/3
to the less restrictive
\delta_{2k}<\sqrt{2}-1\approx 0.4142
.

{theoremHigh}

[Error bound of (
) under RIP
(
Candes 2008
)
]
Suppose the measurement matrix
{\bm{X}}
satisfies the RIP of order
2k
with constant
\delta_{2k}<\sqrt{2}-1\approx 0.4142
, and let
{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}+{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}
where
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\epsilon
.
Then the solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
to (
) satisfies the error bound

\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\big\rVert_{2}\leq C_{0}\frac{\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})_{1}}{\sqrt{k}}+C_{2}\epsilon,

(5.31)

where

C_{0}=2\frac{1-(1-\sqrt{2})\delta_{2k}}{1-(1+\sqrt{2})\delta_{2k}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad C_{2}=4\frac{\sqrt{1+\delta_{2k}}}{1-(1+\sqrt{2})\delta_{2k}}.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Let
{\bm{d}}\triangleq{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
. Our goal is to bound
\left\lVert{\bm{d}}\right\rVert_{2}\triangleq\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\big\rVert_{2}
.
Since
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\epsilon
,
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\in\mathcal{B}({\bm{y}})=\{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\mid\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\epsilon\}
is feasible, and
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is the minimizer, we have
\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{1}
. Thus we may invoke Lemma
with
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\triangleq{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
and
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\triangleq{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
, and it remains to bound
\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}},{\bm{X}}{\bm{d}}\right\rangle\right\rvert
, where
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
is arbitrary with
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert\leq k
. To do this, using the triangle inequality, we have

\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\bm{d}}\right\rVert_{2}=\big\lVert{\bm{X}}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})\big\rVert_{2}=\big\lVert{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\bm{y}}+{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\big\rVert_{2}\leq\big\lVert{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\bm{y}}\big\rVert_{2}+\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{2}\leq 2\epsilon,

where the last inequality follows since
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\in\mathcal{B}({\bm{y}})
. Combining this with the RIP and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, we obtain

\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}},{\bm{X}}{\bm{d}}\right\rangle\right\rvert\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\bm{d}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq 2\epsilon\sqrt{1+\delta_{2k}}\left\lVert{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}.

Thus,

\left\lVert{\bm{d}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq C_{0}\frac{\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})_{1}}{\sqrt{k}}+C_{1}2\epsilon\sqrt{1+\delta_{2k}}=C_{0}\frac{\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})_{1}}{\sqrt{k}}+C_{2}\epsilon.

This completes the proof.

Consider we have an
oracle estimator
, which provides the exact support of the sparse vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
; that is, the
k
indices corresponding to its nonzero entries, denoted by
{\mathbb{S}}_{0}
.
In this case, a natural reconstruction strategy is to use the pseudo-inverse restricted to the known support:

\displaystyle{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}}

\displaystyle={\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}}^{+}{\bm{y}}=({\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}})^{-1}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}}^{\top}{\bm{y}},\qquad{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}^{c}}=\boldsymbol{0},

where we assume that
{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}}
has full column rank, so that there is a unique solution to the equation
{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}}
.
Under this assumption, and given noisy measurements
{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}+{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}
, the reconstruction error becomes

\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\big\rVert_{2}=\left\lVert({\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}})^{-1}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}}^{\top}({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}+{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}})-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{2}=\left\lVert({\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}})^{-1}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\right\rVert_{2}.

Note that the singulars value of
{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}}
lie in the range
[1/\sqrt{1+\delta_{2k}},1/\sqrt{1-\delta_{2k}}]
(see the discussion following Definition
).
Thus, if we consider the worst-case recovery error over all noise vectors
{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}
satisfying
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq\epsilon
, then the reconstruction error obeys

\frac{\epsilon}{\sqrt{1+\delta_{2k}}}\leq\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\big\rVert_{2}\leq\frac{\epsilon}{\sqrt{1-\delta_{2k}}}.

(5.32)

Thus, even with perfect knowledge of the true support (i.e., in the oracle setting), the best possible recovery guarantee cannot improve upon the bound in Theorem
by more than a constant factor—highlighting the near-optimality of
\ell_{1}
-minimization under the RIP.

We can further refine the recovery guarantees by leveraging the connection between the RIP and the
\ell_{2}
-robust NSP. Specifically, using Corollary
, we obtain the following improved result.

{theoremHigh}
[Error bound of (
) under RIP
(
Mo and Li 2011
)
]
Suppose that the measurement matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
satisfies the RIP of order
2k
with constant

\delta_{2k}<\frac{77-\sqrt{1337}}{82}\approx 0.4931,

(5.33)

and let the observations be given by
{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}+{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}
, where
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\epsilon
.
Then any solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
of problem (
) satisfies the error bounds

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq C\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})_{1}+D\sqrt{k}\epsilon,

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\frac{C}{\sqrt{k}}\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})_{1}+D\epsilon,

where the constants
C,D>0
depend only on
\delta_{2k}
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
The RIP condition (
) implies that
{\bm{X}}
satisfies the
\ell_{2}
-robust NSP of order
k
(w.r.t.
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert=\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{2}
) by Theorem
.
The stated error bounds then follow directly from Corollary
.

In fact, interpolation arguments immediately yield corresponding
\ell_{s}
-error estimates for all
1\leq s\leq 2
.

\paragrapharrow

Gaussian noise.
We can also analyze the performance of these methods in the presence of Gaussian noise
(
Haupt and Nowak 2006
)
.
To simplify the discussion, we restrict our attention to the case where the true signal
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
is exactly
k
-sparse, i.e.,
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]\triangleq\{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\mid\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{0}\leq k\}
.
In this setting, the best
k
-term approximation error vanishes:
\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})_{1}=0
, and thus the error bounds in Theorem
depend only on the noise vector
{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}
.
Assume that the entries of
{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\in\real^{n}
are i.i.d. according to a Gaussian distribution with mean zero and variance
\sigma^{2}
, i.e.,
\epsilon_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2})
.
Since the Gaussian distribution
\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2})
is itself sub-Gaussian (as a hindsight, see Chapter
for more details), we may apply concentration results such as Theorem
.
Specifically, there exists a constant
\kappa_{0}>0
such that for any
e>0
,

\Pr\left(\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\geq(1+e)n\sigma^{2}\right)\leq\exp\left(-\kappa_{0}ne^{2}\right).

(5.34)

Setting
e=3
, we obtain

\Pr\left(\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\right\rVert_{2}\geq 2\sqrt{n}\sigma\right)\leq\exp\left(-9\kappa_{0}n\right).

(5.35)

This leads to the following corollary for the special case of Gaussian noise.

Corollary 187
(Error bound of (
) under RIP and Gaussian noise).

Suppose that the measurement matrix
{\bm{X}}
satisfies the RIP of order
2k
with
\delta_{2k}<\sqrt{2}-1
.
Assume further that
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]
and that the observations are given by
{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}+{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}
, where the entries of
{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}
are i.i.d.
\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2})
.
Then when
\mathcal{B}({\bm{y}})=\{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\mid\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq 2\sqrt{n}\sigma\}
, the solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
to (
) with
\epsilon=2\sqrt{n}\sigma
satisfies

\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\big\rVert_{2}\leq 8\frac{\sqrt{1+\delta_{2k}}}{1-(1+\sqrt{2})\delta_{2k}}\sqrt{n}\sigma

(5.36)

with probability at least
1-\exp(-9\kappa_{0}n)
.

The proof follows directly from Theorem
by noting that
\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})_{1}=0
if
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]
.
A similar result can also be derived for Theorem
, yielding analogous
\ell_{1}
- and
\ell_{2}
-error bounds under Gaussian noise with high probability.

5.3.5
Signal Recovery with Dantzig Selector

We now consider a slightly different noise model. Whereas Theorems
and
assumed that the
\ell_{2}
-norm of the noise,
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\right\rVert_{2}
is small, the theorem below analyzes the performance of a different recovery algorithm known as the
Dantzig selector
under the assumption that
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\right\rVert_{\infty}
is small
(
Candes and Tao 2007
)
; see Problem
. As we will see, this assumption leads to a particularly simple analysis of the algorithm’s performance in the presence of Gaussian noise.

{theoremHigh}

[Error bound of Dantzig selector under RIP]
Suppose that the measurement matrix
{\bm{X}}
satisfies the RIP of order
2k
with
\delta_{2k}<\sqrt{2}-1
, and that we observe measurements of the form
{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}+{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}
, where
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq\epsilon
.
Then when
\mathcal{B}({\bm{y}})=\{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\mid\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\bm{y}})\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq\epsilon\}
, the solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
to (
) (p.
) satisfies

\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\big\rVert_{2}\leq C_{0}\frac{\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})_{1}}{\sqrt{k}}+C_{3}\sqrt{k}\epsilon,

(5.37)

where

C_{0}=2\frac{1-(1-\sqrt{2})\delta_{2k}}{1-(1+\sqrt{2})\delta_{2k}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad C_{3}=\frac{4\sqrt{2}}{1-(1+\sqrt{2})\delta_{2k}}.

(5.38)

Proof
[of Theorem
]
The proof closely follows that of Theorem
.
Since
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq\epsilon
, we again have that
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\in\mathcal{B}({\bm{y}})
, so
\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{1}
.
Hence, Lemma
applies.
Let
{\bm{d}}={\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
.
As in the earlier proof, we aim to bound
\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}},{\bm{X}}{\bm{d}}\right\rangle\right\rvert
.
First, by the triangle inequality,

\big\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}{\bm{d}}\big\rVert_{\infty}\leq\big\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}({\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\bm{y}})\big\rVert_{\infty}+\big\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}({\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})\big\rVert_{\infty}\leq 2\epsilon,

where the last inequality holds because both
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
and
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
belong to
\mathcal{B}({\bm{y}})
.
Applying the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives

\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}},{\bm{X}}{\bm{d}}\right\rangle\right\rvert=\left\lvert\left\langle{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}},{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}{\bm{d}}\right\rangle\right\rvert\leq\left\lVert{\bm{d}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}{\bm{d}}\right\rVert_{2}.

Finally, since
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}{\bm{d}}\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq 2\epsilon
, each entry of
{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}{\bm{d}}
is bounded in absolute value by
2\epsilon
.
Because
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert=\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}_{0}\right\rvert+\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}_{1}\right\rvert=2k
from Lemma
, we obtain
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}{\bm{d}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\sqrt{2k}(2\epsilon)
. Combining these estimates yields

\left\lVert{\bm{d}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq C_{0}\frac{\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})_{1}}{\sqrt{k}}+C_{1}2\sqrt{2k}\epsilon=C_{0}\frac{\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})_{1}}{\sqrt{k}}+C_{3}\sqrt{k}\epsilon,

This completes the proof.

\paragrapharrow

Gaussian noise for Dantzig selector.
We can similarly apply Theorem
to the case of Gaussian noise.
Assume that the columns of
{\bm{X}}
are normalized to unit
\ell_{2}
-norm. Then each component of
{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}
is a Gaussian random variable with mean zero and variance
\sigma^{2}
.
Using standard Gaussian tail bounds (see Lemma
), we have

\Pr\left(\left\lvert({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}})_{i}\right\rvert\geq t\sigma\right)\leq\exp\left(-\frac{t^{2}}{2}\right),\quad\text{for $i=1,2,\ldots,p$}.

(5.39)

Applying the union bound over all
p
coordinates (Theorem
) and setting
t=2\sqrt{\ln p}
, we obtain

\Pr\left(\big\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\big\rVert_{\infty}\geq 2\sqrt{\ln p}\sigma\right)\leq p\exp(-2\ln p)=\frac{1}{p}.

(5.40)

Substituting this into Theorem
, and noting that
\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})_{1}=0
when
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]
, we arrive at the following corollary.

Corollary 188
(Error bound of Dantzig selector under RIP and Gaussian noise
(
Candes and Tao 2007
)
).

Suppose that the measurement matrix
{\bm{X}}
has unit-norm columns and satisfies the RIP of order
2k
with
\delta_{2k}<\sqrt{2}-1
. Further assume that
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]
and that the measurements are given by
{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}+{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}
, where the entries of
{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}
are i.i.d.
\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2})
. Then when
\mathcal{B}({\bm{y}})=\{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\mid\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\bm{y}})\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq 2\sqrt{\ln p}\sigma\}
, the solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
to (
) satisfies

\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\big\rVert_{2}\leq\frac{8\sqrt{2}}{1-(1+\sqrt{2})\delta_{2k}}\sqrt{k\ln p}\sigma,

(5.41)

with probability at least
1-\frac{1}{p}
.

Ignoring precise constants and the exact success probabilities (which we have not optimized), we observe that if
n=\mathcal{O}(k\ln p)
, then Corollaries
and
yield essentially comparable error bounds. However, there is a subtle but important distinction: for fixed
n
and
p
, the bound in Corollary
adapts to the sparsity level
k
, providing a tighter guarantee when
k
is small. In contrast, the bound in Corollary
does not improve as
k
decreases. Thus, while both methods offer similar overall performance, the Dantzig selector may be preferable in settings where the true sparsity
k
is significantly smaller than the ambient dimension. See
Candes and Tao 2007
for a more detailed comparison of the relative merits of these approaches.

5.4
Sparse Linear Regression

In many modern data problems—from genomics to finance—we encounter datasets where the number of features
p
far exceeds the number of observations
n
.
In such high-dimensional settings, classical linear regression breaks down: it becomes unstable, prone to overfitting, and often produces models that are difficult or impossible to interpret. Sparse linear regression addresses these challenges by seeking solutions in which only a small subset of coefficients are nonzero, effectively performing feature selection while fitting the model.

At its core, sparse linear regression builds on the familiar linear model

{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}},

where
{\bm{y}}\in\real^{n}
is the response vector,
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
contains the predictors,
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
is the coefficient vector we wish to estimate, and
{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}
represents noise. The key assumption in the sparse setting is that most entries of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
are exactly zero—that is, only a few predictors truly influence the outcome. This assumption not only reflects scientific reality in many domains (e.g., only a handful of genes may affect a disease), but also leads to models that generalize better and are easier to interpret.

The most widely used method for achieving sparsity is the LASSO (least absolute shrinkage and selection operator), introduced by Robert Tibshirani in 1996
(
Tibshirani 1996
)
. The LASSO estimator solves the optimization problem

{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\text{lasso}}=\arg\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\left\{\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\lambda\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\right\},

where
\lambda\geq 0
is a tuning parameter that controls the degree of sparsity. The
\ell_{1}
penalty
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}=\sum_{j=1}^{p}\left\lvert\beta_{j}\right\rvert
encourages many coefficients to be exactly zero—a property not shared by the
\ell_{2}
penalty used in ridge regression. As
\lambda
increases, more coefficients are shrunk to zero, yielding increasingly sparse models. In practice,
\lambda
is typically selected via cross-validation to balance prediction accuracy and model simplicity.

Although LASSO is computationally efficient and performs well in many scenarios, it has limitations. For instance, when predictors are highly correlated, LASSO tends to select only one variable from a group, potentially omitting other relevant ones. It can also introduce bias by overshrinking large coefficients. Alternatives such as the
Elastic Net
—which combines
\ell_{1}
and
\ell_{2}
penalties—help mitigate these issues, especially when features are grouped or highly correlated. At the other extreme, best subset selection directly minimizes prediction error subject to a constraint on the number of nonzero coefficients (i.e.,
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{0}\leq k
). While statistically appealing, this approach is combinatorially hard and generally infeasible for large
p
, though recent advances in optimization have renewed interest in it.

The appeal of sparse regression extends beyond computation. In applications like genome-wide association studies, researchers may measure expression levels for tens of thousands of genes but expect only a few dozen to be biologically relevant. A sparse model not only improves predictive performance but also highlights candidate genes for further experimental validation. Similarly, in signal processing, sparse representations underpin techniques like compressed sensing, where a signal can be accurately reconstructed from far fewer measurements than traditionally required—provided it is sparse in some basis.

From a theoretical perspective, consistent recovery of the true support (i.e., the set of nonzero coefficients) is possible even when
p\gg n
, provided certain conditions on the design matrix
{\bm{X}}
hold. Notable among these are the restricted eigenvalue condition, which essentially require that relevant and irrelevant features are not too strongly correlated. Under such assumptions, methods like LASSO can provably recover the correct sparse structure with high probability as the sample size grows.

Of course, sparsity involves trade-offs. Imposing a sparse structure introduces bias into coefficient estimates, but this is often offset by a substantial reduction in variance—leading to lower overall prediction error. Moreover, while convex formulations like LASSO scale well to large problems, non-convex penalties (e.g., SCAD or MCP
(
Kim et al. 2008
;
Zhang 2010
)
) can offer improved statistical properties at the cost of greater computational complexity and the risk of converging to local minima.

In summary, sparse linear regression transforms an ill-posed high-dimensional problem into a tractable one by embracing the principle of parsimony: the simplest explanation is often the best. This section has focused primarily on the theoretical foundations of the LASSO—particularly the conditions under which it consistently recovers the true sparse model.
It is worth noting that LASSO is closely related to the broader framework of sparse recovery from compressed sensing and signal processing.
Thus, LASSO can be viewed as the statistical instantiation of
\ell_{1}
-based sparse recovery, adapted to settings where data are noisy and the primary goals are prediction and consistent support estimation rather than exact reconstruction. By automatically identifying and retaining only the most informative features, it delivers models that are not only accurate but also interpretable—a rare and valuable combination in the era of big data. Whether in biology, economics, engineering, or machine learning, sparse regression remains a foundational tool for turning overwhelming complexity into actionable insight.

5.4.1
LASSO and Robust Linear Regression

The problem of regression analysis is fundamental across many fields, including statistics, supervised machine learning, and optimization.
Minimizing the squared error often yields solutions that are highly sensitive to small changes in the data.
To mitigate this sensitivity, various regularization methods have been proposed. Among the most well-known and widely cited are Tikhonov regularization (
\ell_{2}
penalty)
(
Tikhonov 1963
)
and the LASSO
(
Tibshirani 1996
)
.

To reduce the computational complexity of solving the optimization problem (
) directly, consider a linear regression setting: given an observed response vector
{\bm{y}}\in\real^{n}
and a design matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
, the goal is to find a coefficient vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
such that

\widehat{y}_{i}=\beta_{1}x_{i1}+\beta_{2}x_{i2}+\cdots+\beta_{p}x_{ip},\quad i=1,2,\ldots,n,

(5.42)

or equivalently
\widehat{{\bm{y}}}=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\beta_{i}{\bm{x}}_{i}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.

Tibshirani 1996
introduced the LASSO (least absolute shrinkage and selection operator) for linear regression.
The core idea of LASSO is to minimize the sum of squared prediction errors subject to an upper bound
\Sigma
on the
\ell_{1}
-norm of the coefficient vector, i.e., model (
LC
) (p.
LC
):

\text{(L${}_{C}$)}\qquad\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\qquad\text{s.t.}\quad\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\left\lvert\beta_{i}\right\rvert\leq\Sigma.

(5.43)

The bound
\Sigma
is a tuning parameter.
When
\Sigma
is sufficiently large, the constraint becomes inactive, and the solution reduces to ordinary least squares regression. However, for smaller values of
\Sigma
, some coefficients are driven exactly to zero, resulting in a sparse estimate of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.
Selecting an appropriate
\Sigma
thus enables automatic variable selection.

An equivalent formulation uses the Lagrangian form of the LASSO, i.e., model (
LL
) (p.
LL
):

\text{(L${}_{L}$)}\qquad\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\left\{\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\lambda\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\right\},

(5.44)

where
\lambda\geq 0
controls the strength of regularization and is related to
\Sigma
(see Corollary
).

The LASSO combines
\ell_{1}
-norm regularization with linear regression and exhibits two key properties:

1.

Contraction effect
. It shrinks the estimated coefficients toward zero, reducing model complexity.

2.

Selection effect
. It automatically sets some coefficients exactly to zero, thereby performing feature selection and yielding a sparse solution.

Consequently, LASSO serves as both a shrinkage and a variable selection method. It is closely related to soft-thresholding of wavelet coefficients and forward stagewise regression; see Section
.

In practical applications, the observed design matrix
{\bm{X}}
may be corrupted by noise or even adversarial perturbations. To ensure robustness against such uncertainties,
robust linear regression
considers the worst-case scenario by solving the following minimax problem:

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\max_{\Delta{\bm{X}}\in{\mathbb{U}}}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-({\bm{X}}+\Delta{\bm{X}}){\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2},

(5.45)

where
\Delta{\bm{X}}=[{\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{1},{\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{2},\ldots,{\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{p}]
represents the perturbation applied to each column (feature) of
{\bm{X}}
, and

{\mathbb{U}}\triangleq\big\{[{\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{1},{\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{2},\ldots,{\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{p}]\mid\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}\leq c_{i},\ i=1,2,\ldots,p\big\}

(5.46)

is called the
uncertainty set
, or the set of admissible perturbations of the matrix
{\bm{X}}
.
This uncertainty set is featurewise uncoupled, meaning that perturbations to different features are constrained independently—unlike coupled uncertainty sets, which impose joint constraints across features.

Remarkably, when the uncertainty set is uncoupled and bounded in the
\ell_{2}
-norm per feature, the robust regression problem admits a tractable reformulation, as stated in the following theorem.

{theoremHigh}

[Robust regression
(
Xu et al. 2008
)
]
The robust regression problem (
) with uncertainty set
{\mathbb{U}}
given by (
) is equivalent to the following
\ell_{1}
-regularized regression problem:

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\left\{\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}+\sum_{i=1}^{p}c_{i}\left\lvert\beta_{i}\right\rvert\right\}.

(5.47)

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Fix
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
. We show that

\max_{\Delta{\bm{X}}\in{\mathbb{U}}}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-({\bm{X}}+\Delta{\bm{X}}){\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{2}=\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{2}+\sum_{i=1}^{p}c_{i}\left\lvert\beta_{i}^{*}\right\rvert.

By the triangle inequality, the left-hand side can be written as

\displaystyle\max_{\Delta{\bm{X}}\in{\mathbb{U}}}\big\lVert{\bm{y}}-({\bm{X}}+\Delta{\bm{X}}){\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\big\rVert_{2}

(5.48)

\displaystyle=\max_{[{\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{1},\ldots,{\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{p}]:\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}\leq c_{i}}\big\lVert{\bm{y}}-\left({\bm{X}}+[{\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{1},\ldots,{\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{p}]\right){\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\big\rVert_{2}=\max_{[{\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{1},\ldots,{\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{p}]:\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}\leq c_{i}}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-\sum_{i=1}^{p}\beta_{i}^{*}{\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}

\displaystyle\leq\max_{[{\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{1},\ldots,{\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{p}]:\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}\leq c_{i}}\left\{\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{2}+\sum_{i=1}^{p}\left\lVert\beta_{i}^{*}{\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}\right\}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{2}+\sum_{i=1}^{p}\left\lvert\beta_{i}^{*}\right\rvert c_{i}.

To establish equality, define a unit vector
{\bm{v}}
as

{\bm{v}}\triangleq\begin{cases}{({\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})}/{\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{2}},&\text{if }{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\neq{\bm{y}};\\
\text{any unit norm vector},&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}\qquad\text{and}\qquad{\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{i}^{*}\triangleq-c_{i}\mathrm{sign}(\beta_{i}^{*}){\bm{v}},\,\forall\,i.

Since
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{i}^{*}\right\rVert_{2}\leq c_{i}
, it follows that
\Delta{\bm{X}}^{*}\triangleq[{\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{1}^{*},{\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{2}^{*},\ldots,{\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{p}^{*}]\in{\mathbb{U}}
, whence we have

\displaystyle\max_{\Delta{\bm{X}}\in{\mathbb{U}}}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-({\bm{X}}+\Delta{\bm{X}}){\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{2}\geq\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-({\bm{X}}+\Delta{\bm{X}}^{*}){\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{2}

(5.49)

\displaystyle=\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-\left({\bm{X}}+[{\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{1}^{*},{\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{2}^{*},\ldots,{\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{p}^{*}]\right){\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{2}=\big\lVert\left({\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right)-\sum_{i=1}^{p}\left(-\beta_{i}^{*}c_{i}\mathrm{sign}(\beta_{i}^{*}){\bm{v}}\right)\big\rVert_{2}

\displaystyle=\big\lVert\left({\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right)+\left(\sum_{i=1}^{p}c_{i}\left\lvert\beta_{i}^{*}\right\rvert\right){\bm{v}}\big\rVert_{2}=\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{2}+\sum_{i=1}^{p}c_{i}\left\lvert\beta_{i}^{*}\right\rvert.

Combining (
) and (
) yields the desired equality for any fixed
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}

\max_{\Delta{\bm{X}}\in{\mathbb{U}}}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-({\bm{X}}+\Delta{\bm{X}}){\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{2}=\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{2}+\sum_{i=1}^{p}c_{i}\left\lvert\beta_{i}^{*}\right\rvert.

Minimizing both sides over
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
completes the proof.

When the
\ell_{1}
-norm is replaced by an arbitrary norm
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{s}
, the previous result generalizes as follows.

Corollary 189
(Robust regression).

Let

{\mathbb{U}}_{a}\triangleq\big\{[\boldsymbol{\delta}_{1},\ldots,\boldsymbol{\delta}_{p}]\mid\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\delta}_{i}\right\rVert_{s}\leq c_{i},\ i=1,2,\ldots,p\big\}.

(5.50)

Then the following robust regression problem

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\max_{\Delta{\bm{X}}\in{\mathbb{U}}_{a}}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-({\bm{X}}+\Delta{\bm{X}}){\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{s},

with uncertainty set
{\mathbb{U}}_{a}
is equivalent to the following arbitrary norm
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{s}
-regularized regression problem:

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\left\{\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{s}+\sum_{i=1}^{p}c_{i}\left\lvert\beta_{i}\right\rvert\right\}.

(5.51)

Thus, robust regression yields an objective that combines an
\ell_{2}
(or more generally,
\ell_{s}
) loss with a weighted
\ell_{1}
penalty. The following result shows that, in the case of the
\ell_{2}
loss, this formulation is essentially equivalent to the standard regularized least squares model used in LASSO.

{theoremHigh}
[Equivalent forms
(
Xu et al. 2008
)
]
The optimization problems

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\{\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}+\lambda_{1}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\{\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}2}}+\lambda_{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\}

(5.52)

are equivalent in the sense that, for every choice of
\lambda_{1}>0
, there exists a corresponding
\lambda_{2}>0
(and vice versa) such that both problems share the same set of minimizers.

Proof

See Appendix of
Xu et al. 2008
.

Now, suppose we set
c_{i}=\lambda
for all
i
and assume that the columns
{\bm{x}}_{i}
of
{\bm{X}}
are orthonormal. Under these conditions, the robust regression problem (
) simplifies to

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\left\{\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}+\lambda\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\right\}.

(5.53)

By Theorem
, this problem is equivalent to the Lagrangian LASSO formulation (
). In other words, a robust linear regression problem—with featurewise
\ell_{2}
-bounded perturbations and orthonormal design—is equivalent to the LASSO problem.

Viewing the LASSO solution as the solution to a robust regression problem has two important implications:

1.

Interpretability of regularization.
Robustness provides a concrete interpretation of the
\ell_{1}
regularizer—it corresponds to protection against worst-case data perturbations, linking the mathematical penalty to a tangible physical property (noise resilience).

2.

Analytical leverage.
More importantly, robustness is a powerful structural property that can be used to analyze the behavior of the solution. For instance, the sparsity of the LASSO estimator can be understood as a consequence of its robustness: under adversarial perturbations, the optimal strategy is to rely only on the most stable (i.e., nonzero) features. Moreover, by construction, a robust solution is optimal under the worst-case scenario, which offers strong guarantees in uncertain or noisy environments.

5.4.2
Error Bounds of LASSO

We conclude this section by presenting several theoretical results for the LASSO problem.
Given a LASSO estimate
\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\in\real^{p}
, its quality can be assessed in multiple ways, depending on the goals of the application.
In some settings, the primary concern is the predictive performance of
\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
.
In such cases, we evaluate it using the
(in-sample) prediction loss
:

\mathcal{L}_{\text{pred}}(\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}};{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})=\frac{1}{n}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},

(5.54a)

which measures the mean squared prediction error over the observed design matrix
{\bm{X}}
.
In other applications—such as medical imaging, remote sensing, and compressed sensing—the main interest lies in accurately recovering the unknown parameter vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
itself.
Here, it is more appropriate to consider the
parameter estimation loss
, defined as the squared
\ell_{2}
-distance between the estimator and the true parameter:

\mathcal{L}_{2}(\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}};{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})=\big\lVert\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}.

(5.54b)

Finally, when the goal is variable selection or support recovery, one may use a discrete loss that checks whether the estimated and true vectors share the same signed support:

\mathcal{L}_{\text{vs}}(\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}};{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})=\begin{cases}0,&\text{if }\sign(\widehat{\beta}_{i})=\sign(\beta_{i}^{*})\text{ for all }i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\};\\
1,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

(5.54c)

This loss equals zero only when
\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
correctly identifies both the locations and signs of the nonzero entries of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
.

For brevity, this subsection focuses on theoretical guarantees for the first two loss functions—prediction and parameter estimation. To establish these results, we require the following technical lemma.

Lemma 190
.

Let
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
satisfy
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{1}
, where
\mathrm{supp}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\triangleq{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
.
Denote
{\bm{e}}\triangleq{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
. Then
\left\lVert{\bm{e}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{e}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}
, i.e.,
{\bm{e}}\in{\mathbb{C}}[{\mathbb{S}};1]
(see definition in (
)), where
{\mathbb{S}}^{c}
denotes the complement of
{\mathbb{S}}
.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Let
{\mathbb{T}}\triangleq\mathrm{supp}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
. The assumption
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{1}
indicates that

\displaystyle\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{T}}}\left\lvert\beta_{i}\right\rvert\leq\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}}\left\lvert\alpha_{i}\right\rvert\quad\implies\quad\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{T}}\setminus{\mathbb{S}}}\left\lvert\beta_{i}\right\rvert+\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}\cap{\mathbb{T}}}\left\lvert\beta_{i}\right\rvert\leq\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}\setminus{\mathbb{T}}}\left\lvert\alpha_{i}\right\rvert+\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}\cap{\mathbb{T}}}\left\lvert\alpha_{i}\right\rvert

\displaystyle\implies\quad\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{T}}\setminus{\mathbb{S}}}\left\lvert\beta_{i}\right\rvert\leq\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}\setminus{\mathbb{T}}}\left\lvert\alpha_{i}\right\rvert+\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}\cap{\mathbb{T}}}\left\lvert\alpha_{i}-\beta_{i}\right\rvert,

which obtains the desired result.

With this intuition in place, we now present a result that provides a bound on the parameter estimation error
\big\lVert\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\big\rVert_{2}
under the linear observation model
{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}+{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}
, where
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
is
k
-sparse and supported on a subset
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
(i.e.,
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert=k
).

{theoremHigh}

[Bounds of optimizer error for LASSO]
Assume the observations follow the linear model
{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}+{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}
, where
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
, and
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
is
k
-sparse with support
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
(i.e.,
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert=k
).
Suppose the design matrix
{\bm{X}}
satisfies the restricted eigenvalue (RE) property (Definition
) with constant
n\mu>0
over
{\mathbb{C}}[{\mathbb{S}};3]
.
Then the following error bounds hold:

1.

Constrained LASSO.
Any estimate
\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
based on the constrained LASSO (
LC
) with
\Sigma=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{1}
satisfies the bound

\left\lVert\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\frac{4\sqrt{k}}{\mu n}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\right\rVert_{\infty}.

(5.55)

2.

Lagrangian LASSO.
Given a regularization parameter
\lambda\geq{2}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\right\rVert_{\infty}>0
, any estimate
\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
from the regularized LASSO (
LL
) satisfies the bound

\left\lVert\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\frac{3}{\mu}\sqrt{{k}}\frac{\lambda}{n}.

(5.56)

Proof
[of Theorem
]

(i) Constrained LASSO.
Since
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
is feasible and
\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is optimal, we have the inequality
\big\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
. Defining the error vector
\widehat{\bm{e}}\triangleq\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
, substituting in the relation
{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}+{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}
yields

\text{(Constrained LASSO)}:\qquad{\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\widehat{\bm{e}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}\leq{2}{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}\widehat{\bm{e}}.

(5.57)

Applying Hölder’s inequality (Theorem
) to the right-hand side yields the upper bound
{2}\left\lvert{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}\widehat{\bm{e}}\right\rvert\leq{2}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\right\rVert_{\infty}\left\lVert\widehat{\bm{e}}\right\rVert_{1}
. The inequality
\big\lVert\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}\leq\Sigma=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{1}
implies that
\widehat{\bm{e}}\in{\mathbb{C}}[{\mathbb{S}};1]
(Lemma
):

\big\lVert\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{1}\;\;\implies\;\;\left\lVert\widehat{\bm{e}}\right\rVert_{1}=\left\lVert\widehat{\bm{e}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}+\left\lVert\widehat{\bm{e}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq 2\left\lVert\widehat{\bm{e}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\dagger}}}{{\leq}}2\sqrt{k}\left\lVert\widehat{\bm{e}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq 2\sqrt{k}\left\lVert\widehat{\bm{e}}\right\rVert_{2},

(5.58)

where the inequality (
{\dagger}
) follows from the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality (Equation (
)):

\left\lVert\widehat{\bm{e}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}=\left\lvert\widehat{\bm{e}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rvert^{\top}{\bm{1}}\leq\left\lVert\widehat{\bm{e}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\bm{1}}\right\rVert_{2}=\sqrt{k}\left\lVert\widehat{\bm{e}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\sqrt{k}\left\lVert\widehat{\bm{e}}\right\rVert_{2}.

(5.59)

Note that (
) holds under the condition
\big\lVert\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{1}
, while (
) is valid for any
{\mathbb{S}}
and
\widehat{\bm{e}}
.
On the other hand, applying the RE property to the left-hand side of the inequality (
) yields
n\mu\left\lVert\widehat{\bm{e}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\widehat{\bm{e}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
. Combining these inequalities yields the desired result.

(ii) Lagrangian LASSO.

Define the function

G({\bm{e}})\triangleq\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}+{\bm{e}})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\lambda\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}+{\bm{e}}\right\rVert_{1}.

(5.60)

Noting that
\widehat{\bm{e}}\triangleq\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
minimizes
G
by construction, we have
G(\widehat{\bm{e}})\leq G(\boldsymbol{0})
.
Substituting in the relation
{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}+{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}
yields

\text{(Lagrangian LASSO)}:\qquad{\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\widehat{\bm{e}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}\leq{2}{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}\widehat{\bm{e}}+2\lambda\left\{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{1}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}+\widehat{\bm{e}}\right\rVert_{1}\right\}.

(5.61)

Since
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}^{*}=\boldsymbol{0}
, we have
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{1}=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}^{*}\right\rVert_{1}
, and

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}+\widehat{\bm{e}}\right\rVert_{1}=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}^{*}+\widehat{\bm{e}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}+\left\lVert\widehat{\bm{e}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}\geq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}^{*}\right\rVert_{1}-\left\lVert\widehat{\bm{e}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}+\left\lVert\widehat{\bm{e}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}.

Substituting these relations into the inequality (
) and applying Hölder’s yield

\displaystyle{\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\widehat{\bm{e}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}

\displaystyle\leq{2}{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}\widehat{\bm{e}}+2\lambda\left\{\left\lVert\widehat{\bm{e}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}-\left\lVert\widehat{\bm{e}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}\right\}

(5.62)

\displaystyle\leq{2}\big\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\big\rVert_{\infty}\left\lVert\widehat{\bm{e}}\right\rVert_{1}+2\lambda\left\{\left\lVert\widehat{\bm{e}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}-\left\lVert\widehat{\bm{e}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}\right\}.

Since
{2}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq\lambda
by assumption, using the fact that
\left\lVert\widehat{\bm{e}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\sqrt{k}\left\lVert\widehat{\bm{e}}\right\rVert_{2}
from (
), we have:

0\leq{\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\widehat{\bm{e}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}\leq{\lambda}\left\{\left\lVert\widehat{\bm{e}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}+\left\lVert\widehat{\bm{e}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}\right\}+2\lambda\left\{\left\lVert\widehat{\bm{e}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}-\left\lVert\widehat{\bm{e}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}\right\}\leq{3}\sqrt{k}\lambda\left\lVert\widehat{\bm{e}}\right\rVert_{2}.

(5.63)

The inequality (
) also implies that
\left\lVert\widehat{\bm{e}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq 3\left\lVert\widehat{\bm{e}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{1}
such that
\widehat{\bm{e}}\in{\mathbb{C}}[{\mathbb{S}};3]
(see definition in (
)).
Applying the
\mu
-RE condition to
\widehat{\bm{e}}
ensures that
\mu\left\lVert\widehat{\bm{e}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\frac{1}{n}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\widehat{\bm{e}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
.
Combining this lower bound with the inequality (
) yields

{\mu}\left\lVert\widehat{\bm{e}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq{3}\sqrt{k}\frac{\lambda}{n}\left\lVert\widehat{\bm{e}}\right\rVert_{2},

which implies the desired result.

{theoremHigh}

[Bounds of prediction error for LASSO]
Assume the observations follow the linear model
{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}+{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}
, where
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
.
Consider the Lagrangian LASSO (
LL
) with a regularization parameter
\lambda\geq{2}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\right\rVert_{\infty}
.

1.

If
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{1}<R_{1}
, then any optimal solution
\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
satisfies

{\left\lVert{\bm{X}}(\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}\leq 12\,R_{1}\,\lambda.\penalty\

(5.64)

2.

Suppose further that
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
is
k
-sparse, supported on the subset
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
(i.e.,
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert=k
).
If the model matrix
{\bm{X}}
satisfies the restricted eigenvalue property with parameter
n\mu>0
over
{\mathbb{C}}[{\mathbb{S}};3]
, then any optimal solution
\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
satisfies

{\left\lVert{\bm{X}}(\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}\leq 9\frac{k\lambda^{2}}{n\mu}.

(5.65)

Proof
[of Theorem
]
The proof is a slight adaptation based on
Hastie et al. 2015
;
Lu 2025
.

(i).

Once again, we define the error vector
\widehat{\bm{e}}\triangleq\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
. Following the inequality (
), we have

\displaystyle 0

\displaystyle\leq{\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\widehat{\bm{e}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}\leq{2}\big\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\big\rVert_{\infty}\left\lVert\widehat{\bm{e}}\right\rVert_{1}+2\lambda\big\{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{1}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}+\widehat{\bm{e}}\right\rVert_{1}\big\}

(5.66)

\displaystyle\overset{{\dagger}}{\leq}2\left\{{\big\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\big\rVert_{\infty}}-\lambda\right\}\left\lVert\widehat{\bm{e}}\right\rVert_{1}+4\lambda\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{1}\overset{{\ddagger}}{\leq}\lambda\Big\{-\left\lVert\widehat{\bm{e}}\right\rVert_{1}+4\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{1}\Big\},

(5.67)

where the inequality
({\dagger})
follows from the triangular inequality

-(\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{1}-\left\lVert\widehat{\bm{e}}\right\rVert_{1})\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-(-\widehat{\bm{e}})\right\rVert_{1}
, and the inequality
({\ddagger})
follows from the assumption that
\lambda\geq{2}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\right\rVert_{\infty}
.
This indicates that
\left\lVert\widehat{\bm{e}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq 4\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{1}\leq 4R_{1}
. Combining these inequalities and applying the triangle inequality
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{1}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}+\widehat{\bm{e}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}+\widehat{\bm{e}})\right\rVert_{1}=\left\lVert\widehat{\bm{e}}\right\rVert_{1}
in (
5.66
) yield that

{\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\widehat{\bm{e}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}\leq 2\left\{{\big\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\big\rVert_{\infty}}+\lambda\right\}\left\lVert\widehat{\bm{e}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq 12\lambda R_{1},

(5.68)

which establishes the desired result.

(ii).

Following (
), we have

{\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\widehat{\bm{e}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}\leq 3\sqrt{k}\lambda\left\lVert\widehat{\bm{e}}\right\rVert_{2}.

By the proof of Theorem
, the error vector
\widehat{\bm{e}}
belongs to the cone

Remark 191
(Compatibility condition,
\ell_{1}
estimation bound).

Another related condition is the compatibility condition on the design matrix
{\bm{X}}
.
It is defined with respect to the true support set
{\mathbb{S}}=\mathrm{supp}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})
and requires that, for some compatibility constant
\mu>0
,

\frac{1}{n}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\bm{u}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\geq\frac{\mu}{k}\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{1}^{2},\quad\text{for all }{\bm{u}}\in{\mathbb{C}}[{\mathbb{S}};3],\text{ i.e., }\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq 3\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{1},

(5.69)

where
k\triangleq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{0}
.
Intuitively, this condition ensures that the truly active predictors are not too highly correlated.
Note that inequality (
) also implies

\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq 3\lambda\left\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{S}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{1}.

(5.70)

Since
\widehat{\bm{e}}={\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\in{\mathbb{C}}[{\mathbb{S}};3]
by (
),
we can combine this with the compatibility condition to bound the parameter estimation error. Specifically, applying the lower bound from (
) to the left-hand side of (
) yields

\frac{n\mu}{k}\left\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{S}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{1}^{2}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq 3\lambda\left\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{S}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{1}.

Dividing both sides by
\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{S}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}_{\mathbb{S}}\big\rVert_{1}
, and using the fact that
\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\big\rVert_{1}\leq 3\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{S}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}_{\mathbb{S}}\big\rVert_{1}
, which implies
\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\big\rVert_{1}\leq 4\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{S}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}_{\mathbb{S}}\big\rVert_{1}
, we get

\left\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\frac{k\lambda}{n\mu}.

(5.71)

This provides an
\ell_{1}
-bound for the parameter estimation loss.
Compared to the
\ell_{1}
-bound in (
), the dependence on the sparsity level is now linear in
k
rather than
\sqrt{k}
.

5.4.3
Gaussian Noise and Oracle Inequality

We consider the linear model
{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}+{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}
, where the noise vector
{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\in\real^{n}
has i.i.d. Gaussian entries with mean zero and variance
\sigma^{2}
.
The design matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
is assumed fixed, and each column satisfies
\max_{i=1,2,\ldots,p}\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\sqrt{n}
.
(Note that this normalization can always be achieved by rescaling.)
Under these assumptions, the random vector
{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}
has independent Gaussian entries with mean zero and variance at most
\max_{i=1,2,\ldots,p}\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\sigma^{2}\leq n\sigma^{2}
.
Using standard Gaussian tail bounds (see Lemma
), we have

\Pr\left(\left\lvert({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}})_{i}\right\rvert\geq t\sqrt{n}\sigma\right)\leq\exp\left(-\frac{t^{2}}{2}\right),\quad\text{for $i=1,2,\ldots,p$}.

Applying the union bound over all
p
coordinates (Theorem
) and setting the parameter
t=\sqrt{2(\ln(2p)+\xi)}
, we obtain

\Pr\left(\big\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\big\rVert_{\infty}\geq\sigma\sqrt{2n(\ln(2p)+\xi)}\right)\leq\frac{1}{2}\exp(-\xi),\quad\forall\,\xi>0.

(5.72)

Thus, choosing
\lambda=2\sigma\sqrt{2n(\ln(2p)+\xi)}=\mathcal{O}\big(\sqrt{n{\ln(p)}}\big)
is valid for Theorem
with probability at least
1-\exp(-\xi)/2
.
Consequently, the prediction loss bounds take the form:

\displaystyle\frac{\left\lVert{\bm{X}}(\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}{n}

\displaystyle\leq\mathcal{O}\big(R_{1}\,\sqrt{\frac{\ln(p)}{n}}\big);

(5.73a)

\displaystyle\frac{\left\lVert{\bm{X}}(\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}{n}

\displaystyle\leq\mathcal{O}\big(\frac{\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert\,\ln(p)}{n}\big).

(5.73b)

The first bound (
5.73a
), which depends only on the
\ell_{1}
-norm radius
R_{1}
, is known as the “slow rate,” since the mean squared prediction error decays at the rate
1/\sqrt{n}
.
In contrast, the second bound (
5.73b
) is referred to as the “fast rate,” exhibiting a faster
1/n
decay.

Note that the fast rate relies on stronger assumptions: specifically, that
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
is exactly
k
-sparse (i.e., hard sparsity), and—more critically—that the design matrix
{\bm{X}}
satisfies the RE condition.
In principle, good prediction performance should not require such structural conditions on
{\bm{X}}
, suggesting that the RE assumption may be an artifact of the current proof technique rather than a fundamental requirement.

When analyzing the constrained form of the LASSO (problem (
LC
)),
where
\Sigma\geq 0
serves as the tuning parameter.
Setting
\Sigma=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{1}
ensures that the true coefficient vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
is feasible for (
LC
); under this choice, the same bounds in (
) hold with probability at least
1-\exp(-\xi)/2
.

Even without assuming a linear model
{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}+{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}
, we can still derive a meaningful bound on the prediction loss that quantifies its excess risk relative to the best linear predictor.
Suppose instead that

{\bm{y}}=f_{0}({\bm{X}})+{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}},

for some unknown function
f_{0}:\real^{p}\to\real
, where
f_{0}({\bm{X}})=[f_{0}({\bm{x}}^{1}),\ldots,f_{0}({\bm{x}}^{n})]^{\top}\in\real^{n}
denotes the row-wise application of
f_{0}
to the rows of
{\bm{X}}
.
Then, for any solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
of the constrained LASSO problem (
LC
) and any
{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}
satisfying
\left\lVert{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\Sigma
, we have

\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

Rearranging terms gives

\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\bm{X}}{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle\leq\left\langle{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}},{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\bm{X}}{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}\right\rangle=\left\langle f_{0}({\bm{X}})-{\bm{X}}{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}},{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\bm{X}}{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}\right\rangle+\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}},{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\bm{X}}{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}\right\rangle.

Applying the polarization identity
\left\lVert{\bm{a}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\left\lVert{\bm{b}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\left\lVert{\bm{a}}-{\bm{b}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=2\left\langle{\bm{a}},{\bm{b}}\right\rangle
to the first inner product on the right-hand side yields

\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\bm{X}}{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}-f_{0}({\bm{X}})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\bm{X}}{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}-f_{0}({\bm{X}})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+2\left\langle{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}},{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}\right\rangle.

After rearranging, we obtain

\displaystyle\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-f_{0}({\bm{X}})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}-f_{0}({\bm{X}})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+2\left\langle{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}},{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}\right\rangle\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}-f_{0}({\bm{X}})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+4\Sigma\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\right\rVert_{\infty}

\displaystyle\leq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}-f_{0}({\bm{X}})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+4\Sigma\sigma\sqrt{{2n(\ln(2p)+\xi)}},

where the last inequality holds with probability at least
1-\exp(-\xi)/2
.
Since this holds simultaneously for all
{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}
with
\left\lVert{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\Sigma
and probability at least
1-\exp(-\xi)/2
, we may take the infimum over such
{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}
on the right-hand side, yielding the
oracle inequality
:

\frac{1}{n}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-f_{0}({\bm{X}})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\min_{\left\lVert{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\Sigma}\left(\frac{1}{n}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}-f_{0}({\bm{X}})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right)+4\Sigma\sigma\sqrt{\frac{2(\ln(2p)+\xi)}{n}},

(5.74)

with probability at least
1-\exp(-\xi)/2
.
This inequality states that, in terms of prediction loss, the constrained LASSO performs nearly as well as the best
\ell_{1}
-constrained linear predictor of
f_{0}
.

Let
{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}^{*}
denote a minimizer of
\frac{1}{n}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}-f_{0}({\bm{X}})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
over
\left\lVert{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\Sigma
.
Then, by the triangle inequality and (
), we further obtain

\frac{1}{n}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\bm{X}}{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}^{*}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq 4\Sigma\sigma\sqrt{\frac{2(\ln(2p)+\xi)}{n}},

(5.75)

with probability at least
1-\exp(-\xi)/2
.
This result is stronger than the oracle inequality: it shows that the LASSO’s predictions are close to those of the best
\ell_{1}
-constrained linear predictor—even when that predictor itself is far from the true regression function
f_{0}
.
