Chapter 6
Design of Sensing Matrices Using Gaussian Ensembles

S
Since properties such as the restricted isometry property (RIP), the restricted eigenvalue (RE) condition, nullspace property (NSP), and the restricted strong convexity (RSC) are crucial for guaranteed sparse recovery, it is important to study problem settings in which real-world or constructed data matrices actually satisfy these conditions.
Significant research has focused on explicitly constructing matrices that provably satisfy the RIP—for example, see
Baraniuk et al. 2008
;
Bourgain et al. 2011
;
Jain et al. 2017
.

To build intuition, we begin by introducing the necessary probabilistic tools related to Gaussian distributions.
We first analyze sparse recovery using random Gaussian matrices and then extend the results to sub-Gaussian random matrices in Chapter
.

6.1
Covering Numbers

Before discussing Gaussian random variables and their application in ensuring the restricted isometry property, we introduce some essential mathematical tools concerning covering numbers.

A covering number refers to the minimum number of sets—typically balls in a metric space or substructures in a combinatorial setting—required to completely cover a given space or set.
Conversely, a packing number measures how many points can be placed within a set
{\mathbb{S}}
such that any two are at least
\varepsilon
apart. This captures the “spread” or “separatedness” of the set.

Formally, we have the following definition.

Definition 192
(Covering number, packing number).

Let
{\mathbb{S}}
be a subset of a metric space
({\mathbb{X}},d)
, where
d(\cdot,\cdot)
denotes the metric.
For
\varepsilon>0
, the
\varepsilon
-covering number (or simply covering number) of
{\mathbb{S}}
, denoted
\mathcal{C}({\mathbb{S}},d,\varepsilon)
, is defined as the smallest integer
\mathcal{C}
such that
{\mathbb{S}}
can be covered by
\mathcal{C}
closed balls of radius
\varepsilon
,
{\mathbb{B}}_{d}[{\bm{x}}_{i},\varepsilon]\triangleq\{{\bm{y}}\in{\mathbb{X}}\mid d({\bm{x}}_{i},{\bm{y}})\leq\varepsilon\}
,
{\bm{x}}_{i}\in{\mathbb{S}}
,
i=1,2,\ldots,\mathcal{C}
.
That is,

\mathcal{C}\equiv\mathcal{C}({\mathbb{S}},d,\varepsilon)=\min\left\{k\in\mathbb{N}\mid\exists\,{\bm{x}}_{1},{\bm{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\bm{x}}_{k}\in{\mathbb{X}}\text{ such that }{\mathbb{S}}\subset\bigcup_{i=1}^{k}{\mathbb{B}}[{\bm{x}}_{i},\varepsilon]\right\}.

Any such set
{\mathbb{C}}_{\varepsilon}\triangleq\{{\bm{x}}_{1},{\bm{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\bm{x}}_{\mathcal{C}}\}
is then called an
\varepsilon
-covering of
{\mathbb{S}}
.
Note that the centers
{\bm{x}}_{i}
do
not
necessarily have to lie in
{\mathbb{S}}
.

For
\varepsilon>0
, the
\varepsilon
-packing number (or simply packing number) of
{\mathbb{S}}
, denoted
\mathcal{P}({\mathbb{S}},d,\varepsilon)
,
is the largest number
\mathcal{P}
of disjoint closed balls of radius
\varepsilon
centered at points in
{\mathbb{S}}
. Equivalently, it is the maximum number
\mathcal{P}
of points

{\bm{x}}_{1},{\bm{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\bm{x}}_{\mathcal{P}}
such that
d({\bm{x}}_{i},{\bm{x}}_{i})>\varepsilon
for all
i\neq j
(i.e., it is the maximum number of disjoint closed balls of radius
\varepsilon/2
centered at points in
{\mathbb{S}}
).
Such a set
{\mathbb{P}}_{\varepsilon}\triangleq\{{\bm{x}}_{1},{\bm{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\bm{x}}_{\mathcal{P}}\}
is called an
\varepsilon
-packing or
\varepsilon
-separated set.

As
\varepsilon\rightarrow 0
, finer resolution is required, so the covering number
\mathcal{C}({\mathbb{S}},d,\varepsilon)
generally increases.

When
{\mathbb{X}}=\real^{n}
is a vector space and the metric is induced by a norm, i.e.,
d({\bm{a}},{\bm{b}})=\left\lVert{\bm{a}}-{\bm{b}}\right\rVert
, we often write the following for brevity:

\mathcal{C}({\mathbb{S}},\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert,\varepsilon)\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathcal{P}({\mathbb{S}},\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert,\varepsilon).

We now list several basic properties of covering numbers; packing numbers satisfy analogous properties.
For arbitrary sets
{\mathbb{M}},{\mathbb{S}}\subset{\mathbb{X}}
, the “triangle inequality” holds:

\mathcal{C}({\mathbb{M}}\cup{\mathbb{S}},d,\varepsilon)\leq\mathcal{C}({\mathbb{M}},d,\varepsilon)+\mathcal{C}({\mathbb{S}},d,\varepsilon).

(6.1a)

For any
\eta>0
,

\mathcal{C}({\mathbb{S}},\eta d,\varepsilon)=\mathcal{C}({\mathbb{S}},d,\varepsilon/\eta).

(6.1b)

If
{\mathbb{X}}=\real^{n}
and
d(\cdot,\cdot)
is induced by a norm
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert
, then

\mathcal{C}(\eta{\mathbb{S}},d,\varepsilon)=\mathcal{C}({\mathbb{S}},d,\eta^{-1}\varepsilon).

(6.1c)

Moreover, if
d^{\prime}(\cdot,\cdot)
is another metric on
{\mathbb{X}}
satisfying
d^{\prime}({\bm{a}},{\bm{b}})\leq d({\bm{a}},{\bm{b}})
for all
{\bm{a}},{\bm{b}}\in{\mathbb{X}}
, then

\mathcal{C}({\mathbb{S}},d^{\prime},\varepsilon)\leq\mathcal{C}({\mathbb{S}},d,\varepsilon).

(6.1d)

There is a fundamental relationship between covering and packing numbers:

Lemma 193
(Key relationship between covering and packing numbers).

Let
{\mathbb{S}}
be a subset of a metric space
({\mathbb{X}},d)
, and let
\varepsilon>0
. Then,

\mathcal{P}({\mathbb{S}},d,2\varepsilon)\leq\mathcal{C}({\mathbb{S}},d,\varepsilon)\leq\mathcal{P}({\mathbb{S}},d,\varepsilon).

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Let
\{{\bm{x}}_{1},{\bm{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\bm{x}}_{\mathcal{P}}\}
be a
2\varepsilon
-packing set such that each
{\bm{x}}_{i}\in{\mathbb{S}}
and
d({\bm{x}}_{i},{\bm{x}}_{j})>2\varepsilon
for
i\neq j
,
and let

\{{\bm{y}}_{1},{\bm{y}}_{2},\ldots,{\bm{y}}_{\mathcal{C}}\}
be an
\varepsilon
-covering set such that
{\mathbb{S}}\subset\bigcup_{i=1}^{\mathcal{C}}{\mathbb{B}}[{\bm{y}}_{i},\varepsilon]
.
Each
{\bm{x}}_{j}
must lie in at least one (closed) ball
{\mathbb{B}}_{d}[{\bm{y}}_{i},\varepsilon]
.
That is, we can assign to each point
{\bm{y}}_{i}
a point
{\bm{x}}_{j}
with
d({\bm{y}}_{i},{\bm{x}}_{j})\leq\varepsilon
.
Crucially, each ball
{\mathbb{B}}_{d}[{\bm{y}}_{i},\varepsilon]
can contain
at most one
point from the
2\varepsilon
-packing set.
Indeed, if two distinct points
{\bm{x}}_{i},{\bm{x}}_{k}
(
i\neq k
) both belonged to
{\mathbb{B}}_{d}[{\bm{y}}_{i},\varepsilon]
, satisfying

d({\bm{x}}_{i},{\bm{y}}_{j})\leq\varepsilon\qquad\text{and}\qquad d({\bm{x}}_{k},{\bm{y}}_{j})\leq\varepsilon,

then by the triangle inequality,

d({\bm{x}}_{i},{\bm{x}}_{k})\leq d({\bm{x}}_{i},{\bm{y}}_{j})+d({\bm{x}}_{k},{\bm{y}}_{j})\leq 2\varepsilon,

contradicting the definition of a
2\varepsilon
-packing set. This proves the first inequality.

For the second inequality, let
\{{\bm{x}}_{1},{\bm{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\bm{x}}_{\mathcal{P}}\}
be an
\varepsilon
-packing of
{\mathbb{S}}
.
Since it’s maximal, for any point
{\bm{x}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
, there exists some
{\bm{x}}_{i}
such that
d({\bm{x}}_{i},{\bm{x}})\leq\varepsilon
. Otherwise, we could add
{\bm{x}}
to the packing, contradicting maximality. Thus,
{\mathbb{S}}\subset\bigcup_{i=1}^{\mathcal{P}}{\mathbb{B}}[{\bm{y}}_{i},\varepsilon]
. This means
\mathcal{P}
is at least the covering number.

The following result bounds the packing (and hence covering) number of a norm-induced unit sphere (norm-sphere) in finite dimensions.

{theoremHigh}
[Covering and packing numbers of a norm-sphere]
Let
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert
be some norm on
n
, and let
{\mathbb{A}}
be a subset of the unit ball
{\mathbb{B}}\triangleq{\mathbb{B}}_{\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert}[\boldsymbol{0},1]=\{{\bm{x}}\in\real^{n}\mid\left\lVert{\bm{x}}\right\rVert\leq 1\}
. Then the packing and covering numbers of the
n
-dimensional sphere
{\mathbb{B}}
at scale
\varepsilon<1
satisfy

\mathcal{C}({\mathbb{A}},\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert,\varepsilon)\leq\mathcal{P}({\mathbb{A}},\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert,\varepsilon)\leq\left(1+\frac{2}{\varepsilon}\right)^{n}\leq\left(\frac{3}{\varepsilon}\right)^{n}.

(6.2)

Proof
[of Theorem
]
The first inequality follows from Lemma
.
Let
\{{\bm{x}}_{1},{\bm{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\bm{x}}_{\mathcal{P}}\}\subset{\mathbb{A}}
be a maximal
\varepsilon
-packing of
{\mathbb{A}}
.
Then the balls
{\mathbb{B}}_{\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert}[{\bm{x}}_{\ell},\varepsilon/2]
are pairwise disjoint, and they are all contained in the scaled ball
(1+\varepsilon/2){\mathbb{B}}
with radius
(1+\varepsilon/2)
.
Comparing volumes yields

\mathrm{Vol}\left(\bigcup_{\ell=1}^{\mathcal{P}}{\mathbb{B}}_{\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert}[{\bm{x}}_{\ell},\frac{\varepsilon}{2}]\right)=\mathcal{P}\,\mathrm{Vol}\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{2}{\mathbb{B}}\right)\leq\mathrm{Vol}\left(\big(1+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\big){\mathbb{B}}\right).

Since the volume satisfies

\mathrm{Vol}(\varepsilon{\mathbb{B}})=\varepsilon^{n}\,\mathrm{Vol}({\mathbb{B}})\quad\text{ on $\real{}^{n}$},

we obtain

\mathcal{P}\big(\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\big)^{n}\,\mathrm{Vol}({\mathbb{B}})\leq\big(1+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\big)^{n}\,\mathrm{Vol}({\mathbb{B}})\qquad\implies\qquad\mathcal{P}\leq\big(1+\frac{2}{\varepsilon}\big)^{n}.

This completes the proof.

Specifically, the following corollary provides a bound for the covering and packing numbers of the
n
-dimensional sphere

{\mathbb{U}}^{n-1}\triangleq\{{\bm{x}}\in\real^{n}\mid\left\lVert{\bm{x}}\right\rVert=1\},

which contains the unit (
\ell_{2}
) norm vectors in
n
.
Note the distinction between the unit ball in
n
and the
n
-dimensional sphere, for the given norm
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert:\real^{n}\rightarrow\real
:

\displaystyle{\mathbb{B}}_{\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert}[\boldsymbol{0},1]

\displaystyle\triangleq\{{\bm{x}}\in\real^{n}\mid\left\lVert{\bm{x}}\right\rVert\leq 1\};

(6.3a)

\displaystyle{\mathbb{U}}^{n-1}

\displaystyle\triangleq\{{\bm{x}}\in\real^{n}\mid\left\lVert{\bm{x}}\right\rVert=1\}.

(6.3b)

Corollary 194
(Covering number of a sphere).

The covering and packing numbers of the
n
-dimensional sphere
{\mathbb{U}}^{n-1}
at scale
\varepsilon<1
satisfy

\mathcal{C}\left({\mathbb{U}}^{n-1},\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert,\varepsilon\right)\leq\mathcal{P}\left({\mathbb{U}}^{n-1},\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert,\varepsilon\right)\leq\left(\frac{2+\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}\right)^{n}\leq\left(\frac{3}{\varepsilon}\right)^{n}.

(6.4)

We construct an
\varepsilon
-packing set
{\mathbb{P}}_{\varepsilon}\subseteq{\mathbb{U}}^{n-1}
recursively as follows:

We initialize
{\mathbb{P}}_{\varepsilon}
to the empty set.

We choose a point
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{U}}^{n-1}
such that
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert>\varepsilon
for any
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{P}}_{\varepsilon}
. We add
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
to
{\mathbb{P}}_{\varepsilon}
until there are no points in
{\mathbb{U}}^{n-1}
that are
\varepsilon
away from any point in
{\mathbb{P}}_{\varepsilon}
.

This procedure terminates after finitely many steps because
{\mathbb{U}}^{n-1}
is compact; an infinite sequence would admit a convergent subsequence, contradicting the separation condition.

6.2
Concentration of Gaussian Vectors

In low dimensions, the joint p.d.f. of i.i.d. standard Gaussian vectors is highly concentrated near the origin. However, this behavior changes dramatically as the dimension of the ambient space increases.
Specifically, consider an
n
-dimensional vector
{\mathbf{x}}=[{\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{n}]^{\top}
whose entries are i.i.d. standard Gaussian random variables.

The squared
\ell_{2}
-norm of
{\mathbf{x}}
, given by
\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\textnormal{x}}_{i}^{2}
, follows a Chi-squared (
\chi^{2}
) distribution with
n
degrees of freedom (see Definition
). As
n
grows, the p.d.f. of this
\chi^{2}
random variable becomes increasingly concentrated around its mean, which equals
n
:

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}]

\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\textnormal{x}}_{i}^{2}\right]=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{i}^{2}]=n.

(6.5)

Moreover, we present simple results concerning the expected values of the
\ell_{1}
-,
\ell_{2}
- and
\ell_{\infty}
-norms of standard Gaussian random vectors. The bound for the
\ell_{\infty}
-norm relies on properties of sub-Gaussian random variables discussed in Section
.

{theoremHigh}
[Norms of standard Gaussian vectors]
Let
{\mathbf{x}}=[{\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{n}]^{\top}
be a vector of (not necessarily independent) standard Gaussian random variables. Then,

1.

\mathbb{E}[\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{1}]=\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}n
.

2.

It holds that

\mathbb{E}[\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}]=n\qquad\text{and}\qquad\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\sqrt{n}\leq\mathbb{E}[\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{2}]\leq\sqrt{n}.

(6.6)

If the entries of
{\mathbf{x}}
are independent, then

\frac{n}{\sqrt{n+1}}\leq\mathbb{E}[\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{2}]\leq\sqrt{2}\frac{\Gamma((n+1)/2)}{\Gamma(n/2)}\leq\sqrt{n},

(6.7)

and consequently
\mathbb{E}[\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{2}]\sim\sqrt{n}
as
n\to\infty
.

3.

It holds that

\mathbb{E}[\max_{i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}}{\textnormal{x}}_{i}]\leq\sqrt{2\ln(n)}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathbb{E}[\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{\infty}]\leq\sqrt{2\ln(2n)}.

(6.8)

If the entries of
{\mathbf{x}}
are independent then, for
n\geq 2
, then

\mathbb{E}[\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{\infty}]\geq C\sqrt{\ln(n)},\quad\text{with $C\approx 0.265$}.

(6.9)

Proof
[of Theorem
]

(i).
Using the density of a standard Gaussian random variable,

\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\right\rvert]=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\left\lvert x\right\rvert\exp(-\frac{x^{2}}{2})dx=\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\int_{0}^{\infty}x\exp(-\frac{x^{2}}{2})dx=\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}.

By linearity of expectation,
\mathbb{E}[\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{1}]=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\right\rvert]=\sqrt{2/\pi}n
.

(ii).

Clearly,
\mathbb{E}[\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}]=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{i}^{2}]=n
for standard Gaussian random variables
{\textnormal{x}}_{i}
.
Jensen’s inequality for expectations of the square function gives
\mathbb{E}[\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{2}]\leq\sqrt{\mathbb{E}[\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}]}=\sqrt{n}
, while the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality for the inner product on
n
gives
\mathbb{E}[\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{2}]\geq\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\mathbb{E}[\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{1}]=\sqrt{2/\pi}\sqrt{n}
; see Exercise
for more details.

If the entries of
{\mathbf{x}}
are independent, then
\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
follows the
\chi^{2}_{(n)}
Chi-squared distribution (Definition
).
Therefore,

\mathbb{E}[\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{2}]=\int_{0}^{\infty}x^{\frac{1}{2}}\cdot\frac{x^{\frac{n}{2}-1}}{2^{\frac{n}{2}}\Gamma(\frac{n}{2})}e^{-\frac{x}{2}}dx=\frac{2^{\frac{n}{2}+\frac{1}{2}}}{2^{\frac{n}{2}}\Gamma(\frac{n}{2})}\int_{0}^{\infty}t^{\frac{n}{2}-\frac{1}{2}}e^{-t}dt=\sqrt{2}\frac{\Gamma((n+1)/2)}{\Gamma(n/2)},

where the last equality follows from that the Gamma function is
\Gamma(x)=\int_{0}^{\infty}t^{x-1}\exp(-t)dt
.
Let
T_{n}\triangleq\mathbb{E}[\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{2}]\leq\sqrt{n}
, where the upper bound for Gaussian vector
{\mathbf{x}}
of length
n
was already shown above.
By the fact that
\Gamma(x+1)=x\Gamma(x)
for
x>0
, we have

T_{n+1}T_{n}=2\frac{\Gamma(n/2+1)}{\Gamma(n/2)}=n,

which implies
T_{n}=n/T_{n+1}\geq n/\sqrt{n+1}
, since
T_{n+1}\leq\sqrt{n+1}
.
Therefore,
n/\sqrt{n+1}\leq T_{n}\leq\sqrt{n}
, and this proves the desired result.

(iii).

The bounds in (
) follow from Proposition
(on maxima of sub-Gaussian variables).
Indeed, Lemma
shows that
\mathbb{E}[\exp(\theta{\textnormal{x}}_{i})]\leq\exp(\theta^{2}/2)
for all
\theta\in\real
so that the parameter
C
is
C=1/2
in Proposition
for Gaussian random variables.

For the lower bound under independence, by Exercise

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{\infty}]

\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{\infty}\Pr\left(\max_{i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}}\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\right\rvert>x\right)dx=\int_{0}^{\infty}\left(1-\Pr\left(\max_{i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}}\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\right\rvert\leq x\right)\right)dx

\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{\infty}\left(1-\prod_{i=1}^{n}\Pr(\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\right\rvert\leq x)\right)dx\geq\int_{0}^{\delta}\big(1-\big(\Pr(\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert\leq x)\big)^{n}\big)dx

\displaystyle\geq\delta\big(1-\big(1-\Pr(\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert>\delta)\big)^{n}\big),

where
\delta>0
. For any
\delta>0
, we also have

\Pr(\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert>\delta)=\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\int_{\delta}^{\infty}e^{-t^{2}/2}dt\geq\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\int_{\delta}^{2\delta}e^{-t^{2}/2}dt\geq\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\delta e^{-2\delta^{2}}.

Choosing
\delta=\sqrt{\ln n/2}
, for
n\geq 2
,

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{\infty}]

\displaystyle\geq\sqrt{\frac{\ln n}{2}}\left(1-\left(1-\sqrt{\frac{\ln n}{\pi}}\frac{1}{n}\right)^{n}\right)\geq\sqrt{\frac{\ln n}{2}}\left(1-\exp\left(-\sqrt{\frac{\ln n}{\pi}}\right)\right),

where the second inequality follows since
(1-\frac{x}{n})^{n}\leq\exp(-x)
if
n>x>0
.
For
n\geq 2
, the factor in parentheses is bounded below by a positive constant, yielding the claimed lower bound with
C=(1-\exp(-\sqrt{\ln(2)/\pi}))/\sqrt{2}\approx 0.265
.

We can further extend part (iii) of the previous theorem to bound the maximum squared
\ell_{2}
-norm over a sequence of standard Gaussian random vectors.

{theoremHigh}
[Maximum of norms of Gaussian vectors]
Let
{\mathbf{x}}_{1},{\mathbf{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\mathbf{x}}_{n}\in\real^{p}
be a sequence of (not necessarily independent) standard Gaussian random vectors. Then, for any
\nu>0
,

\mathbb{E}\left[\max_{i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}}\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right]\leq 2(1+\nu)\ln(n)+p(1+\nu)\ln(1+\nu^{-1}).

Consequently,

\mathbb{E}\left[\max_{i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}}\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right]\leq(\sqrt{2\ln(n)}+\sqrt{p})^{2}.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
By the concavity of the logarithm and Jensen’s inequality, for any
\theta>0
,

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\max_{i}\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right]

\displaystyle=\theta^{-1}\mathbb{E}\left[\ln\max_{i}\exp(\theta\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}^{2})\right]\leq\theta^{-1}\ln\mathbb{E}\left[\max_{i}\exp(\theta\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}^{2})\right]

\displaystyle\leq\theta^{-1}\ln\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}[\exp(\theta\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}^{2})]\right),

For each standard Gaussian random vector
{\mathbf{x}}={\mathbf{x}}_{i}
,
by the independence of the components of
{\mathbf{x}}
and Lemma
, we have for
\theta<1/2
,

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\exp(\theta\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2})]

\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\exp\left(\theta\sum_{i=1}^{p}{\textnormal{x}}_{i}^{2}\right)\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\prod_{i=1}^{p}\exp(\theta{\textnormal{x}}_{i}^{2})\right]=\prod_{i=1}^{p}\mathbb{E}[\exp(\theta{\textnormal{x}}_{i}^{2})]\leq(1-2\theta)^{-\frac{p}{2}},

Therefore,

\mathbb{E}\left[\max_{i}\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right]\leq\min_{0<\theta<1/2}\theta^{-1}\left(\ln n+\frac{p}{2}\ln\left((1-2\theta)^{-1}\right)\right).

Choosing
\theta=(2+2\nu)^{-1}
yields the first claim. Using the fact that
\ln(1+\nu^{-1})\leq\nu^{-1}
and choosing
\nu=\sqrt{p/(2\ln(n))}
, we obtain

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\max_{i}\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right]

\displaystyle\leq 2(1+\nu)\ln(n)+p(1+\nu^{-1})

\displaystyle=2\ln(n)+2\sqrt{2p\ln(n)}+p=(\sqrt{2\ln(n)}+\sqrt{p})^{2}.

This completes the proof.

The following result quantifies the variability of the squared
\ell_{2}
-norm of a standard Gaussian vector.

Proposition 195
(Variance of the squared
\ell_{2}
-norm of a Gaussian vector).

Let
{\mathbf{x}}\in\real^{n}
be an i.i.d. standard Gaussian random vector. The variance of
\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
is
2n
.

Proof
[of Proposition
]
Recall that
\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}]=\mathbb{E}[(\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2})^{2}]-(\mathbb{E}[\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}])^{2}
.
We compute:

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right)^{2}\right]

\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\textnormal{x}}_{i}^{2}\right)^{2}\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}{\textnormal{x}}_{i}^{2}{\textnormal{x}}_{j}^{2}\right]=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{i}^{2}{\textnormal{x}}_{j}^{2}]

\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{i}^{4}]+\sum_{i\neq j}^{n,n}\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{i}^{2}]\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{j}^{2}]\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\dagger}}}{{=}}3n+n(n-1)=n(n+2),

where the equality (
{\dagger}
) follows since the 4-th moment of a standard Gaussian equals 3.
Thus,

\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}]=n(n+2)-n^{2}=2n
by Theorem
.

This result shows that as
n
grows, the relative fluctuations of
\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{2}
around its mean decay like
1/\sqrt{n}
. In other words, the squared norm becomes increasingly concentrated near
n
. The following theorem makes this concentration precise by providing a non-asymptotic tail bound.

{theoremHigh}

[Chebyshev tail bound for the
\ell_{2}
-norm of an i.i.d. standard Gaussian vector]
Let
{\mathbf{x}}\in\real^{n}
be an i.i.d. standard Gaussian random vector.
Then, for any
\varepsilon>0
,

\Pr\left(n(1-\varepsilon)\leq\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq n(1+\varepsilon)\right)\geq 1-\frac{2}{n\varepsilon^{2}}.

(6.10)

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Let
{\textnormal{y}}\triangleq\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
. Then Theorem
shows
{\textnormal{y}}-n={\textnormal{y}}-\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{y}}]
.
Markov’s inequality (Theorem
) shows that

\Pr\big(({\textnormal{y}}-\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{y}}])^{2}\geq n^{2}\varepsilon^{2}\big)\leq\frac{\mathbb{E}[({\textnormal{y}}-\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{y}}])^{2}]}{n^{2}\varepsilon^{2}}=\frac{\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{y}}]}{n^{2}\varepsilon^{2}}=\frac{2n}{n^{2}\varepsilon}.

Taking the complement yields the desired bound (
).

The bound in Theorem
relies only on the variance to control the probability that the squared norm deviates from its mean. Consequently, it is significantly weaker than the following result, which leverages the favorable behavior of higher moments of the standard Gaussian distribution.

{theoremHigh}
[Chernoff tail bound for the
\ell_{2}
-norm of an i.i.d. standard Gaussian vector]
Let
{\mathbf{x}}\in\real^{n}
be an i.i.d. standard Gaussian random vector.
For any
\varepsilon\in(0,1)
, we have

\Pr\left(n(1-\varepsilon)\leq\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq n(1+\varepsilon)\right)\geq 1-2\exp\left(-\frac{n\varepsilon^{2}}{8}\right).

(6.11)

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Let
{\textnormal{y}}\triangleq\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
. The desired inequality follows from the two one-sided bounds:

\displaystyle\Pr({\textnormal{y}}\geq n(1+\varepsilon))

\displaystyle\leq\exp\left(-\frac{n\varepsilon^{2}}{8}\right);

\displaystyle\Pr({\textnormal{y}}\geq n(1-\varepsilon))

\displaystyle\leq\exp\left(-\frac{n\varepsilon^{2}}{8}\right).

We prove the first; the second is analogous.
Fix
\theta\in(0,1/2)
.
By Markov’s inequality (Theorem
) and the independence of the components of
{\mathbf{x}}
, we have for any
\tau>0
:

\displaystyle\Pr({\textnormal{y}}>\tau)

\displaystyle=\Pr(\exp(\theta y)>\exp(\theta\tau))\leq\exp(-\theta\tau)\,\mathbb{E}[\exp(\theta y)]

\displaystyle\leq\exp(-\theta\tau)\,\mathbb{E}\left[\exp\left(\theta\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\textnormal{x}}_{i}^{2}\right)\right]=\exp(-\theta\tau)\prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}[\exp(\theta{\textnormal{x}}_{i}^{2})]=\frac{\exp(-\theta\tau)}{(1-2\theta)^{n/2}},

where the last equality is a consequence of the the moment lemma of standard Gaussian variables (Lemma
).
Set
\tau\triangleq n(1+\varepsilon)
and

\theta\triangleq\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2(1+\varepsilon)}
.
By taking the infimum over
\theta\in(0,1/2)
, we have

\Pr({\textnormal{y}}>n(1+\varepsilon))\leq(1+\varepsilon)^{n/2}\exp\left(-\frac{n\varepsilon}{2}\right)=\exp\left(-\frac{n}{2}(\varepsilon-\ln(1+\varepsilon))\right)\leq\exp\left(-\frac{n\varepsilon^{2}}{8}\right),

where the last equality follows from the fact that the function
g(x)\triangleq x-\frac{x^{2}}{4}-\ln(1+x)
is nonnegative between 0 and 1 (the derivative is nonnegative and
g(0)=0
).
A similar argument gives the lower-tail bound, completing the proof.

\paragrapharrow

Tail bound after projection.
It is well known that the
\ell_{2}
-norm of the projection of i.i.d. standard Gaussian noise onto a fixed subspace concentrates around the square root of the subspace dimension. This is because, in any orthonormal basis of the subspace, the projected coordinates remain i.i.d. standard Gaussian.

Lemma 196
(Projection of an i.i.d. Gaussian vector onto a subspace).

Let
\mathcal{V}
be a
k
-dimensional subspace of
n
, and let
{\mathbf{x}}\in\real^{n}
be a vector with i.i.d. standard Gaussian entries.
Then the squared norm of the orthogonal projection of
{\mathbf{x}}
onto
\mathcal{V}
, denoted
\left\lVert\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{V}}{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
, follows
a
\chi^{2}
distribution with
k
degrees of freedom.
Equivalently, it has the same distribution as

{\textnormal{y}}\triangleq\sum_{i=1}^{k}{\textnormal{y}}_{i}^{2}

(6.12)

where
{\textnormal{y}}_{1},{\textnormal{y}}_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{y}}_{k}
are i.i.d. standard Gaussian random variables.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Let
{\bm{Q}}\in\real^{n\times k}
be a matrix whose columns form an orthonormal basis for
\mathcal{V}
(i.e.,
{\bm{Q}}^{\top}{\bm{Q}}={\bm{I}}_{k}
).
Then
{\bm{Q}}{\bm{Q}}^{\top}
is the orthogonal projection matrix for the subspace
\mathcal{V}
(Lemma
).
Thus, we have

\displaystyle\left\lVert\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{V}}{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle=\left\lVert{\bm{Q}}{\bm{Q}}^{\top}{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}={\mathbf{x}}^{\top}{\bm{Q}}{\bm{Q}}^{\top}{\bm{Q}}{\bm{Q}}^{\top}{\mathbf{x}}={\mathbf{x}}^{\top}{\bm{Q}}{\bm{Q}}^{\top}{\mathbf{x}}\triangleq{\mathbf{z}}^{\top}{\mathbf{z}}=\sum_{i=1}^{k}{\textnormal{z}}_{i}^{2},

where by Lemma
, the random vector
{\mathbf{z}}\triangleq{\bm{Q}}^{\top}{\mathbf{x}}\in\real^{k}
is Gaussian with mean zero and covariance matrix

\displaystyle\Sigma_{{\mathbf{z}}}={\bm{Q}}^{\top}\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\mathbf{x}}]{\bm{Q}}={\bm{Q}}^{\top}{\bm{I}}{\bm{Q}}={\bm{I}}_{k}.

Therefore, the entries are independent standard Gaussians.

Because the projected norm squared is distributed as a
\chi^{2}_{(k)}
random variable, we can directly apply Theorem
with
n
replaced by
k
.

Corollary 197
(Chernoff tail bound for the
\ell_{2}
-norm of projection an i.i.d. standard Gaussian vector).

Let
\mathcal{V}
be a
k
-dimensional subspace of
n
, and let
{\mathbf{x}}\in\real^{n}
a vector of i.i.d. Gaussian entries.
For any
\varepsilon\in(0,1)
, we have

\Pr\left(\sqrt{k(1-\varepsilon)}\leq\left\lVert\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{V}}{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\sqrt{k(1+\varepsilon)}\right)\geq 1-2\exp\left(-\frac{k\varepsilon^{2}}{8}\right).

This follows immediately from Lemma
and Theorem
, applied to the
k
-dimensional Gaussian vector
{\bm{Q}}^{\top}{\mathbf{x}}
.

6.3
Randomized Projections under Gaussian Random Matrices

Previously, we showed that projections of Gaussian random vectors exhibit strong concentration properties.
We now turn to a key property of Gaussian random matrices.

In an introductory linear algebra course, one learns that dimensionality reduction via principal component analysis (PCA) involves projecting data onto low-dimensional subspaces that are optimal in the sense of preserving as much energy (i.e., variance) as possible. The principal directions correspond to the directions of maximum variation in the data and are obtained from the singular value decomposition (SVD) of the data matrix. However, computing the SVD can be computationally expensive—and may even be infeasible—when dealing with streaming data or when the projection must be applied in real time.

In such scenarios, a non-adaptive alternative to PCA is needed: one that selects the projection matrix before observing the data. A simple and effective approach is to use a random linear map, represented by a random matrix
{\mathbf{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
whose entries are sampled independently from the standard Gaussian distribution. The following lemma shows that applying such a matrix to any fixed unit vector yields a Gaussian random vector.

Lemma 198
(Randomized projections under i.i.d. standard Gaussian matrix).

Let
{\mathbf{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
be a matrix with i.i.d. standard Gaussian entries.
If
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
is a deterministic vector with
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}=1
, then
{\mathbf{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{n}
is an i.i.d. standard Gaussian random vector.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
For each
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}
, the
i
-th entry of
{\mathbf{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is given by
({\mathbf{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}})_{i}=\left\langle{\mathbf{x}}^{i},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle
, i.e., the inner product between
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
and the
i
-th row
{\mathbf{x}}^{i}
(viewed as a column vector in
p
).
Since
{\mathbf{x}}^{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},{\bm{I}}_{p})
and
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is deterministic, Lemma
implies that
\left\langle{\mathbf{x}}^{i},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle
is Gaussian.
Its mean is zero because
\mathbb{E}[{\mathbf{x}}^{i}]=\boldsymbol{0}
. The variance is

\displaystyle\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}\left[\left\langle{\mathbf{x}}^{i},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle\right]

\displaystyle={\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\top}\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}[{\mathbf{x}}^{i}]{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\top}{\bm{I}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=1.

(6.13)

Thus, each component of
{\mathbf{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is a standard normal random variable.
Moreover, the components are independent because each depends only on a distinct row of
{\mathbf{X}}
, and the rows are mutually independent by construction. Hence,
{\mathbf{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},{\bm{I}})
.

A direct consequence of this result is a non-asymptotic concentration bound on the
\ell_{2}
-norm of
{\mathbf{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
for any fixed unit vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.

Corollary 199
(Chernoff tail bound for the
\ell_{2}
-norm of random Gaussian projection).

Let
{\mathbf{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
be a matrix with i.i.d. standard Gaussian entries.
Then, for any deterministic
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
with unit norm and any
\varepsilon\in(0,1)
, we have

\Pr\left(\sqrt{n(1-\varepsilon)}\leq\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\sqrt{n(1+\varepsilon)}\right)\geq 1-2\exp\left(-\frac{n\varepsilon^{2}}{8}\right).

(6.14)

This follows immediately from Lemma
, which shows that
{\mathbf{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is an
n
-dimensional i.i.d. standard Gaussian vector, together with Theorem
applied to its squared norm.

6.4
Randomized Projections and Johnson–Lindenstrauss Lemma

Dimensionality-reduction techniques are useful when they preserve the information we are interested in.
In many applications, it is essential that the projection approximately preserves pairwise distances between data points. This property enables us to apply distance-based algorithms—such as nearest neighbors, clustering, or kernel methods—in the lower-dimensional space without significant loss of accuracy.

The following result, known as the Johnson–Lindenstrauss (JL) lemma, guarantees that random projections achieve precisely this: they preserve all pairwise distances among a finite set of points with high probability, even in a non-asymptotic setting. Remarkably, the required target dimension
n
depends only logarithmically on the number of points
k
, and not at all on the ambient dimension
p
. The proof follows the classical argument of
Johnson et al. 1984
.

{theoremHigh}

[Johnson–Lindenstrauss (JL) lemma]
Let
{\mathbf{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
be a random matrix with i.i.d. standard Gaussian entries. Let
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2},\ldots,{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{k}\in\real^{p}
be any fixed (deterministic) set of
k
vectors.
Then, for any
\delta\in(0,1)
and any pair
i\neq j
,

(1-\delta)\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{i}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{j}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\left\lVert\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}{\mathbf{X}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{i}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{j})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq(1+\delta)\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{i}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{j}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},

(6.15)

with probability at least
1-\frac{1}{k}
as long as

n\geq\frac{24\ln(k)}{\delta^{2}}.

(6.16)

Proof
[of Theorem
]
We analyze the action of
{\bm{X}}
on the normalized difference vectors

{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{ij}\triangleq\frac{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{i}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{j}}{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{i}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{j}\right\rVert_{2}},\quad 1\leq i<j\leq k.

which satisfy
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{ij}\right\rVert_{2}=1
whenever
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{i}\neq{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{j}
(if
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{i}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{j}
, the distance is zero and trivially preserved).
Define the concentration event

\mathcal{E}_{ij}=\left\{n(1-\delta)<\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{ij}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}<n(1+\delta)\right\},\quad 1\leq i<j\leq k.

By Corollary
, each event
\mathcal{E}_{ij}
holds with high probability under condition (
):

\Pr\left(\mathcal{E}_{ij}^{c}\right)\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{n\delta^{2}}{8}\right)\leq\frac{2}{k^{3}},\quad\text{if }n\geq\frac{24\ln(k)}{\delta^{2}}.

There are
\binom{k}{2}=k(k-1)/2
such pairs. Applying the union bound (Theorem
),

\displaystyle\Pr\left(\bigcup_{i,j}\mathcal{E}_{ij}^{c}\right)\leq\sum_{i,j}\Pr\left(\mathcal{E}_{ij}^{c}\right)\leq\frac{k(k-1)}{2}\cdot\frac{2}{k^{3}}\leq\frac{k-1}{k^{2}}=\frac{1}{k}.

Thus, with probability at least
1-1/k
, inequality (
) holds simultaneously for all pairs
i\neq j
. This completes the proof.

Many algorithms—such as nearest neighbor search, clustering, and kernel methods—depend critically on the geometry of the data, particularly pairwise distances. The JL lemma guarantees that after projecting the data randomly into a space of dimension
n\ll p
, these distances remain nearly intact. Consequently, algorithmic behavior is preserved even though computations now occur in a dramatically smaller space.

In essence, the JL lemma decouples accuracy from ambient dimensionality: randomness enables extreme data compression while maintaining geometric fidelity. This makes randomized algorithms—for example, Gaussian sketching—simultaneously fast, scalable, simple to implement, and theoretically sound, a rare and powerful combination in algorithm design
(
Woodruff et al. 2014
;
Lu 2021a
;
Lu 2021b
)
.

Figure 6.1:

Approximate 2D projection of the Iris dataset using (left) two random Gaussian directions and (right) PCA. Each point represents an iris sample, colored by species.

Example 200
(Dimensionality reduction via randomized projections).

We consider the Iris dataset, introduced in
Fisher 1936
, which is a benchmark multivariate data set consisting of 150 samples from three iris species—Iris setosa, Iris versicolor, and Iris virginica (50 samples each). Each sample is described by four continuous features: sepal length, sepal width, petal length, and petal width (all in centimeters). The dataset is widely used in machine learning and statistics due to its clear class structure—I. setosa is linearly separable from the other two species, while I. versicolor and I. virginica exhibit partial overlap—making it ideal for illustrating classification, clustering, and dimensionality reduction techniques.
The objective is to project the data onto 2D for visualization. In Figure
, we compare the result of randomly projecting the data by applying a
2\times 4
i.i.d. standard Gaussian matrix, with the result of PCA-based dimensionality reduction.
In terms of keeping the different types of iris species, the randomized projection preserves the structure in the data as effectively as PCA.

This result also reveals a close connection between the concentration inequality (
) and the JL lemma.
Since (
) implies the RIP via Theorems
and
, in this sense, one may say that the JL lemma implies the RIP.

We now show a partial converse: under suitable conditions, a matrix satisfying the RIP can be turned into a JL embedding for a point set
{\mathbb{S}}
by randomizing the signs of its columns.
Indeed, without such sign randomization, the claim would be false. Randomizing the column signs ensures that the probability of the point set
{\mathbb{S}}
falling (or nearly falling) into the null space of
{\bm{X}}{\bm{D}}
is exponentially small.

{theoremHigh}

Let
{\mathbb{S}}\subset\real^{p}
be a finite set of cardinality
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert=S
. Fix
\delta\in(0,1)
.
Let
{\mathbf{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
be a matrix satisfying the RIP of order
2k
with constant
\delta_{2k}\leq\delta/4
for some integer
k\geq 16\ln(4S/\varepsilon)
.
Then, with probability at least
1-\varepsilon

(1-\delta)\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}{\mathbf{D}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq(1+\delta)\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},\quad\text{for all }{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}},

where
{\mathbf{D}}\triangleq\mathrm{diag}({\boldsymbol{\epsilon}})\in\real^{p\times p}
, and

{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}=[\epsilon_{1},\epsilon_{2},\ldots,\epsilon_{p}]^{\top}
is a Rademacher vector (i.e., each
\epsilon_{i}
is an independent random variable taking values +1 and
-1
with equal probability).

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Without loss of generality, assume that all vectors in
{\mathbb{S}}
are normalized:
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}=1
.
Fix any
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
.
We partition
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
into blocks of size
k
based on the magnitudes of its entries.
Specifically, let
{\mathbb{T}}_{1}\subset\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
index the
k
largest (in absolute value) entries of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
,
{\mathbb{T}}_{2}\subset\{1,2,\ldots,p\}\setminus{\mathbb{T}}_{1}
index the next
k
largest entries among the remaining coordinates, and so on.
This yields a decomposition
{{\mathbf{X}}{\mathbf{D}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}={{\mathbf{X}}{\mathbf{D}}\sum_{i}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{T}}_{i})}
.

Now expand the squared norm:

\displaystyle\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}{\mathbf{D}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}{\mathbf{D}}\sum_{i}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{T}}_{i})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle=\sum_{i}\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}{\mathbf{D}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{T}}_{i})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+2\left\langle{\mathbf{X}}{\mathbf{D}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{T}}_{1}),{\mathbf{X}}{\mathbf{D}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{T}}_{1}^{c})\right\rangle+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j\geq 2\\
i\neq j\end{subarray}}\left\langle{\mathbf{X}}{\mathbf{D}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{T}}_{i}),{\mathbf{X}}{\mathbf{D}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{T}}_{j})\right\rangle.

(6.17)

Bound the first term.

Because
{\mathbf{X}}
satisfies the RIP of order
2k
with constant
\delta_{2k}\leq\delta/4
, and because
\big\lVert{\mathbf{D}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{T}}_{i})\big\rVert_{2}=\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{i}}\big\rVert_{2}
, the first term satisfies

(1-\delta/4)\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=(1-\delta/4)\sum_{i}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{i}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\sum_{i}\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}{\mathbf{D}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{T}}_{i})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq(1+\delta/4)\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

Bound the second term.

To bound the second term in (
6.17
), we define the random variable

{\textnormal{y}}\triangleq\left\langle{\mathbf{X}}{\mathbf{D}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{T}}_{1}),{\mathbf{X}}{\mathbf{D}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{T}}_{1}^{c})\right\rangle=\left\langle{\mathbf{u}},{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{1}^{c}}\right\rangle=\sum_{i\notin{\mathbb{T}}_{1}}\epsilon_{i}{\textnormal{u}}_{i},

where

{\mathbf{u}}\triangleq\mathrm{diag}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{1}^{c}}){\mathbf{X}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{1}^{c}}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{1}}{\mathbf{D}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{1}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{1}}\in\real^{\left\lvert{\mathbb{T}}_{1}^{c}\right\rvert}
.

Since
{\mathbf{u}}
and
{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{1}^{c}}
are stochastically independent, Hoeffding’s inequality for Rademacher sequences (Corollary
) shows that

\Pr(\left\lvert{\textnormal{y}}\right\rvert\geq\mu)\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{\mu^{2}}{2\left\lVert{\mathbf{u}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}\right).

(6.18)

We now bound
\left\lVert{\mathbf{u}}\right\rVert_{2}
above.
By the definition of dual norm (
), Cauchy–Schwarz ienquality, and the submultiplicativity of spectral norms (Theorem
), we obtain

\displaystyle\left\lVert{\mathbf{u}}\right\rVert_{2}

\displaystyle=\max_{\left\lVert{\bm{a}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq 1}\left\langle{\bm{a}},{\mathbf{u}}\right\rangle=\max_{\left\lVert{\bm{a}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq 1}\sum_{i\geq 2}\left\langle{\bm{a}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{i}},\mathrm{diag}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{i}}){\mathbf{X}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{i}}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{1}}{\mathbf{D}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{1}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{1}}\right\rangle

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\dagger}}}{{\leq}}\max_{\left\lVert{\bm{a}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq 1}\sum_{i\geq 2}\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{i}}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{1}}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\bm{a}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{i}}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{i}}\right\rVert_{\infty}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{1}}\right\rVert_{2}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\ddagger}}}{{\leq}}\frac{\delta_{2k}}{\sqrt{k}}\max_{\left\lVert{\bm{a}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq 1}\sum_{i\geq 2}\left\lVert{\bm{a}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{i}}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{i-1}}\right\rVert_{2}

\displaystyle\leq\frac{\delta_{2k}}{\sqrt{k}}\max_{\left\lVert{\bm{a}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq 1}\sum_{i\geq 2}\frac{1}{2}\left(\left\lVert{\bm{a}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{i}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{i-1}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right)\leq\frac{\delta_{2k}}{\sqrt{k}},

where the inequality (
{\dagger}
) follows since
\left\lVert\mathrm{diag}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rVert_{2}=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{\infty}
(the largest singular value of the diagonal matrix
\mathrm{diag}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
is
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{\infty}
) and
\left\lVert{\bm{D}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{1}}\right\rVert_{2}=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\right\rVert_{\infty}=1
.
The inequality (
{\ddagger}
) follows from
\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{i}}\big\rVert_{\infty}\leq k^{-1/2}\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{i-1}}\big\rVert_{2}
by the construction of the partitioning the ordered sets
{\mathbb{T}}_{1},{\mathbb{T}}_{2},\ldots
(Lemma
),
\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{i}}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{1}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\delta_{2k}
for
i\geq 2
by the standard consequence of RIP (Proposition
), and the fact that
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{1}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}=1
.
Therefore, (
) becomes

\Pr(\left\lvert{\textnormal{y}}\right\rvert\geq\mu)\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{\mu^{2}}{2\left\lVert{\mathbf{u}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}\right)\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{k\mu^{2}}{2\delta_{2k}^{2}}\right)\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{8k\mu^{2}}{\delta^{2}}\right).

(6.19)

Bound the third term.

Consider the remaining cross terms, we define the following random variable

{\textnormal{z}}\triangleq\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j\geq 2\\
i\neq j\end{subarray}}\left\langle{\mathbf{X}}{\mathbf{D}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{T}}_{i}),{\mathbf{X}}{\mathbf{D}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}({\mathbb{T}}_{j})\right\rangle=\sum_{i,j\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}}\epsilon_{i}\epsilon_{j}{\textnormal{a}}_{ij}={\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}^{\top}{\mathbf{A}}{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}},

where
{\mathbf{A}}\in\real^{p\times p}
is a symmetric matrix with zero diagonal and off-diagonal entries:

{\textnormal{a}}_{ij}=\begin{cases}\beta_{i}{\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\mathbf{x}}_{j}\beta_{j}&\text{if }i,j\in{\mathbb{T}}_{1}^{c}\text{ and }i,j\text{ are contained in different blocks }{\mathbb{T}}_{\ell};\\
0&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

The expression
{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}^{\top}{\mathbf{A}}{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}
a homogeneous Rademacher chaos of order two.
To bound
\left\lvert{\textnormal{z}}\right\rvert
, we apply Problem
, which requires estimates on
\left\lVert{\mathbf{A}}\right\rVert_{2}
and
\left\lVert{\mathbf{A}}\right\rVert_{F}
.
Since
{\mathbf{A}}
is symmetric, its spectral norm can be obtained by using the RIP and the block structure as before:

\displaystyle\left\lVert{\mathbf{A}}\right\rVert_{2}

\displaystyle=\max_{\left\lVert{\bm{a}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq 1}\left\langle{\mathbf{A}}{\bm{a}},{\bm{a}}\right\rangle=\max_{\left\lVert{\bm{a}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq 1}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j\geq 2\\
i\neq j\end{subarray}}\left\langle{\bm{a}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{i}},\mathrm{diag}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})_{{\mathbb{T}}_{i}}{\mathbf{X}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{i}}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{j}}\mathrm{diag}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})_{{\mathbb{T}}_{j}}{\bm{a}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{j}}\right\rangle

\displaystyle\leq\max_{\left\lVert{\bm{a}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq 1}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j\geq 2\\
i\neq j\end{subarray}}\left\lVert{\bm{a}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{i}}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\bm{a}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{j}}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{i}}\right\rVert_{\infty}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{j}}\right\rVert_{\infty}\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{i}}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{j}}\right\rVert_{2}

\displaystyle\leq\delta_{2k}\max_{\left\lVert{\bm{a}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq 1}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j\geq 2\\
i\neq j\end{subarray}}\left\lVert{\bm{a}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{i}}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\bm{a}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{j}}\right\rVert_{2}k^{-1/2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{i-1}}\right\rVert_{2}k^{-1/2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{j-1}}\right\rVert_{2}

\displaystyle\leq\frac{\delta_{2k}}{k}\max_{\left\lVert{\bm{a}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq 1}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j\geq 2\\
i\neq j\end{subarray}}\Bigg(\frac{\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{i-1}}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}+\left\lVert{\bm{a}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{i}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}{2}\Bigg)\Bigg(\frac{\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{j-1}}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}+\left\lVert{\bm{a}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{j}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}{2}\Bigg)\leq\frac{\delta_{2k}}{k}\leq\frac{\delta}{4k}.

For the Frobenius norm, observe that

\displaystyle\left\lVert{\mathbf{A}}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}

\displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}s,t\geq 2\\
s\neq t\end{subarray}}\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{T}}_{s}}\sum_{j\in{\mathbb{T}}_{t}}(\beta_{i}{\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\mathbf{x}}_{j}\beta_{j})^{2}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}s,t\geq 2\\
s\neq t\end{subarray}}\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{T}}_{s}}\beta_{i}^{2}{\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\in{\mathbb{T}}_{t}}\beta_{j}{\mathbf{x}}_{j}\beta_{j}{\mathbf{x}}_{j}^{\top}\right){\mathbf{x}}_{i}

\displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}s,t\geq 2\\
s\neq t\end{subarray}}\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{T}}_{s}}\beta_{i}^{2}\left\lVert\mathrm{diag}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{t}}){\mathbf{X}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{t}}^{\top}{\mathbf{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}s,t\geq 2\\
s\neq t\end{subarray}}\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{T}}_{s}}\beta_{i}^{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{t}}\right\rVert_{\infty}^{2}\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{t}}^{\top}{\mathbf{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\dagger}}}{{\leq}}\delta_{2k}^{2}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}s,t\geq 2\\
s\neq t\end{subarray}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{s}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}k^{-1}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{t}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\frac{\delta_{2k}^{2}}{k}\leq\frac{\delta^{2}}{16k},

where the inequality (
{\dagger}
) follows from the fact that
\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{t}}^{\top}{\mathbf{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}=\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}_{{\mathbb{T}}_{t}}^{\top}{\mathbf{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\delta_{k+1}\leq\delta_{2k}
by the standard consequence of RIP (Proposition
).
Problem
shows that
\left\lvert{\textnormal{z}}\right\rvert
satisfies

\displaystyle\Pr(\left\lvert{\textnormal{z}}\right\rvert\geq\tau)

\displaystyle\leq 2\exp\left(-\min\left\{\frac{3\tau^{2}}{128\,\left\lVert{\mathbf{A}}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}},\frac{\tau}{32\,\left\lVert{\mathbf{A}}\right\rVert_{2}}\right\}\right)\leq 2\exp\left(-k\min\left\{\frac{3\tau^{2}}{8\delta^{2}},\frac{\tau}{8\delta}\right\}\right).

Combining bounds.

Choosing
\mu\triangleq\delta/4
and
\tau\triangleq\delta/2
,
and plugging the three estimates into (
6.17
) shows that

(1-\delta)\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}{\mathbf{D}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq(1+\delta)\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},\quad\text{for any ${\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}$}

(6.20)

with probability at least

1-2\exp(-k/2)-2\exp\left(-k\min\{3/32,1/16\}\right)\geq 1-4\exp(-k/16).

Finally, applying the union bound over all
S
points in
{\mathbb{S}}
, the inequality holds simultaneously for all
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
with probability at least

1-4S\exp(-k/16)\geq 1-\varepsilon

under the condition
k\geq 16\ln(4S/\varepsilon)
.
This completes the proof.

n\times p
matrices with i.i.d. standard Gaussian entries as the aspect ratio
n/p
increases.
Providing also the theoretical Marchenko–Pastur distribution for each empirical distribution.

6.5
Singular Values of Gaussian Random Matrices

In this section, we analyze the singular values of random matrices whose entries are i.i.d. standard Gaussian random variables.
Specifically, consider an
n\times p
matrix
{\bm{X}}
with
n>p
. Numerical experiments show that as
n
grows (with
p
fixed), all
p
singular values of
{\bm{X}}
concentrate tightly around

n
, as illustrated in Figure
. Consequently,

{\bm{X}}\approx{\bm{U}}(\sqrt{n}{\bm{I}}){\bm{V}}^{\top}=\sqrt{n}{\bm{U}}{\bm{V}}^{\top},

(6.21)

which means that
{\bm{X}}
behaves like a scaled orthogonal matrix. Geometrically, this implies that if we draw a fixed number of i.i.d. Gaussian vectors in increasingly high-dimensional ambient spaces, these vectors become nearly orthogonal with high probability as the dimension grows.

The following result provides a non-asymptotic probabilistic bound on the extreme singular values of such a matrix. The proof uses a covering number argument from
Vershynin 2010
, which is flexible enough to extend to other sub-Gaussian distributions and settings.

{theoremHigh}

[Singular values of a Gaussian matrix]
Let
{\mathbf{X}}\in\real^{n\times k}
be a random matrix with i.i.d. standard Gaussian entries, where
n>k
.
For any fixed
\varepsilon\in(0,1)
, the smallest and largest singular values of
{\mathbf{X}}
satisfy

\sqrt{n}(1-\varepsilon)\leq\sigma_{k}\leq\sigma_{1}\leq\sqrt{n}(1+\varepsilon)

(6.22)

with probability at least
1-2\left(\frac{12}{\varepsilon}\right)^{k}\exp\left(-\frac{n\varepsilon^{2}}{32}\right)
,
or
with probability at least
1-1/k
as long as

n>\frac{32}{\varepsilon^{2}}\ln\left(2k\left(\frac{12}{\varepsilon}\right)^{k}\right).

(6.23)

The theorem gives a concrete formula for how large
n
needs to be (relative to
k
and
\varepsilon
) to guarantee this behavior with probability at least
1-1/k
.
By the variational characterization of singular values (see (
)), the bounds in (
) are equivalent to

\sqrt{n}(1-\varepsilon)<\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}<\sqrt{n}(1+\varepsilon),\quad\text{for all }{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{U}}^{k-1},

(6.24)

where
{\mathbb{U}}^{k-1}\triangleq\{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{k}\mid\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}=1\}
is the
k
-dimensional sphere in
k
, which contains the unit
\ell_{2}
-norm vectors in
k
.
Since this set is uncountably infinite, a direct union bound—such as the one used in the proof of the JL lemma—is not applicable. Instead, we use a net-based argument.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Let
\varepsilon_{1}\triangleq\varepsilon/4
and
\varepsilon_{2}\triangleq\varepsilon/2
. Consider the
\varepsilon_{1}
-packing set
{\mathbb{P}}_{\varepsilon_{1}}
of
{\mathbb{U}}^{k-1}
as that is constructed below Corollary
.
For any fixed
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{U}}^{k-1}
, define the event

\mathcal{A}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}},\varepsilon_{2}}\triangleq\left\{n(1-\varepsilon_{2})\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq n(1+\varepsilon_{2})\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right\}.

By Corollary
, for any fixed
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{U}}^{k-1}
,
\Pr\left(\mathcal{A}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}},\varepsilon_{2}}^{c}\right)\leq 2\exp\left(-n\varepsilon^{2}/32\right)
.
Applying the union bound (Theorem
) over the finite set
{\mathbb{P}}_{\varepsilon_{1}}
gives

\displaystyle\Pr\left(\bigcup_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{P}}_{\varepsilon_{1}}}\mathcal{A}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}},\varepsilon_{2}}^{c}\right)

\displaystyle\leq\sum_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{P}}_{\varepsilon_{1}}}\Pr\left(\mathcal{A}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}},\varepsilon_{2}}^{c}\right)\leq\left\lvert{\mathbb{P}}_{\varepsilon_{1}}\right\rvert\cdot\Pr\left(\mathcal{A}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}},\varepsilon_{2}}^{c}\right)\leq 2\left(\frac{12}{\varepsilon}\right)^{k}\exp\left(-\frac{n\varepsilon^{2}}{32}\right)\leq\frac{1}{k},

where
\left\lvert{\mathbb{P}}_{\varepsilon_{1}}\right\rvert\leq\left({12}/{\varepsilon}\right)^{k}
by Corollary
, and the last inequality follows from condition (
).

Thus, with probability at least
1-1/k
, the event
\mathcal{A}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}},\varepsilon_{2}}
holds simultaneously for all
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{P}}_{\varepsilon_{1}}
.
To finish the proof, we need to show that if
\cup_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{P}}_{\varepsilon_{1}}}\mathcal{A}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}},\varepsilon_{2}}^{c}
holds, then the bound holds for every element in
{\mathbb{U}}^{k-1}
, not only for those in the packing set
{\mathbb{P}}_{\varepsilon_{1}}
.

For any arbitrary vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{U}}^{k-1}
on the sphere, there exists a vector in the
\varepsilon/4
-packing set
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{P}}_{\varepsilon_{1}}
such that
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\varepsilon_{1}=\varepsilon/4
.
Assuming the good event
(\cup_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{P}}_{\varepsilon_{1}}}\mathcal{A}_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},\varepsilon_{2}}^{c})^{c}
holds (which has probability at least
1-1/k
), by the triangle inequality and the definition of the spectral norm (Definition
), this implies

\displaystyle\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}

\displaystyle\leq\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}+\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\right\rVert_{2}\leq\sqrt{n}\left(1+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\right)+\sigma_{1}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\sqrt{n}\left(1+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\right)+\frac{\sigma_{1}\varepsilon}{4},

where the second inequality follows because we assume
\cup_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{P}}_{\varepsilon_{1}}}\mathcal{A}_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},\varepsilon_{2}}^{c}
holds.
The definition of the spectral norm also implies
\sigma_{1}
is the smallest upper bound on
\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}
for all
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
on the sphere
{\mathbb{U}}^{k-1}
, so the bound in the above inequality cannot be smaller:

\sigma_{1}\leq\sqrt{n}\left(1+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\right)+\frac{\sigma_{1}\varepsilon}{4}.

Rearranging yields

\sigma_{1}\leq\sqrt{n}\left(\frac{1+\varepsilon/2}{1-\varepsilon/4}\right)=\sqrt{n}\left(1+\varepsilon-\frac{\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)}{4-\varepsilon}\right)\leq\sqrt{n}(1+\varepsilon).

(6.25)

For the lower bound, again under the same good event,
(\cup_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{P}}_{\varepsilon_{1}}}\mathcal{A}_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},\varepsilon_{2}}^{c})^{c}
(which has probability at least
1-1/k
), the triangle inequality also implies

\displaystyle\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}

\displaystyle\geq\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}-\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\right\rVert_{2}\geq\sqrt{n}\left(1-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\right)-\sigma_{1}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}

\displaystyle\geq\sqrt{n}\left(1-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\right)-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}\sqrt{n}(1+\varepsilon)\geq\sqrt{n}(1-\varepsilon),

where the penultimate inequality follows form (
), and the last inequality follows since
\varepsilon<1
.
By the singular value property (
),
\sigma_{k}
is the largest lower bound on
\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}
for all
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
on the sphere
{\mathbb{U}}^{k-1}
, so
\sigma_{k}\geq\sqrt{n}(1-\varepsilon)
as long as
(\cup_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{P}}_{\varepsilon_{1}}}\mathcal{A}_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},\varepsilon_{2}}^{c})^{c}
holds.
This completes the proof.

6.6
Sparse Optimization with Gaussian Random Matrices

With these tools in hand, we can easily establish the recovery guarantee of Gaussian random matrices in compressed sensing problems.

A common strategy to prove that compressed sensing succeeds for a given class of signals is to construct a dual certificate (see Theorem
and its application in Theorem
using RIP to find the certificate) and verify that it is valid for every signal in that class. We illustrate this approach using Gaussian measurement matrices.

{theoremHigh}

[Exact recovery of (
) under standard Gaussian matrix
(
Baraniuk et al. 2008
)
]
Let
{\mathbf{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
be a random matrix with i.i.d. standard Gaussian entries, and let the measurements
{\bm{y}}={\mathbf{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\in\real^{n}
, where
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\in\real^{p}
is
k
-sparse (i.e., has at most
k
nonzero entries).
Then
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
is the unique solution to the
\ell_{1}
-minimization problem (
) (p.
) with probability at least
1-\frac{1}{p}
, provided that the number of measurements satisfies

n\geq Ck\ln p,

(6.26)

for some universal constant
C
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
The proof relies on the dual certificate condition for
\ell_{1}
-minimization (Theorem
).
According to that result, it suffices to show that for any support set
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
with
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert=k
and any possible sign pattern
{\bm{w}}\triangleq\mathrm{sign}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}_{\mathbb{S}})\in\real^{k}
of the nonzero entries of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
, there exists a valid dual certificate
{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n}
satisfying

{\mathbf{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}={\bm{w}}.

We construct the candidate certificate as the least squares solution (see (
)):

{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}_{\text{LS}}={\mathbf{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}({\mathbf{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{\mathbb{S}})^{-1}{\bm{w}}
.
To control
{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}_{\mathrm{LS}}
, we resort to the bound on the singular values of a fixed
n\times k
submatrix by Theorem
. Setting
\varepsilon\triangleq 0.5
,
we denote by
\mathcal{E}
the event that

\mathcal{E}\triangleq\{0.5\sqrt{n}\leq\sigma_{k}\leq\sigma_{1}\leq 1.5\sqrt{n}\},

where

\Pr(\mathcal{E})\geq 1-2\left(\frac{12}{\varepsilon}\right)^{k}\exp\left(-\frac{n\varepsilon^{2}}{32}\right)\approx 1-\exp\left(-C^{\prime}\frac{n}{k}\right)

for some absolute constant
C^{\prime}>0
.
Conditioned on
\mathcal{E}
, the submatrix
{\mathbf{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}
has full rank and
{\mathbf{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}
is invertible,
so
{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}_{\mathrm{LS}}
is well-conditioned and guarantees
{\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}_{\text{LS}}=\sign(\beta_{i}^{*})
for
i\in{\mathbb{S}}
.
To verify the second condition
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}_{\text{LS}}\right\rVert_{\infty}<1
(see Theorem
), consider any index
i\in{\mathbb{S}}^{c}
, and let
{\mathbf{x}}_{i}
denote the
i
-th column of
{\mathbf{X}}
.
We need to bound
\left\lvert{\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}_{\mathrm{LS}}\right\rvert
for all indices
i\in{\mathbb{S}}^{c}
.
Let
{\mathbf{U}}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}{\mathbf{V}}^{\top}
be the reduced SVD of
{\mathbf{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}
.
Conditioned on
\mathcal{E}
, we have

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}_{\mathrm{LS}}\right\rVert_{2}=\left\lVert{\mathbf{V}}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}{\mathbf{U}}^{\top}{\bm{w}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\frac{\left\lVert{\bm{w}}\right\rVert_{2}}{\sigma_{k}}\leq 2\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}.

(6.27)

For a fixed
i\in{\mathbb{S}}^{c}
and a fixed vector
{\bm{v}}\in\real^{n}
,
{\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{v}}/\left\lVert{\bm{v}}\right\rVert_{2}
is a standard Gaussian random variable by the definition of Gaussian random vectors and the linear transformation lemma (Lemma
or Lemma
), which, by Exercise
, implies

\displaystyle\Pr\left(\left\lvert{\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{v}}\right\rvert\geq 1\right)

\displaystyle=\Pr\left(\frac{\left\lvert{\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{v}}\right\rvert}{\left\lVert{\bm{v}}\right\rVert_{2}}\geq\frac{1}{\left\lVert{\bm{v}}\right\rVert_{2}}\right)\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{1}{\left\lVert{\bm{v}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}/2\right).

Note that if
i\notin{\mathbb{S}}
, then
{\mathbf{x}}_{i}
and
{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}_{\mathrm{LS}}
are independent (they depend on different and hence independent entries of
{\mathbf{X}}
). This means that due to (
),

\Pr\left(\left\lvert{\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}_{\mathrm{LS}}\right\rvert\geq 1\mid\mathcal{E}\right)=\Pr\left(\left\lvert{\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{v}}\right\rvert\geq 1\right)\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{n}{8k}\right),\quad\text{for $\left\lVert{\bm{v}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq 2\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}$},\;i\notin{\mathbb{S}}.

As a result,

\displaystyle\Pr\left(\left\lvert{\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}_{\mathrm{LS}}\right\rvert\geq 1\right)

\displaystyle\leq\Pr\left(\left\lvert{\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}_{\mathrm{LS}}\right\rvert\geq 1\mid\mathcal{E}\right)+\Pr(\mathcal{E}^{c})\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{n}{8k}\right)+\exp\left(-C^{\prime}\frac{n}{k}\right).

Applying the union bound over all
i\in{\mathbb{S}}^{c}
(at most
p
indices),

\Pr\left(\bigcup_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\left\{\left\lvert{\mathbf{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}_{\mathrm{LS}}\right\rvert\geq 1\right\}\right)\leq p\left(2\exp\left(-\frac{n}{8k}\right)+\exp\left(-C^{\prime}\frac{n}{k}\right)\right).

Choosing a constant
C
so that

n\geq Ck\ln p

ensures this probability is at most
\frac{1}{p}
.
Hence, with probability at least
1-1/p
, the dual certificate conditions hold for all
k
-sparse vectors, which implies exact recovery via
\ell_{1}
-minimization.

Rather than constructing a dual certificate, one can alternatively use the RIP to guarantee exact recovery. While verifying RIP for a deterministic matrix is computationally intractable—requiring checks over all
\binom{p}{k}
submatrices—it can be shown that random matrices satisfy RIP with high probability. The next two theorems establish this for i.i.d. Gaussian matrices.

{theoremHigh}

[RIP for Gaussian matrices]
Let
{\mathbf{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
have i.i.d. standard Gaussian entries.
For any
\eta,\varepsilon\in(0,1)
, suppose

n\geq 32\eta^{-2}\left(k\ln\left(\frac{ep}{k}\right)+k\ln\left(\frac{12}{\eta}\right)+\ln(2/\varepsilon)\right).

(6.28)

Then, with probability at least
1-\varepsilon
, the restricted isometry constant
\delta_{k}
of the scaled matrix
\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}{\mathbf{X}}
satisfies

\delta_{k}\leq\eta(2+\eta).

(6.29)

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Fix a support set
{\mathbb{S}}\subset\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
with
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert=k
.
The submatrix
{\mathbf{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}
is an
n\times k
Gaussian matrix.
The eigenvalues of
\frac{1}{{n}}{\mathbf{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}-{\bm{I}}
lie in
[\sigma_{\min}^{2}-1,\sigma_{\max}^{2}-1]
, where
\sigma_{\min}
and
\sigma_{\max}
are the smallest and largest singular values of
\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}{\mathbf{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}
.
Denote
\widetilde{{\mathbf{X}}}_{\mathbb{S}}\triangleq\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}{\mathbf{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}
.
For
\eta>0
, Theorem
implies that

\left\lVert\widetilde{{\mathbf{X}}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}\widetilde{{\mathbf{X}}}_{\mathbb{S}}-{\bm{I}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\max\left\{(1+\eta)^{2}-1,1-(1-\eta)^{2}\right\}=2\eta+\eta^{2},

with probability at least
1-2\left(\frac{12}{\eta}\right)^{k}\exp\left(-\frac{n\eta^{2}}{32}\right)
.
Taking the union bound over all
\binom{p}{k}
possible supports, by the definition of the restricted isometry constant (see Definition
),
\delta_{k}=\max_{{\mathbb{S}}\subset\{1,2,\ldots,p\},\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert=k}\left\lVert\widetilde{{\mathbf{X}}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}\widetilde{{\mathbf{X}}}_{\mathbb{S}}-{\bm{I}}\right\rVert_{2}
,
we obtain

\Pr\left(\delta_{k}>2\eta+\eta^{2}\right)\leq 2\binom{p}{k}\left(\frac{12}{\eta}\right)^{k}\exp\left(-\frac{n\eta^{2}}{32}\right)\leq 2\left(\frac{ep}{k}\right)^{k}\left(\frac{12}{\eta}\right)^{k}\exp\left(-\frac{n\eta^{2}}{32}\right),

where the second inequality follows from the bound on the binomial coefficient (see Problem
). The last term is dominated by
\varepsilon
due to condition (
).
This completes the proof.

Since
\delta_{k}\leq 2\eta+\eta^{2}
, choosing
\eta=0.22
yields
\delta_{k}\leq 0.4884<0.4931
(compare Theorem
concerning
\ell_{1}
-minimization) under the condition
n\geq 662\big(k\ln(ep/k)+k\ln(12/\eta)+\ln(2/\varepsilon)\big)
in this asymptotic regime.

Foucart and Rauhut 2013
improves this bound to
n\geq 78.13\left(k\ln(ep/k)+\ln(2/\varepsilon)\right)
by improving the bound in Theorem
; we omit the details here.

{theoremHigh}

[Exact recovery of (

Let
{\mathbf{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}

Suppose

and

If

for universal constants

Then with probability at least

).

Proof
[of Theorem
]
This follows by combining Theorem
(which establishes RIP for Gaussian matrices) with Theorem

Once the RIP is established, recovery via

Additionally, these results are not limited to Gaussian matrices. They also hold for any random matrix ensemble satisfying the concentration inequality (

Chapter 7
Design of Sensing Matrices Using Sub-Gaussian Ensembles

W
While Gaussian random matrices offer strong theoretical guarantees for compressed sensing and sparse recovery, their practical use is often limited by computational and implementation constraints. In this chapter, we extend the analysis to sub-Gaussian ensembles—random matrices whose entries satisfy sub-Gaussian tail bounds—and demonstrate that many desirable properties of Gaussian matrices, such as the restricted isometry property and stable sparse recovery, continue to hold under much broader and more flexible distributions.

7.1
Sub-Gaussian (SG) Random Variables

Several common distributions, notably the Gaussian and Rademacher, are known to satisfy certain concentration-of-measure inequalities.
We analyze this phenomenon from a more general perspective by considering the class of sub-Gaussian distributions
(
Buldygin and Kozachenko 2000
;
Vershynin 2010
)
.

We begin by presenting the general definition of sub-Gaussian random variables and then specialize to the zero-mean case in the following section.

Definition 201
(Sub-Gaussian random variables using concentration inequality).

A random variable
x
is called sub-Gaussian if there exist constants
\Phi,\xi>0
such that

\Pr(\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert\geq\tau)\leq\Phi e^{-\xi\tau^{2}},\quad\text{for all }\tau>0.

(7.1)

It is called sub-exponential if

\Pr(\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert\geq\tau)\leq\Phi e^{-\xi\tau},\quad\text{for all }\tau>0.

(7.2)

Clearly, a random variable
x
is sub-Gaussian if and only if
{\textnormal{x}}^{2}
is sub-exponential.

By Exercise
or Lemma
, a standard Gaussian random variable
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)
is sub-Gaussian with
\Phi=1
and
\xi=1/2
.
Moreover, Rademacher (i.e., symmetric Bernoulli) and bounded random variables are also sub-Gaussian.
According to Theorem
and Corollary
, sums of independent Rademacher variables are sub-Gaussian as well.

Lemmas
and
are converse to one another and establish a fundamental relationship between the tail probabilities and moments of a random variable—a connection essential for understanding the behavior of sub-Gaussian random variables. These lemmas build on the foundational notion of sub-Gaussianity by providing conditions under which concentration around the mean can be tightly controlled, thereby offering deeper insight into the probabilistic structure of such variables.

Lemma 202
(Basic concentration lemma).

Let
x
be a random variable satisfying

\left\lVert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rVert_{s}\triangleq\big(\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert^{s}]\big)^{\frac{1}{s}}\leq\alpha\Phi^{\frac{1}{s}}s^{\frac{1}{\nu}},\quad\text{for all }s_{0}\leq s\leq s_{1}

for some constants
\alpha,\Phi,\nu>0
and
s_{1}>s_{0}>0
. Then

\Pr(\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert\geq e^{\frac{1}{\nu}}\alpha\mu)\leq\Phi e^{-\frac{\mu^{\nu}}{\nu}},\quad\text{for all $\mu\in[s_{0}^{1/\nu},s_{1}^{1/\nu}]$}.

(7.3)

Proof
[of Lemma
]
By Markov’s inequality (Theorem
), for any
\kappa>0
, we have

\Pr(\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert\geq e^{\kappa}\alpha\mu)\leq\frac{\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert^{s}]}{(e^{\kappa}\alpha\mu)^{s}}\leq\Phi\left(\frac{\alpha s^{\frac{1}{\nu}}}{e^{\kappa}\alpha\mu}\right)^{s}.

Choosing
s=\mu^{\nu}
gives

\Pr(\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert\geq e^{\kappa}\alpha\mu)\leq\Phi e^{-\kappa\mu^{\nu}}
, and setting
\kappa=\frac{1}{\nu}
yields the claim.

Important special cases of Lemma
arise when
\nu=1
and
\nu=2
.
Indeed,
if
(\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert^{s}])^{\frac{1}{s}}\leq\alpha\Phi^{\frac{1}{s}}s
for all
s\geq 2
then

\Pr(\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert\geq e\alpha\mu)\leq\Phi e^{-\mu},\quad\text{for all }\mu\geq 2.

(7.4)

Similarly, if
(\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert^{s}])^{\frac{1}{s}}\leq\alpha\Phi^{\frac{1}{s}}\sqrt{s}
for all
s\geq 2
, then

\Pr(\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert\geq e^{1/2}\alpha\mu)\leq\Phi e^{-\mu^{2}/2},\quad\text{for all }\mu\geq\sqrt{2}.

(7.5)

The converse of Lemma
also holds.

Lemma 203
(Basic moment bound lemma).

Suppose a random variable
x
satisfies, for some
\nu>0
,

\Pr(\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert\geq e^{\frac{1}{\nu}}\alpha\mu)\leq\Phi e^{-\frac{\mu^{\nu}}{\nu}},\quad\text{for all }\mu>0.

Then, for all
s>0
,

\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert^{s}]\leq\Phi\alpha^{s}(e\nu)^{\frac{s}{\nu}}\Gamma\left(\frac{s}{\nu}+1\right),

(7.6a)

where
\Gamma(x)=\int_{0}^{\infty}t^{x-1}\exp(-t)dt
is the Gamma function.
As a consequence, for
s\geq 1
,

\big(\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert^{s}]\big)^{\frac{1}{s}}\leq T_{1}\alpha(T_{2,\nu}\Phi)^{\frac{1}{s}}s^{\frac{1}{\nu}},

(7.6b)

where
T_{1}=e^{1/(2e)}\approx 1.2019
and
T_{2,\nu}=\sqrt{\frac{2\pi}{\nu}}e^{\frac{\nu}{12}}
.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Using the absolute moments lemma (Lemma
) and two changes of variables (i.e.,
\tau\triangleq e^{\frac{1}{\nu}}\alpha\mu
and
x=\frac{\mu^{\nu}}{\nu}
), we obtain

\displaystyle\footnotesize\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert^{s}]

\displaystyle=s\int_{0}^{\infty}\Pr(\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert>\tau)\tau^{s-1}d\tau\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\tau\triangleq e^{\frac{1}{\nu}}\alpha\mu}}{{\mathrel{\rule[2.15277pt]{20.00003pt}{0.5pt}\hskip-20.00003pt\rule[-2.15277pt]{20.00003pt}{0.5pt}}}}s\alpha^{s}e^{\frac{s}{\nu}}\int_{0}^{\infty}\Pr(\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert\geq e^{\frac{1}{\nu}}\alpha\mu)\mu^{s-1}d\mu

\displaystyle\leq s\alpha^{s}e^{\frac{s}{\nu}}\int_{0}^{\infty}\Phi e^{-\frac{\mu^{\nu}}{\nu}}\mu^{s-1}d\mu\stackrel{{\scriptstyle x=\frac{\mu^{\nu}}{\nu}}}{{\mathrel{\rule[2.15277pt]{20.00003pt}{0.5pt}\hskip-20.00003pt\rule[-2.15277pt]{20.00003pt}{0.5pt}}}}s\Phi\alpha^{s}e^{\frac{s}{\nu}}\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-x}(x)^{\frac{s}{\nu}-1}(\nu)^{\frac{s}{\nu}-1}dx

\displaystyle=\Phi\alpha^{s}(e\nu)^{\frac{s}{\nu}}\frac{s}{\nu}\Gamma\left(\frac{s}{\nu}\right),

where the inequality follows from the assumption.
and the last equality follows from the definition of Gamma function (see (
)):

\Gamma(x)=\int_{0}^{\infty}t^{x-1}e^{-t}dt
for
x\geq 0
.
This proves (
) by the property of the Gamma function.
Applying Stirling’s formula—
\Gamma(x)=\sqrt{2\pi}x^{x-1/2}e^{-x}\exp\left(\frac{\theta(x)}{12x}\right)
for positive
x
and a correction term
0\leq\theta(x)\leq 1
—yields

\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert^{s}]\leq\Phi\alpha^{s}(e\nu)^{\frac{s}{\nu}}\sqrt{2\pi}\left(\frac{s}{\nu}\right)^{\frac{s}{\nu}+\frac{1}{2}}e^{-\frac{s}{\nu}}e^{\frac{\nu}{12s}}=\sqrt{2\pi}\Phi\alpha^{s}e^{\frac{\nu}{12s}}\left(s\right)^{\frac{s}{\nu}+\frac{1}{2}}\nu^{-\frac{1}{2}}.

For
s\geq 1
, taking the
s
-th root gives

\big(\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert^{s}]\big)^{\frac{1}{s}}\leq\left(\frac{\sqrt{2\pi}}{\sqrt{\nu}}e^{\frac{\nu}{12}}\Phi\right)^{\frac{1}{s}}\alpha s^{\frac{1}{2s}}s^{\frac{1}{\nu}}.

Finally, the function
s^{{1}/{2s}}=\sqrt{s^{{1}/{s}}}
attains its maximum at
s=e
(see Problem
), so
s^{{1}/{2s}}\leq e^{{1}/{2e}}
. This completes the proof.

Remark 204
(Standard consequences for sub-Gaussian and sub-exponential variables).

Setting
\alpha\triangleq(2e\xi)^{-1/2}
and
\nu\triangleq 2
, and applying Lemma
with the change of variable
\tau=(2\xi)^{-1/2}\mu
, we find that the moments of a sub-Gaussian variable
x
satisfy

\big(\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert^{s}]\big)^{1/s}\leq\widetilde{T}\xi^{-1/2}\Phi^{1/s}s^{1/2},\quad\forall\,s\geq 1,\text{ with $\widetilde{T}\triangleq T_{1}T_{2,2}/\sqrt{2e}\approx 1.0794$. }

(7.7)

Similarly, setting
\alpha\triangleq(e\xi)^{-1}
and
\nu\triangleq 1
, and using the change of variable
\tau=\xi^{-1}\mu
,
the moments of a sub-exponential variable
x
satisfy

\big(\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert^{s}]\big)^{1/s}\leq\widehat{T}\xi^{-1}\Phi^{1/s}s,\quad\forall\,s\geq 1,\text{ with $\widehat{T}\triangleq T_{1}T_{2,1}/e\approx 1.2047$. }

(7.8)

We now present an equivalent characterization of sub-Gaussian random variables.

{theoremHigh}
[Equivalent statement of sub-Gaussian]
Let
x
be a random variable.

1.

If
x
is sub-Gaussian, then there exist constants
c_{1}>0
and
c_{2}>1
such that
\mathbb{E}[\exp(c_{1}{\textnormal{x}}^{2})]\leq c_{2}
.

2.

Conversely, if
\mathbb{E}[\exp(c_{1}{\textnormal{x}}^{2})]\leq c_{2}
for some constants
c_{1},c_{2}>0
, then
x
is sub-Gaussian. More precisely, we have
\Pr(\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert\geq\tau)\leq c_{2}\exp(-c_{1}\tau^{2})
for all
\tau>0
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]

(i).

Using the well-known Taylor expansion
\exp(z)=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^{i}}{i!}
for all
z\in\real
around 0, we have

\mathbb{E}[\exp(c_{1}{\textnormal{x}}^{2})]=1+\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\frac{c_{1}^{i}\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}^{2i}]}{i!}

Applying the moment bound (
) and Stirling’s inequality—
i!\geq\sqrt{2\pi i}(i/e)^{i}\geq\sqrt{2\pi}(i/e)^{i}
for
i\geq 1
—we obtain

\mathbb{E}[\exp(c_{1}{\textnormal{x}}^{2})]=1+\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\frac{c_{1}^{i}\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}^{2i}]}{i!}\leq 1+\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\frac{c_{1}^{i}\widetilde{T}^{2i}\xi^{-i}\Phi(2i)^{i}}{\sqrt{2\pi}(i/e)^{i}}=1+\frac{\Phi}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\left(\frac{c_{1}\widetilde{T}^{2}(2e)}{\xi}\right)^{i}.

If
\big({c_{1}\widetilde{T}^{2}(2e)}/{\xi}\big)<1
, the series converges, and we may define
c_{2}

accordingly:
c_{2}\triangleq 1+\frac{\Phi}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\big({c_{1}\widetilde{T}^{2}(2e)}/{\xi}\big)^{i}
.

(ii).

By Markov’s inequality (Theorem
),

\Pr(\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert\geq\tau)=\Pr\big(\exp(c_{1}{\textnormal{x}}^{2})\geq\exp(c_{1}\tau^{2})\big)\leq\mathbb{E}[\exp(c_{1}{\textnormal{x}}^{2})]e^{-c_{1}\tau^{2}}\leq c_{2}e^{-c_{1}\tau^{2}}.

This completes the proof.

We now consider the moment generating function of a zero-mean sub-Gaussian random variable.

{theoremHigh}

[Standard characterization of zero-mean sub-Gaussian variables]
Let
x
be a random variable.

1.

If
x
is sub-Gaussian with
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]=0
, then there exists a constant
C>0
or a constant
c>0
(depending only on
\Phi
and
\xi
) such that

\mathbb{E}[\exp(\theta{\textnormal{x}})]\leq\exp(\theta^{2}\cdot C)=\exp(\theta^{2}\cdot c^{2}/2),\quad\text{for all }\theta\in\real,

(7.9)

where
C=c^{2}/2
.

2.

Conversely, if (
) holds for some
C>0
,
then
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]=0
and
x
is sub-Gaussian with parameters
\Phi=2
and
\xi=\frac{1}{4C}
in Definition
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]

(i).

It suffices to consider
\theta\geq 0
, since the case
\theta<0
follows by replacing
x
with
-{\textnormal{x}}
, which preserves sub-Gaussianity and zero mean.
Using the well-known Taylor expansion
\exp(z)=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^{i}}{i!}
for all
z\in\real
around 0, we obtain

\mathbb{E}[\exp(\theta{\textnormal{x}})]=1+\theta\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]+\sum_{i=2}^{\infty}\frac{\theta^{i}\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}^{i}]}{i!}=1+\sum_{i=2}^{\infty}\frac{\theta^{i}\mathbb{E}[\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert^{i}]}{i!},

where we used
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]=0
.
First, suppose
0\leq\theta\leq\theta_{0}
, where
\theta_{0}>0
will be chosen later.
Applying the moment bound (
) and Stirling’s formula—
i!\geq\sqrt{2\pi i}(i/e)^{i}
for
i\geq 1
—we get

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\exp(\theta{\textnormal{x}})]

\displaystyle\leq 1+\Phi\sum_{i=2}^{\infty}\frac{\theta^{i}\widetilde{T}^{i}i^{i/2}\xi^{-i/2}}{i!}\leq 1+\Phi\sum_{i=2}^{\infty}\frac{\theta^{i}\widetilde{T}^{i}i^{i/2}\xi^{-i/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi i}(i/e)^{i}}

\displaystyle\leq 1+\frac{\Phi(\widetilde{T}e\theta)^{2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}\xi}\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\left(\widetilde{T}e\theta_{0}\xi^{-1/2}\right)^{i}\leq 1+\theta^{2}\frac{\Phi(\widetilde{T}e)^{2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}\xi}\frac{1}{1-\widetilde{T}e\theta_{0}\xi^{-1/2}}

\displaystyle=1+C_{1}\theta^{2}\leq\exp(C_{1}\theta^{2}),

where the third inequality holds since
i^{-(i+1)/2}<1
for
i\geq 2
, and the penultimate inequality holds when
\widetilde{T}e\theta_{0}\xi^{-1/2}<1
(using the inequality
\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}a^{i}\leq\frac{a}{1-a}
for
0\leq a<1
).
The last inequality is satisfied by setting

\theta_{0}\triangleq(2\widetilde{T}e)^{-1}\sqrt{\xi},

which gives the constant
C_{1}=\sqrt{2}\Phi(\widetilde{T}e)^{2}\xi^{-1}/\sqrt{\pi}
.

Now consider
\theta>\theta_{0}
. We aim to show
\mathbb{E}[\exp(\theta{\textnormal{x}}-C_{2}\theta^{2})]\leq 1
for a suitable
C_{2}>0
.
Observe that

\theta{\textnormal{x}}-C_{2}\theta^{2}=-(\sqrt{C_{2}}\theta-\frac{{\textnormal{x}}}{2\sqrt{C_{2}}})^{2}+\frac{{\textnormal{x}}^{2}}{4C_{2}}\leq\frac{{\textnormal{x}}^{2}}{4C_{2}}.

Invoking Theorem
(i) with
\widetilde{c}_{1}>0
and
\widetilde{c}_{2}\geq 1
, and choosing
C_{2}=1/(4\widetilde{c}_{1})
,
we have

\mathbb{E}[\exp(\theta{\textnormal{x}}-C_{2}\theta^{2})]\leq\mathbb{E}[\exp(\widetilde{c}_{1}{\textnormal{x}}^{2})]\leq\widetilde{c}_{2}.

Define
\nu\triangleq\ln(\widetilde{c}_{2})\theta_{0}^{-2}
.
The above inequality and the condition
\theta>\theta_{0}
show that
