\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\exp(\theta{\textnormal{x}})]

\displaystyle\leq\widetilde{c}_{2}\exp(C_{2}\theta^{2})=\widetilde{c}_{2}\exp(-\nu\theta^{2})\exp((C_{2}+\nu)\theta^{2})

\displaystyle\leq\widetilde{c}_{2}\exp(-\nu\theta_{0}^{2})\exp((C_{2}+\nu)\theta^{2})\leq\exp((C_{2}+\nu)\theta^{2}).

Setting
C\triangleq\max\{C_{1},C_{2}+\nu\}
completes the proof of part (i).

(ii).

Conversely, suppose (
) holds for some
C>0
.
Let
\theta,\tau>0
.
By Markov’s inequality,

\Pr({\textnormal{x}}\geq\tau)=\Pr(\exp(\theta{\textnormal{x}})\geq\exp(\theta\tau))\leq\frac{\mathbb{E}[\exp(\theta{\textnormal{x}})]}{\exp(\theta\tau)}\leq\exp(C\theta^{2}-\theta\tau).

Optimizing over
\theta
gives the minimum at
\theta=\tau/(2C)
, yielding

\Pr({\textnormal{x}}\geq\tau)\leq\exp(-\tau^{2}/(4C)).

Applying the same argument to
-{\textnormal{x}}
gives

\Pr(-{\textnormal{x}}\geq\tau)\leq\exp(-\tau^{2}/(4C))
.
By the union bound,

\Pr(\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert\geq\tau)\leq 2\exp(-\tau^{2}/(4C)),

which shows that
x
is sub-Gaussian with
\Phi=2
and
\xi=1/(4C)
, as claimed.
To verify that
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]=0
, note that for any real
\theta
,
1+\theta{\textnormal{x}}\leq\exp(\theta{\textnormal{x}})
.
Taking expectations and using (
), we obtain for
\left\lvert\theta\right\rvert<1
,

1+\theta\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]\leq\mathbb{E}[\exp(\theta{\textnormal{x}})]\leq\exp(C\theta^{2})\leq 1+(C/2)\theta^{2}+\mathcal{O}(\theta^{4}).

Letting
\theta\to 0
forces
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]=0
, completing the proof.

7.2
Strictly Sub-Gaussian (SSG) Random Variables

As previously mentioned, when a sub-Gaussian random variable has zero mean, its moment generating function (MGF; see Definition
) satisfies a specific bound (see Theorem
).
Moreover, key results concerning concentration inequalities and design properties—such as the restricted isometry property (RIP) for sub-Gaussian random matrices in Theorem
—assume that the underlying random variables are zero-mean sub-Gaussian.
We therefore adopt the MGF-based characterization to define this important subclass of sub-Gaussian random variables and explore how it enables fine-grained control over the behavior of design matrices.

Definition 205
((Zero-mean) sub-Gaussian random variables).

A random variable
x
is called (zero-mean) sub-Gaussian (SG), denoted
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{SG}(c^{2})
, if there exists a constant
c>0
such that

\mathbb{E}[\exp(\theta{\textnormal{x}})]\leq\exp(\theta^{2}c^{2}/2),\quad\forall\,\theta\in\real.

(7.10)

The quantity
c^{2}
is referred to as the variance proxy of the sub-Gaussian distribution.

This definition means that a random variable
x
to is (zero-mean) sub-Gaussian if its Laplace transform (i.e., its MGF) is pointwise dominated by the MGF of a zero-mean Gaussian random variable with variance
c^{2}
.
Indeed, the function
\mathbb{E}[\exp(\theta{\textnormal{x}})]
is the MGF of
x
, while the right-hand side of (
) is precisely the MGF of a Gaussian random variable
\mathcal{N}(0,c^{2})
.
.
Consequently, a (zero-mean) sub-Gaussian distribution is one whose tails decay at least as rapidly as those of a Gaussian distribution with variance
c^{2}
(see also Theorem
for more insights).

Examples of such (zero-mean) sub-Gaussian distributions include the Gaussian distribution itself, the Rademacher distribution (symmetric Bernoulli variable) taking values
\pm 1
, and more generally, any zero-mean distribution with bounded support.

Example 206
(Gaussian SG).

If
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2})
, i.e.,
x
is a zero-mean Gaussian random variable with variance
\sigma^{2}
, then
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{SG}(\sigma^{2})
. Indeed, as mentioned above, the MGF of a Gaussian is given by
\mathbb{E}[\exp(\theta{\textnormal{x}})]=\exp(\theta^{2}\sigma^{2}/2)
, and thus (
) is trivially satisfied.

Example 207
(Bounded SG and Rademacher).

Let
x
be a zero-mean random variable satisfying
\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert\leq B
almost surely for some
B>0
.
Then
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{SG}(B^{2})
.
In particular, a Rademacher random variable (i.e.,
\Pr({\textnormal{x}}=\pm 1)=1/2
) satisfies
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{SG}(1)

A common way to characterize (zero-mean) sub-Gaussian random variables is through their moments. The following theorem, due to Buldygin and Kozachenko
(
Buldygin and Kozachenko 2000
)
, relates the first two moments to the variance proxy.

{theoremHigh}

[Buldygin–Kozachenko
(
Buldygin and Kozachenko 2000
)
]
If
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{SG}(c^{2})
, then,

\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]=0\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}^{2}]\leq c^{2}.

(7.11)

In other words, the variance of
x
does not exceed its variance proxy
c^{2}
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Using the Taylor expansion
\exp(z)=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^{i}}{i!}
for the exponential function, for any
\theta\in\real
,

\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{\theta^{k}}{k!}\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}^{k}]=\mathbb{E}[\exp(\theta{\textnormal{x}})]\leq\exp(c^{2}\theta^{2}/2)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{c^{2k}\theta^{2k}}{2^{k}k!}.

Comparing terms up to second order as
\theta\rightarrow 0
, we obtain

\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]\theta+\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}^{2}]\frac{\theta^{2}}{2!}\leq\frac{c^{2}\theta^{2}}{2}+o(\theta^{2})\quad\text{as }\theta\to 0.

Dividing both sides by
\theta>0
and letting
\theta\to 0^{+}
yields
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]\leq 0
. Dividing through by
\theta<0
and letting
\theta\to 0^{-}
gives
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]\geq 0
.
Hence,
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}]=0
. (This was also shown in Theorem
(ii).)
With the mean established as zero, divide the inequality by
\theta^{2}
and let
\theta\to 0
.
This gives
\mathbb{V}\mathrm{ar}[{\textnormal{x}}]\leq c^{2}
.

Theorem
shows that if
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{SG}(c^{2})
, then
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}^{2}]\leq c^{2}
.
In certain applications, it is useful to consider a more restrictive class of random variables for which this inequality becomes an equality.

Definition 208
(Strictly sub-Gaussian random variables).

A random variable
x
is called strictly sub-Gaussian (SSG) if it satisfies
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{SG}(\sigma^{2})
with
\sigma^{2}=\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}^{2}]
, denoted
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{SSG}(\sigma^{2})
, i.e.,

\mathbb{E}[\exp(\theta{\textnormal{x}})]\leq\exp(\theta^{2}\sigma^{2}/2),\text{ with }\sigma^{2}=\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}^{2}],\quad\forall\,\theta\in\real.

(7.12)

Example 209
(Strictly sub-Gaussian random variables).

The following are examples of SSG random variables:

If
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2})
, then
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{SSG}(\sigma^{2})
.

If
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\text{Uniform}(-1,1)
, then
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}^{2}]=1/3
, and one can verify that
\mathbb{E}[\exp(\theta{\textnormal{x}})]\leq\exp(\theta^{2}/6)
for all
\theta\in\real
. Hence,
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{SSG}(1/3)
.

Consider the symmetric three-point distribution defined by

\Pr({\textnormal{x}}=1)=\Pr({\textnormal{x}}=-1)=\frac{1-s}{2},\quad\Pr({\textnormal{x}}=0)=s,\quad s\in[0,1).

(7.13)

Its variance is
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}^{2}]=1-s
. This random variable is strictly sub-Gaussian if and only if
s\in[0,2/3]
. For
s\in(2/3,1)
, the tail behavior violates the strict sub-Gaussian condition, so
x
is not SSG.

Buldygin and Kozachenko 2000
provide an equivalent characterization of sub-Gaussian and strictly sub-Gaussian random variables in terms of their tail decay, which directly reflects their concentration-of-measure properties.

{theoremHigh}
[Buldygin–Kozachenko
(
Buldygin and Kozachenko 2000
)
]
A random variable
x
is sub-Gaussian with variance proxy
c^{2}
, i.e.,
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{SG}(c^{2})
, if and only if there exist constants
\tau_{0}\geq 0
and
a\geq 0
such that

\Pr(\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert\geq\tau)\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{\tau^{2}}{2a^{2}}\right),\quad\text{for all $\tau\geq\tau_{0}$}.

(7.14)

Moreover, if
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{SSG}(\sigma^{2})
, then the above inequality holds for all
\tau>0
with
a=\sigma
.

The proof follows directly from Theorem
(ii).
This matches the bound obtained by applying the Chernoff method directly to Gaussian variables (see Exercise
).
In fact, for a Gaussian random variable
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2})
, Lemma
provides a slightly tighter tail bound:

\Pr(\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}\right\rvert\geq\tau)\leq\exp\left(-\frac{\tau^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right),\quad\text{for all $\tau\geq 0$}.

(7.15)

Finally, sub-Gaussian distributions share a key stability property with Gaussian distributions: the sum of independent sub-Gaussian random variables is itself sub-Gaussian.
This closure property is formalized in the following more general result.

Proposition 210
.

Suppose that
{\mathbf{x}}=[{\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{p}]
, where each
{\textnormal{x}}_{i}
is i.i.d. with
{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\sim\mathcal{SG}(c^{2})
.
Then,

\left\langle{\mathbf{x}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rangle\sim\mathcal{SG}(c^{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}),\quad\text{for any ${\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}$}.

(7.16)

Similarly, if each
{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\sim\mathcal{SSG}(\sigma^{2})
, then

\left\langle{\mathbf{x}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rangle\sim\mathcal{SSG}(\sigma^{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}),\quad\text{for any ${\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}$}.

(7.17)

Moreover, it follows that

\Pr\left(\left\lvert\left\langle{\mathbf{x}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rangle\right\rvert\geq\tau\right)\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{\tau^{2}}{4C\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}\right),\quad\text{for all }\tau>0.

where
C={c^{2}}/{2}
in the SG and
C={\sigma^{2}}/{2}
in the SSG case.

Proof
[of Proposition
]
Since the variables
{\textnormal{x}}_{i}
are i.i.d., the joint distribution factors and simplifies as:

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\exp\left(\theta\sum_{i=1}^{p}\alpha_{i}{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\right)\right]

\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\prod_{i=1}^{p}\exp(\theta\alpha_{i}{\textnormal{x}}_{i})\right]=\prod_{i=1}^{p}\mathbb{E}\left[\exp(\theta\alpha_{i}{\textnormal{x}}_{i})\right]

\displaystyle\leq\prod_{i=1}^{p}\exp(\theta^{2}\alpha_{i}^{2}\cdot c^{2}/2)=\exp\left(\left(\sum_{i=1}^{p}\alpha_{i}^{2}\right)\theta^{2}c^{2}/2\right).

Thus,
\left\langle{\mathbf{x}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rangle
is sub-Gaussian with variance proxy
c^{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
.
If the variables
{\textnormal{x}}_{i}
are strictly sub-Gaussian, the same argument applies with
c^{2}=\sigma^{2}
, and one can verify that
\mathbb{E}[\left\langle{\mathbf{x}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rangle^{2}]=\sigma^{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
, confirming strict sub-Gaussianity.
This proves the first part.
The tail bound then follows directly from Theorem
(ii).

As a concrete example, let
{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}=[\epsilon_{1},\ldots,\epsilon_{p}]^{\top}
be a Rademacher sequence, and
{\textnormal{y}}=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\alpha_{i}\epsilon_{i}
.
Then

\mathbb{E}[\exp(\theta{\textnormal{y}})]\leq\exp(\theta^{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}/2),

confirming that
y
is sub-Gaussian with variance proxy
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
.

The expected maximum of a finite collection of (possibly dependent) zero-mean sub-Gaussian random variables can be bounded as follows.

Proposition 211
(Maximum of zero-mean sub-Gaussian variables).

Let
{\mathbf{x}}=[{\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{p}]
, where each
{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\sim\mathcal{SG}(c_{i}^{2})
(not necessarily independent)
satisfies
\mathbb{E}[\exp(\theta{\textnormal{x}}_{i})]\leq\exp(c_{i}^{2}\theta^{2}/2)
,
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
.
Define
C\triangleq\max_{i}c_{i}^{2}/2
.
Then

\mathbb{E}[\max_{i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}}{\textnormal{x}}_{i}]\leq\sqrt{4C\ln(p)},\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathbb{E}[\max_{i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}}\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\right\rvert]\leq\sqrt{4C\ln(2p)}.

(7.18)

And for any
\tau>0
, it holds that

\Pr\left(\max_{i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}}{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\right)\leq p\exp(-\frac{\tau^{2}}{4C})\quad\text{and}\quad\Pr\left(\max_{i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}}\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\right\rvert\right)\leq 2p\exp(-\frac{\tau^{2}}{4C}).

(7.19)

Proof
[of Proposition
]
The case
p=1
is trivial; assume
p\geq 2
.
Let
\Theta>0
be a parameter to be chosen later. Using the monotonicity of the exponential and Jensen’s inequality,

\displaystyle\Theta\mathbb{E}[\max_{i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}}{\textnormal{x}}_{i}]

\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\ln\max_{i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}}\exp(\Theta{\textnormal{x}}_{i})]\leq\mathbb{E}\left[\ln\left(\sum_{i=1}^{p}\exp(\Theta{\textnormal{x}}_{i})\right)\right]

\displaystyle\leq\ln\left(\sum_{i=1}^{p}\mathbb{E}[\exp(\Theta{\textnormal{x}}_{i})]\right)\leq\ln(p\exp(C\Theta^{2}))=C\Theta^{2}+\ln(p).

Choosing
\Theta\triangleq\sqrt{C^{-1}\ln(p)}
yields

\sqrt{C^{-1}\ln(p)}\mathbb{E}[\max_{i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}}{\textnormal{x}}_{i}]\leq\ln(p)+\ln(p),

which implies
\mathbb{E}[\max_{i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}}{\textnormal{x}}_{i}]\leq\sqrt{4C\ln(p)}
.

For the absolute maximum, we can rewrite the expectation by
\mathbb{E}[\max_{i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}}\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\right\rvert]=\mathbb{E}[\max\{{\textnormal{x}}_{1},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{p},-{\textnormal{x}}_{1},\ldots,-{\textnormal{x}}_{p}\}]
.
Applying the previous bound to this set of
2p
variables gives the second expectation inequality.

The tail bounds follow from the union bound together with the sub-Gaussian tail inequality

The bounds in this proposition are nearly sharp: for a sequence of independent standard Gaussian random variables, the expected maximum scales as
\sqrt{2\ln(p)}
, matching the above up to constant factors (see Theorem
(iii)).

7.3
Isotropic Sub-Gaussian Random Vectors

Sub-Gaussian distributions are closely connected to the concentration of measure phenomenon
(
Ledoux 2001
)
. For instance, combining Theorem
and Proposition
yields deviation bounds for weighted sums of sub-Gaussian random variables.

More broadly, sub-Gaussian random matrices belong to a larger class of random matrices that exhibit strong concentration properties—specifically, they approximately preserve the Euclidean norm of vectors under linear transformation. This property is central to applications such as compressed sensing and high-dimensional statistics.

We begin by introducing key definitions.

Definition 212
(Isotropic and sub-Gaussian random vectors).

Let
{\mathbf{x}}
be a random vector in
p
.

1.

If
\mathbb{E}[\left\langle{\mathbf{x}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle^{2}]=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
for all
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
, then
{\mathbf{x}}
is called isotropic.

2.

If, for every unit vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
(i.e.,
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}=1
), the scalar random variable
\left\langle{\mathbf{x}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle
is sub-Gaussian with sub-Gaussian parameter
C\equiv c^{2}/2
(see its Definition in Theorem
or Definition
) being independent of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
(and ideally independent of
p
); that is,

\mathbb{E}[\exp(\theta\left\langle{\mathbf{x}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle)]\leq\exp(\theta^{2}\cdot C),\quad\text{for all }\theta\in\real,\quad\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}=1,

(7.20)

then
{\mathbf{x}}
is called a sub-Gaussian random vector.

Note that isotropic sub-Gaussian random vectors need not have independent entries.

The following proposition shows that a random vector with independent, mean-zero, unit-variance sub-Gaussian entries is both isotropic and sub-Gaussian; see Problem
for further discussions.

Proposition 213
(Isotropic and sub-Gaussian random vector).

Let
{\mathbf{x}}\in\real^{p}
be a random vector whose entries are independent, mean-zero, sub-Gaussian random variables with variance
1
nd a common sub-Gaussian parameter
C\equiv c^{2}/2
as in (
).
5Then
{\mathbf{x}}
is an isotropic and sub-Gaussian random vector, with constants independent of the dimension
p
.

Proof
[of Proposition
]
Let
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
with
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}=1
.
Since the the entries
{\textnormal{x}}_{i}
of
{\mathbf{x}}
are independent, zero-mean, and have unit variance,

\mathbb{E}[\left\langle{\mathbf{x}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle^{2}]=\sum_{i,j=1}^{p}\beta_{i}\beta_{j}\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{i}{\textnormal{x}}_{j}]=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\beta_{i}^{2}=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

Therefore,
{\mathbf{x}}
is isotropic. Furthermore, according to Proposition
and Theorem
, the random variable
{\textnormal{y}}=\left\langle{\mathbf{x}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle
is sub-Gaussian
\mathcal{SG}(c^{2}/2)
(or with parameters
\Phi=2
and
\xi=1/(4C\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2})=1/(4C)
). Hence,
{\mathbf{x}}
is a sub-Gaussian random vector with parameters independent of
p
.

Now consider a matrix
{\mathbf{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
whose entries are (unit-variance sub-Gaussian) random variables.
Such a matrix is referred to as a
(sub-Gaussian) random matrix
or
(sub-Gaussian) random matrix ensemble
.
More specifically, we focus on random matrices
{\mathbf{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
whose rows are independent, isotropic, and sub-Gaussian random vectors in
p
:

{\mathbf{X}}=\begin{bmatrix}{\mathbf{x}}_{1}^{\top}\\
{\mathbf{x}}_{2}^{\top}\\
\vdots\\
{\mathbf{x}}_{n}^{\top}\end{bmatrix}.

where each
{\mathbf{x}}_{i}\in\real^{p}
satisfies the conditions in Definition
.

Example 214
(Sub-Gaussian random matrices).

Let
{\mathbf{X}}
be an
n\times p
random matrix.

1.

If the entries of
{\mathbf{X}}
are independent Rademacher variables (i.e., taking values
\pm 1
with equal probability), then
{\mathbf{X}}
is called a Rademacher random matrix.

2.

If the entries of
{\mathbf{X}}
are independent standard normal distributed random variables, then
{\mathbf{X}}
is called a Gaussian random matrix.

3.

More generally, if all entries of
{\mathbf{X}}
are independent mean-zero sub-Gaussian random variables of variance
1
with the same constants
\Phi,\xi
in the Definition
of sub-Gaussian random variables, that is,

\Pr(\left\lvert{\textnormal{x}}_{ij}\right\rvert\geq\tau)\leq\Phi e^{-\xi\tau^{2}},\quad\text{for all }\tau>0,\quad i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\},j\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\},

(7.21)

then
{\mathbf{X}}
is called a sub-Gaussian random matrix.
Equivalently, one may require the moment-generating function bound

\mathbb{E}[\exp(\theta{\textnormal{x}}_{ij})]\leq\exp(\theta^{2}C),\quad\text{for all }\theta\in\real,\quad i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\},j\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\},

(7.22)

for some constant
C\equiv c^{2}/2
that is independent of
i,j
, and
p
(see Theorem
).

Both Gaussian and Rademacher matrices are special cases of sub-Gaussian random matrices. Note that the entries of a sub-Gaussian matrix need not be identically distributed—only that they share uniform sub-Gaussian parameters.

A crucial property of random matrices with sub-Gaussian rows is their norm-preserving behavior, which underpins the restricted isometry property (RIP), which will be discussed in the sequel.

{theoremHigh}
[Norm preservation under sub-Gaussian rows]
Let
{\mathbf{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
be a random matrix with independent, isotropic, and sub-Gaussian rows with the same sub-Gaussian parameter
C\equiv c^{2}/2
in (
). Then,

\Pr\left(\left\lvert n^{-1}\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right\rvert\geq\varepsilon\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right)\leq 2\exp(-\widetilde{C}\varepsilon^{2}n),\quad\text{for all ${\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}$, all $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$},

where
\widetilde{C}
depends only on
C
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Let
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
. Without loss of generality, assume that
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}=1
.
Let
{\mathbf{x}}^{(1)},{\mathbf{x}}^{(2)},\ldots,{\mathbf{x}}^{(n)}\in\real^{p}
denote the rows of
{\mathbf{X}}
, and define the random variables

{\textnormal{y}}_{i}=\left\langle{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle^{2}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left\langle{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle^{2}-1,\quad i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}.

Since
{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)}
is isotropic, we have
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{y}}_{i}]=0
.
Moreover, because
\left\langle{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle
is sub-Gaussian,
{\textnormal{y}}_{i}
is sub-exponential;
that is, there exist constants
\Phi,\xi
(depending only on
C
) such that
\Pr(\left\lvert{\textnormal{y}}_{i}\right\rvert\geq\varepsilon)\leq\Phi\exp(-\xi\varepsilon)
.
Observe that

n^{-1}\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\big(\big\langle{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\big\rangle^{2}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\big)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\textnormal{y}}_{i}.

Since the
{\textnormal{y}}_{i}
are independent, Bernstein’s inequality for sub-exponential random variables (Corollary
) yields

\displaystyle\Pr\left(\left\lvert n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\textnormal{y}}_{i}\right\rvert\geq\varepsilon\right)

\displaystyle=\Pr\left(\left\lvert\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\textnormal{y}}_{i}\right\rvert\geq\varepsilon n\right)

\displaystyle\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{\xi^{2}\varepsilon^{2}n^{2}/2}{2\Phi n+\xi\varepsilon n}\right)\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{\xi^{2}\varepsilon^{2}n}{4\Phi+2\xi}\right),

where the last inequality follows since
\varepsilon\in(0,1)
.
Therefore, the claim follows with
\widetilde{C}\triangleq\frac{\xi^{2}}{4\Phi+2\xi}
.

Finally, note that the scaled matrix
\widetilde{{\mathbf{X}}}\triangleq\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}{\mathbf{X}}
, with
{\mathbf{X}}
satisfying the assumptions of the previous result, satisfies

\Pr\left(\left\lvert\left\lVert\widetilde{{\mathbf{X}}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right\rvert\geq\varepsilon\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right)\leq 2\exp(-\widetilde{C}\varepsilon^{2}n),\quad\text{for all ${\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}$, all $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$}.

(7.23)

This concentration inequality serves as the foundation for proving the restricted isometry property of sub-Gaussian random matrices;
see Proposition
.

7.4
Concentration of Measure for SSG Random Variables

In this section, we show that when the entries are strictly sub-Gaussian, the constant
\widetilde{C}
in (
) can be made explicit.
Moreover, for our purposes, it is particularly insightful to study the Euclidean norm of a vector composed of sub-Gaussian random variables.
Specifically, suppose
{\mathbf{x}}=[{\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{n}]^{\top}
, where each
{\textnormal{x}}_{i}
is i.i.d. with
{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\sim\mathcal{SG}(c)
.
We are interested in how
\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{2}
deviates from its expected value.

To establish the main result, we will use Markov’s inequality for nonnegative random variables (Theorem
) together with the following bound on the exponential moment of a sub-Gaussian random variable.

Lemma 215
.

Suppose
{\textnormal{x}}\sim\mathcal{SG}(c^{2})
. Then, for any
\lambda\in[0,1)
,

\mathbb{E}[\exp\left(\lambda{\textnormal{x}}^{2}/2c^{2}\right)]\leq\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\lambda}},

Proof
[of Lemma
]
The claim is trivial when
\lambda=0
.
Assume now that
\lambda\in(0,1)
.
Let
f(x)
denote the probability density function of
x
. By the definition of sub-Gaussianity,

\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\exp(\theta x)f(x)\,dx\leq\exp(\theta^{2}c^{2}/2),\quad\forall\,\theta\in\real.

Multiplying both sides by
\exp(-\theta^{2}c^{2}/2\lambda)
gives

\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\exp\left(\theta x-\theta^{2}c^{2}/2\lambda\right)f(x)\,dx\leq\exp(\theta^{2}c^{2}(\lambda-1)/2\lambda).

Integrating both sides with respect to
\theta\in\real
yields

\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\left(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\exp\left(\theta x-\theta^{2}c^{2}/2\lambda\right)d\theta\right)f(x)\,dx\leq\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\exp(\theta^{2}c^{2}(\lambda-1)/2\lambda)\,d\theta.

Evaluating the Gaussian integrals on both sides leads to

\frac{1}{c}\sqrt{{2\pi\lambda}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\exp\left(\lambda x^{2}/2c^{2}\right)f(x)\,dx\leq\frac{1}{c}\sqrt{\frac{2\pi\lambda}{1-\lambda}},

which simplifies to the desired inequality. This completes the proof.

This lemma refines the properties of zero-mean sub-Gaussian variables and complements part (i) of Theorem
.

We now present a key concentration result, which generalizes findings from
Dasgupta and Gupta 2003
and extends the well-known behavior of Gaussian vectors (see Section
).

{theoremHigh}
[Concentration of SG variables
(
Dasgupta and Gupta 2003
;
Baraniuk et al. 2011
)
]
Let
{\mathbf{x}}=[{\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{n}]^{\top}
, where each
{\textnormal{x}}_{i}
is i.i.d. with
{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\sim\mathcal{SG}(c^{2})
and
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{i}^{2}]=\sigma^{2}
. Then,

\mathbb{E}[\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}]=n\sigma^{2}.

(7.24)

Moreover, for any
\mu\in(0,1)
and for any
\nu\in[c^{2}/\sigma^{2},\nu_{\max}]
, there exists a constant
\kappa\geq 4
depending only on
\nu_{\max}
and the ratio
\sigma^{2}/c^{2}
such that

\Pr(\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\mu n\sigma^{2})\leq\exp\left(-n(1-\mu)^{2}/\kappa\right)

(7.25)

and

\Pr(\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\geq\nu n\sigma^{2})\leq\exp\left(-n(\nu-1)^{2}/\kappa\right).

(7.26)

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Equation (
) follows immediately from independence:

\mathbb{E}[\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}]=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{i}^{2}]=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma^{2}=n\sigma^{2}

Since
\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
is nonnegative and the exponential function is monotone, we can apply Markov’s inequality (Theorem
):

\displaystyle\Pr(\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\geq\nu n\sigma^{2})

\displaystyle=\Pr\left(\exp\big(\lambda\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\big)\geq\exp\big(\lambda\nu n\sigma^{2}\big)\right)

\displaystyle\leq\frac{\mathbb{E}\left[\exp\left(\lambda\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right)\right]}{\exp\left(\lambda\nu n\sigma^{2}\right)}=\frac{\prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}\left[\exp\left(\lambda{\textnormal{x}}_{i}^{2}\right)\right]}{\exp\left(\lambda\nu n\sigma^{2}\right)}.

Since
{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\sim\mathcal{SG}(c^{2})
, for
\lambda\in[0,1/(2c^{2}))
, we have from Lemma
that

\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\exp\left(\lambda{\textnormal{x}}_{i}^{2}\right)\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\exp\left(2c^{2}\lambda{\textnormal{x}}_{i}^{2}/2c^{2}\right)\right]\leq\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-2c^{2}\lambda}}

\displaystyle\implies

\displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}\left(\exp\left(\lambda{\textnormal{x}}_{i}^{2}\right)\right)\leq\left(\frac{1}{1-2c^{2}\lambda}\right)^{n/2}.

Combining the preceding two results shows that

\Pr(\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\geq\nu n\sigma^{2})\leq\left(\frac{\exp\left(-2\lambda\nu\sigma^{2}\right)}{1-2c^{2}\lambda}\right)^{n/2}.

Optimizing over
\lambda
yields the choice

\lambda=\frac{\nu\sigma^{2}-c^{2}}{2c^{2}\sigma^{2}\nu},

which lies in
[0,1/(2c^{2})]
provided
\nu\in[c^{2}/\sigma^{2},\nu_{\max}]
.
Substituting this optimal
\lambda
gives

\Pr(\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\geq\nu n\sigma^{2})\leq\left(\nu\frac{\sigma^{2}}{c^{2}}\exp\left(1-\nu\frac{\sigma^{2}}{c^{2}}\right)\right)^{n/2}.

(7.27)

A similar calculation yields

\Pr(\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\mu n\sigma^{2})\leq\left(\mu\frac{\sigma^{2}}{c^{2}}\exp\left(1-\mu\frac{\sigma^{2}}{c^{2}}\right)\right)^{n/2}.

(7.28)

To simply these bounds, define

\kappa\triangleq\max\left\{4,2\frac{(\nu_{\max}\sigma^{2}/c^{2}-1)^{2}}{(\nu_{\max}\sigma^{2}/c^{2}-1)-\ln(\nu_{\max}\sigma^{2}/c^{2})}\right\}.

Then, for all
\gamma\in[0,\nu_{\max}\sigma^{2}/c^{2}]
, one has

\ln(\gamma)\leq(\gamma-1)-\frac{2(\gamma-1)^{2}}{\kappa}\quad\implies\quad\gamma\leq\exp\left((\gamma-1)-\frac{2(\gamma-1)^{2}}{\kappa}\right).

Since
\sigma^{2}\leq c^{2}
by Theorem
,
setting
\gamma=\nu\sigma^{2}/c^{2}\leq\nu\leq\nu_{\max}
in (
) gives (
).
Similarly, setting
\gamma=\mu\sigma^{2}/c^{2}
in (
) yields (
).

This result shows that the squared norm of a sub-Gaussian vector concentrates sharply around its mean
n\sigma^{2}
, with exponentially decaying tail probabilities as
n
grows. However, note that the upper-tail bound (
) only applies for
\nu\geq c^{2}/\sigma^{2}\geq 1
, as implied by Theorem
. Thus, for a general sub-Gaussian distribution, the concentration may not be arbitrarily tight.

Crucially, for strictly sub-Gaussian distributions—where
c^{2}=\sigma^{2}
—this restriction disappears. In this favorable case, we obtain the following simplified and symmetric concentration inequality.

{theoremHigh}

[Concentration of SSG variables]
Let
{\mathbf{x}}=[{\textnormal{x}}_{1},{\textnormal{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\textnormal{x}}_{n}]^{\top}
, where each
{\textnormal{x}}_{i}
is i.i.d. with
{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\sim\mathcal{SSG}(\sigma^{2})
. Then,

\mathbb{E}[\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}]=n\sigma^{2}

(7.29)

and for any
\varepsilon\in(0,1)
,

\Pr\left(\left\lvert\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-n\sigma^{2}\right\rvert\geq\varepsilon n\sigma^{2}\right)\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{n\varepsilon^{2}}{\kappa}\right)

(7.30)

with
\kappa=2/(1-\ln(2))\approx 6.52
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Since each
{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\sim\mathcal{SSG}(\sigma^{2})
, we have that
{\textnormal{x}}_{i}\sim\mathcal{SG}(\sigma^{2})
and
\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{i}^{2}]=\sigma^{2}
.
Invoking Theorem
with
\mu=1-\varepsilon
and
\nu=1+\varepsilon
allows us to simplify and combine
the bounds in (
) and (
) to obtain (
).
Since
\nu<2
for
\varepsilon\in(0,1)
, we may take
\nu_{\max}=2
.
Thus,
\kappa=2/(1-\ln(2))\approx 6.52
.
This completes the proof.

As an immediate application, consider a noise vector
{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\in\real^{n}
with i.i.d. entries
\epsilon_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2})
. Since the Gaussian distribution is strictly sub-Gaussian, Theorem
implies that there exists a constant
c_{0}>0
such that for any
e>0
,

\Pr\left(\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\right\rVert_{2}\geq(1+e)\sqrt{n}\sigma\right)\leq\exp\left(-c_{0}ne^{2}\right).

(7.31)

In particular, setting
e=1
gives

\Pr\left(\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\right\rVert_{2}\geq 2\sqrt{n}\sigma\right)\leq\exp\left(-c_{0}n\right).

(7.32)

Finally, Theorem
also implies the following useful corollary, which shows that the transformation of a vector by a random matrix exhibits a concentration phenomenon.
The result is a special case of Theorem
where the constant is determined.

Corollary 216
(Norm preservation for SSG matrices).

Let
{\mathbf{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
be a random matrix with i.i.d. entries
{\textnormal{x}}_{ij}\sim\mathcal{SSG}(1/n)
.
For any fixed
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
, define
{\mathbf{y}}={\mathbf{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.
Then

\mathbb{E}[\left\lVert{\mathbf{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}]=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

(7.33)

and for any
\varepsilon\in(0,1)
,

\displaystyle\Pr\left(\left\lvert\left\lVert{\mathbf{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right\rvert\geq\varepsilon\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right)\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{n\varepsilon^{2}}{\kappa}\right)

(7.34)

\displaystyle\implies\Pr\left((1-\varepsilon)\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\left\lVert{\mathbf{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq(1+\varepsilon)\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right)\geq 1-2\exp\left(-\frac{n\varepsilon^{2}}{\kappa}\right),

(7.35)

where
\kappa=2/(1-\ln(2))\approx 6.52
.

Proof
[of Corollary
]
Let
{\bm{x}}^{(i)}
denote the
i
-th row of
{\mathbf{X}}
. Then
{\textnormal{y}}_{i}=\left\langle{\bm{x}}^{(i)},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle
, and thus by Proposition
,
{\textnormal{y}}_{i}\sim\mathcal{SSG}(\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}/n)
. Applying Theorem
to the
n
-dimensional random vector
{\mathbf{y}}
, we obtain (
7.34
).

7.5
Design Properties under Sub-Gaussian Random Matrices

We now return to again the question of how to construct matrices that satisfy the RIP.
While it is possible to deterministically construct
n\times p
matrices that satisfy the RIP of order
k
, early approaches relied on mutual coherence.
A matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
with unit-norm columns is said to be
\mu
-coherent if
\left\langle{\bm{x}}_{i},{\bm{x}}_{j}\right\rangle\leq\mu
for all
i\neq j\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
(see Definition
).
Such a matrix satisfies the RIP of order
k
with constant
\delta=(k-1)\mu
(see Proposition
).

Deterministic constructions of
\mu
-coherent matrices with
\mu=\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{\ln p}{\sqrt{n\ln n}}\right)
have been known since the work of
Kashin 1975
.
However, these constructions require
n=\widetilde{O}\left(\frac{k^{2}\ln^{3}p}{\delta^{2}}\right)
, which is quadratically larger than the number of rows needed by random constructions.
Other explicit constructions fare little better:

DeVore 2007
achieves
n=\mathcal{O}(k^{2}\ln p)
, while
Indyk 2008
requires
n=\mathcal{O}(kp^{\mu})
for some constant
\mu>0
.
In many practical settings, such requirements on
n
are prohibitively large.
The first significant improvement came from
Bourgain et al. 2011
, who introduced deterministic combinatorial constructions satisfying the RIP with

n=\widetilde{O}\left(\frac{k^{(2-\epsilon)}}{\delta^{2}}\right)
for some constant
\epsilon>0
.
Although this reduces the quadratic dependence on
k
, the constructions remain complex and still fall short of the near-linear scaling achieved by random matrices.

Fortunately, these limitations can be overcome by randomizing the matrix construction.
A simple and effective approach is as follows: given dimensions
n
and
p
, generate a random matrix
{\mathbf{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
by sampling its entries
{\textnormal{x}}_{ij}
independently from a suitable probability distribution.
One might first observe that if we only require
\delta_{2k}>0
(i.e., mere injectivity on
2k
-sparse vectors), then setting
n=2k
and drawing
{\mathbf{X}}
from a continuous distribution—such as the Gaussian—suffices. With probability 1, every subset of
2k
columns is linearly independent, so the RIP holds for some
\delta_{2k}\in(0,1)
.

However, in practice we typically need a specified RIP constant
\delta_{2k}

(e.g.,
\delta_{2k}<0.1
). To guarantee such a bound, we must control the singular values of all
\binom{p}{k}
submatrices corresponding to
k
-sparse supports—a task that is computationally infeasible for realistic values of
p
and
k
. Moreover, when
n=2k
, the resulting
\delta_{2k}
is typically very close to 1, rendering the matrix unsuitable for applications like compressed sensing.

Therefore, we focus instead on constructing matrices that satisfy the RIP of order
2k
with a prescribed constant
\delta_{2k}\in(0,1)
. Our approach follows the simple framework introduced by
Baraniuk et al. 2008
and later extended by
Mendelson et al. 2008
to broader classes of random matrices.

In this section, we show how the concentration-of-measure properties of sub-Gaussian distributions yield a straightforward proof that random sub-Gaussian matrices satisfy the RIP. Specifically, we aim to prove that if an
n\times p
matrix
{\mathbf{X}}
is drawn at random with sufficiently large
n
, then with high probability there exists a constant
\delta_{k}\in(0,1)
such that

(1-\delta_{k})\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq(1+\delta_{k})\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

(7.36)

holds for all
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]\triangleq\{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\mid\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{0}\leq k\}
;
that is, for all
k
-sparse vectors.
As is seen in the Gaussian case (see Theorem
).

To ensure the RIP, we impose two conditions on the underlying distribution:

Sub-Gaussianity.
We assume the entries of
{\mathbf{X}}
are sub-Gaussian.
This allows us to apply the clean concentration bound in Theorem
or Theorem
.
The argument can be adapted to strictly sub-Gaussian distributions using Corollary
, which yields explicit constants.

Approximate norm preservation.
We require that the matrix preserves the Euclidean norm in expectation. This is achieved by requiring isotropic or by setting

\mathbb{E}[{\textnormal{x}}_{ij}^{2}]=\frac{1}{n},

(7.37)

so that each entry has variance
1/n
. Under this normalization, for any fixed vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
, we have
\mathbb{E}[\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}]=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
, making the RIP a statement about concentration around the mean.

7.5.1
RIP under Isotropic and Sub-Gaussian Random Ensembles

We now show that a random matrix satisfying either the concentration inequality (
)—which holds when the rows are isotropic and sub-Gaussian—or inequality (
7.34
)—which holds under strictly sub-Gaussian entries—also satisfies the restricted isometry property (RIP) of order
k
, provided that the number of rows scales at least as
k
times a logarithmic factor. We begin by showing that any
k
-column submatrix of such a random matrix is well-conditioned, under an appropriate condition on its dimensions.
This is an extension to the singular values theorem of a matrix under Gaussian entries; see Theorem
.

Proposition 217
(RIP via tail bounds).

Let
{\mathbb{S}}\subset\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
with
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert=k
. Suppose that an
n\times p
random matrix
{\mathbf{X}}
is drawn from a distribution satisfying the concentration inequality (
) holds, that is,

\Pr\left(\left\lvert\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right\rvert>\tau\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right)\leq 2\exp(-\widetilde{C}\tau^{2}n),\quad\text{for all }\tau\in(0,1),\,{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}.

(7.38)

Equivalently, Theorem
shows that
\sqrt{n}{\mathbf{X}}
has
independent, isotropic, and sub-Gaussian rows with the same sub-Gaussian parameter
C
in (
).
If

n\geq\frac{2}{3\widetilde{C}\delta^{2}}(7k+2\ln(2/\varepsilon)),\quad\text{for $\varepsilon,\delta\in(0,1)$,}

(7.39)

then, with probability at least
1-\varepsilon
,

\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}-{\bm{I}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\delta.

Proof
[of Proposition
]
By Theorem
,
for
\rho\in(0,1/2)
, there exists a finite subset
{\mathbb{A}}
of the unit sphere
{\mathbb{U}}=\{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}\mid\mathrm{supp}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\subset{\mathbb{S}},\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}=1\}
such that

\left\lvert{\mathbb{A}}\right\rvert\leq\left(1+\frac{2}{\rho}\right)^{k}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\min_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{A}}}\left\lVert\mathbf{z}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\rho\quad\text{for all }\mathbf{z}\in{\mathbb{U}}.

That is,
{\mathbb{A}}
is the
\rho
-packing set of itself (Definition
).
For any
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{A}}
, the concentration inequality (
) gives, for
\tau\in(0,1)
depending on
\delta
and
\rho
to be determined later,

\displaystyle\Pr\left(\left\lvert\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right\rvert>\tau\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right)

\displaystyle\leq\sum_{{\bm{a}}\in{\mathbb{A}}}\Pr\left(\left\lvert\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}{\bm{a}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\left\lVert{\bm{a}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right\rvert>\tau\left\lVert{\bm{a}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right)

\displaystyle\leq 2\,\left\lvert{\mathbb{A}}\right\rvert\exp(-\widetilde{C}\tau^{2}n)\leq 2\left(1+\frac{2}{\rho}\right)^{k}\exp(-\widetilde{C}\tau^{2}n).

Since
{\mathbb{A}}
is a subset of the unit sphere
{\mathbb{U}}
, the above inequality shows that the random matrix
{\mathbf{X}}
satisfies

\left\lvert\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right\rvert\leq\tau,\quad\text{for all }{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{A}}.

(7.40)

with probability at least

D\triangleq 1-2\left(1+\frac{2}{\rho}\right)^{k}\exp(-\widetilde{C}\tau^{2}n).

(7.41)

We now show that (
) implies
\big\lvert\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\big\rvert\leq\delta
for all
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{U}}
, i.e.,
\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}-{\bm{I}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\delta
once
\rho,\tau
are chosen appropriately. Let
{\mathbf{H}}\triangleq{\mathbf{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}-{\bm{I}}
. Then (
) means that
\left\lvert\left\langle{\mathbf{H}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rangle\right\rvert\leq\tau
for all
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{A}}
with probability exceeding
D
.
Now consider a vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{U}}
, for which we choose another vector
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{A}}
satisfying
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\rho<1/2
.
Using the triangle inequality and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality (Theorem
), we obtain

\displaystyle\left\lvert\left\langle{\mathbf{H}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rangle\right\rvert

\displaystyle=\left\lvert\left\langle{\mathbf{H}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rangle+\left\langle{\mathbf{H}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}+{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}),{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rangle\right\rvert

\displaystyle\leq\left\lvert\left\langle{\mathbf{H}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rangle\right\rvert+\left\lvert\left\langle{\mathbf{H}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}+{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}),{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rangle\right\rvert

\displaystyle\leq\tau+\left\lVert{\mathbf{H}}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}+{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\tau+2\left\lVert{\mathbf{H}}\right\rVert_{2}\rho.

By the definition of the spectral norm (Definition
) and taking the supremum over all
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{U}}
, we deduce that

\left\lVert{\mathbf{H}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\tau+2\left\lVert{\mathbf{H}}\right\rVert_{2}\rho\quad\implies\quad\left\lVert{\mathbf{H}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\frac{\tau}{1-2\rho}.

Choosing
\tau\triangleq(1-2\rho)\delta\in(0,1)
ensures
\left\lVert{\mathbf{H}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\delta
. By (
) we conclude that

\Pr\left(\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}-{\bm{I}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\delta\right)\geq 1-2\left(1+\frac{2}{\rho}\right)^{k}\exp(-\widetilde{C}(1-2\rho)^{2}\delta^{2}n).

(7.42)

Thus, the event
\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}-{\bm{I}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\delta
occurs with probability at least
1-\varepsilon
whenever

n\geq\frac{1}{\widetilde{C}(1-2\rho)^{2}\delta^{2}}\left(k\ln(1+2/\rho)+\ln(2/\varepsilon)\right).

The choice
\rho\triangleq 0.2/(e^{3/2}-1)<0.5
makes
(\ln(1+2/\rho))/(1-2\rho)^{2}\leq 14/3
and
1/(1-2\rho)^{2}\leq 4/3
.
Consequently, the required condition on
n
is fulfilled if

n\geq\frac{2}{3\widetilde{C}\delta^{2}}\left(7k+2\ln(2/\varepsilon)\right),

which completes the proof.

The above argument applies unchanged when replacing coordinate subspaces indexed by
{\mathbb{S}}
with arbitrary
k
-dimensional subspaces of
p
. Moreover, the result depends only on the columns of
{\mathbf{X}}
indexed by
{\mathbb{S}}
; thus, it equally holds for an
n\times k
sub-Gaussian random matrix
{\mathbf{Z}}
(see Example
). In particular, for such a matrix,

\left\lVert\frac{1}{n}{\mathbf{Z}}^{\top}{\mathbf{Z}}-{\bm{I}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\delta

with probability at least
1-\varepsilon
provided that condition (
) is satisfied.

We now present the main result of this section: the RIP for random matrices whose entries exhibit sub-Gaussian behavior.

{theoremHigh}
[RIP via tail bounds]
Let
{\mathbf{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
be a random matrix drawn from a distribution satisfying the concentration inequality (
):

\Pr\left(\left\lvert\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right\rvert>\tau\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right)\leq 2\exp(-\widetilde{C}\tau^{2}n),\quad\text{for all $\tau\in(0,1)$ and ${\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}$}.

Equivalently, Theorem
shows that
\sqrt{n}{\mathbf{X}}
has
independent, isotropic, and sub-Gaussian rows with the same sub-Gaussian parameter
C
in (
).
Then the following statements hold:

If

n\geq\frac{2}{3\widetilde{C}\delta^{2}}\left[k\ln(e^{9}(p/k)^{2})+2\ln(2/\varepsilon)\right],\quad\text{for $\delta,\varepsilon\in(0,1)$},

then with probability at least
1-\varepsilon
the restricted isometry constant
\delta_{k}
of order
k
of
{\mathbf{X}}
satisfies
\delta_{k}\leq\delta
.

Setting
\varepsilon=\exp(-3\widetilde{C}\delta^{2}n/8)
yields the condition

n\geq\frac{8}{3\widetilde{C}\delta^{2}}k\ln\left(\frac{ep}{k}\right)+\frac{12k}{\widetilde{C}\delta^{2}},

(7.43)

which guarantees that
\delta_{k}\leq\delta
with probability at least
1-2\exp\left(-\delta^{2}n/(2C)\right)
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
The conditioning of a single
k
-column submatrix
{\mathbf{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}
(with
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert=k
) was analyzed in Proposition
; we adopt the same notation here.
Recall from Definition
that the restricted isometry constant of order
k

is given by

\delta_{k}=\max_{{\mathbb{S}}\subset\{1,2,\ldots,p\},\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert=k}\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}-{\bm{I}}\right\rVert_{2}.

Applying the union bound over all
\binom{p}{k}
subsets
{\mathbb{S}}\subset\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
of size
k
, and using (
), we obtain

\displaystyle\Pr(\delta_{k}>\delta)

\displaystyle\leq\sum_{{\mathbb{S}}\subset\{1,2,\ldots,p\},\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert=k}\Pr\left(\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\mathbf{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}-{\bm{I}}\right\rVert_{2}\geq\delta\right)

\displaystyle\leq 2\binom{p}{k}\left(1+\frac{2}{\rho}\right)^{k}\exp(-\widetilde{C}(1-2\rho)^{2}\delta^{2}n)

\displaystyle\leq 2\left(\frac{ep}{k}\right)^{k}\left(1+\frac{2}{\rho}\right)^{k}\exp(-\widetilde{C}(1-2\rho)^{2}\delta^{2}n),

where the last inequality follows from Problem
.
This shows that the event
\delta_{k}\leq\delta
holds with probability at least
1-\varepsilon
provided that

n\geq\frac{1}{\widetilde{C}(1-2\rho)^{2}\delta^{2}}\left(k\ln(1+2/\rho)+k\ln(ep/k)+\ln(2/\varepsilon)\right).

Once again, the choice
\rho\triangleq 0.2/(e^{3/2}-1)<0.5
yields that
\delta_{k}\leq\delta
with probability at least
1-\varepsilon
provided

n\geq\frac{1}{\widetilde{C}\delta^{2}}\left(\frac{4}{3}k\ln(ep/k)+\frac{14}{3}k+\frac{4}{3}\ln(2/\varepsilon)\right).

This completes the proof.

Since the entries of Gaussian and Rademacher random matrices are sub-Gaussian with variance 1 (see Example
and Problem
), it follows immediately that these matrices satisfy the RIP under condition (
).

Corollary 218
.

Let
{\mathbf{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
be a Gaussian or Rademacher random matrix.
Then there exists a universal constant
C>0
such that the restricted isometry constant of
\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}{\mathbf{X}}
satisfies
\delta_{k}\leq\delta
with probability at least
1-\varepsilon
provided

n\geq C\delta^{-2}(k\ln(ep/k)+\frac{7}{2}k+\ln(2/\varepsilon)).

(7.44)

The normalization
\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}{\mathbf{X}}
is natural:
for any fixed vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
, we have

\mathbb{E}[\big\lVert\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}{\mathbf{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}]=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},

provided that the entries of
{\mathbf{X}}
are independent, mean-zero, and have unit variance (as is the case for both Gaussian and Rademacher ensembles, or a
\mathcal{SSG}(1/n)
variable).
Consequently, the restricted isometry constant
\delta_{k}
quantifies the maximal deviation of

\big\lVert\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}{\mathbf{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}
from its expectation, uniformly over all
k
-sparse vectors
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.

For Gaussian matrices we will slightly improve on (
) in the next subsection by making the constants explicit.

7.5.2
RIP under SSG Random Ensembles

We shall now show how the concentration of measure inequality in Corollary
(which tells us that the norm of a sub-Gaussian random vector strongly concentrates about its mean) can be used together with covering arguments to prove the RIP for sub-Gaussian random matrices.
Similarly, our general approach will again be to construct nets of points in each
k
-dimensional subspace, apply (
7.34
) to all of these points through a union bound, and then extend the result from our finite set of points to all possible
k
-dimensional signals.
The resulting statement is often found in the literature.

{theoremHigh}

[RIP under SSG, Theorem 5.2 of
Baraniuk et al. 2008
]
Fix
\delta\in(0,1)
.
Let
{\mathbf{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
be a random matrix whose entries
{\textnormal{x}}_{ij}
are i.i.d. with
{\textnormal{x}}_{ij}\sim\mathcal{SSG}(1/n)
. If

n\geq\kappa_{1}k\ln\left(\frac{p}{k}\right),

(7.45)

then
{\mathbf{X}}
satisfies the RIP of order
k
with the prescribed constant
\delta
, with probability exceeding
1-2\exp(-\kappa_{2}n)
.
Here,
\kappa_{1}>1
is an arbitrary constant, and
\kappa_{2}=\delta^{2}/2\kappa-1/\kappa_{1}-\ln(42e/\delta)
, where
\kappa=2/(1-\ln(2))\approx 6.52
.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
First, observe that it suffices to verify inequality (
) for vectors
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
satisfying
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}=1
, since
{\mathbf{X}}
is linear.
Next, fix an index set
{\mathbb{S}}\subset\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
with
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert=k
, and let
{\mathbb{C}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
denote the
k
-dimensional subspace spanned by the columns of
{\mathbf{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
.
We construct a finite set of points
{\mathbb{A}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\subseteq{\mathbb{C}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
such that
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}=1
for all
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{A}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
, and for every
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{C}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
with
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}=1
, there exists some
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{A}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
satisfying:

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{A}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\delta/14.

By Theorem
, such a set
{\mathbb{A}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
can be chosen with cardinality at most
\left\lvert{\mathbb{A}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\right\rvert\leq(42/\delta)^{k}
.
Repeating this construction for every possible index set
{\mathbb{S}}
of size
k
, we define the union

{\mathbb{A}}=\bigcup_{{\mathbb{S}}:\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert=k}{\mathbb{A}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}.

There are
\binom{p}{k}
such index sets
{\mathbb{S}}
.
Using Problem
, we can bound this number by
\binom{p}{k}\leq\left(\frac{ep}{k}\right)^{k}
.
Hence,
\left\lvert{\mathbb{A}}\right\rvert\leq(42ep/\delta k)^{k}
.
Since the entries of
{\mathbf{X}}
follow a SSG distribution, Corollary
implies inequality (
7.34
):

\Pr\left(\left\lvert\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right\rvert\geq\varepsilon\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right)\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{n\varepsilon^{2}}{\kappa}\right),\quad\text{for any ${\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}$}.

Applying the union bound over all
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
with
\varepsilon=\delta/\sqrt{2}
, we find that with probability at least

\widetilde{p}\triangleq 1-2\left(\frac{42ep}{\delta k}\right)^{k}\exp\left(-\frac{n\delta^{2}}{2\kappa}\right),

(7.46)

the following holds for all
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{A}}
:

(1-\delta/\sqrt{2})\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq(1+\delta/\sqrt{2})\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},\quad\text{for all }{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{A}}.

(7.47)

Now, if
n
satisfies condition (
), then

\ln\left(\frac{42ep}{\delta k}\right)^{k}\leq k\left(\ln\left(\frac{p}{k}\right)+\ln\left(\frac{42e}{\delta}\right)\right)\leq\frac{n}{\kappa_{1}}+n\ln\left(\frac{42e}{\delta}\right).

Consequently, the probability
\widetilde{p}
in (
) exceeds
1-2\exp(-\kappa_{2}n)
, as required.

However, (
) holds for all
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
. We now define
D
as the smallest number such that

\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\sqrt{1+D},\quad\text{for all }{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k],\;\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}=1,

(7.48)

where the first inequality follows from the definition of the spectral norm.
To prove the RIP condition, our goal is to show that
D\leq\delta
. For this, by the construction of the set
{\mathbb{A}}
, for any
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]
with
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}=1
, there exists a vector
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{A}}
such that
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\delta/14
and
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]
.
Applying the triangle inequality,

\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}+\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\right\rVert_{2}\leq\sqrt{1+\delta/\sqrt{2}}+\sqrt{1+D}\cdot\delta/14.

Because
D
is defined as the smallest constant satisfying (
), it follows that
\sqrt{1+D}\leq\sqrt{1+\delta/\sqrt{2}}+\sqrt{1+D}\cdot\delta/14
.
Rearranging gives

\sqrt{1+D}\leq\frac{\sqrt{1+\delta/\sqrt{2}}}{1-\delta/14}\leq\sqrt{1+\delta}.

This establishes the upper bound of the RIP condition.
The lower bound follows similarly:

\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}\geq\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}-\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\right\rVert_{2}\geq\sqrt{1-\delta/\sqrt{2}}-\sqrt{1+\delta}\cdot\delta/14\geq\sqrt{1-\delta},

which completes the proof.

Note that, in light of the measurement bounds for the RIP established in Theorem
, condition (
) achieves the optimal number of measurements—up to a constant factor.

7.5.3
Other Issues

Using random matrices to construct
{\mathbf{X}}
offers several additional benefits. To illustrate these, we again focus on the RIP condition.

First, random constructions yield democratic measurements: any sufficiently large subset of the measurements suffices for stable signal recovery
(
Davenport et al. 2009
;
Laska et al. 2011
)
. Consequently, systems based on random
{\mathbf{X}}
are inherently robust to the loss or corruption of a small fraction of measurements.

Second—and perhaps more importantly—in practice we are often interested in signals that are sparse not in the standard basis, but with respect to some other orthonormal basis
{\bm{Q}}
; see the next section.
In such cases, what we actually require is that the product
{\mathbf{X}}{\bm{Q}}
satisfies the RIP. If
{\mathbf{X}}
were constructed deterministically, we would need to tailor it specifically to the structure of
{\bm{Q}}
. However, when
{\mathbf{X}}
is drawn at random, this dependency disappears. For example, if
{\mathbf{X}}
has i.i.d. Gaussian entries and
{\bm{Q}}
is any fixed orthonormal basis, then
{\mathbf{X}}{\bm{Q}}
also has i.i.d. Gaussian entries (see Lemma
).
Therefore, as long as
n
is sufficiently large,
{\mathbf{X}}{\bm{Q}}
satisfies the RIP with high probability—just as
{\mathbf{X}}
does on its own. Although less immediate, analogous results hold for sub-Gaussian ensembles as well
(
Baraniuk et al. 2008
)
. This desirable feature is often referred to as
universality
, and it represents a major advantage of random matrix constructions.

On the other hand, the work of
Agarwal et al. 2010
shows that the restricted strong convexity (RSC) and restricted strong smoothness (RSS) properties (Definition
) hold whenever the rows of
{\mathbf{X}}
are drawn independently from a sub-Gaussian distribution over
p

with a nonsingular covariance matrix. This result is particularly valuable because many real-world datasets—such as those arising in gene-expression analysis—can be reasonably modeled as sub-Gaussian random vectors. Hence, with high probability, such data matrices satisfy RSC/RSS, enabling the use of sparse recovery algorithms in practical applications.

If one is willing to accept a modest increase in the number of rows of
{\mathbf{X}}
, even more efficient constructions become available—particularly those that support fast matrix-vector multiplication. The seminal work of
Candes and Tao 2005
showed that selecting each row of a Fourier matrix independently with probability
\mathcal{O}\left({k\ln^{4}p}/{p}\right)
yields a matrix satisfying the RIP with high probability. This was later improved by
Haviv and Regev 2017
, who reduced the required sampling rate to
\mathcal{O}\left(k\ln^{2}k{\ln(p)}/{p}\right)
. Crucially, multiplying such a structured matrix by a
k
-sparse vector takes only
\mathcal{O}(k\ln^{2}p)
time, compared to
\mathcal{O}(k^{2}\ln p)
time for a dense Gaussian matrix (under the typical scaling
n\sim k\ln(p/k)
).

7.6
Sparse Optimization under Sub-Gaussian Ensembles

Towards this end, observe that all the
\ell_{1}
-minimization results presented so far are deterministic: they hold simultaneously for all vectors
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
, provided the measurement matrix
{\mathbf{X}}
satisfies the RIP
(see Section
).
This is a powerful theoretical property. However, as noted earlier, it is generally infeasible in practice to verify or guarantee that a given deterministic matrix satisfies the RIP. In fact, the only known constructions that provably satisfy the RIP do so with high probability—thanks to randomness. For instance, recall Theorem
or Theorem
, which illustrate how randomness enables slightly weaker—but still highly useful—probabilistic guarantees.

We now combine the results of this chapter to state the main theorem on sparse recovery via the
\ell_{1}
-minimization problem (
) (p.
) from random measurements.

{theoremHigh}

[Recovery of (
) under Sub-Gaussian]
Let
{\mathbf{X}}
be an
n\times p
random matrix with independent isotropic sub-Gaussian rows. Let
k<p
,
\varepsilon\in(0,1)
, and suppose

n\geq C_{1}k\ln(ep/k)+C_{2}k+C_{3}\ln(2/\varepsilon),

where the constants
C_{1},C_{2},C_{3}>0
depend only on the sub-Gaussian parameters
\Phi,\xi
.
Then, with probability at least
1-\varepsilon
, every
k
-sparse vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is exactly recovered from
{\mathbf{y}}={\mathbf{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
by solving the
\ell_{1}
-minimization problem (
).

Proof
[of Theorem
]
The result follows by combining Theorem
(which ensures the RIP holds with high probability for sub-Gaussian matrices) and Theorem
(which guarantees exact recovery under the RIP). Note that exact sparse recovery is invariant under rescaling of the measurement matrix, so normalization does not affect the conclusion.

7.6.1
Sparsity in an Orthonormal Basis

In many applications, sparsity is not expressed in the canonical basis but rather in some other orthonormal basis. That is, the signal of interest takes the form
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}={\bm{Q}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
, where
{\bm{Q}}\in\real^{p\times p}
is an orthogonal matrix and
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
is
k
-sparse. Taking measurements of
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
with a random matrix
{\mathbf{X}}
gives

{\mathbf{y}}={\mathbf{X}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}={\mathbf{X}}{\bm{Q}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}.

To recover
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
, it suffices to first recover the sparse coefficient vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
and then compute
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}={\bm{Q}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
. Thus, this generalized setting reduces to the standard compressive sensing problem with effective measurement matrix
{\mathbf{X}}^{\prime}={\mathbf{X}}{\bm{Q}}
.

Consequently, we consider the model where
{\mathbf{X}}
is a random
n\times p
matrix and
{\bm{Q}}
is a fixed (deterministic) orthogonal matrix. Importantly, the analysis developed in the preceding sections extends naturally to this scenario.

Corollary 219
.

Let
{\bm{Q}}\in\real^{p\times p}
be a (fixed) orthogonal matrix.
Suppose the
n\times p
random matrix
{\mathbf{X}}
satisfies the concentration inequality

\Pr\left(\left\lvert\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right\rvert>\tau\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right)\leq 2\exp(-\widetilde{C}\tau^{2}n),\quad\text{for all $\tau\in(0,1)$ and ${\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}$},

(7.49)

for some constant
\widetilde{C}>0
.
Let
\delta,\varepsilon\in(0,1)
. Then the restricted isometry constant
\delta_{k}
of
{\mathbf{X}}{\bm{Q}}
satisfies
\delta_{k}\leq\delta
with probability at least
1-\varepsilon
, provided that

n\geq\frac{1}{\widetilde{C}\delta^{2}}\left(\frac{4}{3}k\ln(ep/k)+\frac{14}{3}k+\frac{4}{3}\ln(2/\varepsilon)\right).

Proof
[of Corollary
]
The key observation is that the concentration inequality (
) also holds for the matrix
{\mathbf{X}}{\bm{Q}}
.
Indeed, for any
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
, define
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}\triangleq{\bm{Q}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
. Orthogonality of
{\bm{Q}}
shows

\displaystyle\Pr\left(\left\lvert\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}{\bm{Q}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right\rvert>\tau\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right)

\displaystyle=\Pr\left(\left\lvert\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\left\lVert{\bm{Q}}^{-1}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right\rvert>\tau\left\lVert{\bm{Q}}^{-1}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right)

\displaystyle=\Pr\left(\left\lvert\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right\rvert>\tau\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right)\leq 2\exp(-\widetilde{C}\tau^{2}n).

Therefore, the claim follows directly from Theorem
.

This result implies that sparse recovery using sub-Gaussian random matrices is universal with respect to the choice of orthonormal basis in which the signal is sparse. Crucially, the orthogonal matrix
{\bm{Q}}
can be arbitrary—and notably, it need not be known at the encoding stage when measurements
{\mathbf{y}}={\mathbf{X}}{\bm{Q}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
are acquired. Knowledge of
{\bm{Q}}
is only required during decoding, when solving the
\ell_{1}
-minimization problem.

However, it is important to emphasize that this universality is probabilistic and basis-specific: it does not mean that a single fixed matrix
{\bm{X}}
works for all possible bases simultaneously. In fact, for any given deterministic
{\bm{X}}
, one can construct an orthonormal basis
{\bm{Q}}
for which sparse recovery fails. The corollary only guarantees that, for any fixed
{\bm{Q}}
, a randomly drawn
{\mathbf{X}}
will enable successful recovery with high probability.

7.6.2
Sparse Recovery with Strictly Sub-Gaussian

To establish a robust recovery guarantee, we rely on the fact that strictly sub-Gaussian random matrices preserve the Euclidean norm of any fixed vector with high probability.
Specifically, a slight modification of Corollary
shows that for any
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
,

\Pr\left(\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\geq 2\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right)\leq\exp(-\kappa_{3}n),\quad\text{with $\kappa_{3}\triangleq 1/\kappa$ and $\kappa=2/(1-\ln(2))\approx 6.52$.}

(7.50)

We now use this concentration property to derive the following result.

{theoremHigh}

[Error bound of (
) under SSG]
Let
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\in\real^{p}
be a fixed vector, and assume
\delta_{2k}<\sqrt{2}-1
.
Let
{\mathbf{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
be a strictly sub-Gaussian random matrix (
{\textnormal{x}}_{ij}\sim\mathcal{SSG}(1/n)
) satisfying
n\geq 2\kappa_{1}k\ln(p/2k)
.
Suppose we observe measurements
{\bm{y}}={\mathbf{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
. Then with probability at least
1-2\exp(-\kappa_{2}n)-\exp(-\kappa_{3}n)
, the solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
to problem (
) can be reduced to the problem (
) (p.
) with
\epsilon=2\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})_{2}
, and
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
satisfies

\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\big\rVert_{2}\leq\frac{8\sqrt{1+\delta_{2k}}-(1+\sqrt{2})\delta_{2k}+1}{1-(1+\sqrt{2})\delta_{2k}}\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})_{2}.

(7.51)

Proof
[of Theorem
]
First, by Theorem
, the matrix
{\mathbf{X}}
satisfies the RIP of order
2k
with probability at least
1-2\exp(-\kappa_{2}n)
, provided
n\geq 2\kappa_{1}k\ln(p/2k)
.
Next, let
{\mathbb{S}}
denote the index set corresponding to the
k
entries of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
with largest magnitude, and decompose
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
as
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}({\mathbb{S}})+{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}({\mathbb{S}}^{c})
; note that
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{2}=\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})_{2}
is the best
k
-term approximation error.
Since
{\mathbf{X}}
is strictly sub-Gaussian, Proposition
implies that the vector
{\mathbf{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}
is also strictly sub-Gaussian.
Applying (
), we obtain that with probability at least
1-\exp(-\kappa_{3}n)
,
\left\lVert{\mathbf{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq 2\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{2}=2\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})_{2}
.
Now observe that
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}({\mathbb{S}})\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]
, so we can write the measurement vector as
{\mathbf{y}}={\mathbf{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}={\mathbf{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}_{\mathbb{S}}+{\mathbf{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}={\mathbf{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}_{\mathbb{S}}+{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}
, where
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\epsilon
.
By the union bound, both the RIP condition (for order
2k
) and the above noise bound hold simultaneously with probability at least

1-2\exp(-\kappa_{2}n)-\exp(-\kappa_{3}n)
.
Under these conditions, we may apply Theorem
to recover
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}({\mathbb{S}})
from noisy measurements

{\mathbf{y}}={\mathbf{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}_{\mathbb{S}}+{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}
.
Since
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}({\mathbb{S}})
is exactly
k
-sparse, its best
k
-term
\ell_{1}
approximation error is zero, i.e.,
\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}({\mathbb{S}}))_{1}=0
.
Therefore,

\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}({\mathbb{S}})\big\rVert_{2}\leq C_{2}\epsilon\leq 2C_{2}\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})_{2},

where
C_{2}=4\frac{\sqrt{1+\delta_{2k}}}{1-(1+\sqrt{2})\delta_{2k}}
, as defined in Theorem
.
Finally, by the triangle inequality,

\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\big\rVert_{2}=\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}({\mathbb{S}})+{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}({\mathbb{S}})-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\big\rVert_{2}\leq\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}({\mathbb{S}})\big\rVert_{2}+\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}({\mathbb{S}})-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{2}\leq(2C_{2}+1)\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})_{2},

which yields the claimed error bound after substituting the expression for
C_{2}
and simplifying the numerator.

Thus, although a deterministic guarantee of the form in (
) would require a prohibitively large number of measurements, it is possible to achieve comparable performance with high probability using far fewer measurements—significantly fewer than suggested by Theorem
.

We note, however, that the above result assumes the noise level parameter
\epsilon
is chosen as
2\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})_{2}
, which requires partial knowledge of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
. In practice, this limitation can be addressed using data-driven parameter selection methods such as cross-validation
(
Ward 2009
)
. Moreover, more refined analyses of
\ell_{1}
-minimization show that similar recovery guarantees can be obtained without oracle knowledge of
\sigma_{k}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})_{2}

(
Wojtaszczyk 2010
)
.
