Chapter 8
A Unified Algorithm for Sparse Optimization Problems

W
We will discuss algorithms for solving sparse regression and sparse recovery problems in greater detail in Chapters
and
.
This Chapter primarily introduces a unified yet simple algorithm—
primal-dual algorithm
—for solving the four core optimization problems covered in this book, namely the Lagrangian LASSO, the constrained LASSO,
\ell_{1}
-minimization, and
\ell_{1}
-minimization with noise measurements.

8.1
Fenchel’s Duality Theorem: Revisited

Motivated by these considerations, we now examine the following convex optimization problem, which is central to this book:

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}F({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}})+G({\boldsymbol{\beta}}),

(PG)

with
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
, and
F:\real^{n}\to(-\infty,\infty]
,
G:\real^{p}\to(-\infty,\infty]
are proper convex functions..
Introducing an auxiliary variable
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\triangleq{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
, we obtain the equivalent constrained formulation:

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{n}}F({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+G({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=\boldsymbol{0}.

(PG
′
)

The Lagrange dual function to this problem is given by

\displaystyle D({\boldsymbol{\lambda}})

\displaystyle=\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}\left\{F({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+G({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+\left\langle{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle-\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rangle\right\}

\displaystyle=-\max_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{n}}\left\{\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rangle-F({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\right\}-\max_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\left\{\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\beta}},-{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rangle-G({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\}

\displaystyle=-F^{*}({\boldsymbol{\lambda}})-G^{*}(-{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}),

(8.1)

where
F^{*}
and
G^{*}
denote the convex conjugate functions of
F
and
G
, respectively (Definition
). Consequently, the dual problem of (
) is

\max_{{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n}}D({\boldsymbol{\lambda}})\equiv-F^{*}({\boldsymbol{\lambda}})-G^{*}(-{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}).

(DG)

Strictly speaking, (
) is not the Lagrange dual of the original unconstrained problem (
), since unconstrained problems do not naturally give rise to dual variables. However, because (
) and its constrained reformulation (
) are equivalent—and share the same optimal value—we refer to (
) as the dual of (
).

A variant of Fenchel’s duality theorem (Theorem
), stated below, provides sufficient conditions under which strong duality holds between the primal problem (
) and its dual (
).

Corollary 220
(Fenchel’s duality theorem;
Rockafellar 1970
, Theorem 31.1).

Let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
, and let
F:\real^{n}\to(-\infty,\infty]
and
G:\real^{p}\to(-\infty,\infty]
be proper convex functions.
Suppose that either
\mathrm{dom}(F)=\real^{n}
or
\mathrm{dom}(G)=\real^{p}
, and that there exists some
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
such that
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\mathrm{dom}(F)
.
If the the optima in both (
) and (
) are attained, then strong duality holds:

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}F({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}})+G({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\max_{{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n}}-F^{*}({\boldsymbol{\lambda}})-G^{*}(-{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}).

(8.2)

Under the same conditions as in the theorem above, strong duality implies the
saddle-point property
(
) of the Lagrange function:

L(({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}),{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})\leq L(({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}),{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{*})\leq L(({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}),{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{*})\quad\text{for all }{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{n},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n},

(8.3)

where
({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*})
and
{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{*}
denote primal and dual optimal points, respectively.
From (
8.1
), the optimal value can also be expressed as the solution to the following min-max problem:

\displaystyle\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}}\max_{{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n}}F({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+G({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+\left\langle{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle-\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rangle

\displaystyle=\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\max_{{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n}}\left(\min_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{n}}-\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rangle+F({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\right)+\left\langle{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle+G({\boldsymbol{\beta}})

\displaystyle=\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\max_{{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n}}\left\langle{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rangle+G({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-F^{*}({\boldsymbol{\lambda}}),

(8.4)

where the last equality follows directly from the definition of the convex conjugate.
The interchange of the minimum and maximum is justified because if
(({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}),{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{*})
is a saddle point of the full Lagrangian
L(({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}),{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})
, then
({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{*})
is a saddle point of the reduced Lagrangian
\mathcal{L}({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})\triangleq\min_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}L(({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}),{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})
.
Thus, any primal-dual optimal pair
({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{*})
solves the saddle-point problem

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\max_{{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n}}\left\langle{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rangle+G({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-F^{*}({\boldsymbol{\lambda}}).

(8.5)

Moreover, the reduced Lagrangian
\mathcal{L}
satisfies the saddle-point inequality:

\mathcal{L}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})\leq\mathcal{L}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{*})\leq\mathcal{L}({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{*})\quad\text{for all }{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n}.

(8.6)

8.2
Primal-Dual Algorithm

We consider a general optimization framework for problems of the form

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}F({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}})+G({\boldsymbol{\beta}}),

(8.7)

where
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
, and
F:\real^{n}\to(-\infty,\infty]
,
G:\real^{p}\to(-\infty,\infty]
are proper closed and convex functions.
From (
8.1
), the dual problem associated with (
) is

\max_{{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n}}\left\{D({\boldsymbol{\lambda}})\triangleq-F^{*}({\boldsymbol{\lambda}})-G^{*}(-{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})\right\}.

(8.8)

where
F^{*}
and
G^{*}
denote the convex conjugate functions of
F
and
G
, respectively (Definition
).

By Fenchel’s duality theorem (Corollary
), strong duality holds for the primal-dual pair (
) and (
) under mild regularity conditions on
F
and
G
. These conditions are always satisfied in the special cases of interest in this book.
Moreover, as shown in (
8.4
), jointly solving the primal and dual problems is equivalent to finding a saddle point of the Lagrangian:

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\max_{{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n}}\left\langle{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rangle+G({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-F^{*}({\boldsymbol{\lambda}}).

(8.9)

The algorithm described below relies on the proximal mappings of
F^{*}
and
G
(Definition
).
For convenience, we introduce step-size parameters
\gamma>0
and
\phi>0
and define

\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{G}(\gamma;{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\triangleq\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{\gamma G}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\arg\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\left\{\gamma G({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right\},\quad{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p},

(8.10)

and analogously,

\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{F^{*}}(\phi;{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\triangleq\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{\phi F^{*}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\arg\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{n}}\left\{\phi F^{*}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right\},\quad{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{n}.

(8.11)

We assume that both
\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{F^{*}}(\phi;{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
and
\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{G}(\gamma;{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
can be evaluated efficiently—either in closed form or via simple linear-time algorithms. Note that, by the Moreau decomposition (Theorem
or Theorem
), the proximal operator of
F^{*}
can be computed easily once that of
F
is known. Although the algorithm is well-defined for arbitrary convex
F
and
G
, its practical efficiency hinges on the ability to compute these proximal maps repeatedly and cheaply.
Thus, the following algorithm works only when the proximal mappings are inexpensive.

Algorithm 1

Primal-Dual Method: the General Case
(
Chambolle and Pock 2011
)

1:

Functions
F({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}})
and
G({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
;

2:

input:

\xi\in[0,1]
,
\gamma,\phi>0
such that
\gamma\phi\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}<1
;

3:

initialize:

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(0)}\in\real^{p}
,
{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(0)}\in\real^{n}
,
{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(0)}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(0)}
;

4:

for

t=0,1,2,\ldots

do

5:

{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t+1)}\leftarrow\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{F^{*}}(\phi;{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}+\phi{\bm{X}}{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t)})
;
\triangleright
(PDM
1
), dual proximal step

6:

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}\leftarrow\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{G}(\gamma;{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-\gamma{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t+1)})
;
\triangleright
(PDM
2
), primal proximal step

7:

{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t+1)}\leftarrow{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}+\xi({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})
;
\triangleright
(PDM
3
), extrapolation

8:

Exit if stopping criterion is met at
t=\bar{t}
;

9:

end

for

10:

return:
Approximation
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(\bar{t})}
to the solution of primal problem (
);

11:

return:
Approximation
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}}={\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(\bar{t})}
to the solution of dual problem (
).

Algorithm
outlines the primal-dual method for solving (
).
The parameter
\xi
controls the amount of extrapolation applied to the primal iterate
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
. Specifically:

When
\xi=1
, we have
{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t+1)}=2{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}
(full extrapolation).

When
\xi=0
,
{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t+1)}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}
(no extrapolation). The method reduces to the classical Arrow–Hurwicz algorithm, originally proposed in 1958
(
Arrow et al. 1958
)
.

The choice of step sizes
\gamma
and
\phi
critically affects convergence; see Theorem
for details.
In this work, we analyze Algorithm
with
\xi=1
. If either
F^{*}
or
G
is uniformly convex, further acceleration can be achieved by adaptively adjusting the parameters
\xi,\gamma,
and
\phi
during the iterations; see
Chambolle and Pock 2011
.

\paragrapharrow

Variant.
A symmetric variant of the algorithm is obtained by swapping the order of the primal and dual updates (i.e.,
{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t+1)}
and
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}
) and introducing an auxiliary dual variable
{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}}^{(t)}
:

\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}

\displaystyle\leftarrow\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{G}(\gamma;{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-\gamma{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}}^{(t)});

(8.12a)

\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t+1)}

\displaystyle\leftarrow\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{F^{*}}(\phi;{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}+\phi{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)});

(8.12b)

\displaystyle{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}}^{(t+1)}

\displaystyle\leftarrow{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t+1)}+\xi({\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t+1)}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}).

(8.12c)

\paragrapharrow

Stopping criterion.
A natural stopping criterion is based on the primal-dual gap (see (
)), which in this setting takes the form

H({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})=F({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}})+G({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+F^{*}({\boldsymbol{\lambda}})+G^{*}(-{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})\geq 0.

At optimality
({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}},{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}})
, we have
H({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}},{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}})=0
.
Thus, one may terminate the algorithm at iteration
t
when

H({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)})\leq\varepsilon
for a prescribed tolerance
\varepsilon>0
.

However, in four of the key problems presented in the next section, the function
F
may take the value
+\infty
, which can cause the primal-dual gap
H
to be infinite during intermediate iterations—rendering it uninformative about the quality of the current iterate. In such cases, the algorithm can be modified (e.g., by restricting iterates to the effective domain of
F
) to avoid infinite values.

8.3
Different Problems under the Primal-Dual Framework

Before proceeding with the convergence analysis of the algorithm, we illustrate how the primal-dual framework applies to several sparse optimization problems.

8.3.1
Lagrangian LASSO

The Lagrangian LASSO (also known as the
\ell_{1}
-regularized least squares) problem (
LL
) (p.
LL
) is given by

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}+\frac{\eta}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},

(8.13)

with some regularization parameter
\eta>0
.
This formulation is equivalent to the standard Lagrangian LASSO (
LL
) after the reparameterization
\lambda=\eta^{-1}
.
It fits the general form (
) with
G({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}
and
F({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\frac{\eta}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
.
Clearly,
F
is not only convex but also smooth.
The convex conjugate of
F
(see Example
) is given by

F^{*}({\boldsymbol{\lambda}})=\left\langle{\bm{y}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rangle+\frac{1}{2\eta}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

The convex conjugate of
G
(see Problem
) is the indicator function of the unit
\ell_{\infty}
-ball:

G^{*}({\boldsymbol{\nu}})=\delta_{{\mathbb{B}}_{\infty}[1]}({\boldsymbol{\nu}})=\begin{cases}0,&\text{if }\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq 1;\\
\infty,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}

(8.14)

where
{\mathbb{B}}_{\infty}[1]
denotes the closed unit-ball under the
\ell_{\infty}
-norm (Definition
).
Consequently, the dual problem associated with (
) is

\max_{{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n}}-\left\langle{\bm{y}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rangle-\frac{1}{2\eta}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq 1,

and the corresponding saddle-point problem becomes

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\max_{{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n}}\left\langle{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rangle-\frac{1}{2\eta}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}.

A straightforward computation yields the proximal operator of
F
:

\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{F}(\phi;{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})=\frac{\phi\eta}{\phi\eta+1}{\bm{y}}+\frac{1}{\phi\eta+1}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}.

(8.15)

By the extended Moreau decomposition (Theorem
), the proximal mapping of
F^{*}
is given by

\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{F^{*}}(\phi;{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})=\left(1-\frac{\eta}{\eta+\phi}\right){\boldsymbol{\lambda}}-\frac{\phi^{2}}{\eta+\phi}{\bm{y}}.

The proximal mapping of
\gamma G({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\gamma\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}
is the well-known soft-thresholding operator (see Example
):

\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{G}(\gamma;{\bm{z}})=\mathcal{T}_{\gamma}({\bm{z}})=\left\{\mathcal{T}_{\gamma}(z_{i})\right\}_{i=1}^{p}=[\left\lvert{\bm{z}}\right\rvert-\gamma{\bm{1}}]_{+}\circ\sign({\bm{z}}),

where
\circ
denotes element-wise multiplication and
[\cdot]_{+}
applies the positive part component-wise.

Combining these components, the primal-dual algorithm for the Lagrangian LASSO (
) takes the following form:

\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t+1)}

\displaystyle\leftarrow\left(1-\frac{\eta}{\eta+\phi}\right){\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}+\frac{\phi^{2}}{\eta+\phi}({\bm{X}}{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t)}-{\bm{y}});

(8.16a)

\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}

\displaystyle\leftarrow\mathcal{T}_{\gamma}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-\gamma{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t+1)});

(8.16b)

\displaystyle{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t+1)}

\displaystyle\leftarrow{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}+\xi({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}).

(8.16c)

8.3.2
Constrained LASSO

The constrained LASSO (or the
\ell_{1}
-constrained least squares) problem (
LC
) (p.
LC
) is

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\Sigma.

(8.17)

This can be cast in the form (
) by setting
G({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\delta_{{\mathbb{B}}_{1}[\Sigma]}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
and
F({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
, where
{{\mathbb{B}}_{1}[\Sigma]}
denotes the
\ell_{1}
-ball with radius
\Sigma
.
The function
G
is closed convex since the set
{\mathbb{B}}_{1}[\Sigma]
is closed and convex; see Exercises
and
.
As before,
F
is still continuous in this case.
The convex conjugate of
F
is given by

F^{*}({\boldsymbol{\lambda}})=\left\langle{\bm{y}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rangle+\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

For
G
, its conjugate is

G^{*}({\bm{z}})=\max_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\left\langle{\bm{z}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle-G({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\max_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{{\mathbb{B}}_{1}[\Sigma]}}\left\langle{\bm{z}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\left\lVert{\bm{z}}\right\rVert_{\infty},

where the last equality follows from Hölder’s inequality (Theorem
).
Thus, the dual problem becomes

\max_{{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n}}-\left\langle{\bm{y}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rangle-\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rVert_{\infty}.

and the associated saddle-point problem is

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\max_{{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n}}\left\langle{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rangle-\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\delta_{{\mathbb{B}}_{1}[\Sigma]}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}).

From (
) with
\eta=1
, we obtain

\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{F}(\phi;{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})=\frac{\phi}{\phi+1}{\bm{y}}+\frac{1}{\phi+1}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}.

By extended Moreau decomposition (Theorem
), the proximal mapping of
F^{*}
is given by

\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{F^{*}}(\phi;{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})=\left(1-\frac{1}{1+\phi}\right){\boldsymbol{\lambda}}-\frac{\phi^{2}}{1+\phi}{\bm{y}}.

The proximal mapping of
G
is equivalent to the projection onto the
\ell_{1}
-ball
{\mathbb{B}}_{1}[\Sigma]
(see Definition
), which will be introduced in Section
for
projected gradient descent methods
.

Putting everything together, the primal-dual method for the constrained LASSO (
) reads:

\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t+1)}

\displaystyle\leftarrow\left(1-\frac{1}{1+\phi}\right){\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}+\frac{\phi^{2}}{1+\phi}({\bm{X}}{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t)}-{\bm{y}});

(8.18a)

\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}

\displaystyle\leftarrow\mathcal{P}_{{\mathbb{B}}_{1}[\Sigma]}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-\gamma{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t+1)});

(8.18b)

\displaystyle{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t+1)}

\displaystyle\leftarrow{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}+\xi({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}).

(8.18c)

8.3.3
\ell_{1}
-Minimization

The
\ell_{1}
-minimization problem (
) (p.
) is

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\bm{y}}.

(8.19)

This problem fits the general primal-dual form (
) with
G({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}
and

F({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\delta_{\{{\bm{y}}\}}({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\begin{cases}0,&\text{if }{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\bm{y}};\\
\infty,&\text{if }{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\neq{\bm{y}},\end{cases}

i.e.,
F
is the indicator function of the singleton set
\{{\bm{y}}\}
(see Exercise
for its definition).
Note that
F
is trivially closed (Exercise
).
The convex conjugate of
G
is given by (
), and the conjugate of
F
is given by

\displaystyle F^{*}({\boldsymbol{\lambda}})

\displaystyle=\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\bm{y}}\right\rangle.

Because terms where the objective takes the value
-\infty
can be ignored in maximization, we may explicitly enforce the constraint arising from the domain of
G^{*}
. Consequently, the dual problem (
) becomes

\max_{{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n}}-\left\langle{\bm{y}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rangle\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq 1.

The associated saddle-point problem is

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\max_{{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n}}\left\langle{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rangle+\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}-\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}},{\bm{y}}\right\rangle.

(8.20)

By the extended Moreau decomposition (Theorem
), the proximal mapping of
F^{*}
is therefore

\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{F^{*}}(\phi;{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})={\boldsymbol{\lambda}}-\phi\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{\phi^{-1}F}({\boldsymbol{\lambda}}/\phi)={\boldsymbol{\lambda}}-\phi{\bm{y}},

where the proximal mapping of
F
is the projection onto
\{{\bm{y}}\}
, that is, the constant map
\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{F}(\phi;{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})={\bm{y}}
, for all
{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n}
.

Combining these components, the primal-dual algorithm for the
\ell_{1}
-minimization problem (
) reads:

\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t+1)}

\displaystyle\leftarrow{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}+\phi({\bm{X}}{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t)}-{\bm{y}});

(8.21a)

\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}

\displaystyle\leftarrow\mathcal{T}_{\gamma}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-\gamma{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t+1)});

(8.21b)

\displaystyle{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t+1)}

\displaystyle\leftarrow{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}+\xi({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}).

(8.21c)

8.3.4
\ell_{1}
-Minimization with Noise Measurements

The quadratically-constrained
\ell_{1}
-minimization problem (
) (p.
) is

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\epsilon,

(8.22)

where
\epsilon>0
models the noise level.
This can be expressed in the form (
) with
G({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}
and

F({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\delta_{{\mathbb{B}}[{\bm{y}},\epsilon]}({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\begin{cases}0,&\text{if }\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\epsilon;\\
\infty,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

The function
F
is closed because the set
{\mathbb{B}}[{\bm{y}},\epsilon]
is closed (Exercise
).
Its convex conjugate (see Problem
) is the support function of the ball:

F^{*}({\boldsymbol{\lambda}})=\max_{{\bm{z}}:\,\left\lVert{\bm{z}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\epsilon}\left\langle{\bm{z}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rangle=\left\langle{\bm{y}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rangle+\epsilon\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rVert_{2}.

The convex conjugate of
G
remains as in (
).
Therefore, the dual problem becomes

\max_{{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n}}-\left\langle{\bm{y}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rangle-\epsilon\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rVert_{2}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq 1,

and the corresponding saddle-point formulation is

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\max_{{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n}}\left\langle{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rangle-\epsilon\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rVert_{2}+\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}.

Example
shows that the proximal mapping of
F
is the orthogonal projection onto the ball
{\mathbb{B}}[{\bm{y}},\epsilon]
,

\displaystyle\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{F}(\phi;{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})

\displaystyle=\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{{\bm{z}}\in\real^{n}:\,\left\lVert{\bm{z}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\epsilon}\left\lVert{\bm{z}}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rVert_{2}={\bm{y}}+\frac{\epsilon}{\max\{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2},\epsilon\}}({\boldsymbol{\lambda}}-{\bm{y}})

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}&\text{if }\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\epsilon;\\
\displaystyle{\bm{y}}+\frac{\epsilon}{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}}({\boldsymbol{\lambda}}-{\bm{y}})&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

Applying the extended Moreau decomposition again yields the proximal mapping of
F^{*}
:

\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{F^{*}}(\phi;{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})=\begin{cases}\boldsymbol{0},&\text{if }\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}-\phi{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\epsilon\phi;\\
\displaystyle\left(1-\frac{\epsilon\phi}{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}-\phi{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}}\right)({\boldsymbol{\lambda}}-\phi{\bm{y}}),&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

Finally, the primal-dual algorithm for the quadratically constrained
\ell_{1}
-minimization problem (
) is given by:

\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t+1)}

\displaystyle\leftarrow\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{F^{*}}(\phi;{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}+\phi{\bm{X}}{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t)});

(8.23a)

\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}

\displaystyle\leftarrow\mathcal{T}_{\gamma}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-\gamma{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t+1)});

(8.23b)

\displaystyle{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t+1)}

\displaystyle\leftarrow{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}+\xi({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}).

(8.23c)

8.4
Optimality Condition of the Primal-Dual Algorithm

The algorithm can be interpreted as a fixed point iteration:

{theoremHigh}

[Optmality condition of the primal-dual method]
A point
({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}},{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}})
is a fixed point of the iterations (PDM
1
), (PDM
2
), (PDM
3
) (for any choice of
\xi
) if and only if
({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}},{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}})
is a saddle point
of (
), that is, a primal-dual optimal point for the problems (
) and (
).

Proof
[of Theorem
]
From Algorithm
, a fixed point must satisfy

\displaystyle{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}}=\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{F^{*}}(\phi;{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}}+\phi{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})\qquad\text{and}\qquad{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}=\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{G}(\gamma;{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-\gamma{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}}).

Since
F^{*}
and
G
are proper closed and convex functions (
F^{*}
is proper closed and convex by Lemma
and Exercise
),
it follows from the Proximal Property-I (Lemma
) that a fixed point
({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}},{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}})
satisfies

\displaystyle\phi{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\in\phi\partial F^{*}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}})\qquad\text{and}\qquad-\gamma{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}}\in\gamma\partial G({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}),

where
\partial F^{*}
and
\partial G
denote the subdifferentials of
F^{*}
and
G
, respectively (Definition
).
Dividing both inclusions by the positive scalars
\phi
and
\gamma
, we obtain the equivalent conditions

\boldsymbol{0}\in-{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}+\partial F^{*}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}})\qquad\text{and}\qquad\boldsymbol{0}\in{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}}+\partial G({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}).

By the optimality condition under subdifferential (Theorem
), these relations are equivalent to
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
being the minimum of the function
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\mapsto\big\langle{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}}\big\rangle+G({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-F^{*}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}})
and
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}}
being the maximum of the function
{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\mapsto\big\langle{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\big\rangle+G({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})-F^{*}({\boldsymbol{\lambda}})
.
Together, this means that
({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}},{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}})
satisfies the saddle-point condition for the Lagrangian in (
). Hence, it is a saddle point of that problem.

Conversely, any saddle point of (
) satisfies the above subdifferential inclusions, which—by the same proximal characterization—implies it is a fixed point of the primal-dual iterations. This completes the proof.

Primal-dual algorithms are often derived heuristically by splitting the primal and dual updates. This theorem validates that design:
The specific proximal steps for
G
and
F^{*}

are not arbitrary—they precisely encode the subdifferential optimality conditions required for a saddle point.

8.5
Convergence of the Primal-Dual Algorithm

We now discuss the convergence of the primal-dual method.
Recall that for the saddle-point problem (
), we define the (reduced) Lagrangian function

\mathcal{L}({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})\triangleq\left\langle{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rangle+G({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-F^{*}({\boldsymbol{\lambda}}),

Note that this Lagrangian gives rise to the primal-dual gap, defined as

H({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})\triangleq\max_{{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{\prime}\in\real^{n}}\mathcal{L}({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{\prime})-\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}\in\real^{p}}\mathcal{L}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}).

(8.24)

It follows that
H({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})\geq 0
for all
{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}
, and
H({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})=0
if and only if
({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})
is a saddle point of
\mathcal{L}
; see the saddle-point characterization in (
).

We begin by establishing key properties of the primal-dual algorithm, which will later be used to prove its convergence.
To simplify notation, consider a sequence
({\bm{a}}^{(t)})_{t\in\mathbb{N}_{0}}
(of scalars or vectors).
We introduce the
divided difference
operator:

\displaystyle\Delta_{\theta}{\bm{a}}^{(t)}

\displaystyle\triangleq\frac{{\bm{a}}^{(t)}-{\bm{a}}^{(t-1)}}{\theta};

(8.25)

\displaystyle\Delta_{\theta}\left\lVert{\bm{a}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle\triangleq\frac{\left\lVert{\bm{a}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\left\lVert{\bm{a}}^{(t-1)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}{\theta},\quad t\in\mathbb{N}.

(8.26)

This quantity can be interpreted as a discrete derivative with step size
\theta
. The following identities closely mirror familiar rules from continuous calculus.

Lemma 221
.

Let
{\bm{a}},{\bm{a}}^{(t)}\in\real^{p}
,
t\in\mathbb{N}_{0}
. Then

2\left\langle\Delta_{\theta}{\bm{a}}^{(t)},{\bm{a}}^{(t)}-{\bm{a}}\right\rangle=\Delta_{\theta}\left\lVert{\bm{a}}^{(t)}-{\bm{a}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\theta\left\lVert\Delta_{\theta}{\bm{a}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

(8.27)

Moreover, if
{\bm{b}}^{(t)}
,
t\in\mathbb{N}_{0}
, is another sequence of vectors, then the following discrete integration-by-parts formula holds for any
T\in\mathbb{N}
,

\theta\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(\left\langle\Delta_{\theta}{\bm{a}}^{(t)},{\bm{b}}^{(t)}\right\rangle+\left\langle{\bm{a}}^{(t-1)},\Delta_{\theta}{\bm{b}}^{(t)}\right\rangle\right)=\left\langle{\bm{a}}^{(T)},{\bm{b}}^{(T)}\right\rangle-\left\langle{\bm{a}}^{(0)},{\bm{b}}^{(0)}\right\rangle.

(8.28)

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Let
\widetilde{\bm{a}}^{(t)}\triangleq{\bm{a}}^{(t)}-{\bm{a}}
.
Then
\Delta_{\theta}\widetilde{\bm{a}}^{(t)}=\Delta_{\theta}{\bm{a}}^{(t)}
, and

\displaystyle 2\theta\left\langle\Delta_{\theta}{\bm{a}}^{(t)},{\bm{a}}^{(t)}-{\bm{a}}\right\rangle

\displaystyle=2\theta\left\langle\Delta_{\theta}\widetilde{\bm{a}}^{(t)},\widetilde{\bm{a}}^{(t)}\right\rangle=2\left\langle\widetilde{\bm{a}}^{(t)}-\widetilde{\bm{a}}^{(t-1)},\widetilde{\bm{a}}^{(t)}\right\rangle

\displaystyle=\left\langle\widetilde{\bm{a}}^{(t)}-\widetilde{\bm{a}}^{(t-1)},\widetilde{\bm{a}}^{(t)}-\widetilde{\bm{a}}^{(t-1)}\right\rangle+\left\langle\widetilde{\bm{a}}^{(t)}-\widetilde{\bm{a}}^{(t-1)},\widetilde{\bm{a}}^{(t)}+\widetilde{\bm{a}}^{(t-1)}\right\rangle

\displaystyle=\left\lVert\widetilde{\bm{a}}^{(t)}-\widetilde{\bm{a}}^{(t-1)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\theta\Delta_{\theta}\left\lVert\widetilde{\bm{a}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

This proves (
).

For the second part, we observe that

\Delta_{\theta}\left\langle{\bm{a}}^{(t)},{\bm{b}}^{(t)}\right\rangle=\frac{\left\langle{\bm{a}}^{(t)},{\bm{b}}^{(t)}\right\rangle-\left\langle{\bm{a}}^{(t-1)},{\bm{b}}^{(t-1)}\right\rangle}{\theta}=\left\langle\Delta_{\theta}{\bm{a}}^{(t)},{\bm{b}}^{(t)}\right\rangle+\left\langle{\bm{a}}^{(t-1)},\Delta_{\theta}{\bm{b}}^{(t)}\right\rangle.

Telescoping the sum over
t=1,2,\ldots,T
proves the desired result.

Lemma 222
(Iterate inequality of primal-dual algorithm).

Let
\{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)},{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t)},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}\}_{t\geq 0}
be the sequence generated by
(PDM
1
), (PDM
2
), (PDM
3
)
in Algorithm
, and let
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
,
{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n}
be arbitrary. Then, for
t\in\mathbb{N}
,

\displaystyle\quad\frac{1}{2}\Delta_{\phi}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\Delta_{\gamma}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac{\phi}{2}\left\lVert\Delta_{\phi}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac{\gamma}{2}\left\lVert\Delta_{\gamma}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle\leq\mathcal{L}({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)})-\mathcal{L}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})+\left\langle{\bm{X}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t-1)}),{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}\right\rangle.

(8.29)

Furthermore, assume that
\xi=1
in Algorithm
.
Telescoping the sum of inequality (
8.29
) over
t=1,2,\ldots,T
gives

\displaystyle\frac{1}{2\phi}\left(\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(T)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(0)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right)+\frac{1}{2\gamma}\left(\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(T)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(0)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right)

\displaystyle+\frac{1}{2\phi}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t-1)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac{1}{2\gamma}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t-1)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle\leq\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(\mathcal{L}({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)})-\mathcal{L}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})\right)+\gamma^{2}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left\langle{\bm{X}}\Delta_{\gamma}^{2}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}\right\rangle,

(8.30)

where
\Delta_{\gamma}^{2}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\triangleq\Delta_{\gamma}(\Delta_{\gamma}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})
.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
From (PDM
1
), (PDM
2
), and Proximal Property-I (Lemma
),
the iterates satisfy the relations (replacing
t+1
by
t
)

{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t-1)}+\phi{\bm{X}}{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t-1)}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}\in\phi\partial F^{*}({\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}),\qquad{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t-1)}-\gamma{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\in\gamma\partial G({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}),

where
\partial F^{*}
and
\partial G
denote the subdifferentials of
F^{*}
and
G
, respectively.
Applying the subgradient inequality (Definition
), we obtain:

\displaystyle\phi F^{*}({\boldsymbol{\lambda}})-\phi F^{*}({\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)})

\displaystyle\geq\left\langle-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}+{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t-1)}+\phi{\bm{X}}{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t-1)},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}\right\rangle;

\displaystyle\gamma G({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-\gamma G({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})

\displaystyle\geq\left\langle-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}+{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t-1)}-\gamma{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\right\rangle.

Dividing by
\phi
and
\gamma
, respectively, and rewriting using the definition of the divided difference gives:

\displaystyle F^{*}({\boldsymbol{\lambda}})-F^{*}({\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)})

\displaystyle\geq\left\langle\Delta_{\phi}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rangle+\left\langle{\bm{X}}{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t-1)},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}\right\rangle;

\displaystyle G({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-G({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})

\displaystyle\geq\left\langle\Delta_{\gamma}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle-\left\langle{\bm{X}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}),{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}\right\rangle.

Summing these two inequalities and applying Lemma
(
) yields:

\displaystyle\left(\frac{1}{2}\Delta_{\phi}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac{\phi}{2}\left\lVert\Delta_{\phi}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right)+\left(\frac{1}{2}\Delta_{\gamma}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac{\gamma}{2}\left\lVert\Delta_{\gamma}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right)

\displaystyle\leq F^{*}({\boldsymbol{\lambda}})-F^{*}({\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)})+G({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-G({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})+\left\langle{\bm{X}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}),{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}\right\rangle-\left\langle{\bm{X}}{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t-1)},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}\right\rangle

\displaystyle=\mathcal{L}({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)})-\mathcal{L}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})+\left\langle{\bm{X}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t-1)}),{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}\right\rangle.

This proves (
8.29
).

Now suppose
\xi=1
. In this case, the extrapolation satisfies
{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t-1)}=2\beta^{(t-1)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t-2)}
so that

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t-1)}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t-1)}-({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t-1)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t-2)})=\gamma^{2}\Delta_{\gamma}(\Delta_{\gamma}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})\triangleq\gamma^{2}\Delta_{\gamma}^{2}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)},\quad\text{for }t\geq 2.

The formula holds for
t=1
if we set
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(-1)}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(0)}
, which implies
{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(0)}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(0)}
and
\Delta_{\gamma}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(0)}=\boldsymbol{0}
.
Telescoping the sum of inequality (
8.29
) over
t=1,2,\ldots,T
proves (
8.30
).

Inequality (
8.29
) suggests that the ideal choice would be
{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t-1)}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}
, which would eliminate the last inner-product term.
However, this would result in an implicit scheme, where each iteration requires solving a coupled system as difficult as the original problem.

Using the telescoped iterate inequality (
8.30
), we now establish an upper bound on the cumulative primal-dual gap.

Lemma 223
(Primal-dual gap inequality).

Let
\{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)},{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t)},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}\}_{t\geq 0}
be the sequence generated by (PDM
1
), (PDM
2
), (PDM
3
) in Algorithm
with the parameter choice
\xi=1
, and let
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
,
{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in\real^{n}
be arbitrary. Then, for any
T\in\mathbb{N}
,

\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(\mathcal{L}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})-\mathcal{L}({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)})\right)+\frac{1-\gamma\phi\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}{2\phi}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(T)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac{1}{2\gamma}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(T)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle\quad+\frac{1-\sqrt{\gamma\phi}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}}{2\phi}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t-1)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac{1-\sqrt{\gamma\phi}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}}{2\gamma}\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t-1)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{2\phi}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(0)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac{1}{2\gamma}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(0)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

(8.31)

Proof
[of Lemma
]
We begin with the summed iterate inequality (Lemma
(
8.30
)).
Using the discrete integration-by-parts formula Lemma
(
), together with the initialization
\Delta_{\gamma}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(0)}=\boldsymbol{0}
(by initializing
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(-1)}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(0)}
), and the definition
\Delta_{\gamma}^{2}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\triangleq\Delta_{\gamma}(\Delta_{\gamma}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})
,
we rewrite the second-order term as:

\displaystyle\gamma^{2}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left\langle{\bm{X}}\Delta_{\gamma}^{2}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}\right\rangle=\gamma^{2}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left\langle{\bm{X}}\Delta_{\gamma}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t-1)},\Delta_{\gamma}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}\right\rangle+\gamma\left\langle{\bm{X}}\Delta_{\gamma}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(T)},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(T)}\right\rangle

\displaystyle\quad\quad=\gamma\phi\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left\langle{\bm{X}}\Delta_{\gamma}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t-1)},\Delta_{\phi}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}\right\rangle+\gamma\left\langle\Delta_{\gamma}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(T)},{\bm{X}}^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\lambda}}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(T)})\right\rangle.

(8.32)

For the first term on the right-hand side, by setting
\eta\triangleq\sqrt{\gamma/\phi}
, we have

\displaystyle\gamma\phi\left\langle{\bm{X}}\Delta_{\gamma}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t-1)},\Delta_{\phi}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}\right\rangle\leq\gamma\phi\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert\Delta_{\gamma}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t-1)}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert\Delta_{\phi}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}

\displaystyle\quad\leq\frac{\gamma\phi\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}}{2}\left(\eta\left\lVert\Delta_{\gamma}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t-1)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\eta^{-1}\left\lVert\Delta_{\phi}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right)

\displaystyle\quad=\frac{\phi\eta\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}}{2\gamma}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t-1)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t-2)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac{\gamma\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}}{2\eta\phi}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t-1)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle\quad\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\eta=\sqrt{\gamma/\phi}}}{{\mathrel{\rule[2.15277pt]{20.00003pt}{0.5pt}\hskip-20.00003pt\rule[-2.15277pt]{20.00003pt}{0.5pt}}}}\frac{\sqrt{\gamma\phi}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}}{2\gamma}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t-1)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t-2)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac{\sqrt{\gamma\phi}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}}{2\phi}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t-1)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},

(8.33)

where the first inequality follows from the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality (Theorem
), and the second inequality follows from the fact that
2ab\leq\eta a^{2}+b^{2}/\eta
for positive
a,b,\eta
.
Similarly, the second term satisfies

\displaystyle\footnotesize\gamma\left\langle\Delta_{\gamma}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(T)},{\bm{X}}^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\lambda}}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(T)})\right\rangle

\displaystyle\leq\frac{\gamma}{2}\left(\left\lVert\Delta_{\gamma}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(T)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(T)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right)

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2\gamma}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(T)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(T-1)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac{\gamma\phi\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}{2\phi}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(T)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

Substituting these estimates into (
8.32
) and using that
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(-1)}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(0)}
, we obtain:

\displaystyle\gamma^{2}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left\langle{\bm{X}}\Delta_{\gamma}^{2}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}\right\rangle\leq\frac{\sqrt{\gamma\phi}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}}{2\gamma}\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t-1)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle\quad+\frac{\sqrt{\gamma\phi}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}}{2\phi}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t-1)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac{1}{2\gamma}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(T)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(T-1)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac{\gamma\phi\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}{2\phi}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(T)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

Plugging this bound back into the summed iterate inequality (Lemma
(
8.30
)), and rearranging terms, yields the desired inequality (
8.31
).

Using the results above, we now establish a descent lemma for the primal-dual algorithm.

Lemma 224
(Decent lemma of primal-dual algorithm).

Let
({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}},{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}})
be a primal dual optimum, that is, a saddle point of the saddle-point problem (
).
Let
\{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)},{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t)},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}\}_{t\geq 0}
be the sequence generated by (PDM
1
), (PDM
2
), (PDM
3
) in Algorithm
with the parameter choice
\xi=1
and
\gamma\phi\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}<1
. Then, for any
T\in\mathbb{N}
,

\frac{1}{2\phi}\left\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(T)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac{1}{2\gamma}\left\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(T)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq C\left(\frac{1}{2\phi}\left\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(0)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac{1}{2\gamma}\left\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(0)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right),

where
C\triangleq(1-\gamma\phi\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2})^{-1}
. In particular, the iterates
\{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}\}
remain bounded.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
For a saddle point
({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}},{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}})
, the terms
\mathcal{L}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}},{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}})-\mathcal{L}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)})
are non-negative so that all terms on the left-hand side of (
8.31
) are positive.
Consequently

\frac{1-\gamma\phi\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}{2\phi}\left\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(T)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac{1}{2\gamma}\left\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(T)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\frac{1}{2\phi}\left\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(0)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac{1}{2\gamma}\left\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(0)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

This completes the proof.

The convergence of the primal-dual method is then established in the following theorem.

{theoremHigh}
[Convergence of primal-dual algorithm]
Let
\{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)},{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t)},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}\}_{t\geq 0}
be the sequence generated by (PDM
1
), (PDM
2
), (PDM
3
) in Algorithm
with the parameter choice
\xi=1
and
\gamma\phi\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}<1
.
Suppose that the saddle-point problem (
) has a saddle point.
Then the iterates
\{({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)})\}
converges to a saddle point
({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}},{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}})
of (
) so that
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}
converges to a minimizer of problem (
).

Proof
[of Theorem
]
By Lemma
, the sequence
\{({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)})\}
is bounded. Hence, there exists a convergent subsequence
\{({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t_{k})},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t_{k})})\}_{k}
such that

({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t_{k})},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t_{k})})\to({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\star},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{\star})
as
k\to\infty
. Choosing
({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})
to be a saddle point
({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}},{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}})
in (
8.31
) makes all terms nonnegative.
Since all terms on the left-hand side are nonnegative, we obtain in particular:

\frac{1-\sqrt{\gamma\phi}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}}{2\gamma}\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t-1)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\frac{1}{2\gamma}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(0)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac{1}{2\phi}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(0)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

Because the right-hand side is independent of
T
and
\sqrt{\gamma\phi}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}<1
, we conclude that the series
\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t-1)}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}
converges;
hence,
\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t-1)}\big\rVert_{2}\to 0
as
t\to\infty
.
An identical argument shows
\lim_{t\to\infty}\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t-1)}\big\rVert_{2}=0
.
In particular, the subsequence
({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t_{k}-1)},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t_{k}-1)})
also converges to
({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\star},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{\star})
.
It follows that
({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\star},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{\star})
is a fixed point of the primal dual algorithm. By Theorem
, it is primal-dual optimal (a saddle point).

Invoking
({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})=({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\star},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{\star})
in (
8.29
), we have
\mathcal{L}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{\star})-\mathcal{L}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\star},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)})\geq 0
by the primal-dual gap property.
Similarly to the proof of (
8.30
), telescoping the sum of (
8.29
) over
t=t_{k}
to
t=T>t_{k}
results in

\displaystyle\frac{1}{2\phi}\left(\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{\star}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(T)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{\star}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t_{k})}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right)+\frac{1}{2\gamma}\left(\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\star}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(T)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\star}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t_{k})}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right)

\displaystyle+\frac{1}{2\phi}\sum_{t=t_{k}}^{T}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t-1)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac{1}{2\gamma}\sum_{t=t_{k}}^{T}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t-1)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\gamma^{2}\sum_{t=t_{k}}^{T}\left\langle{\bm{X}}\Delta_{\gamma}^{2}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{\star}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}\right\rangle

\displaystyle=\gamma\phi\sum_{t=t_{k}}^{T}\left\langle{\bm{X}}\Delta_{\gamma}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t-1)},\Delta_{\phi}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}\right\rangle+\gamma\left\langle{\bm{X}}\Delta_{\gamma}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(T)},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{\star}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(T)}\right\rangle-\gamma\left\langle{\bm{X}}\Delta_{\gamma}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t_{k})},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{\star}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t_{k})}\right\rangle,

where the last equality follows from the discrete integration-by-parts Lemma
(
).
Inequality (
8.33
) therefore implies

\displaystyle\frac{1}{2\phi}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{\star}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(T)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac{1}{2\gamma}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\star}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(T)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac{1-\sqrt{\gamma\phi}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}}{2\phi}\sum_{t=t_{k}}^{T}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t-1)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle+\frac{1-\sqrt{\gamma\phi}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}}{2\gamma}\sum_{t=t_{k}}^{T-1}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t-1)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle+\frac{1}{2\gamma}\left(\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(T)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(T-1)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\sqrt{\gamma\phi}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t_{k}-1)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t_{k}-2)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right)

\displaystyle+\left\langle{\bm{X}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(T)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(T-1)}),{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{\star}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(T)}\right\rangle-\left\langle{\bm{X}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t_{k})}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t_{k}-1)}),{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{\star}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t_{k})}\right\rangle

\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{2\phi}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{\star}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t_{k})}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac{1}{2\gamma}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\star}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t_{k})}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

Since
\lim_{t\to\infty}\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t-1)}\big\rVert_{2}=\lim_{t\to\infty}\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t-1)}\big\rVert_{2}=0
and
\lim_{k\to\infty}\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\star}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t_{k})}\big\rVert_{2}=\lim_{k\to\infty}\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{\star}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t_{k})}\big\rVert_{2}=0
, it follows that
\lim_{T\to\infty}\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\star}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(T)}\big\rVert_{2}=\lim_{T\to\infty}\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{\star}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(T)}\big\rVert_{2}=0
.
This completes the proof.

8.6
Rate of Convergence of the Primal-Dual Algorithm

To analyze the rate of convergence of the primal-dual algorithm, we introduce the
partial primal-dual gap
.
For two sets
{\mathbb{S}}_{1}\subset\real^{p}
and
{\mathbb{S}}_{2}\subset\real^{n}
, this quantity is defined as

\mathcal{P}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{1},{\mathbb{S}}_{2}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})\triangleq\max_{{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{\prime}\in{\mathbb{S}}_{2}}\mathcal{L}({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{\prime})-\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime}\in{\mathbb{S}}_{1}}\mathcal{L}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\prime},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}).

(8.34)

This is a variant of the standard primal-dual gap defined in (
).
It is particularly convenient in our setting and is naturally motivated by the saddle-point problem (
).
Whenever the product set
{\mathbb{S}}_{1}\times{\mathbb{S}}_{2}
contains a saddle point
({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}},{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}})
, the partial gap satisfies
\mathcal{P}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{1},{\mathbb{S}}_{2}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})\geq 0
for all
{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}
, and
\mathcal{P}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{1},{\mathbb{S}}_{2}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})=0
if and only if
({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})
is itself a saddle point; see the saddle-point property (
).
Thus,
\mathcal{P}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{1},{\mathbb{S}}_{2}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})
serves as a natural measure of how far the pair
({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})
is from optimality in the saddle-point problem (
).

{theoremHigh}

[Rate of convergence of primal-dual algorithm]
Assume the same conditions as in Theorem
.
Define the averaged iterates
{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}^{(T)}\triangleq T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^{T}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}
and
{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}}}^{(T)}\triangleq T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^{T}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}
. Let
{\mathbb{S}}_{1}\subset\real^{p},{\mathbb{S}}_{2}\subset\real^{n}
be bounded sets such that
{\mathbb{S}}_{1}\times{\mathbb{S}}_{2}
contains at least one saddle point
({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}},{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}})
. Then,

\mathcal{P}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{1},{\mathbb{S}}_{2}}({\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}^{(T)},{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}}}^{(T)})\leq\frac{D({\mathbb{S}}_{1},{\mathbb{S}}_{2})}{T},

(8.35)

where
D({\mathbb{S}}_{1},{\mathbb{S}}_{2})\triangleq(2\phi)^{-1}\max_{{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\in{\mathbb{S}}_{2}}\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}+(2\gamma)^{-1}\max_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}_{1}}\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}
,
and
\mathcal{P}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{1},{\mathbb{S}}_{2}}
denotes the partial primal-dual gap defined in (
).

Proof
[of Theorem
]
By the convexity of
G
and the convex conjugate
F^{*}
, and using the primal-dual gap inequality (
8.31
), we have for any
({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})
,

\displaystyle\mathcal{L}({\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}^{(T)},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})-\mathcal{L}({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}}}^{(T)})

\displaystyle\quad=\left(\left\langle{\bm{X}}{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}^{(T)},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rangle+G({\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}}^{(T)})-F^{*}({\boldsymbol{\lambda}})\right)-\left(\left\langle{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\overline{{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}}}^{(T)}\right\rangle+G({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-F^{*}({\overline{{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}}}^{(T)})\right)

\displaystyle\quad\leq\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(\left\langle{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\right\rangle+G({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})-F^{*}({\boldsymbol{\lambda}})\right)-\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(\left\langle{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}\right\rangle+G({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-F^{*}({\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)})\right)

\displaystyle\quad\leq\frac{1}{T}\left(\frac{1}{2\phi}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}-{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(0)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac{1}{2\gamma}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(0)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right).

Taking the supremum over all
({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\lambda}})\in{\mathbb{S}}_{1}\times{\mathbb{S}}_{2}
proves (
).

The inequality (
) shows that the primal-dual algorithm achieves an
\mathcal{O}(1/T)
convergence rate in terms of the partial primal-dual gap.
Note that this bound remains valid even when
{\mathbb{S}}_{1}\times{\mathbb{S}}_{2}
does not contain a saddle point; however, in that case the partial gap
\mathcal{P}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{1},{\mathbb{S}}_{2}}
may become negative and thus loses its interpretation as a meaningful error measure.

Importantly, inequality (
) does not imply an
\mathcal{O}(1/T)
rate for the individual sequences
\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{2}
or
\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{(t)}-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}}\big\rVert_{2}
. Nevertheless, in practice the iterates often converge reasonably fast in these norms as well.

Chapter 9
Algorithms for Sparse Regression Problems

This chapter presents a comprehensive overview of algorithms designed to solve sparse optimization problems, with a focus on the
\ell_{0}
-constrained and LASSO formulations. We begin by examining iterative methods for
\ell_{0}
-constrained problems, such as the iterative hard-thresholding (IHT) method, which directly enforces sparsity constraints.
We then turn to constrained LASSO problems, discussing key approaches including projected gradient descent, proximal gradient methods, conditional gradient (Frank–Wolfe), and least angle regression (LARS).
The chapter further explores Lagrangian formulations of the LASSO, covering advanced techniques like smoothing with Huber loss, FISTA, penalty methods, ADMM, and block coordinate descent.
Finally, we extend the framework to other sparse models, including generalized LASSO, group LASSO, and sparse noise models.
Together, these algorithms form the backbone of modern sparse recovery and feature selection methods in machine learning and signal processing.

9.1
Algorithms for
\ell_{0}
-Constrainted Problems

In Section
, we will introduce several algorithms for solving the constrained LASSO problem (
LC
) (p.
LC
), including
projected gradient descent
,
proximal gradient method
, and
conditional gradient method
.
These methods are also applicable to general constrained optimization problems of the form
\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
s.t.
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
, provided that the feasible set
{\mathbb{S}}
is closed and convex.
However, in this section, we focus on sparse optimization problems where the constraint set is non-convex—specifically,
\ell_{0}
-constrained problems. Consequently, the aforementioned convex optimization techniques cannot be directly applied. Although there are some superficial similarities between the convex and non-convex settings, the theoretical guarantees and algorithmic behaviors differ significantly. To address this class of problems, we introduce the iterative hard-thresholding (IHT) algorithm.

In particular, we address the challenge of minimizing a general continuously differentiable objective function subject to a sparsity constraint, see (
) (p.
):

\text{(S${}_{0}$)}\qquad\begin{aligned} \min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{0}\leq k,\end{aligned}

(9.1)

where
f:\real^{p}\to\real
is
L_{b}
-smooth (see Definition
and Theorem
),
k>0
is an integer satisfying
k<p
, and
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{0}
denotes the so-called “
\ell_{0}
-norm” of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
, which counts the number of nonzero components in
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
:

\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{0}=\big\lvert\{i\mid\beta_{i}\neq 0,\forall\,i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}\}\big\rvert.

It is important to note that the
\ell_{0}
-norm is not a true norm, as it fails to satisfy the homogeneity property: for any scalar
\lambda\neq 0
(Definition
), we have
\left\lVert\lambda{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{0}=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{0}
(see Definition
).
Moreover, we do not assume that
f
is convex, and the constraint set is inherently non-convex.
As a result, much of the standard convex optimization theory does not apply to problem (
). Nevertheless, this problem is of central importance in applications such as compressed sensing, motivating the development of specialized algorithms and adapted analytical tools.

We recall some useful notation. For any vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
, define its support set and its complement as

{\mathbb{I}}_{1}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\triangleq\mathrm{supp}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\triangleq\{i\mid\beta_{i}\neq 0\}\qquad\text{and}\qquad{\mathbb{I}}_{0}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\triangleq\{i\mid\beta_{i}=0\}.

(9.2)

A vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is called
k
-sparse
if
\left\lvert\mathrm{supp}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rvert\leq k
, or equivalently, if
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]
(the closed
\ell_{0}
-ball of radius
k
centered at the origin:
{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]={\mathbb{B}}_{0}[\boldsymbol{0},k]
for brevity; see Definition
).
Using this notation, problem (
) can be rewritten as:

\min\;f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\qquad\text{s.t.}\quad{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k].

(9.3)

For a vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
and
i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
, let
[{\boldsymbol{\beta}}]_{i}
denote the
i
-th largest absolute value among its components
, so that

[{\boldsymbol{\beta}}]_{1}\geq[{\boldsymbol{\beta}}]_{2}\geq\ldots\geq[{\boldsymbol{\beta}}]_{p},

(9.4)

where

[{\boldsymbol{\beta}}]_{1}=\max_{i=1,\ldots,p}\left\lvert\beta_{i}\right\rvert\quad\text{and}\qquad[{\boldsymbol{\beta}}]_{p}=\min_{i=1,\ldots,p}\left\lvert\beta_{i}\right\rvert.

(9.5)

9.1.1
Optimity Condition under
L
-Stationarity

Our goal now is to explore necessary optimality conditions for problem (
). Because the
\ell_{0}
-constraint is non-convex, classical stationarity conditions from convex optimization do not generally apply. However, alternative notions of optimality—specifically tailored to the structure of sparsity constraints—can be formulated and analyzed.

We begin by extending the concept of stationarity to problem (
), using the characterization of stationarity via the projection operator. Recall that a point
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}

is stationary for the problem of minimizing a continuously differentiable function over a closed and convex set
{\mathbb{S}}
if and only if

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}=\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{S}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-\eta\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})),

(9.6)

where
\eta>0
is an arbitrary positive scalar (see Corollary
).
Although condition (
) is expressed in terms of
\eta
, it is actually independent of the choice of
\eta
.
However, this characterization does not extend directly to the case where
{\mathbb{S}}={\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]
, because the orthogonal projection onto non-convex sets such as
{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]
is not unique. Instead, the projection becomes a set-valued mapping defined by

\mathcal{P}_{{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\mathop{\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}}_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}\{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}\mid{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]\}.

By the Weierstrass theorem (Theorem

),
the existence of elements in
\mathcal{P}_{{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
follows from the closedness of
{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]
and the coercivity of the function
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}
(with respect to
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
).
To generalize condition (
) to the sparsity-constrained problem (
), we introduce the notion of “
L
-stationarity.”

Definition 225
(
L
-Stationarity).

A vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]
is called an
L
-stationary point of problem (
) if it satisfies

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\in\mathcal{P}_{{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]}\left({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-\frac{1}{L}\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})\right).

(9.7)

Because the projection operator
\mathcal{P}_{{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]}(\cdot)
is set-valued, its output consists of all vectors obtained by keeping the

k
entries of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
with the largest absolute values and setting the rest to zero.
For example,

\mathcal{P}_{{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[2]}([3,1,1]^{\top})=\big\{[3,1,0]^{\top},[3,0,1]^{\top}\big\}.

We now show that, under the assumption that
f
is
L_{b}
-smooth,
L
-stationarity is a necessary condition for optimality whenever
L>L_{b}
.
Before proving this result, we first provide a more explicit characterization of
L
-stationarity.

Lemma 226
(
L
-Stationarity).

For any
L>0
, a vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]
satisfies
L
-stationarity if and only if

\left\lvert\frac{\partial f}{\partial\beta_{i}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})\right\rvert\begin{cases}\leq L\cdot[{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}]_{k},&\text{if }i\in{\mathbb{I}}_{0}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*});\\
=0,&\text{if }i\in{\mathbb{I}}_{1}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}),\end{cases}

(9.8)

where
[{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}]_{k}
denotes the
k
-th largest absolute value among the components of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Suppose that
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
satisfies
L
-stationarity.
Note that for any index
j\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
, the
j
-th component of any vector in
\mathcal{P}_{{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-\frac{1}{L}\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}))
is either zero or equal to
x_{j}^{*}-\frac{1}{L}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{j}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})
. On the other hand, since
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\in\mathcal{P}_{{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-\frac{1}{L}\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}))
, it follows that if
i\in{\mathbb{I}}_{1}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})
, then
\beta_{i}^{*}=\beta_{i}^{*}-\frac{1}{L}\frac{\partial f}{\partial\beta_{i}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})
, so that
\frac{\partial f}{\partial\beta_{i}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})=0
. If
i\in{\mathbb{I}}_{0}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})
, then
\left\lvert\beta_{i}^{*}-\frac{1}{L}\frac{\partial f}{\partial\beta_{i}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})\right\rvert\leq[{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}]_{k}
and
\beta_{i}^{*}=0
, which yields
\big\lvert\frac{\partial f}{\partial\beta_{i}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})\big\rvert\leq L\cdot[{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}]_{k}
.
Thus, condition (
) holds.

Conversely, suppose that
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
satisfies (
). If
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{0}<k
, then
[{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}]_{k}=0
, and by (
) it follows that
\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})=\boldsymbol{0}
; therefore, in this case,
\mathcal{P}_{{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]}\left({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-\frac{1}{L}\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})\right)=\mathcal{P}_{{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})
is the set
\{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\}
, which apparently satisfies the
L
-stationarity.
On the other hand, if
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{0}=k
, then
[{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}]_{k}\neq 0
and
\left\lvert{\mathbb{I}}_{1}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})\right\rvert=k
. By (
),

\left\lvert\beta_{i}^{*}-\frac{1}{L}\frac{\partial f}{\partial\beta_{i}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})\right\rvert\begin{cases}\leq[{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}]_{k},&i\in{\mathbb{I}}_{0}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}),\\
=\left\lvert\beta_{i}^{*}\right\rvert,&i\in{\mathbb{I}}_{1}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}).\end{cases}

Therefore, the vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-\frac{1}{L}\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})
contains the
k
components of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
with the largest absolute values and all other components are smaller or equal to them in magnitude. This also implies the
L
-stationary and completes the proof.

Clearly, condition (
) depends on the constant
L
; it becomes more restrictive as
L
decreases.
This underscores a fundamental difference between the non-convex and convex settings. Before investigating the conditions under which
L
-stationarity constitutes a necessary optimality condition, we first establish a technical yet useful result.

Lemma 227
(Descent lemma for sparse projection under SS).

Let
f:\real^{p}\rightarrow\real
be an
L_{b}
-smooth function, and let
L>L_{b}
. Then for any
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]
and any
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}
satisfying

{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\mathcal{P}_{{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]}\left({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\frac{1}{L}\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right),

we have

f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\geq\frac{L-L_{b}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Since
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\mathcal{P}_{{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]}\left({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\frac{1}{L}\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right)
,
it follows that

\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}

\displaystyle\in\mathop{\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}}_{{\bm{u}}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]}\left\lVert{\bm{u}}-\left({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\frac{1}{L}\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right)\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\mathop{\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}}_{{\bm{u}}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]}\frac{L}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{u}}-\left({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\frac{1}{L}\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right)\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+C_{{\bm{u}}}

(9.9)

\displaystyle=\mathop{\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}}_{{\bm{u}}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]}\left\{f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+\left\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}),{\bm{u}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle+\frac{L}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{u}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\triangleq\Psi_{L}({\bm{u}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\},

where
C_{{\bm{u}}}\triangleq f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-\frac{1}{2L}\left\lVert\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
denotes a constant with respect to
{\bm{u}}
.
This implies that

\Psi_{L}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\leq\Psi_{L}({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}})=f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}).

By the
L_{b}
-smoothness of
f
(Definition
), we also have

f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\geq f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-\Psi_{L_{b}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\Psi_{L}({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}})-\Psi_{L_{b}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}).

Combining the preceding properties and the fact that
\Psi_{L_{b}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\Psi_{L}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}})-\frac{L-L_{b}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
yields the desired result.

We are now ready to demonstrate the necessity of
L
-stationarity for optimality when
L>L_{b}
and
f
is
L_{b}
-smooth.

{theoremHigh}

[Necessity under
L
-stationarity and smoothness]
Let
f:\real^{p}\rightarrow\real
be an
L_{b}
-smooth function (Definition
), and let
L>L_{b}
.
If
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
is an optimal solution of problem (
), then:

1.

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
is an
L
-stationary point.

2.

The set
\mathcal{P}_{{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]}\left({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-\frac{1}{L}\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})\right)
is a singleton.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Suppose, for contradiction, that the projection set contains a vector
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\neq{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
, i.e.,

{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\mathcal{P}_{{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]}\left({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-\frac{1}{L}\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})\right)
.
By Lemma
, it follows that

f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})-f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\geq\frac{L-L_{b}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},

contradicting the optimality of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
.
Thus,
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
is the only vector in the set
\mathcal{P}_{{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]}\left({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-\frac{1}{L}\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})\right)
, and
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
is
L
-stationary.

In summary, we have shown that for any
L_{b}
-smooth objective function,
L
-stationarity with any
L>L_{b}
is a necessary condition for optimality in problem (
).

9.1.2
The Iterative Hard-Thresholding (IHT) Method

Algorithm 2

Iterative Hard-Thresholding (IHT) Method

1:

Sparsity level
s
;

2:

input (a).
A differential function
f
;

3:

input (b).

f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\frac{1}{2n}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}
: design matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
and response
{\bm{y}}\in\real^{n}
;

4:

initialize:

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(1)}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[s]
;

5:

for

t=1,2,\ldots

do

6:

Pick a stepsize
\eta_{t}
;

7:

{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(a)}}{{\leftarrow}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-\eta_{t}\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})\quad\text{ or }\quad\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(b)}}{{\leftarrow}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-\eta_{t}\frac{1}{n}{\bm{X}}^{\top}({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-{\bm{y}})
;

8:

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}\in\mathcal{P}_{{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[s]}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)})
;
\triangleright
Selecting the
s
largest elements in magnitude of
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)}

9:

end

for

10:

return
final
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\leftarrow{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}
;

We previously introduced optimality conditions for general
\ell_{0}
-constrained optimization problems in Section
:

\text{(S${}_{0}$)}\qquad\begin{aligned} \min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{0}\leq k,\end{aligned}

(9.10)

A natural approach to solving problem (
) is to generalize the projected gradient descent (PGD) framework by alternating between a gradient descent step and a projection onto the non-convex sparsity set
{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]=\{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\mid\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{0}\leq k\}
(see Section
for further details).
This yields the iterative scheme

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}\in\mathcal{P}_{{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]}\left({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-\frac{1}{L}\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})\right),\quad t=1,2,\ldots.

(9.11a)

The method is known in the literature as the
iterative hard-thresholding (IHT) method
(see Algorithm
), and we adopt this terminology.
It applies both to general smooth functions
f
(under the assumptions stated in Lemma
) and to least squares objectives of the form
f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\frac{1}{2n}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}
(which satisfies certain design properties as previously discussed).
It can shown that the general step of the IHT method is equivalent to the relation

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}\in\mathop{\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]}\Psi_{L}({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}),\quad t=1,2,\ldots,

(9.11b)

where the surrogate function is defined as
\Psi_{L}({\bm{u}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\triangleq f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+\left\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}),{\bm{u}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle+\frac{L}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{u}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
as in (
).

When the constraint set
{\mathbb{S}}
is closed convex, projected gradient descent (see Algorithm
) can be interpreted as a fixed-point method for solving
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}=\mathcal{P}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\big({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-\eta\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})\big)
(Corollary
).
Although
{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]
is non-convex, the IHT method can similarly be viewed as a fixed-point iteration aimed at enforcing the
L
-stationarity condition (Definition
). Specifically, under the assumption that
f
is
L_{b}
-smooth and
L>L_{b}
, any limit point of the IHT iterates satisfies

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}=\mathcal{P}_{{\mathbb{S}}}\big({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-\frac{1}{L}\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})\big)

which, by Theorem
, is a necessary condition for optimality.
