Several fundamental convergence properties of the IHT method are summarized in the following lemma.

Lemma 228
(Properties of IHT under smoothness).

Let
f:\real^{p}\rightarrow\real
be an
L_{b}
-smooth and lower-bounded function.
Suppose
\{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\}_{t>0}
is the sequence generated by the IHT method (Algorithm
(a)) with constant stepsize
\eta\triangleq\eta_{t}\triangleq\frac{1}{L}
, where
L>L_{b}
, and a projection sparsity level
s=k
. Then,

1.

f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})-f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)})\geq\frac{L-L_{b}}{2}\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}
.

2.

The sequence
\{f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})\}_{t>0}
is nonincreasing.

3.

\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}\big\rVert_{2}\to 0
as
t\rightarrow\infty
.

4.

For every
t=1,2,\ldots
, if
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\neq{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}
, then
f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)})<f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})
.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Part (i) follows directly from Lemma
by setting
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}
and
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}
.
Part (ii) is an immediate consequence of (i), since the right-hand side is nonnegative.
To prove (iii), observe that
\{f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})\}_{t>0}
is nonincreasing and bounded below, hence convergent to some limit
B\in\real
.
Therefore,
f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}))-f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)})\to B-B=0
as
t\to\infty
. By part (i) and the fact that
L>L_{b}
, it follows that
\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}\big\rVert_{2}\to 0
.
Finally, (iv) follows directly from (i): if
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\neq{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}
, then the norm difference is positive, so the objective strictly decreases.

As previously discussed, the IHT algorithm can be interpreted as a fixed-point method for enforcing the
L
-stationarity condition.
The following theorem establishes that every accumulation point of the sequence generated by IHT with a constant stepsize
\frac{1}{L}
is indeed an
L
-stationary point.

{theoremHigh}

[Convergence of IHT
(
Beck 2014
)
]
Assume the same conditions as in Lemma
.
Let
\{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\}_{t>0}
be the sequence generated by the IHT method (Algorithm
(a)) with constant stepsize
\eta\triangleq\eta_{t}\triangleq\frac{1}{L}
, where
L>L_{b}
, and sparsity level
s=k
.
Then, any accumulation point of
\{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\}_{t>0}
is an
L
-stationary point.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Let
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
be an accumulation point of the sequence
\{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\}_{t>0}
.
Then there exists a subsequence
\{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t_{j})}\}_{j>0}
such that
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t_{j})}\rightarrow{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
as
j\rightarrow\infty
.
From Lemma
, we have

f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t_{j})})-f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t_{j}+1)})\geq\frac{L-L_{b}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t_{j})}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t_{j}+1)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

(9.12)

Since
\{f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t_{j})})\}_{j>0}
and
\{f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t_{j}+1)})\}_{j>0}
, as nonincreasing and lower-bounded sequences,
they both converge to the same limit.
Consequently,
f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t_{j})})-f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t_{j}+1)})\to 0
as
j\to\infty
, which combined with (
) yields that

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t_{j}+1)}\to{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\text{ as }j\to\infty.

Recall that for all
j>0
,

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t_{j}+1)}\in\mathcal{P}_{{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]}\left({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t_{j})}-\frac{1}{L}\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t_{j})})\right).

We then consider the following two cases.

Let
i\in{\mathbb{I}}_{1}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})
(i.e., in the support set;
{\mathbb{I}}_{1}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\triangleq\mathrm{supp}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\triangleq\{i\mid\beta_{i}\neq 0\}
). By the convergence of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t_{j})}
and
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t_{j}+1)}
to
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
, it follows that there exists an integer
J
such that

\beta_{i}^{(t_{j})},\beta_{i}^{(t_{j}+1)}\neq 0\text{ for all }j>J,

and therefore, for
j>J
,

\beta_{i}^{(t_{j}+1)}=\beta_{i}^{(t_{j})}-\frac{1}{L}\frac{\partial f}{\partial\beta_{i}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t_{j})}).

Taking the limit as
j\rightarrow\infty
and using the continuity of
f
, we obtain that

\frac{\partial f}{\partial\beta_{i}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})=0
for
i\in{\mathbb{I}}_{1}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})
.

Now let
i\in{\mathbb{I}}_{0}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})
. If there exist an infinite number of indices
t_{j}
for which
\beta_{i}^{(t_{j}+1)}\neq 0
, then as in the previous case, we obtain that
\beta_{i}^{(t_{j}+1)}=\beta_{i}^{(t_{j})}-\frac{1}{L}\frac{\partial f}{\partial\beta_{i}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t_{j})})
for these indices, implying (by taking the limit) that
\frac{\partial f}{\partial\beta_{i}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})=0
. In particular,
\left\lvert\frac{\partial f}{\partial\beta_{i}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})\right\rvert\leq L[{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}]_{k}
. On the other hand, if there exists an
M>0
such that for all
j>M
,
\beta_{i}^{(t_{j}+1)}=0
, then

\left\lvert\beta_{i}^{(t_{j})}-\frac{1}{L}\frac{\partial f}{\partial\beta_{i}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t_{j})})\right\rvert\leq\big[{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t_{j})}-\frac{1}{L}\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t_{j})})\big]_{k}=\big[{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t_{j}+1)}\big]_{k}.

Taking the limit as
j\rightarrow\infty
, and using the continuity of the mapping
[\cdot]_{k}
(which holds at points where the
k
-th and
(k+1)
-th largest magnitudes are distinct—a condition satisfied along the subsequence due to convergence to
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
), we obtain that

\left\lvert\frac{\partial f}{\partial\beta_{i}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})\right\rvert\leq L[{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}]_{k},\quad i\in{\mathbb{I}}_{0}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}).

Combining both cases, we conclude that
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}

satisfies the
L
-stationarity by Lemma
.

We now establish an important result: if the design matrix satisfies the restricted isometry property (RIP; see Definition
) with suitable constants, then the IHT algorithm guarantees universal sparse recovery for the least squares objective:
f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\frac{1}{2n}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}
.

{theoremHigh}
[Rate of convergence of IHT under RIP
(
Jain et al. 2014
;
Jain et al. 2017
)
]
Suppose
\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
satisfies the RIP of order
3k
with constant
\delta_{3k}<\frac{1}{2}
.
Let
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]\subset\real^{p}
be any
k
-sparse vector, and let
{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
. Then the IHT algorithm (Algorithm
(b)), when executed with constant stepsize
\eta_{t}=1
and sparsity level
s=k
,
produces a sequence
\{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\}
such that
\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\big\rVert_{2}\leq\epsilon
after at most
t=\mathcal{O}\left(\ln\frac{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{2}}{\epsilon}\right)
iterations.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Let
{\mathbb{S}}^{*}\triangleq\text{supp}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})
and
{\mathbb{S}}^{t}\triangleq\text{supp}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})
.
Define the index set
{\mathbb{I}}^{t}\triangleq{\mathbb{S}}^{t}\cup{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}\cup{\mathbb{S}}^{*}
, which contains the supports of two consecutive iterates and the true support.
Since each set has cardinality at most
k
, we have
\left\lvert{\mathbb{I}}^{t}\right\rvert\leq 3k
.
Crucially, both error vectors
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
and
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
are supported on
{\mathbb{I}}^{t}
.

With stepsize
\eta_{t}=1
, the gradient step in Algorithm
(b) yields
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-\frac{1}{n}{\bm{X}}^{\top}({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-{\bm{y}})
.
Although
{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]
is non-convex, the projection
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}=\mathcal{P}_{{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)})
satisfies the basic optimality property (Projection Property-O; see Lemma
):

\displaystyle\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle\implies\quad\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}^{(t+1)}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}^{(t+1)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}^{c}}^{(t+1)}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{I}}^{c}}^{(t+1)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}^{*}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}^{(t+1)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}^{c}}^{*}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{I}}^{c}}^{(t+1)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},

where, for brevity, we denote
{\mathbb{I}}\triangleq{\mathbb{I}}^{t}
such that
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}^{c}}^{(t+1)}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}^{c}}^{*}=\boldsymbol{0}
.
Using the fact that
{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
, and denoting
\widetilde{\bm{X}}\triangleq\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}{\bm{X}}
and
\widetilde{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}\triangleq\widetilde{\bm{X}}[:,{\mathbb{I}}]
, we obtain

\displaystyle\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{2}

\displaystyle=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}^{(t+1)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}^{*}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}^{(t+1)}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}^{(t+1)}\right\rVert_{2}+\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}^{(t+1)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}^{*}\right\rVert_{2}\leq 2\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}^{(t+1)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}^{*}\right\rVert_{2}

\displaystyle=2\left\lVert\left({\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}^{(t)}-\widetilde{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}^{\top}\widetilde{\bm{X}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})\right)-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}^{*}\right\rVert_{2}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\dagger}}}{{=}}2\left\lVert({\bm{I}}-\widetilde{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}^{\top}\widetilde{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{I}}})({\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}^{*})\right\rVert_{2}

\displaystyle\leq 2\left\lVert\widetilde{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}^{\top}\widetilde{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}-{\bm{I}}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}^{*}\right\rVert_{2}\leq 2\delta_{3k}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{2},

where the equality (
{\dagger}
) follows since
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}^{c}}^{(t)}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}^{c}}^{*}=\boldsymbol{0}
,
and the last inequality follows from the RIP condition (Definition
or Remark
).
To achieve
\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\big\rVert_{2}\leq\epsilon
, it suffices to take

t=\mathcal{O}\left(\ln\frac{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{2}}{\epsilon}\right)
with initialization
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(1)}=\boldsymbol{0}
, which completes the proof.

The above theorem establishes the convergence rate of the IHT algorithm for the least squares objective.
To extend this result to a general smooth objective function, we first require the following lemma concerning the sparsity projection operator.

Lemma 229
(Sparsity projection property).

Let
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
, and let
{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\triangleq\mathcal{\mathcal{P}}_{{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
denote its best
k
-sparse approximation.
Then, for any
k^{*}
-sparse vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k^{*}]\subseteq\real^{p}
with
k^{*}\leq k\leq p
, the following inequality holds:

\frac{\big\lVert{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}}{p-k}\leq\frac{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}{p-k^{*}}\qquad\implies\qquad\big\lVert{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\frac{p-k}{p-k^{*}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
Without loss of generality, assume the coordinates of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
are ordered so that
\left\lvert\beta_{1}\right\rvert\geq\left\lvert\beta_{2}\right\rvert\geq\ldots\geq\left\lvert\beta_{p}\right\rvert
.
Since the projection operator
\mathcal{\mathcal{P}}_{{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
operates by selecting the largest elements by magnitude, we have
{\widetilde{\beta}}_{1}=\beta_{1},{\widetilde{\beta}}_{2}=\beta_{2}\ldots,{\widetilde{\beta}}_{k}=\beta_{k}
and
{\widetilde{\beta}}_{k+1}={\widetilde{\beta}}_{k+2}=\ldots={\widetilde{\beta}}_{p}=0
.

Similarly, define
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\triangleq\mathcal{P}_{{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k^{*}]}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})

so that
{\widehat{\beta}}_{1}=\beta_{1},{\widehat{\beta}}_{2}=\beta_{2},\ldots,{\widehat{\beta}}_{k^{*}}=\beta_{k^{*}}
and
{\widehat{\beta}}_{k^{*}+1}={\widehat{\beta}}_{k^{*}+2}=\ldots={\widehat{\beta}}_{p}=0
.
Since
k^{*}\leq k
, we compute

\displaystyle(p-k)

\displaystyle(p-k^{*})\bigg(\frac{\left\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}{p-k^{*}}-\frac{\big\lVert{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}}{p-k}\bigg)=(p-k)\sum_{i=k^{*}+1}^{p}\beta_{i}^{2}-(p-k^{*})\sum_{i=k+1}^{p}\beta_{i}^{2}

(9.13)

\displaystyle=(p-k)\sum_{i=k^{*}+1}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}k}}\beta_{i}^{2}+\big((p-k)-(p-k^{*})\big)\sum_{i=k+1}^{p}\beta_{i}^{2}

\displaystyle\geq(p-k)(k-k^{*})\beta_{k}^{2}+(k^{*}-k)(p-k)\beta_{k+1}^{2}\geq 0.

Finally, by the optimality of the projection (the Projection Property-O; see Lemma
), we have
\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\big\rVert_{2}\leq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}
for any
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k^{*}]
, which establishes the desired result when combining with the above inequality.

For a more general objective function
f
(not necessarily least squares), suppose there exists an optimal
k^{*}
-sparse parameter
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}=\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{0}\leq k^{*}}f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
.
Our analysis combines the above projection property with the restricted strong convexity (RSC) and restricted smoothness (RSS) assumptions on
f
to establish geometric convergence of IHT.

{theoremHigh}

[Rate of convergence of IHT under RSC & RSS
(
Jain et al. 2014
)
]
Assume
f
satisfies RSC and RSS with parameters
\mu_{2k+k^{*}}(f)=L_{a}>0
and
\nu_{2k+k^{*}}(f)=L_{b}>0
, respectively (Definition
or Definition
).
Let Algorithm
be invoked with
f
,
s\triangleq k\geq 32\left(\frac{L_{b}}{L_{a}}\right)^{2}k^{*}
, and a constant stepsize
\eta_{t}=\frac{2}{3L_{b}}
. Also let
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}=\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{0}\leq k^{*}}f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
. Then, the
T
-th iterate of Algorithm
(a), for
T=\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{L_{b}}{L_{a}}\cdot\ln\left(\frac{f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(1)})}{\epsilon}\right)\right)
satisfies:

f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(T)})-f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})\leq\epsilon.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Denote
{\bm{g}}^{(t)}\triangleq\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})
, recall that
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}=\mathcal{\mathcal{P}}_{{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-\frac{\gamma}{L_{b}}{\bm{g}}^{(t)})
where
\gamma=\frac{2}{3}<1
. Let
{\mathbb{S}}^{t}\triangleq\mathrm{supp}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})
,
{\mathbb{S}}^{*}\triangleq\mathrm{supp}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})
, and
{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}\triangleq\mathrm{supp}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)})
. Also, let
{\mathbb{I}}\triangleq{\mathbb{S}}^{*}\cup{\mathbb{S}}^{t}\cup{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}
.
Given the RSS property (Definition
) and the fact that
\mathrm{supp}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})\subseteq{\mathbb{I}}
and
\mathrm{supp}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)})\subseteq{\mathbb{I}}
(implying that
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}^{c}}^{(t+1)}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}^{c}}^{(t)}=\boldsymbol{0}
), along with the fact that
\left\lVert{\bm{u}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{{\mathbb{I}}^{c}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
for any vector
{\bm{u}}\in\real^{p}
, we have:

\displaystyle f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)})-f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})\leq\left\langle{\bm{g}}^{(t)},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\right\rangle+\frac{L_{b}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},

(9.14)

\displaystyle=\frac{L_{b}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}_{{\mathbb{I}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}_{{\mathbb{I}}}+\frac{\gamma}{L_{b}}\cdot{\bm{g}}^{(t)}_{{\mathbb{I}}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\frac{\gamma^{2}}{2L_{b}}\left\lVert{\bm{g}}^{(t)}_{{\mathbb{I}}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+(1-\gamma)\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)},{\bm{g}}^{(t)}\right\rangle.

Since
{\mathbb{S}}^{t}\setminus{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}
and
{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}
are disjoint, we have:

\displaystyle\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)},{\bm{g}}^{(t)}\right\rangle=\left\langle\,\cancel{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t}\setminus{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t}\setminus{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}},{\bm{g}}^{(t)}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t}\setminus{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}}\right\rangle+\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}},{\bm{g}}^{(t)}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}}\right\rangle

(9.15)

\displaystyle\overset{{\dagger}}{=}-\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t}\setminus{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}},{\bm{g}}^{(t)}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t}\setminus{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}}\right\rangle-\frac{\gamma}{L_{b}}\left\lVert{\bm{g}}^{(t)}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle\overset{{\ddagger}}{\leq}\frac{\gamma}{2L_{b}}\left\lVert{\bm{g}}^{(t)}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}\setminus{\mathbb{S}}^{t}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\frac{\gamma}{2L_{b}}\left\lVert{\bm{g}}^{(t)}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t}\setminus{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\frac{\gamma}{L_{b}}\left\lVert{\bm{g}}^{(t)}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\cancel{-\left(\frac{L_{b}}{2\gamma}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t}\setminus{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right)}

\displaystyle\overset{*}{=}-\frac{\gamma}{2L_{b}}\left\lVert{\bm{g}}^{(t)}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}\setminus{\mathbb{S}}^{t}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\frac{\gamma}{2L_{b}}\left\lVert{\bm{g}}^{(t)}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t}\setminus{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\frac{\gamma}{L_{b}}\left\lVert{\bm{g}}^{(t)}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t}\cap{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq-\frac{\gamma}{2L_{b}}\left\lVert{\bm{g}}^{(t)}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t}\cup{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},

where the equality
({\dagger})
follows from the gradient step, i.e.,
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}}-\frac{\gamma}{L_{b}}{\bm{g}}^{(t)}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}}
, the inequality
({\ddagger})
follows using the fact that
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}
is obtained using hard-thresholding (
{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}
contains the indices of largest
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}\right\rvert=\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}^{t}\right\rvert
magnitudes) and the fact that
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}^{t}\setminus{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}\right\rvert=\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}\setminus{\mathbb{S}}^{t}\right\rvert
, such that

\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t}\setminus{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}}^{(t)}-\frac{\gamma}{L_{b}}{\bm{g}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t}\setminus{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}}^{(t)}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}\setminus{\mathbb{S}}^{t}}^{(t+1)}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}=\frac{\gamma^{2}}{L_{b}^{2}}\big\lVert{\bm{g}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}\setminus{\mathbb{S}}^{t}}^{(t)}\big\rVert_{2}^{2},

and the equality
(*)
follows from
\big\lVert{\bm{g}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}}^{(t)}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}=\big\lVert{\bm{g}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}\setminus{\mathbb{S}}^{t}}^{(t)}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}+\big\lVert{\bm{g}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t}\cap{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}}^{(t)}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}
.
Combining (
) and (
) yields

\displaystyle f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)})-f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})

(9.16)

\displaystyle\leq\frac{L_{b}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}^{(t+1)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}^{(t)}+\frac{\gamma}{L_{b}}{\bm{g}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\frac{\gamma^{2}}{2L_{b}}\left\lVert{\bm{g}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\frac{\gamma(1-\gamma)}{2L_{b}}\left\lVert{\bm{g}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t}\cup{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle=\frac{L_{b}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}^{(t+1)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}^{(t)}+\frac{\gamma}{L_{b}}{\bm{g}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\frac{\gamma^{2}}{2L_{b}}\left\lVert{\bm{g}}_{{\mathbb{I}}\setminus({\mathbb{S}}^{t}\cup{\mathbb{S}}^{*})}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle-\frac{\gamma^{2}}{2L_{b}}\left\lVert{\bm{g}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t}\cup{\mathbb{S}}^{*}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\frac{\gamma(1-\gamma)}{2L_{b}}\left\lVert{\bm{g}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t}\cup{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

Next, we will upper bound the first two terms on the right-hand side of the above inequality. Since
{\mathbb{I}}\setminus({\mathbb{S}}^{t}\cup{\mathbb{S}}^{*})={\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}\setminus({\mathbb{S}}^{t}\cup{\mathbb{S}}^{*})\subseteq{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}
, we have
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}\setminus({\mathbb{S}}^{t}\cup{\mathbb{S}}^{*})}^{(t+1)}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}\setminus({\mathbb{S}}^{t}\cup{\mathbb{S}}^{*})}^{(t)}-\frac{\gamma}{L_{b}}{\bm{g}}_{{\mathbb{I}}\setminus({\mathbb{S}}^{t}\cup{\mathbb{S}}^{*})}^{(t)}
.
However, since
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}\setminus{\mathbb{S}}^{t}}^{(t)}=\boldsymbol{0}
, the preceding equality reduces to
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}\setminus({\mathbb{S}}^{t}\cup{\mathbb{S}}^{*})}^{(t+1)}=-\frac{\gamma}{L_{b}}{\bm{g}}_{{\mathbb{I}}\setminus({\mathbb{S}}^{t}\cup{\mathbb{S}}^{*})}^{(t)}
.
Let
{\mathbb{T}}\subseteq{\mathbb{S}}^{t}\setminus{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}
such that
\left\lvert{\mathbb{T}}\right\rvert=\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}\setminus({\mathbb{S}}^{t}\cup{\mathbb{S}}^{*})\right\rvert
. Such a choice is possible since
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}\setminus({\mathbb{S}}^{t}\cup{\mathbb{S}}^{*})\right\rvert=\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}^{t}\setminus{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}\right\rvert-\left\lvert({\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}\cap{\mathbb{S}}^{*})\setminus{\mathbb{S}}^{t}\right\rvert
(which itself is a consequence of the fact that
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}\right\rvert=\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}^{t}\right\rvert
such that
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}^{t}\setminus{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}\right\rvert=\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}\setminus{\mathbb{S}}^{t}\right\rvert
). Moreover, since
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}
is obtained by hard-thresholding
\left({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-\frac{\gamma}{L_{b}}{\bm{g}}^{(t)}\right)
, for any choice of
{\mathbb{T}}
made above, we have:

\frac{\gamma^{2}}{L_{b}^{2}}\left\lVert{\bm{g}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}\setminus({\mathbb{S}}^{t}\cup{\mathbb{S}}^{*})}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}\setminus({\mathbb{S}}^{t}\cup{\mathbb{S}}^{*})}^{(t+1)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\geq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\mathbb{T}}^{(t)}-\frac{\gamma}{L_{b}}{\bm{g}}_{\mathbb{T}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

(9.17)

Using the above equation, the fact that
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\mathbb{T}}^{(t+1)}=\boldsymbol{0}
(since
{\mathbb{T}}\nsubseteq{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}
), and the fact that
{\mathbb{I}}\setminus({\mathbb{S}}^{t}\cup{\mathbb{S}}^{*})={\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}\setminus({\mathbb{S}}^{t}\cup{\mathbb{S}}^{*})
, the first two terms of equality (
) becomes

\displaystyle\frac{L_{b}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}^{(t+1)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}^{(t)}+\frac{\gamma}{L_{b}}{\bm{g}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\frac{\gamma^{2}}{2L_{b}}\left\lVert{\bm{g}}_{{\mathbb{I}}\setminus({\mathbb{S}}^{t}\cup{\mathbb{S}}^{*})}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

(9.18)

\displaystyle\leq\frac{L_{b}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}^{(t+1)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}^{(t)}+\frac{\gamma}{L_{b}}{\bm{g}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\frac{L_{b}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\mathbb{T}}^{(t+1)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\mathbb{T}}^{(t)}+\frac{\gamma}{L_{b}}{\bm{g}}_{\mathbb{T}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle=\frac{L_{b}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}\setminus{\mathbb{T}}}^{(t+1)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}\setminus{\mathbb{T}}}^{(t)}+\frac{\gamma}{L_{b}}{\bm{g}}_{{\mathbb{I}}\setminus{\mathbb{T}}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

Since we construct the set
{\mathbb{T}}
such that
{\mathbb{T}}\subseteq{\mathbb{S}}^{t}\setminus{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}
satisfying
\left\lvert{\mathbb{T}}\right\rvert=\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}\setminus({\mathbb{S}}^{t}\cup{\mathbb{S}}^{*})\right\rvert=\left\lvert{\mathbb{I}}\setminus({\mathbb{S}}^{t}\cup{\mathbb{S}}^{*})\right\rvert
, we can bound the size of
{\mathbb{I}}\setminus{\mathbb{T}}
as
\left\lvert{\mathbb{I}}\setminus{\mathbb{T}}\right\rvert\leq\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}^{t}\right\rvert+\left\lvert({\mathbb{S}}^{t}\setminus{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1})\setminus{\mathbb{T}}\right\rvert+\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}^{*}\right\rvert\leq k+\left\lvert({\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}\cap{\mathbb{S}}^{*})\setminus{\mathbb{S}}^{t}\right\rvert+k^{*}\leq k+2k^{*}
. Also, since
{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}\subseteq({\mathbb{I}}\setminus{\mathbb{T}})
, we have
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}\setminus{\mathbb{T}}}^{(t+1)}=\mathcal{P}_{{\mathbb{B}}_{0}[k]}\left({\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}\setminus{\mathbb{T}}}^{(t)}-\frac{\gamma}{L_{b}}{\bm{g}}_{{\mathbb{I}}\setminus{\mathbb{T}}}^{(t)}\right)
.

Given the above observation with (
) and the assumption that
k\geq 32\left(\frac{L_{b}}{L_{a}}\right)^{2}k^{*}
, Lemma
is valid with
{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\triangleq{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}\setminus{\mathbb{T}}}^{(t+1)}+\frac{\gamma}{L_{b}}{\bm{g}}_{{\mathbb{I}}\setminus{\mathbb{T}}}^{(t)}
and
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\triangleq{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}\setminus{\mathbb{T}}}^{(t)}
, whence we reduce the first two terms of equality (
) to

\displaystyle\frac{L_{b}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}^{(t+1)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}^{(t)}+\frac{\gamma}{L_{b}}{\bm{g}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\frac{\gamma^{2}}{2L_{b}}\left\lVert{\bm{g}}_{{\mathbb{I}}\setminus({\mathbb{S}}^{t}\cup{\mathbb{S}}^{*})}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\frac{L_{b}}{2}\cdot\frac{\left\lvert{\mathbb{I}}\setminus{\mathbb{T}}\right\rvert-k}{\left\lvert{\mathbb{I}}\setminus{\mathbb{T}}\right\rvert-k^{*}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}\setminus{\mathbb{T}}}^{*}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}\setminus{\mathbb{T}}}^{(t)}+\frac{\gamma}{L_{b}}{\bm{g}}_{{\mathbb{I}}\setminus{\mathbb{T}}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

(9.19)

\displaystyle\overset{{\dagger}}{\leq}\frac{L_{b}}{2}\cdot\frac{2k^{*}}{k+k^{*}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}^{*}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}^{(t)}+\frac{\gamma}{L_{b}}{\bm{g}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\frac{2k^{*}}{k+k^{*}}\cdot\left(\gamma\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)},{\bm{g}}^{(t)}\right\rangle+\frac{L_{b}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac{\gamma^{2}}{2L_{b}}\left\lVert{\bm{g}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right)

\displaystyle\overset{{\ddagger}}{\leq}\frac{2k^{*}}{k+k^{*}}\cdot\left(\gamma f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})-\gamma f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})+\frac{L_{b}-\gamma L_{a}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac{\gamma^{2}}{2L_{b}}\left\lVert{\bm{g}}_{{\mathbb{I}}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right),

where the inequality
({\dagger})
follows from
\left\lvert{\mathbb{I}}\setminus{\mathbb{T}}\right\rvert\leq k+2k^{*}
as shown earlier and the observation that
\frac{z-a}{z-b}
is a positive and increasing function on the interval
z\geq a
if
a\geq b\geq 0
. Note that since we already have
{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}\subseteq({\mathbb{I}}\setminus{\mathbb{T}})
, we get
\left\lvert{\mathbb{I}}\setminus{\mathbb{T}}\right\rvert\geq k
. The inequality
({\ddagger})
follows by the RSC property of functions (Definition
).

Plugging (
) into the first two terms of equality (
), and using the fact that
{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}\setminus({\mathbb{S}}^{t}\cup{\mathbb{S}}^{*})\subseteq({\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}\cup{\mathbb{S}}^{t})
, we get:

\displaystyle f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)})-f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})

\displaystyle\leq\frac{2k^{*}}{k+k^{*}}\cdot\left(\gamma f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})-\gamma f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})+\frac{L_{b}-\gamma L_{a}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac{\gamma^{2}}{2L_{b}}\left\lVert{\bm{g}}_{\mathbb{I}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right)

(9.20)

\displaystyle-\frac{\gamma^{2}}{2L_{b}}\left\lVert{\bm{g}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t}\cup{\mathbb{S}}^{*}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\frac{\gamma(1-\gamma)}{2L_{b}}\left\lVert{\bm{g}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}\setminus({\mathbb{S}}^{t}\cup{\mathbb{S}}^{*})}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

Since
\gamma=2/3
and
k\geq 32\left(\frac{L_{b}}{L_{a}}\right)^{2}k^{*}
, so that we have
\frac{2k^{*}}{k+k^{*}}\leq\frac{L_{a}^{2}}{16L_{b}(L_{b}-\gamma L_{a})}
. Since
L_{b}\geq L_{a}
, we also have
\frac{L_{a}^{2}}{16L_{b}(L_{b}-\gamma L_{a})}\leq\frac{3}{16}
. Using these inequalities, rearrange the terms in (
) above:

\displaystyle f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)})-f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})

\displaystyle\leq\frac{2k^{*}}{k+k^{*}}\cdot\gamma\cdot\left(f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})-f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})\right)+\frac{L_{a}^{2}}{32L_{b}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac{1}{24L_{b}}\left\lVert{\bm{g}}_{\mathbb{I}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

(9.21)

\displaystyle-\frac{2}{9L_{b}}\left\lVert{\bm{g}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t}\cup{\mathbb{S}}^{*}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\frac{1}{9L_{b}}\left\lVert{\bm{g}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}\setminus({\mathbb{S}}^{t}\cup{\mathbb{S}}^{*})}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

Decomposing
\big\lVert{\bm{g}}_{\mathbb{I}}^{(t)}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}=\big\lVert{\bm{g}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t}\cup{\mathbb{S}}^{*}}^{(t)}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}+\big\lVert{\bm{g}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}\setminus({\mathbb{S}}^{t}\cup{\mathbb{S}}^{*})}^{(t)}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}
implies

\displaystyle f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)})-f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})

\displaystyle\leq\frac{2k^{*}}{k+k^{*}}\cdot\gamma\cdot\left(f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})-f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})\right)-\frac{1}{2L_{b}}\left(\frac{13}{36}\left\lVert{\bm{g}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t}\cup{\mathbb{S}}^{*}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\frac{L_{a}^{2}}{16}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right)

(9.22)

\displaystyle-\frac{1}{2L_{b}}\cdot\left(\frac{4}{9}-\frac{1}{12}\right)\left\lVert{\bm{g}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t+1}\setminus({\mathbb{S}}^{t}\cup{\mathbb{S}}^{*})}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle\leq\frac{2k^{*}}{k+k^{*}}\cdot\gamma\cdot\left(f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})-f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})\right)-\frac{13}{72L_{b}}\left(\left\lVert{\bm{g}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t}\cup{\mathbb{S}}^{*}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\frac{L_{a}^{2}}{4}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right).

Using the RSC property, we have:

\displaystyle f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})-f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})

\displaystyle\leq\left\langle{\bm{g}}^{(t)},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rangle-\frac{L_{a}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left\langle{\bm{g}}^{(t)}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t}\cup{\mathbb{S}}^{*}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t}\cup{\mathbb{S}}^{*}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t}\cup{\mathbb{S}}^{*}}\right\rangle-\frac{L_{a}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle\leq\left\lVert{\bm{g}}^{(t)}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t}\cup{\mathbb{S}}^{*}}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{2}-\frac{L_{a}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

This shows

\displaystyle\left\lVert{\bm{g}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t}\cup{\mathbb{S}}^{*}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle-\frac{L_{a}^{2}}{4}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left(\left\lVert{\bm{g}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t}\cup{\mathbb{S}}^{*}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}-\frac{L_{a}}{2}{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}}\right)\left(\left\lVert{\bm{g}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t}\cup{\mathbb{S}}^{*}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}+\frac{L_{a}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}\right)

\displaystyle\geq\frac{(f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})-f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}))}{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{2}}\cdot\left(\left\lVert{\bm{g}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{t}\cup{\mathbb{S}}^{*}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}+\frac{L_{a}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}\right)\geq\frac{L_{a}}{2}\cdot(f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})-f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})).

Plugging this inequality into (
) yields

\displaystyle f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)})-f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})

\displaystyle\leq\frac{2k^{*}}{k+k^{*}}\cdot\gamma\cdot\left(f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})-f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})\right)-\frac{L_{a}}{12L_{b}}\left(f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})-f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})\right)

(9.23)

\displaystyle=-\left(\frac{2k^{*}}{k+k^{*}}\cdot\gamma+\frac{L_{a}}{12L_{b}}\right)\left(f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})-f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})\right).

The result follows by observing that
\frac{2k^{*}}{k+k^{*}}\geq 0
.

9.2
Algorithms for Constrained LASSO Problems

Instead of enforcing an
\ell_{0}
-constraint—as in the IHT method—the original formulation of the constrained LASSO (
LC
) (p.
LC
) is given by:

\mathop{\min}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\triangleq\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\Sigma\}\equiv\{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{B}}_{1}[\Sigma]\},

(9.24)

where
{\mathbb{B}}_{1}[\Sigma]\triangleq\{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}\mid\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\Sigma\}
denotes the closed
\ell_{1}
-ball of radius
\Sigma
.
Since
{\mathbb{B}}_{1}[\Sigma]
is convex, a natural approach to solving this problem is
projected gradient descent (PGD)
, which alternates between a gradient descent step and a projection onto the feasible set
{\mathbb{B}}_{1}[\Sigma]
.

Algorithm 3

Projected (Sub)Gradient Descent (PGD) Method

1:

A function
f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
and a set
{\mathbb{S}}
;

2:

initialize:

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(1)}
;

3:

for

t=1,2,\ldots

do

4:

Choose a stepsize
\eta_{t}
;

5:

{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)}\leftarrow{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-\eta_{t}\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})
or
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)}\leftarrow{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-\eta_{t}f^{\prime}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})
, where
f^{\prime}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})\in\partial f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})
;

6:

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}\in\mathcal{P}_{{\mathbb{S}}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)})
;

7:

Stop if a stopping criterion is satisfied at iteration
t=T
;

8:

end

for

9:

(Output Option 1) Output
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{final}}\leftarrow{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(T)}
;

10:

(Output Option 2) Output
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{avg}}\leftarrow\frac{1}{T}(\sum_{t=1}^{t}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})
or
\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{2t}{T(T+1)}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}
;

11:

(Output Option 3) Output
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{best}}\leftarrow\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{t\in\{1,2,\ldots,T\}}f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})
;

9.2.1
Projected Gradient Descent (PGD)

Standard gradient descent is designed for unconstrained optimization problems. To handle constraints, the projected gradient descent (PGD) method—described in Algorithm
—solves problems of the form:

\text{(C1)}:\qquad\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}.

(9.25)

Section
discusses optimality conditions for such constrained problems.
PGD is the most straightforward first-order method for solving (C1) and serves as a foundational building block in constrained optimization. Many advanced algorithms—including the proximal gradient method—are natural extensions of PGD; see Chapter 4 of
Lu 2025
for further discussion.

When
{\mathbb{S}}
is closed and convex and the stepsize
\eta_{t}\equiv\eta
is constant, a fixed point
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
of the PGD update satisfies the stationarity condition:

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}=\mathcal{P}_{{\mathbb{S}}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-\eta\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}))

as stated in Corollary
.
Because PGD closely resembles the proximal gradient method, we will analyze its convergence within the proximal framework in the following sections.

More precisely, the PGD update from iteration
t
to
t+1
can be equivalently written as:

\small\textbf{(PGD)}:\hskip 9.24994pt\begin{aligned} {\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}&\leftarrow\mathcal{P}_{{\mathbb{S}}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-\eta_{t}\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}))\\
&=\mathop{\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\left({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-\eta_{t}\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})\right)\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\\
&=\mathop{\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}}\left\{\frac{1}{2\eta_{t}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})+\left\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}),{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\right\rangle\right\}.\end{aligned}

(9.26)

In the third line, the constant term
f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})
does not affect the minimizer and is included only for interpretability.
This formulation reveals that each PGD step minimizes a local linear model of the objective
f
, regularized by a quadratic proximity term that penalizes large deviations from the current iterate
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}
.

The linear term encourages progress in the direction of decreasing
f
, while the quadratic term ensures stability by keeping the next iterate close to the current one. This decomposition provides key intuition for designing more sophisticated first-order methods—such as the proximal gradient method, conditional gradient (Frank–Wolfe) method, and mirror descent—all of which balance local approximation with regularization tailored to the problem geometry.

Projection onto
\ell_{1}
-Ball

To apply PGD to the constrained LASSO (
LC
), we must solve the following subproblem at each iteration: given a vector
{\bm{v}}\in\real^{p}
, compute its Euclidean projection onto the
\ell_{1}
-ball of radius
\Sigma
i.e., solve:

\mathcal{P}_{{\mathbb{B}}_{1}[\Sigma]}({\bm{v}})\equiv\left\{\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{v}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\Sigma\right\}.

This is a convex optimization problem with a unique solution that can be computed efficiently
(
Duchi et al. 2008
)
.

The projection
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}=\mathcal{P}_{{\mathbb{B}}_{1}[\Sigma]}({\bm{v}})
is obtained via
soft-thresholding
(see Example
) and proceeds as follows:

1.

If
\left\lVert{\bm{v}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\Sigma
, then
{\bm{v}}
already lies in the in the
\ell_{1}
-ball, so
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}={\bm{v}}
.

2.

Otherwise (i.e.,
\left\lVert{\bm{v}}\right\rVert_{1}>\Sigma
), the projection is given by

\beta^{*}_{i}=\sign(v_{i})\cdot[\left\lvert v_{i}\right\rvert-\lambda]_{+},\quad\forall\,i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\},

where
[\cdot]_{+}\triangleq\max(\cdot,0)
, and
\lambda\geq 0
is chosen such that:

\sum_{i=1}^{p}[\left\lvert v_{i}\right\rvert-\lambda]_{+}=\Sigma.

In other words,
\lambda
is the unique nonnegative scalar that ensures the soft-thresholded vector has
\ell_{1}
-norm exactly equal to
\Sigma
.
Intuitively, we uniformly shrink the magnitudes of all components of
{\bm{v}}
until the total
\ell_{1}
-norm reaches the constraint boundary
\Sigma
.

Equivalently, we seek
\lambda
such that
\left\lVert\mathcal{T}_{\lambda}({\bm{v}})\right\rVert_{1}=\Sigma
,
where the soft-thresholding operator
\mathcal{T}_{\lambda}({\bm{v}})
acts componentwise as
\big(\mathcal{T}_{\lambda}({\bm{v}})\big)_{i}=\sign(v_{i})[\left\lvert v_{i}\right\rvert-\lambda]_{+}
.
This reduces to solving the scalar equation:

\sum_{i=1}^{p}[\left\lvert v_{i}\right\rvert-\lambda]_{+}=\Sigma
.
Let
b_{i}\triangleq\left\lvert v_{i}\right\rvert
, and sort them in descending order:
b_{(1)}\geq b_{(2)}\geq\ldots\geq b_{(p)}
.
An efficient algorithm to compute
\lambda
proceeds as follows:

1.

Compute
b_{i}=\left\lvert v_{i}\right\rvert
for all
i
.

2.

Sort
{\bm{b}}
in descending order:
b_{(1)}\geq b_{(2)}\geq\ldots\geq b_{(p)}
.

3.

Compute cumulative sums
S_{t}\triangleq\sum_{i=1}^{t}b_{(i)}
.

4.

Find the largest
t\in\{1,2,\dots,p\}
such that
b_{(t)}>\frac{S_{t}-\Sigma}{t}
.
This ensures
\lambda<b_{(t)}
.

5.

Set

\lambda\triangleq\frac{S_{t}-\Sigma}{t}.

(9.27)

6.

Apply soft-thresholding:

\beta^{*}_{i}=\sign(v_{i})\cdot[\left\lvert v_{i}\right\rvert-\lambda]_{+}.

(9.28)

Example 230
.

Let
{\bm{v}}=[3,-2,1]
,
\Sigma=3
.
Since
\left\lVert{\bm{v}}\right\rVert_{1}=6>3
, projection is required.
The absolute values are
{\bm{b}}=[3,2,1]
, already sorted in descending order.

Try
t=1
:
S_{1}=3
, so
\lambda=(3-3)/1=0
, and
b_{(1)}=3>0
, so
t=1
is valid.

Try
t=2
:
S_{2}=3+2=5
, so
\lambda=(5-3)/2=1
. Check
b_{(2)}=2>1
so
t=2
is valid.

Try
t=3
:
S_{3}=3+2+1=6
, so
\lambda=(6-3)/3=1
. Check Check
b_{(3)}=1\ngtr 1
, so
t=3
is not valid.

Thus,
\lambda=1
and we project:

\displaystyle\beta^{*}_{1}

\displaystyle=\sign(3)(3-1)=2;

\displaystyle\beta^{*}_{2}

\displaystyle=\sign(-2)(2-1)=-1;

\displaystyle\beta^{*}_{3}

\displaystyle=\sign(1)(1-1)=0.

The projection result is
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}=[2,-1,0]
with
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{1}=3=\Sigma
.

Constrained LASSO with PGD

Applying Algorithm
with the constraint set
{\mathbb{S}}\triangleq{\mathbb{B}}_{1}[\Sigma]
to the least squares objective
f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\triangleq\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
yields a practical numerical method for solving the constrained LASSO problem.
Provided that we can project efficiently onto the
\ell_{1}
-ball, PGD behaves similarly to standard gradient descent applied to the unconstrained least squares problem.
In particular, when the Gram matrix
{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}
is well-conditioned, PGD enjoys a linear convergence rate—and this rate is fast when the condition number is small.

To formally establish this convergence guarantee, we introduce the proximal gradient method in the next subsection and clarify its relationship to projected gradient descent.

Algorithm 4

Proximal Gradient Method

1:

A function
f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
and a closed convex function
g
(usually non-smooth) satisfying (A1) and (A2) in Theorem
;

2:

initialize:

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(1)}
;

3:

for

t=1,2,\ldots

do

4:

Choose a stepsize
\eta_{t}
;

5:

{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)}\leftarrow{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-\eta_{t}\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})
;
\triangleright
(PROX
1
)

6:

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}\leftarrow\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{\eta_{t}g}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)})\triangleq\mathcal{T}_{L_{t}}^{f,g}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})
;
\triangleright
(PROX
2
)

7:

Stop if a stopping criterion is satisfied at iteration
t=T
;

8:

end

for

9:

(Output Option 1) Output
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{final}}\leftarrow{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(T)}
;

10:

(Output Option 2) Output
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{avg}}\leftarrow\frac{1}{T}(\sum_{t=1}^{t}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})
or
\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{2t}{T(T+1)}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}
;

11:

(Output Option 3) Output
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{best}}\leftarrow\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{t\in\{1,2,\ldots,T\}}f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})
;

9.2.2
Proximal Gradient Method

\paragrapharrow

Proximal gradient method.
In Section
, we highlighted the close relationship between projection and proximal operators. Specifically, recall the identity

\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{\delta_{\mathbb{S}}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\mathcal{P}_{\mathbb{S}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}),

where
\delta_{\mathbb{S}}
denotes the indicator function of the set
{\mathbb{S}}
.
This allows us to reinterpret the projection step in projected gradient descent as a proximal operation:

\left\{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}\leftarrow\mathcal{P}_{{\mathbb{S}}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)})\right\}\qquad\leadsto\qquad\left\{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}\leftarrow\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{\delta_{\mathbb{S}}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)})\right\}.

The
proximal gradient method
(Algorithm
) generalizes this idea by replacing the indicator function with an arbitrary closed, convex, and possibly non-smooth function
g
:

\left\{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}\leftarrow\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{\delta_{\mathbb{S}}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)})\right\}\qquad\leadsto\qquad\left\{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}\leftarrow\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\eta_{t}g}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)})\right\},

(9.29)

where
\eta_{t}>0
is the stepsize at iteration
t
(its role will become clear shortly)..
We assume that
g
is closed and convex, which ensures that the proximal operator satisfies the standard properties (Proximal Properties-O, I, II, III, IV; see Lemmas
\sim
).
When
g\equiv\delta_{\mathbb{S}}
, the proximal gradient method reduces exactly to projected gradient descent.

Recall that in PGD, the update from iteration
t
to
t+1
can be written as:

\small\textbf{(PGD)}:\hskip 9.24994pt\begin{aligned} {\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}&\leftarrow\mathop{\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\left({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-\eta_{t}\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})\right)\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\\
&=\mathop{\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}}\left\{\frac{1}{2\eta_{t}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})+\left\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}),{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\right\rangle\right\}.\end{aligned}

(9.30)

Here, the constant term
f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})
does not affect the minimizer and is included only for interpretability.
Thus, the PGD update minimizes a linear approximation of the smooth function
f
around
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}
, regularized by a quadratic proximity term. The linear term drives progress toward lower objective values, while the quadratic term keeps the new iterate close to the current one, ensuring stability.

The proximal gradient method extends this framework to unconstrained composite optimization by incorporating a non-smooth penalty
g
directly into the objective:

\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}

\displaystyle\leftarrow\mathop{\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\real{}^{p}}}\left\{\frac{1}{2\eta_{t}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})+\left\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}),{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\right\rangle+{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}g({\boldsymbol{\beta}})}\right\}

(9.31a)

\displaystyle\textbf{(Prox)}:\hskip 18.49988pt\,\,\,

\displaystyle=\mathop{\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\real{}^{p}}}\eta_{t}g({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\left({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-\eta_{t}\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})\right)\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

(9.31b)

\displaystyle=\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{\eta_{t}g}\left({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-\eta_{t}\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})\right)\triangleq\mathcal{T}_{L_{t}}^{f,g}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}),

(9.31c)

where
L_{t}\triangleq\frac{1}{\eta_{t}}
, and
\mathcal{T}_{L}^{f,g}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\triangleq\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{\frac{1}{L}g}\left({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\frac{1}{L}\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right)
denotes the
prox-grad operator
.
We also define the
gradient mapping
as

\mathcal{G}_{L}^{f,g}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\triangleq L\big({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\mathcal{T}_{L}^{f,g}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\big).

(9.31d)

The update (
9.31c
) is computationally efficient whenever the proximal operator
\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{\eta_{t}g}
admits a closed-form solution or can be evaluated quickly (e.g., via soft-thresholding for
\ell_{1}
-regularization).
This formulation (
9.31c
) is particularly well-suited for statistical learning problems that use penalized objectives—such as the Lagrangian (unconstrained) LASSO—rather than hard constraints of the form
g({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\leq\Sigma
(see Section
for details).

Moreover, the update (
9.31c
) can be rewritten as

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}\leftarrow\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{\eta_{t}g}\left({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-\eta_{t}\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})\right)\triangleq\mathcal{T}_{L_{t}}^{f,g}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})\triangleq{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-\frac{1}{L_{t}}\mathcal{G}_{L_{t}}^{f,g}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}),

(9.31e)

which closely resembles a standard gradient descent (GD) step.
For this reason,
\mathcal{G}_{L_{t}}^{f,g}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})
is called the
gradient mapping
.
When the functions
f
and
g
are clear from context,
we simplify notation by writing
\mathcal{T}_{L_{t}}(\cdot)
and
\mathcal{G}_{L_{t}}(\cdot)
instead of
\mathcal{T}_{L_{t}}^{f,g}(\cdot)
and
\mathcal{G}_{L_{t}}^{f,g}(\cdot)
.

Equation (
) justifies the scaling by
\eta_{t}
in (
).
Altogether, the proximal gradient method is designed to minimize the composite objective

\min\{F({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\triangleq f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+g({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\},

(9.32)

where
f
is smooth and
g
is closed, convex, and possibly non-smooth.

Before presenting convergence results, we state the following descent lemma for the proximal gradient method.

Lemma 231
(Descent lemma for proximal gradient method).

Let
f
be a proper
closed
and
L_{b}
-smooth function, and let
g
be a proper closed and convex function.
Assume the following conditions hold:

(A1)

g:\real^{p}\rightarrow(-\infty,\infty]
is proper, closed, and convex.

(A2)

f:\real^{p}\rightarrow(-\infty,\infty]
is proper, closed, and convex,
\mathrm{dom}(f)
is convex,
\mathrm{dom}(g)\subseteq{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\text{int}}(\mathrm{dom}(f))
, and
f
is
L_{b}
-smooth over
{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\text{int}}(\mathrm{dom}(f))
.

Consider the composite function
F\triangleq f+g
and the prox-grad operator
\mathcal{T}_{L}\triangleq\mathcal{T}_{L}^{f,g}
.
Then, for any
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\text{int}(\mathrm{dom}(f))
and
L\in\left(\frac{L_{b}}{2},\infty\right)
, the following inequality holds:

F(\mathcal{T}_{L}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}))-F({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\leq\frac{\frac{L_{b}}{2}-L}{L^{2}}\left\lVert\mathcal{G}_{L}^{f,g}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq 0,

(9.33)

where
\mathcal{G}_{L}^{f,g}:\text{int}(\mathrm{dom}(f))\rightarrow\real^{p}
is the operator defined by
\mathcal{G}_{L}^{f,g}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\triangleq L\big({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\mathcal{T}_{L}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\big)
for all
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\text{int}(\mathrm{dom}(f))
.

Moreover, for any
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}
,
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\text{int}(\mathrm{dom}(f))
, consider the proximal gap
\mathcal{D}_{f}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\triangleq f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-\left\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}),{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle
and
L\triangleq L_{b}
. Then it holds that

F(\mathcal{T}_{L}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}))-F({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\leq\frac{L}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\frac{L}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-\mathcal{T}_{L}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\mathcal{D}_{f}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}).

(9.34)

When
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}
, (
) reduces to (
) by setting
L\triangleq L_{b}
.

Proof
[of Lemma
]

Equation (
).

For brevity, denote
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{+}\triangleq\mathcal{T}_{L}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
. By the smoothness of
f
(Definition
),

f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{+})\leq f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+\left\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}),{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{+}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle+\frac{L_{b}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{+}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

By the Proximal Property-I (Lemma
), since
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{+}=\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{\frac{1}{L}g}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\frac{1}{L}\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}))
, we have

\displaystyle\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\frac{1}{L}\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{+},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{+}\right\rangle\leq\frac{1}{L}g({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-\frac{1}{L}g({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{+}),\quad\forall\,{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}

\displaystyle\implies\quad g({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{+})\leq g({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-L\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{+}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\left\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}),{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{+}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle.

Combining the preceding two inequalities, we have

f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{+})+g({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{+})\leq f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+g({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+\left(-L+\frac{L_{b}}{2}\right)\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{+}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

Thus, taking into account the definitions of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{+}
,
\mathcal{G}_{L}^{f,g}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
, and the identities
F({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+g({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
,
F({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{+})=f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{+})+g({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{+})
, the desired result follows.

Equation (
).

Define the auxiliary function

\varphi({\bm{u}})\triangleq f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+\left\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}),{\bm{u}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle+g({\bm{u}})+\frac{L}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{u}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

This is precisely the first objective minimized in the proximal gradient update in (
).
Since
\varphi
is an
L
-strongly convex function and
\mathcal{T}_{L}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\arg\min_{{\bm{u}}\in\real^{p}}\varphi({\bm{u}})
, it follows by Theorem
(ii) that

\varphi({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\varphi(\mathcal{T}_{L}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}))\geq\frac{L}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-\mathcal{T}_{L}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rVert_{2}^{2},\quad\text{for all }{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}.

(9.35)

This implies, by the smoothness of
f
, that

\displaystyle\varphi(\mathcal{T}_{L}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}))

\displaystyle=f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+\left\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}),\mathcal{T}_{L}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle+\frac{L}{2}\left\lVert\mathcal{T}_{L}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+g(\mathcal{T}_{L}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}))

(9.36)

\displaystyle\geq f(\mathcal{T}_{L}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}))+g(\mathcal{T}_{L}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}))=F(\mathcal{T}_{L}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})).

Thus, combining (
) and (
) yields that

\displaystyle\underbrace{f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+\left\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}),{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle+g({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\frac{L}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}_{=\varphi({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})}-F(\mathcal{T}_{L}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}))

\displaystyle\geq\frac{L}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-\mathcal{T}_{L}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rVert_{2}^{2},\quad\forall\,\text{${\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}$}.

This proves the desired result.

When
f
is convex and strongly smooth, the proximal gradient method enjoys the following convergence guarantee.

{theoremHigh}
[Convergence of proximal gradient for convex and SS
f
:
\mathcal{O}(1/T)

(
Lu 2025
)
]
Let
f
be a proper
closed
and
L_{b}
-smooth function, and let
g
be a proper closed and convex function.
Assume the following conditions hold:

(A1)

g:\real^{p}\rightarrow(-\infty,\infty]
is proper, closed, and convex.

(A2)

f:\real^{p}\rightarrow(-\infty,\infty]
is proper, closed, and convex,
\mathrm{dom}(f)
is convex,
\mathrm{dom}(g)\subseteq{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\text{int}}(\mathrm{dom}(f))
, and
f
is
L_{b}
-smooth over
{\color[rgb]{0,0.08,0.45}\text{int}}(\mathrm{dom}(f))
.

Let
\{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\}_{t>0}
be the sequence generated by the proximal gradient method (Algorithm
) applied to the composite problem
\min\{F({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\triangleq f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+g({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\}
with a constant stepsize rule in which
L_{t}\triangleq L_{b}
for all
t>0
.
Then, for any optimal solution
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
of
F\triangleq f+g
and any integer
T>1
,
the following bound holds:

F({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(T)})-F({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})\leq\frac{L_{b}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(1)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}{2(T-1)}.

Consequently, for any tolerance
\epsilon>0
, we have

F({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(T)})\leq F({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})+\epsilon,\quad\text{for all $T\geq\frac{L_{b}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(1)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}{2\epsilon}+1$}.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Since
f
is convex, the proximal gap
\mathcal{D}_{f}
qualifies a Bregman distance such that
\mathcal{D}_{f}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})\geq 0
(Remark
).
For any
t>0
, using the descent lemma in (
), we obtain

\displaystyle\frac{2}{L_{b}}\left(F({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)})-F({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})\right)

\displaystyle\leq\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}-\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}-\frac{2}{L_{b}}\mathcal{D}_{f}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})

\displaystyle\leq\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}-\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}.

Summing the above inequality over
t=\{1,2,\ldots,T-1\}
yields a telescoping sum:

\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\left(F({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)})-F({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})\right)\leq\frac{L_{b}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(1)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\frac{L_{b}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(T)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\frac{L_{b}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(1)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

By the monotonicity of
\{F({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})\}_{t>0}
(Equation (
) and Lemma
), we can conclude that

\displaystyle(T-1)\left(F({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(T)})-F({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})\right)

\displaystyle\leq\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\left(F({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)})-F({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})\right)\leq\frac{L_{b}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(1)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},

which implies the desired result.

\paragrapharrow

Constrained LASSO with proximal.
Using an indicator function, the constrained LASSO problem in (
) can be equivalently rewritten as the composite optimization problem:

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}F({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\triangleq f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+g({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\triangleq\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\delta_{{\mathbb{B}}_{1}[\Sigma]}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}).

(9.37)

Here,
\delta_{{\mathbb{B}}_{1}[\Sigma]}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
denotes the indicator function of the scaled
\ell_{1}
-ball
{\mathbb{B}}_{1}[\Sigma]
.

F({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\triangleq f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+g({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
and
g({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\triangleq\delta_{{\mathbb{B}}_{1}[\Sigma]}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
is the indicator function.
Since this set is closed and convex, the indicator function
g
is proper, closed, and convex (see Exercises
and
).

Applying the proximal gradient method (Algorithm
) to this formulation yields the following update rule at the
t
-th iteration:

\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)}

\displaystyle\leftarrow{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-\eta_{t}{\bm{X}}^{\top}({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-{\bm{y}});

(9.38a)

\displaystyle\lambda^{(t+1)}

\displaystyle\leftarrow\text{Using the projection onto $\ell_{1}$-ball in \eqref{equation:projec_ell1_st1}};

(9.38b)

\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}

\displaystyle\leftarrow\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{\eta_{t}g}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)})=\mathcal{T}_{\eta_{t}\lambda^{(t+1)}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)})=\big[\big\lvert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)}\big\rvert-\eta_{t}\lambda^{(t+1)}{\bm{1}}\big]_{+}\circ\sign({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)}),

(9.38c)

where
\mathcal{T}_{\lambda}(\cdot)
denotes the soft-thresholding operator (Example
).
This is equivalent to the PGD update for constrained LASSO problem.
In words, the algorithm first takes a gradient descent step on the smooth loss
f
, then applies a proximal (shrinkage) step that enforces the
\ell_{1}
-norm constraint by projecting onto the feasible set. This shrinkage promotes sparsity in the iterates, which explains why the proximal gradient method is particularly well-suited for sparse recovery problems like the constrained LASSO.

Convergence of this scheme is guaranteed by Theorem
. Specifically, since
f
is
L_{b}
-smooth with
L_{b}=\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}
(Example
),
a constant stepsize
\eta_{t}=1/L_{b}=\frac{1}{\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}}
ensures the
\mathcal{O}(1/T)
convergence rate established in the theorem.

Conditional Gradient Method

1:

A function
f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
and a set

;

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(0)}
;

3:

\triangleright
