9.2.3
Conditional Gradient (Frank–Wolfe) Method

\paragrapharrow

Conditional gradient (CG, Frank–Wolfe) method
We investigate the
conditional gradient method
, commonly known as the
Frank–Wolfe (FW) algorithm
.
This method offers an attractive alternative for solving constrained optimization problems, especially because it avoids the potentially expensive projection step required in PGD methods.
Consider again the following constrained optimization problem:

\mathop{\min}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}.

(9.39)

In the conditional gradient method, the next iterate is computed as a convex combination of the current iterate and a minimizer of a linear approximation of the objective function over the feasible set
{\mathbb{S}}
(see Algorithm
).

Recall that in the PGD method, the update from the
t
-th to the
(t+1)
-th iteration is given by:

\small\textbf{(PGD)}:\hskip 18.49988pt\begin{aligned} {\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}&\leftarrow\mathop{\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-\left({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-\eta_{t}\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})\right)\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\\
&=\mathop{\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}}\left\{\frac{1}{2}\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}+\eta_{t}\left\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}),{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle\right\},\end{aligned}

(9.40)

where the quadratic term acts as a regularizer, ensuring the new iterate stays close to the current point
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}
.

In contrast—while closely connected to the PGD update—the conditional gradient method computes the next iterate as a convex combination of a solution to the linear subproblem

\mathop{\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}}\big\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}),{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\big\rangle
and the current iterate
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}
.
This approach avoids quadratic regularization entirely. Nevertheless, the convex combination itself serves as a form of implicit regularization, preventing large deviations from the current iterate:

\small\textbf{(CG)}:\hskip 18.49988pt\begin{aligned} {\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}&\leftarrow(1-\eta_{t}){\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}+\eta_{t}\mathop{\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}}\left\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}),{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle.\end{aligned}

(9.41)

Like PGD and proximal gradient method, the CG method achieves a convergence rate of
\mathcal{O}(T)
for convex and smooth objective functions.

{theoremHigh}
[FW for convex and SS:
\mathcal{O}(1/T)
]
Let
f:{\mathbb{S}}\rightarrow\real
be a proper, differentiable, convex, and
L_{b}
-smooth function defined over the convex domain
{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\real^{p}
.
Assume that
f
attains its global minimum at some point
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\in{\mathbb{S}}
, and let
D
denote the diameter of
{\mathbb{S}}
, defined as
D\triangleq\max_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\bm{u}}\in{\mathbb{S}}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{u}}\right\rVert_{2}
.
Let
\{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\}_{t\geq 0}

be the sequence generated by the Frank–Wolfe method (Algorithm
) for solving problem
\mathop{\min}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
subject to
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\mathbb{S}}
with a dynamic stepsize rule in which
\eta_{t}=\frac{2}{t+2}
at the
t
-th iteration.
Then, for any
T\geq 0
,

f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(T)})-f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})\leq\frac{2L_{b}D^{2}}{T+2}.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
By the smoothness, convexity, and the progress rule of conditional gradient method, we have

\displaystyle f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)})

\displaystyle\leq f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})+\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})+\frac{L_{b}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\quad

\displaystyle(\text{smoothness})

\displaystyle=f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})+\eta_{t}\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})^{\top}({\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})+\frac{\eta_{t}^{2}L_{b}}{2}\left\lVert{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\quad

\displaystyle\text{(update rule)}

\displaystyle\leq f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})+\eta_{t}\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})+\frac{\eta_{t}^{2}L_{b}D^{2}}{2}.

\displaystyle\text{(linear update rule)}

By convexity of
f
, we also have:

\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})\leq f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})-f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})
(see Theorem
);
Combining these two inequalities yields:

f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)})-f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})\leq(1-\eta_{t})(f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})-f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}))+\frac{\eta_{t}^{2}L_{b}D^{2}}{2}.

(9.42)

We now prove by induction that
f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})-f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})\leq\frac{2L_{b}D^{2}}{t+2}
for all
t\geq 0
.

Base case
t=0
.

When
t=0
, we have
\eta_{0}=\frac{2}{2}=1
and
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(0)}=\boldsymbol{0}
, and (
) reduces to

\displaystyle f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(1)})-f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})

\displaystyle\leq(1-\eta_{0})(f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(0)})-f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}))+\frac{L_{b}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(1)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\frac{L_{b}D^{2}}{2}\leq\frac{2L_{b}D^{2}}{2}.

Inductive step.

Assume the claim holds for some
t\geq 0
, i.e.,

f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})-f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})\leq\frac{2L_{b}D^{2}}{t+2}

holds for all integers up to
t
and we show the claim for
t+1
. Using (
) with
\eta_{t}=\frac{2}{t+2}
, we obtain:

\displaystyle f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)})-f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})

\displaystyle\leq\left(1-\frac{2}{t+2}\right)\left(f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})-f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})\right)+\frac{2L_{b}D^{2}}{(t+2)^{2}}

\displaystyle\leq\left(1-\frac{2}{t+2}\right)\frac{2L_{b}D^{2}}{t+2}+\frac{2L_{b}D^{2}}{(t+2)^{2}}=2L_{b}D^{2}\frac{t+1}{(t+2)^{2}}

\displaystyle=2L_{b}D^{2}\frac{t+1}{t+2}\cdot\frac{1}{t+2}\leq 2L_{b}D^{2}\frac{t+2}{t+3}\cdot\frac{1}{t+2}=2L_{b}D^{2}\frac{1}{t+3}.

Thus, the inequality also holds for the
t+1
case, completing the induction.

Algorithm 6

Conditional Gradient Method

1:

Matrix
{\bm{X}}
, vector
{\bm{y}}
, scalar
\Sigma>0
, tolerance
\delta
;

2:

goal:

Find
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
such that
\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
is minimized subject to
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\Sigma
;

3:

initialize:

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(0)}=\boldsymbol{0}
(or any point in
{\mathbb{S}}
);

4:

for

t=0,1,2,\ldots

do

5:

Compute gradient:

{\bm{g}}^{(t)}\leftarrow\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})={\bm{X}}^{\top}({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-{\bm{y}})
;

6:

Find coordinate with largest absolute gradient:

i^{*}=\operatorname*{\text{arg max}}_{i=1,2\ldots,p}\left\lvert g_{i}^{(t)}\right\rvert
;

7:

Compute linear minimizer:

{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t)}\leftarrow-\mathrm{sign}(g_{i^{*}}^{(t)})\Sigma{\bm{e}}_{i^{*}}

(i.e.,
-\Sigma
in coordinate
i^{*}
, zero elsewhere);

8:

Choose stepsize
\eta_{t}\in[0,1]
(e.g.,
\eta_{t}=\frac{2}{t+2}
);

9:

Update:

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}\leftarrow(1-\eta_{t}){\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}+\eta_{t}{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t)}
;

10:

Stop if a stopping criterion is satisfied at iteration
t=T
;

11:

end

for

12:

return

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\text{final}}\leftarrow{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(T)}
;

\paragrapharrow

Constrained LASSO with FW method.
We apply the conditional gradient method to the constrained LASSO problem (
LC
); see Algorithm
.
At the
t
-th iteration, the linear subproblem requires computing the gradient
{\bm{g}}\triangleq\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})={\bm{X}}^{\top}({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-{\bm{y}})
.
We then minimize the linear function
{\bm{g}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
subject to the constraint
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\Sigma
.
By the duality between the
\ell_{1}
- and
\ell_{\infty}
-norms, the optimal value of this subproblem is

{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}=\min_{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\Sigma}{\bm{g}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=-\Sigma\left\lVert{\bm{g}}\right\rVert_{\infty}.

(9.43)

An optimal
{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
is obtained by allocating the entire
\ell_{1}
budget
\Sigma
to a single coordinate
j
that achieves the maximum absolute gradient component, i.e., where
\left\lvert g_{j}\right\rvert=\left\lVert{\bm{g}}\right\rVert_{\infty}
, and choosing the sign opposite to
g_{j}
:

{\widetilde{\beta}}_{i}=\begin{cases}-\Sigma\mathrm{sign}(g_{j}),&i=j,\\
0,&i\neq j.\end{cases}

This choice yields
{\bm{g}}^{\top}{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}=-\Sigma\left\lVert{\bm{g}}\right\rVert_{\infty}
.
If multiple coordinates attain the maximum absolute value (i.e., there is a tie in
\left\lVert{\bm{g}}\right\rVert_{\infty}
), the optimal solution is not unique. In such cases, one may distribute the
\ell_{1}
budget among any subset of those coordinates, provided that each selected coordinate
i
receives a sign opposite to
g_{i}
.
If
{\bm{g}}=\boldsymbol{0}
, then every feasible
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
(i.e., every
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
with
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\Sigma
) is optimal, and the objective value is zero.

Since the feasible set is the
\ell_{1}
-ball
{\mathbb{B}}_{1}[\Sigma]
, its diameter (in the Euclidean norm) satisfies
D=\max_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\bm{u}}\in{\mathbb{S}}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{u}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq 2\Sigma
,
because any two points in the
\ell_{1}
-ball are at most
2\Sigma
apart in
\ell_{1}
-norm, and
\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{2}\leq\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{1}
(Exercise
).
Thus, the method achieves an
\mathcal{O}(1/T)
convergence rate, with constants depending on
\Sigma
.

9.2.4
Least Angle Regression (LARS)

Least angle regression (LARS)
is an efficient model-fitting algorithm that provides a unified framework for understanding several key regression techniques, including forward selection, forward stagewise regression, and the LASSO. It offers a geometrically intuitive approach to building linear models by iteratively adding predictors in a direction that maintains equal angles with their current correlations to the residual—hence the name least angle.

The algorithm proceeds sequentially, starting with the predictor most correlated with the response. Rather than fully including this variable in the model right away, LARS gradually increases its coefficient, moving it continuously toward its least squares estimate. As the coefficient grows, the correlation between this predictor and the current residual decreases. The process pauses as soon as another predictor “catches up”—that is, when its correlation with the residual becomes equal in magnitude. At this point, the second predictor joins the active set, and both coefficients are updated jointly, maintaining equal absolute correlation (i.e., equal angular distance) with the residual. This collaborative updating continues until all variables have been included, ultimately converging to the full least squares solution.

Before presenting the LARS algorithm, we first review two related methods: forward selection and forward stagewise regression, which serve as conceptual precursors to LARS
(
Efron et al. 2004
;
Weisberg 2005
)
.

Forward Selection Algorithm

LARS is closely related to the classical model-selection method known as the
forward selection algorithm
(a.k.a.,
forward stepwise regression
).
Forward selection is a greedy algorithm that builds a model by sequentially adding the most informative predictor at each step.

Consider the linear model
{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
, where
{\bm{y}}\in\real^{n}
is the response vector and
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
is the design matrix of
p
predictors.
The algorithm begins with all coefficients set to zero and the initial residual defined as

{\bm{y}}^{(0)}\triangleq{\bm{y}}
.
Among all candidate predictors in
{\bm{X}}
, it selects the one—say,
{\bm{x}}_{k}
—that is most correlated with the current residual (equivalently, forms the smallest angle with it, or has the largest absolute cosine similarity).
The procedure then proceeds as follows:
The algorithm proceeds as follows:

1.

Compute the projection of
{\bm{y}}^{(0)}
onto
{\bm{x}}_{k}
, yielding the fitted component
\beta_{k}{\bm{x}}_{k}
, and update the residual:
{\bm{y}}^{(1)}={\bm{y}}^{(0)}-\beta_{k}{\bm{x}}_{k}
.
By construction,
{\bm{y}}^{(1)}
and
{\bm{x}}_{k}
are orthogonal.

2.

Treat
{\bm{y}}^{(1)}
as the new response variable, remove
{\bm{x}}_{k}
from the pool of available predictors, and repeat the process using the remaining features
\{{\bm{x}}_{i}\mid i\neq k\}
.

3.

Continue iterating until a stopping criterion is met—such as exhausting all predictors, achieving a sufficiently small residual, or reaching a pre-specified model size. The final estimate is
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=[\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\ldots,\beta_{p}]^{\top}
, where unused predictors have coefficient zero.

To illustrate, consider a simple two-dimensional example (see Figure
). In the first step,
{\bm{x}}_{1}
forms the smallest angle with
{\bm{y}}^{(0)}
. Its projection,
\beta_{1}{\bm{x}}_{1}
, serves as the initial approximation to
{\bm{y}}
, and the residual is
{\bm{y}}^{(1)}={\bm{y}}^{(0)}-\beta_{1}{\bm{x}}_{1}
. In the next step,
{\bm{y}}^{(1)}

becomes the new target, and the only remaining predictor is
{\bm{x}}_{2}
. After projecting onto
{\bm{x}}_{2}
, the algorithm terminates, yielding the solution
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=[\beta_{1},\beta_{2}]^{\top}
.

Because forward selection performs only one update per selected variable, it is computationally efficient and fast. However, this simplicity comes at the cost of coarseness: once a variable is added, its coefficient is fixed, which can lead to suboptimal fits compared to more refined methods like LARS or LASSO.

(a)

Step 1.

(b)

Step 2.

Figure 9.1:
An example of the forward selection algorithm.

Forward Stagewise Algorithm

Similar to the forward selection algorithm, the forward stagewise algorithm begins by identifying, among the set of feature variables
{\bm{X}}
, the predictor
{\bm{x}}_{k}
that is most correlated with the initial residual vector
{\bm{y}}^{(0)}\equiv{\bm{y}}
—that is, the one forming the smallest angle (or equivalently, having the largest absolute cosine similarity) with
{\bm{y}}
.
Let the stepsize be denoted by
\eta>0
. The algorithm proceeds as follows:

1.

Take a small step of size
\eta
in the direction of
{\bm{x}}_{k}
: update the fit by adding
\eta{\bm{x}}_{k}
, and compute the new residual
{\bm{y}}^{(1)}={\bm{y}}^{(0)}-\eta{\bm{x}}_{k}
.

2.

Treat
{\bm{y}}^{(1)}
as the new response (residual), and retain all feature variables
\{{\bm{x}}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{p}
—including those already used—as candidates for the next step. Repeat step (i), always selecting the predictor most correlated with the current residual, until a termination condition is met. Termination occurs when either the residual becomes sufficiently small or no further meaningful progress can be made.

Figure
illustrates this process in a two-dimensional setting.
Suppose
{\bm{x}}_{1}
initially forms the smallest angle with
{\bm{y}}^{(0)}
. The algorithm takes repeated small steps in the direction of
{\bm{x}}_{1}
, each of size
\eta{\bm{x}}_{1}
, with the corresponding residuals shown as orange vectors. As the residual evolves, its correlation with
{\bm{x}}_{2}
increases. Once
{\bm{x}}_{2}
becomes more aligned with the residual than
{\bm{x}}_{1}
i.e., forms a smaller angle), the algorithm switches direction and begins taking steps along
{\bm{x}}_{2}
instead.

This procedure continues iteratively: at every step, all predictors remain eligible for selection, and any variable may be used multiple times. When the stepsize
\eta
is chosen to be very small, the algorithm can closely approximate the optimal solution—but at the expense of increased computational cost due to the large number of iterations required.

The resulting path resembles a staircase, which is characteristic of the stagewise approach—hence the name forward stagewise algorithm.

Figure 9.2:
Several steps in the forward stagewise algorithm for a two-dimensional case.
Blue segments indicate movement in the direction of
{\bm{x}}_{1}
, red segments indicate movement in the direction of
{\bm{x}}_{2}
, and the orange vectors represent the residuals after each step.
The staircase-like trajectory reflects the incremental, piecewise nature of the stagewise path.

LARS

Least angle regression (LARS)
algorithm is a compromise between the two algorithms above: it is computationally more efficient than stagewise regression and more accurate than forward selection.

Let
\{\widehat{\bm{y}}_{0},\widehat{\bm{y}}_{1},\widehat{\bm{y}}_{2},\ldots,\widehat{\bm{y}}_{p}\}
denote the sequence of fitted value vectors generated by LARS as it progresses toward approximating the response vector
{\bm{y}}
.
The algorithm is initialized with
\widehat{\bm{y}}_{0}=\boldsymbol{0}
(corresponding to a model with only an intercept, which we assume has already been accounted for).
The process terminates when one of the following conditions is met:
there is no remaining residual to explain, all available predictors have been included, or the residual norm falls below a pre-specified tolerance.

In the one-dimensional case, LARS coincides exactly with forward selection. We compute

\widehat{\bm{y}}_{1}=\widehat{\bm{y}}_{0}+{\widehat{\gamma}}_{1}{\bm{u}}_{1}
,
where
{\bm{u}}_{1}
is the unit vector in the direction of the selected predictor
{\bm{x}}_{1}
.
By choosing
{\widehat{\gamma}}_{1}
appropriately,
\widehat{\bm{y}}_{1}
is aligned with
\overline{\bm{y}}_{1}
(the orthogonal projection of the response variable
{\bm{y}}
onto the one-dimensional subspace spanned by
{\bm{x}}_{1}
), and the algorithm stops once the termination condition is satisfied.

In the two-dimensional case, suppose we have two predictors
{\bm{x}}_{1}
and
{\bm{x}}_{2}
.
Let
\overline{\bm{y}}_{2}
denote the projection of
{\bm{y}}
onto the column space
\mathcal{C}([{\bm{x}}_{1},{\bm{x}}_{2}])
.
LARS first identifies the predictor most correlated with the current residual
\overline{\bm{y}}_{2}
—in this case, say
{\bm{x}}_{1}
.
Rather than moving all the way to
\overline{\bm{y}}_{2}
along
{\bm{x}}_{1}
, LARS takes a step of size
{\widehat{\gamma}}_{1}
in the direction of
{\bm{u}}_{1}
(unit vector along
{\bm{x}}_{1}
), yielding

\widehat{\bm{y}}_{1}=\widehat{\bm{y}}_{0}+{\widehat{\gamma}}_{1}{\bm{u}}_{1},

chosen so that the new residual
\overline{\bm{y}}_{2}-\widehat{\bm{y}}_{1}
lies on the angle bisector between

{\bm{x}}_{1}
and
{\bm{x}}_{2}
.
Next, the algorithm proceeds along this bisector direction. Let
{\bm{u}}_{2}

be the unit vector pointing along the bisector of the angle between
{\bm{x}}_{1}
and
{\bm{x}}_{2}
.
Then

\widehat{\bm{y}}_{2}=\widehat{\bm{y}}_{1}+{\widehat{\gamma}}_{2}{\bm{u}}_{2}.

By adjusting
{\widehat{\gamma}}_{2}
, we can move directly to
\overline{\bm{y}}_{2}
, completing the fit in two dimensions; see Figure
.

For the general high-dimensional case, consider the
t
-th iteration of the algorithm:

1.

Move a step of size
{\widehat{\gamma}}_{t}
in the equiangular (i.e., angle-bisecting) direction among the currently active predictors. Specifically, set

\widehat{\bm{y}}_{t}=\widehat{\bm{y}}_{t-1}+{\widehat{\gamma}}_{t}{\bm{u}}_{t},

where
{\bm{u}}_{t}
is the unit vector in the equiangular direction defined by the active set.
This direction is chosen so that the updated residual remains equally correlated (in absolute value) with all active predictors. The next predictor to enter the active set—denoted
{\bm{x}}_{t+1}
—is the one that becomes equally correlated with the residual at the end of this step. That is, the current residual
\overline{\bm{y}}_{t+1}-\widehat{\bm{y}}_{t}
lies on the angle bisector between
{\bm{u}}_{t}
and
{\bm{x}}_{t+1}
.

2.

Repeat step (i) until a termination condition is met.

(a)

Two-dimensional case of LARS.

(b)

Three-dimensional case of LARS.

Figure 9.3:

Illustration of the LARS algorithm.
When
{\bm{X}}
is a two-dimensional matrix with two covariates (or features, predictors)
{\bm{x}}_{1}
and
{\bm{x}}_{2}
, we find the component that is closest to
\overline{\bm{y}}_{2}
(i.e., smallest angle, largest cosine value, and
\overline{\bm{y}}_{2}
is the projection of
{\bm{y}}
onto
\mathcal{C}([{\bm{x}}_{1},{\bm{x}}_{2}])
), say
{\bm{x}}_{1}
. We move along the direction of
{\bm{x}}_{1}
by a stepsize
{\widehat{\gamma}}_{1}{\bm{u}}_{1}
such that the resulting residual
\overline{\bm{y}}_{2}-\widehat{\bm{y}}_{1}
lies on the angle bisector between the feature vectors
{\bm{x}}_{1}
and
{\bm{x}}_{2}
(where
{\bm{u}}_{1}
is the unit vector along
{\bm{x}}_{1}
). Let
\widehat{\bm{y}}_{2}=\widehat{\bm{y}}_{1}+{\widehat{\gamma}}_{2}{\bm{u}}_{2}
, where
{\bm{u}}_{2}
is the unit vector along the angle bisector. By adjusting
{\widehat{\gamma}}_{2}
, we can directly align
\widehat{\bm{y}}_{2}
with
\overline{\bm{y}}_{2}
until the termination condition is met.
Note that
\widehat{\bm{y}}_{2}=\overline{\bm{y}}_{2}
in the case
p=2
, but not for
p>2
, for example in Fig.
.

The key innovation of LARS occurs after the first predictor is selected. Unlike forward selection—which fully fits the selected variable before considering others—or stagewise regression—which takes tiny incremental steps—LARS moves in a direction that maintains equal angles (or equal absolute correlations) between the current residual and all active predictors.
This equiangular direction ensures a balanced contribution from the selected variables. The algorithm continues along this path until another predictor “catches up” in correlation with the residual, at which point it joins the active set, and a new equiangular direction is computed. This process yields a piecewise-linear solution path that is both efficient and geometrically elegant.

\paragrapharrow

Illustrating example.
To further clarify the LARS algorithm, we make the following standard preprocessing assumptions:

Each predictor
{\bm{x}}_{i}
is standardized to have mean zero and unit Euclidean norm.

The response vector
{\bm{y}}
is centered so that it has mean zero.

These steps simplify computations and ensure all variables are on a comparable scale. Under this standardization, the (absolute) correlation between any predictor and the residual is proportional to their inner product, so angles can be interpreted directly via dot products.
Let
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
denote the current coefficient vector and
\widehat{\bm{y}}
be the current estimate.
LARS builds up estimates

\widehat{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}

(9.44)

in successive steps, each step adding one covariate to the model, so that after
t
steps just
t
of the coefficients
{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}
are nonzero.
Let
{\bm{c}}(\widehat{\bm{y}})
be the vector of
current correlations

\widehat{\bm{c}}\triangleq{\bm{c}}(\widehat{\bm{y}})={\bm{X}}^{\top}({\bm{y}}-\widehat{\bm{y}})\equiv{\bm{X}}^{\top}({\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}),

(9.45)

such that
\widehat{c}_{i}=c_{i}(\widehat{\bm{y}})
denotes the correlation between the
i
-th covariate
{\bm{x}}_{i}
and the current residual vector
{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
.

Figure
illustrates the algorithm in the case of
p=2
predictors,
{\bm{X}}=[{\bm{x}}_{1},{\bm{x}}_{2}]
.
Because the predictors span a two-dimensional subspace, the current correlations depend only on the projection of
{\bm{y}}
onto this space, denoted
\overline{\bm{y}}_{2}=\mathcal{P}_{[{\bm{x}}_{1},{\bm{x}}_{2}]}({\bm{y}})
.
Thus,

{\bm{c}}(\widehat{\bm{y}})\triangleq{\bm{X}}^{\top}({\bm{y}}-\widehat{\bm{y}})={\bm{X}}^{\top}(\overline{\bm{y}}_{2}-\widehat{\bm{y}}),

(9.46)

where the
i
-th component
c_{i}(\widehat{\bm{y}})
is precisely the cosine of the angle between
{\bm{x}}_{i}
and the residual
(\overline{\bm{y}}_{2}-\widehat{\bm{y}})
since the covariates
{\bm{x}}_{i}
have unit norms.

The algorithm starts at
\widehat{\bm{y}}_{0}=\boldsymbol{0}
.
In Figure
(and similarly in Figure
), the initial residual

\overline{\bm{y}}_{2}-\widehat{\bm{y}}_{0}=\overline{\bm{y}}_{2}
forms a smaller angle with
{\bm{x}}_{1}
than with
{\bm{x}}_{2}
, i.e.,
c_{1}(\widehat{\bm{y}}_{0})>c_{2}(\widehat{\bm{y}}_{0})
.
LARS then moves from
\widehat{\bm{y}}_{0}
in the direction of
{\bm{x}}_{1}
:

\widehat{\bm{y}}_{1}=\widehat{\bm{y}}_{0}+\widehat{\gamma}_{1}\frac{{\bm{x}}_{1}}{\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{1}\right\rVert_{2}}=\widehat{\bm{y}}_{0}+\widehat{\gamma}_{1}{\bm{u}}_{1}.

(9.47)

Classic forward selection algorithm would take
\widehat{\gamma}_{1}
large enough to make
\widehat{\bm{y}}_{1}
equal
\overline{\bm{y}}_{1}\triangleq\mathcal{P}_{[{\bm{x}}_{1}]}({\bm{y}})
, the orthogonal projection of
{\bm{y}}
onto
\mathcal{C}([{\bm{x}}_{1}])
;
while the forward stagewise algorithm suggests to choose
\widehat{\gamma}_{1}
equal to some small value
\eta
, and then repeat the process many times.
LARS adopts an intermediate strategy: it selects
\widehat{\gamma}_{1}
such that the new residual
\overline{\bm{y}}_{2}-\widehat{\bm{y}}_{1}
becomes
equally
correlated with both
{\bm{x}}_{1}
and
{\bm{x}}_{2}
.
Geometrically, this means the residual
\overline{\bm{y}}_{2}-\widehat{\bm{y}}_{1}
lies along the angle bisector between
{\bm{x}}_{1}
and
{\bm{x}}_{2}
, so that

c_{1}(\widehat{\bm{y}}_{1})=c_{2}(\widehat{\bm{y}}_{1}).

Let
{\bm{u}}_{2}\triangleq\frac{\overline{\bm{y}}_{2}-\widehat{\bm{y}}_{1}}{\left\lVert\overline{\bm{y}}_{2}-\widehat{\bm{y}}_{1}\right\rVert_{2}}
denote the unit vector pointing along this bisector. The next LARS update is

\widehat{\bm{y}}_{2}=\widehat{\bm{y}}_{1}+\widehat{\gamma}_{2}{\bm{u}}_{2},

(9.48)

with
\widehat{\gamma}_{2}
chosen so that
\widehat{\bm{y}}_{2}=\overline{\bm{y}}_{2}
in the case
p=2
(Figure
).
With
p>2
covariates, however,
\widehat{\gamma}_{2}
would be
smaller
, leading to another change of direction, as illustrated in Figure
such that the new residual
\overline{\bm{y}}_{3}-\widehat{\bm{y}}_{2}
lies on the angle bisector between
{\bm{u}}_{2}
and
{\bm{x}}_{3}
for some given
{\bm{x}}_{3}
.

Subsequent LARS steps generalize this idea: once
k
predictors are active, the algorithm proceeds in the equiangular direction—a unique direction that maintains equal absolute correlation with all active predictors. This direction generalizes the geometric notion of an angle bisector to higher dimensions, as exemplified by the vector
{\bm{u}}_{3}
in Figure
.

Mathematical Formulas of LARS Algorithm

With the geometric intuition behind the LARS algorithm established, we now turn to its precise mathematical formulation.

\paragrapharrow
Obtaining angle bisector with unit norm.
Assume that the covariate vectors
{\bm{x}}_{1},{\bm{x}}_{2},\ldots,{\bm{x}}_{p}
are
linearly independent
.
Suppose LARS has just completed step
t-1
, yielding the current estimate
\widehat{\bm{y}}_{t-1}
, and is about to begin step
t
.
Let
{\mathbb{S}}
denote the active set—the set of indices of predictors currently included in the model—with cardinality
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert=t
. Define the signed design matrix for the active variables as

{\bm{X}}_{t}\triangleq[\ldots,s_{i}{\bm{x}}_{i},\ldots]_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}},

(9.49a)

where the signs
s_{i}
equal
\pm 1
.

Next, define the Gram matrix and a scaling constant:

{\bm{G}}_{t}\triangleq{\bm{X}}_{t}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{t}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\sigma_{t}\triangleq({\bm{1}}_{t}^{\top}{\bm{G}}_{t}^{-1}{\bm{1}}_{t})^{-1/2},

(9.49b)

where
{\bm{1}}_{t}
is a vector of ones of length
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert=t
.
Then the vector

{\bm{u}}_{t}={\bm{X}}_{t}{\bm{w}}_{t},\quad\text{where }{\bm{w}}_{t}\triangleq\sigma_{t}{\bm{G}}_{t}^{-1}{\bm{1}}_{t},

(9.49c)

is a unit vector, satisfying

{\bm{X}}_{t}^{\top}{\bm{u}}_{t}={\bm{X}}_{t}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{t}{\bm{w}}_{t}=\sigma_{t}{\bm{1}}_{t}.

(9.49d)

Equality (
) shows
\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{t}\right\rVert_{2}=1
such that
{\bm{u}}_{t}
is a unit-length vector;
while (
) implies that the inner product (and hence the cosine of the angle) between
{\bm{u}}_{t}
and each signed predictor
s_{i}{\bm{x}}_{i}
(
i\in{\mathbb{S}}
) is identical and equal to
\sigma_{t}>0
(hence, the angles between
{\bm{x}}_{i}
,
i\in{\mathbb{S}}
and
{\bm{u}}_{t}
are equal and less than
90^{\circ}
). Consequently,
{\bm{u}}_{t}
makes equal acute angles with all active predictors.
Such a vector
{\bm{u}}_{t}
is known as the
equiangular vector
or
angle bisector
of the columns of
{\bm{X}}_{t}
.

\paragrapharrow

The general step the LARS Algorithm.
We can now describe the full LARS procedure.
Starting from
\widehat{\bm{y}}_{0}=\boldsymbol{0}
, the algorithm constructs the fitted values
\widehat{\bm{y}}
through a sequence of steps, each typically larger than those in stagewise regression.
Suppose that
\widehat{\bm{y}}_{t-1}
is the current LARS estimate, lying in the column space of
{\bm{X}}_{t-1}
corresponding to an active set
{\mathbb{S}}_{-}
with
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}_{-}\right\rvert=\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert-1=t-1
. Let the current correlation vector be

\widehat{\bm{c}}={\bm{X}}^{\top}({\bm{y}}-\widehat{\bm{y}}_{t-1}),

(9.50)

where
{\bm{y}}-\widehat{\bm{y}}_{t-1}
is the current residual.
The general step consists of two parts:
(i) updating the estimate by moving in the equiangular direction within the current active subspace (i.e., column space of
{\bm{X}}_{t}
), and
(ii) determining when a new predictor should enter the active set so as to update the active set to
{\mathbb{S}}_{+}
such that
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}_{+}\right\rvert=\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert+1
.

The
active set

{\mathbb{S}}\subseteq\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
at step
t
consists of all indices achieving the maximal absolute current correlation:

\widehat{C}_{t}=\max_{i}\{\left\lvert\widehat{c}_{i}\right\rvert\}\qquad\text{and}\qquad{\mathbb{S}}=\left\{i\mid\left\lvert\widehat{c}_{i}\right\rvert=\widehat{C}_{t}\right\}.

(9.51)

For each
i\in{\mathbb{S}}
, define the sign

s_{i}\triangleq\mathrm{sign}\{\widehat{c}_{i}\},\quad\text{for }i\in{\mathbb{S}},

(9.52)

and construct
{\bm{X}}_{t}
,
\sigma_{t}
, and
{\bm{u}}_{t}
as in (
).
Additionally, compute the vector of directional correlations:

{\bm{z}}\triangleq{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{u}}_{t}.

(9.53)

The next LARS estimate is obtained by moving from
\widehat{\bm{y}}_{t-1}
in the direction
{\bm{u}}_{t}
:

\widehat{\bm{y}}_{t}=\widehat{\bm{y}}_{t-1}+\widehat{\gamma}_{t}{\bm{u}}_{t},

(9.54)

where

\widehat{\gamma}_{t}=\mathop{\text{min}^{+}}_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}\left\{\frac{\widehat{C}_{t}-\widehat{c}_{i}}{\sigma_{t}-z_{i}},\frac{\widehat{C}_{t}+\widehat{c}_{i}}{\sigma_{t}+z_{i}}\right\};

(9.55)

“
\min^{+}
” indicates that the minimum is taken over only positive components within each choice of
i
in (
).

To understand this choice of the stepsize
\widehat{\gamma}_{t}
(
), consider a candidate update for any
\gamma>0
.
We define the potential next LARS estimate

{\bm{y}}(\gamma)\triangleq\widehat{\bm{y}}_{t-1}+\gamma{\bm{u}}_{t},

(9.56)

which yields the updated correlation for predictor
i

c_{i}(\gamma)={\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}\big({\bm{y}}-{\bm{y}}(\gamma)\big)=\widehat{c}_{i}-\gamma z_{i},\quad\text{for all }i.

(9.57)

For active indices
i\in{\mathbb{S}}
, (
) along with the fact that
{\bm{X}}_{t}^{\top}{\bm{u}}_{t}=\sigma_{t}{\bm{1}}_{t}
in (
) yield

\left\lvert c_{i}(\gamma)\right\rvert=\widehat{C}_{t}-\gamma\sigma_{t},\quad\text{for all }i\in{\mathbb{S}},

(9.58)

showing that all of the maximal absolute current correlations decline equally.
For
i\in{\mathbb{S}}^{c}
, equating (
) with (
) shows that
c_{i}(\gamma)
equals the maximal value at
\gamma=(\widehat{C}_{t}-\widehat{c}_{i})/(\sigma_{t}-z_{i})
. Likewise
-c_{i}(\gamma)
, the current correlation for the reversed covariate
-{\bm{x}}_{i}
, achieves maximality at
(\widehat{C}_{t}+\widehat{c}_{i})/(\sigma_{t}+z_{i})
.
Therefore,
\widehat{\gamma}_{t}
in (
) is the smallest positive value of
\gamma
such that some new index
i_{+}
joins the active set;
i_{+}
is the minimizing index in (
),
and the new active set
{\mathbb{S}}_{+}
is
{\mathbb{S}}_{+}={\mathbb{S}}\cup\{i_{+}\}
; the new maximum absolute correlation is
\widehat{C}_{t+1}=\widehat{C}_{t}-\widehat{\gamma}_{t}\sigma_{t}
for
i\in{\mathbb{S}}_{+}
.

\paragrapharrow

Geometric property of LARS path.
Let

\widehat{C}_{t}{\bm{1}}_{t}\triangleq{\bm{X}}_{t}^{\top}({\bm{y}}-\widehat{\bm{y}}_{t-1})

(9.59)

denote the vector of correlations at the step
t
, where all active predictors share the same absolute correlation
\widehat{C}_{t}
by construction.
Let
\overline{\bm{y}}_{t}
denote the orthogonal projection of
{\bm{y}}
onto the column space
\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}_{t})
.
Since
\widehat{\bm{y}}_{t-1}\in\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}_{t-1})\subseteq\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}_{t})
, this projection can be written as

\overline{\bm{y}}_{t}=\widehat{\bm{y}}_{t-1}+{\bm{X}}_{t}{\bm{G}}_{t}^{-1}{\bm{X}}_{t}^{\top}({\bm{y}}-\widehat{\bm{y}}_{t-1})=\widehat{\bm{y}}_{t-1}+\frac{\widehat{C}_{t}}{\sigma_{t}}{\bm{u}}_{t},

(9.60)

where
\widehat{\bm{y}}_{t-1}+{\bm{X}}_{t}{\bm{G}}_{t}^{-1}{\bm{X}}_{t}^{\top}({\bm{y}}-\widehat{\bm{y}}_{t-1})
denotes the projection of the residual
{\bm{y}}-\widehat{\bm{y}}_{t-1}
onto
\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}_{t})
(Lemma
),
and the last equality follows from (
) and the fact that the signed current correlations all equal
\widehat{C}_{t}
from (
).
Since
{\bm{u}}_{t}
is a unit vector, (
) says that
\overline{\bm{y}}_{t}-\widehat{\bm{y}}_{t-1}
has length

\overline{\gamma}_{t}\triangleq\frac{\widehat{C}_{t}}{\sigma_{t}}\quad\implies\quad\overline{\bm{y}}_{t}-\widehat{\bm{y}}_{t-1}=\overline{\gamma}_{t}{\bm{u}}_{t}.

(9.61)

Remark 232
(Geometric property of LARS path).

Comparison with (
)—the update of estimate
\widehat{\bm{y}}_{t}=\widehat{\bm{y}}_{t-1}+\widehat{\gamma}_{t}{\bm{u}}_{t}
—shows that the LARS estimate
\widehat{\bm{y}}_{t}
lies on the line from
\widehat{\bm{y}}_{t-1}
to
\overline{\bm{y}}_{t}
,

\widehat{\bm{y}}_{t}-\widehat{\bm{y}}_{t-1}=\widehat{\gamma}_{t}{\bm{u}}_{t}=\frac{\widehat{\gamma}_{t}}{\overline{\gamma}_{t}}(\overline{\bm{y}}_{t}-\widehat{\bm{y}}_{t-1}).

(9.62)

By (
), it is easy to see that
\widehat{\gamma}_{t}
is always less than
\overline{\gamma}_{t}
, so that
\widehat{\bm{y}}_{t}
lies closer than
\overline{\bm{y}}_{t}
to
\widehat{\bm{y}}_{t-1}
.
Therefore, the successive LARS estimates
\widehat{\bm{y}}_{t}
are always approaching but never reaching the OLS estimates
\overline{\bm{y}}_{t}
.

The only exception occurs at the final step.
When the active set includes all
p
predictors, i.e.,
{\mathbb{S}}=\{1,2,\ldots,p\}
, the stepsize formula (
) is no longer applicable (as there are no inactive variables).
By convention, the algorithm takes
\widehat{\gamma}_{p}=\overline{\gamma}_{p}=\widehat{C}_{p}/\sigma_{p}
, making the current estimate
\widehat{\bm{y}}_{p}=\overline{\bm{y}}_{p}
and and the current coefficient
\widehat{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{p}
equal the OLS estimate for the full set of
p
covariates.

For notational clarity, we define:
{\bm{c}}_{t}\triangleq{\bm{X}}_{t}^{\top}({\bm{y}}-\widehat{\bm{y}}_{t-1})
as the vector of correlations at step
t
, with
c_{ti}
denoting the
i
-th entry of
{\bm{c}}_{t}
.
And we let
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{t}
denote the full regression coefficient vector satisfying
\widehat{\bm{y}}_{t}={\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{t}
, and let
{\widehat{\beta}}_{ti}
denote the
i
-th entry of
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{t}
.
We now establish an important property of the LARS algorithm: new variables enter the model in the direction consistent with their current correlation with the residual.

Lemma 233
(Sign restriction of LARS).

Suppose LARS has completed step
t-1
, yielding the estimate
\widehat{\bm{y}}_{t-1}
and active set
{\mathbb{S}}_{t}
for step
t
,
where the predictor
{\bm{x}}_{t}
is the newest addition to the active set (i.e.,
{\mathbb{S}}_{t}={\mathbb{S}}_{t-1}\cup\{t\}
).
If
{\bm{x}}_{t}
is the only addition to the active set at the end of step
t-1
, then the coefficient vector
{\bm{w}}_{t}=\sigma_{t}{\bm{G}}_{t}^{-1}{\bm{1}}_{t}
for the equiangular vector
{\bm{u}}_{t}={\bm{X}}_{t}{\bm{w}}_{t}
, (
), has its
t
-th component
w_{tt}
agreeing in sign with the current correlation
c_{tt}={\bm{x}}_{t}^{\top}({\bm{y}}-\widehat{\bm{y}}_{t-1})
. Moreover, the regression vector
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{t}
for
\widehat{\bm{y}}_{t}={\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{t}
has its
t
-th component
{\widehat{\beta}}_{tt}
agreeing in sign with
c_{tt}
.

Proof
[Lemma
]
The case
t=1
is immediate, since the first predictor enters in the direction of its correlation with
{\bm{y}}
.
For
t\geq 2
, recall from (
) that

\\
bX_{t}^{\top}({\bm{y}}-\widehat{\bm{y}}_{t-1})=\widehat{C}_{t}{\bm{1}}_{t}
.
Using (
), we can express

{\bm{w}}_{t}=\sigma_{t}{\bm{G}}_{t}^{-1}{\bm{1}}_{t}=\sigma_{t}\widehat{C}_{t}^{-1}[({\bm{X}}_{t}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{t})^{-1}{\bm{X}}_{t}^{\top}({\bm{y}}-\widehat{\bm{y}}_{t-1})]\triangleq\sigma_{t}\widehat{C}_{t}^{-1}\widehat{\bm{w}}_{t}.

The term in square braces is the least squares coefficient vector in the regression of the current residual on
{\bm{X}}_{t}
, and the term preceding it is positive.

Now observe that

{\bm{X}}_{t}^{\top}({\bm{y}}-\overline{\bm{y}}_{t-1})=[\boldsymbol{0},\delta]^{\top},\quad\text{with }\delta>0,

(9.63)

since
{\bm{X}}_{t-1}^{\top}({\bm{y}}-\overline{\bm{y}}_{t-1})=\boldsymbol{0}_{t-1}
by definition (because
\overline{\bm{y}}_{t-1}
is the projection of
{\bm{y}}
onto
\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}_{t-1})
), and
c_{t}(\gamma)={\bm{x}}_{t}^{\top}({\bm{y}}-\gamma{\bm{u}}_{t-1})
decreases more slowly in
\gamma
than
c_{i}(\gamma)
for
i\in{\mathbb{S}}_{t-1}
:

c_{t}(\gamma)\begin{cases}<c_{i}(\gamma),&\text{if }\gamma<\widehat{\gamma}_{t-1};\\
=c_{i}(\gamma)=\widehat{C}_{t},&\text{if }\gamma=\widehat{\gamma}_{t-1};\\
>c_{i}(\gamma),&\text{if }\widehat{\gamma}_{t-1}<\gamma<\overline{\gamma}_{t-1}.\end{cases}

Thus,

\displaystyle\widehat{\bm{w}}_{t}

\displaystyle=({\bm{X}}_{t}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{t})^{-1}{\bm{X}}_{t}^{\top}({\bm{y}}-\overline{\bm{y}}_{t-1}+\overline{\bm{y}}_{t-1}-\widehat{\bm{y}}_{t-1})

\displaystyle=({\bm{X}}_{t}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{t})^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{0}\\
\delta\end{bmatrix}+({\bm{X}}_{t}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{t})^{-1}{\bm{X}}_{t}^{\top}[(\overline{\gamma}_{t-1}-\widehat{\gamma}_{t-1}){\bm{u}}_{t-1}],

(9.64)

where the last equality follows from (
) and (
).
The
t
-th element of
\widehat{\bm{w}}_{t}
is positive, because it is in the first term in (
9.64
) (since
{\bm{X}}_{t}
has full column rank and thus
{\bm{X}}_{t}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{t}
is positive definite), and in the second term it is 0 since
{\bm{u}}_{t-1}={\bm{X}}_{t-1}{\bm{w}}_{t-1}\in\mathcal{C}({\bm{X}}_{t-1})
.
This proves the first statement.

For the second claim, note that the full coefficient vector updates as

{\widehat{\beta}}_{tt}={\widehat{\beta}}_{t-1,t}+\widehat{\gamma}_{t}w_{tt},

(9.65)

where
{\widehat{\beta}}_{t-1,t}=0
, since
{\bm{x}}_{t}
was not active before step
t
.
Because both
\widehat{\gamma}_{t}>0
and
w_{tt}
share the sign of
c_{tt}
, it follows that

{\widehat{\beta}}_{tt}
also shares that sign.

Lemma
shows that new variables enter the LARS model in the “correct” direction—i.e., with a coefficient sign matching their current correlation with the residual. This is a weaker but essential property compared to the stricter sign consistency required by the LASSO (see condition (
)). As we shall see, this alignment is a key ingredient in the deep connection between LARS and the LASSO.

LARS for Constrained LASSO Problems

LARS proceeds along the most natural compromise direction—the equiangular vector defined in (
)—whereas the constrained LASSO imposes additional restrictions on this equiangular strategy.

We now briefly show that the entire set of LASSO solutions can be generated by a minor modification of the standard LARS algorithm (
)
\sim
(
).

\paragrapharrow

Piecewise linear update of the fitted values in LARS–LASSO.
We begin by discussing the relationship between LARS and the LASSO.
Let
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}={\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}(\Sigma)
denote a solution to the constrained LASSO problem (
LC
), and define the corresponding fitted values as
\widehat{\bm{y}}=\widehat{\bm{y}}(\Sigma)={\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}(\Sigma)
, where
\Sigma\geq 0
is the constraint radius satisfying
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\Sigma
.
Since both the loss function
f({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})=\frac{1}{2}\big\lVert{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\bm{y}}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}
and the constraint
g({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})=\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}
are convex functions of
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
—and
f
is strictly convex—it follows from standard convex analysis that
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}(\Sigma)
and
\widehat{\bm{y}}(\Sigma)
are unique and continuous functions of the constraint radius
\Sigma
.

For a fixed
\Sigma
, define the active set as

{\mathbb{S}}\triangleq\{i\mid{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}(\Sigma)\neq 0\}.

Indeed,
{\mathbb{S}}
is also the active set that determines the equiangular direction
{\bm{u}}_{\mathbb{S}}
in the LARS–LASSO computations.

We wish to characterize the trajectory of the LASSO solutions
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}(\Sigma)
or equivalently of
\widehat{\bm{y}}(\Sigma)
as
\Sigma
increases from 0 to its maximum effective value. Let
{\mathbb{M}}
be an open interval of the
\Sigma
axis, with infimum
\Sigma_{0}\triangleq\inf({\mathbb{M}})
, within which the set
{\mathbb{S}}
of nonzero LASSO coefficients
{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}(\Sigma)
remains constant:

{\mathbb{S}}\equiv\{i\mid{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}(\Phi)\neq 0\},\quad\text{for all }\Phi\in{\mathbb{M}}.

Lemma 234
(Piecewise linear update of the fitted values in LARS–LASSO).

For
\Sigma\in{\mathbb{M}}
, the LASSO estimates
\widehat{\bm{y}}(\Sigma)
satisfy

\widehat{\bm{y}}(\Sigma)=\widehat{\bm{y}}(\Sigma_{0})+\sigma_{\mathbb{S}}(\Sigma-\Sigma_{0}){\bm{u}}_{\mathbb{S}}

(9.66)

where
{\bm{u}}_{\mathbb{S}}
is the equiangular vector
{\bm{u}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}={\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\bm{w}}_{\mathbb{S}}
,
{\bm{w}}_{\mathbb{S}}=\sigma_{\mathbb{S}}{\bm{G}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{-1}{\bm{1}}_{\mathbb{S}}
.
Equivalently, in terms of the nonzero regression coefficients
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{S}}(\Sigma)
,

{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{S}}(\Sigma)={\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{S}}(\Sigma_{0})+{\bm{S}}_{\mathbb{S}}\sigma_{\mathbb{S}}(\Sigma-\Sigma_{0}){\bm{w}}_{\mathbb{S}},

(9.67)

where
{\bm{S}}_{\mathbb{S}}\triangleq\mathrm{diag}({\bm{s}}_{\mathbb{S}})
is the diagonal matrix with diagonal elements
s_{i}=\sign({\widehat{\beta}}_{i})
,
i\in{\mathbb{S}}
, and
{\bm{s}}_{\mathbb{S}}
is a vector containing these sign elements.

Note that (
) implies that the maximum absolute correlation
\widehat{C}(\Sigma)
equals
\widehat{C}(\Sigma_{0})-\sigma_{\mathbb{S}}^{2}(\Sigma-\Sigma_{0})
by (
), so that
\widehat{C}(\Sigma)
is a piecewise linear decreasing function of the LASSO parameter
\Sigma
.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
The lemma says that, for
\Sigma
in
{\mathbb{M}}
where the active set
{\mathbb{S}}
and signs
{\bm{s}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}

remain fixed,
\widehat{\bm{y}}(\Sigma)
moves linearly along the equiangular vector
{\bm{u}}_{\mathbb{S}}
determined by
{\mathbb{S}}
.
Since
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}(\Sigma)
satisfies the constrained LASSO problem (
LC
) and has support
{\mathbb{S}}
, it also minimizes

f({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{S}})=\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\bm{S}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

subject to

\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}}s_{i}{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}=\Sigma\qquad\text{and}\qquad\sign({\widehat{\beta}}_{i})=s_{i}\quad\text{for }i\in{\mathbb{S}}.

(9.68)

The inequality constraint in the constraint LASSO problem (
LC
) can be replaced by
\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}=\Sigma
as long as
\Sigma
is less than
\sum\big\lvert{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}\big\rvert
for the full
p
-variable OLS solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{p}
.
Moreover, the fact that the minimizing point
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{S}}(\Sigma)
occurs strictly inside the simplex (
), combined with the strict convexity of
f({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{S}})
, implies we can drop the second condition in (
) so that
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{S}}(\Sigma)
solves

\min\quad\{f({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{S}})\}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}}s_{i}{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}=\Sigma.

(9.69)

Introducing a Lagrange multiplier
\lambda
, (
) becomes

\min\quad\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\bm{S}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{S}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\lambda\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}}s_{i}{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}.

Differentiating with respect to
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\mathbb{S}}
and setting the gradient to zero yields

\displaystyle-{\bm{S}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}({\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\bm{S}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{S}})+\lambda{\bm{S}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\bm{1}}_{\mathbb{S}}=\boldsymbol{0}

(9.70)

\displaystyle\quad\implies\quad{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\mathbb{S}}=({\bm{S}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\bm{S}}_{\mathbb{S}})^{-1}({\bm{S}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\bm{y}}-\lambda{\bm{s}}_{\mathbb{S}}).

(9.71)

Now consider two values
\Sigma_{1},\Sigma_{2}\in{\mathbb{M}}
with
\Sigma_{0}<\Sigma_{1}<\Sigma_{2}
,
and let
\lambda_{1}>\lambda_{2}
be the corresponding Lagrange multipliers (since larger
\Sigma
implies smaller penalty weight).
Subtracting the optimality conditions for
\Sigma_{1}
and
\Sigma_{2}
gives

{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\bm{S}}_{\mathbb{S}}\big({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{S}}(\Sigma_{2})-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{S}}(\Sigma_{1})\big)=(\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{2}){\bm{1}}_{\mathbb{S}},

which implies

{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{S}}(\Sigma_{2})-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{S}}(\Sigma_{1})=(\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{2}){\bm{S}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\bm{G}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{-1}{\bm{1}}_{\mathbb{S}}.

However, we can also prove
{\bm{s}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}[{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{S}}(\Sigma_{2})-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{S}}(\Sigma_{1})]=\Sigma_{2}-\Sigma_{1}
according to the LASSO definition:

For the active set,
\Sigma=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}=\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}}\left\lvert\beta_{i}\right\rvert={\bm{s}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\mathbb{S}}
.
Substitute (
9.71
):

\Sigma={\bm{s}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}({\bm{S}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\bm{S}}_{\mathbb{S}})^{-1}({\bm{S}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\bm{y}}-\lambda{\bm{s}}_{\mathbb{S}}).

Define

a\triangleq{\bm{s}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}({\bm{S}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\bm{S}}_{\mathbb{S}})^{-1}{\bm{S}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\bm{y}}

and
b\triangleq{\bm{s}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}({\bm{S}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\bm{S}}_{\mathbb{S}})^{-1}{\bm{s}}_{\mathbb{S}}
.
Then

\Sigma=a-\lambda b\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\lambda=\frac{a-\Sigma}{b}.

Thus,
\lambda
is an affine (linear) function of
\Sigma

while
{\mathbb{S}}
and
{\bm{s}}_{\mathbb{S}}
remain fixed.
Differentiate (
9.71
) with respect to
\Sigma
:

\frac{\partial{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\mathbb{S}}}{\partial\Sigma}=-({\bm{S}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\bm{S}}_{\mathbb{S}})^{-1}{\bm{s}}_{\mathbb{S}}\cdot\frac{\partial\lambda}{\partial\Sigma}
.
From
\lambda=(a-\Sigma)/b
, we get
\dfrac{\partial\lambda}{\partial\Sigma}=-\dfrac{1}{b}
.
Hence

\frac{\partial{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{\mathbb{S}}}{\partial\Sigma}=\frac{({\bm{S}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\bm{S}}_{\mathbb{S}})^{-1}{\bm{s}}_{\mathbb{S}}}{{\bm{s}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}({\bm{S}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\bm{S}}_{\mathbb{S}})^{-1}{\bm{s}}_{\mathbb{S}}},\qquad\frac{\partial{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{{\mathbb{S}}^{c}}}{\partial\Sigma}=\boldsymbol{0}.

If
\Sigma_{1}
and
\Sigma_{2}
lie within the same region
where the active set
{\mathbb{S}}
and sign vector
{\bm{s}}_{\mathbb{S}}
remain unchanged, then

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1}=(\Sigma_{2}-\Sigma_{1})\frac{({\bm{S}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\bm{S}}_{\mathbb{S}})^{-1}{\bm{s}}_{\mathbb{S}}}{{\bm{s}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}({\bm{S}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\bm{S}}_{\mathbb{S}})^{-1}{\bm{s}}_{\mathbb{S}}}.

(9.72)

That is,
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
changes linearly with
\Sigma

along the fixed direction

{\bm{v}}\triangleq\frac{({\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}})^{-1}{\bm{s}}_{\mathbb{S}}}{{\bm{s}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}({\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{\mathbb{S}})^{-1}{\bm{s}}_{\mathbb{S}}}
.

Therefore,

\Sigma_{2}-\Sigma_{1}=(\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{2}){\bm{s}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\bm{S}}_{\mathbb{S}}{\bm{G}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{-1}{\bm{1}}_{\mathbb{S}}=(\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{2}){\bm{1}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{\top}{\bm{G}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{-1}{\bm{1}}_{\mathbb{S}}=(\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{2})\sigma_{\mathbb{S}}^{-2},

and hence

{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{S}}(\Sigma_{2})-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{\mathbb{S}}(\Sigma_{1})={\bm{S}}_{\mathbb{S}}\sigma_{\mathbb{S}}^{2}(\Sigma_{2}-\Sigma_{1}){\bm{G}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{-1}{\bm{1}}_{\mathbb{S}}={\bm{S}}_{\mathbb{S}}\sigma_{\mathbb{S}}(\Sigma_{2}-\Sigma_{1}){\bm{w}}_{\mathbb{S}}.

(9.73)

Invoking
\Sigma_{2}=\Sigma
and
\Sigma_{1}\to\Sigma_{0}
gives (
) by the continuity of
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}(\Sigma)
, and implying the desired result (
).

Lemma
(
) shows that, for
\Sigma\in{\mathbb{M}}
, the constrained LASSO regression estimates
\widehat{\bm{y}}(\Sigma)
move in the LARS equiangular direction
{\bm{u}}_{\mathbb{S}}
defined in (
).
Moreover, the LASSO solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}(\Sigma)
lies on the boundary of the diamond-shaped convex polytope (i.e., the “
\ell_{1}
-norm” ball with radius
\Sigma
):

{\mathbb{B}}_{1}[\boldsymbol{0},\Sigma]=\left\{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\mid\sum\left\lvert\alpha_{i}\right\rvert\leq\Sigma\right\},

(9.74)

This set
{\mathbb{B}}_{1}[\boldsymbol{0},\Sigma]
expands monotonically as
\Sigma
increases. Lemma
(
) further shows that, for
\Sigma\in{\mathbb{M}}
, the regression coefficients
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}(\Sigma)
move linearly along edge
{\mathbb{S}}
of the polytope, namely, the face where
\beta_{i}=0
for all
i\notin{\mathbb{S}}
.

\paragrapharrow

Sign restriction.
Let
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
be a solution to the constrained LASSO problem (
LC
), and let
\widehat{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
denote the corresponding fitted values.
It is straightforward to show that for any nonzero component
{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}
, its sign must match the sign
s_{i}
of the current correlation
\widehat{c}_{i}={\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}({\bm{y}}-\widehat{\bm{y}})
,

\mathrm{sign}({\widehat{\beta}}_{i})=\mathrm{sign}(\widehat{c}_{i})=s_{i}.

(9.75)

Lemma 235
(Sign restriction of LARS–LASSO).

For any LASSO solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
, the current correlations satisfy

\widehat{c}_{i}=\widehat{C}\cdot\sign({\widehat{\beta}}_{i}),\quad\text{for }i\in{\mathbb{S}},

(9.76)

where
\widehat{c}_{i}
is the current correlation
{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}({\bm{y}}-\widehat{\bm{y}})={\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}({\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})
. In particular, this implies that

\sign({\widehat{\beta}}_{i})=\sign(\widehat{c}_{i}),\quad\text{for }i\in{\mathbb{S}}.

(9.77)

Proof
[of Lemma
]
This follows immediately from the stationary condition (
9.70
) by observing that the
i
-th element of the left-hand side is
\widehat{c}_{i}
, and the right-hand side is
\lambda\cdot\sign({\widehat{\beta}}_{i})
for
i\in{\mathbb{S}}
.
Moreover,
\lambda=\left\lvert\widehat{c}_{i}\right\rvert=\widehat{C}
, which completes the proof.

The standard LARS algorithm does not enforce the sign restriction (
), so it cannot be used directly to compute LASSO solutions. However, it can be easily modified to incorporate this constraint.

\paragrapharrow
LASSO modification.
Suppose we have just completed a LARS step, giving a new active set
{\mathbb{S}}
from the previous active set
{\mathbb{S}}_{-}
, as in (
), and that the current LARS estimate
\widehat{\bm{y}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{-}}
coincides with a valid LASSO solution
\widehat{\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
.
At the beginning of this LARS step, we know (assume) that the sign restriction (
) holds.
However, this may no longer be true after moving further along the current equiangular direction.
To analyze this, define

{\bm{w}}_{\mathbb{S}}=\sigma_{\mathbb{S}}{\bm{G}}_{\mathbb{S}}^{-1}{\bm{1}}_{\mathbb{S}},

(9.78)

a vector of length the size of
\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}\right\rvert
.
Now construct the
p
-dimensional direction vector

\widehat{\bm{d}}
by setting

\widehat{d}_{i}=\begin{cases}s_{i}w_{{\mathbb{S}},i},&i\in{\mathbb{S}};\\
0,&i\notin{\mathbb{S}}.\end{cases}

Moving in the positive
\gamma
direction along the LARS path (
),
the coefficient path is given by

{\bm{y}}(\gamma)={\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}(\gamma),\quad\text{where }\beta_{i}(\gamma)\triangleq{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}+\gamma\widehat{d}_{i},\text{ for $i\in{\mathbb{S}}$},

(9.79)

see also (
).
Therefore,
\beta_{i}(\gamma)
will change sign at

\gamma_{i}\triangleq-{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}/\widehat{d}_{i};

(9.80)

the first sign change happens at

\widetilde{\gamma}\triangleq\min_{\gamma_{i}>0}\{\gamma_{i}\},

(9.81)

say for covariate
\beta_{i_{+}}
.
If no such
\gamma_{i}
exists (i.e., all
\gamma_{i}\leq 0
), we define
\widetilde{\gamma}=\infty
.

If
\widetilde{\gamma}<\widehat{\gamma}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
—where
\widehat{\gamma}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
is the stepsize to the next variable joining the active set, as defined in (
)—then the path
\beta_{i}(\gamma)
ceases to be a valid LASSO solution for any
\gamma>\widetilde{\gamma}
since the sign restriction (
) would be violated:
\beta_{i}(\gamma)
changes sign, but the corresponding correlation
c_{i}(\gamma)
does not.
This is because the continuous function
c_{i}(\gamma)
cannot change sign within a single LARS step since
\left\lvert c_{i}(\gamma)\right\rvert=\widehat{C}_{{\mathbb{S}}}-\gamma\sigma_{\mathbb{S}}>0
by (
).
This leads to the following modification for computing LASSO paths:

Remark 236
(LASSO modification).

If
\widetilde{\gamma}<\widehat{\gamma}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
, stop the ongoing LARS step at
\gamma=\widetilde{\gamma}
and remove the index
i_{+}
(the one achieving
{\widetilde{\gamma}}
) from the calculation of the next equiangular direction.
Specifically, update the fit and active set as

\widehat{\bm{y}}_{{\mathbb{S}}}=\widehat{\bm{y}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{-}}+\widetilde{\gamma}{\bm{u}}_{\mathbb{S}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad{\mathbb{S}}_{+}={\mathbb{S}}-\{i_{+}\}

(9.82)

instead of proceeding with the standard update (
).
Otherwise, if

\widetilde{\gamma}\geq\widehat{\gamma}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
, proceed with the usual LARS update (
).

In the original LARS algorithm, the active set
{\mathbb{S}}
grows monotonically. The LASSO modification, however, allows variables to be dropped from
{\mathbb{S}}
when their coefficients cross zero.
The LASSO modification also assumes a “one-at-a-time” condition
which means that at each step, at most one variable is either added to or removed from the active set. This condition typically holds for continuous (quantitative) data and can always be enforced by adding an infinitesimal random perturbation to the response vector
{\bm{y}}
if necessary.
The complete procedure is summarized in Algorithm
.

{theoremHigh}

[LARS–LASSO relationship]
Under the above LASSO modification, and assuming the “one-at-a-time” condition, the LARS algorithm generates the entire LASSO solution path.

Proof

See
Efron et al. 2004
.

Algorithm 7

LARS algorithm with LASSO modification
(
Efron et al. 2004
)

1:

The data vector
{\bm{y}}\in\real^{n}
and the input matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
.

2:

Initialization:

{\mathbb{S}}_{0}=\varnothing
,
\widehat{\bm{y}}=\boldsymbol{0}
, and
{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{0}}={\bm{X}}
;

3:

for

t=1,2,\ldots

do

4:

Compute the current correlation vector
\widehat{\bm{c}}_{t}={\bm{X}}^{\top}({\bm{y}}-\widehat{\bm{y}}_{t-1})
;

5:

Update the active set
{\mathbb{S}}_{t}={\mathbb{S}}_{t-1}\cup\left\{i\mid\left\lvert\widehat{c}_{ti}\right\rvert=C\right\}
with
C=\max\left\{\left\lvert\widehat{c}_{t1}\right\rvert,\left\lvert\widehat{c}_{t2}\right\rvert,\ldots\right\}
, and
\widehat{c}_{ti}
being the
i
-th element of
\widehat{\bm{c}}_{t}
;

6:

Update the input matrix
{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{t}}=[\ldots,s_{i}{\bm{x}}_{i},\ldots]_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}_{t}}
, where
s_{i}=\sign(\widehat{c}_{ti})
;

7:

Find the direction of the current minimum angle:

\displaystyle{\bm{G}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{t}}

\displaystyle={\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{t}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{t}}\in\real^{\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}_{t}\right\rvert\times\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}_{t}\right\rvert},

\displaystyle\sigma_{{\mathbb{S}}_{t}}=({\bm{1}}_{t}^{\top}{\bm{G}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{t}}^{-1}{\bm{1}}_{t})^{-1/2},

\displaystyle{\bm{w}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{t}}

\displaystyle=\sigma_{{\mathbb{S}}_{t}}{\bm{G}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{t}}^{-1}{\bm{1}}_{t}\in\real^{\left\lvert{\mathbb{S}}_{t}\right\rvert},

\displaystyle{\bm{u}}_{t}={\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{t}}{\bm{w}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{t}}\in\real^{n}.

8:

Compute
{\bm{z}}={\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{u}}_{t}=[z_{1},z_{2},\ldots,z_{p}]^{\top}
and estimate the coefficient vector

{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{t}=({\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{t}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{t}})^{-1}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{t}}^{\top}{\bm{y}}={\bm{G}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{t}}^{-1}{\bm{X}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{t}}^{\top}{\bm{y}}.

9:

By (
), compute

{\widehat{\gamma}}=\mathop{\text{min}^{+}}_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}_{t}^{c}}\left\{\frac{C-\widehat{c}_{ti}}{\sigma_{{\mathbb{S}}_{t}}-z_{i}},\frac{C+\widehat{c}_{ti}}{\sigma_{{\mathbb{S}}_{t}}+z_{i}}\right\},\qquad{\widetilde{\gamma}}=\min_{i\in{\mathbb{S}}_{t}}\left\{-\frac{z_{i}}{s_{i}w_{{\mathbb{S}}_{t},i}}\right\}^{+},

where
w_{{\mathbb{S}}_{t},i}
is the
i
-th entry of
{\bm{w}}_{{\mathbb{S}}_{t}}=[w_{1},w_{2},\ldots]^{\top}
, and
(\cdot)^{+}
denotes the positive minimum term. If there is no positive term then
{\text{min}^{+}}\{\cdot\}=\infty
;

10:

if

{\widetilde{\gamma}}<{\widehat{\gamma}}

then

11:

The fitted vector
\widehat{\bm{y}}_{t}
and the active set
{\mathbb{S}}_{t}
are modified as follows:

\widehat{\bm{y}}_{t}=\widehat{\bm{y}}_{t-1}+{\widetilde{\gamma}}{\bm{u}}_{t},\qquad{\mathbb{S}}_{t}={\mathbb{S}}_{t}\setminus\{i_{+}\},

where the removed index
i_{+}
is the index
i\in{\mathbb{S}}_{t}
such that
{\widetilde{\gamma}}
is a minimum;

12:

else

13:

The fitted vector
\widehat{\bm{y}}_{t}
and the active set
{\mathbb{S}}_{t}
are modified as follows:

\widehat{\bm{y}}_{t}=\widehat{\bm{y}}_{t-1}+{\widehat{\gamma}}{\bm{u}}_{t},\qquad{\mathbb{S}}_{t}={\mathbb{S}}_{t}\cup\{i_{+}\},

where the added index
i_{+}
is the index
i\in{\mathbb{S}}_{t}^{c}
such that
{\widehat{\gamma}}
is a minimum;

14:

end

if

15:

Exit if some stopping criterion is satisfied;

16:

end

for

17:

return

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{t}
;

LARS–LASSO Relationship

We now briefly discuss Theorem
, which establishes the equivalence between the modified LARS algorithm and the constrained LASSO problem. This equivalence stems from the fact that the sequence of coefficient estimates—the so-called solution path—generated by the modified LARS algorithm, as it proceeds step by step, coincides exactly with the set of solutions to the constrained LASSO problem as the constraint parameter
\Sigma
increases from 0 to
\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{OLS}\big\rVert_{1}
, the
\ell_{1}
-norm of the ordinary least squares (OLS) solution.

The standard constrained LASSO problem is

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
subvject to
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\Sigma
, where
\Sigma
is a nonnegative scalar that controls the total “budget” for the sum of the absolute values of the coefficients.
As
\Sigma
increases from 0, the behavior of the solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}(\Sigma)
evolves as follows:

When
\Sigma=0
, the only solution is
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\boldsymbol{0}
.

As
\Sigma
increases slightly, the optimal solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}(\Sigma)
will have one or a few nonzero coefficients, chosen to reduce the least squares loss as much as possible per unit of “
\ell_{1}
-cost.”

As
\Sigma\to\infty
, the constraint becomes inactive, and
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}(\Sigma)
approaches the OLS solution.

The solution path
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}(\Sigma)
is the set of all optimal solutions as
\Sigma
varies.

The equivalence between the modified LARS and constrained LASSO arises from the optimality conditions (KKT conditions) of the LASSO problem and how LARS satisfies them at each step.
At the optimal solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
for a given constraint
\Sigma
, the following KKT conditions (Theorem
) must hold:

1.

Subgradient condition.
The gradient of the least squares loss (
-{\bm{X}}^{\top}({\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})
) must be in the subdifferential of
\lambda\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}
, where
\lambda
is the Lagrangian dual variable.
This translates to:

For any
i
where
{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}\neq 0
:
\big\lvert{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}({\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})\big\rvert=\lambda
(the absolute correlation between predictor
i
and the residual is exactly
\lambda
).

For any
i
where
{\widehat{\beta}}_{i}=0
:
\big\lvert{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}({\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})\big\rvert\leq\lambda
(the absolute correlation is less than or equal to
\lambda
).

2.

Complementary slackness.

\lambda(\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}-\Sigma)=0
. If
\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}<\Sigma
, then
\lambda=0
(no regularization). If
\lambda>0
, then
\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\big\rVert_{1}=\Sigma
(the constraint is active).

The modified LARS algorithm satisfies these KKT conditions by the following:

Equal correlations.
At the start of each LARS step, the algorithm ensures that all predictors in the active set have
equal absolute correlation
with the current residual. This matches the KKT condition that nonzero coefficients must have
\left\lvert{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{r}}\right\rvert=\lambda
for some
\lambda
, where
{\bm{r}}
denotes the residual.

Maximal correlation.
The algorithm also ensures that no inactive predictor has a higher absolute correlation with the residual than the active ones. This matches the KKT condition
\left\lvert{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{r}}\right\rvert\leq\lambda
for
i
not in the active set.

Increasing
\Sigma
.
As LARS takes each step and moves the coefficients, the
\ell_{1}
-norm
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}
increases. The point where LARS changes direction (when a new variable enters or an old one leaves) corresponds to a specific value of
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}=\Sigma_{t}
.

Path as
\Sigma
increases.
The piecewise linear path generated by LARS, parameterized by the step or by
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}
, satisfies the KKT conditions for the constrained LASSO problem at every point along the path. The “
\lambda
” in the KKT conditions is implicitly determined by the common absolute correlation value of the active predictors at each step.

Importantly, neither the standard nor the modified LARS algorithm (Algorithm
) takes the constraint parameter
\Sigma
as an explicit input.
Instead, it proceeds via geometric steps dictated by predictor–residual correlations.
Nevertheless, at the end of each LARS step
t
, the resulting coefficient vector
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{t}
is precisely the solution to the constrained LASSO problem with
\Sigma_{t}=\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{t}\big\rVert_{1}
:

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\quad\text{ s.t. }\quad\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\Sigma_{t}.

In other words, the LARS path
is
the LASSO solution path. Although
\Sigma
is not an input to the algorithm, it serves as the natural parameter that indexes the path: each point on the LARS trajectory corresponds to a unique value of
\Sigma=\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}
. Consequently, the full regularization path is obtained automatically, and one can subsequently select the optimal
\Sigma
—for example, via cross-validation.

9.3
Algorithms for Lagrangian LASSO Problems

We introduce several algorithms for solving the constrained LASSO problem (
LC
).
We now turn to the Lagrangian (or penalized) form of the LASSO problem. This formulation is more commonly used in machine learning due to its simplicity: it casts the problem as an unconstrained optimization with a single objective function, which is algorithmically easier to handle than a constrained problem like (
LC
). Moreover, it integrates naturally into regularization frameworks.

In machine learning, regularization is a fundamental technique for preventing overfitting and promoting desirable model properties—such as sparsity; see Section
.
The Lagrangian LASSO explicitly captures this trade-off between data fidelity (measured by the loss) and model complexity (penalized via the
\ell_{1}
-norm).

The standard form of the Lagrangian LASSO (
LL
) (p.
LL
) is:

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\quad F({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\triangleq f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+g({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\triangleq\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\lambda\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1},

(9.83)

where
g({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\triangleq\lambda\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}
.

Since both
f
and
g
are convex (Exercise
), one might consider applying gradient descent as a straightforward approach.
However, the objective function
F({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
is non-smooth at points where any component of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
is zero (due to the nondifferentiability of the
\ell_{1}
-norm).
Consequently, the classical gradient does not exist everywhere, and standard gradient descent cannot be applied directly.

To address this, subgradient methods can be employed. While
f
is smooth—specifically,
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}
-smooth (see Example
)—and
g
is Lipschitz continuous, their sum
F=f+g
is neither smooth nor differentiable. As a result, subgradient methods applied to
F
generally exhibit slow convergence and lack strong theoretical guarantees (e.g., no linear or even accelerated rates without additional structure).

9.3.1
Smoothing with Huber Loss

An alternative approach to handling the non-smoothness of the LASSO objective is to recognize that the
\ell_{1}
-norm,
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\left\lvert\beta_{i}\right\rvert
, is a sum of absolute-value functions—each of which is nondifferentiable at zero. If we replace each absolute value with a smooth approximation, then standard gradient-based optimization methods become applicable.
One common choice for such an approximation is the
Huber loss function
, defined as:

h_{\delta}(x)=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{2\delta}x^{2},&\left\lvert x\right\rvert<\delta;\\
\left\lvert x\right\rvert-\frac{\delta}{2},&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

(9.84)

When
\delta\to 0
, the smooth function
h_{\delta}(x)
approaches the absolute value function
\left\lvert x\right\rvert
. Figure
illustrates the graph of
h_{\delta}(x)
for various values of
\delta
.

Figure 9.4:
Illustration of Huber loss function
h_{\delta}(x)
for different values of
\delta
.

By substituting
\left\lvert\beta_{i}\right\rvert
with
h_{\delta}(\beta_{i})
, we obtain a
smoothed LASSO
problem:

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\quad F_{\delta}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\lambda H_{\delta}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}),\quad\text{with }H_{\delta}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\triangleq\sum_{i=1}^{p}h_{\delta}(\beta_{i}),

(9.85)

where
\delta
is the given smoothing parameter.
The objective
F_{\delta}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
is now continuously differentiable, and its gradient can be computed as:

\nabla F_{\delta}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})={\bm{X}}^{\top}({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}})+\lambda\nabla H_{\delta}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}),

(9.86)

where
\nabla H_{\delta}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
is defined component-wise by:

(\nabla H_{\delta}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}))_{i}=\begin{cases}\sign(\beta_{i}),&\left\lvert\beta_{i}\right\rvert>\delta;\\
{\beta_{i}}/{\delta},&\left\lvert\beta_{i}\right\rvert\leq\delta,\end{cases}\quad i\in\{1,2,\ldots,p\}.

(9.87)

Since both terms in
F_{\delta}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
are convex and the gradient
\nabla F_{\delta}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
is Lipschitz continuous, the function
F_{\delta}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
is
L_{b}
-smooth with Lipschitz constant

L_{b}=\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}+\frac{\lambda}{\delta}

(see Example
and Exercise
).
Therefore, by Problem
, gradient descent with a constant stepsize
\eta=1/L_{b}
is guaranteed to converge to the global minimum of
F_{\delta}
.

However, when
\delta
is very small—i.e., when the smoothed problem closely approximates the original LASSO—the Lipschitz constant
L_{b}
becomes large due to the
\lambda/\delta
term. In this regime, the required stepsize
\eta=1/L_{b}
becomes very small, which can lead to slow convergence in practice. Thus, careful tuning of
\delta
(or the use of adaptive stepsize strategies) is essential when using this smoothing approach.

9.3.2
Proximal Gradient and Minorization-Maximization Methods

Given that both functions
f
and
g
in the Lagrangian LASSO problem (
) are convex, where
f
is differentiable and
g
is non-differentiable, problem (
) can be considered a composite model.
We have already introduced the proximal gradient method to address such composite problems (Section
).
Although alternative approaches exist—such as generalized conditional gradient and generalized mirror descent methods
(
Lu 2025
)
—these typically require solving, at each iteration, a subproblem of the form
\mathop{\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in{\real{}^{p}}}\big\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}),{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\big\rangle+g({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
.
In the LASSO setting, this subproblem is essentially as difficult as the original problem (
).
Therefore, the proximal gradient method remains the most practical and efficient choice.

Following Algorithm
, the update rule for the proximal gradient method applied to the Lagrangian LASSO problem (
) at the
t
-th iteration is:

\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)}

\displaystyle\leftarrow{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-\eta_{t}{\bm{X}}^{\top}({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-{\bm{y}});

(9.88a)

\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}

\displaystyle\leftarrow\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{\eta_{t}g}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)})=\mathcal{T}_{\eta_{t}\lambda}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)})=\big[\big\lvert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)}\big\rvert-\eta_{t}\lambda{\bm{1}}\big]_{+}\circ\sign({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)}),

(9.88b)

where
\mathcal{T}_{\lambda}(\cdot)
denotes the soft-thresholding operator (Example
).
This two-step procedure first performs a standard gradient descent step on the smooth loss
f
, followed by a shrinkage (thresholding) operation that promotes sparsity in the iterates.
Convergence of this scheme is guaranteed by Theorem
when using a constant stepsize
\eta_{t}=\frac{1}{\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}}
since
f
is
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}
-smooth (Example
).

Note that this update closely resembles the proximal gradient step for the constrained LASSO problem in (
); however, in the constrained formulation, the regularization parameter
\lambda
is not fixed but instead varies adaptively with the constraint level at each iteration.

Finally, when the proximal gradient method is applied specifically to the Lagrangian LASSO problem, it is commonly referred to in the literature as the
iterative shrinkage-thresholding algorithm (ISTA)
—a name that reflects how each iteration shrinks small coefficients toward zero, thereby encouraging sparse solutions.

Minorization-Maximization Method

We further turn to a class of methods, known either as
minorization-maximization
or
majorization-minimization (MM)
algorithms.
These are particularly useful for nonconvex problems and belong to the family of
auxiliary-variable methods
: they introduce an auxiliary function that locally upper-bounds (i.e., majorizes) the original objective, turning a difficult minimization into a sequence of simpler ones.

Although MM methods apply to both constrained and unconstrained settings, we describe them here for an unconstrained problem of the form
\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
, where
f:\real^{p}\to\real
may be nonconvex.

Definition 237
(Auxiliary function (majorizer)).

A function
\Psi({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})
is called an auxiliary function for
F({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
(or a majorizer of
F
at
{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
) if it satisfies:

\Psi({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})\geq F({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\quad\text{and}\quad\Psi({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}})=F({\boldsymbol{\beta}}).

(9.89)

In other words, the auxiliary function
\Psi(\cdot,{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})
is an upper bound of
F(\cdot)
, and the bound is tight at
{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.

Lemma 238
(Nonincreasing in auxiliary functions).

If
\Psi
is an auxiliary function for
F
, then the sequence generated by

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}=\mathop{\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\,\Psi({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}),\quad\text{for }t=0,1,2,\ldots

(9.90)

satisfies
F({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)})\leq F({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})
.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
By definition of the auxiliary function and the update rule:
F({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)})\leq\Psi({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})\leq\Psi({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})=F({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})
.

An MM algorithm proceeds by initializing
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(0)}
and iteratively applying the update (
).
The objective value decreases monotonically:

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}=\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\Psi\left({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\right),\quad\text{for }t=0,1,2,\ldots

(9.91)

Note that
F({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)})=F({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})
only if
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}
is a local minimum of
\Psi({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})
w.r.t.
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
. If the partial derivatives of
F
exist and are continuous in a small neighborhood of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}
, this also implies that the gradient
\nabla F({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})=\boldsymbol{0}
. Thus, by iterating the update in (
), we obtain a sequence of estimates that converge to a local minimum
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}=\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}F({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
of the objective function:

F({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(0)})\geq F({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(1)})\geq F({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(2)})\geq\ldots\geq F({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})\geq F({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)})\geq\ldots\geq F({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}).

(9.92)

Definition
finds a majorizer
\Psi
of
F
, and Lemma
shows the minimization property in
\Psi
, hence the algorithm is often referred to as the
majorization-minimization (MM) framework
.
The key advantage of the MM framework is that if the surrogate function
\Psi(\cdot,{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})
admits a closed-form minimizer or can be minimized efficiently, then each iteration becomes computationally tractable—even when direct minimization of
F
is not.
Moreover, if
F
is strictly convex, the MM algorithm converges to the global minimizer.

\paragrapharrow

Proximal gradient as an MM algorithm for Lagrangian LASSO problems.

Recall from Sections
and
that the proximal gradient method applies to objectives of the form
F=f+g
, where
f=\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
is convex and differentiable, and
g=\lambda\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}
is convex and nondifferentiable. By applying the linear approximation theorem (Theorem
) to
f
, we obtain

\displaystyle F({\boldsymbol{\beta}})

\displaystyle=f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+g({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=f({\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})+\left\langle\nabla f({\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}),{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle+\frac{1}{2}\left\langle{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}},\nabla^{2}f({\boldsymbol{\xi}})({\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rangle+g({\boldsymbol{\beta}}),

where
{\boldsymbol{\xi}}=\gamma{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+(1-\gamma){\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
for some
\gamma\in[0,1]
.
Since
f
is
L_{b}
-smooth with
L_{b}\triangleq\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}
(Example
),
we have an upper bound on the Hessian, namely
\nabla^{2}f({\boldsymbol{\xi}})\preceq L_{b}{\bm{I}}_{p\times p}
, from which we obtain the inequality

F({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\leq f({\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})+\left\langle\nabla f({\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}),{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle+\frac{L_{b}}{2}\left\lVert{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+g({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\triangleq{\Psi({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})},

with equality holding when
{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.
At
{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}
, the update at the
t
-th iteration becomes:

\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}

\displaystyle=\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\Psi\left({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\right)

(9.93)

\displaystyle\implies\frac{\lambda}{L_{b}}\sign({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-\frac{1}{L_{b}}{\bm{X}}^{\top}({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-{\bm{y}}),

(9.94)

which is precisely the proximal gradient step with stepsize
\eta_{t}={1}/{L_{b}}
.
Thus, the proximal gradient method for the Lagrangian LASSO can be interpreted as an instance of the MM framework, where the surrogate function
\Psi
is constructed via a quadratic upper bound on the smooth part
f
.

Algorithm 8

FISTA-V1

1:

{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(1)}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(1)}\in\real^{p}
,
\gamma_{1}=\frac{1}{\zeta_{1}}=1
;

for

do

3:

Choose
\eta_{t}
and
\zeta_{t}=\frac{1}{\gamma_{t}}
;
