9.3.3
Fast Proximal Gradient Method—FISTA

The
fast proximal gradient
method, also known as the
fast iterative shrinkage-thresholding algorithm (FISTA)
(Algorithm
) is an accelerated variant of the proximal gradient method introduced by
Beck and Teboulle 2009
.
Recall that the standard proximal gradient method achieves a convergence rate of
\mathcal{O}\left({1}/{T}\right)
for minimizing a sum of a smooth convex function and a non-smooth convex regularizer (Theorem
).
A natural question is whether this rate can be improved. FISTA addresses this by incorporating momentum, leading to a faster convergence
\mathcal{O}\left({1}/{T^{2}}\right)
.

FISTA operates in two steps at each iteration
t
:

It constructs an extrapolated point
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)}
using information from the two most recent iterates.

It performs a proximal gradient step at this extrapolated point.

Specifically, the update takes the form:

\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)}

\displaystyle\leftarrow{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}+\frac{t-2}{t+1}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t-1)});

(9.95a)

\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}

\displaystyle\leftarrow\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{\eta_{t}g}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)}-\eta_{t}\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)})).

(9.95b)

The key distinction from the standard proximal gradient method is the
momentum term
,
\frac{t-2}{t+1}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t-1)})
, which leverages historical iterates to accelerate convergence.
Crucially, this acceleration incurs negligible additional computational cost per iteration, yet yields significantly faster empirical and theoretical performance.
If the stepsize
\eta_{t}
is fixed and satisfies
\eta_{t}={1}/{L_{b}}
(where
f
is assumed to be
L_{b}
-smooth), then FISTA guarantees a convergence rate of
\mathcal{O}\left({1}/{T^{2}}\right)
; see Theorem
.
With this intuition, the complete FISTA algorithm is presented in Algorithm
, where we define
\zeta_{t}=\frac{1}{\gamma_{t}}
for all
t>0
.
When
\frac{1}{\gamma_{t}}=\zeta_{t}\triangleq\frac{t+1}{2}
, Algorithm
is equivalent to the intuitive update in (
).

To facilitate theoretical analysis, an equivalent reformulation of FISTA is often used—shown in Algorithm
. While Algorithm
makes the momentum mechanism explicit and is thus more interpretable, Algorithm
structures the updates in a way that simplifies the convergence proof (see Theorem
).

\paragrapharrow

Convergence requirement.
To achieve the accelerated
\mathcal{O}\left({1}/{T^{2}}\right)
rate, the stepsizes
\eta_{t}

and
\gamma_{t}=\frac{1}{\zeta_{t}}
must satisfy certain conditions. Specifically, the following three requirements ensure the desired convergence behavior:

\displaystyle f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})\leq f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)})+\left\langle\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)}),{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)}\right\rangle+\frac{1}{2\eta_{t}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},\text{ i.e., $\eta_{t}\leq\frac{1}{L_{b}}$};

(9.96a)

\displaystyle\gamma_{1}=1,\hskip 9.24994pt\frac{(1-\gamma_{t+1})\eta_{t+1}}{\gamma_{t+1}^{2}}\leq\frac{\eta_{t}}{\gamma_{t}^{2}},\hskip 9.24994ptt>1;

(9.96b)

\displaystyle\frac{\gamma_{t}^{2}}{\eta_{t}}=\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{t^{2}}\right).

(9.96c)

\paragrapharrow

Choice of
\gamma_{t}=\frac{1}{\zeta_{t}}
.
A common and effective choice is to set
\eta_{t}=\frac{1}{L_{b}}
and
\frac{1}{\zeta_{t}}=\gamma_{t}=\frac{2}{t+1}
for
t>0
.
This selection satisfies all conditions in (
) and recovers the intuitive FISTA update in (
).
However, this choice is not unique. Another valid sequence is defined recursively by:

\displaystyle\gamma_{1}=1,\hskip 9.24994pt\frac{1}{\gamma_{t+1}}=\frac{1}{2}\left(1+\sqrt{1+\frac{4}{\gamma_{t}^{2}}}\right)\iff\zeta_{t+1}=\frac{1+\sqrt{1+4\zeta_{t}^{2}}}{2},\hskip 9.24994ptt>0.

where
\{\gamma_{t}\}=\{\frac{1}{\zeta_{t}}\}
.
This sequence also yields an
\mathcal{O}\left({1}/{T^{2}}\right)
convergence rate.
The following lemma confirms that this recursive choice satisfies condition in (
).

Lemma 239
.

Let
\{\frac{1}{\gamma_{t}}\}_{t>0}=\{\zeta_{t}\}_{t>0}
be the sequence (see Algorithm
) defined by

\zeta_{1}=1,\;\zeta_{t+1}=\frac{1+\sqrt{1+4\zeta_{t}^{2}}}{2},t\geq 0.

Then,
\zeta_{t}\geq\frac{t+1}{2}
for all
t>0
.

Proof
[of Lemma
]
We proceed by induction.
Obviously, for
t=1
,
\zeta_{1}=1\geq\frac{1+1}{2}
, so the claim holds.
Suppose that the claim holds for
t>1
such that
\zeta_{t}\geq\frac{t+1}{2}
.
We will prove that
\zeta_{t+1}\geq\frac{t+2}{2}
. By the recursive relation defining the sequence and the induction assumption,

\zeta_{t+1}=\frac{1+\sqrt{1+4\zeta_{t}^{2}}}{2}\geq\frac{1+\sqrt{1+(t+1)^{2}}}{2}\geq\frac{1+\sqrt{(t+1)^{2}}}{2}=\frac{t+2}{2}
.
This completes the induction.

\paragrapharrow

Monotone issue.
The original FISTA algorithm is not a descent method—that is, the objective value

F({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})
may increase at some iterations.
To address this, we present a monotone (descent) variant of FISTA that requires only a minor modification to Algorithm
:
instead of always accepting the new iterate
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}
, we choose

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}\in\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}\left\{F({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\mid{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)},{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{(t)}\}\right\}

ensuring that
F({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)})\leq\min\{F({\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{(t)}),F({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})\}
.
This modified procedure is given in Algorithm
.
In practice, after computing the proximal update
{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{(t)}
, we compare its objective value with that of the current iterate
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}
.
Only if
F({\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{(t)})\leq F({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)})
do we accept
{\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{(t)}
as the next iterate; otherwise, we keep
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}
unchanged.
More compactly, Steps 6 to 10 of Algorithm
can be equivalently expressed as:

{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}+\frac{\zeta_{t}}{\zeta_{t+1}}({\boldsymbol{\xi}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)})+\frac{\zeta_{t}-1}{\zeta_{t+1}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}).

\paragrapharrow

Line search methods.
In Algorithms
and
, the stepsize must satisfy
\eta_{t}\leq\frac{1}{L_{b}}
to ensure condition (
9.96a
) holds.
However, in many practical problems, the Lipschitz constant
L_{b}
of
\nabla f
is unknown.
In such cases, we can still satisfy condition (
9.96a
) by using a backtracking line search to adaptively select
\eta_{t}
at each iteration. Meanwhile, the sequence
\{\gamma_{t}\}
can be chosen to simultaneously satisfy conditions (
9.96b
) and (
9.96c
), thereby preserving the accelerated convergence rate of
\mathcal{O}\left({1}/{T^{2}}\right)
.

Algorithm
implements such a line search strategy. At iteration
t
, it initializes
\eta_{t}
with the previous stepsize
\eta_{t-1}
and then decreases
\eta_{t}
geometrically until condition (
9.96a
) is met. Since this condition is guaranteed to hold for sufficiently small
\eta_{t}
(due to the smoothness of
f
), the line search always terminates in finite steps.
Moreover, it is straightforward to verify that the other two conditions—(
9.96b
) and (
9.96c
)—remain satisfied throughout the iterative process when
\{\gamma_{t}\}
is updated appropriately (e.g., via the recursive rule in Lemma
).

The following theorem establishes the convergence rate for FISTA with a fixed stepsize. The analysis for the adaptive (line search) variant follows analogously and is omitted for brevity.

{theoremHigh}

By the subgradient inequality (Definition

\eta_{t}g({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\geq\eta_{t}g({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)})+\left\langle-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}+{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)}-\eta_{t}\nabla f({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)}),{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}\right\rangle.

\displaystyle F({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)})=f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)})+g({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)})

where the last equality follows from the fact that

\paragrapharrow

Applied to LASSO.
Note that the FISTA method (Algorithm
and Lemma
) is a slight acceleration of the standard proximal gradient method. When applied to the LASSO problem

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\lambda\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1},

the FISTA updates take the following form:

\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)}

\displaystyle\leftarrow\mathcal{T}_{{\eta_{t}\lambda}}\left({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-\eta_{t}{\bm{X}}^{\top}({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-{\bm{y}})\right);

(9.99a)

\displaystyle\zeta_{t+1}

\displaystyle\leftarrow\frac{1+\sqrt{1+4\zeta_{t}^{2}}}{2};

(9.99b)

\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}

\displaystyle\leftarrow{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)}+\left(\frac{\zeta_{t}-1}{\zeta_{t+1}}\right)({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)}),

(9.99c)

where
\eta_{t}=1/\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}
and
\zeta_{1}=1
.

9.3.4
Penalty Function Method

We have now introduced several approaches for solving the Lagrangian LASSO problem.
Note that when the regularization parameter
\lambda
is small, the objective is dominated by the smooth loss term
f=\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
.
The proximal gradient method typically uses a fixed stepsize
\eta=1/L_{b}=1/\left\lVert{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}\right\rVert_{2}
,which depends only on the data matrix
{\bm{X}}
and is independent of
\lambda
.
More critically, when
\lambda
is very small, the proximal (soft-thresholding) step applies only very weak shrinkage. As a result, sparsity is barely enforced, and the iterates behave almost like those of standard gradient descent applied to an ill-conditioned least squares problem—leading to extremely slow convergence.
To address this issue, we turn to the penalty function method.

Quadratic Penalty Function Method

Consider optimization problems with equality constraints:

\displaystyle\mathop{\min}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}

\displaystyle f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})

\displaystyle,

(9.100)

\displaystyle\text{s.t.}

\displaystyle g_{i}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})

\displaystyle=0,\,\,i\in\mathcal{E},\,\,\text{with $\left\lvert\mathcal{E}\right\rvert=k$}.

Among various possible penalty formulations, the quadratic penalty is the simplest and most widely used. It is defined as follows:

Definition 240
(Quadratic penalty function for equality constraints).

For the equality-constrained optimization problem (
),
the quadratic penalty function is defined as

f_{\sigma}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\triangleq f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+\frac{1}{2}\sigma\sum_{i\in\mathcal{E}}g_{i}^{2}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\triangleq f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+\frac{1}{2}\sigma\left\lVert{\bm{g}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rVert_{2}^{2},

(9.101)

where
{\bm{g}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}):\real^{p}\rightarrow\real^{k}
is the vector-valued constraint function whose
i
-th component is
g_{i}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
.
The term
\frac{1}{2}\sigma\left\lVert{\bm{g}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
is called the penalty term, and
\sigma>0
is the penalty parameter (or penalty factor).

This penalty function assigns a high cost to points that violate the constraints. During optimization, iterates often lie outside the feasible region. As
\sigma
increases, the penalty term dominates the objective, pushing the minimizer of
f_{\sigma}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
closer to the feasible set.

Conversely, within the feasible region (i.e., where
{\bm{g}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\boldsymbol{0}
), the penalty term vanishes, and minimizing
f_{\sigma}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
is equivalent to minimizing the original objective
f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
. Thus, as
\sigma\rightarrow\infty
, the minimizers of
f_{\sigma}
converge to the solution of the original constrained problem (
), under mild regularity conditions.

Algorithm 12

)

1:

A function

and a set of constraints
\{g_{i}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\}
;

2:

input:

\rho>1
;

3:

input:

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(1)}
and
\sigma_{1}>0
;

4:

for

t=1,2,\ldots

do

5:

With
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}
as the initial point, solve
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}=\mathop{\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}f_{\sigma_{t}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
;
\triangleright
(QPF
1
)

6:

Update penalty parameter:
\sigma_{t+1}=\rho\sigma_{t}
;
\triangleright
(QPF
2
)

7:

;
\triangleright
(QPF

)

9:

return:
Final

;

The quadratic penalty function method, as outlined in Algorithm
, proceeds as follows: it generates a sequence of penalty parameters
\{\sigma_{t}\}
that increase exponentially (e.g.,
\sigma_{t+1}=\rho\sigma_{t}
with
\rho>1
), and for each
\sigma_{t}
, it approximately minimizes the penalized objective
f_{\sigma_{t}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
.
The subproblem in Step (QPF
1
)—an unconstrained optimization problem—can be solved using any iterative method suitable for smooth objectives, such as gradient descent, quasi-Newton methods, or Newton-type algorithms.

Importantly, the interpretation of argmin in Step (QPF
1
) may vary depending on the problem and solver:

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}
is the global minimizer of
f_{\sigma_{t}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
;

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}
is a local minimizer of
f_{\sigma_{t}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
;

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}
is not necessarily a strict minimizer but satisfies the first-order optimality condition approximately, i.e.,
\nabla f_{\sigma_{t}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)})\approx\boldsymbol{0}
.

Based on this, three practical considerations are essential when implementing Algorithm
:

Choice of penalty parameter schedule.

The rate at which
\sigma_{t}
increases significantly affects performance. If
\sigma_{t}
grows too rapidly, the subproblems become increasingly ill-conditioned and difficult to solve. Conversely, if
\sigma_{t}
increases too slowly, the algorithm requires many outer iterations, leading to slow overall convergence. A more adaptive strategy is to adjust the growth of
\sigma_{t}
based on the observed difficulty of solving the current subproblem: if the previous subproblem converged quickly, one may safely increase
\sigma_{t+1}
more aggressively; otherwise, a more conservative update is advisable.

Risk of unboundedness for small
\sigma_{t}
.

When
\sigma_{t}
is too small, the penalty term may be insufficient to enforce feasibility, and
f_{\sigma_{t}}(\boldsymbol{\beta})
can become unbounded below. In such cases, the subproblem solver may diverge. If divergence is detected during Step (QPF
1
), the algorithm should halt the current inner solve, increase
\sigma_{t}
, and retry.

Required accuracy of subproblem solutions.

To ensure convergence of the overall method, the subproblems must be solved with sufficient accuracy. In particular, the error in satisfying the first-order optimality conditions should tend to zero as
t\to\infty
.

Convergence Analysis

We now examine the convergence properties of the quadratic penalty method for equality-constrained problems. For simplicity, we assume that for each
\sigma_{t}>0
, the penalized function
f_{\sigma_{t}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
admits at least one minimizer. Note that this assumption may fail for certain problems—for instance, if the penalty is too weak to prevent the objective from decreasing indefinitely along infeasible directions. In such cases, the quadratic penalty method is not applicable, and we restrict our analysis to problems satisfying this basic regularity condition.

{theoremHigh}

[Penalty function method with optimal subproblem]
Let
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}
be a global minimizer of
f_{\sigma_{t}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
,

and suppose the penalty parameters
\{\sigma_{t}\}
satisfy
\sigma_{t}\rightarrow\infty
monotonically in Algorithm
.
Then every limit point
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
of the sequence
\{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\}_{t>0}
is a global minimizer of the original constrained problem (
).

Proof
[of Theorem
]
Let
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
be a global minimum of the original problem (
), i.e.,

f({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})\leq f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
, for all
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
satisfies
g_{i}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=0
,
i\in\mathcal{E}
.
Since
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}
minimizes
f_{\sigma_{t}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
, we have
f_{\sigma_{t}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)})\leq f_{\sigma_{t}}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}),

i.e.,

\displaystyle f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)})+\frac{\sigma_{t}}{2}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{E}}g_{i}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)})^{2}\leq f({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})+\frac{\sigma_{t}}{2}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{E}}g_{i}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})^{2}

(9.102)

\displaystyle\quad\implies\quad\sum_{i\in\mathcal{E}}g_{i}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)})^{2}\leq\frac{2}{\sigma_{t}}\big(f({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})-f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)})\big).

(9.103)

Let
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
be any limit point of the sequence
\{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\}
.
Taking the limit as
t\rightarrow\infty
in (
9.103
), and using the continuity of
f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
and
g_{i}({\boldsymbol{\beta}})

together with
\sigma_{t}\rightarrow+\infty
, we obtain

\sum_{i\in\mathcal{E}}g_{i}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})^{2}=0
,
so
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
is feasible for the original problem.
Moreover, from (
9.102
), we have

f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)})\leq f({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})
for all
t
.
Passing to the limit gives
f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})\leq f({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})
.
By the optimality of
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
, it follows that
f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*})=f({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}})
, and thus
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
is also a global minimizer.
