Penalty Function Method Applied to Lagrangian LASSO

Recall the Lagrangian LASSO problem (
LL
):

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\lambda\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1},

where
\lambda>0
is a regularization parameter. Solving the LASSO problem can be viewed as an approximation to solving the following basis pursuit (BP) problem:

\displaystyle\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\bm{y}},

The BP problem is a non-smooth optimization problem with linear equality constraints. By applying a quadratic penalty function to enforce the constraint
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\bm{y}}
, we obtain the penalized formulation:

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}+\frac{\sigma}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

Setting
\lambda\triangleq\frac{1}{\sigma}
reveals a direct correspondence: the above penalized problem is precisely the LASSO problem with regularization parameter
\lambda
. This observation leads to two important insights:

The solutions of the LASSO and BP problems are generally not identical. However, as
\lambda\rightarrow 0^{+}
(equivalently,
\sigma\rightarrow\infty
), the solution of the LASSO problem converges to a solution of the BP problem—provided a feasible solution exists.

When
\lambda
is very small (i.e.,
\sigma
is large), the quadratic term becomes dominant and highly sensitive to constraint violations, but the overall objective remains non-smooth due to the
\ell_{1}
-norm. Moreover, if one attempts to solve the BP problem directly via the penalty method with a fixed large
\sigma
, the resulting subproblem can become ill-conditioned, leading to slow convergence.

In the classical penalty function framework, the penalty parameter
\sigma
is gradually increased toward infinity to enforce feasibility more strictly over successive iterations. Translating this into the LASSO context, this strategy corresponds to starting with a relatively large
\lambda
(i.e., weak enforcement of the data-fitting term) and progressively decreasing
\lambda
toward the desired value.
This homotopy-like approach improves numerical stability and convergence behavior. The specific procedure is detailed in Algorithm
.

9.3.5
Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM)

Alternating direction methods of multipliers (ADMM)
is widely used to solve problems such as LASSO, sparse logistic regression, and basis pursuit. These applications benefit from ADMM’s ability to efficiently handle sparsity constraints. Moreover, ADMM can also be applied to optimization problems arising in the training of support vector machines (SVMs; see Problem
), particularly when dealing with large-scale datasets
(
Boyd et al. 2011
)
.
We first provide a brief introduction to ADMM and then discuss its application to the LASSO problem.

\paragrapharrow

Fixed Augmented Lagrangian Method.
Consider the following convex optimization problem:

\mathop{\min}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}F({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\triangleq f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+g({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+{\bm{Z}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}={\bm{f}},

(9.104a)

where
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
,
{\bm{Z}}\in\real^{n\times q}
,
{\bm{f}}\in\real^{n}
, and
f:\real^{p}\to(-\infty,\infty]
and
g:\real^{q}\to(-\infty,\infty]
are proper closed convex functions.
The Lagrangian function is

L({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\nu}})=f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+g({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\nu}},{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+{\bm{Z}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\bm{f}}\right\rangle.

(9.104b)

The dual objective function is obtained by minimizing the Lagrangian with respect to the primal variables
{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
(see Section
):

Q({\boldsymbol{\nu}})=\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}L({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\nu}})=-f^{*}(-{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\nu}})-g^{*}(-{\bm{Z}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\nu}})-\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\nu}},{\bm{f}}\right\rangle.

Thus, the dual problem becomes

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\in\real^{n}}f^{*}(-{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\nu}})+g^{*}(-{\bm{Z}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\nu}})+\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\nu}},{\bm{f}}\right\rangle.

(9.104c)

If
f
and
g
are proper closed and convex, the dual problem can be solved using the
proximal point method
(Problem
, which is a consequence of the primal gradient method), due to the properness, closedness, and convexity of the conjugate functions (Lemma
, Exercise
).
Given a parameter
\rho>0
, the update at the
t
-th iteration is

{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t+1)}\leftarrow\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\in\real^{n}}\left\{G({\boldsymbol{\nu}})\triangleq f^{*}(-{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\nu}})+g^{*}(-{\bm{Z}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\nu}})+\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\nu}},{\bm{f}}\right\rangle+\frac{1}{2\rho}\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\nu}}-{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t)}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}\right\}.

By the first-order necessary and sufficient conditions of convex functions (Theorem
), it follows that

\boldsymbol{0}\in\partial G({\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t+1)})=-{\bm{X}}\partial f^{*}(-{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t+1)})-{\bm{Z}}\partial g^{*}(-{\bm{Z}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t+1)})+{\bm{f}}+\frac{{{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t+1)}-{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t)}}}{\rho}.

From the definition of conjugate functions (Definition
), we have

\displaystyle\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\left\langle{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t+1)},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle+f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=f^{*}(-{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t+1)});

\displaystyle\min_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{q}}\left\langle{\bm{Z}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t+1)},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rangle+g({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=g^{*}(-{\bm{Z}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t+1)}).

By the conjugate subgradient theorem (Theorem
), this is equivalent to updating
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
,
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
, and
{\boldsymbol{\nu}}
by

\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}

\displaystyle\in\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\left\langle{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t+1)},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle+f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\partial f^{*}(-{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t+1)});

\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)}

\displaystyle\in\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{q}}\left\langle{\bm{Z}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t+1)},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rangle+g({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\partial g^{*}(-{\bm{Z}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t+1)});

\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t+1)}

\displaystyle\leftarrow{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t)}+\rho\left({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}+{\bm{Z}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)}-{\bm{f}}\right).

Substituting the expression for
{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t+1)}
into the first two equalities and applying the first-order necessary and sufficient conditions of convex functions (Theorem
) again (since
f
and
g
are proper closed and convex), it follows that

\displaystyle\boldsymbol{0}

\displaystyle\in{\bm{X}}^{\top}\left({\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t)}+\rho\big({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}+{\bm{Z}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)}-{\bm{f}}\big)\right)+\partial f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)});

(9.105a)

\displaystyle\boldsymbol{0}

\displaystyle\in{\bm{Z}}^{\top}\left({\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t)}+\rho\big({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}+{\bm{Z}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)}-{\bm{f}}\big)\right)+\partial g({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)});

(9.105b)

\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t+1)}

\displaystyle\leftarrow{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t)}+\rho\left({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}+{\bm{Z}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)}-{\bm{f}}\right).

(9.105c)

Given
{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t)}
, the quantities (
9.105b
) and (
9.105c
) correspond to the optimality conditions of the function

L_{\rho}({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t)})=f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+g({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t)},{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+{\bm{Z}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\bm{f}}\right\rangle+\frac{\rho}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+{\bm{Z}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\bm{f}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},

(9.106)

which is known as the
augmented Lagrangian function

(
Lu 2025
)
.
When
\rho=0
, the augmented Lagrangian function reduces to the standard Lagrangian function; when
\rho>0
, it acts as a penalized version of the Lagrangian function.
The
augmented Lagrangian method
proceeds iteratively (at the
t
-th iteration) as follows:

\text{augmented Lagrangian:}\quad\left\{\begin{aligned} ({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)})&\in\mathop{\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}L_{\rho}({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t)});\\
{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t+1)}&\leftarrow{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t)}+\rho({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}+{\bm{Z}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)}-{\bm{f}}).\end{aligned}\right.

However, unlike in standard augmented Lagrangian methods
(
Lu 2025
)
, the parameter
\rho
can remain fixed across iterations due to the convergence guarantees of the proximal point method (Problem
).

\paragrapharrow

ADMM.
One significant challenge in solving the problem is the coupling term between the variables
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
and
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
, which appears as
\rho({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{Z}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
.
ADMM addresses this issue by replacing the joint minimization over
({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})
with a single iteration of alternating minimization.
Specifically, at the
t
-th iteration, ADMM updates
{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
, and the dual variable
{\boldsymbol{\nu}}
from (
) sequentially as follows:

\text{ADMM:}\quad\left\{\small\begin{aligned} {\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}&\in\mathop{\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\left\{f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+\frac{\rho}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+{\bm{Z}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)}-{\bm{f}}+\frac{1}{\rho}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right\};\\
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)}&\in\mathop{\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}}_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}\left\{g({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\frac{\rho}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}+{\bm{Z}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\bm{f}}+\frac{1}{\rho}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right\};\\
{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t+1)}&\leftarrow{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t)}+\rho({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}+{\bm{Z}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)}-{\bm{f}}).\end{aligned}\right.

(9.107a)

Let
{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}\triangleq\frac{1}{\rho}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}
, this scheme can be equivalently rewritten in terms of the scaled dual variable
{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}
:

\text{ADMM:}\quad\left\{\small\begin{aligned} {\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}&\in\mathop{\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\left\{f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+\frac{\rho}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+{\bm{Z}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)}-{\bm{f}}+{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right\};\\
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)}&\in\mathop{\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}}_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}\left\{g({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\frac{\rho}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}+{\bm{Z}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\bm{f}}+{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right\};\\
{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}^{(t+1)}&\leftarrow{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}^{(t)}+({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}+{\bm{Z}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)}-{\bm{f}}).\end{aligned}\right.

(9.107b)

Note that the scaled-form ADMM update in (
) can be derived from the following augmented Lagrangian expressed in terms of the scaled dual variable
{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}
:

L_{\rho}({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\nu}}})=f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+g({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\frac{\rho}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}+{\bm{Z}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\bm{f}}+{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\frac{\rho}{2}\left\lVert{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

(9.108)

This iterative procedure enables the algorithm to converge to a solution that minimizes the objective function while satisfying the constraints. The main strength of ADMM lies in its ability to efficiently handle complex objectives and constraints—particularly in high-dimensional settings that are common in modern statistical learning and large-scale optimization problems.

\paragrapharrow

Stopping criteria.
ADMM iterations continue until both the primal and dual residuals fall below prescribed tolerance levels. These residuals are defined as:

\displaystyle{\bm{r}}^{(t+1)}

\displaystyle={\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)}\quad\text{(primal residual)},

\displaystyle{\bm{s}}^{(t+1)}

\displaystyle=\rho({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)})\quad\text{(dual residual)}.

The algorithm terminates when

\left\lVert{\bm{r}}^{(t+1)}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\varepsilon_{\text{pri}}\quad\text{and}\quad\left\lVert{\bm{s}}^{(t+1)}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\varepsilon_{\text{dual}}.

where
\varepsilon_{\text{pri}}
and
\varepsilon_{\text{dual}}
are user-specified tolerances.

\paragrapharrow

Convergence of ADMM.
The following theorem
demonstrates an
\mathcal{O}(1/T)
rate of convergence for the sequence generated by ADMM.
To state the result, we make the following assumptions.
For any
{\bm{u}}\in\real^{p}
and
{\bm{v}}\in\real^{q}
, the optimal solution sets of the problems

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\left\{f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+\frac{\rho}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{D}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\left\langle{\bm{u}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rangle\right\}

and

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{q}}\left\{g({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\frac{\rho}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{Z}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\left\langle{\bm{v}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rangle\right\}

are nonempty.
Moreover, we assume there exist
\widetilde{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\in\mathrm{dom}(f)
and
\widetilde{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}\in\mathrm{dom}(g)
such that
{\bm{D}}\widetilde{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}+{\bm{Z}}\widetilde{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}={\bm{f}}
.
These conditions ensure that the ADMM iterates are well-defined.

{theoremHigh}
[Convergence of ADMM,
\mathcal{O}(1/T)
]
Suppose the above assumptions hold,
and let
f:\real^{p}\to(-\infty,\infty]
and
g:\real^{q}\to(-\infty,\infty]
be proper closed convex functions.
Let
\big\{({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)})\big\}_{t>0}
be the sequence generated by ADMM for solving problem (
). Let
({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*})
be an optimal solution of problem (
) and
{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{*}
an optimal solution of the dual problem (
).
Assume
\zeta>0
is any constant satisfying
\zeta\geq\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{*}\right\rVert_{2}
.
Then for all
T>0
,

\displaystyle F(\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(T)},\overline{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}^{(T)})-F({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*})

\displaystyle\leq\frac{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(1)}\right\rVert_{{\bm{C}}}^{2}+\frac{1}{\rho}\big(\zeta+\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(1)}\big\rVert_{2}\big)^{2}}{2T},

(9.109)

where
{\bm{C}}\triangleq\rho{\bm{Z}}^{\top}{\bm{Z}}
,
\left\lVert{\bm{a}}\right\rVert_{{\bm{C}}}=({\bm{a}}^{\top}{\bm{C}}{\bm{a}})^{1/2}
,
and the averaged iterates are defined as

\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(T)}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\overline{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}^{(T)}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)}.

Proof
[of Theorem
]
From the first-order optimality conditions for convex functions (Theorem
) and the ADMM update rules (
), it follows that
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}
and
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)}
satisfy

\displaystyle-\rho{\bm{X}}^{\top}\left({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}+{\bm{Z}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)}-{\bm{f}}+\frac{1}{\rho}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t)}\right)

\displaystyle\in\partial f({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}),

(9.110)

\displaystyle-\rho{\bm{Z}}^{\top}\left({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}+{\bm{Z}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)}-{\bm{f}}+\frac{1}{\rho}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t)}\right)

\displaystyle\in\partial g({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)}).

(9.111)

Define the auxiliary variables

\displaystyle{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t)}

\displaystyle\triangleq{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)},\qquad{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}^{(t)}

\displaystyle\triangleq{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)},\qquad{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}^{(t)}

\displaystyle\triangleq{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t)}+\rho({\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}+{\bm{Z}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)}-{\bm{f}}).

Using the above optimality conditions and the subgradient inequality (Definition
), we obtain that for any
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\mathrm{dom}(f)
and
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\mathrm{dom}(g)
,

\displaystyle f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-f({\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t)})+\left\langle\rho{\bm{X}}^{\top}\left({\bm{X}}{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t)}+{\bm{Z}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)}-{\bm{f}}+\frac{1}{\rho}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t)}\right),{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t)}\right\rangle

\displaystyle\geq 0,

\displaystyle g({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-g({\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}^{(t)})+\left\langle\rho{\bm{Z}}^{\top}\left({\bm{X}}{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t)}+{\bm{Z}}{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}^{(t)}-{\bm{f}}+\frac{1}{\rho}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t)}\right),{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}^{(t)}\right\rangle

\displaystyle\geq 0.

By the definition of
{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}^{(t)}
, these inequalities can be rewritten as

\displaystyle f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})-f({\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t)})+\left\langle{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}^{(t)},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t)}\right\rangle

\displaystyle\geq 0,

\displaystyle g({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-g({\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}^{(t)})+\left\langle{\bm{Z}}^{\top}{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}^{(t)}+{\bm{C}}({\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)}),{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}^{(t)}\right\rangle

\displaystyle\geq 0,

where
{\bm{C}}=\rho{\bm{Z}}^{\top}{\bm{Z}}
.
Adding the two inequalities and using the dual update for
{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t+1)}
:

{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t+1)}-{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t)}=\rho({\bm{X}}{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t)}+{\bm{Z}}{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}^{(t)}-{\bm{f}}),

we obtain that for any
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\mathrm{dom}(f)
,
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\mathrm{dom}(g)
, and
{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\in\real^{n}
,

\displaystyle F({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-F({\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t)},{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}^{(t)})+\left\langle\begin{bmatrix}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t)}\\
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}^{(t)}\\
{\boldsymbol{\nu}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}^{(t)}\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}^{(t)}\\
{\bm{Z}}^{\top}{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}^{(t)}\\
-{\bm{X}}{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t)}-{\bm{Z}}{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}^{(t)}+{\bm{f}}\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{0}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t)})\\
{\bm{C}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}^{(t)})\\
\frac{1}{\rho}\big({\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t+1)}\big)\end{bmatrix}\right\rangle\geq 0.

(9.112)

For any vectors
{\bm{a}},{\bm{b}},{\bm{c}},{\bm{d}}
, and a positive semidefinite matrix
{\bm{H}}
, we have:

({\bm{a}}-{\bm{b}})^{\top}{\bm{H}}({\bm{c}}-{\bm{d}})=\frac{1}{2}\left(\left\lVert{\bm{a}}-{\bm{d}}\right\rVert_{{\bm{H}}}^{2}-\left\lVert{\bm{a}}-{\bm{c}}\right\rVert_{{\bm{H}}}^{2}+\left\lVert{\bm{b}}-{\bm{c}}\right\rVert_{{\bm{H}}}^{2}-\left\lVert{\bm{b}}-{\bm{d}}\right\rVert_{{\bm{H}}}^{2}\right).

Applying this with
{\bm{H}}={\bm{C}}
yields

\displaystyle({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}^{(t)})^{\top}{\bm{C}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}^{(t)})

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{{\bm{C}}}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{{\bm{C}}}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{{\bm{C}}}^{2}.

(9.113)

Similarly, using the definition of
{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}^{(t)}
and
{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t+1)}
, we derive

\displaystyle 2({\boldsymbol{\nu}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}^{(t)})^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t+1)})=\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\nu}}-{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t+1)}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}-\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\nu}}-{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t)}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}+\big\lVert{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t)}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}-\big\lVert{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t+1)}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}

\displaystyle=\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\nu}}-{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t+1)}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}-\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\nu}}-{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t)}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}+\rho^{2}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t)}+{\bm{Z}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)}-{\bm{f}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\rho^{2}\left\lVert{\bm{Z}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}^{(t)})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

Therefore,

\displaystyle\frac{1}{\rho}({\boldsymbol{\nu}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}^{(t)})^{\top}({\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t+1)})\geq\frac{1}{2\rho}\left(\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\nu}}-{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t+1)}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}-\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\nu}}-{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t)}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}\right)-\frac{\rho}{2}\big\lVert{\bm{Z}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}^{(t)})\big\rVert_{2}^{2}.

(9.114)

Now define the block-diagonal matrix and the stacked vectors:

{\bm{A}}\triangleq\small\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&{\bm{C}}&\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}&\frac{1}{\rho}{\bm{I}}\end{bmatrix},\normalsize\qquad{\bm{u}}\triangleq\small\begin{bmatrix}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\\
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\\
{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\end{bmatrix},\normalsize\qquad{\bm{u}}^{(t)}\triangleq\small\begin{bmatrix}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}\\
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)}\\
{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t)}\end{bmatrix},\normalsize\quad\text{and}\quad\widetilde{\bm{u}}^{(t)}\triangleq\small\begin{bmatrix}{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t)}\\
{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}^{(t)}\\
{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}^{(t)}\end{bmatrix}.\normalsize

Combining (
) and (
), we obtain

\left\langle\small\begin{bmatrix}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t)}\\
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}^{(t)}\\
{\boldsymbol{\nu}}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}^{(t)}\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{0}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t)}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t)})\\
{\bm{C}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)}-{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}^{(t)})\\
\frac{1}{\rho}({\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t+1)})\end{bmatrix}\normalsize\right\rangle\geq\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{u}}-{\bm{u}}^{(t+1)}\right\rVert_{{\bm{A}}}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{u}}-{\bm{u}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{{\bm{A}}}^{2}.

Combining the preceding inequality with (
), we obtain that for any
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\mathrm{dom}(f)
,
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\mathrm{dom}(g)
, and
{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\in\real^{n}
,

F({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-F({\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t)},{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}^{(t)})+\left\langle{\bm{u}}-\widetilde{\bm{u}}^{(t)},{\bm{G}}\widetilde{\bm{u}}^{(t)}+\widetilde{{\bm{f}}}\right\rangle\geq\frac{1}{2}\big\lVert{\bm{u}}-{\bm{u}}^{(t+1)}\big\rVert_{{\bm{A}}}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\big\lVert{\bm{u}}-{\bm{u}}^{(t)}\big\rVert_{{\bm{A}}}^{2},

(9.115)

where

{\bm{G}}\triangleq\small\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}&{\bm{X}}^{\top}\\
\boldsymbol{0}&\boldsymbol{0}&{\bm{Z}}^{\top}\\
-{\bm{X}}&-{\bm{Z}}&\boldsymbol{0}\end{bmatrix}\normalsize\qquad\text{and}\qquad\widetilde{{\bm{f}}}\small\triangleq\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{0}\\
\boldsymbol{0}\\
{\bm{f}}\end{bmatrix}.

Note that

\left\langle{\bm{u}}-\widetilde{\bm{u}}^{(t)},{\bm{G}}\widetilde{\bm{u}}^{(t)}+\widetilde{{\bm{f}}}\right\rangle=\left\langle{\bm{u}}-\widetilde{\bm{u}}^{(t)},{\bm{G}}(\widetilde{\bm{u}}^{(t)}-{\bm{u}})+{\bm{G}}{\bm{u}}+\widetilde{{\bm{f}}}\right\rangle=\left\langle{\bm{u}}-\widetilde{\bm{u}}^{(t)},{\bm{G}}{\bm{u}}+\widetilde{{\bm{f}}}\right\rangle,

where the last equality follows from the fact that
{\bm{G}}
is skew-symmetric (i.e.,
{\bm{G}}^{\top}=-{\bm{G}}
).
Therefore, (
) can be rewritten as

F({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-F({\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t)},{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}^{(t)})+\left\langle{\bm{u}}-\widetilde{\bm{u}}^{(t)},{\bm{G}}{\bm{u}}+\widetilde{{\bm{f}}}\right\rangle\geq\frac{1}{2}\big\lVert{\bm{u}}-{\bm{u}}^{(t+1)}\big\rVert_{{\bm{A}}}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\big\lVert{\bm{u}}-{\bm{u}}^{(t)}\big\rVert_{{\bm{A}}}^{2}.

Performing sum of the above inequality over
t=1,2,\ldots,T
yields the inequality

T\cdot F({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-\sum_{t=1}^{T}F({\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(t)},{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}^{(t)})+\left\langle T\cdot{\bm{u}}-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\widetilde{\bm{u}}^{(t)},{\bm{G}}{\bm{u}}+\widetilde{{\bm{f}}}\right\rangle\geq-\frac{1}{2}\big\lVert{\bm{u}}-{\bm{u}}^{(1)}\big\rVert_{{\bm{A}}}^{2}.

Defining

\overline{{\bm{u}}}^{(T)}\triangleq\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\widetilde{\bm{u}}^{(t)},\qquad\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(T)}\triangleq\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)},\qquad\overline{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}^{(T)}\triangleq\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)},

and using the convexity of
F
, we obtain that

\displaystyle F({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-F(\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(T)},\overline{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}^{(T)})+\left\langle{\bm{u}}-\overline{{\bm{u}}}^{(T)},{\bm{G}}{\bm{u}}+\widetilde{{\bm{f}}}\right\rangle+\frac{1}{2T}\big\lVert{\bm{u}}-{\bm{u}}^{(1)}\big\rVert_{{\bm{A}}}^{2}\geq 0

\displaystyle\implies F({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})-F(\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(T)},\overline{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}^{(T)})+\left\langle{\bm{u}}-\overline{{\bm{u}}}^{(T)},{\bm{G}}\overline{{\bm{u}}}^{(T)}+\widetilde{{\bm{f}}}\right\rangle+\frac{1}{2T}\big\lVert{\bm{u}}-{\bm{u}}^{(1)}\big\rVert_{{\bm{A}}}^{2}\geq 0,

where the implication follows again from the skew-symmetry of
{\bm{G}}
.
In other words, for any
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\mathrm{dom}(f)
and
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\mathrm{dom}(g)
,

F(\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(T)},\overline{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}^{(T)})-F({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\left\langle\overline{{\bm{u}}}^{(T)}-{\bm{u}},{\bm{G}}\overline{{\bm{u}}}^{(T)}+\widetilde{{\bm{f}}}\right\rangle\leq\frac{1}{2T}\big\lVert{\bm{u}}-{\bm{u}}^{(1)}\big\rVert_{{\bm{A}}}^{2}.

(9.116)

Let
({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*})
be an optimal solution of problem (
). Then
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}+{\bm{Z}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}={\bm{f}}
.
Let
\overline{{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}^{(T)}\triangleq\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t)}
. Plugging
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}
,
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}={\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}
, and the expressions for
\overline{{\bm{u}}}^{(T)}
,
{\bm{u}}
,
{\bm{u}}^{(1)}
,
{\bm{G}}
,
{\bm{Z}}
,
\widetilde{{\bm{f}}}
into (
), we obtain

\displaystyle F(\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(T)},\overline{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}^{(T)})-F({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*})+\left\langle\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(T)}-{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*},{\bm{X}}^{\top}\overline{{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}^{(T)}\right\rangle+\left\langle\overline{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}^{(T)}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*},{\bm{Z}}^{\top}\overline{{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}^{(T)}\right\rangle

\displaystyle+\left\langle\overline{{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}^{(T)}-{\boldsymbol{\nu}},-{\bm{X}}\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(T)}-{\bm{Z}}\overline{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}^{(T)}+{\bm{f}}\right\rangle\quad\leq\quad\frac{1}{2T}\left\{\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(1)}\big\rVert_{{\bm{C}}}^{2}+\frac{1}{\rho}\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\nu}}-{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(1)}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}\right\}.

Cancelling terms and using the fact that
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*}+{\bm{Z}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}={\bm{f}}
, the above inequality reduces to

\displaystyle F(\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(T)},\overline{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}^{(T)})-F({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*})+\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\nu}},{\bm{X}}\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(T)}+{\bm{Z}}\overline{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}^{(T)}-{\bm{f}}\right\rangle\leq\frac{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(1)}\right\rVert_{{\bm{C}}}^{2}+\frac{1}{\rho}\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\nu}}-{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(1)}\big\rVert_{2}^{2}}{2T}.

Taking
{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\in{\mathbb{B}}[\boldsymbol{0},\zeta]
as the maximum of both sides obtains

\displaystyle F(\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(T)},\overline{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}^{(T)})-F({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{*},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*})+\zeta\left\lVert{\bm{X}}\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(T)}+{\bm{Z}}\overline{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}^{(T)}-{\bm{f}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\frac{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(1)}\right\rVert_{{\bm{C}}}^{2}+\frac{1}{\rho}(\zeta+\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(1)}\big\rVert_{2})^{2}}{2T}.

This completes the proof.

In fact, by leveraging the strong duality between the primal problem (
) and its dual (
), and under the assumption that
\zeta\geq 2\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{*}\right\rVert_{2}
, one can also establish the following bound on the feasibility residual:

\left\lVert{\bm{D}}\overline{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}^{(T)}+{\bm{Z}}\overline{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}^{(T)}-{\bm{f}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\frac{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{*}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(1)}\right\rVert_{{\bm{C}}}^{2}+\frac{1}{\rho}\big(\zeta+\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(1)}\big\rVert_{2}\big)^{2}}{\zeta T},

See
Beck 2017
for more details.

\paragrapharrow

ADMM applied to LASSO.
Note that the Lagrangian LASSO problem (
LL
) can be equivalently reformulated using an auxiliary variable as follows:

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}F({\boldsymbol{\beta}})\triangleq f({\boldsymbol{\beta}})+g({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\triangleq\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\lambda\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{1}\quad\text{ s.t. }{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\boldsymbol{\alpha}}.

This formulation fits the standard ADMM framework.
Given a smoothing parameter
\rho>0
, the updates at the
t
-th iteration are:

\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}

\displaystyle\leftarrow\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\left\{\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac{\rho}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)}+\frac{1}{\rho}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right\}

\displaystyle=\Big({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}+\rho{\bm{I}}\Big)^{-1}\Big({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{y}}+\rho{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t)}\Big);

\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)}

\displaystyle\leftarrow\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}\left\{\lambda\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{1}+\frac{\rho}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+\frac{1}{\rho}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\right\}

\displaystyle=\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{(\lambda/\rho)\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{1}}\left({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}+\frac{1}{\rho}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t)}\right)=\mathcal{T}_{(\lambda/\rho)}({\boldsymbol{\beta}});

\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t+1)}

\displaystyle\leftarrow{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t)}+\rho({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)}),

where
\mathcal{T}_{\lambda}(\cdot)
denotes the soft-thresholding operator (Example
).

Since
\rho>0
,
{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}+\rho{\bm{I}}
is always invertible. The update for
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
essentially solves a ridge regression problem (an
\ell_{2}
-norm squared regularization least squares problem); while the update for
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
involves an
\ell_{1}
-norm proximal operator, which admits a closed-form solution via soft thresholding.
When solving the
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
-subproblem, if a fixed penalty parameter
\rho
is used throughout the iterations, one can precompute and cache a matrix factorization (e.g., Cholesky decomposition) of
{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}+\rho{\bm{I}}
; see, for example,
Lu 2022
. This significantly reduces the computational cost in subsequent iterations, as the expensive factorization need only be performed once.

9.3.6
Block Coordinate Descent

We briefly introduce how to solve the LASSO problem using the
block coordinate descent (BCD)
method.
Because the
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}
term in the objective function is separable, each block variable corresponds to a single coordinate of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.
For convenience, when updating the
i
-th block, we represent
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
as:

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\begin{bmatrix}\beta_{i}\\
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{-i}\end{bmatrix},

where
\beta_{i}
denotes the
i
-th component of
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
, and
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{-i}\in\real^{p-1}
contains all components except the
i
-th.
Similarly, we partition the design matrix
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
as:

{\bm{X}}=\begin{bmatrix}{\bm{x}}_{i}&{\bm{X}}_{-i}\end{bmatrix},

where
{\bm{x}}_{i}\in\real^{n}
is the
i
-th column of
{\bm{X}}
, and
{\bm{X}}_{-i}\in\real^{n\times{p-1}}
consists of all columns except the
i
-th.
This reordering does not change the problem—it merely isolates the variable being optimized.

During the update of the
i
-th coordinate, the LASSO objective becomes:

\min_{\beta_{i}}\,\lambda\left\lvert\beta_{i}\right\rvert+\lambda\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{-i}\right\rVert_{1}+\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{i}\beta_{i}-({\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}_{-i}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{-i})\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

Since
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{-i}
is fixed during this step, the term
\lambda\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{-i}\right\rVert_{1}
is constant and can be ignored for optimization purposes. Define the residual vector

{\bm{r}}_{i}\triangleq{\bm{y}}-{\bm{X}}_{-i}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{-i}
.
Then the subproblem reduces to:

\min_{\beta_{i}}\,f_{i}(\beta_{i})\triangleq\lambda\left\lvert\beta_{i}\right\rvert+\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\beta_{i}^{2}-{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{r}}_{i}\beta_{i}.

(9.117)

The minimizer of (
) has a closed-form solution given by soft thresholding:

\beta_{i}^{(t)}\leftarrow\operatorname*{\text{arg min}}_{\beta_{i}}f_{i}(\beta_{i})=\begin{cases}\frac{{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{r}}_{i}-\lambda}{\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}},&{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{r}}_{i}>\lambda;\\
\frac{{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{r}}_{i}+\lambda}{\left\lVert{\bm{x}}_{i}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}},&{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}{\bm{r}}_{i}<-\lambda;\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

(9.118)

Thus, the block coordinate descent algorithm for the LASSO problem proceeds by cyclically updating each coordinate using (
). The full procedure is summarized in Algorithm
.

Algorithm 14

Block Coordinate Descent Method for LASSO

1:

input:

{\bm{X}},{\bm{y}}
, parameter
\lambda
;

2:

initialize:

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(1)}
;

3:

for

t=1,2,\ldots

do

4:

for

i=1,2,\ldots,p

do

5:

Compute
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{-i},{\bm{r}}_{i}
according to definitions;

6:

Compute
\beta_{i}^{(t)}
by (
);

7:

end

for

8:

Stop if a stopping criterion is satisfied at iteration
t=T
;

9:

end

for

10:

return:
Final
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(T)}
;

9.3.7
Barzilai–Borwein Gradient Projection Algorithm

Consider the standard
bound-constrained quadratic program (BCQP)
problem

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}\left\{Q({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\triangleq\frac{1}{2}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{\top}{\bm{Y}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}-{\bm{z}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\bm{\ell}\leq{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\leq{\bm{u}}.

(9.119)

Projected gradient descent (PGD; see Algorithm
) methods provide a way of solving large-scale BCQP problems.
Let
{\mathbb{S}}
denote the feasible set of (
):

{\mathbb{S}}\triangleq\left\{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\in\real^{p}\mid\bm{\ell}\leq{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\leq{\bm{u}}\right\}\quad\implies\quad\mathcal{P}_{{\mathbb{S}}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\mathrm{mid}(\bm{\ell},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\bm{u}}),

(9.120)

where
\mathcal{P}_{{\mathbb{S}}}
denote the projection operator onto
{\mathbb{S}}
, which has a simple closed form; that is,
\mathcal{P}_{{\mathbb{S}}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})=\mathrm{mid}(\bm{\ell},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\bm{u}})
is the vector whose
i
-th component is the median of the set
\{\ell_{i},\alpha_{i},u_{i}\}
.
Given a current feasible iterate
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)}
, the projected gradient method computes the next iterate as

{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)}=\mathcal{P}_{{\mathbb{S}}}({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)}-\eta_{t}{\bm{g}}^{(t)}),

where
\eta_{t}>0
is some stepsize and
{\bm{g}}^{(t)}\triangleq{\bm{Y}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)}-{\bm{z}}
denotes the gradient; see Section
.

Barzilai and Borwein 1988
proposed a highly effective strategy for choosing the stepsize
\eta_{t}
, now known as the
Barzilai–Borwein (BB) rule
.
Two common variants are:

\eta_{t}^{BB1}=\frac{{\bm{s}}^{(t-1)\top}{\bm{s}}^{(t-1)}}{{\bm{s}}^{(t-1)\top}{\bm{t}}^{(t-1)}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\eta_{t}^{BB2}=\frac{{\bm{s}}^{(t-1)\top}{\bm{t}}^{(t-1)}}{{\bm{t}}^{(t-1)\top}{\bm{t}}^{(t-1)}},

(9.121)

where
{\bm{s}}^{(t-1)}={\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t-1)}
and
{\bm{t}}^{(t-1)}={\bm{g}}^{(t)}-{\bm{g}}^{(t-1)}
.

When combined with BB stepsizes, the projected gradient method is referred to as the
Barzilai–Borwein gradient projection (BBGP)
method.
A notable feature of BBGP is that it is non-monotonic: the objective value
Q({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)})
may increase on some iterations. Nevertheless, the method is simple, requires no matrix factorizations, and often exhibits fast practical convergence.

\paragrapharrow

Lagrangian LASSO with BB gradient projection.
Interestingly, the Lagrangian LASSO problem (
LL
)—originally an unconstrained convex optimization problem—can be reformulated as a BCQP. Specifically, consider

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\left\{\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\lambda\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}\right\},\quad{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p},{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p},{\bm{y}}\in\real^{n}.

(9.122)

To transform this into a bound-constrained problem, we use the standard variable-splitting technique: for each component
\beta_{i}
,
introduce nonnegative variables
u_{i}=(\beta_{i})_{+}
and
\ell_{i}=(-\beta_{i})_{+}
for all
i=1,2,\ldots,p
, where
(\beta)_{+}=\max(\beta,0)
denotes the positive-part operator. Then, the coefficient vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
can be split into a difference between nonnegative vectors:

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\bm{u}}-\bm{\ell},\quad{\bm{u}}\geq\boldsymbol{0},\quad\bm{\ell}\geq\boldsymbol{0}.

(9.123)

And consequently,
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}={\bm{1}}_{p}^{\top}{\bm{u}}+{\bm{1}}_{p}^{\top}\bm{\ell}
, where
{\bm{1}}_{p}=[1,1,\ldots,1]^{\top}
is a
p\times 1
summing vector consisting of
p
ones. By setting
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\bm{u}}-\bm{\ell}
, the Lagrangian LASSO problem (
) can be rewritten as the following BCQP problem
(
Figueiredo et al. 2008
)
:

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}\left\{F({\boldsymbol{\alpha}})\triangleq{\bm{c}}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+\frac{1}{2}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{\top}{\bm{Y}}{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\geq\boldsymbol{0},

(9.124)

where

{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=\begin{bmatrix}{\bm{u}}\\
\bm{\ell}\end{bmatrix},\qquad{\bm{c}}=\lambda{\bm{1}}_{2p}+\begin{bmatrix}-{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{y}}\\
{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{y}}\end{bmatrix},\qquad{\bm{Y}}=\begin{bmatrix}{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}&-{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}\\
-{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}&{\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}\end{bmatrix}.

(9.125)

To solve this BCQP problem (
) with nonnegative constraint,
Figueiredo et al. 2008
proposed the following two-step update:

\displaystyle{\bm{w}}^{(t)}

\displaystyle\leftarrow\big({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)}-\eta_{t}\nabla F({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)})\big)_{+};

(9.126a)

\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)}

\displaystyle\leftarrow{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)}+\lambda_{t}({\bm{w}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)}),

(9.126b)

where
\lambda_{t}\in[0,1]
.
Step (
9.126a
) corresponds to a standard projected gradient descent step (projection onto the nonnegative orthant).
Step (
9.126b
) introduces an extrapolation (or relaxation) similar in spirit to the conditional gradient method discussed in Section
.
The parameter
\lambda_{t}
is typically chosen via a backtracking line search to ensure sufficient decrease in the objective
F

(
Bertsekas 1997
)
.

9.4
Other Sparse Optimization Formulations

Apart from the standard LASSO problem, we also briefly introduce three important variants: the generalized LASSO, group LASSO, and sparse noise LASSO.

In the generalized LASSO, we assume that the regression coefficients exhibit a specific structural pattern—such as smoothness, piecewise constancy, or underlying trends. Rather than penalizing only the magnitude of the coefficients, this formulation penalizes their differences or higher-order variations. It is widely used in signal processing, image denoising, and time-series analysis, where such structural assumptions are natural.

The group LASSO is designed for settings in which predictors naturally form groups—for example, genes within biological pathways, dummy variables encoding a categorical feature, or multi-channel sensor measurements. In such cases, group LASSO selects or discards entire groups of variables simultaneously. This approach preserves model interpretability and respects the inherent grouping structure of the data.

The sparse noise LASSO (also known as robust LASSO) addresses scenarios where observations are corrupted by occasional large errors or outliers. Instead of assuming that all noise is small and Gaussian, it explicitly models sparse but significant (i.e., “gross”) errors in the data. This variant is particularly useful in real-world applications such as financial data analysis, sensor networks, or clinical measurements, where rare but severe anomalies can compromise data integrity.

9.4.1
Generalized LASSO Problem

The
generalized LASSO problem
is defined as:

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\,\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\lambda\left\lVert{\bm{Z}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1},

(9.127)

where
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
,
{\bm{Z}}\in\real^{l\times p}
, and
{\bm{y}}\in\real^{n}
.
In standard LASSO, the
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\right\rVert_{1}
penalty promotes sparsity in
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
.
However, in many applications,
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
itself may not be sparse, but becomes sparse after a linear transformation.
A key example arises when
{\bm{Z}}\in\real^{(p-1)\times p}
is the first-order difference matrix:

z_{ij}=\begin{cases}1,&j=i+1,\\
-1,&j=i,\\
0,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}

and
{\bm{X}}={\bm{I}}
.
In this case, the generalized LASSO reduces to:

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\,\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\lambda\sum_{i=1}^{p-1}\left\lvert\beta_{i+1}-\beta_{i}\right\rvert,

This formulation corresponds to the
total variation (TV)
model used in image denoising. When
{\bm{X}}={\bm{I}}
and
{\bm{Z}}
is instead a second-order difference matrix, problem (
) is known as
trend filtering

(
Rudin et al. 1992
;
Kim et al. 2009
)
.

\paragrapharrow

Generalized LASSO with ADMM.
In Section
, we introduced the use of ADMM to solve the standard (Lagrangian) LASSO problem. Here, we extend that approach to the generalized LASSO.
To apply ADMM to problem (
), we introduce an auxiliary variable

{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}

and enforce the constraint
{\bm{Z}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
.
This yields the equivalent constrained problem:

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}\quad\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\lambda\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{1}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\bm{Z}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=\boldsymbol{0}.

Let
{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\in\real^{l}
be the Lagrange multiplier associated with this constraint (assuming
{\bm{Z}}\in\real^{l\times p}
).
The augmented Lagrangian is then:

L_{\rho}({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\nu}})=\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\lambda\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{1}+{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{\top}({\bm{Z}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})+\frac{\rho}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{Z}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},

where
\rho>0
is the penalty parameter.
As in the standard LASSO case, the ADMM updates decouple the smooth quadratic term from the non-smooth
\ell_{1}
penalty. Specifically, the
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
-update requires solving a linear system:

\Big({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}+\rho{\bm{Z}}^{\top}{\bm{Z}}\Big){\boldsymbol{\beta}}={\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{y}}+\rho{\bm{Z}}^{\top}\Big({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)}-\frac{1}{\rho}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t)}\Big),

while the
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
-update is performed via the proximal operator of the
\ell_{1}
-norm.
Thus, for a given
\rho>0
, the ADMM iterations (cf. Section
) are:

\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}

\displaystyle\leftarrow\Big({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}+\rho{\bm{Z}}^{\top}{\bm{Z}}\Big)^{-1}\Big({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{y}}+\rho{\bm{Z}}^{\top}\Big({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)}-\frac{1}{\rho}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t)}\Big)\Big);

(9.128a)

\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)}

\displaystyle\leftarrow\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{(\lambda/\rho)\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{1}}\Big({\bm{Z}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}+\frac{1}{\rho}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t)}\Big);

(9.128b)

\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t+1)}

\displaystyle\leftarrow{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t)}+\rho({\bm{Z}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)}).

(9.128c)

9.4.2
Group LASSO and Dual Polytope Projections

When the columns of
{\bm{X}}
can be naturally partitioned into disjoint subsets
{\mathbb{G}}=\{g_{1},g_{2},\ldots,g_{G}\}
,
where each subset corresponds to a coherent group of features (e.g., genes in a pathway or dummy variables from a categorical predictor), the group LASSO enforces sparsity at the group level rather than on individual coefficients
(
Yuan and Lin 2006
)
. Specifically, the groups cover all
p
columns of
{\bm{X}}
, i.e.,

\bigcup_{\scriptsize g\in{\mathbb{G}}}g=\{1,2,\ldots,p\},

and typically the groups are assumed to be non-overlapping (though extensions exist for overlapping cases).
To achieve group-level sparsity, we apply an
\ell_{1}
penalty to a vector in
|G|
, whose entries are the
\ell_{2}
-norms of the coefficient subvectors within each group. (Using the
\ell_{2}
-norm within groups would not induce group-wise selection on its own.) This strategy avoids penalizing individual coefficients directly and instead encourages entire groups of coefficients to be zero or nonzero together.

This approach is especially valuable when domain knowledge suggests that predictors form meaningful groups, enabling the model to select or discard whole sets of related features—enhancing both interpretability and statistical efficiency.

More formally, let
{\bm{X}}\in\real^{n\times p}
and
{\bm{y}}\in\real^{n}
denote the design matrix and response vector based on
n
observations.
The parameter vector
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}
is partitioned into
G=\left\lvert{\mathbb{G}}\right\rvert
blocks:

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=[{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{1}^{\top},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{2}^{\top},\ldots,{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{G}^{\top}]^{\top}\in\real^{p},

where
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{g}\in\real^{p_{g}}
corresponds to group
g
, with
\sum_{g=1}^{G}p_{g}=p
.
The group LASSO assumes that only a few of the
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{g}
are nonzero.
The corresponding optimization problem is:

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\,\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\lambda\sum_{g=1}^{G}\sqrt{p_{g}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{g}\right\rVert_{2},

with feature groups
{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\sum_{g=1}^{G}{\bm{X}}_{g}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{g}
, where
{\bm{X}}_{g}\in\real^{n\times p_{g}}
denoting the submatrix of
{\bm{X}}
containing the columns in group
g
.
The factor
\sqrt{p_{g}}
compensates for varying group sizes, ensuring fair penalization across groups of different dimensions. The regularization parameter
\lambda>0
controls the trade-off between data fidelity and group sparsity.
Note that the penalty uses the (unsquared) Euclidean norm
\big\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{g}\big\rVert_{2}
for each group, making this a sum-of-norms regularization
(
Ohlsson et al. 2010
)
.

Group LASSO with ADMM

Following the ADMM framework (see Section
), we introduce auxiliary variables
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=[{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{1}^{\top},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{2}^{\top},\ldots,{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{G}^{\top}]^{\top}\in\real^{p}
to decouple the smooth loss from the non-smooth group penalty. The problem is equivalently rewritten as:

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\lambda\sum_{g=1}^{G}\sqrt{p_{g}}\,\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{g}\right\rVert_{2}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{g}={\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{g},\ \forall\,g.

Let
{\boldsymbol{\nu}}=[{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{1}^{\top},{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{2}^{\top},\ldots,{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{G}^{\top}]^{\top}\in\real^{p}

denote the scaled dual variables associated with these constraints. The scaled-form augmented Lagrangian is:

L_{\rho}({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},{\boldsymbol{\nu}})=\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\lambda\sum_{g=1}^{G}\sqrt{p_{g}}\,\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{g}\right\rVert_{2}+\left\langle{\boldsymbol{\nu}},{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right\rangle+\frac{\rho}{2}\sum_{g=1}^{G}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{g}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{g}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},

where
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{g}
are scaled Lagrange multipliers associated with the equality constraints
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{g}={\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{g}
, and
\rho>0
is a penalty parameter.

ADMM proceeds by iteratively updating
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
,
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
, and
{\boldsymbol{\nu}}
; see (
).
The
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
-update is

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}=\arg\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\frac{\rho}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)}+{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

This is a ridge regression-type problem, with a closed-form solution:

{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}=({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}+\rho{\bm{I}})^{-1}({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{y}}+\rho({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t)})).

For large-scale problems, iterative solvers such as conjugate gradient or precomputed factorizations can be used to accelerate computation
(
Lu 2025
)
.

The
{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}
-update is

{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)}=\arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\lambda\sum_{g=1}^{G}\sqrt{p_{g}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{g}\right\rVert_{2}+\frac{\rho}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}+{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}

This decomposes group-wise. For each group
g\in\{1,2,\ldots,G\}
, the update is given by the proximal operator of the scaled
\ell_{2}
-norm

\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{g}^{(t+1)}

\displaystyle=\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{(\lambda\sqrt{p_{g}}/\rho)\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{2}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{g}^{(t+1)}+{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{g}^{(t)})

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\left(1-\dfrac{\lambda\sqrt{p_{g}}}{\rho\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{g}^{(t+1)}+{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{g}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}}\right)({\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{g}^{(t+1)}+{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{g}^{(t)}),&\text{if }\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{g}^{(t+1)}+{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{g}^{(t)}\right\rVert_{2}>\dfrac{\lambda\sqrt{p_{g}}}{\rho};\\
0,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}

which is known as the
block soft-thresholding operator
(see Example
).

The scaled dual variable
{\boldsymbol{\nu}}
-update is

{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t+1)}={\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t)}+({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)})

Combining these steps, the full ADMM iteration at step
t
is:

\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}

\displaystyle\leftarrow({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}+\rho{\bm{I}})^{-1}({\bm{X}}^{\top}{\bm{y}}+\rho({\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t)}-{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t)}));

(9.129a)

\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{g}^{(t+1)}

\displaystyle\leftarrow\mathcal{P}\mathrm{rox}_{(\lambda\sqrt{p_{g}}/\rho)\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{2}}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{g}^{(t+1)}+{\boldsymbol{\nu}}_{g}^{(t)}),\quad\forall\,g;

(9.129b)

\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t+1)}

\displaystyle\leftarrow{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{(t)}+({\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{(t+1)}-{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{(t+1)}).

(9.129c)

Group LASSO Dual

Let again the design matrix be partitioned into
G
groups,
{\bm{X}}=[{\bm{X}}_{1},{\bm{X}}_{2},\ldots,{\bm{X}}_{g}]
, where
{\bm{X}}_{g}\in\real^{n\times p_{g}}
and
p=\sum_{g=1}^{G}p_{g}
.
The group LASSO problem is equivalently given by:

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}-\sum_{g=1}^{G}{\bm{X}}_{g}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{g}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\lambda\sum_{g=1}^{G}\sqrt{p_{g}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{g}\right\rVert_{2}.

(9.130)

Introducing the residual vector
{\bm{r}}\triangleq{\bm{y}}-\sum_{g=1}^{G}{\bm{X}}_{g}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{g}
,
we reformulate the problem as:

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\bm{r}}}\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{r}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\lambda\sum_{g=1}^{G}\sqrt{p_{g}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{g}\right\rVert_{2}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\bm{r}}={\bm{y}}-\sum_{g=1}^{G}{\bm{X}}_{g}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{g}.

(9.131)

Let
{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\in\real^{n}
denote the dual variable associated with the equality constraint.
The Lagrangian of problem (
) is:

L({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\bm{r}},{\boldsymbol{\nu}})=\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{r}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\lambda\sum_{g=1}^{G}\sqrt{p_{g}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{g}\right\rVert_{2}+{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{\top}\left({\bm{y}}-\sum_{g=1}^{G}{\bm{X}}_{g}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{g}-{\bm{r}}\right).

(9.132)

The dual function
D({\boldsymbol{\nu}})
is obtained by minimizing the Lagrangian over
{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
and
{\bm{r}}
:

\displaystyle D({\boldsymbol{\nu}})

\displaystyle=\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\bm{r}}}L({\boldsymbol{\beta}},{\bm{r}},{\boldsymbol{\nu}})

\displaystyle={\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{\top}{\bm{y}}+\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\in\real^{p}}\left(-{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{\top}\sum_{g=1}^{G}{\bm{X}}_{g}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{g}+\lambda\sum_{g=1}^{G}\sqrt{p_{g}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{g}\right\rVert_{2}\right)+\min_{{\bm{r}}\in\real^{n}}\left(\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{r}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{\top}{\bm{r}}\right).

The last term matches the standard LASSO dual (
) and evaluates to
-\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}
.
We now analyze the second term.
Define

\displaystyle h({\boldsymbol{\beta}})

\displaystyle=-{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{\top}\sum_{g=1}^{G}{\bm{X}}_{g}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{g}+\lambda\sum_{g=1}^{G}\sqrt{p_{g}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{g}\right\rVert_{2};

\displaystyle h_{g}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{g})

\displaystyle=-{\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{g}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{g}+\lambda\sqrt{p_{g}}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{g}\right\rVert_{2},\qquad g=1,2,\ldots,G.

Since the groups are disjoint, and the minimization decouples across groups.
Then we can split
h({\boldsymbol{\beta}})
into a set of subproblems. Clearly
h_{g}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{g})
is convex but not smooth because it has a singular point at
\boldsymbol{0}
.
Consider the subgradient of
h_{g}
,

\partial h_{g}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{g})=-{\bm{X}}_{g}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}+\lambda\sqrt{p_{g}}{\bm{u}}_{g},\quad{\bm{u}}_{g}\in\partial\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{g}\right\rVert_{2},\qquad g=1,2,\ldots,G,

where
{\bm{u}}_{g}
is the subgradient of
\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{g}\right\rVert_{2}
(Exercise
):

{\bm{u}}_{g}\in\begin{cases}{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{g}}/{\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{g}\right\rVert_{2}},&\text{if }{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{g}\neq\boldsymbol{0};\\
{\mathbb{B}}_{2}[\boldsymbol{0},1],&\text{if }{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{g}=\boldsymbol{0},\end{cases}

(9.133)

and
{\mathbb{B}}_{2}[\boldsymbol{0},1]
denotes the unit
\ell_{1}
-ball.
The optimal solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{g}
of
h_{g}
satisfies

\exists\widehat{\bm{u}}_{g}\in\partial\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{g}\big\rVert_{2},\quad-{\bm{X}}_{g}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}+\lambda\sqrt{p_{g}}\widehat{\bm{u}}_{g}=\boldsymbol{0}.

If
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{g}=\boldsymbol{0}
, clearly
h_{g}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{g})=0
. Otherwise, since
\lambda\sqrt{p_{g}}\widehat{\bm{u}}_{g}={\bm{X}}_{g}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}
and
\widehat{\bm{u}}_{g}={{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{g}}/{\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{g}\big\rVert_{2}}
, we have

h_{g}({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{g})=-\lambda\sqrt{p_{g}}\frac{{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{g}^{\top}}{\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{g}\big\rVert_{2}}{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{g}+\lambda\sqrt{p_{g}}\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{g}\big\rVert_{2}=0.

Therefore, this shows

\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{g}}h_{g}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{g})=0,\;g=1,2,\ldots,G

and thus

\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}h({\boldsymbol{\beta}})=\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\sum_{g=1}^{G}h_{g}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{g})=\sum_{g=1}^{G}\min_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{g}}h_{g}({\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{g})=0.

From (
), it is easy to see
\left\lVert{\bm{u}}_{g}\right\rVert_{2}\leq 1
. Since
\lambda\sqrt{p_{g}}\widehat{\bm{u}}_{g}={\bm{X}}_{g}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}
, we get a constraint on
{\boldsymbol{\nu}}
, i.e.,
{\boldsymbol{\nu}}
should satisfy:

\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{g}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\lambda\sqrt{p_{g}},\quad g=1,2,\ldots,G.

(9.134)

Therefore, the dual function
D({\boldsymbol{\nu}})
is:

D({\boldsymbol{\nu}})={\boldsymbol{\nu}}^{\top}{\bm{y}}-\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\nu}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

and the dual formulation of the group LASSO problem is:

\max_{{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\in\real^{n}}D({\boldsymbol{\nu}})=\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\nu}}-{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{g}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\lambda\sqrt{p_{g}},\;\forall\,g.

(9.135)

As in the standard LASSO, a simple re-scaling of the dual variables
{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\triangleq\frac{{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}{\lambda}
yields an equivalent formulation:

\max_{{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\in\real^{n}}D({\boldsymbol{\mu}})=\frac{1}{2}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}-\frac{\lambda^{2}}{2}\left\lVert{\boldsymbol{\mu}}-\frac{{\bm{y}}}{\lambda}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{g}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\sqrt{p_{g}},\;\forall\,g.

(9.136)

\paragrapharrow

Dual feasibility condition for sparsity.
Clearly, problem (
) is convex and its constraints are all affine.
By Slater’s condition, strong duality holds whenever the primal is feasible.
Let (
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}
,
\widehat{\bm{r}}
,
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}
) be optimal primal-dual solutions.
From the Lagrangian function (
) and KKT conditions (Theorem
), we have

\displaystyle\boldsymbol{0}\in\partial_{{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{g}}L({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}},\widehat{\bm{r}},{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}})

\displaystyle=-{\bm{X}}_{g}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}+\lambda\sqrt{p_{g}}{\bm{u}}_{g},\quad\text{where }{\bm{u}}_{g}\in\partial\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{g}\big\rVert_{2},\quad\forall\,g;

(9.137a)

\displaystyle\nabla_{{\bm{r}}}L({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}},\widehat{\bm{r}},{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}})

\displaystyle=\widehat{\bm{r}}-{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}=\boldsymbol{0};

(9.137b)

\displaystyle\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\nu}}L({\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}},\widehat{\bm{r}},{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}})

\displaystyle={\bm{y}}-\sum_{g=1}^{G}{\bm{X}}_{g}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{g}-\widehat{\bm{r}}=\boldsymbol{0}.

(9.137c)

From (
9.137b
) and (
9.137c
), we have:

{\bm{y}}=\sum_{g=1}^{G}{\bm{X}}_{g}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{g}+{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}.

(9.138)

From (
9.137a
), we know there exists
\widehat{\bm{u}}_{g}\in\partial\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{g}\big\rVert_{2}
such that

{\bm{X}}_{g}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}=\lambda\sqrt{p_{g}}\widehat{\bm{u}}_{g}.

(9.139)

Then, for each group
g=1,2,\ldots,G
, the following holds:

{\bm{X}}_{g}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}\in\begin{cases}\lambda\sqrt{p_{g}}\dfrac{{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{g}}{\big\lVert{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{g}\big\rVert_{2}},&\text{if }{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{g}\neq\boldsymbol{0};\\
\lambda\sqrt{p_{g}}{\mathbb{B}}[\boldsymbol{0},1],&\text{if }{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{g}=\boldsymbol{0}.\end{cases}

The dual problem is then important in the sense that it leads to a group-wise sparsity screening rule.
That is, the knowledge of
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}
allows us to identify the
zeros in
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{g}
by checking the optimality condition:

\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{g}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}\right\rVert_{2}<\lambda\sqrt{p_{g}}\quad\implies\quad{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{g}=\boldsymbol{0}.

(9.140)

This condition is analogous to the standard LASSO dual feasibility condition (
), but enforces sparsity at the group level rather than on individual coefficients.
Note that this condition is sufficient but not necessary: it is possible to have

{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{g}=\boldsymbol{0}
even when
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{g}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}\right\rVert_{2}=\lambda\sqrt{p_{g}}
(i.e., on the boundary of the dual feasible set).

Group LASSO with Dual Polytope Projections

In Section
, we introduced dual polytope projection (DPP) rules to efficiently identify and eliminate inactive predictors—those with zero coefficients in the final solution—from the standard LASSO problem before solving it, by exploiting geometric properties in the dual space.
We now extend this idea to the group LASSO problem (
).

Consider the dual formulation (
) or (
).
It is easy to see that the dual optimal
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}
is the projection of
{{\bm{y}}}
onto the feasible set. For each group
g
, the constraint
\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{g}^{\top}{\boldsymbol{\nu}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\lambda\sqrt{p_{g}}
confines
{\boldsymbol{\nu}}
to an ellipsoid which is closed and convex. Therefore, the feasible set of the dual problem (
) is the intersection of ellipsoids and thus closed and convex. Hence the dual solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}(\lambda)
under the penalty parameter
\lambda
is also nonexpansive for the group LASSO problem.

Similarly to the standard LASSO problem, let
\lambda_{\max}\triangleq\max_{g}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{g}^{\top}{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}/\sqrt{p_{g}}
, we can see that
\frac{{\bm{y}}}{\lambda_{\max}}
is itself feasible, and
\lambda_{\max}
is the largest parameter such that problem (
) has a nonzero solution. That is, if
\lambda>\lambda_{\max}
, the primal solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{g}(\lambda)=\boldsymbol{0}
,
\forall\,g=1,2,\ldots,G
.
Clearly, the dual solution of (
) under
\lambda=\lambda_{\max}
is
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}(\lambda_{\max})={{\bm{y}}}
.

Building on the DPP theorem for the standard LASSO (Theorem
), we obtain the following result for the group LASSO.

{theoremHigh}
[Dual polytope projections (DPP) for group LASSO]
Suppose we are given a solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}(\lambda^{\prime})
to the group LASSO dual (
) and a primal solution
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}(\lambda^{\prime})
for a specific
0<\lambda^{\prime}\leq\lambda_{\max}
.
Let
\lambda
be a nonnegative value different from
\lambda^{\prime}
.
For each group
g\in\{1,2,\ldots,G\}
, if the following holds:

\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{g}^{\top}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\nu}}}(\lambda^{\prime})\right\rVert_{2}<\lambda^{\prime}\sqrt{p_{g}}-\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{g}\right\rVert_{F}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lvert 1-\frac{\lambda^{\prime}}{\lambda}\right\rvert.

(9.141)

then the
g
-th group coefficient vector satisfies
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{g}(\lambda)=\boldsymbol{0}
.

The above theorem shows that if the following holds:

\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{g}^{\top}\big({\bm{y}}-\sum_{g}{\bm{X}}_{g}{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{g}(\lambda^{\prime})\big)\right\rVert_{2}<\lambda^{\prime}\sqrt{p_{g}}-\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{g}\right\rVert_{F}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}\left\lvert 1-\frac{\lambda^{\prime}}{\lambda}\right\rvert,

(9.142a)

then group
g
is guaranteed to be inactive at
\lambda
, i.e.,
{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{g}(\lambda)=\boldsymbol{0}
.
In particular, when
\lambda^{\prime}=\lambda_{\max}\equiv\max_{g}\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{g}^{\top}{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}/\sqrt{p_{g}}
, we have

{\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}}_{g}(\lambda_{\max})=\boldsymbol{0}
for all
g
, so the residual equals
{\bm{y}}
.
The above inequality becomes

\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{g}^{\top}{{\bm{y}}}\right\rVert_{2}<\lambda_{\max}\sqrt{p_{g}}-\left\lVert{\bm{X}}_{g}\right\rVert_{F}\left\lVert{\bm{y}}\right\rVert_{2}\left(\frac{\lambda_{\max}}{\lambda}-1\right).

(9.142b)

\paragrapharrow

Sequential DPP for group LASSO.
As in Corollary
, we can derive a sequential DPP rule for the group LASSO.
Consider the group LASSO problem (
) along a decreasing sequence of regularization parameters:
\lambda_{\max}=\lambda_{0}>\lambda_{1}>\ldots>\lambda_{m}
. For any integer
0\leq t<m
